# The Frontispiece Binding

<note>This page describes the physical exterior of the book, which was crafted with significant expense and skill.</note>

->**H  D**<-

The volume is protected by a highly ornate, dark leather cover featuring elaborate **gold tooling** <term>a decorative technique where gold leaf is pressed into leather using heated metal stamps</term>. The central focus of the binding is a large, symmetrical **cartouche** <term>an ornamental frame, often oval or rectangular, used to highlight a central motif</term> composed of intricate **strapwork** <term>decorative bands that appear to be folded or interlaced</term> and elegant scrollwork. 

In the center of this arrangement, a detailed oval medallion is positioned between two stamped gold initials:

->**H** &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; **D**<-
<note>original: "H D"</note>
<note>These initials likely represent the original owner or the patron for whom the manuscript was produced.</note>

The background field within the rectangular border is densely decorated with a repeating **diaper pattern** <term>a design of small, repeated shapes covering a surface</term> of golden **fleurons** <term>stylized flower-shaped ornaments</term>. The corners are further enhanced with scrolling **foliate motifs** <note>patterns designed to look like leaves or vines</note>.

# Decorative Endpaper

This page features a full-page illustration of traditional **marbled paper** <term>marbled paper: paper decorated with patterns produced by floating pigments on a liquid surface and then transferring them to the sheet</term>. In historical bookmaking, these vibrant designs were frequently used as endpapers <term>endpapers: the sheets of paper pasted to the inside covers of a book to reinforce the binding</term> or as decorative covers.

The pattern displayed here is known as a **"peacock"** or **"combed"** style. It is characterized by densely packed, overlapping scalloped shapes that mimic the appearance of bird feathers. The artisan would have achieved this effect by using a tool resembling a comb to pull colors across a prepared "size" (a thick liquid bath) before laying the paper down to absorb the ink.

The color palette consists of:
*   Deep madder red <note>a warm red pigment traditionally derived from the root of the madder plant</note>
*   Navy blue
*   Ochre yellow
*   Cream

The intricate, repeating rows of these "feathers" create a sense of movement and rich texture across the entire surface of the page.

<summary>This page features a traditional peacock-patterned marbled endpaper in red, blue, and yellow, serving as a decorative transition between the library's bookplate and the manuscript's contents.</summary>
<keywords>marbled paper, peacock pattern, bookbinding, endpaper, combed marbling, decorative arts, 19th-century binding</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the "Preface to the Reader" from the 1582 Rheims New Testament. The translators are explaining the Catholic Church's policy on translating the Bible into "vulgar" (common) languages, distinguishing their approach from that of the Protestant reformers.</meta>

# THE PREFACE

<margin>Concerning translation into the common language.</margin>
Finding a balance between the common people and their rebellious leaders, on one hand, is a matter of great wisdom. 

<margin>Matthew 24:45; 1 Corinthians 4:1.</margin>
These latter individuals—partly out of naivety, partly out of meddling curiosity, and especially out of pride and disobedience—have claimed that the common people have a right to the Bible. They use many appealing excuses, but offer no good reasons at all. On the other hand, those * to whom Christ has given the care of our souls, the distribution of God’s mysteries and treasures (among which the Holy Scripture is a significant portion), and the feeding of his family in due season with food suitable for every type of person, have never—neither in ancient times nor recently—wholly condemned all common-language versions of Scripture. Nor have they ever generally forbidden the faithful from reading them. Yet, they have not, by public authority, prescribed, commanded, or officially recommended any such translation to be used indiscriminately by everyone.

<margin>
The Scriptures in the common languages of various nations.

Holy Library <note>original: "Bib. Sāct." referring to Sixtus Senensis's *Bibliotheca Sancta*</note>, book 4.

Jerome <note>original: "Hiero."</note>, epistle 134.

Holy Library, book 4.

Ancient Catholic translations of the Bible into the Italian, French, and English tongues.

History of the English People <note>original: "hiſt. Angl."</note>, book 1, chapter 1.

An ancient provincial law in England concerning English translations. See Lyndwood <note>original: "Lin-vvod"</note>, book 5, title "Concerning Teachers" <note>original: "de Magiſtris"</note>.
</margin>
The Armenians say they have the Book of Psalms and some other parts of the Bible translated by St. Chrysostom into their language when he was banished among them; and George the Patriarch, in writing his life, indicates the same. The Slavonians claim they have the Scriptures in their common tongue, translated by St. Jerome, and some would conclude as much from his own words in his letter to Sophronius, though the text does not actually prove it. Ulfilas <note>original: "Vulpilas"</note> certainly gave the Scriptures to the Goths in their own tongue, and did so before he became an Arian <note>term: Arian — A follower of Arianism, a 4th-century belief that denied the full divinity of Christ, considered a major heresy by the Church.</note>. It has been almost three hundred years since James, Archbishop of Genoa, is said to have translated the Bible into Italian. More than two hundred years ago, in the days of King Charles V of France, it was published faithfully in French, specifically to remove the false, heretical translations of a sect called the Waldensians <note>term: Waldensians — A medieval movement that advocated for poverty and lay preaching, often translating the Bible into local dialects against Church regulations.</note> from the hands of the deceived people. In our own country, even though the Latin language was always (to use the words of the Venerable Bede) common to all the provinces for meditation or study of the Scriptures, and no common-language translation was used by the general public, such translations were nonetheless available in English even before the troubles that Wycliffe <note>original: "Vvicleffe"</note> and his followers caused in our Church. This is clear both from some pieces still remaining and from a local church law <note>original: "prouincial Conſtitution"</note> by Thomas Arundel, Archbishop of Canterbury, in a Council held at Oxford. There, a strict provision was made that no heretical version published by Wycliffe or his followers should be allowed, nor any other version in or after his time be published or permitted to be read, unless it was first approved by the local Bishop <note>original: "Dioceſan"</note>. This law cited St. Jerome regarding the difficulty and danger of translating the Holy Scripture from one language into another, even by learned and Catholic men. It was also suggested there that neither the translations published before that heretic’s time, nor others afterward that were approved by the lawful authorities <note>term: Ordinaries — Church officials, usually bishops, with the legal authority to execute church laws.</note>, were ever wholly forbidden in our country. However, in truer and more peaceful times (and much less when people were prone to disruption, heresy, or novelty), they were not hastily allowed or commonly read by the general public. Instead, they were used only, or especially, by certain devout religious and prayerful people, in reverence, secrecy, and silence, for their spiritual comfort.

<margin>Similar Catholic and common-language translations in many countries since Luther’s time.</margin>
Now, since the revolt of Luther as well, various learned Catholics have published the Bible in the several languages of almost all the main provinces of the Latin Church. This was done to more quickly abolish many false and wicked translations put out by various sects, and to better protect or reclaim many good souls endangered by them. No other books in the world are as destructive as heretical translations of the Scriptures, which poison the people under the guise of divine authority; and there are not many other remedies

<meta>catchword: being</meta>

<summary>This page argues that while the Catholic Church has historically permitted vernacular Bible translations under strict supervision, it opposes the unregulated and "heretical" translations spread by groups like the Waldensians and Wycliffites. It provides a historical list of approved translations in various languages to prove that the Church does not flatly forbid the Bible in common tongues.</summary>

# TO THE READER.
<sig>a iij</sig>

...nothing is a more powerful remedy against the same (if it be used with order, discretion, and humility) than the true, faithful, and sincere interpretation offered against it.

<margin>The Church’s order and decision concerning the reading of Catholic translations of the Bible in common languages.</margin>
This is why the holy Church does not utterly forbid every Catholic translation, even though she does not allow the publishing or reading of every single one without exception or limitation. In her divine and most sincere wisdom, she knows how, where, when, and to whom these gifts from her Master and Spouse <note>Referring to Christ and the Holy Spirit as the source of the scriptures.</note> should be given for the greatest benefit of the faithful. Therefore, she neither generally permits what must surely harm those who are unworthy, nor absolutely condemns what might do much good for those who are worthy.

<margin>Index of Prohibited Books, Rule 4. <note>original: "Ind. lib. prohibit. regula 4."</note></margin>
Consequently, the order that many wise men had wished for previously was established by the deputies of the late, famous Council of Trent <note>A major council of the Catholic Church (1545–1563) held to address the challenges of the Protestant Reformation.</note> regarding this matter, and confirmed by supreme authority. This rule states that the Holy Scriptures—even when truly and Catholically translated into common languages—may not be read indiscriminately by everyone. They may only be read by those who have express permission from their lawful Ordinaries <note>A church official with ordinary jurisdiction, like a Bishop.</note>, along with a good testimonial from their priests or confessors stating that they are humble, discreet, and devout people who are likely to benefit much and suffer no harm from the reading. This instruction, though it cannot be as strictly followed in these days of ours <note>The translators are writing from exile in France during a time of religious conflict in England.</note> as in other times and places where there is more respect for the Church’s authority and discipline, we nevertheless trust that all wise and godly people will handle the matter in the meantime with such moderation, meekness, and submissiveness of heart as is required by the handling of so sacred a book, the sincere understanding of God’s truth within it, and the holy laws, councils, reason, and religion.

<margin>The Holy Scriptures were never read by all persons indiscriminately at their pleasure.</margin>
In this matter—to preserve this divine work from abuse and profanation, and to better restrain the intolerable arrogance of proud, meddling, and argumentative minds—the leaders of the Church, guided by God’s Spirit, have established more exact orders for readers and translators in these later ages than in the past. This was done based on more experience with the "sickness" of this present time. However, we must not imagine that in the early Church, everyone who understood the learned languages in which the Scriptures were written (or other languages into which they were translated) could read, debate, dispute, or flip through the Scriptures without being corrected. Nor should we think that our ancestors allowed every schoolmaster, student, or student of grammar who knew a little Greek or Latin to immediately take the Holy Testament into their hands. We must not think that translated Bibles in common languages were in the hands of every farmer, craftsman, apprentice, boy, girl, mistress, or maid. Nor were they sung, played, or cited by every traveling repairman, tavern-goer, rhymester, or minstrel; they were not meant for dinner-table talk, for tavern benches, for boats and barges, or for every profane person and company. No; in those better times, people were neither so wicked nor so meddling as to abuse the blessed book of Christ in that way. Furthermore, before printing was invented, there was no such easy way to distribute copies into everyone's hands as there is now.

<margin>Where and in whose hands the Scriptures were in the early Church.</margin>
They were then kept in libraries, monasteries, colleges, and churches, or in the houses and hands of bishops, priests, and some other devout, high-ranking laypeople. These people used them with fear and reverence, especially those parts concerning a good life and moral behavior. They did not meddle with the difficult and high mysteries or passages of great difficulty, except in the pulpit and in schools—and even then, they did so with moderation.

The poor plowman could then, while working the soil, sing the hymns
and

<meta>This page continues the "Preface to the Reader" from the 1582 Rheims New Testament. Having established the Council of Trent's rules on Bible reading, the authors now contrast the humble, devout reading habits of the early Christians with the "presumptuous" and "arrogant" reading they observe in their own time.</meta>

# THE PREFACE

<meta>catchword: greediness</meta>

<margin>How the laity of those days did read them, with what humility and religion, and training of life and manners.</margin>
and psalms, either in known or unknown languages, as they heard them in the Holy Church, even if they could neither read nor understand the sense, meaning, and mysteries of the same. Such holy persons of both sexes—to whom **Saint Jerome** <note>A prominent 4th-century scholar and Father of the Church who translated the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</note> in various Epistles to them, commends the reading and meditation of Holy Scriptures—were diligent to search all the godly histories and imitable examples of chastity, humility, obedience, clemency, poverty, penance, and renouncing the world. They noted especially the places that bred a hatred of sin, fear of God’s judgment, and delight in spiritual thoughts. They deferred in all difficult passages to the judgment of the ancient Fathers and their masters in religion, never presuming to contend, control, teach, or talk of their own sense and fantasy in deep questions of divinity. Then the virgins did meditate upon the places and examples of chastity, modesty, and demureness; the married, on conjugal faith and continence; the parents, how to bring up their children in the faith and fear of God; the Prince, how to rule; the subject, how to obey; the Priest, how to teach; and the people, how to learn.

<margin>The Fathers sharply rebuke as an abuse that all people, without distinction, should read, explain, and talk of the Scriptures.</margin>
Then the scholar did not teach his master, the sheep did not control the Pastor, the young student did not set the Doctor to school, nor reproved their fathers for error and ignorance. Or if there were any in those better days (as in all times of heresy such must necessarily be) who had itching ears, talkative tongues and wits, or were curious and contentious disputers—hearers and talkers rather than doers of God’s word—the Fathers always sharply rebuked such people, counting them unworthy and unprofitable readers of the Holy Scriptures. **Saint Jerome**, in his Epistle to Paulinus, after declaring that no manual trade is so base, nor liberal science so easy, that it can be learned without a master (which **Saint Augustine** also affirms in *On the Utility of Believing, chapter 7* <note>original: "De vtilitate cred. cap. 7."</note>), and that men do not presume in any occupation to teach what they never learned, <margin>Jerome’s Letter 103, chapter 6. <note>original: "Hiero. ep. 103. c. 6."</note></margin> writes: *“Only (he says) the art of Scripture is that which every man claims for himself: this the chatting old wife, this the doting old man, this the babbling sophister <note>A person who uses clever but misleading arguments.</note>, this on every hand, men presume to teach before they learn it.”* Again, *“Some with a weight of lofty words devise matters of Scripture among women; others (shame on it!) learn from women what to teach men, and lest that be not enough, by facility of tongue—or rather audacity—teach to others that which they do not understand a bit themselves. I say nothing of those of my own profession: who, stepping from secular learning to the Holy Scriptures, and being able to tickle the ears of the multitude with a smooth tale, think all they speak is the Law of God.”* He wrote this at a time when this malady of arrogance and presumption in divine matters was not nearly as outrageous as it is now.

<margin>From the speech concerning the moderation to be observed in disputes. <note>original: "In orat. de moderatio. in disputa. seruanda."</note></margin>
**Saint Gregory Nazianzen** <note>A 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople and theologian.</note> gave a speech on the moderation that was to be used in these matters, where he says that some in his time thought themselves to have all the wisdom in the world when they could once repeat two or three words (and those poorly put together) out of the Scriptures. But he there divinely discourses on the orders and differences of degrees: how in Christ’s mystical body, some are ordained to learn and some to teach; that all are not Apostles, all Doctors, all interpreters, all gifted with tongues and knowledge, nor all learned in Scriptures and divinity. He notes that the people did not go up to talk with God on the mountain, but Moses, Aaron, and Eleazar did—and even they only according to the difference of their callings. He argues that those who rebel against this ordinance are guilty of the conspiracy of Korah <note>original: "Corè" - A biblical figure who led a rebellion against the leadership of Moses and Aaron (Numbers 16).</note> and his accomplices; and that in Scripture there is both milk for babes and meat for men, to be dispensed not according to everyone’s greediness...

<summary>This page describes the humble manner in which early Christians read the Bible, contrasting it with the "arrogance" of those who teach without proper training. It cites Saints Jerome, Augustine, and Gregory Nazianzen to argue that Scripture requires guidance and should not be interpreted by everyone indiscriminately.</summary>

<margin>
The Scriptures must be delivered with measure and discretion, according to each person's need and capacity.
</margin>
...greediness of appetite or willfulness, but as is most fitting for each person’s necessity and capacity: for just as it is a shame for a Bishop or Priest to be unlearned in God’s mysteries, so for the common people it is often profitable for salvation not to be overly curious, but to follow their Pastors in sincerity and simplicity. Regarding this, **Saint Augustine** <note>A highly influential 4th-century theologian and Bishop of Hippo.</note> says excellently, *“Being fed with the simplicity and sincerity of faith, as if with milk, so let us be nourished in Christ; and when we are little ones, let us not crave the foods of the older sort.”* <note>original: "Fidei simplicitate & sinceritate lactati, nutriamur in Christo: & cum parui sumus, maiorum cibos non appetamus."</note> In another place, he testifies that the word of God cannot be preached nor certain mysteries uttered to all men alike, but are to be delivered according to the capacity of the hearers. He proves this both by **Saint Paul’s** example—who gave not <term>strong meat</term> <note>A biblical metaphor for advanced theological doctrines.</note> to every sort, but milk to many, as they were not spiritual but carnal and incapable—and also by our Lord’s example, who spoke to some plainly and to others in parables, and affirmed that He had many things to utter which the hearers were not able to bear.

<margin>
In his oration on moderation in disputes, near the end.
Jerome in the prologue to his commentary on Ezekiel.
</margin>
<margin>
The Jewish law regarding not reading certain books of Holy Scripture until a certain time.
</margin>
How much more may we gather that all things written are not suited for the capacity and "diet" of every simple reader, but that very many mysteries of Holy Writ are far above their reach? Therefore, they can and ought to be (for equally good reason) delivered to them in a measure and manner most fitting for them. This can hardly be done when the whole book of the Bible lies before every man in his mother tongue, allowing him to choose whatever he likes. For this reason, the aforementioned **Gregory Nazianzen** <note>A 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople known as "The Theologian."</note> wishes the Christians had as good a law as the Hebrews of old had. As **Saint Jerome** <note>The scholar who translated the Bible into the Latin Vulgate.</note> also witnesses, the Hebrews took an order among themselves that no one should read the *Song of Songs* <note>original: "Cantica Canticorum"; a book of the Bible often interpreted as an allegory of divine love.</note> nor certain other pieces of the most difficult Scriptures until they were thirty years of age.

<margin>
Ephesians 4.
Romans 10, 17.
Book 2 to Gratian.
</margin>
And truly, there is no reason why men should be more reluctant to be ordered and moderated in this point by God’s Church and their Pastors than they are in the use of the holy <term>Sacraments</term> <note>Sacred rites of the Church, such as Baptism or the Eucharist.</note>. For just as Christ has appointed Priests and ministers from whose hands we must receive the Sacraments rather than being our own "carvers" <note>An old expression meaning to serve oneself or take what one wants without permission.</note>, so He has given us doctors, prophets, expounders, interpreters, teachers, and preachers, to receive the law and our faith from their mouths. This is because our faith and religion do not come to us properly or principally by reading Scriptures, but (as the Apostle says) by hearing preachers who are lawfully sent—though reading in order and humility greatly confirms and advances that faith. Therefore, this holy book of the Scriptures is called by **Saint Ambrose** <note>A 4th-century Bishop of Milan.</note> the *Priestly Book* <note>original: "Liber sacerdotalis"</note>, signifying it is a book for priests, from whose hands and at whose discretion we must receive and use it.

<margin>
Genesis 3.
1 Timothy 6, 20.
Romans 12, 3.
</margin>
<margin>
The popular objections about withholding the Scriptures from the people are answered.
</margin>
<margin>
Why the Church does not permit everyone to read the Scripture at their own pleasure.
</margin>
The wise will not pay attention to what some willful people mutter: that the Scriptures are made for all men, and that it is out of envy that the Priests keep the holy book from them. This suggestion comes from the same serpent that seduced our first parents, persuading them that God had forbidden them that Tree of Knowledge lest they should be as clever as Himself and like the Highest. No, no: the Church does this to keep them from blind, ignorant presumption, and from that which the Apostle calls *knowledge falsely so called* <note>original: "falsi nominis scientiam"</note>, and not to bar them from the true knowledge of Christ. She would have all be wise, but *unto sobriety* <note>original: "usque ad sobrietatem"; meaning with moderation and restraint.</note>, as the Apostle speaks. She knows the Scriptures are ordained for every state of life, just as food, the elements, fire, water, candles, knives, and swords are...

It cites historical precedents, such as Jewish restrictions on difficult texts and the warnings of Church Fathers, to justify priestly oversight of Scripture reading.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Preface to the Reader" of the 1582 Rheims New Testament. The text here picks up mid-sentence regarding the profit of the Scriptures for different types of people.</meta>

# THE PREFACE

<margin>
The holy Scriptures to carnal men and Heretics are like pearls to swine.
Matthew 7:6.
Tertullian, *On Prescription against Heretics*.
Origen, on Romans 2.
Luke 24.
</margin>
...which are as necessary (most of them) for children as for old folks, for the simple as for the wise: but yet they would ruin everything if they were under the guidance of anyone other than wise men, or were in the hands of everyone, for whose protection they are intended to be profitable. She <note>The Church.</note> does not forbid the reading of them in any language, nor does she envy any man’s benefit, but she gives order on how to do it for <term>edification</term> <note>Spiritual building up or improvement.</note> and not for destruction: how to do it without casting what is holy to dogs, or pearls to hogs. (See *Saint Chrysostom’s 24th Homily on Matthew*, declaring these hogs and dogs to be carnal men and <term>Heretics</term> <note>Those who hold beliefs contrary to established Church doctrine.</note>, who gain no good from the holy mysteries, but thereby hurt both themselves and others.) She teaches how to do it in a way that agrees with the sovereign sincerity, majesty, and depth of the Mystery contained in the same. She would have the presumptuous Heretic—even though he cites them ever so fast, flying as it were through the whole Bible, and quoting the Psalms, Prophets, Gospels, and Epistles ever so readily for his purpose, as **Vincent of Lérins** says such men's fashion is—yet she would, according to **Tertullian’s** rule, have such mere usurpers quite discharged from all occupation and possession of the holy Testament. For the Testament is her old and only right and inheritance, and does not belong to Heretics at all, whom **Origen** calls <note>original: "scripturarũ fures"</note> thieves of the Scriptures. She would have the unworthy repelled, the curious repressed, the simple measured, the learned humbled, and all sorts either to use them or abstain from them as is most convenient for each one’s salvation. This comes with this general admonition: that none can understand the meaning of God in the Scriptures unless Christ opens their understanding and makes them partakers of his holy Spirit in the unity of his mystical body. For the rest, she commits it to the Pastor of every province and people—according to the differences of time, place, and persons—how and in what manner the reading of the Scriptures is more or less to be encouraged or permitted.

<margin>
Saint Chrysostom’s exhortations to the reading of holy Scriptures, and when the people should be so exhorted.
In the *Life of Athanasius*.
* Homily 2 on Matthew; Homily 3 on Lazarus; Homily 3 on 2 Thessalonians; and often elsewhere.
</margin>
In this, the variety of circumstances causes them to deal in various ways. We see this with **Saint Chrysostom** <note>A 4th-century Church Father known for his eloquent preaching.</note> and the people of Constantinople, who were so delicate, dull, worldly, and so much given to dice, cards, and especially stage-plays or theaters (as **Saint Gregory Nazianzen** witnesses) that the Scriptures and all holy readings of divine things were loathsome to them. Because of this, their holy Bishop was forced in many of his sermons to cry out against their extreme negligence and contempt for God’s word. He declared that not only Hermits and Religious <note>Monks or those living under religious vows.</note> (as the people claimed for their excuse) but secular men of all sorts might read the Scriptures, and often have more need of it for themselves than those who live in more purity and contemplation. He further suggested that although various things therein are high and hard, yet many godly histories, lives, examples, and precepts of life and doctrine are plain. Finally, he argued that when the <term>Gentiles</term> <note>Non-Christians, specifically pagans in this context.</note> were so clever and diligent in attacking their faith, it was not good for Christians to be simple or negligent in its defense. In truth, it is more necessary for a Catholic man in these days—when our adversaries are industrious in attacking our belief—to be skillful in the Scriptures than at other times when the Church had no such enemies.

<margin>
Saint Chrysostom provides no support for the popular and unrestrained reading of Scriptures used among the Protestants nowadays.
</margin>
In this sense, **Saint Chrysostom** said various things, not as a teacher in a school making exact and general rules to be observed in all places and times, but as a man in the pulpit, speaking to that specific audience and his people’s faults. He did not make it (as some perversely gather from his words) a thing absolutely necessary for every poor craftsman to read or study the Scriptures. Nor did he in any way favor the presumptuous, curious, and contentious arguing and searching of God’s secrets, which was reproved by the aforementioned fathers—much less did he approve of the excessive pride and

They do not feel, as Saint Jerome did, that the text has a hard shell that must be broken before we reach the kernel. For as the right and reverent use of that book is precious, so much more ruinous is the abuse and profanation of it—as any man of experience may easily see by the evidence of these few years, comparing the former days and manners to our own.

<margin>Scriptures are quoted as profanely as pagan poets.</margin>
...the Priest. Look whether the most chaste and sacred sentences of God's holy word are not turned by many into mirth, mockery, amorous ballads, and detestable letters of love and lewdness; their delicate rhymes, tunes, and translations much increasing the same.

<margin>Scriptures are erroneously explained according to every wicked man’s private fancy.</margin>
This decline of a good life and the profaning of the divine mysteries is something everyone sees. But the great corruption and decay of faith caused by this is seen only by wise men. They alone know that, even if the Scriptures were translated perfectly, heretics and wicked men—who follow their own spirit and know nothing but their private fantasies rather than the sense of the holy Church and its <term>Doctors</term> <note>The "Doctors of the Church" are influential theologians whose writings are considered authoritative in Catholic tradition.</note>—must inevitably abuse them to their own damnation. And curious, simple, and <margin>* 1 Corinthians 2</margin> sensual men, who have no taste for the things of the Spirit of God, may find occasion for destructive errors in countless places. For though the letter or text itself has no error, yet (as Saint Ambrose says) the <term>Arian</term> <note>Arianism was an early Christian heresy that denied the full divinity of Jesus Christ.</note>—or as we might say now, the <term>Calvinist</term> <note>Followers of John Calvin, a major figure in the Protestant Reformation.</note>—interpretation has errors. <note>original Latin reference: *lib. 2 ad Gratianum ca. 1.*; "Book 2 of 'To Gratian,' chapter 1."</note> And Tertullian says, *The sense corrupted is as perilous as the text itself being corrupted.* <note>original Latin: *De Præscript.*; "On the Prescription of Heretics."</note> Saint Hilary also speaks thus: *Heresy arises from the understanding, not from the writing; the fault is in the meaning, not in the word.* <note>original Latin: *lib. 2 de Trinit. in principio*; "Book 2 of 'On the Trinity,' at the beginning."</note> And Saint Augustine says *that many hold the Scriptures as they do the Sacraments, "for the outward appearance, and not for salvation."* <note>original Latin: *ad speciem, & non ad salutem*; *de Baptis. cont. Donat. lib. 3 ca. 19.*; "On Baptism against the Donatists, Book 3, chapter 19."</note>

<margin>All heretics claim the Scriptures.</margin>
Finally, all sect-leaders and ravening wolves—yes, <margin>* Matthew 4</margin> the devils themselves—claim the Scriptures, quote the Scriptures, and entirely shroud themselves in the Scriptures, as if in the wool and fleece of simple sheep. Because of this, the common people in these days of general disputes cannot help but be in extreme danger of error, even if their books were truly translated and were indeed God’s own word.

<margin>The Scriptures have been falsely and heretically translated into the common languages, and sacrilegiously abused in various other ways, and then given to the people to read.</margin>
But the case now is even more lamentable. For the Protestants—whom Saint Paul calls <margin>* 2 Corinthians 4</margin> *walking in craftiness* <note>original Latin: *ambulantes in astutia*</note>—have so deceived the people and many others in the world (who are not unwise) that through their false translations, they have given them their own wicked writings and fantasies instead of God’s Law and Testament, and in place of Christ’s written will and word. They have most shamefully corrupted both the letter and the meaning in all their versions—Latin, English, and other languages—by false translation: adding, removing, altering, rearranging, punctuating, and using all other deceitful means, especially where it serves the advantage of their private opinions. Because of this, they are also bold enough to either completely strip of authority or cast doubt upon various whole books that have been accepted as <term>Canonical Scripture</term> <note>The list of books officially recognized as divinely inspired and belonging in the Bible.</note> by the universal Church of God for over a thousand years. They alter all the authentic and Church-related words used since the beginning of our Christianity into new, profane novelties of speech that agree with their doctrine. They change the titles of works, remove the names of authors, <margin>* <term>Beza</term> <note>Theodore Beza, a major Protestant Reformer and successor to John Calvin.</note>'s notes on Luke 1:78.</margin> charge the Evangelist himself with untrue translation, and add entire sentences specific to their sect into their psalms in meter—<margin>* See the tenth article of their Creed in verse.</margin> even into the very Creed in rhyme. All of this the poor, deceived people say and sing as if it were God’s own word, when in fact, through such sacrilegious treachery, it has been made the Devil's word.

<margin>All of their dealings are noted (as the opportunity arises) in the annotations of this Testament, and more extensively in a book recently written specifically on that subject, titled *A Discovery*, etc.</margin>
Not to mention their intolerable liberty and license to change the accustomed names for God, Angels, men, places, and things used by the Apostles and all antiquity in Greek, Latin, and all other languages of Christian nations. They replace these with new names—sometimes false, and always ridiculous and done for show—taken from the Hebrew. They frame and refine the phrases of holy Scriptures according to the style of secular writers, not hesitating to supply, add, alter, or diminish text as freely as if they were translating <term>Livy</term>, <term>Virgil</term>, or <term>Terence</term> <note>Ancient Roman authors of history, epic poetry, and comedy, respectively.</note>. We trust that after diligently reading it, you may be encouraged to set aside those impure versions you have been forced to use until now. How well we have done this, we must not judge, but refer everything to God’s Church and our superiors within it. To them we submit ourselves and this work, along with all our other labors, to be reformed, corrected, altered, or entirely abolished. We most humbly ask for pardon if, through our ignorance, recklessness, or other human frailty, we have anywhere mistaken the meaning of the Holy Ghost. Furthermore, we promise that if we later discover any of our own errors, or if anyone else—whether a friend out of goodwill or an adversary seeking to criticize—points them out to us, we will not (as Protestants do) willfully persist in them to defend our reputation or out of pride and contention. Instead, we will be most glad to hear of them and correct them in the next edition or otherwise. For it is the truth we seek, and God’s honor; if that is achieved, whether by our good intention or by the occasion of others, all is well. We only declare that we have done our best with prayer, much fear, and trembling, lest we should dangerously err in such a sacred, high, and divine work. We have done it with all faith, diligence, and sincerity. We have used no partiality to the disadvantage of our adversaries, nor taken more liberty than is allowable in translating the Holy Scriptures. <margin>Heresies make Catholics more diligent to search and find the meanings of holy Scripture for the refuting of the same.</margin>
...similar doctrine against our adversaries, which perhaps he had thought before this diligent search, either not to be consonant to God’s word, or at least not contained in the same, and finally he shall prove this saying of **Saint Augustine** to be most true: *“Many senses of holy Scriptures lie hidden, and are known to some few of greater understanding: neither are they at any time vouched for more conveniently and acceptably than at such times, when the care to answer heretics forces men thereto.* <note>original: "Multi sensus &c." — Augustine explains that conflict with heretics forces the Church to define its doctrines more clearly.</note> *For then, even they that be negligent in matters of study and learning, shaking off sluggishness, are stirred up to diligent hearing, so that the adversaries may be refuted. Again, how many senses of holy Scriptures, concerning Christ’s Godhead, have been vouched for against **Photinus**; how many, of his Manhood, against **Manichæus**; how many, of the Trinity, against **Sabellius**; how many, of the unity in Trinity, against the **Arians**, **Eunomians**, **Macedonians**; how many, of the Catholic Church dispersed throughout the whole world, and of the mixture of good and bad in the same until the end of the world, against the **Donatists** and **Luciferians** and others of the like error; how many against all other heretics, which it would be too long to rehearse? Of which senses and expositions of holy Scripture the approved authors and vouchers, would otherwise either not be known at all, or not so well known, as the contradictions of proud heretics have made them.”* <note>These groups represent various early Christian heresies: Photinus denied Christ's divinity; Manichæus taught dualism; Sabellius denied the distinction of the Trinity; Arians denied Christ's co-equality with the Father; and Donatists argued the Church should only consist of the "pure."</note>

Thus he says of such things as, while not seeming to be in holy Scriptures to the ignorant or heretics, yet indeed are there. But in other points doubted of, that indeed are not decided by Scripture, he gives us this goodly rule to be followed in all, as he exemplifies in one: *“Then do we hold (he says) the truth of the Scriptures, when we do that which now has seemed good to the Universal Church, which the authority of the Scriptures themselves does commend: so that, because the holy Scripture cannot deceive, whoever is afraid to be deceived by the obscurity of questions, let him therein ask counsel of the same **CHURCH**, which the holy Scripture most certainly and evidently shows and points unto.”* **Augustine**, book 1, *Against Cresconius*, chapter 13.

<margin>Many causes why this New Testament is translated according to the ancient vulgar Latin text.</margin>
NOW TO GIVE thee also intelligence in particular, most gentle Reader, of such things as it behooves thee specially to know concerning our Translation: We translate the old <term>vulgar Latin text</term> <note>Now commonly known as the **Vulgate**, this was the standard Latin translation used by the Catholic Church for over a millennium.</note>, not the common Greek text, for these causes:

<margin>It is most ancient.</margin>
1. It is so ancient, that it was used in the Church of God above 1,300 years ago, as appears by the fathers of those times.

<margin>Corrected by Saint Jerome.</margin>
2. It is that (by the common received opinion and by all probability) which **Saint Jerome** afterward corrected according to the Greek, by the appointment of **Damasus** then Pope, as he makes mention in his preface before the four Evangelists, unto the said Damasus: and in the *Catalogue at the end*, and *Letter 102*.

<margin>Letter 10.</margin>
<margin>Commended by Saint Augustine.</margin>
3. Consequently, it is the same which **Saint Augustine** so commends and allows in a Letter to **Saint Jerome**.

<margin>Used and expounded by the fathers.</margin>
4. It is that which for the most part ever since has been used in the Church’s service, expounded in sermons, alleged and interpreted in the Commentaries and writings of the ancient fathers of the Latin Church.

<margin>Session 4.</margin>
<margin>Only <term>authentical</term>, by the holy Council of Trent.</margin>
5. The holy <term>Council of Trent</term> <note>The 16th-century ecumenical council that responded to the Protestant Reformation; "authentical" here means it is the official, authoritative version for public use.</note>, for these and many other important considerations, has declared and defined this only of all other Latin translations, to be authentical, and so only to be used and taken in public lessons, disputations, preachings, and expositions, and that no man presume upon any pretense to reject or refuse the same.

<margin>Most grave, least partial.</margin>
6. It is the gravest, sincerest, of greatest majesty, and least partiality, as being without any respect to the controversies and contentions, especially those of our time.

time, as it appears by those places which Erasmus and others at this day translate much more to the advantage of the Catholic cause.

<margin>Precise in following the Greek.</margin>
7. It is so exact and precise according to the Greek, both in phrase and word, that fastidious Heretics <note>The translators use "heretics" to refer to Protestant reformers, and "delicate" or "fastidious" to suggest they care more about polished language than accurate theology.</note> therefore criticize it for its rudeness. And to show that it follows the Greek far more exactly than the Protestants' translations, besides infinite other places, we appeal to these: *Titus 3:14, "Let them be careful to excel in good works"* <note>original: "Curent bonis operibus præ-esse," matching the Greek "προῗστασθαι" (proistasthai).</note>. The English Bible of 1577 translates this as *to maintain good works.* And *Hebrews 10:20, "He initiated a way for us"* <note>original: "Viam nobis initiauit," matching the Greek "ἐνεκαίνισεν" (enekainisen).</note>. The English Bible says, *be prepared.* So also in these words: *Justifications, Traditions, Idols,* etc. In all of which they do not come near the Greek, but avoid it on purpose.

<margin>Preferred by Beza himself.</margin>
8. Our adversaries themselves, namely Beza <note>Theodore Beza was a major Protestant reformer and successor to Calvin.</note>, prefer it before all the rest. *In the preface to his New Testament, year 1556.* And again he says that the old Interpreter translated very religiously. *Annotations on Luke chapter 1, verse 1.*

<margin>All the rest are disliked by the Sectaries themselves, each criticizing the other.</margin>
9. In the rest, there is such diversity and dissension, and no end of criticizing one another, and every man translating according to his own fantasy, that <margin>* Johannes Cochlaeus, chapter 11, on the authority of the Canonical Scriptures.</margin> *Luther said: "If the world should stand any long time, we must receive again (which he thought absurd) the Decrees of Councils, for preserving the unity of faith, because of such diverse interpretations of the Scripture."* And Beza (in the place mentioned above) notes the "itching ambition" of his fellow-translators, who would much rather disagree and dissent from the best, than seem to have said or written nothing themselves. And Beza’s translation itself, being so esteemed in our country that the Geneva <note>The Geneva Bible was the most popular English Protestant translation before the King James Version.</note> English Testaments are translated according to it, yet sometimes goes so far from the Greek and from the meaning of the Holy Ghost, that those who profess to translate it dare not follow it. For example, *Luke 3:36,* they have put these words, *The son of Cainan,* which he knowingly and willfully left out; and *Acts 1:14,* they say, *With the women,* agreeing with the vulgar Latin, where he says, *With their wives* <note>original: "Cum uxoribus."</note>. <margin>The New Testament printed in the year 1580, in the title.</margin>

<margin>It is truer than the common Greek text itself.</margin>
10. It is not only better than all other Latin translations, but better than the Greek text itself in those places where they disagree.

<margin>The ancient fathers as proof, and the adversaries themselves.</margin>
The proof of this is evident, because most of the ancient Heretics were Greeks, and therefore the Scriptures in Greek were more corrupted by them, as the ancient fathers often complain. Tertullian notes the Greek text which is used today (*1 Corinthians 15:47*) to be an old corruption by Marcion the Heretic, and the truth to be as in our vulgar Latin: <margin>Book 5 against Marcion.</margin> *"The second man from heaven is heavenly"* <note>original: "Secundus homo de cœlo cœlestis."</note>. <margin>Ambrose. Jerome.</margin> Other ancient fathers read it this way, and Erasmus thinks it must be so, and Calvin himself follows it in his *Institutes, book 2, chapter 13, paragraph 2.* Again, Saint Jerome notes that the Greek text (*1 Corinthians 7:33*) as it is today is not the Apostolic truth or the true text of the Apostle; but rather that which is in the vulgar Latin: <margin>Book 1, against Jovinian, chapter 7.</margin> *"He that is with a wife is careful of worldly things, how he may please his wife, and is divided"* <note>original: "Qui cum vxore est, solicitus est quæ sunt mundi, quomodo placeat vxori, & diuisus est."</note> (or distracted). The ecclesiastical history called the *Tripartite* notes that the Greek text now used (*1 John 4:3*) is an old corruption of the ancient Greek copies by the Nestorian Heretics, and the true reading is as in our vulgar Latin: <margin>Book 12, chapter 4.</margin> *"Every spirit that dissolves Jesus is not of God"* <note>original: "Omnis spiritus qui soluit IESVM, ex Deo non est." The term "dissolves" refers to the Nestorian heresy of separating Christ's human and divine natures.</note>; and Beza confesses that Socrates in his ecclesiastical history reads it this way in the Greek: *"every spirit that looses [dissolves] Jesus Christ"* <note>original: "πᾶν πνεῦμα ὃ λύει τὸν ἰησοῦν χριστὸν" (pan pneuma ho lyei ton Iesoun Christon).</note>, etc. <margin>Book 7, chapter 32.</margin>

# TO THE READER.

<margin>covenant / tabernacle <note>original: "διαθήκη" / "σκηνὴ"</note></margin>
<margin>at the time / to the Lord <note>original: "καιρῷ" / "κυρίῳ"</note></margin>
<margin>into hypocrisy <note>original: "ἐς ὑπόκρισιν"</note></margin>
<margin>The Calvinists themselves often abandon the Greek as corrupted, and translate according to the ancient Latin Vulgate text.</margin>
...namely Beza and his students, the English translators of the Bible, in these places. *Hebrews chapter 9, verse 1:* saying, *the first covenant*, for that which is in the Greek: *The first tabernacle* <note>original: "σκηνή" (skēnē)</note>. Where they put *covenant*, not as the actual text, but in a different font as something to be understood, following the Latin Vulgate, which most honestly leaves it out entirely, saying, *The former also indeed had justifications, etc.* <note>original: "Habuit quidem & prius iustificationes &c."</note>. Again, *Romans 11, verse 21:* They do not translate according to the Greek text, *serving the time* <note>original: "Tempori seruientes"</note>—which Beza says must certainly be a corruption—but according to the Latin Vulgate, *serving our Lord* <note>original: "Domino seruientes"</note>. Again, *Revelation 11, verse 2:* they do not translate the Greek text, *the court which is within the temple* <note>original: "Atrium quod intra templum est"</note>, but exactly the opposite, according to the Latin Vulgate, which Beza says is the true reading, *the court which is outside the temple* <note>original: "Atrium quod est foris templum"</note>. Only in this last place, one English Bible from the year 1562 follows the error of the Greek. Again, *2 Timothy 2, verse 14:* they add "but," which is more than what is in the Greek, to make the sense more convenient and easy, just as it is in the Latin Vulgate. Again, *James 5:12:* they leave the Greek and follow the Latin Vulgate, saying, *lest you fall into condemnation* <note>original: "ἐς ὑπόκρισιν," which literally means "into hypocrisy" but is translated here as condemnation</note>. "I do not doubt," says Beza, "but this is the true and honest reading, and I suspect the corruption in the Greek happened like this, etc." It would be an endless task to list all such places where our opponents (especially Beza) follow the old Latin Vulgate and the Greek manuscripts that agree with it, condemning the current Greek text as corrupted.

<margin>See the Greek New Testament of Robert Stephens in folio, and Crispin’s edition.</margin>
<margin>Extra additions in the Greek, which Erasmus calls trifling and reckless additions.</margin>
Furthermore, Erasmus—the best translator of all the recent ones, according to Beza's judgment—says that the Greek sometimes has extra parts corruptedly added to the text of Holy Scripture. For example, at *Matthew 6*, at the end of the *Our Father* <note>original: "Pater noster"</note>, these words: *Because yours is the kingdom, the power, and the glory, forevermore.* Which he calls *trifles* <note>original: "nugas"</note> recklessly added to our Lord’s prayer, and he rebukes Valla <note>Lorenzo Valla (c. 1407–1457) was an Italian humanist who used philology to critique the Vulgate; here, the author defends the Vulgate against Valla's critiques.</note> for blaming the old Latin Vulgate because it does not have it. Likewise, *Romans 11:6*, these words are in the Greek but not in the Latin Vulgate: *But if of works, it is no longer grace; otherwise the work is no more a work.* And *Mark 10:29*, these words: *or wife*, and such like. Indeed, the Greek text in these extra additions condemns itself and justifies the Latin Vulgate immensely, as it is marked throughout in many places indicating that such and such words or sentences are extra. In all these places, our Latin Vulgate has no such thing, but agrees with the Greek that remains after the extra parts are removed. For example, the one mentioned before at the end of the *Our Father* has a mark of extra content in the Greek text like this: '''. And *Mark 6:11*, these words: *Amen I say to you, it shall be more tolerable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah in the day of judgment, than for that city.* And *Matthew 10:22*, these words: *And be baptized with the baptism that I am baptized with?* which is also extra and repeated in verse 23; and very many such places. Since these are noted as extra in the Greek and are not in the Latin Vulgate, they prove the Latin in those places to be better, truer, and more honest than the Greek.

<margin>Beza’s preface to the New Testament, 1556. See also his notes on Acts 13:20.</margin>
<margin>The Latin Vulgate translation agrees with the best Greek manuscripts, by Beza's own judgment.</margin>
Therefore, we conclude from these facts that it is no insult to the Latin Vulgate text which we translate to disagree with the Greek text, since it may nevertheless be not only as good, but even better. And this the opponent himself—their greatest and most recent translator of the Greek—affirms against Erasmus in defense of the old Latin Vulgate translation, in these well-known words: "How unworthily and without cause," says he, "does Erasmus blame the old Interpreter for differing from the Greek? He differed, I admit, from those Greek manuscripts which he had obtained; but we have found, in more than one place, that the same in—"

# THE PREFACE

<margin>When the Church Fathers say that the Latin text must yield to the Greek and be corrected by it, they mean the true and uncorrupted Greek text.</margin>
...interpretation which he blames, is grounded upon the authority of other Greek copies, and those most ancient. Indeed, in a number of places we have observed that the reading or the Latin text of the old Interpreter <note>The "old Interpreter" refers to the original translator of the Latin Vulgate, traditionally thought to be St. Jerome.</note>, though it does not always agree with our current Greek copies, is much more convenient, because it seems he followed some better and truer copy. Thus far Beza <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605) was a major Protestant reformer and scholar who succeeded Calvin in Geneva.</note> says. In which words he unwittingly, but most truly, justifies and defends the old common [Vulgate] Translation against himself and all other objectors who accuse it because it is not always in agreement with the Greek text. It was translated out of other Greek copies (partly still existing, partly not existing today) that were either as good and as ancient, or better and more ancient, such as St. Augustine speaks of, calling them *more learned and more diligent* <note>original: "doctiores & diligentiores"</note> Greek copies, to which the Latin translations that fail in any place must necessarily yield. *Book 2 on Christian Doctrine, chapter 15.*

And if it were not too long to give examples and prove this, which would require a treatise of its own, we could show through many and most clear examples throughout the New Testament these various means of justifying the old translation.

<margin>The common Latin Translation is justified in many ways by the most ancient Greek copies and the Church Fathers.</margin>
First, if it agrees with the Greek text (as it commonly does, and in the most important places concerning the controversies of our time, it does most certainly), so far the Adversaries have nothing to complain about—unless they will complain about the Greek also, as they do in *James chapter 4, verse 2* and *1 Peter chapter 3, verse 21*, where the common Latin follows the Greek text exactly, saying, *You kill* <note>original: "Occiditis"</note> and, *Which in a similar form [saves you]* <note>original: "Quod vos similis forma"</note>, etc. But Beza in both places corrects the Greek text as well, claiming it is false.

2.  If it disagrees here and there from the Greek text, it often agrees with another Greek copy cited in the margin. See examples of this throughout the Greek Testaments of Robert Stephens and Crispin <note>Robert Stephens (Estienne) and Jean Crispin were famous 16th-century printers of scholarly Bibles.</note>. For example: *2 Peter 1:10, Strive that through good works you may make your calling sure* <note>original Latin: "Satagite vt per bona opera certam vestram vocationem faciatis"; original Greek: "Διὰ τῶν ἀγαθῶν ἔργων"</note>; and *Mark 8:7, And he blessed them* <note>original Latin: "Et ipsos benedixit"; original Greek: "εὐλογήσας αὐτὰ"</note>.

3.  If these marginal Greek copies are thought to be less authentic than the main Greek text, the Adversaries themselves tell us the contrary, as they often follow the marginal copies in their own translations and abandon the Greek text, as is evident in the examples mentioned above: *Romans 11, Revelation 11, 2 Timothy 2, James 5,* etc.

4.  If all of Erasmus's <note>Desiderius Erasmus, the humanist scholar who produced the first widely used printed Greek New Testament.</note> Greek copies do not have what is in the common Latin, Beza had copies which do have it, and those were most ancient (as he says) and better. And if all of Beza’s copies fail in this point and will not help us, Gagneie—the French king's preacher who had access to all the royal libraries—found Greek copies that match the common Latin exactly, even in places that might otherwise seem less probable. For instance: *James 3:5, Behold how much fire what a great wood it kindles!* <margin>Verona manuscript: how great a fire <note>original: "ἥλικον πῦρ"</note></margin> A man would think it should rather be as it is in the standard Greek text, *A little fire what a great wood it kindles!* But an approved ancient Greek copy cited by Gagneie has it as it is in the common Latin. And if Gagneie’s copies also fail sometimes, there Beza and Crispin provide Greek copies fully agreeable to the common Latin, such as: *Jude verse 5, Knowing all things once, that JESUS,* etc. and *verse 19, They separate themselves* <margin>all things, that Jesus; themselves <note>original: "πάντα, ὅτι ἰησοῦς. ἑαυτοὺς"</note></margin>. Likewise *Ephesians 2 [actually 2 Thessalonians 2:13], Because he has chosen you as firstfruits* <note>original: "ἀπαρχὰς"</note> in some Greek copies (Gagneie); and *2 Corinthians 9:2, Your zeal* <note>original: "ὁ ὑμῶν ζῆλος"</note>, as one Greek copy has it (Beza).

5.  If all their copies are insufficient, the ancient Greek Fathers had copies and explained them in a way that agrees with our common Latin. For example: *1 Timothy 6:20, Profane novelties of words* <margin>novelties of speech <note>original: "καινοφωνίας"</note></margin>. So St. Chrysostom reads and explains it as being against heretical and erroneous novelties. Yet now we know of no Greek copy that reads it that way.

# THE PREFACE

...comfortable and godly sense thereof.

<margin>The few and small faults that have negligently crept into the common Latin translation.</margin>
Thus then we see that by all means the old common <note>The "common Latin" refers to the Vulgate, the standard Bible of the Catholic Church.</note> Latin translation is approved as good, and better than the Greek text itself, and that there is no cause why it should give place to any other text, copies, or readings. Indeed, if there be any faults evidently crept in by those who previously wrote or copied out the Scriptures (as there are some), we grant them no less than we would grant faults nowadays committed by the Printer. These are exactly noted by Catholic writers, namely in all Plantin's Bibles <note>Bibles produced by the famous printer Christophe Plantin in Antwerp.</note> set forth by the theologians of Leuven. The holy Council of Trent <margin>Session 4.</margin> desires that the common Latin text be thoroughly mended in such points, and so be made most authentic. Such faults are these: "In faith" for "in the end" <note>original Latin: *In fide* for *in fine*</note>; "Foreknowledge" for "presence" <note>original Latin: *Praefcientiam* for *praefentiam*</note>; "Receiving" for "looking up" <note>original Latin: *Sufcipiens* for *Sufpiciens*</note>; and others like these, which are very rare. These are evident corruptions made by the copyists, or grown by the similarity of words. These being taken away—which are no part of those corruptions and differences we are discussing—we translate that text which is most sincere, and in our opinion (as we have proved), incorrupt. The adversaries <note>A term used by the translators to refer to Protestant reformers.</note> on the contrary translate that text which they themselves confess, both by their writings and actions, to be corrupt in a number of places, and more corrupt than our common Latin, as was declared before.

<margin>The Calvinists confessing the Greek to be most corrupt, yet translate that only, and hold that only for authentic Scripture.</margin>
And if we would stand here to recite the places in the Greek which Beza <note>Theodore Beza, a prominent successor to John Calvin and a major biblical scholar.</note> pronounces to be corrupted, we should make the reader wonder how they can either so plead otherwise for the Greek text (as though there were no other truth of the New Testament but that) or how they translate only that (to deface, as they think, the old common Latin) which they themselves so shamefully disgrace—more so than the common Latin—inventing corruptions where none are, nor can be, in such universal consent of all both Greek and Latin copies. For example, *Matthew 10*: "The first, Simon, who is called Peter." <margin>In his Annotations on the New Testament, year 1556.</margin> I think (says Beza) this word "first" <note>original Greek: πρῶτος</note> has been added to the text by some who would establish Peter's Primacy. Again, *Luke 22*: "The chalice, that is shed for you." It is most likely (says he) that these words, being at one time but a marginal note, came by corruption out of the margin into the text. Again, *Acts 7*: "Figures which they made, to adore them." It may be suspected (says he) that these words, as many others, have crept by corruption into the text out of the margin. And in *1 Corinthians 15*, he thinks the Apostle said not "victory" <note>original Greek: νῖκος</note> as it is in all Greek copies, but "contention" <note>original Greek: νᾶκος</note>. And in *Acts 13*, he calls it a manifest error that in the Greek it is "400 years" for "300." And in *Acts 7, verse 16*, he reckons up a whole catalogue of corruptions: namely *Mark 12, verse 42*, "a farthing" <note>original Greek: κόδράντης, a small Roman coin</note>; and *Acts 8, verse 26*, "this is desert" <note>original Greek: αὕτη ἐστὶν ἔρημος</note>; and *Acts 7, verse 16*, the name of Abraham, and such like. All of which he thinks to have been added or altered into the Greek text by corruption.

But among other places, he labors exceedingly to prove a great corruption in *Acts 7, verse 14*, where it is said (according to the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Old Testament.</note>, that is, the Greek text of the Old Testament) that Jacob went down into Egypt with 75 souls. And in *Luke 3, verse 36*, he thinks these words "of Cainan" <note>original Greek: τοῦ καινὰν</note>, <margin>They standing precisely upon the Hebrew of the old, and Greek text of the new Testament, must of necessity deny one of them.</margin> <margin>Years of Our Lord 1556 and 1565.</margin> "who was of Cainan," to be so false that he leaves them clean out in both his editions of the New Testament, saying that he is bold so to do by the authority of Moses. By which he means to signify that it is not in the Hebrew text of Moses or of the Old Testament, and therefore it is false in the Greek of the New Testament. This consequence of theirs (for it is common among them and concerns all Scriptures) if it were true, all places of the Greek text of the New Testament cited out of the Old according to the Septuagint, and not accor-

<sig>c ij</sig>
<meta>Catchword: But</meta>

...according to the Hebrew (which they know are very many) should be false. And so, by tying themselves only to the Hebrew in the Old Testament, they are forced to forsake the Greek of the New; or if they will maintain the Greek of the New, they must sometimes forsake the Hebrew in the Old. But this argument shall be pressed against them elsewhere.

<margin>They claim the Greek is more corrupt than we will grant them.</margin>
By this little example, the Reader may see what fine patrons they are of the Greek text, and how little cause they have in their own judgments to translate it, or boast of it as a way to disparage the common Latin translation. We might easily answer them in a word as to why we do not translate from the Greek: namely, because it is so infinitely corrupted. But the truth is, we do by no means grant it to be as corrupted as they claim, though in comparison we know it to be less pure and incorrupt than the common Latin; and for that cause, and others previously mentioned, we prefer the said Latin and have translated it.

<margin>We do not prefer the common Latin text simply because it favors our position.</margin>
If there still remains one thing which they might say when they cannot answer our reasons mentioned above: namely, that we prefer the common Latin before the Greek text because the Greek works more against us; we protest that, just as we prefer the Latin for other causes, in this respect of "working for us" or "against us," we value the Greek as much as the Latin. Indeed, in various places we value it more than the Latin, being assured that they have not one advantage, and that we have many advantages in the Greek more than in the Latin, as will clearly appear by the Annotations of this New Testament. Specifically, we see this in all those places where they dare not translate the Greek accurately because it favors us and goes against them. 

For example, they translate the Greek word for <term>justifications</term> <note>original Greek: δικαιώματα (dikaiomata)</note> as "ordinances," and not "justifications"—and that on purpose, as the reformer Beza confesses in his notes on <term>Luke 1:6</term>. They translate the word for <term>traditions</term> <note>original Greek: παραδόσεις (paradoseis)</note> as "ordinances" or "instructions," and not "traditions," even when used in a positive sense, as in <term>2 Thessalonians 2:15</term>. They use "Elders" for the word for <term>Priests</term> <note>original Greek: πρεσβυτέρους (presbyteros)</note>, and "images" rather than "idols" <note>original Greek: εἴδωλα (eidola)</note>. 

<margin>The Greek text supports our positions more than the common Latin does.</margin>
<margin>Luke 22:20.</margin>
<margin>For the real presence.</margin>
<margin>For fasting.</margin>
<margin>For free will.</margin>
<margin>Against faith alone.</margin>
<margin>Against the absolute assurance of salvation.</margin>
<margin>For the sacrifice of Christ's body and blood.</margin>
Furthermore, when Saint Luke in the Greek so clearly supports our position (while the common Latin could be interpreted as supporting either side), Beza claims the Greek is a corruption that crept from the margin into the text. What need is there for these absurd devices and false dealings with the Greek text if it truly favored them more than us? 

But to see that the Greek favors us more, consider <term>1 Corinthians 7</term>. In the Latin it says, *Defraud not one another, except for a time, that you may give yourselves to prayer.* In the Greek it says, *to fasting and prayer.* In <term>Acts 10:30</term>, the Latin says *Cornelius says, "From the fourth day past until this hour I was praying in my house, and behold a man..." etc.* In the Greek it says, *I was fasting and praying.* In <term>1 John 5:18</term>, the Latin says, *We know that every one which is born of God, sinneth not: but the generation of God preserveth him, etc.* In the Greek it says, *but he that is born of God preserveth himself.* 

In <term>Revelation 22:14</term>, the Latin says, *Blessed are they that wash their garments in the blood of the lamb, etc.* In the Greek it says, *Blessed are they that do his commandments.* In <term>Romans 8:38</term>, the Latin says <term>I am sure</term> <note>original Latin: Certus sum</note> *that neither death nor life, nor other creature is able to separate us from the charity of God*—as though he were absolutely certain, or as if we should assure ourselves of our predestination. But in the Greek, the word is <term>I am persuaded</term> <note>original Greek: πέπεισμαι (pepeismai)</note>, meaning *I am probably persuaded that neither death nor life, etc.* 

Finally, in the Gospels regarding the Sacrifice and the Blessed Sacrament, the Latin says: *This is my blood that shall be shed for you,* and in Saint Paul, *This is my body which shall be betrayed or delivered for you*—both referring to the future sacrifice on the cross. But in the Greek, it says, *This is my blood which **is** shed for you,* and *my body which **is** broken for you.* Both refer to that present time when Christ gave his body and blood at his supper, shedding the one and breaking the other then—that is, sacrificing it sacramentally and mystically. Behold, these and similar points are our advantages in the Greek, even more than in the Latin.

They accuse Protestant translators like Beza of intentionally mistranslating Greek terms to avoid Catholic conclusions.</summary>

# TO THE READER.

<margin>The method of this translation, and what has been observed within it.</margin>
IN THIS OUR TRANSLATION, because we wish it to be most sincere, as becomes a Catholic translation, and have endeavored to make it so: we are very precise and scrupulous in following our copy, the old vulgar approved Latin <note>This refers to the "Vulgate," the Latin Bible translation used by the Catholic Church for centuries.</note>: not only in the sense, which we hope we always do, but sometimes in the very words also and phrases. These may seem to the common reader and to common English ears not yet acquainted with them to be rudeness or ignorance. But to the discrete reader who deeply weighs and considers the importance of sacred words and speeches, and how easily a translator following his own will may miss the true sense of the Holy Ghost, we doubt not but our consideration and actions therein shall seem reasonable and necessary. Indeed, we believe that all sorts of Catholic readers will in a short time think that familiar which at first may seem strange, and will value it more when they are otherwise taught to understand it than if it were the common, well-known English.

<margin>Certain words not English nor as yet familiar in the English tongue.</margin>

And just as when we end with *Amen*, it sounds much better than saying *So be it*; so in the beginning, *Amen, Amen* must necessarily, through use and custom, sound much better than *Verily, verily*. The latter does not truly express the affirmation and assurance signified in this Hebrew word. Besides, it is the solemn and usual word of our Savior to express a forceful affirmation,

<meta>This page continues the preface of the 1582 Rheims New Testament. # THE PREFACE

<margin>
Why we say "our Lord," not "the Lord" (except in certain cases); see the Annotations on 1 Timothy 6, page 585.
</margin>
...cation of the word as *a young scholar*. <note>original: "a yong scholer"</note> Whereas it is a specific word used to signify those who were lately baptized, just as *Catechumen* <note>original: "Catechumenus"</note> signifies one newly instructed in the faith but not yet baptized—who is actually more of a "young scholar" than the other—and many who have been "old scholars" in years may still be *Neophytes* <note>A term for the newly baptized</note> by delaying their baptism. And if *Phylacteries* <note>Small boxes containing scripture verses worn during prayer</note> are allowed in English in Matthew 23, we hope that *Didragmes* <note>A silver coin; original: "Didragmes"</note> also, *Prepuce* <note>Foreskin</note>, *Paraclete* <note>The Holy Spirit as Advocate or Comforter</note>, and such similar terms will easily become current and familiar. In truth, there is such a necessity for all these that they cannot be conveniently translated. For example, when St. Paul says *division, not circumcision* <note>original Latin: "concisio, non circumcisio," a wordplay in Philippians 3:2-3</note>, how can we do anything but follow his very words and allusion? And how is it possible to express the verb *to Evangelize* <note>original: "Euangelizo"</note> except as we do? For if *Evangelium* is the Gospel, what is *to Evangelize* but to show the glad tidings of the Gospel, of the time of grace, and of all Christ’s benefits? All of this meaning is lost by translating as the English Protestant Bibles do: *I bring you good tidings* in Luke 2:10. Therefore, we use the terms *Deposit* <note>original: "Depositum," referring to the "deposit of faith" committed to the Church</note> in 1 Timothy 6, and *He emptied himself* <note>original: "exinanited him self," referring to Christ's humility</note> in Philippians 2, and *You have flourished again* <note>original: "reflorished"</note> in Philippians 4, and *to take away* <note>original Latin: "exhaust," in the sense of draining or carrying away sins</note> in Hebrews 9:28. We do this because we cannot possibly fully express these words in English. We think it much better that the reader, paused by the difficulty of them, should take the opportunity to look in the table following or otherwise ask for their full meaning, rather than for us to deceive the reader by using common English words that do not fully express the sense.

<margin>
Catholic terms proceeding from the very text of Scripture.
</margin>
Sometimes we also do this for another reason: as when we say *the Advent of our Lord* and *the imposing of hands*. We do this because one is a solemn season and the other a solemn action in the Catholic Church; we want to signify to the people that these and similar names come directly out of the Latin text of the Scripture. In the same way, terms like *Penance*, *doing penance*, *Chalice*, *Priest*, *Deacon*, *Traditions*, *altar*, and *host* <note>The bread offered in the Eucharist; original: "host"</note> (which we strictly keep as Catholic terms) proceed from the very words of Scripture.

<margin>
Certain difficult speeches and phrases.
</margin>
Furthermore, we do not presume to "soften" the speech or phrases in difficult passages, but religiously keep them word-for-word and point-for-point. We do this for fear of missing or restricting the meaning intended by the Holy Spirit to fit our own imagination. For example, in Ephesians 6: *Against the spirits of wickedness in the high places.* <note>original: "Against the spirituals of vvickednes in the celestials"</note> And in John 2: <margin>John 2.</margin> *What is that to me and to thee, woman?* <note>A literal translation of the Greek and Latin idiom used by Jesus to Mary at Cana</note>—see the Annotation on this place. Also in 1 Peter 2: *As infants even now born, reasonable, milk without guile desire ye.* We intentionally place the word *reasonable* <note>original: "reasonable," representing the Greek "logikos," which implies both "rational" and "spiritual"</note> where we do so that it may apply either to the "infants" mentioned before (as in our Latin text) or to the "milk" that follows after (as in other Latin copies and the Greek).

<margin>
The Protestants' presumptuous boldness and liberty in translating.
</margin>
In John 3, we translate: *The spirit breathes where he will, etc.*, leaving it open to mean either the Holy Spirit or the wind. By translating it only as *wind*, the Protestants take away the other meaning, which was more common and usual among the ancient Church Fathers. In Luke 8:23, we translate *They were filled*, without adding our own words *with water* to "soften" the sentence as the Protestants do. In chapter 22: *This is the chalice, the new Testament, etc.*, not *This chalice is the new Testament.* Likewise, in Mark 13: *Those days shall be such tribulation, etc.*, and not—as our adversaries put it—*In those days*, since both our text and theirs say otherwise. Similarly, in James 4:6: *And giveth greater grace*, leaving it open to refer either to the Scripture or to the Holy Spirit, both of which are mentioned before. Whereas the adversaries, with too much boldness and presumption, add words saying, *The Scripture giveth*, thereby taking away the other meaning, which is far more probable. Likewise, in Hebrews 12:21, we translate: *So terrible was it which was seen, Moses said, etc.* Neither the Greek nor the Latin allows us to add *that Moses said*, as the Protestants presume to do. So we say, *Men brethren*, *A widow woman*, *A woman a sister*, *James of Alphaeus*, and the like. Sometimes also we intentionally follow the phrasing of the Scripture, as in Matthew 5: <margin>Matthew 5.</margin> *The hell of fire*, according to both the Greek and Latin.

<meta>catchword: Latin</meta>

<summary>The translators justify using specific Latinate and technical terms like "Paraclete" and "Chalice" to preserve the precise theological meaning of the Vulgate. They also criticize Protestant translators for adding explanatory words that limit the possible interpretations of the Holy Spirit.</summary>
