<meta>This page continues the 1582 Rheims New Testament preface. It explains the translators' philosophy regarding the preservation of specific Hebrew, Greek, and Latin idioms. The previous page justified the use of technical ecclesiastical terms; this page focuses on why they occasionally include Greek and Latin references in the margins to clarify the translation or defend Catholic doctrine against Protestant ("heretical") versions.</meta>

# TO THE READER.

<margin>
*Fiery Gehenna.* <note>original Latin: "Gehenna ignis"</note>
</margin>
...which we might say perhaps, *the fiery hell*, according to the Hebrew phrase used in such speeches, but not *hell fire*, as it is commonly translated. Likewise Luke 4:36: *What word is this, that with power and authority he commands the unclean spirits?* As also, Luke 2: *Let us pass over, and see the word that is done.* In this case, we might say *thing*, following the Hebrew phrase, but there is a certain majesty and deeper significance in these expressions; therefore, both the Greek and Latin keep them, although they are no more native to the Greek or Latin phrase than they are to the English. And why should we be squeamish about new words or phrases in the Scripture, which are necessary, when we so easily admit and follow new words coined in court and in courtly or other secular writings?

<margin>
The Greek is often added in the margin for many reasons.
</margin>
We add the Greek in the margin for various causes. Sometimes when the sense is difficult, so that the learned reader may consider it and see if he can help himself better than by our translation. For example, Luke 11: *Do not be lifted up.* <note>original Latin: "Nolite extolli"; Greek: "mè meteōrizesthe"</note> And again: *Give as alms that which remains.* <note>original Latin: "Quod superest date eleemosynam"; Greek: "ta enonta"</note> Sometimes it is to take away the ambiguity of the Latin or English, as in Luke 11: *And house shall fall upon house.* Although we must necessarily translate it as *and house upon house shall fall*, by looking at the Greek, the sense is not that one house shall fall on top of another, but that if a house rises up against itself, it shall perish—just as he speaks of a kingdom divided against itself in the words before. And in Acts 14: *The priest of Jupiter who was.* In the Greek, the word *who* refers back to Jupiter <note>clarifying that it was the temple of Jupiter located at the entrance of the city</note>. Sometimes it is to satisfy the reader, who might otherwise think the translation is false. For example, Philippians 4:6: *But in everything by prayer, etc.* <note>original Greek: "en panti proseuchē"</note>, not *in all prayer*, as it may seem in the Latin. Sometimes when the Latin neither does, nor can, reach the full meaning of the Greek word, we add the Greek as more significant. <margin>Matthew 4.</margin> *Him only shall you serve* <note>original Latin: "Illi soli servies"; Greek: "latreuseis," referring to a specific type of worship due to God alone</note>. And Acts 6: *Nicolas, a stranger of Antioch* <note>original Greek: "prosēlytos," or proselyte</note>; and Romans 9: *The service* <note>original Greek: "hē latreia"</note>; and Ephesians 1: *To restore all things in Christ* <note>original Latin: "instaurare omnia in Christo"; Greek: "anakephalaiōsasthai"</note>. And: *Wherein he has gratified us* <note>original Greek: "echaritōsen"</note>; and Ephesians 6: *Put on the armor* <note>original Greek: "panoplian," meaning the "whole armor" or "suit of armor"</note>, and many others like these. Sometimes, when the Greek has two meanings and the Latin only one, we add the Greek. In 2 Corinthians 1: *By the exhortation wherewith we also are exhorted*, the Greek also signifies "consolation" and so forth; and 2 Corinthians 10: *But having hope of your faith increasing, to be etc.*, where the Greek may also mean *as when your faith increases*. Sometimes it is for the advantage of the Catholic cause, when the Greek supports us more than the Latin. For instance, <margin>Acts 15.</margin> *Elders* <note>original Latin: "Seniores"; Greek: "presbyterous," referring to Priests</note>; *That you may be counted worthy* <note>original Greek: "hina axiōthēte"</note>; *Which shall be shed* <note>original Greek: "to ekchynnomenon," used in the context of the Eucharist</note>; <margin>2 Thessalonians 2.</margin> *Precepts* <note>original Latin: "Praecepta"; Greek: "paradoseis," meaning traditions</note>; and John 21: *Feed and rule* <note>original Greek: "poimaine"; Latin: "Pasce & rege"</note>. And sometimes it is to show the <margin>1 Corinthians 11.</margin> false translation of the Heretic, such as when Beza <note>Theodore Beza, a prominent Protestant reformer and translator</note> says: *This cup in my blood which [is shed]* <note>original Latin: "Hoc poculum in meo sanguine qui..."; Greek: "to potērion en tō emō haimati to ekchynnomenon," Luke 22</note>, and *Whom heaven must contain* <note>original Latin: "Quem oportet caelo contineri"; Greek: "hon dei ouranon dechesthai," Acts 3</note>. Thus we use the Greek in various ways and value it as it deserves, taking all advantages from it for the better understanding of the Latin—which, being a translation itself, cannot always reach the full sense of the original tongue, as we see in all translations.

<margin>
The Latin text is sometimes noted in the margin.
</margin>
Furthermore, we add the Latin word sometimes in the margin when we cannot fully express it (as in Acts 8: *They took order for Stephen’s funeral* <note>original Latin: "Curaverunt Stephanum"</note>; and *All do not take this word* <note>original Latin: "Non omnes capiunt"</note>) or when the reader might think it cannot be as we translate it. For example, Luke 8: *A storm of wind descended into the lake, and they were filled* <note>original Latin: "et complebantur"</note>; and John 5: *When Jesus knew that he had now a long time* <note>original Latin: "quia iam multum tempus haberet"</note>, meaning in his infirmity.

This precise following of our Latin text, neither adding nor subtracting, is the reason why we do not say in the title of the books, on the first page, Saint Mat—

# THE PREFACE TO THE READER.

<margin>
In the beginning of books, [we write] Matthew, Paul, etc., not Saint Matthew, Saint Paul, etc.
</margin>
...thew, Saint Paul: because it is titled this way in neither the Greek nor the Latin. However, in the headers at the top of the following pages, where we may be more flexible, we add "Saint Matthew," etc., to satisfy the reader. This is much unlike the Protestants, our opponents, who have no hesitation in leaving out the name of Paul in the title of the *Epistle to the Hebrews*, even though it is present in every Greek manuscript they translate. 
<margin>
Bibles from the years 1579, 1580, 1577, 1562.
</margin>
And their most authorized English Bibles omit the word "Catholic" in the title of Saint James's Epistle and the rest, which were famously known in the early Church by the name of the *Catholic Epistles*. <note>Reference to Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 2, chapter 22.</note>

<margin>
Another reading provided in the margin.
</margin>
Likewise, in places of some importance, we provide the reader with an alternative reading in the margin, especially when the Greek agrees with it. For example, in John 5:24 <note>The source text cites "IO. 4," likely a printer's error for John 5:24</note>, the text reads *will pass from death to life* <note>original Latin: "transiet de morte ad vitam"</note>. Other Latin copies read *has passed* <note>original Latin: "transiit"</note>, and so it is in the Greek.

<margin>
The punctuation is sometimes altered.
</margin>
We do not bind ourselves to the <term>pointing|An early modern term for punctuation</term> of any single copy, print, or edition of the Vulgate Latin in places where there is no controversy. Instead, we follow the punctuation most agreeable to the Greek and to the commentaries of the Church Fathers. For example, in Colossians 1:10, we punctuate as: *Walking worthy of God, in all things pleasing.* <note>original Latin: "Ambulantes dignè Deo, per omnia placentes"; original Greek: "axiōs tou kyriou eis pasan areskeian"</note>. In Ephesians 1:17, we punctuate thus: *The God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the father of glory,* <note>original Latin: "Deus Domini nostri Iesu Christi, pater gloriae"</note> as it is in the Greek, and as Saint Chrysostom and Saint Jerome do in both their texts and commentaries. The Catholic reader must especially take note of this, lest he find fault when he sees our translation disagree in such places from the punctuation of his own Latin Testament.

<margin>
The marginal reading is sometimes preferred over the text.
</margin>
We sometimes translate the word that is in the Latin margin rather than the one in the main text, when—by looking at the Greek or the Church Fathers—we see it is a clear error made by previous scribes who mistook one word for another. For example, we use "In the end" <note>original Latin: "In fine"</note> instead of "in faith" <note>original Latin: "in fide"</note> in 1 Peter 3:8; "presence" <note>original Latin: "praesentiam"</note> instead of "foreknowledge" <note>original Latin: "praescientiam"</note> in 2 Peter 1:16; and "were hidden" <note>original Latin: "latuerunt"</note> instead of "were pleasing" <note>original Latin: "placuerunt"</note> in Hebrews 13.

Thus we have endeavored by all means to satisfy the <term>indifferent|In this context, meaning impartial or unbiased</term> reader, and to help his understanding in every way, both in the text and by the Annotations. Furthermore, we aim to deal most sincerely before God and man in translating and explaining the most sacred text of the Holy Testament. Farewell, good Reader, and if you profit at all from our poor labors, let us—for God's sake—share in your devout prayers. Together, with humble and contrite hearts, let us call upon our Savior Christ to end these troubles and storms facing his dearest spouse <note>A traditional metaphor for the Church</note>. In the meantime, let us comfort ourselves with this saying of Saint Augustine: *That heretics, when they receive power to physically afflict the Church, exercise her patience; but when they oppose her only by their evil doctrine or opinion, then they exercise her wisdom.* <note>Reference to Augustine's *The City of God*, book 18, chapter 51.</note>

# THE SIGNIFICANCE OR MEANING
## OF THE NUMBERS AND MARKS
### used in this New Testament.

The numbers in the inner margin of the text show the number of verses in every chapter.

The numbers in the Arguments <note>In this context, "Arguments" refers to the brief summaries or introductions placed at the beginning of each chapter.</note> before every chapter point to the same numbers of verses in the text that deal with that same subject matter.

The numbers at the beginning of the Annotations signify that the specific annotation refers to that particular verse of the text.

The numbers in the inner margin, or elsewhere, joined to the citations of Scripture, follow these rules: if they are written thus, Genesis 4, 16 <note>original: "Gen. 4, 16."</note>, the first is the chapter and the second is the verse. If written thus, Genesis 4. 16. <note>original: "Gen. 4. 16."</note>, both are chapters. If written thus, Genesis 4, 16. 17. 18. <note>original: "Gen. 4, 16. 17. 18."</note>, the first is the chapter and all the rest are verses. If written thus, Genesis 4, 16. 5, 7. <note>original: "Gen. 4, 16. 5, 7."</note>, it signifies chapter 4, verse 16, and chapter 5, verse 7.

† This cross signifies the beginning of every verse.

¶ This mark in the text <note>The pilcrow, or paragraph mark.</note> signifies that there is an Annotation upon the word or words which follow the said mark.

* This star in the text, or in the Annotations, signifies the reference cited across from it in the margin, or some other thing corresponding to it.

<margin>a</margin> This mark shows an alternative reading in the margin. And if there is nothing in the margin, it signifies that those words are not found in some manuscript copies.

<margin>c b</margin> These notes in the text refer the reader to the exact same letters in the margin.

<margin>Matthew <note>original: "Mt."</note></margin> for Matthew.

<margin>Mark <note>original: "Mr."</note></margin> for Mark.

☞ This mark <note>The manicule, or pointing hand.</note> signifies the ending of the Gospel and Epistle readings <note>These refer to the specific passages of the New Testament assigned to be read during the Mass.</note>.

Their beginning is identified by the margin, where directly at their start is placed: *The Gospel, or, The Epistle upon such a day.* And if it could not be placed directly there (because of other marginal notes), then <gloss>b</gloss> is the mark of their beginning. If a few, by oversight, are not noted in the margin, the information is provided in the table of Epistles and Gospels at the end of this book.

<margin>1 The infallible authority and excellence of them above all other writings.</margin>
->Saint Augustine, Book 11, against Faustus, chapter 5. <note>original: "S. Auguſtine li. 11. cont. Fauſtum. cap. 5." Faustus was a prominent Manichaean teacher whom Augustine debated.</note><-

> The excellence of the Canonical authority of the Old and New Testament is distinguished from the books of later writers: which, being confirmed in the Apostles' times by the successions of Bishops and the spreading of Churches, is placed as it were on a certain throne on high, whereunto every faithful and godly understanding must be subject and obedient. There, if anything moves or troubles you as absurd, you may not say, "The author of this book held not the truth": but rather, either the copy is faulty, or the Translator erred, or you do not understand it. But in the works of those who wrote afterward, which are contained in infinite books, but are in no case equal to that most sacred authority of **CANONICAL SCRIPTURES**: in whichever of them even the same truth is found, yet the authority is far unequal.

---

<margin>2 The discerning of Canonical from not Canonical, and of their infallible truth and sense, comes to us only by the credit we give unto THE CATHOLIC CHURCH: through whose commendation we believe both the Gospel and Christ himself. Whereas the Sectaries <note>A term used here to describe Protestant Reformers who separated from the Catholic Church.</note> measure the matter by their fantasies and opinion.</margin>
->Saint Augustine, Against the Fundamental Epistle, chapter 5. <note>original: "S. Auguſtine cont. Epiſt. fundamenti cap. 5."</note><-

> I for my part would not believe the Gospel, unless the authority of the **CATHOLIC CHURCH** moved me. They therefore whom I obeyed when they said, "Believe the Gospel": why should I not believe them when they say, "Believe not <margin>Luther, Calvin.</margin>Manichaeus"? <note>Manichaeus was the founder of Manichaeism, a religion Augustine once followed and later rejected.</note> Choose which you will. If you will say, "Believe the Catholics": lo, they warn me that I give no credit unto you; and therefore believing them, I must needs not believe you. If you say, "Believe not the Catholics": it is not the right way, by the Gospel to drive me to the faith of Manichaeus, because I believed [the Gospel]...

Whereas thou sayest, "This is Scripture," or, "This is such an Apostle's, and that is not," because this sounds in my favor and the other against me; Thou then art the rule of truth. Whatsoever is against thee is not true.

<meta>This page continues the argument for the necessity of Church tradition alongside the Bible. While the previous page established the Catholic Church as the rightful owner of the Scriptures, this page addresses how heretics use the Bible to deceive the faithful and why an "Ecclesiastical understanding" is required to interpret the text correctly.</meta>

->Vincent of Lérins in his book against the profane novelties of heresies.<- <note>original: "Vincentius Lirinensis li. cont. prophanas hæresum Nouationes." Vincent was a 5th-century monk whose writings defined how to distinguish ancient Catholic truths from new errors.</note>

<margin>* Concerning Calvin, Jewel, and the others.</margin> <note>The author is comparing the Protestant Reformers John Calvin and John Jewel to the ancient heretics described in the text.</note>
Here perhaps some man may ask, whether heretics also do not use the testimonies of divine Scripture. Yes indeed they do, and they do so vehemently. For you shall see them fly through every one of the sacred books of the Law: through **Moses**, the books of the **Kings**, the **Psalms**, the **Apostles**, the **Gospels**, and the **Prophets**. For, whether among their own followers or strangers; whether privately or publicly; whether in talk or in their books; whether at banquets or in the streets; they (I say) allege nothing of their own which they do not endeavor to shadow with the words of Scripture also. Read the works of Paulus Samosatenus, of Priscillian, of Eunomius, of Jovinian, * and of those other plagues and pestilences: you shall find an infinite heap of examples, with almost no page omitted or empty that is not painted and colored with sentences from the New or Old Testament. 

But they are to be all the more carefully avoided and feared the more secretly they lurk under the shadows of God’s divine law. For they know their foul ideas would not easily please almost anyone if they were breathed out nakedly and simply by themselves; therefore, they sprinkle them as if with certain precious spices of the heavenly word. They do this so that he who would easily despise the error of man may not easily disregard the oracles of God. They act like those who, when they wish to prepare certain bitter potions for children, first coat the rims of the cup with honey; so that the unwary child, when he first tastes the sweetness, may not fear the bitterness.

---

### ¶ The reason why, though the Scriptures are perfect, we still use other Church writings and tradition.

->Vincent of Lérins in his "golden book" cited above, *Against the Profane Novelties of Heresies*.<-

<margin>* This refers to the Church’s sense and the Church Fathers’ interpretations of Scriptures.</margin>
Here some man perhaps may ask: since the **Canon of the Scriptures** is perfect and in all points very sufficient in itself, what need is there to join to it the authority of the * **Ecclesiastical understanding**? 

The cause is surely this: that not everyone takes the Holy Scripture in one and the same sense because of its great depth. Instead, some interpret its words one way, and some another way, so that there may be almost as many interpretations picked out of it as there are men. For **Novatian** expounds it one way, and **Sabellius** another way; **Donatus** differently, and **Arius**, **Eunomius**, and **Macedonius** differently; **Photinus**, **Apollinaris**, and **Priscillian** differently; and differently still by **Jovinian**, **Pelagius**, **Celestius**, and finally **Nestorius**. * Therefore, it is very necessary—because of such great windings and turnings of various errors—that the standard of Prophetic and Apostolic interpretation be directed according to the rule of the **Ecclesiastical sense** or understanding. <note>The author lists ancient heretics to show that without the Church's guidance, individuals inevitably create conflicting and "erroneous" versions of Christianity.</note>
<margin>* Otherwise Wycliffe, Luther, Calvin, and the Puritans.</margin>

---

->Saint Basil, in his book *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 27.<- <note>original: "s. Basil li. de Spiritu sancto cap. 27." Basil the Great was a 4th-century bishop and one of the most influential theologians in Christian history.</note>

Of such articles of religion as are kept and preached in the Church, some were taught by the written word, while others we have received by the **tradition of the Apostles**, delivered to us as if from hand to hand in a hidden mystery. Both of these have equal force for Christian religion; no man will deny this if he has even a little skill in the Church's rites or customs. For if we attempt to reject the customs not contained in Scripture as being of little force, we shall unwittingly and unawares mangle the **GOSPEL** itself in its principal parts. Or rather, we shall reduce the very preaching of the Gospel to nothing but a bare name.

# THE SUMMARY OF THE NEW TESTAMENT.

<margin>
Augustine, *On the Catechizing of the Uninstructed*, chapters 3 and 4.
</margin>
That which was the essence of the Old Testament—namely, Christ and his Church, as St. Augustine says when teaching the basics of the faith to the unlearned—is the very same essence of the New Testament as well. For (as the same St. Augustine says elsewhere) in the Old Testament there is the hiding of the New, and in the New <margin>In *Questions on Exodus*, question 73.</margin> Testament there is the revealing of the Old. And in another place: "In the Old the New lies hidden, and in the New the Old lies open." <margin>Matthew 5.</margin> And because of this, our Savior said: "I have not come to break the Law or the Prophets, but to fulfill them. For assuredly I say to you, until heaven and earth pass away, not one jot or one tittle <note>The "jot" (Greek: iota) is the smallest letter, and the "tittle" refers to the smallest stroke of a pen in Hebrew script.</note> shall pass from the Law until all is fulfilled." In these words, he shows plainly that the New Testament is nothing else but the fulfilling of the Old.

Therefore, to come to the parts: The **Gospels** tell of Christ himself (whom the Old Testament foretold) from his coming into the world until his departure from it again. The **Acts of the Apostles** tell of his Church beginning at Jerusalem, the capital city of the Jews, and of its spread to the Gentiles and their capital city, Rome. And the **Apocalypse** <note>The Greek name for the Book of Revelation.</note> prophesies about the Church until its final completion at the end of the world. The **Epistles** of the Apostles deal partly with questions that were raised at that time, and partly with living a good life and maintaining good order.

### The Summary of the 4 Gospels.

<margin>
John 20:31.
</margin>
The Gospels give a historical account of the life of our Lord Jesus, showing clearly that he is the Christ, or the King of the Jews, whom they had expected throughout the entire time of the Old Testament. They also show that the Jews—out of their own pure malice and blindness (a wickedness that began with the elders <note>Refers to the Sanhedrin, the Jewish high council.</note> but eventually involved the common people as well)—would not receive him, but constantly sought his death. For the redemption of the world, he eventually allowed them to succeed in this, which resulted in them justly deserving to be rejected by him. Thus, his Kingdom or Church was taken away from them and given to the Gentiles. For the gathering of this Church after his departure, he chose **Twelve**, and appointed one of them <note>A reference to St. Peter, reflecting the Catholic emphasis on the Papacy.</note> to be the chief of all, giving instructions to both the group and to him specifically.

<margin>
Ezekiel 1.
Revelation 4.
</margin>
The story of these events was written by four authors, who in the books of Ezekiel and Revelation are compared to four living creatures, each according to how his book begins. **St. Matthew** is likened to a **Man**, because he begins with the family lineage of Christ as a man. **St. Mark** is likened to a **Lion**, because he begins with the preaching of St. John the Baptist, which was like the roaring of a lion in the wilderness. **St. Luke** is likened to a **Calf** <note>Also interpreted as an Ox, an animal used for sacrifice.</note>, because he begins with a priest of the Old Testament (Zachary, the father of St. John the Baptist), whose duty was to sacrifice calves to God. **St. John** is likened to an **Eagle**, because he begins with the Divinity of Christ, flying as high as is possible for the mind to reach.

<meta>This page continues the introduction to the New Testament, moving from a general overview of the books to a specific comparison of the four Gospels' timelines and a detailed introduction to the Gospel of Matthew.</meta>

The first three Gospels report in detail what Christ did in Galilee after the imprisonment of St. John the Baptist. Therefore, St. John the Evangelist, writing after all the others, omits his deeds in Galilee (except for one which they had not written about—the wonderful bread which he told the people of Capernaum <note>original: "Capharnaites"</note> he could and would give, in John 6). Instead, he reports first what Christ did while John the Baptist was still preaching and baptizing; then, after John’s imprisonment, what he did in Judea <note>original: "Iurie"</note> every year around Easter. However, all four write in detail about his Passion. It should be noted that from his baptism (which is thought to have occurred on the Epiphany <note>original: "Twelfth day," the feast celebrating the visit of the Magi and Christ's baptism.</note>, at which time he was beginning to be about 30 years old, Luke 3) until his passion, three years and three months are counted, during which there were also four Easters.

## The argument of St. Matthew’s Gospel.
<note>"Argument" here refers to the summary or central theme of the book.</note>

St. Matthew’s Gospel may be well divided into five parts. The first part concerns the infancy of our Lord Jesus: Chapters 1 and 2.
The second concerns the preparation that was made for his manifestation: Chapter 3 and a portion of Chapter 4.
The third concerns the manifesting of himself through preaching and miracles, specifically in Galilee: the remaining portion of Chapter 4 through Chapter 18.
The fourth concerns his coming into Judea toward his Passion: Chapters 19 and 20.
The fifth concerns the Holy Week of his Passion in Jerusalem: Chapter 21 through the end of the book.

Regarding St. Matthew, we read in Matthew 9, Mark 2, and Luke 5 how, having previously been a tax collector <note>original: "Publican," a Roman tax official often despised by the Jewish community.</note>, he was called by our Lord and made a disciple. Then in Luke 6, Mark 3, and Matthew 10, we see how out of the whole number of disciples he was chosen to be one of the twelve Apostles. And out of them again he was chosen (and none but he and St. John) to be one of the four Evangelists. Among those four, he was the first who wrote, about 8 or 10 years after Christ’s Ascension.

3. *Thamar.*] Christ did not abhor taking flesh from some who were evil, just as he chose Judas among his Apostles: Let us not disdain to receive our spiritual birth and sustenance from those who are not always good.

23. *A Virgin.*] As our Lady, being both a virgin and a mother, brought forth Christ the head corporally: so the Church, being both a virgin and a mother, brings forth the members of this head spiritually. *Augustine, Book on Virginity, chapter 2.*

23. *And bring forth.*] The Heretic Jovinian is here refuted, as he held that her virginity was corrupted in the act of bringing forth Christ. *Augustine, On Heresies, 82; Book 1, Against Julian, chapter 2.*

## ANNOTATIONS
### C H A P. II.

1. *Behold.*] Our Lord’s apparition or <term>Epiphany</term> <note>From the Greek 'epiphaneia', meaning 'manifestation' or 'appearance'.</note> to these Sages being Gentiles, their Pilgrimage to him, and in them the first homage of the Gentile world done unto him the twelfth day after his Nativity: and therefore is *Twelfth day* highly celebrated in the Catholic Church for joy of the calling of us Gentiles. His baptism also and first miracle are celebrated on the same day.

2. *Star.*] Christ’s Nativity depended not upon this star, as the <term>Priscillianists</term> <note>A 4th-century heretical sect that believed human souls were tied to the stars and fate.</note> falsely surmised: but the star upon his Nativity, for the service of which it was created. <note>original Latin: "Grego. Ho. 10." refers to Saint Gregory the Great, Homily 10 on the Gospels.</note>

<margin>Pilgrimage.</margin>
3. *Come to adore.*] This coming so far out of devotion to visit and adore Christ in the place of his birth, was properly a Pilgrimage to his person: and warrants the faithful in the like kind of external worship done to holy persons, places, and things.

4. *Inquired of them.*] The high Priests were rightly consulted in questions of their law and religion, and be they ever so ill, are often forced to say the truth by privilege of their <term>unction</term> <note>The spiritual grace or authority given through their formal anointing or office.</note>: as here and after, they did concerning the true <term>Messiah</term>.

<margin>Adoration of the Blessed Sacrament.</margin>
11. *Adored him*] This body (says <note>original Latin: "S. Chrysostom."</note>) the Sages adored in the crib. Let us at the least imitate them: thou seest him not now in the crib, but on the altar: not a woman holding him, but the Priest present, and the Holy Ghost poured out abundantly upon the sacrifice. <note>original Latin: "Ho. 24. in 1. Cor. Ho. 7. in Mt. Ho. de sancto Philogonio." refers to Saint John Chrysostom’s 24th Homily on 1 Corinthians, 7th Homily on Matthew, and his Homily on Saint Philogonius.</note>

<margin>The three kings.</margin>
<margin>Psalm 71. Isaiah 60. Chrysostom. Theophylact. <note>original Latin: "Cic. de Diuinat. Plin. li. 20." refers to Cicero’s *On Divination* and Pliny the Elder’s *Natural History*, Book 20.</note></margin>
11. *Treasures.*] These treasures are as it were the first fruits of those riches and gifts, (according to the Prophecies of David and Isaiah) that the Gentile world should offer to Christ and his Church, and now have offered, especially from the time of Constantine the Great. As also these three Sages, being principal men of their Country, represent the whole state of Princes, kings, and Emperors, that were (according to the said Prophecies) to believe in Christ, to humble themselves to his cross, to foster, enrich, adorn and defend his Church. Whereupon it is also a very convenient and agreeable tradition of antiquity, and a received opinion among the faithful, not lacking testimonies of ancient Writers, and much for the honor of our Savior, that these three also were kings: to wit, either according to the state of those Countries, where the Princes

...were Magi, and *Magi* [were] the greatest officials around the Prince: or as we read in the Scriptures regarding Melchizedek king of Salem, and many other kings who lived within a small territory: or as * Job’s three friends are called kings. 11. **Gifts.**] These Sages were three, and their gifts were three, and each one offered every one of the three gifts to express our faith in the Trinity. The Gold signifies that he was a King; the frankincense, that he was God; the myrrh, that he was to be buried as a man. <note>original: "Aug. ser. 1. de Epiph." — St. Augustine, Sermon 1 on the Epiphany.</note>

15. **Out of Egypt.**] This passage from the Prophet (and similar ones in the New Testament) is applied here to Christ; whereas in the literal letter <note>The "letter" refers to the historical or literal meaning of the Old Testament text.</note> it might seem to mean something else, it teaches us how to interpret the Old Testament and shows that the principal meaning refers to Christ and his Church.

<margin>The naming and honoring of Saints.</margin>
16. **Murdered.**] By this example we learn how much trust we owe to the Church in the <term>Canonizing of Saints: The formal process by which the Church declares a person to be a saint.</term> and the celebration of their holy days; by whose authority alone, without any specific word in the Scriptures, these Holy Innocents have been honored as Martyrs, and their holy day kept ever since the time of the Apostles—even though they did not die voluntarily, and perhaps not all were circumcised, and some were the children of Pagans. <note>original: "Aug. ep. 28. Orig. ho. 3. in diuersos." — St. Augustine, Letter 28; Origen, Homily 3 on various topics.</note>

### ->A N N O T A T I O N S<-
### ->C H A P. III.<-

<margin>Hermits. Magdeburg Centuriators <note>A massive Protestant history of the church</note> Cent. 5, c. 6. p. 711. Cent. 1. li. 1. c. 10. Chytraeus on 3rd chap. Matthew. Bucer ibid.</margin>
1. *Desert.*] From this Word *desert* (in Greek *eremus*) comes the name <term>Hermitages: isolated dwellings for religious recluses</term>, and <term>Hermits: those who live a solitary, religious life</term>, who live a religious and austere life in deserts and solitary places, following the example of St. John the Baptist. The holy Doctors of the church therefore call him the Prince and, as it were, the author of such a profession. <note>original: "S. Chrys. ho. 1 in Marcum & ho. de Io. Baptista. Hiero. ad Eustoch. de custod. virg. Isid. li. 2. c. 15 de diu off. Bernardus de excel. Io. Baptista." — References to St. Chrysostom, Jerome, Isidore, and Bernard.</note> The Protestants are so offended by this that they say St. Chrysostom spoke rashly and untruly. And it is no wonder, for whereas the Evangelist himself in this place makes John a perfect pattern of penance and the hermit’s life—by his living in the desert or wilderness, his rough and rude apparel, and his abstaining from all delicate meats (according to our Savior’s testimony of him in Matthew 11:8 and Luke 7:33)—they are not ashamed to pervert everything with this strange commentary: that it was a "desert" full of towns and villages, his garment was "chamlet" <note>A fine, expensive fabric; the author is mocking the idea that John wore luxury items</note>, and his meat was such as the country gave and the people there used. They do this to make him nothing more than a common man like the rest in his manner of life, which is completely against the Scriptures, the Church Fathers, and reason.

<margin>See Canisius regarding the corruptions of the Word of God <note>original: "de verb. Dei corruptelis"</note> book 1. c. 2. 3. 4. Penance. Mt. 4, 17. Lu. 13, 3. 5. Lu. 24, 47. Act. 2, 38. 26, 20. Annotations in this place. Μετανοέιν. Μετάνοια.</margin>
2. *Do penance.*] This follows the Latin word for word <note>original: "paenitentiam agite"</note>, as all antiquity reads it—namely St. Cyprian (Epistle 52) and St. Augustine (Confessions, Book 13, c. 12). It is a very common phrase in the New Testament, especially in the preaching of St. John the Baptist, Christ himself, and the Apostles. It signifies perfect repentance, which includes not only confession and amendment, but also contrition (sorrow for the offense) and <term>Satisfaction: performing acts to make up for the harm caused by sin</term>, such as St. Cyprian speaks of in his entire epistle. But our adversaries, on purpose (as Beza specifically protests), dislike that interpretation because it favors "Satisfaction" for sin, which they cannot abide. If they claim the Greek word <note>original: "Μετάνοια" (Metanoia)</note> means otherwise, we send them to these places: Matthew 11:21, Luke 10:13, and 1 Corinthians 7:9. In these contexts, it must necessarily signify sorrowful, painful, and satisfactory repentance. We also tell them that St. Basil, a Greek Doctor, calls the repentance of the Ninevites—done with fasting, haircloth, and ashes—by that same Greek word *repentance* <note>original: "μετάνοιαν"</note>. We will say more on this in other places.

6. *Confessing their sins.*] John prepared the Way for Christ and his Sacraments not only by his baptism, but by leading the people to the confession of their sins. This means not just acknowledging in general that they are "sinners," but for every man to actually speak <note>original: "utter"</note> his specific sins.

8. *Fruit Worthy.*] He preaches satisfaction by doing "worthy fruits" or works of penance, which are (as St. Jerome says on Joel 2) fasting, praying, almsgiving, and the like.

10. *The axe.*] Here, preachers are taught to <term>dehort: to strongly discourage</term> people from doing evil for fear of Hell, and to exhort them to do good in hope of Heaven—a kind of preaching which our adversaries condemn.

<margin>John's baptism and Christ's.</margin>
11. *In Water.*] John’s baptism did not remit sins, nor was it comparable to Christ’s Baptism, as is plain here and in many other places. <note>original: "Hiero. adu. Lucifer. Aug. de Bapt. cont. Donat. li. 5. c. 9. 10. 11." — Jerome and Augustine on baptism.</note> Yet it is a belief <note>original: "article"</note> of our adversaries that the one is no better than the other. They say this not to exalt John’s baptism, but to take away from Christ’s baptism, making it of no more value or efficacy for the forgiveness of sins, grace, and justification than John’s was. They do this to maintain their many heresies: that Baptism does not take away sins, that a man is no cleaner or more just by the Sacrament of Baptism than before, and that it is not necessary for children for their salvation.

12. **Floor.**) This floor is his Church militant <note>The "Church militant" refers to the body of believers currently living on earth, as opposed to those in heaven.</note> here on earth, wherein are both good and bad (here signified by grain <note>original: "corne"</note> and chaff) until the separation be made in the day of judgment: contrary to the doctrine of the Heretics <note>The authors use "Heretics" to refer to Protestant reformers who argued that the true Church consisted only of the elect or the godly.</note>, that hold the Church to consist only of the good.

## ANNOTATIONS
### C H A P. 4.

<margin>Hermits <note>original: "Eremites"</note>.</margin>
1. *Desert.*] As John the Baptist, so our Savior by going into the desert and there living in contemplation even among brute beasts, and subject to the assaults of the Devil for our sins, gives a warrant and example to such holy men as have lived in the wilderness for penance and contemplation, called Hermits <note>original: "Eremites"; from the Greek 'eremos' for desert.</note>.

<margin>The Lent fast.</margin>
2. *Fasted forty days.*] Elijah <note>original: "Elias"</note> and Moses (says St. Jerome) by the fast of 40 days were filled with the familiarity of God, and our Lord himself in the wilderness fasted as many, to leave unto us the solemn days of fast, (that is, Lent.) *Jerome on Isaiah chapter 58.* <note>original: "Hiero. in c. 58 Esa."</note> St. Augustine also has the very like words in *Epistle 119.* And generally all the ancient fathers that by occasion or of purpose speak of the Lent fast, make it not only an imitation of our Savior's fast, but also an Apostolic tradition, and of necessity to be kept. <margin>Ignatius, Epistle 5.</margin> *Despise not Lent (says St. Ignatius) for it contains the imitation of our Lord's way of life.* <note>original: "conuersation"</note> <margin>Ambrose, On Lent, sermon 36, 34.</margin> And St. Ambrose says plainly, that *it was not ordained by men, but consecrated by God: nor invented by any earthly thought, but commanded by the heavenly Majesty.* <margin>Jerome, Epistle 54 to Marcella against Montanus.</margin> And again, that *it is sin not to fast all the Lent.* St. Jerome’s words also are most plain: *we (says he) fast forty days, or, make one Lent in a year, according to the tradition of the Apostles, in a convenient time.* This most convenient time is (as St. Augustine says in *Epistle 119*) immediately before Easter, thereby to communicate with our Savior's Passion: and (as other Writers do add) thereby to come better prepared and more worthily to the great solemnity of Christ’s Resurrection: beside many other goodly reasons in the ancient fathers which for brevity we omit. See (good Christian Reader) 12 notable sermons of St. Leo the Great *On Lent* <note>original: "de Quadragesima"</note>: namely *Sermon 6 and 9,* where he calls it the Apostles' ordinance by the doctrine of the Holy Ghost. See St. Ambrose from the 23rd sermon forward: in St. Bernard 7 sermons, and in many other fathers the like. <margin>Augustine, Sermon 69, On Time.</margin> Last of all, note well the saying of St. Augustine, who affirms that by due observation thereof, the wicked are separated from the good, infidels from Christians, Heretics from faithful Catholics.

<header>CHAPTER 5 ACCORDING TO ST. MATTHEW.</header>

6. *It is written.*] Heretics allege scriptures, as the Devil does here, in a false sense; the Church uses them, as Christ does, in the true sense, and to refute their falsehood. <margin>Augustine, *Against the Letters of Petilian*, book 2, chapter 51, volume 7.</margin>

11. *Him only serve.*] It was not said, says St. Augustine, "The Lord thy God only shalt thou adore," as it was said, "Him only shalt thou serve": in Greek, <note>original: "λατρεύσεις" (latreuseis)</note> "thou shalt serve with divine worship." <margin>Augustine, *Questions on Genesis*, question 61. <term>Latria</term> <note>Worship given to God alone.</note>. <term>Dulia</term> <note>Veneration or honor given to Saints and holy things.</note>.</margin> Whereupon the Catholic Church has always used this most true and necessary distinction: <margin>Latria. Dulia.</margin> that there is an honor due to God only, which to give unto any creature would be idolatry; and there is an honor due to creatures also according to their dignity, as to Saints, holy things, and holy places. <margin>See Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 4, chapter 14; St. Jerome, *Against Vigilantius*, epistle 53; Augustine, *City of God*, book 10, chapter 1; *On the Trinity*, book 1, chapter 6; Second Council of Nicaea; John Damascene, *On Images*, book 1; Bede on Luke 4.</margin>

17. *Do penance.*] That penance is necessary also before baptism, for those who are of age: as John’s preaching, so our Savior’s preaching declares, both beginning with penance. <note>The Rheims translators use "penance" to emphasize the sacrament and outward acts of contrition, contrasting with Protestant translations that used "repentance" to signify only an inner change of mind.</note>

23. *Healing every malady.*] Christ (*says St. Augustine*) by miracles gained authority, by authority found credit, by credit drew together a multitude, by a multitude obtained antiquity, by antiquity fortified a Religion, which not only the most sound "new rising" of Heretics using deceitful wiles, but neither the drowsy old error of the very Heathen with violence setting against it, might in any part shake and cast down. <margin>Augustine, *On the Profit of Believing*, chapter 14.</margin>

## ANNOTATIONS
### CHAPTER 5.

<margin>False Martyrs.</margin>
10. *For justice.*) Heretics and other wrongdoers sometimes suffer willingly and stoutly: but they are not blessed, because they suffer not for justice. For (says *St. Augustine*) they cannot suffer for justice who have divided the Church. And, where sound faith or charity is not, there cannot be justice. <note>original: "Cont. ep. Parm. li. 1. c. 9. Ep. 50. Psal. 34. Conc. 2." — Against the Letter of Parmenian, Book 1, chapter 9; Letter 50; Psalm 34, Commentary 2.</note> And so by this scripture are excluded all false Martyrs, as *St. Augustine* often declares, and *St. Cyprian* in his work <note>original: "de Unit. Eccl. nu. 8." — On the Unity of the Church, number 8.</note>.

<margin>Reward. Μισθός.</margin>
12. *Reward.*) In Latin and Greek the word <note>original Latin: "merces"; original Greek: "misthos" (μισθός)</note> signifies very wages and hire due for works, and so presupposes a meritorious deed.

<summary>In this portion of the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus reinterprets the Law regarding divorce, oaths, and retaliation, urging his followers toward a higher standard of love and perfection. The accompanying annotations argue that true martyrdom requires unity with the Church and that "reward" in heaven implies merit for good works.</summary>

<margin>The Church visible.</margin>
15. *The light.*] This light of the world, and city on a mountain, and candle upon a candlestick, signify the Clergy and the whole Church, so built upon Christ the mountain that it must necessarily be visible, and cannot be hidden nor unknown. <note>original: "Aug. cont. Fulg. Donat. c. 18. Li. 16. cont. Faust. c. 17." — St. Augustine, *Against Fulgentius the Donatist*, chapter 18; and *Against Faustus*, book 16, chapter 17.</note> And therefore, the Church being a candle not under a bushel, but shining to all in the house (that is, in the world), what shall I say more (says St. Augustine) than that they are blind who shut their eyes against the candle that is set on the candlestick? <note>original: "Tract. 2. in ep. Io." — St. Augustine, *Tractate 2 on the Epistle of John*.</note>

17. *Your light.*] The good life of the Clergy edifies much and is God's great honor, whereas the contrary dishonors him.

20. *One of these.*] Behold how necessary it is, not only to believe, but to keep all the commandments, even the very least.

<margin>True inherent justice.</margin>
21. *Your justice.*] It is our justice <term>justice: here meaning righteousness or moral standing before God</term> when it is given to us by God. <note>original: "Aug. in Psal. 30. Conc. 1. De Sp. & lit. c. 9." — St. Augustine, *Commentary on Psalm 30*, Sermon 1; and *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 9.</note> So that Christians are truly just and have in themselves inherent justice by doing God's commandments. Without which justice of works no man of age can be saved. <note>original: "Aug. de fid. & oper. c. 16." — St. Augustine, *On Faith and Works*, chapter 16.</note> By this we see that salvation, justice, and justification do not come from faith alone, or the mere "imputation" of Christ’s justice <note>Imputation is the Protestant idea that Christ’s righteousness is credited to a believer's account, rather than the person becoming righteous through their own actions.</note>.

<margin>Venial sins.</margin>
23. *Hell of fire.*] Here is a plain difference between sins: some are mortal <note>sins that sever one's relationship with God</note> and bring one to Hell, and some are less serious and less punished, called venial <note>sins that damage but do not destroy the life of grace in the soul</note>.

24. *Gift at the altar.*] Beware of coming to the holy altar or any Sacrament while lacking charity. But be first reconciled to your brother, and much more to the Catholic Church, which is the whole brotherhood of Christian men. <note>original: "Heb. 13:1." — Hebrews 13:1.</note>

32. *Excepting the cause of fornication.*] This exception is only to show that for this one cause a man may put away his wife forever, but not that he may marry another. This is most plain 
<margin>Marriage is a Sacrament, and is not dissolved by divorce.</margin>
<margin>Mark 10:11. Luke 16:18.</margin>
in St. Mark and St. Luke, who leave out this exception, saying: *Whoever dismisses his wife and marries another, commits adultery.* See the Annotations on Luke 19:9. But if both parties are in one and the same fault, then neither of them can even divorce or put away the other.

33. *Committeth adultery.*] The knot of Marriage is so great a Sacrament that it cannot be loosened even by the separation of the parties; it is not lawful for either the one part or the other to marry again upon divorce. <note>original: "Aug. de bo. Coniug. c. 7." — St. Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage*, chapter 7.</note>

35. *Not to swear.*] The Anabaptists <note>A radical Reformation group</note> here, not following the Church’s judgment but the bare letter (as other heretics do in other cases), hold that no oath is lawful, not even before a judge. Whereas Christ speaks against rash and usual swearing in common talk when there is no cause.

39. *Not to Resist evil.*] Here also the Anabaptists gather from the letter that it is not lawful to go to law for our rights, just as Luther also held regarding this place, that Christians might not resist the Turk <note>The Ottoman Empire</note>. Whereas by this, as by that which follows, only patience is signified and a will to suffer more rather than to seek revenge. For neither Christ nor St. Paul followed the letter by literally "turning the other cheek." <note>original: "Io. 18. Act. 23." — John 18 and Acts 23.</note>

## ANNOTATIONS
### CHAPTER VI.

<margin>Good works justify.</margin> 1. *Justice.*] By this it is plain that good works are justice, and that a person doing them performs justice, and is thereby just and justified, and not by faith alone. All this justice of a Christian man our Savior here comprises in these three works: in alms, fasting, and prayers. <note>original: "Aug. li. perf. iust. c. 8." refers to Saint Augustine’s Book on the Perfection of Justice, chapter 8.</note> So that to give alms is to do justice, and the works of mercy are justice. <note>original: "Aug. in Ps. 49, v. 5." refers to Saint Augustine’s commentary on Psalm 49, verse 5.</note>

<margin>Merits.</margin> 4. *Repay.*] This repaying and rewarding of good works in heaven, often mentioned here by our Savior, declares that the said works are meritorious, and that we may do them in respect of that reward.

<margin>Hypocrisy.</margin> 5. *Hypocrites.*] Hypocrisy is forbidden in all these three works of justice, but not the doing of them openly for the glory of God and the profit of our neighbor and our own salvation: for Christ before (chapter 5) commanded, saying: *Let your light so shine before men, etc.* And in all such works Saint Gregory's rule is to be followed: *The work should be in public in such a way that the intention remains in secret.* <note>original: "Ho. 11. in Euang. c. 10." refers to Saint Gregory the Great's 11th Homily on the Gospels, chapter 10.</note>

<margin>Luke 6:12; 18:1; 21:36. 1 Thessalonians 5:17. Cyprian on the Lord's Prayer, at the end.</margin> 7. *Much speaking.*] Long prayer is not forbidden, for Christ himself spent whole nights in prayer, and he says we must pray always, and the Apostle exhorts us to pray without intermission, and the holy Church from the beginning has had her Canonical hours <note>Scheduled times of day set aside for specific prayers and psalms.</note> of prayer: but idle and voluntary babbling is forbidden, whether of the heathens to their gods, or of Heretics, who think to persuade God by long rhetorical prayers; whereas the <term>Collects <note>Brief, formal prayers used in the liturgy of the Church.</note></term> of the Church are most brief and most effectual. <note>original: "See S. Augustine ep. 121, c. 8, 9. 10." refers to Saint Augustine’s 121st Letter.</note>

<margin>the essential bread <note>original: τὸν ἐπιούσιον (ton epiousion)</note>. The Blessed Sacrament.</margin> 11. *Supersubstantial bread.*] By this bread, so called here according to the Latin word and the Greek, we ask not only for all necessary sustenance for the body, but much more for all spiritual food, namely the <term>Blessed Sacrament <note>The Eucharist or Holy Communion.</note></term> itself, which is Christ the true bread that came from heaven, and the bread of life to us who eat his body. <note>original: "Cypr. de orat. Do." (Cyprian on the Lord's Prayer); "Aug. ep. 121 c. 11." (Augustine's Letter 121).</note> And therefore it is called here "Supersubstantial," that is, the bread that surpasses and excels all creatures. <note>original references: Saint Jerome on Titus chapter 2 and Matthew chapter 6; Saint Ambrose, Book 5 on the Sacraments, chapter 4; Saint Augustine, Sermon 28 on the Words of the Lord according to Matthew; Saint Germanus in his Mystical Theory.</note>

<margin>Venial sins.</margin> 12. *Debts.*] These debts signify not only mortal sins, but also <term>venial <note>Lesser sins that do not fully separate a person from God's grace, as opposed to "mortal" or deadly sins.</note></term> sins, as Saint Augustine often teaches: and therefore every person, no matter how just, because they cannot live without venial sins, may very truly and ought to say this prayer. <note>original: "Aug. cont. du. ep. Pelag. li. 1. c. 14." (Augustine against the two letters of the Pelagians) and "li. 21 de Ciuit. c. 27." (The City of God, Book 21).</note>

<meta>catchword: 13. Lead us not</meta>

<meta>This page continues the scholarly and polemical annotations for Matthew Chapter 6, specifically focusing on the Lord’s Prayer and the merits of good works, before transitioning into the text of Matthew Chapter 7, which concludes the Sermon on the Mount.</meta>

<page-num>17</page-num>
<header>CHAPTER VII. ACCORDING TO SAINT MATTHEW.</header>

<margin>In the Exposition of the Lord’s Prayer; James 1.</margin> 13. *Lead us not.*] Saint Cyprian reads, "Suffer us not to be led," <note>original: "Ne patiaris nos induci." Cyprian was a 3rd-century Bishop of Carthage.</note> as Saint Augustine <margin>God is not the author of evil.</margin> notes in his *Book on the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 6, <note>original: "li. de bo. perseu. c. 6." refers to De bono perseverantiae.</note> and so the holy Church understands it, because God (as Saint James says) tempts no man: though for our sins, or for our testing and crown of glory, he permits us to be tempted. Beware then of Beza's exposition <note>Theodore Beza was a major French Protestant reformer and successor to John Calvin.</note> upon this place, who (according to the Calvinists' opinion) says that God leads them into temptation into whom he himself brings in Satan to fill their hearts: so making God the author of sin.

14. *If you forgive.*] This point—of forgiving our brother when we ask forgiveness of God—our Savior repeats again as a thing much to be considered: and therefore commended in the parable also of the servant that would not forgive his fellow servant, *Matthew 18.*

<margin>Judges 20, 26; 2 Esdras 9; Joel 2, 15; Jonah 3.</margin> 16. *Fast.*] He does not forbid open and public fasts, which in the <margin>Public fast.</margin> Scriptures were commanded and proclaimed to the people of God; even the Ninevites <note>The inhabitants of Nineveh who repented at the preaching of Jonah.</note> appeased God's wrath by such fasting. Rather, he forbids fasting for vain glory and the praise of men, or being desirous to be recognized as a faster by one's very face and look; that is forbidden, and that is hypocrisy.

20. *Treasures in heaven.*] Treasures laid up in heaven must signify not faith only, but plentiful alms, deeds of mercy, and other good works. God keeps these as if in a book and <margin>Meritorious works.</margin> will reward them accordingly: as, on the contrary, the Apostle says, *He that sows sparingly, shall reap sparingly. 2 Corinthians 9.*

24. *Two Masters.*] Two religions: God and Baal, Christ and Calvin, Mass and Communion, the Catholic Church and Heretical Conventicles <note>Conventicles were secret or unauthorized religious meetings, here used as a derogatory term for Protestant gatherings.</note>. Let them mark this lesson of our Savior who think they may serve all masters, all times, and all religions. Again, these two masters signify God and the world, the flesh and the spirit, justice and sin.

25. *Careful.*] Prudent provision is not prohibited, but rather too much doubt and fear of God’s provision for us: to whom we ought to commit the rest with patience once we have done sufficiently for our part.

### ANNOTATIONS
#### CHAPTER 7.

1. *Judge not.*] It is no Christian part to judge poorly of men's acts which are in themselves good and may proceed from good meaning, or of man's inward meanings and intentions which we cannot see: of which fault they must beware who are too suspicious and given to always deem the worst of other men. But to say that Judas, or a Heretic evidently known to die obstinately in heresy, is damned, and in all other plain and manifest cases to judge, is not forbidden.

6. *Holy to dogs.*] No holy Sacrament, and especially that of our Savior's blessed body <note>The Eucharist or Holy Communion</note>, must be <margin>Worthy receiving.</margin> given knowingly to the unworthy—that is, to those who have not examined and proved themselves by confession of all mortal sins. See the Annotations for 1 Corinthians 11:27, 28, 29.

8. *Every one that asketh.*] All things that we ask which are necessary to salvation with humility, attention, persistence, and other due circumstances, God will undoubtedly grant when it is best for us.

<margin>Romans 16:18. Heretics are wolves in sheep’s skins.</margin>
15. *Clothing of sheep.*] An extraordinary appearance of zeal and holiness is the "sheep’s coat" in some Heretics: but those of this time do not wear that garment much, being men of insatiable sin. This is rather their garment, common to them with all other heretics: to brag much of the word of the Lord, and by pretended allegations and sweet words of blessing, and especially by promise of knowledge, light, and liberty of the Gospel, to seduce the simple and the sinful.

<margin>Heretics known by their fruits.</margin>
16. *Fruits.*] These are the fruits by which Heretics are known: division from the whole Church, division among themselves, taking to themselves new names and new masters, inconstancy in doctrine, disobedience both to others and namely to spiritual officers <note>Bishops and Church authorities</note>, love and liking of themselves, pride and intolerable vaunting of their own knowledge above all the holy Doctors <note>The early Church Fathers and theologians</note>, corruption, falsification, and quite denying of the parts of Scriptures that specially make against them; and these are common to all heretics generally. Some others are more peculiar to those of our time, such as incestuous marriages of vowed persons <note>referring to monks or nuns who left their vows to marry</note>, the spoiling of Churches, sacrilege and profanation of all holy things, and many other special points of doctrine directly tending to the corruption of good life in all states.

<margin>Not only faith.</margin>
21. *Lord, Lord.*] These men have faith, otherwise they could not call out, *Lord, Lord* (Romans 10). But here we see that to believe is not enough, and that not only infidelity <note>lack of faith</note> is sin, as Luther teaches. Yea, Catholics also who work true miracles in the name of our Lord, and by never so great faith, yet without the works of justice <note>righteousness or good works</note> shall not be saved (1 Corinthians 13). Again, consider here who they are that have "The Lord, the Lord" so often in their mouth, and how little it shall avail them who set so little by good works and despise Christian justice.

### A N N O T A T I O N S
#### C H A P T E R 8.

<margin>Priests forgive sins.</margin>
4. **Priest.**] The Priests of the old law (says St. Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), a prominent Early Church Father.</note>) had authority and privilege only to discern who were healed of leprosy, and to announce the same to the people: but the Priests of the new law have power to purge in very deed <note>Truly or effectively.</note> the filth of the soul. Therefore whosoever despises them, is more worthy to be punished than the rebel Dathan and his accomplices <note>Referencing Numbers 16, where Dathan rebelled against the spiritual authority of Moses and Aaron.</note>. *St. Chrysostom, Book 3, On the Priesthood.*

4. **Gift.**] Our Savior wills him to go and offer his gift or sacrifice according as Moses prescribed in that case, because the other sacrifice being the holiest of all holies, which is his body, was not yet begun. *So says St. Augustine, Book 2, Questions on the Gospels, question 3; and Against the Adversaries of the Law and Prophets, Book 1, chapters 19, 20.*

<margin>Lord, I am not worthy. <note>Original Latin: "DOMINE, non sum dignus."</note></margin>
8. **Not Worthy.**] *Origen, homily 5, on various subjects.* When thou eatest (says he) and drinkest the body and <margin>* Greek Liturgy of St. Chrysostom, near the end.</margin> blood of our Lord, he enters under thy roof. Thou also therefore humbling thyself, say: Lord I am not worthy, etc. So said * St. Chrysostom in his Mass, and so does the Catholic Church use at this day in every Mass. *See St. Augustine, epistle 118 to Januarius.*

<margin>Priests' marriage.</margin>
14. **His Wife’s mother.**] Of Peter specially among the rest it is evident that he had a wife, but <margin>Book 1 against Jovinian, chapter 14; Matthew 19:29; Epiphanius, Heresy 59; * Sozomen, Book 1, chapter 22; Socrates, Book 1, chapter 8.</margin> (as St. Jerome says) after they were called to be Apostles, they had no more carnal company with their wives, as he proves there by the very words of our Savior, *He that hath left Wife etc.* And so in the Latin Church has been always used, that married men may be and are daily made Priests, either after the death of the wife, or with her consent to live in perpetual continence. And if the Greeks have Priests that do otherwise, St. Epiphanius a Greek Doctor tells them that they do it against the ancient Canons, and * Paphnutius <note>A 4th-century bishop who argued at the Council of Nicaea that while clergy should not marry after ordination, those already married should not be forced to separate.</note> plainly signifies the same in the first Council of Nice <note>Nicaea (325 AD).</note>. But this is most plain, that there was never either in the Greek Church or the Latin, authentic example of any that married after holy Orders.

## ANNOTATIONS
### CHAPTER 9.

3. *He blasphemeth.*] When the Jews heard Christ remit sins, they charged him with blasphemy, just as heretics now charge his priests of the New Testament because they remit sins; to whom he said, *Whose sins you shall forgive, they are forgiven etc. John 20.* <note>The author is comparing the Protestant rejection of the Sacrament of Penance/Confession to the Pharisees' rejection of Christ's authority.</note>

<margin>Men have power to forgive sins.</margin>
5. *Whether is easier.*] The faithless Jews thought (as heretics do nowadays) that to forgive sins was so unique to God that it could not be communicated to man: but Christ shows that just as working miracles is otherwise unique to God alone, and yet this power is communicated to men, so also is the power to forgive sins.

6. *The son of man in earth.*] Christ had power to remit sins, and often performed this, not only as he was God, but also as he was a man, because he was head of the Church and our chief Bishop and Priest according to his manhood, in respect of which all power was given him in heaven and earth. *Matthew 28, v. 18.*

8. *Glorified.*] The faithful people glorified God who gave such power to men to remit sins and to perform miracles, knowing that what God commits to men does not take away from his honor, but adds to his glory: he himself remains the principal worker of that effect, while men are only his ministers, substitutes, and workers under him and by his commission and authority.

8. *To men.*] Not only Christ, as he was man, had this power to forgive sins, but through him and from him the Apostles, and consequently Priests, received it. *Matthew 28: All power is given to me.* *Matthew 18: Whatever you shall loose on earth, shall be loosed in heaven.* *John 20: Whose sins you shall forgive, they are forgiven.*

<margin>External Sacrifice.</margin>
13. *Not sacrifice.*] These are the words of the Prophet <note>Referring to Hosea 6:6.</note>, who spoke them even when sacrifices were being offered by God’s commandment: so this does not argue against sacrifice itself, but rather he says that sacrifice alone, without mercy and charity, and especially when performed in a state of mortal sin, is not acceptable. The Jews offered their sacrifices duly, but in the meantime, they had no pity or mercy on their brethren; that is what God dislikes.

<margin>Fasting.</margin>
14. *Fast often.*] From the frequent fasting of his disciples, we may easily gather that he appointed for them a prescribed manner of fasting, just as it is certain he taught them a form of prayer. *Luke 5 and 11.*

17. *New Wine.*] By this "new wine," he plainly signifies fasting and a stricter kind of life; by the "old bottles," he refers to those who cannot cope with such rigor.

19. *Twelve years.*] This woman, a Gentile, had her disease for twelve years, and the Governor’s daughter, a Jew (who is here raised to life), was twelve years old, *Luke 8.* Observe then the allegory here regarding the Jews and Gentiles. Just as that woman fell sick when the girl was born, so the Gentiles went their own way into idolatry when the Jews, through Abraham, believed. Again, as Christ went here to raise the girl, and along the way the woman was first healed and then the girl revived: so Christ came to the Jews, but the Gentiles believed first and were saved, and in the end, the Jews shall believe also. <note>original: "Hiero. in Mat." Refers to Saint Jerome’s commentary on Matthew.</note>

<margin>Relics and Images.</margin>
<margin>Eusebius, book 7, chapter 14 of his History.</margin>
<margin>book 5, chapter 20.</margin>
21. *Touch only.*] Not only Christ’s words, but his garment and the touch of it—or anything belonging to him—could and did perform miracles, as power proceeded from his holy person to those objects. Indeed, this woman, returning home, * set up an image of Christ to remember this benefit, and the hem of that same image also performed miracles. This image Julian the Apostate <note>A Roman Emperor who tried to revive paganism and suppress Christianity.</note> threw down and set up his own in its place, which was immediately destroyed by fire from heaven. But the image of Christ, though broken in pieces by the heathens, was later gathered up by Christians and placed in the Church: where it remained (as Sozomen <note>An early Christian church historian.</note> writes) until his time.

CHAPTER 10. ACCORDING TO ST. MATTHEW.

28. *Do you believe that I can.]* We see here that for the physical healing of these men he requires only this faith: that he is able to do it. This specific faith is not sufficient to justify them <note>In this context, "justify" means to be made righteous or saved in a theological sense.</note>. How then do the heretics <note>The author uses "heretics" to refer to Protestant Reformers who taught "sola fide," or salvation by faith alone.</note> use this and similar passages to plead for their "faith alone" doctrine? *See the Annotations for Mark 5:36.*

38. *Pray therefore.)* Therefore the Church prays and fasts during the Ember Days <note>The "Imber dayes" or Ember Days are four separate sets of three days within the church calendar dedicated to fasting and prayer, often coinciding with the ordination of new clergy.</note>, when holy Orders are given—that is, when workmen are prepared to be sent into the harvest. *See Acts 13:2.*

# A N N O T A T I O N S
## C H A P T E R. X.

1. *Power.*) Miracles were so necessary to the confirmation of their doctrine <note>The "doctrine" refers to the teachings of the Apostles as they began to preach.</note> beginning then to be preached, that not only Christ himself performed miracles, but he also gave his Apostles power to do them.

<margin>
Beza in Annotations on the New Testament, 1556.
</margin>
<margin>
Peter's Primacy.
</margin>
2. *First Simon.*) Peter is called "the first," not because he was called first to follow Jesus, but in terms of his preeminence <term>Primacy: the Catholic doctrine that Peter held the highest authority among the Apostles</term>. For (as Saint Ambrose says in his commentary on 2 Corinthians 12) *Andrew followed our Savior before Peter; and yet Andrew did not receive the Primacy, but Peter did.* This preeminence of Saint Peter above the other Apostles is so plainly indicated by this word "First," that even the judgment of the Heretics <note>The author uses "Heretics" to refer to Protestant reformers.</note> acknowledges it. Theodore Beza, even though he confesses that all copies in both Latin and Greek agree, is not ashamed to say that he suspects this word was shoved into the text by someone favoring Peter's Primacy. By this we see that they care no more for the Greek text than for the Latin when it goes against them, but they claim at their pleasure that everything is corrupted.

9. *Do not possess.*) Preachers should not carefully seek after the luxuries <note>original: "superfluities"</note> of this life, or anything that might be an obstacle to their duties. As for necessities, they deserve their temporal living from the hands of those for whom they labor spiritually.

<margin>
Augustine, *The City of God*, Book 22, Chapter 8. Emperor Leo in the *Life of St. Chrysostom*, Book 6, Chapter 14.
</margin>
<margin>
Bishops' blessing.
</margin>
12. *Peace to this house.*) Just as Christ himself often used these words or this blessing—*Peace be to you*—so here he commands his Apostles to say the same to the houses they enter. Thus, it has always been a most godly custom for Bishops to give their blessing wherever they go. This blessing must surely be of great grace and profit, since only worthy persons (as we read here) might benefit from it; and it is never lost, but returns to the giver when the other party is not worthy of it. Among other spiritual benefits, it takes away venial sins <term>Venial sins: in Catholic teaching, lesser sins that do not fully separate a person from God's grace</term>. <note>Citing Ambrose in his commentary on Luke 9.</note>

<margin>
It remits venial sins.
</margin>
14. *Shake off the dust.*) To despise <note>original: "contemne"</note> true preachers, or not to receive the truth they preach, is a very damnable sin.

15. *More tolerable.*) By this it is evident that there are degrees and differences of damnation in Hell fire according to people's deserts. <note>Citing Augustine, *On Baptism*, Book 4, Chapter 19.</note>

18. *Kings.*) In the beginning, Kings and Emperors persecuted the Church, so that by the very death and blood of Martyrs it should grow more miraculously. Afterward, when the Emperors and Kings themselves became Christians, they used their power for the Church, against Infidels and Heretics. <note>Citing Augustine, Letter 48.</note>

19. *It shall be given.*) This is proven even at this present time, when many good Catholics who have no great formal learning confound their adversaries with their answers.

25. *How much more.*) It is no wonder, therefore, if Heretics call Christ's Vicar <note>The Pope</note> "Antichrist," when their forefathers, the faithless Jews, called Christ himself "Beelzebub."

<margin>
Acts 9.
</margin>
<margin>
Confessing of Christ and his truth.
</margin>
32. *Confess me.*) See how Christ values the open confessing of him—that is, of his truth in the Catholic Church. For just as when Saul persecuted the Church, Christ said *he himself* was being persecuted; so to confess him and his Church is all one. Conversely, see how he abhors those who deny him before men. This includes not only denying any one small article of the Catholic faith commended to us by the Church, but also to allow or consent to heresy by any means, such as by subscribing,

coming to their service and sermons, furthering them any way against Catholics, and such like.
34. *Not peace but sword.*] Christ came to break the peace of worldlings and sinners: as when the son believes in him, and the father does not; or the wife is a Catholic, and the husband is not. For to agree together in infidelity, heresy, or any other sin, is a naughty peace. This being the true meaning of Christ's words, mark that the Heretics <note>In this context, "Heretics" refers to Protestant reformers.</note> interpret this to maintain their rebellions and troubles which their new gospel breeds. <note>original: "Beza in no. Test. an. 1565." — Refers to the French Protestant reformer Theodore Beza's 1565 edition of the New Testament.</note>

41. *In the name.*] Reward for hospitality, and especially for receiving a holy person, as Prophet, Apostle, Bishop, or Priest persecuted for Christ's sake. For by receiving him in that respect as he is such a one, he shall be partaker of his merits, and be rewarded as for such a one. Whereas on the contrary side, he that receives a Heretic into his house and a false preacher, does communicate with his wicked works. <note>original: "Ep. 2. 10." — Refers to the Second Epistle of John, verse 10, which warns against welcoming those who do not bring the true doctrine.</note>

# THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO ST. MATTHEW, CHAPTER 12

## ANNOTATIONS
### CHAPTER 11

3. *Are you he.*] John himself did not doubt, for he had baptized him and gave great testimony of him before: *John 1.* But because his disciples did not know him, nor esteemed him as much as they did John, their own Master, he sent them to Christ so that, by the occasion of Christ’s answer, he might better instruct them on who he was, and so make them Christ’s disciples, moving them to a better Master.

<margin>Hermit-like life.</margin>
7. *What did you go out [to see].*] This is high praise for John’s holiness, regarding his fasting, rough clothing, solitary life, and constancy, as well as the dignity of his office.

7. *Into the desert.*] Faithful people in all ages have traveled out of devotion into the wilderness to see men of special and rare holiness—prophets, hermits <note>original: "Eremites"</note>, anchorites, etc.—to receive their prayers or spiritual counsel. *See St. Jerome’s On the Life of Hilarion.*

<margin>Elijah.</margin>
14. *Elijah.*] Just as Elijah shall be the messenger of Christ’s second coming, so was John his messenger and forerunner <note>original Latin: "Praecursor"</note> at his first coming; therefore he is called Elijah because of his similar office and spirit. *Luke 1; Gregory, Homily 7 on the Gospels.*

18. *Eating and drinking.*] The wicked critics of the world easily misinterpret the actions and lives of good men. If they are great fasters and live austere lives, they are slandered and counted as hypocrites; if they socialize with other men in an ordinary way, then they are counted as dissolute.

<margin>Penance.</margin>
<margin>Repentance <note>original Greek: "μετάνοια"</note></margin>
21. *Penance in sackcloth.*] By the mention of sackcloth and ashes here and in other places, we see clearly that Penance is not only the leaving behind of former sins and a change or amendment of one's past life, nor merely feeling sorry or recounting offenses already committed. Instead, it requires the punishment and chastisement of our persons by these and other such means as the Scriptures set forth elsewhere. Therefore, regarding the word itself, it is more fittingly called "Penance," as in our translation, rather than "Repentance" or "Amendment of life" (terms used by our opponents <note>The "adversaries" refers to Protestant reformers who preferred "repentance" to "penance."</note> for the purpose of avoiding the word). This is according to the very common meaning of the Greek word used by the most ancient Greek Church writers, who, when referring to the "Penitents" <note>original Latin: "Paenitentes"</note> who performed public penance in the early Church, said: <margin>Dionysius, The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, chapter 3, at the beginning.</margin> \* "those who are in a state of repentance" <note>original Greek: "οἱ ἐν μετανοίᾳ ὄντες"</note>, which means *men who are doing penance.* Regarding the part of penance which is Confession, the history of the Church calls it by the same Greek word, and calls the penitents coming to confession "those repenting" <note>original Greek: "τοὺς μετανοοῦντας"</note>. *Sozomen, book 7, chapter 16; Socrates, book 5, chapter 19.*

<margin>Matthew 18:3.</margin>
25. *Little ones.*] These "little ones" do not signify here only the unlearned—as if shoemakers, weavers, women, and girls had this revelation and therefore understood all Scriptures and were able to explain them. Instead, here are signified the humble, whether they are learned or unlearned; as when he says, *Unless you become as little ones, you shall not enter into the Kingdom of heaven.* Thus, even the greatest Doctors of the Church (who, as they were the most learned, so they most humbled themselves to the judgment of the Catholic Church) are these "little ones." Conversely, heretics—who, although unlearned, boast of their knowledge and their spirit of understanding above all the ancient fathers and the whole Church—cannot be among these little and humble ones.

<margin>The commandments are possible.</margin>
30. *Yoke is sweet.*] What is this light burden and sweet yoke but his commandments, of which St. John says in 1 John 5: *His commandments are not heavy?* This is completely contrary to our opponents who say they are impossible to keep.

---
