## ANNOTATIONS
### CHAPTER 12.

24. *In Beelzebub.*] A similar blasphemy against the Holy Ghost is to attribute the miracles performed by Saints, whether dead or alive, to the Devil.

30. *Not With me.*] Those who are indifferent to all religions, commonly and fittingly called Neuters <note>A term used here for people who refused to take a side during the religious conflicts of the Reformation.</note>, joining themselves to neither side, let them mark these words well; they shall see that <margin>Neuters in religion.</margin> Christ accounted all those to be against him and his Church who are not plainly and flatly with him and it.

<margin>Letter 58.</margin> 30. *Gathereth Not With me.*] He speaks not only of his own person, but of all those to whom he has committed the government of his Church, and especially of the chief Pastors succeeding Peter in the government of the whole. As Saint Jerome, writing to Pope Damasus of Rome, applies these words to him, saying of all Heretics: *He that gathers not with you, scatters: that is to say, He that is not with Christ, is with Antichrist.* <note>original Latin: "Qui tecum non colligit, spargit..."</note>

31. *The blasphemy of the Spirit.*] He does not mean that there is any sin so great that God will not forgive it, or of which a man may not repent in this life (as some Heretics at this day affirm); but that some heinous sins—namely this blasphemy of the Jews against the evident works of the Holy Ghost, and likewise Arch-heretics who willfully resist the known truth and works of the Holy Ghost in God's Church—are hardly forgiven, and such men seldom have the grace to repent. Otherwise, among all the sins against the Holy Ghost (which are commonly reckoned as six), only one shall never be forgiven: that is, dying willfully without repentance, called Final <margin>Final impenitence.</margin> impenitence. A person commits this sin if they die with contempt for the Sacrament of Penance <note>Confession and absolution.</note>, obstinately refusing absolution through the Church's ministry, as Saint Augustine plainly declares in these words: *Whosoever he be that believes not man's sins to be remitted in God's Church, and therefore despises the bountifulness of God in so mighty a work, if he continues in that obstinate mind until his life's <margin>Remission of sins in the Church.</margin> end, he is guilty of sin against the Holy Ghost, in which Holy Ghost Christ remits sins.* (Enchiridion, 83; Letter 50 at the end).

32. *Son of man.*] The Jews in their words sinned against the Son of Man when they criticized those things which he did as a man—namely, calling him a glutton, a heavy wine-drinker, a friend of the tax collectors, and taking offense because he kept company with sinners, broke the Sabbath, and such things. This sin might more easily be forgiven them because they judged him as they would have judged any other man. But they sinned...

and blasphemed against the Holy Ghost (called here the "finger of God" <note>original: "digitus Dei"</note> by which he performed miracles) when out of malice they attributed the evident works of God in casting out devils to the devil himself. This sin shall not be forgiven, because it shall only be forgiven with great difficulty—as we see by the punishment <note>Refers to the "plague" or spiritual blindness mentioned by the author.</note> of their descendants to this day.

<margin>Purgatory.</margin>
31. *Nor in the World to come.*] Saint Augustine and other Holy Doctors <note>Highly influential early Christian theologians.</note> conclude from this that some sins may be forgiven in the next life, and consequently prove the existence of Purgatory by this passage. See *The City of God, Book 21, Chapter 13* <note>original: "De Civit. Dei li. 21 c. 13"</note> and *Saint Gregory, Dialogues, Book 4, Chapter 39* <note>original: "D. Gregor, Dial. li. 4 c. 39"</note>.

36. *Idle Word.*] If we must give an account before God in judgment for every idle word, and yet we are not eternally damned for every such word, then there must necessarily be some temporary punishment in the next life.

<margin>All Heresies claim Scripture.</margin>
48. *Who is my mother.*] Dutiful affection toward our parents and relatives is not being criticized here, but rather the disordered love of them that hinders our service and duty toward God. Based on this passage, some ancient heretics denied that Christ had a mother. See *Augustine, On Faith and the Creed, Chapter 4* <note>original: "Aug. li. de Fid. & Symb. c. 4"</note>. Yet there was never any heresy so absurd that it did not try to claim Scripture as its authority.

## C H A P T E R XIII.

*Speaking in parables (as the Scripture foretold of him, and as was appropriate for the stubborn Jews), he shows by the Parable of the Sower that in the labors of his Church, three parts out of four perish through the fault of the listeners. 24. And yet, by the parable of the good seed and the weeds <note>original: "cockle," a type of weed that looks like wheat.</note> (as also the Net), he shows that his servants must not, for all that, ever create any Schism or Separation while the world lasts. 31. And by the parables of the little mustard seed and the leaven, he shows that despite the three parts perishing and the over-sowing of weeds, that fourth part of good seed shall spread over all the world. 44. And withal, what a treasure and pearl it is. 53. After all this, his own country still will not honor him.*

## ANNOTATIONS
### CHAPTER XIII.

<margin>The difference in merits and rewards.</margin>
8. *One a hundred.*] This difference of fruit is the difference of <term>merits<note>Merit refers to the spiritual value of good works performed through grace.</note></term> in this life, and 
rewards for them in the next life, according to the diversity of lifestyles or other differences 
of state; for instance, the hundredfold reward corresponds to professed virgins, the sixtyfold to 
religious widows, and the thirtyfold to those who are married. <note>original: "Aug. li. de S. Virginit. c. 44 & seq." — Augustine, *Book on Holy Virginity*, chapter 44 and following.</note> This truth the old heretic Jovinian 
denied (as our opponents do today), claiming that there is no difference in merits or rewards. 
<note>Citing: Jerome, *Against Jovinian*, book 2; Ambrose, *Epistle 82*; Augustine, *On Heresies*, 82.</note>

11. *To you is given.*] To the Apostles and such as have the guiding and teaching of others, 
a deeper knowledge of God’s word and mysteries is given than to the common people. This is also 
true for Christians generally, regarding that which was not given to the stubborn Jews.

15. *They have shut.*] In saying that they shut their own eyes—which St. Paul also repeats in 
*Acts 28*—he teaches us the true understanding of all other passages where it might seem by the 
<margin>God is not the author of evil.</margin>
<margin>Irenaeus, cited in Eusebius, book 5, chapter 19. Calvin, *Institutes*, book 2, chapter 4.</margin>
bare words that God is the actual author and worker of this <term>induration<note>A theological term meaning "hardening of the heart."</note></term>, and blindness, and of other 
sins. This was an old condemned blasphemy, and is now the heresy of Calvin. Whereas 
our Savior here teaches us that they shut their own eyes and are the cause of their own sin 
and damnation; God does not do it, but permits it, and allows them to fall further because of 
their former sins, as St. Paul declares regarding the rejected Gentiles in *Romans 1*.

25. *Oversowed.*] First, the truth was planted by Christ and his Apostles, and falsehood came 
afterward, being oversowed by the enemy, the Devil, and not by Christ, who is not the

author

author of evil. <margin>Tertullian, *On the Prescription of Heretics* <note>An early Christian treatise arguing against the innovations of heretics.</note></margin>

<margin>Good and evil in the Church.</margin>
29. *Lest you pluck up also.*] The good must tolerate the evil when the evil is so strong that it cannot be corrected without danger and disturbance to the whole Church; in such cases, the matter should be committed to God’s judgment on the last day. Otherwise, where evil men (be they <term>Heretics<note>Those holding beliefs contrary to established Church doctrine.</note></term> or other wrongdoers) may be punished or suppressed without disturbing or endangering the good, they may and ought to be disciplined or executed by public authority, whether Spiritual or temporal.

30. *Suffer both to grow.*] The good and bad (as we see here) are mingled together in the Church. This fact argues against certain heretics and schismatics who separated themselves in ancient times from the rest of the world under the pretense that they alone were pure and all others—both priests and people—were sinners. It also argues against some modern heretics who claim that evil men are not truly part of or inside the Church.

32. *The least of all seeds.*] The Church of Christ had a small beginning, but afterward became the most glorious and well-known commonwealth on earth, with the greatest powers and the wisest people of the world joining it.

55. *Carpenter’s son.*] Because of this, Julian the Apostate and his flatterer Libanius mocked our Savior. As Julian was going to war against the Persians, he said to the Christians: "What is the Carpenter’s son doing now?" He threatened that after his return, the Carpenter’s son would not be able to save them from his fury. To this, a godly man answered by the Spirit of Prophecy: *“He whom Julian calls the Carpenter’s son is currently making a wooden coffin for him for his death.”* And indeed, not long after, news arrived that Julian had died miserably in that battle. <margin>Sozomen, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 6, Chapter 2; Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 3, Chapter 18.</margin> Heretics use a very similar mockery when they call the body of Christ in the <term>Blessed Sacrament<note>The Eucharist or Holy Communion.</note></term> "baker’s bread." To the physical senses it seems to be so, just as Christ seemed to be Joseph’s biological son, but faith tells us the contrary in both cases.

# ANNOTATIONS
## CHAPTER 14.

3. *Because of Herodias.*) It is common for Princes to put those to death who freely tell them of their faults; women, whom they desire <note>original: "fanſie"</note>, especially incite them to such mischief.

<margin>Sacrilege against holy Relics.</margin>
<margin>Jerome in the Funeral Oration <note>original: "Epitaph."</note> of Paula, chapter 6.</margin>
<margin>Theodoret, book 3, chapter 6. Rufinus, book 2, chapters 28, 27.</margin>
12. *Buried it.*) An example of duty toward the dead bodies of the faithful. Here one may see the difference between Catholic Christian men and all infidels, whether they be Pagans, Apostates, or heretics. For whereas the Christians had laid the body of this blessed Prophet and Martyr in Samaria with the Relics of Elijah <note>original: "Elias"</note> and Obadiah <note>original: "Abdias"</note>, by virtue of which wonderful miracles were performed in that place: in the time of Julian the Apostate, when men might do all mischief freely against the Christian religion, the Pagans opened the tomb of Saint John the Baptist, burnt his bones, and scattered the ashes about the fields. But certain religious Monks coming there on a pilgrimage at the same time, risked their lives and saved as much of the holy Relics as they could, and brought them to their Abbot Philip, a man of God. He, considering them too great a treasure for himself and his followers to keep for their private devotion, sent them to Athanasius the Bishop of Alexandria, and he with all reverence laid them in such a place (as if by the Spirit of Prophecy) where afterward, because of them, a beautiful chapel was built. Note here that the Heretics of our time <note>A reference to the Protestant Reformation's rejection of relics.</note> do as those Pagans did to the bodies and Relics of all blessed Saints that they can destroy; and Catholics, on the contrary, have the religious devotion of those old Christians, as appears by the honor done now to his head at Amiens in France.

<margin>Hermits <note>original: "Eremites"</note>.</margin>
<margin>Jerome, volume 2, in the Life of Paul the Hermit. Sozomen, book 1, chapters 12, 13.</margin>
13. *Retired.*) Christ greatly valued John, and withdrew himself aside to give an example of moderate mourning for the departed, and to show the horror of that terrible <note>original: "execrable"</note> murder. Similarly, in the Early <note>original: "Primitiue"</note> Church many good men, seeing the miserable state of the world in the time of persecution and the sins that abounded, took the opportunity to leave those turmoils and give themselves to contemplation; for that purpose, they retired into the deserts of Egypt and elsewhere to do penance for their own sins and the sins of the world. From this, in part, arose that infinite number of Monks and Hermits, of whom the Church fathers and ecclesiastical histories make mention.

19. *The Disciples to the multitudes.*) A symbol <note>original: "figure"</note> of the ministry of the Apostles, who, just as they here had the distribution and ordering of these miraculous loaves, so they were also to bestow and dispense all the food of our souls by administering the Word and Sacraments; nor may lay people claim <note>original: "chalenge"</note> this same right.

<margin>10. 20.</margin>
<margin>Epiphanius in *The Well-Anchored Man* <note>original: "Anchorato"</note>.</margin>
26. *Walking.*) When not only Christ, but by his power Peter also walks upon the waters, it is evident that he can control <note>original: "diipoſe"</note> his own body beyond nature and contrary to its natural conditions, such as going through a door, or being within the space <note>original: "compasſe"</note> of a little bread <note>This argument was used by Catholic theologians to defend the doctrine of the Real Presence in the Eucharist.</note>.

<margin>Peter’s Primacy.</margin>
<margin>Bernard, book 2 on Consideration <note>original: "de conſid."</note>, chapter 8.</margin>
29. *Walked.*) Peter (says Saint Bernard) walking upon the waters as Christ did, declared himself the only Vicar of Christ, who should be ruler not over one people, but over all. For "many waters" are "many peoples" <note>A reference to Revelation 17:15</note>. See the passage, how he derives from Peter the same authority and jurisdiction for his successor, the Bishop of Rome.

## ANNOTATIONS
### CHAPTER XV.

<margin>1 Corinthians 14.</margin>
8. *With their lips.*] This is to be understood properly of such as always have God in their mouth, the word of our Lord, the Scriptures, and the Gospel, but in their heart and all their life are indeed godless. It may be applied also to those who say their prayers without attention or lifting up of the mind to God, whether they understand the prayers or not. For many a poor Christian man who does not understand the words he speaks has his heart nearer heaven, more fervor and devotion, more personal edification, more profit in spirit (as the Apostle speaks), and fewer distractions, than not only all Heretics <note>The author uses "Heretics" to refer to Protestant reformers who criticized the use of Latin in prayer.</note> who have no true feeling for such things, but even many learned Catholics. Therefore, this is not to be understood as a condemnation of praying in unknown tongues <note>Referencing the use of Latin in the liturgy.</note>, as Heretics sometimes explain it—which is far removed from the context of this passage and Christ’s intention, as he was speaking of the hypocritical Jews.

<margin>
2 Thessalonians 2:15.
1 Corinthians 11.
* Acts 15.
a Augustine, Sermon on the Seasons, 251. See 1 Corinthians 16:2.
b Epiphanius, Against Heresies, 75.
c Jerome, Letter 54 to Marcella against Montanus.
* Luke 2:37.
Tobit 12.
Judith ch. 8.
Esther 4.
Luke 10:16.
* Matthew 18:17.
</margin>
<margin>The difference between Jewish traditions here rebuked, and the Church's traditions.</margin>
9. *Commandments of men.*] Only those things are called traditions, doctrines, or commandments of men which are either contrary to God's laws—such as this practice of defrauding parents under the pretense of religion—or which are at least frivolous, useless, and irrelevant to piety or true worship, such as that other practice of washing hands and vessels so often without regard for inward purity of heart and mind. Let no man therefore be deceived by the Protestants' perverse application of this passage against the holy laws, canons, and precepts of the Church and our spiritual Governors, concerning fasts, festivals, and other rules of discipline and proper order in life and in the service of God. For such things are not contrary but consistent with God's word and all piety; and our Lord is truly honored, worshipped, and served both by the making and the observing of them. * Saint Paul gave commandments both by his epistles and by word of mouth, even in matters where Christ had prescribed nothing at all, and he charges the faithful to observe them. * The Apostles and Priests at Jerusalem made laws, and the Christians were bound to obey them. *a* The keeping of Sunday instead of the Sabbath is the tradition of the Apostles, and dare the Heretics deny that its proper observation is an acceptable worship of God? *b* They prescribed the Feasts of Easter, and <term>Whitsuntide<note>The traditional English name for Pentecost, celebrating the descent of the Holy Spirit.</note></term> and other Solemnities of Christ and his Saints, which the Protestants themselves observe. *c* They appointed <term>Lent<note>The forty-day period of fasting before Easter.</note></term> and <term>Ember fasts<note>Traditional quarterly periods of fasting and prayer in the liturgical calendar.</note></term> and others, as well to discipline the <term>concupiscence<note>Strong worldly desires or lusts.</note></term> of man as to serve and please God thereby, as is plain in the fasting of * Anna, Tobit, Judith, and Esther, who served and pleased God in that way. Therefore, neither these nor other such Apostolic Ordinances, nor any precepts of the holy Church or of our lawful Pastors, are implied in these Pharisaical traditions rebuked here. They are not to be counted or called the doctrines and commandments of men, because they are not made by mere human power, but by Christ's Warrant and authority, and by those whom he has placed to rule his Church, of whom he says, * *He that hears you, hears me: he that despises you, despises me.* They are made by the Holy Ghost, joining with our Pastors in the governance of the faithful; they are made by our Mother the Church, whom whosoever does not obey, * *we are warned to treat as a Heathen.* But on the other side, all laws, doctrines, service, and injunctions of Heretics, however much they pretend to be consistent with the Scriptures, are truly "commandments of men": because both the things they prescribe are impious, and the Authors have neither a mission nor a commission from God.

<margin>Difference of foods.</margin>
11. *Not that which enters.*] Catholics do not abstain from certain foods because they believe any food is "unclean" either by its creation or by Jewish ritual observation: but they abstain for the discipline of their desires. <term>Augustine, Book on the Morals of the Catholic Church, ch. 33.<note>original: "Aug. li. de mor. Ec. Cath. c. 33."</note></term>

<margin>
Genesis 3.
</margin>
<margin>Catholic abstinence.</margin>
18. *Defile a man*] It is sin alone which properly defiles a man, and foods in themselves or of their own nature do not defile; however, they defile to the extent that they accidentally cause a man to sin—for instance, the disobedience of God's commandment or of our Superiors who forbid certain foods for specific times and reasons is a sin. Just as the apple which our first parents ate, though of itself it did not defile them, yet being eaten against the command, it did defile them. So neither meat nor fish of itself defiles, but the breach of the Church's precept defiles.

### CHAPTER XVI.

->The obstinate Pharisees and Sadducees, as though his previously mentioned miracles were not sufficient to prove him to be Christ, demand to see a sign from heaven. 5 Whereupon, leaving them, he warns his disciples to beware of the "leaven" of their doctrine. 13 And Peter (the time now approaching for Jesus to go into Judea for his Passion) for confessing him to be Christ, he makes the Rock of his Church, giving him the fullness of Ecclesiastical power accordingly. 21 And after, he so rebukes him for discouraging his Cross and Passion, that he also affirms that similar suffering in everyone is necessary for salvation.<-

# ANNOTATIONS
## CHAPTER XVI.

<margin>ON PETER’S PRIMACY.</margin>
13. *Whom say men.*] Christ intending here to take order for the founding, government, and stability of his Church after his death, and to name the person to whom he meant to give the general charge thereof, would first by questions draw out (specifically from the one whom he intended to make the chief) the profession of that high and principal Article: That he was the Son of the living God. Which being the ground of the Church's faith, was a necessary quality and condition in him that was to be made Head of the same Church, and the perpetual keeper of the said faith and all other points depending upon it.

14. *But they said.*] When Christ asked the people's opinion of him, the Apostles all indifferently made answer: but when he demanded what they themselves thought of him, then behold, Peter, the mouth and head of the whole fellowship, answered for all. <note>John Chrysostom, Homily 55 on Matthew.</note>

<margin>Hilary, Canon 6 on Matthew & Book 6 on the Trinity. Chrysostom, Homily 55 on Matthew. Basil, Book 2 against Eunomius.</margin>
17. *Blessed art thou.*] Though some others (as Nathanael in John 1:49) seem to have before believed and professed the same thing for which Peter is here counted blessed, yet it may plainly be gathered by this place—and so Saint Hilary and others think—that none before this did further speak of him than that he was the son of God by adoption as other Saints are, though more excellent than others. For it was by fitness <note>original: "congruitie"</note> and Christ’s special appointment, that he upon whom he intended to found his new Church, and whose faith he would make infallible, should have the preeminence of this first profession of Christ’s natural divinity—or, that he was by nature the very Son of God. This is a thing so far above the capacity of nature, reason, flesh and blood, and so contrary to Peter’s sense and sight of Christ’s humanity, flesh, and infirmities, that for the belief and public profession of it he is counted blessed, as Abraham was for his faith. He also receives great promises for himself and his successors <note>original: "posteritie"</note>, as the said Patriarch had for himself and his seed. According as Saint Basil says: *Because he excelled in faith, he received the building of the Church committed to him.*

18. *And I say to thee.*] Our Lord rewards Peter for his confession, giving him a great reward, in that upon him he built his Church. <note>Theophylactus on this passage.</note>

<header>THE GOSPEL CHAPTER 16.</header>

<margin>PETER.</margin>
<margin>Cyril, Book 2, Chapter 12, Commentary on John.</margin>
<margin>Hilary, on this passage.</margin>
<margin>Basil, Book on Penance.</margin>
<margin>Matthew 5:14.</margin>
<margin>Luke 22:19.</margin>

### 18. *Thou art Peter.*
Christ (in John 1:42) foretold and appointed that this man, then named Simon, should afterward be called *Cephas*, or *Petrus* <note>original: "Petrus," the Latin name for Peter, derived from the word for rock</note>, that is to say, a *Rock*. He did not state the reason then, but now expresses it: namely (as St. Cyril writes), because upon him, as upon a firm rock, his Church should be built. St. Hilary, agreeing with this, says, *O happy foundation of the Church in the imposing of thy new name, etc.* And yet Christ here does not so much call him by the name Peter or Rock, as he affirms him to be a rock: signifying by that metaphor both that he was designed for the foundation and groundwork of his house, which is the Church; and also that he should be of invincible force, firmness, durability, and stability, to sustain all the winds, waves, and storms that might fall or beat against it. The adversaries <note>A term used by the authors of this 16th-century Catholic commentary to refer to Protestant Reformers</note> object to this, saying that Christ alone is the Rock or foundation. In doing so, they wrangle against the very express Scriptures and Christ's own words, which give both the name and the thing to this Apostle. The simple may learn from St. Basil's words how the case stands. "Though," he says, "Peter be a rock, yet he is not a rock as Christ is. For Christ is the true unmovable rock of himself; Peter is unmovable by Christ the rock." For Jesus communicates and imparts his honors, not emptying himself of them, but holding them to himself while bestowing them also upon others. He is the *light*, and yet, *You are the light* (Matthew 5:14); he is *the Priest*, and yet he makes *Priests* (Luke 22:19); he is the *rock*, and he made a *rock*.

---

<margin>Thou art Cephas, and upon this Cephas. <note>original: "Πέτρος" (Petros) rock. "πέτρα" (petra) rock.</note></margin>
<margin>Augustine, Book 1 of Retractions, chapter 21. On Psalm 69. On the words of the Lord according to John, sermon 49. Sermons 15, 16, 26, 29 on the Saints, chapter 30.</margin>

### 18. *And upon this rock.*
Upon that which he said Peter was, will he build his Church: and therefore, by the most evident logical sequence, he founds his Church upon Peter. The adversaries who argue against this do so against their own conscience and knowledge, especially since they know and confess that in Christ's words spoken in the Syriac tongue <note>Aramaic, the language Jesus actually spoke</note>, there was no difference at all between *Petrus* and *Petra*. Furthermore, the Greek words, though they have different endings, signify the same thing: a rock or stone, as the reformers themselves translate it in John 1:42. So, those who claim to follow the Hebrew or Syriac and the Greek, and to translate directly from them into Latin or English, should (if they had dealt sincerely) have translated Christ’s words as: *Thou art a rock, and upon this rock*; or, *Thou art Peter, and upon this Peter will I build my Church*. For by their own admission, Christ spoke without any difference in the words.

This expressly stops all their empty excuses—such as the claim that *Petrus* (the first word) refers to the Apostle, while *petra* (the second word) refers either to Christ only or to Peter’s faith only. Neither the original languages nor the sequence of the words—*upon this*—allow for any other reference in the world except to that which was spoken in the same sentence immediately before. Neither the following words, which are addressed directly to Peter’s person, nor Christ’s intention, admit their view. His intention was not to make himself or promise himself to be the head or foundation of the Church; his Father gave him that dignity, and he did not take that honor for himself, nor send himself, nor take the keys of heaven from himself, but received all from his Father. He had his commission from the very hour of his Incarnation.

And though St. Augustine sometimes refers the word *Rock* (*Petra*) to Christ in this sentence (which he no doubt did because the endings in Latin are different, and because he did not examine the nature of the original words Christ spoke, nor the Greek; therefore the adversaries, who usually flee to the original languages, should not cite him in this case), yet he never denies that Peter also is the Rock and head of the Church. He states that he himself explained it as referring to Peter in many places, and also cites St. Ambrose for the same in the hymn which the Church sings. We also cite the holy Council of Chalcedon (Act 3, page 118), Tertullian, Origen, St. Cyprian, St. Hilary, St. Ambrose, St. Jerome, St. Epiphanius, St. Chrysostom, St. Cyril, St. Leo, St. Gregory, and others. Every one of them says expressly that the Church was founded and built upon *this* Peter. For though they sometimes say the Church is built on Peter’s faith, they do not mean faith separated from the man, or in any other man, but upon faith as it existed in him who here confessed that faith.

---

<margin>Theodoret, Book 5 on Heretical Fables, chapter on Penance. Jerome, epistle 7, volume 2. Psalm against the part of Donatus, volume 7. Leo, epistle 89.</margin>

### 18. *Rock.*
The adversaries also hear the Church Fathers sometimes say that Peter received these promises and prerogatives as representing the person of all the Apostles or of the whole Church. From this, they absurdly deny that he himself, in his own person, had these prerogatives. It is as if Peter were merely the spokesperson <note>original: "proctor"</note> for the Church or the Apostles, confessing the faith and receiving these things in other men's names. In reality, the holy Doctors mean only that these prerogatives were not given to him for his own private use, but for the good of the whole Church, to be shared with every office according to the measure of their callings. Furthermore, they mean that these great privileges given to Peter should not decay or die with his person, but be perpetual in the Church through his successors.

Therefore, St. Jerome, writing to Pope Damasus, takes this "Rock" to be not only Peter’s person, but his successors and his Chair <note>The "Apostolic Chair," referring to the office and authority of the Pope in Rome</note>. *I,* he says, *following no chief or principal but Christ, join myself to the communion of Peter’s chair; upon that rock I know the Church was built.* And of that same Apostolic Chair, St. Augustine says, *That same is the Rock which the proud gates of Hell do not overcome.* And St. Leo writes: *Our Lord willed that the sacrament or mystery of this gift should pertain to the office of all the Apostles in such a way that he placed it principally in blessed St. Peter, the chief of all the Apostles; so that from him, as from a certain head, he might pour out his gifts as if through the whole body, so that one might understand himself to be an outsider to the divine mystery if he should presume to revolt from the solidity or steadfastness of Peter.*

<summary>This page provides a detailed Catholic defense of the Primacy of Peter, arguing that Jesus's words in Matthew 16:18 established Peter as the personal and foundational "Rock" of the Church, a role that continues through his successors in the Apostolic Chair.</summary>
<keywords>Apostle Peter, Primacy of Peter, Rock of the Church, Papal Succession, Apostolic Chair, Church Fathers, Catholic-Protestant debate, Matthew 16:18, Cephas, Petros vs Petra</keywords>

It bridges the discussion from Peter as the "Rock" (on the previous page) to the specific administrative and spiritual powers the Catholic Church claims were inherited from him.</meta>

<page-num>47</page-num>
-># CHAPTER 16. ACCORDING TO ST. MATTHEW.<-

18. **Build my Church.**] The Church, or the house of Christ, was only promised here to be built upon him <note>The "him" refers to Peter, as the foundation rock mentioned in the previous verse.</note> (which was fulfilled in John 21:15-17). The foundation stone and other pillars or materials were still being prepared, and Christ himself is not only the supreme foundation but also the founder of the Church. This is a more excellent quality than what was in Peter, which is why he calls it *my Church*: meaning specifically the Church of the New Testament. This Church was not perfectly formed, finished, and distinguished from the Synagogue until Pentecost <note>original: "Whitsunday," the traditional English name for the feast of Pentecost</note>, even though Christ gave Peter and the rest of the Apostles their commissions before his Ascension.

<margin>St. Augustine, *Psalm against the Donatists*.
*On the Profit of Believing*, chapter 17.</margin>
18. **Gates of hell.**] Because the Church is compared to a house or a city, the opposing powers are also likened to a contrary house or town. The "gates" of that town—that is to say, its strength or attacks—shall never prevail against the city of Christ. By this promise, we are assured that no heresies or other wicked attempts can prevail against the Church built upon Peter, which the Church Fathers call "Peter’s See" <term>See: From the Latin 'sedes' (seat), referring to the center of authority or the office of a bishop</term> and the Roman Church. *Count* (says St. Augustine) *the priests from the very See of Peter, and in that order of fathers consider who has succeeded whom: that same is the rock which the proud gates of Hell do not overcome.* And in another place, he says *it is the Church which has obtained the height of authority, while heretics bark around it in vain.*

<margin>Cyprian, *Epistle 73*.
Gregory, Book 4, Epistle 32, indiction 13.</margin>
19. **To thee.**] In saying, *to thee will I give*, it is plain that just as he gave the keys to Peter, so he built the Church upon him. So says St. Cyprian: *To Peter first of all, upon whom our Lord built the Church, and from whom he instituted and showed the beginning of unity, did he give this power: that whatever he loosed on earth should be loosed in the heavens.* This reveals the empty legalism of our adversaries <note>A reference to Protestant Reformers who argued that the "Rock" was Peter's faith or confession, not his person.</note>, who say the Church was built only upon Peter's confession (which was common to him and the rest) and not upon his person specifically.

<margin>The dignities of the keys.
Revelation 1.
Isaiah 22:22.</margin>
19. **The keys.**] This refers to the authority or "Chair" of doctrine: the knowledge, judgment, and discretion to distinguish between true and false doctrine. It signifies the height of government: the power of making laws, calling Councils, having the principal voice in them, confirming them, making Church laws <term>Canons: Religious laws or decrees</term>, and overturning contrary ones. It also includes the power of ordaining, deposing, or suspending Bishops and Pastors, and finally the power to distribute the Church's goods, both spiritual and temporal. The Scripture expresses this preeminent power using the word *keys* in many places: namely, when speaking of Christ, *I have the keys of death and Hell, that is, the rule.* And again, *I will give the key of the house of David upon his shoulder.* Moreover, it signifies that men cannot enter heaven except through him, as the keys also signify authority to open and shut. As it is said in Revelation 3 of Christ: *he who has the key of David, he shuts and no man opens.* From these words, we gather that Peter's authority is marvelous, as he was given the keys—the power to open and shut heaven. Therefore, the name "keys" represents a supreme power called *fullness of power* <note>original: "plenitudo potestatis"</note> when compared to the power granted to other Apostles, Bishops, and Pastors. (*Bernard, Book 2, On Consideration, chapter 8*).

19. **Whatsoever thou shalt bind.**] All kinds of discipline and punishment of offenders—whether spiritual (which is directly meant here) or corporal, so far as it relates to spiritual duties—is included under the word "bind." This includes excommunications, bans <note>original: "Anathematismes"</note>, suspensions, removals from office, and other penalties or penances assigned either in the Sacrament of Confession or in the external Courts of the Church. These are for the punishment of crimes, and especially for heresy and rebellion against the Church and its chief pastors.

<margin>Isaiah 22.
Revelation 3.</margin>
19. **Loose.**] To "loose" means, as the offender's case requires, to release them from any of the previously mentioned bonds. it means restoring them to the Church's Sacraments, the community of the faithful, and their official duties. It also means pardoning all or part of the penances assigned, or whatever debts a person owes to God or the Church as satisfaction for their forgiven sins. This kind of releasing or loosing is called an *Indulgence*. Finally, this word "whatsoever" excludes nothing that can be punished or pardoned by Christ on earth, for he has committed his power to Peter. Thus, the validity of Peter’s sentence in binding or loosing anything shall, by Christ’s promise, be confirmed in heaven. (*Leo, Sermon on the Transfiguration; Hilary, Canon 16 on Matthew; Epiphanius in Anchorato*). If any secular ruler <note>original: "temporal power"</note> can show a warrant from Scripture for such sovereign power as is given here to Peter and his successors, let them try to claim they are the head of the whole universal Church.

<margin>Good works.
Free will.</margin>
27. **Works.**] He says not that he will give to every man according to his mercy (or their faith), but according to their works. (*Augustine, Sermon 11 on the words of the Apostle*). And again: *How should our Savior reward every one according to their works, if there were no free will?* (*Augustine, Book 2 against Felix the Manichaean*).

# ANNOTATIONS
## C H A P. XVII.

<margin>Christ can exhibit his body under what form he chooses.</margin>
2. *Transfigured.*] Mark in this Transfiguration many marvelous points. As, that he made not 
only his own body, which then was mortal, but also the bodies of Moses and Elijah—the one 
dead, the other yet to die—for the time as it were immortal: thereby to represent the state and glory 
of his body and his Saints in heaven. By which marvelous transfiguring of his body, you may the 
less marvel that he can exhibit his body under the form of bread and wine or otherwise 
as he chooses. <note>The author is drawing a parallel between the Transfiguration and the Catholic doctrine of the Real Presence in the Eucharist.</note>

<margin>Saints after their death deal with and for the living.</margin>
3. *Appeared Moses.*] By this, that Moses personally appeared and was present with Christ, it 
is plain that the Saints departed may in person be present at the affairs of the living. <note>original citation: *August. de cura pro mort. c. 15. 16.* Referring to St. Augustine's work "On the Care to be Had for the Dead," chapters 15 and 16.</note> For even as Angels elsewhere, so here the Saints also served our Savior: 
and therefore as Angels both in the old Testament and the new, were present often at the affairs 
of men, so may Saints.

<margin>2 Peter 1:18. Exodus 3:5.</margin>
<margin>Holy places.</margin>
<margin>Devotion and Pilgrimage to the same.</margin>
9. *Mount.*] This mount (commonly esteemed and named by the ancient fathers as Tabor) 
St. Peter calls the *holy Mount* because of this wonderful vision, just as in the old Testament where 
God appeared to *Moses* in the bush and elsewhere to others, he calls the place of such appa-
ritions, *holy ground*. Whereby it is evident that by such apparitions places are sanctified, and there-
upon grows a religion and devotion in the faithful toward such places. Specifically to this 
Mount Tabor (called *Itabirium* in St. Jerome's *Letter 17a*), there was great Pilgrimage in the Early 
Church, as unto those places which our Savior had sanctified with his presence and miracles, 
and

<header>THE GOSPEL CHAPTER XVIII.</header>

<margin>The holy land.</margin>
and therefore to the whole land of promise, for that cause called the holy land. <note>original: *See S. Hiero. in Epitap. Paulæ. & ep. 17. & 18 ad Marcellam.*—See Saint Jerome in the *Epitaph of Paula* and letters 17 and 18 to Marcella.</note>

<margin>Elias <note>The prophet Elijah</note>.</margin>
11. *Elias shall come.*] He distinguishes here plainly between Elias in person, who is yet to come before the judgment: and between Elias in name, to wit, John the Baptist, who is come already <margin>Luke 1:17. Malachi 4:5.</margin> in the spirit and virtue of Elias. So that it is not John the Baptist only nor principally of whom Malachi prophesies (as our adversaries <note>A term often used in this period by Catholic translators to refer to Protestant reformers.</note> say) but Elias also himself in person.

<margin>True miracles only in the Catholic Church.</margin>
19. *Why could not we.*] No marvel if the Exorcists of the Catholic Church who have power to cast out devils, yet do it not always when they will, and many times with much ado: whereas the Apostles having received this power *before over unclean spirits, yet here cannot cast them out.* <margin>Matthew 10.</margin> But as for heretics, they can never do it, nor any other true miracle, to confirm their false faith.

20. *Faith as mustard seed.*] This is the Catholic faith, by which only all miracles are wrought: yet not by everyone that has the Catholic faith, but by such as have a great and forcible faith and withal the gift of miracles. These are able as here we see by Christ’s warrant not only to do other wonderful miracles here signified by this one, but also this very same, that is, to move <margin>1 Corinthians 13.</margin> mountains indeed, as St. Paul also presupposes, and St. Jerome affirms, and Ecclesiastical <margin>Jerome in the Life of St. Hilarion. Nicephorus book 6, chapter 17.</margin> <margin>Gregory the Wonder-worker <note>original: *Gregorius Thaumaturgus*</note>.</margin> histories namely tell of Gregory of Neocaesarea, that he moved a mountain to make room for the foundation of a Church, called therefore and for other his wonderful miracles, the Wonder-worker. And yet faithless Heretics laugh at all such things and believe them not.

<margin>Prayer and Fasting.</margin>
21. *Prayer and fasting.*] The force of fasting and praying: whereby also we may see that the <margin>Gregory of Nyssa on the life of Gregory.</margin> holy Church in Exorcisms acts according to the Scriptures, when she uses beside the name of JESUS, many prayers and much fasting to drive out Devils, because these also are here required beside faith.

<margin>The privileges and exemptions of the Clergy.</margin>
26. *The Children free.*] Though Christ to avoid scandal, paid tribute, yet in deed he shows that both himself ought to be free from such payments (as being the king’s son, as well by his eternal birth of God the Father, as temporal of David) and also his Apostles, as being of his family, and in them their successors the whole Clergy, who are called in Scripture the lot and portion of our Lord. This exemption and privilege being grounded upon the very law of nature itself, and therefore practiced even among the Heathen (Genesis 47:22, 27) good Christian Princes have confirmed and ratified by their laws in the honor of Christ, whose ministers they are, and as it were the king’s sons, as St. Jerome declares plainly in these words, *We for his honor pay not tributes, and as the King’s sons, are free from such payments.* <note>Jerome’s commentary on this passage.</note>

<margin>Peter’s preeminence.</margin>
27. *Me and thee.*] A great mystery in that he paid not only for himself, but for Peter bearing <margin>Augustine, Questions on the New Testament, question 75, volume 4.</margin> the Person of the Church, and in whom as the chief, the rest were contained.

-> A N N O T A T I O N S <-
-> CHAPTER 18. <-

1. *Who is the greater.*] The occasion of this question and of their struggle for superiority—among the rest of their weaknesses which they had before the coming of the Holy Ghost—was (as certain holy Doctors write) out of a sense of rivalry toward Peter, whom only they saw preferred before the rest in the payment of the tribute, by these words of our Savior, *Give it to them for me <margin>Chapter 17, v. 27</margin> and you.* <note>John Chrysostom, Homily 59; Jerome on Matthew, upon this place.</note>

7. *Scandals.*] The simple [faithful] are most harmed by taking offense <note>original: "scandal"</note> at the evil lives of their preachers, priests, and elders: and great damnation comes to the guides of the people whether they be secular or spiritual, but especially to the spiritual, if by their evil example and scandalous life the people are led into sin.

8. *Hand, foot, eye.*] By these parts of the body, so necessary and profitable for a man, it is signified that whatsoever is nearest and dearest to us—wife, children, friends, riches—all are to be disregarded and forsaken in order to save our soul.

10. *Their Angels.*] A great dignity and a marvelous benefit that every one has from his

18. *You shall bind.*] As before he gave this power of binding and loosing over the whole, first of all and principally to Peter, upon whom he built his Church: so here not only to Peter, and in him to his successors, but also to the other Apostles, and in them to their successors, every one in their charge.

18. *Shall loose.*] Our Lord gives no less right and authority to the Church to loose than to <margin>Book 1, *On Penance*, Chapter 2.</margin> bind, but not to loose, as St. Ambrose writes against the Novatians <note>A 3rd-century schismatic group that argued certain sins could not be forgiven by the Church.</note>, who confessed that the Priests had power to bind, but not to loose.

20. *In the midst of them.*] Not all assemblies may claim the presence of Christ, but only Catholic <margin>Catholic Assemblies.</margin> ones, such as are gathered together in the unity of the Church; and therefore no secret meetings <note>original: "conventicles"</note> of Heretics, directly gathering against the Church, are warranted by this passage. <margin>St. Cyprian, *On the Unity of the Church*, numbers 7, 8.</margin>

22. *Seventy times seven.*] There must be no end of forgiving those who are penitent, either in the Sacrament by absolution <note>The formal act of a priest pronouncing forgiveness of sins.</note>, or one man to another for their offenses.

Iouin." refers to Saint Jerome’s first book against Jovinianus.</note></margin> :: wife, or children, or lands for my name's sake: shall receive a hundredfold, and shall possess life everlasting. 30 † And * many shall be first, that are last: and last, that are first.

### A N N O T A T I O N S
#### C H A P T E R 19.

<margin>Marriage after divorce unlawful.</margin>
6. *Not man separate.*] This inseparability between husband and wife arises from the fact that Wedlock is a Sacrament. <note>original: "Aug. li. 2. de pec. origine c. 34. to. 7. De nupt. & concupis. li. 1. c. 10." refers to Saint Augustine’s works *On the Origin of Sin* and *On Marriage and Desire*.</note>

<margin>In the Funeral Oration of Fabiola.</margin>
9. *But for fornication.*) For adultery one may dismiss <note>divorce</note> another (as seen in Matthew 5). But neither party can marry again for any cause during their lifetime. <note>original: "Aug. li. 11. de adult. coniug. c. 21. 22. 24." refers to Augustine’s *On Adulterous Marriages*.</note> For this unlawful act of marrying again, Fabiola—that noble matron of Rome—did public penance even though she was the innocent party, as Saint Jerome writes in high praise of her. And in Saint Paul’s writings (Romans 7), it is plain that she who is with another man while her husband still lives shall be called an adulteress; this is contrary to the doctrine of our adversaries <note>A term used here for Protestant reformers</note>.

<margin>Origen’s 7th treatise on Matthew.</margin>
11. *Not all take.*) Whoever does not have this gift <note>the gift of celibacy</note> given to them, it is either because they do not wish to have it, or because they do not fulfill what they wish for. Those who have this gift or attain to this word have it from God and their own free will. <note>original: "Aug. li. de grat. & lib. arbit. c. 4." refers to Augustine’s *On Grace and Free Will*.</note> Thus it is evident no man is excluded from this gift, but (as Origen says here) it is given to all that ask for it; contrary to our adversaries who say it is impossible, and who wickedly say they do not have the gift as an excuse for breaking their vows.

<margin>Vow of chastity.</margin>
12. *Gelded themselves.*) They "geld themselves" <note>make themselves eunuchs</note> for the kingdom of heaven who vow chastity. <note>original: "Aug. de virginitate c. 24." refers to Augustine’s *On Virginity*.</note> This proves those kinds of vows to be both lawful and more meritorious, and a more certain way to obtain life everlasting than the state of marriage, contrary to our adversaries in all respects.

<margin>Augustine, Sermon 6 on the seasons.</margin>
<margin>Counsels vs. Precepts.</margin>
14. *He that can.*) It is not said of the Precepts <note>Commands necessary for all</note>, "keep them who can," for they must be kept under pain of damnation. But of Counsels only (such as virginity, abstaining from meat and wine, and giving all one's goods to the poor) it is said: "He that can attain to it, let him do it." This is a counsel only, not a commandment. This is contrary to our adversaries who say there are no Counsels, only precepts.

<margin>Bishops' and Religious men’s blessing.</margin>
13. *Impose.*) They knew the value of Christ’s blessing, and therefore brought their children to him; just as good Christian people have at all times brought their children to Bishops to receive their blessing. See the Annotation for Chapter 10, verse 12. Regarding the blessing of Religious men <note>monks or friars</note>, see Rufinus, Saint Jerome, and Theodoret in their histories of the holy Fathers.

<margin>The Religious state of perfection.</margin>
21. *If thou wilt be perfect.*] Lo, he makes a plain difference between keeping the commandments (which is necessary for everyone) and being "perfect," which he counsels only to those who choose it. This is the state of great perfection which Religious men <note>monastics</note> profess, according to Christ’s counsel here, leaving all things and following him.

21. *Follow me.*] To follow Christ in this way is to be without a wife and the care of children, to lack private property, and to live in common. This has a great reward in heaven above other states of life. Saint Augustine says that the Apostles followed this, as did he himself, and that he exhorted others to do it as much as he could.

26. *All things possible.*] This image of the Camel through a needle's eye is possible to God, even though he has not done it nor likely will. This argues against the "blasphemous infidelity" of our adversaries who say God can do no more than he has already done or will do. We see also that God can bring a camel through a needle’s eye, and therefore could bring his body through a closed door, out of a shut tomb, or out of his mother while remaining a virgin—generally doing with his body as he pleases, above and contrary to nature.

<margin>Vow of poverty in respect of reward.</margin>
27. *Left all.*) This perfection of leaving all things was a vow the Apostles took. <note>original: "Aug. li. 17. de Civ. Dei c. 4." refers to *The City of God*.</note>
27. *What shall we have.*) They leave all things in hope of a reward, and Christ allows this motivation in his answer.

<margin>Augustine on Psalm 121.</margin>
-28. *You also shall sit.*) Note that not only Christ—who is the primary and proper judge of the living and the dead—but with him the Apostles and all perfect Saints shall judge. Yet this does nothing to take away from his authority, by whom and under whom they hold this and all other dignities in this life and the next.

<summary>This page concludes Jesus' teachings on the rewards for those who leave everything to follow him, followed by extensive Catholic commentary defending clerical celibacy, monastic poverty, and the distinction between universal commandments and voluntary "counsels of perfection."</summary>

<margin>Holy Week.</margin> Nations. <gloss>Augustine, *Sermons on the Words of the Lord*, sermon 59.</gloss> Briefly, this calling at various hours signifies the calling of the Jews from time to time in the first ages of the world, and of the Gentiles in the latter age of it. It also signifies that God calls countries to the faith, some sooner, some later; and particular men to be his servants, some younger, some older, at various ages.

<margin>Diversity of glory in heaven.</margin> <margin>1 Corinthians 15.</margin> 9. *Penny.*] The penny <note>The 'penny' refers to the Roman denarius, a day's wage mentioned in the parable of the laborers in the vineyard.</note> promised to all was life everlasting, WHICH is common to all who shall be saved: but in that same life there are degrees of glory, just as there are differences * between star and star in the heavens <note>original: "element"</note>. <gloss>Augustine, *On Virginity*, chapter 26.</gloss>

16. *Few elect.*] Those are the "elect" who did not despise the one calling them, but followed and believed him; for men do not believe except by their own free will. <gloss>Augustine, *To Simplician*, book 1, question 2.</gloss>

<margin>Difference of merits and reward.</margin> <margin>Matthew 16:27; Romans 2:6; Matthew 25:34.</margin> 23. *To whom it is prepared.*] The kingdom of heaven is prepared for those who are worthy of it and deserve it by their good deeds, as it is very often stated in holy Scripture: *That God will repay every man according to his works,* and, *Come, you blessed, possess the kingdom prepared for you.* Why? *Because I was hungry, and you gave me meat; thirsty, and you gave me drink,* etc. Therefore Christ says here, <margin>Chrysostom, *Homily 66 on Matthew*.</margin> *It is not mine to give,* because he is just and will not give it to every man without respect for their merits <note>original: "deserts"</note>; indeed, not even alike to everyone, but diversely according to greater or lesser merits. As St. Chrysostom here makes plain, when our Savior tells them that although they suffer martyrdom for his sake, yet it is not his to give them the two chief places. <gloss>See St. Jerome upon this place, and *Against Jovinianus*, book 2, chapter 15.</gloss> This is also a lesson for those who have the duty of bestowing Church offices <note>original: "Ecclesiastical benefices"</note>, that they should have no worldly <note>original: "carnal"</note> partiality for kindred, etc., but focus on the worthiness of the persons.

<margin>10. 13, 15.</margin> 28. *As the son of man.*] Christ himself, as he was the Son of Man, was their and our superior, and Lord and Master, despite his humility; and therefore it is pride and haughtiness which is forbidden, and not superiority or lordship, as some heretics <note>The text likely refers to radical reformers who used these verses to argue against all social and religious hierarchy.</note> would have it.

### ANNOTATIONS
#### CHAPTER 21.

2. *You shall find.*] Christ, by divine power, both knew where these animals were while being absent from them, and commanded them for his own use even though they belonged to another man. He also suddenly made the colt fit to be ridden, though it had never been broken before.

<margin><note>original: "Hiero. in Mat."</note> Jerome's Commentary on Matthew. <note>original: "Aug. li. 12 cōt. Faust. c. 42."</note> Augustine, Book 12 against Faustus, chapter 42.</margin>
7. *The ass and the colt.*] This ass under the yoke signifies the Jews under the Law and under God their Lord, acting as his old and ancient people. The young colt, now ridden for the first time by Christ, signifies the <term>Gentiles</term><note>Non-Jewish nations and peoples.</note>, who were wild until now and not broken, but are now called to the faith to receive our Savior’s yoke. Therefore, the last three Evangelists, writing specifically to the Gentiles, mention only the colt.

<margin>Procession on Palm Sunday with the Blessed Sacrament.</margin>
<margin>All devout services of that kind are extremely pleasing [to God].</margin>
8. *Garments in the way.*] These acts of honor shown to our Savior in such an extraordinary way were very acceptable. In memory of this, the holy Church makes a solemn Procession every year on this day—especially in our Country when it was Catholic—with the <term>Blessed Sacrament</term><note>The consecrated bread of the Eucharist, believed to be the actual body of Christ.</note> reverently carried, representing Christ upon the ass. This includes the strewing of rushes and flowers, the bearing of palms, setting up green branches, and hanging up the richest cloths, with the choir and choristers singing just as the children and people did then. All this is done in a beautiful ceremony to honor Christ and remember his triumph on this day. Similar service and duties performed for him in all other solemn Processions of the Blessed Sacrament, or otherwise, are undoubtedly no less pleasing to him.

<margin>HOSANNA.</margin>
9. *Hosanna.*] The holy Church always uses these very words of joyful cry and triumphant voice of greeting to our Savior in the <term>Preface of the Mass</term><note>The introductory prayer of the Eucharistic service.</note>. It serves as the voice of the Priest and all the people (who are then especially attentive and devout) immediately before the Consecration and Elevation, as if they are waiting for and rejoicing at his coming.

13. *House of prayer.*] Note here that he calls external sacrifice "prayer," quoting the Prophet <term>Isaiah</term><note>original: "Esay"</note>. For he is speaking of the Temple, which was built properly and principally for the purpose of sacrifice.

<margin>Prayers not understood by the person are still acceptable.</margin>
16. *Mouth of infants.*] The prayers of young children, proceeding from the instinct of God's spirit, are acceptable. Likewise, the voices of such children, or of other simple folk now in the Church, are marvelously pleasing to Christ, even if they themselves do not understand particularly every word they say. <note>This is a defense of the use of Latin in the liturgy, arguing that the devotion of the heart matters even if the language is not understood by the layperson.</note>

22. *Believing.*] Because of our own unworthiness, or because what we ask for is not always beneficial for us, we may well doubt whether we shall obtain it when we pray. But on God’s part, we must believe—that is, we must have no doubt or mistrust of either his power or his will, provided we are worthy and the request is appropriate. Therefore, Saint Mark writes: *Have the faith of God.*
<margin><note>original: "Marc. 11, 22."</note> Mark 11:22.</margin>

<margin>Heretics run without being sent.</margin>
23. *In what power?*] <term>Heretics</term><note>In this 16th-century context, this refers to Protestant reformers who the authors believe lack proper apostolic ordination or "mission."</note> presumptuously think they are like Christ in this matter because they are asked by what authority they come and who sent them. But only when they have answered this question as fully as Christ did here—by pointing to the testimony of John the Baptist for his authority—shall they be heard. Until then, they shall be regarded as those of whom God speaks through the Prophet: *They ran, and I did not send them.*
<margin><note>original: "Ier. 23."</note> Jeremiah 23:21.</margin>

28. *The first.*] The first son here represents the Gentile people, because "Gentility" existed before there was a peculiar and chosen people of the Jews. Therefore, the Jews are signified here as the second son.

He then turns and challenges them in return, because they imagined that Christ should be nothing more than a man; 46 and so he puts all the busy Sects to silence.*

2. *Marriage.*) Then did God the Father make this marriage, when by the mystery of the Incarnation he joined to his son our Lord, the holy Church for his spouse. <note>original: "Greg. hom. 38"</note> *Gregory, Homily 38.*

3. *Servants.*) The first servants here sent to invite, were the Prophets: the second, were the Apostles: and all that afterward converted countries, or that have and do reconcile men to the Church.

<margin>Worldly excuses against reconciliation.</margin>
5. *One to his farm.*) Such as refuse to be reconciled to Christ's Church, allege often vain impediments and worldly excuses, which at the day of judgment will not serve them.

<meta>Catchword: 11. A man</meta>

<summary>Jesus successfully answers challenges from the Sadducees regarding the resurrection and from the Pharisees regarding the greatest commandment, ultimately silencing his critics by questioning them about the Messiah's lineage. The accompanying annotations provide a mystical interpretation of the Parable of the Wedding Feast, linking it to the Incarnation and the Church.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Matthew 22, specifically focusing on the relationship between Church and State, the nature of the resurrected, and the priority of charity over faith alone, before beginning Chapter 23's critique of the Scribes and Pharisees.</meta>

<page-num>64</page-num>
<header>THE HOLY GOSPEL CHAPTER XXIII.</header>

<margin>Holy week.</margin>
<margin>The Church consists of good and bad.</margin>
11. *A man not attired.*] It does not profit much to be within the Church and to be a Catholic, unless a person lives a good life; for such a person shall be damned, because with faith he does not have good works. This is evident by the example of this man, who was inside and at the feast like the rest, but lacked the garment of charity and good works. By this man are represented all the bad people who are called; therefore they are also in the Church, just as this man was at the feast. But because he was called, and yet was not one of the elect, it is evident that the Church does not consist of the elect only, contrary to what our adversaries claim <note>This is a critique of the Protestant Reformers' view that the "true" Church consists only of those predestined for salvation.</note>.

<margin>Neither must temporal Princes exact, nor their Subjects give vnto them, Ecclesiastical jurisdiction.</margin>
21. *To Caesar.*] Temporal duties and payments demanded by worldly Princes must be paid, so long as God is not defrauded of His more sovereign duty. Therefore Princes must take heed how they demand, and others how they give to Caesar (that is, to their Prince) the things that are due to God (that is, to His Ecclesiastical ministers). Whereupon Saint Athanasius <note>A 4th-century theologian and defender of orthodoxy against Arianism.</note> recites these excellent words from a letter of the ancient and famous Confessor Hosius of Corduba <note>A prominent bishop who presided at the Council of Nicaea.</note> to Constantius the Arian Emperor: *Stop, I beseech you, and remember that you are mortal; fear the day of judgment, and do not meddle with Ecclesiastical matters, nor command us in these things, but rather learn them from us. To you, God has committed the Empire; to us He has committed the things that belong to the Church. And just as he who looks with malicious eyes upon your Empire speaks against the ordinance of God, so you also must beware, lest by drawing Ecclesiastical matters to yourself, you become guilty of a great crime. It is written: Give the things that are Caesar’s to Caesar, and the things that are God’s to God.* Therefore it is not lawful for us on earth to hold the Empire, nor do you, O Emperor, have power over incense and sacred things. <note>original: "Athan. Ep. ad Solit. vitā agentes" — Athanasius, Letter to those leading a solitary life.</note> And Saint Ambrose to the Emperor Valentinian (who, by the ill counsel of his mother Justina, an Arian, required Saint Ambrose to give up one Church in Milan for the Arian heretics) says: *We pay that which is Caesar’s to Caesar, and that which is God’s to God. Tribute belongs to Caesar and is not denied; the Church belongs to God and truly may not be yielded to Caesar, because the Temple of God cannot be Caesar's right. No man can deny that this is spoken with honor to the Emperor; for what is more honorable than that the Emperor be called the son of the Church? For a good Emperor is within the Church, not above the Church.* <note>original: "Ambr. lib. 5. Epist. Orat. de Basil. trad." — Ambrose, Book 5, Letters, Oration on the handing over of the Basilicas.</note>

<margin>The Saints hear our prayers.</margin>
30. *As Angels.*] As Christ proves here that in heaven they neither marry nor are married because they shall be like Angels, by that very same reason it is proved that Saints may hear our prayers and help us, whether they be near or far off. This is because the Angels do so, and in every moment are present wherever they wish; they do not need to be physically near us when they hear or help us.

<margin>Religious single life is Angelical.</margin>
30. *As Angels.*] To not marry nor be married is to be like the Angels; therefore the state of Religious men, women, and priests, who do not marry, is worthily called by the Church Fathers an "Angelical life." <note>original: "Cyp. lib. 2. de discipl. & hab. Virg. sub finem" — Cyprian, Book 2, On the discipline and dress of virgins, near the end.</note>

<margin>Not only faith.</margin>
32. *Of the dead.*] Saint Jerome uses this passage to disprove the heretic Vigilantius <note>A 4th-century priest who opposed the veneration of relics and the cult of saints.</note>, and through him those of our own time who, in order to diminish the honor of Saints, purposely call them "dead men."

40. *On these two.*] By this it is evident that everything does not depend upon faith alone, but much more upon charity (though faith is the first priority), which is the love of God and of our neighbor. This is the sum of all the Law and the Prophets, because he who has this double charity—expressed here by these two principal commandments—fulfills and accomplishes all that is commanded in the Law and the Prophets.

He concludes with the righteous rejection of that persecuting generation and their mother-city Jerusalem with her Temple.*

# A N N O T A T I O N S
## CHAPTER XXIII.

<margin>The See of Rome preserved in truth.</margin>
2. *Chair of Moses.*] God preserveth the truth of Christian religion in the Apostolic See of Rome, which is in the New Law answerable to the chair of Moses, notwithstanding the Bishops of the same were never so wicked of life: yea though some traitor as evil as Judas were Bishop thereof, it should not be prejudicial to the Church and innocent Christians, for whom our Lord providing said, *Do that which they say, but do not as they do.* <note>original: "August. Epist. 165." refers to a letter by Saint Augustine of Hippo arguing that the office of the Papacy remains holy even if the individual holder is not.</note>

<summary>Jesus delivers a final, scathing condemnation of the Pharisees' hypocrisy and their history of violence against prophets, concluding with a lament over Jerusalem. The accompanying annotations argue that the authority of the Church remains valid regardless of the personal character of the clergy.</summary>
<keywords>Hypocrisy, Pharisees, Whitewashed Sepulchres, Zechariah, Jerusalem, Free Will, Chair of Moses, Apostolic See, St. Stephen's Day</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Matthew 23, providing a Catholic defense of the "Apostolic See" (the Papacy) and the clerical hierarchy against the criticisms of Reformers like Wycliffe, Luther, and Calvin. It argues that the office remains holy even if the individual holding it is flawed.</meta>

->### CHAPTER 23. ACCORDING TO ST. MATTHEW.<-

<margin>Against the Letters of Petilian, Book 2, chapter 51.</margin>
<margin>Against the Letters of Petilian, Book 2, chapter 51.</margin>
<margin>The dignity of the See of Rome, despite some evil Bishops holding the office.</margin>
3. *Whatever they shall say.*] Why (asks St. Augustine) do you call the Apostolic Chair the "chair of pestilence"? If it is because of the men, why? Did our Lord Jesus Christ, because of the Pharisees, do any wrong to the chair where they sat? Did he not commend that <term>Chair of Moses</term> <note>The "Chair of Moses" refers to the seat of authority for teaching the Law; the author compares this to the "Apostolic Chair" or the Papacy.</note> and, while preserving the honor of the office, still rebuke the men? For he says: *They sit upon the Chair of Moses; do what they say.* If you considered these things well, you would not—because of the men you defame—blaspheme the <term>Apostolic See</term> <note>The See of Rome, or the Papacy.</note>, with which you do not communicate. And again he says: *Neither because of the Pharisees (to whom you compare us out of malice, not wisdom) did our Lord command the Chair of Moses to be forsaken—in which chair he truly prefigured his own. For he warns the people to do what they say, and not to do what they do, so that the holiness of the office is never forsaken, nor the unity of the flock divided because of bad pastors.*

6. *Love the first places.*] He does not condemn proper ranks of superiority given to or taken by men according to their degrees, but rather the ambitious seeking after fame, their proud hearts, and their wicked intentions, which he saw within them and therefore could boldly rebuke.

<margin>Many "masters" are many "arch-heretics."</margin>
8. *One is your master.*] In the Catholic Church there is one Master, Christ our Lord, and under him one <term>Vicar</term> <note>The Pope, acting as Christ's representative on Earth.</note>, with whom all Catholic doctors and teachers are united, because they all teach one thing. But among the <term>arch-heretics</term> <note>The leaders of major movements that broke away from the Catholic Church.</note> it is not so; every one of them is a different master and teaches things contrary to the others. Every one wants to be called "Rabbi" and "Master" by their own disciples: Arius among the Arians, Luther among the Lutherans, and Calvin among the Calvinists.

<margin>1 Timothy 2.</margin>
<margin>2 Timothy 1.</margin>
<margin>Ephesians 4.</margin>
<margin>1 Corinthians 4:15.</margin>
<margin>Doctors, Masters, and spiritual fathers.</margin>
10. *Masters.*] Wycliffe and similar heretics of this time use this to condemn academic degrees and the titles of "Doctor" and "Master." By this logic, they might as well rebuke St. Paul for calling himself a *Doctor and Master of the Gentiles*, or for saying that there should always be "Doctors" in the Church. And whereas they use the following words against <term>Religious men</term> <note>Members of monastic orders (monks, friars) who were often addressed as "Father."</note> who are called "fathers," they might as well use this place to take away the name of biological fathers, or blame St. Paul for calling himself the only "spiritual father" of the Corinthians. In truth, nothing is forbidden here but the contentious division and partiality of those who make themselves ringleaders of schisms and sects, such as Donatus, Arius, Luther, and Calvin.

<margin>The honor of Priesthood.</margin>
13. *Scribes and Pharisees.*] In all these rebukes it is very important to note that our Savior, out of honor for the priesthood, never rebukes priests by that name <note>original: *Cypr. ep. 65.*, referring to Cyprian's Letter 65.</note>. Whereas the heretics of our day use this name specifically to reproach and despise them.

<margin>The intention.</margin>
14. *Praying long prayers.*] They are not rebuked here for the things themselves—which for the most part are good, such as long prayer, making <term>proselytes</term> <note>Converts to a religion.</note>, and decorating the tombs of the prophets—but for their wicked purpose and intention, as was said before regarding fasting, prayer, and alms in Matthew 6.

<margin>Not only faith.</margin>
15. *Double more.*] Those who teach that it is enough to have faith alone make such Christians as the Jews made proselytes: children of Hell far more than before <note>original: *August. lib. de fide & oper. cap. 26.*, referring to Augustine's book "On Faith and Works."</note>.

<margin>Theophylact.</margin>
<margin>Matthew 22.</margin>
<margin>The altar is sanctified by our Lord's body upon it.</margin>
19. *Sanctifies.*] Note that <term>donaries</term> <note>Gifts or offerings given to a church.</note> and gifts bestowed upon churches and altars are sanctified by being dedicated to God, and by touching the altar and other holy things. This is especially true now of the vessels used for the sacrifice and Sacrament of Christ's body and blood, through touching the same, and the altar itself where it is consecrated. Regarding this, <term>Theophylact</term> <note>A 11th-century Byzantine Archbishop and biblical commentator.</note> writes on this passage: *In the old law, Christ does not allow the gift to be greater than the altar; but with us, the altar is sanctified by the gift. For the hosts, by divine grace, are turned into our Lord's body, and therefore the altar is also sanctified by them.*

21. *By him that dwells therein.*] By this we see that swearing by created things, such as the Gospel or the Saints, is all referred back to the honor of God, whose Gospel it is and whose Saints they are.

28. *Appear to men.*] Christ could boldly rebuke them so often and so vehemently for hypocrisy because he knew their hearts and intentions. But we, who cannot see inside men, must not presume to call men's outward good deeds "hypocrisy," but must judge men as we see and know them.

29. *Garnish.*] Christ does not blame the Jews for adorning the tombs of the Prophets, but rebukes them for their malice toward him. By his divine knowledge, he foresaw that they would fulfill the wickedness of their fathers by shedding his blood, just as their fathers shed the blood of the Prophets <note>original: *Hilar.*, referring to Hilary of Poitiers.</note>.

# CHAPTER XXV. ACCORDING TO ST. MATTHEW. 71 HOLY WEEK.

`12. *Iniquity shall abound.*]` When heresy and false teachers rule the world, specifically toward the final days, wicked living increases and <term>charity</term> <note>In this context, "charity" refers to "agape"—the supernatural love for God and neighbor.</note> decays.

<margin>The Gospel is now preached to those who do not yet believe.</margin>
`14. *Shall be preached.*]` The Gospel has been preached in recent years, and continues to be, by holy men of various religious orders in many great countries that have never heard the Gospel before, as is believed. <note>This likely refers to Catholic missionary efforts in the Americas and Asia during the 16th century.</note>

<margin>The abomination of desolation. The removal of the holy sacrifice of the Mass by Antichrist and his followers.</margin>
`15. *Abomination of desolation.*]` This foretold "abomination of desolation" was first partially fulfilled through various desecrations of the Temple in Jerusalem when the sacrifice and service of God were stopped. However, it will be especially fulfilled by the Antichrist and his precursors when they shall abolish the Holy Mass, which is the Sacrifice of Christ’s body and blood and the only supreme worship due to God in His Church. As St. Hippolytus writes: *The Churches shall mourn with great lamentation, because there shall be neither <term>oblation</term> <note>An offering or sacrifice made to God.</note> made, nor incense, nor worship pleasing to God. The sacred houses of the Churches shall become like cottages, and the precious body and blood of Christ shall not be present (openly in Churches) in those days; the <term>Liturgy</term> (or Mass) shall be extinguished, the singing of Psalms shall cease, and the reading of the Scriptures shall not be heard.* <note>original: "Hippol. de Antichristo"</note> By this, it is clear that the heretics of these days are the specific forerunners of the Antichrist.

<margin>The Antichrist.</margin>
`22. *Shall be shortened.*]` The reign of the Antichrist shall be short—that is, three and a half years. <note>Citing Daniel 7 and Revelation 11.</note> Therefore, the heretics are blasphemous and ridiculous to claim that the <term>Vicar of Christ</term> <note>The Pope.</note> is the Antichrist, as he has held his seat for 1,500 years.

<margin>2 Thessalonians 2.</margin>
`24. *Great signs.*]` These signs and miracles will only be such in outward appearance; for St. Paul calls them "lying signs" intended to seduce only those who are destined to perish. From this, we see that even if heretics could perform fake or forged miracles, we ought not to believe them—and certainly not now, when they cannot even seem to perform any.

<margin>The secret <term>conventicles</term> <note>Secret or illegal religious meetings.</note> of heretics. Catholic Christians meeting secretly in times of persecution.</margin>
<margin>Augustine, Book 1, Question 38 on the Gospels; Acts 1:12.</margin>
`26. *In closets.*]` Since Christ has made the Church's authority bright and clear to the whole world, He warns the faithful to beware of heretics and <term>schismatics</term> <note>Those who promote a split or division within the Church.</note> who hold their secret meetings in odd places and obscure corners to lure curious people to them. As for Catholics coming together to serve God in secret places, that is a necessary thing in times of persecution; it was used by Christians for three hundred years after Christ, and the Apostles and disciples also met that way in Jerusalem for fear of the Jews. Catholics do the same today in our country, not to pull religion into corners away from the society of the Catholic Church, but to practice secretly the very same faith that shines and appears most gloriously throughout all of Christendom.

<margin>The Antichrist.</margin>
`29. *Immediately.*]` If the Last Day follows immediately after the persecution by the Antichrist (which is to last only three and a half years, as stated before), then it is sheer blasphemy to say the Pope is the Antichrist, as they claim he has held that role for nearly a thousand years.
