HOLY WEEK. THE GOSPEL CHAPTER 26.

## ANNOTATIONS
### CHAPTER 25.

<margin>Good works are necessary.</margin>
1. *Virgins.*] These ten virgins—five wise and five foolish—signify that in the <term>Church militant</term><note>The "Church militant" refers to the body of Christian believers currently living on earth, as opposed to those in heaven.</note> there are both good and bad people. The bad shall be shut out on the last day, even though they have lamps (which represents faith) just like the others. This is because their lamps have gone out; that is, their faith is dead because it lacks the charity and good works needed to provide light. <note>original: "Greg. ho. 12."; Gregory the Great, Homily 12</note>

1. *Lamps.*] These burning lamps represent good works—specifically acts of mercy and a praiseworthy way of living that shines before others. <note>original: "Aug. ep: 120, c. 33."; Augustine, Letter 120, chapter 33</note>

<margin>Right intention.</margin>
3. *Oil.*] This oil represents a righteous inward intention, which directs our works toward God’s glory rather than toward seeking praise for ourselves in the sight of men. <note>original: "Aug. ep. 120, c. 33."; Augustine, Letter 120, chapter 33</note>

27. *With interest* <note>original: "vfurie"; in this period, the term referred to any interest earned on a loan, though here it is used metaphorically for spiritual growth.</note>] Interest is used here to mean the lawful gain a person achieves by employing their goods well. When God gives us any talent or talents, He expects "interest"—that is, a spiritual increase of those gifts through our diligence and hard work.

<margin>We must use God's gifts.</margin>
29. *That which he seems to have.*] A person is said to truly "have" God’s gifts if they use them; to such a person, God will increase his gifts. He who does not use them only "seems" to have them, rather than truly possessing them, and God will withdraw from him what He previously gave.

<margin>Good and bad together in the Church.</margin>
32. *Separate.*] Behold, here is the final separation, for in the Church militant, the good and bad lived together. As for heretics, they left the Church previously and separated themselves; therefore, they are not separated here, as they have been judged already.

<margin>Heaven is the reward for good works, and Hell for the opposite.</margin>
34. *Come you, † get you away.*] It is not inconsistent that God should say "Go into everlasting fire" to those who, by their own free will, have rejected His mercy. Similarly, He says to the others, "Come, you blessed of my Father, take the kingdom prepared for you," to those who by their own free will received faith, confessed their sins, and performed <term>penance</term><note>Acts of devotion or self-denial performed to show sorrow for sin.</note>. <note>original: "Aug. li. 2 act. cum Fel. Manich. c. 8."; Augustine, Book 2 of the proceedings against Felix the Manichaean, chapter 8</note>

35. *You gave me.*] Here we see how much almsgiving and all works of mercy help toward attaining everlasting life and blotting out former sins. <note>original: "Aug. in Pf. 49."; Augustine on Psalm 49</note>

42. *Gave me not.*] He does not charge them here with a lack of belief, but rather with a failure to do good works. For such people did believe, but they did not care for good works, as if they could have reached heaven through a dead faith. <note>original: "Aug. de fid. & op. c. 15. & ad Dulcit. q. 2. to. 4."; Augustine, On Faith and Works, chapter 15, and To Dulcitius, question 2, volume 4</note>

# ANNOTATIONS
## CHAPTER 26.

<margin>Expense upon Churches, altars, etc.</margin>
8. ***This Waste.***] The cost bestowed upon Christ’s body while He was alive, which did not seem necessary for His survival, appeared to the disciples as lost and fruitless. Similarly, money spent today on His body in the Sacrament, or on altars and Churches, seems to the simple-minded to be lost, or less meritorious than if it were given to the poor.

<margin>Relief of the poor.</margin>
<margin>Ambrose, Book 2 of *On the Duties of the Clergy*, chapter 28.</margin>
10. ***Good Work.***] Money spent for religion, devotion, and symbolic purposes is a meritorious work <note>A 'meritorious work' is a deed believed to be spiritually valuable or pleasing to God.</note>, and often more meritorious than giving to the poor, though both are very good. In some cases, the poor are to be preferred; indeed, in certain cases of extreme necessity, the Church will even break the consecrated vessels and jewels of silver and gold to spend them on works of mercy. But we may remember well—and our fathers knew it much better—that the poor were best supported during the times when the most was being given to the Church.

<margin>Christ is always with us in the Blessed Sacrament.</margin>
11. ***Have not.***] We do not have Him in the visible manner in which He walked the earth with His disciples, needing food and relief like other poor men. However, we have Him in another way in the Blessed Sacrament <note>The 'Blessed Sacrament' refers to the Eucharist or Holy Communion.</note>, and yet we truly and really have that very same body. Therefore He said they would not have Him because they would not have Him in that visible way, but in another manner—just as when He said in *Luke 24* "When I was with you," as if He were not then currently with them.

<margin>A wonderful mystery in the institution of the Blessed Sacrament.</margin>
20. ***Twelve.***] It must truly be a great mystery that He was to perform in the institution of the new Sacrifice by the marvelous transmutation <note>original: "transmntatiō." Referring to the change of substance, or Transubstantiation, of bread and wine into the Body and Blood of Christ.</note> of bread and wine into His body and blood. Note that He admitted no one (although many were present in the city) except the twelve Apostles, who had already been taught to believe it without contradiction in *John 6*, and who were to have the administration and consecration of it through the Order of Priesthood, which was also given to them there for that purpose. In contrast, at the eating of the Paschal lamb <note>The Passover meal.</note>, the entire family was accustomed to be present.

<margin>The holy Eucharist is both a Sacrifice and a Sacrament.</margin>
26. ***He took bread.***] Here, all at once, is instituted—for the continuation of the external office of Christ's eternal Priesthood according to the order of Melchisedec <note>Melchisedec was a mysterious king and priest from the Old Testament; Christian theology views him as a "type" or foreshadowing of Christ's eternal priesthood.</note>—both a Sacrifice and a Sacrament. Although the Scriptures give neither of these names to this action, our adversaries <note>A reference to Protestant Reformers who challenged Catholic sacramental theology.</note> unreasonably accept it as a sacrament in some sense but utterly deny it as a sacrifice. It is a Sacrifice in that it is ordained to continue the memory of Christ's death and His offering upon the Cross, applying the general power of that event to our specific needs. This is done by consecrating the elements not into Christ’s whole person as He was born or as He is now in heaven, but the bread into His body specifically as betrayed, broken, and given for us; and the wine into His blood specifically as shed for the remission of sins. In this mystical and unspeakable manner, He intended for the Church to offer and sacrifice Him daily; and He dies in mystery and Sacrament, though [the text continues...]

The annotations argue for the spiritual merit of decorating churches and defend the Catholic doctrine of the Real Presence and the Mass as a sacrifice.</summary>

# CHAPTER 26. ACCORDING TO ST. MATTHEW.

...although now He is not only in heaven, but also in the Sacrament, where He is indeed present <note>original: "per Concomitantiam"</note> by **Concomitance** <note>The doctrine of 'Concomitance' teaches that because the living Christ is indivisible, His Body, Blood, Soul, and Divinity are all present together under the form of either the bread or the wine.</note> (as the Church calls it, that is, by the connection of all His parts to each other) whole, alive, and immortal. Because 
<margin>Matthew 22:29.</margin>
our adversaries <note>In this context, 'adversaries' refers to Protestant Reformers who disagreed with Catholic sacramental theology.</note> do not understand this point, not knowing the Scriptures nor the power of God, they blaspheme and mislead the people to their own damnation. It is also a Sacrament in that it is ordained to be received into our bodies to feed them toward resurrection and immortality, and to give grace and salvation to our souls, if we receive it worthily.

<margin>The blessing of Christ directed toward the created things and producing an effect in them.</margin>
26. ***Blessed.***] Our adversaries, regarding the two words used in Greek and Latin—<note>original: "benedixit" and "gratias egit"</note> **he blessed** and **he gave thanks**—use only the latter. They do this on purpose to suggest that Christ neither blessed nor consecrated the bread and wine, and thus His blessing produced no effect upon them, but that He only gave thanks to His Father, as we do when saying grace before a meal. But the truth is that the word <gloss>to bless</gloss> <note>original: "εὐλογεῖν"</note> properly signifies blessing, and is directed toward the thing being blessed. For example, in *Luke 9* regarding the fishes: <gloss>he blessed them</gloss> <note>original: "εὐλόγησεν αὐτούς / benedixit eis"</note>, and by doing so, performed that wonderful multiplication. Thus, God's blessing is always effective; therefore, here also He blessed the bread, and by that blessing, along with the words that followed, made it His body.
<margin>Consecration.</margin>
*Ambrose, Book on those initiated into the mysteries, chapter 9; Augustine, Epistle 59 to Paulinus.* Now, where it says He took the cup and gave thanks, we say this is the same as blessing. He blessed the cup just as he 
<margin>1 Corinthians 10.</margin>
previously blessed the bread, as is evident from the words of St. Paul: <note>original: "Calix cui benedicimus"</note> **The cup which we bless.** For this reason, he calls it <note>original: "Calicem benedictionis"</note> **the cup of blessing**, using the same Greek 
<margin><gloss>the bread of the Eucharist (thanksgiving).</gloss> <note>original: "τὸν ἄρτον τῆς εὐχαριστίας"</note></margin>
word that is used for the bread. But why is it said here that He "gave thanks"? Because we translate the words faithfully as they appear in the Greek and Latin, and because the meaning is the same, as we are taught by the previously mentioned St. Paul and by the Church Fathers. They call this giving of thanks over the cup or the bread the "blessing" thereof. *St. Justin Martyr at the end of his Second Apology: "The bread made Eucharist"; St. Irenaeus, Book 4, chapter 34: "The bread over which thanks were given"; St. Cyprian on the Lord’s Supper: "The cup consecrated by solemn blessing."* That is to say: the bread was blessed by giving thanks over it, and the cup was consecrated by a solemn blessing.

<margin>Transubstantiation.</margin>
26. ***This is.***] The bread and the wine are turned into the body and blood of Christ by the same omnipotent power by which the world was created and the Word became flesh in the womb of the Virgin. *John Damascene, Book 4, chapter 14; Cyprian on the Lord's Supper; Ambrose, Book on the mysteries, chapter 9.*

<margin>Not a figure, but a real presence.</margin>
26. ***My body.***] He did not say, "This bread is a figure of my body," or, "This wine is a figure of my blood," but **This is my body** and **This is my blood.** *John Damascene, Book 4, chapter 14; Theophylact on this passage; Second Council of Nicaea, Act 6.* It is a real presence. When some Fathers call it a "figure" or "sign," they are referring to the outward appearance of the bread and wine.

28. ***Blood of the new Testament.***] Just as the Old Testament was dedicated with blood using the words: *This is the blood of the Testament, etc. (Hebrews 9)*, so here is the institution of the New Testament in Christ’s blood, with the words: **This is the blood of the New Testament, etc.** This blood is 
<margin><gloss>being shed; being broken; being given.</gloss> <note>original: "ἐκχυνόμενον. κλώμενον. διδόμενον."</note></margin>
mystically shed here, and not only later upon the Cross. In Greek, the present tense is used by all the Evangelists and St. Paul. Likewise, when speaking of the body in *1 Corinthians 11*, the Greek uses the present tense, as do *Luke 22* and the Latin text here. Even the heretics use the present tense in their own translations.

29. ***Fruit of the vine.***] St. Luke places these words before the consecration. Because of this, it seems he is speaking of the wine used for the Passover lamb, which is why he calls it the 
<margin>The elements are called bread and wine even after consecration.</margin>
"fruit of the vine." However, even if he were speaking of the wine that had become His blood, he still calls it "wine," just as St. Paul calls the other "bread," for three reasons. First, because it was wine previously; just as Eve is called Adam’s "bone," and it is said that 
<margin>Genesis 2; Exodus 7; John 2.</margin>
**Aaron’s rod swallowed their rods**, even though they were no longer rods, but 
serpents. Similarly, it says **He tasted the water turned into wine**, even though it was now wine and not water. Second, because it keeps the appearance of bread and wine, and things are often named by how they appear; for example, Raphael is called a "young man" in *Tobit 5*, and **three men appeared to Abraham** in *Genesis 18*, even though they were actually angels. Third, because Christ in this Sacrament is the very true and primary "bread and wine," feeding and refreshing our bodies and souls for everlasting life.

39. ***Not as I Will.***] A perfect example of obedience and of submitting ourselves and our wills to God's will and ordinance in all adversity. We should desire nothing in this world except under the condition of His holy pleasure and appointment.

<margin>Cyprian, On the Lord's Prayer, number 15; Jerome, Against Vigilantius, epistle 53.</margin>
41. ***Watch and pray.***] From this came the practice of **Vigils** and **Nocturnes**—that is, 
<margin>Vigils and Nocturnes.</margin>
watching and praying during the night. This was commonly practiced by all Christians in the primitive Church, as is clear from St. Cyprian and St. Jerome; later, and up to this day, it is practiced especially by those in religious orders.

<margin>The power of the Holy Spirit.</margin>
69. ***Maidservant.*** <note>original: "Wench"</note>] St. Gregory, describing the difference in the Apostles before and after receiving the Holy Spirit, says: "Even this very Pastor of the Church himself, at whose most sacred body we now sit—the maidservant can tell you how weak he was then. But his answer to the high priest in *Acts 5:29* shows how strong he was afterward: *We must obey God rather than men.*" *Gregory, Homily 20 on the Gospels.*

<margin>Human weaknesses.</margin>
74. ***To curse.***] A valuable example and warning regarding human weakness; it teaches us to avoid pride and to rely entirely on God during temptations.

<margin>Peter's tears and repentance.</margin>
75. ***Wept bitterly.***] St. Ambrose, in the hymn the Church uses at Lauds, says of this: <note>original: "Hoc ipsa Petra ecclesiæ canente, culpam diluit."</note> **When the cock crowed, the Rock of the Church himself washed away his fault.** *St. Augustine, Retractions, Book 1, chapter 21.*

## A N N O T A T I O N S
### C H A P T E R 27.

<margin>Horror of conscience.</margin> 
3. *Repenting himself.*] Note how speedily the plague of God falls after sin, and especially men must note what torment of conscience and desperation often follows the shedding of innocent blood.

<margin>Despair.</margin> 
5. *Hung himself.*] If he had rightly repented, notwithstanding his horrible treason, he might have obtained mercy: but by hanging himself he took away all means of mercy and salvation, because he died finally impenitent <note>without remorse or turning back to God</note>.

<margin>They that execute laws against their conscience are like Pilate.</margin> 
24. *Innocent of his blood.*] Though Pilate was much more innocent than the Jews, and would have been free from the murder of our Savior, seeking all the means that he could (without offending the people and the Emperor's laws) to dismiss him: Yet he is damned for being the minister of the people's wicked will against his own conscience. Even as all Officers are, and especially the Judges and Juries which execute laws of earthly princes against Catholic men: for all such are guilty of innocent blood, and are not at all excused by the fact that they execute other men's wills according to the laws, which are unjust. For they should rather suffer death themselves, than put an innocent man to death.

<margin>Christ mocked in the Blessed Sacrament, even as upon the Cross.</margin> 
40. *If thou be the Son.*] Marvel not, when you hear our Savior in the Blessed Sacrament <note>The Eucharist</note> mocked, or see him abused by wicked men, that he does not straightway revenge such blasphemies: or that he shows not himself there visibly and to the senses, when faithless Heretics will say, "Let me see him, taste him," etc. For he suffered the like here on the Cross, when he might at his will have come down with as much ease as he rose when he was dead.

<margin>Calvin's Catechism and Institutes, book 2, chapter 16.</margin> 
<margin>Calvin's blasphemy.</margin> 
46. *Why hast thou forsaken me?*] Beware here of the detestable blasphemy of Calvin and the Calvinists, who, thinking the bodily death of Christ not sufficient, say that he was also here so forsaken and abandoned by his Father that he sustained in soul and conscience the very fears and torments of the damned. And to take away the Article of his descending into Hell after his death (which was with triumph and not in pain), they say that his descending was nothing else but that his soul suffered the very pains of Hell upon the Cross. Whereas in deed by these words out of the Psalm, our Savior will signify no more but that his pains (being now so long on the Cross and ready to die) were very great, and therefore according to the infirmity of his human nature, for very anguish (as before in the garden when he was toward his Passion) he said he was

->### ANNOTATIONS<-
->#### CHAPTER XXVIII.<-

<margin>In Epistle 17, Paula and Eustochium to Marcella, volume 1. <note>original: "In Ep. 17 Paula & Eustoch. ad Marcel. to. 1."</note></margin>
<margin>The holy Sepulcher, and Pilgrimage thereunto.</margin>
1. *To see the Sepulcher.*] The devout Women came to visit our Savior’s sepulcher, and for their devotion first deserved to know of the Resurrection, and to see him risen. St. Jerome declares the honor of this Sepulcher and the Pilgrimage thereunto in the Primitive Church in these words: *The Jews sometime honored the Holy of Holies <note>original: "Sancta Sanctorum"</note>, because there were the Cherubim, and the Mercy Seat <note>original: "Propitiatorie"</note>, and the Ark of the Testament, Manna, Aaron's rod, and the golden altar. Does not the Sepulcher of our Lord seem more honorable unto thee? Which as often as we enter into, so often do we see our Savior lie in the linen shroud <note>original: "findon"</note>; and staying there a while, we see the Angel again sit at his feet, and at his head the napkin wrapped together. We know the glory of his Sepulcher was long prophesied before Joseph [of Arimathea] hewed it out, by Isaiah saying: "And his rest shall be honor" <note>Isaiah 11:10</note>; to write, because the place of our Lord's burial should be honored by all men.* <margin>Isaiah 11.</margin> And at this present time, notwithstanding the rule of the Turks <note>Referring to the Ottoman Empire's control over Jerusalem</note>, yet the Religious Christian Catholic men by God’s mighty providence keep the holy Sepulcher, which is within a beautiful Church, and Christians come from all over the world in Pilgrimage to it.

<margin>The Catholic Church to be gathered of all Nations.</margin>
19. *Going then.*] The commission to baptize and preach to all Nations was given to the Apostles, and grounded upon Christ’s sovereign authority, to whom was given all power in heaven and in earth.

<margin>And Christ's continual protection of the same Church.</margin>
20. *With you all days.*] Here Christ does promise his concurrence with his Apostles and their successors, as well in preaching as ministering the Sacraments, and his protection of the Church never to cease until the world's end: contrary to our Adversaries <note>A common term used by the translators to refer to Protestant reformers</note>, who say that the Church has failed for many hundred years until Luther and Calvin.

# THE ARGUMENT OF
## SAINT MARK'S GOSPEL.

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'S' with floral motifs.</image-desc>
Saint Mark's Gospel may be well divided into four parts.
*The first part, regarding the preparation that was made for the manifestation of Christ: chapter 1, at the beginning.*
*The Second, regarding his manifesting himself by Preaching and Miracles, and that in Galilee: the remainder of the 1st chapter through the 10th chapter.*
*The third, regarding his coming into Judea <note>original: "Iurie"</note>, toward his Passion: chapter 10.*
*The fourth, regarding the Holy week of his Passion in Jerusalem: chapter 11 to the end of the book.*

---

Of *Saint Mark* and his conversation with the two Apostles *Saint Paul* and *Saint Barnabas*, we have accounts at length in *Acts 12 and 15*, and somewhat also in *Colossians 4, 2 Timothy 4, and to Philemon.* Moreover, of his familiarity with the Prince of the Apostles, *Saint Peter*, we have *1 Peter 5.* For so it pleased our Lord, that only two of the Evangelists should be of his twelve Apostles, to wit, *Saint Matthew* and *Saint John.* The other two, *Saint Mark* and *Saint Luke*, he gave unto us from the Disciples of his two most principal and most glorious Apostles, *Saint Peter* and *Saint Paul.* Whose Gospels therefore were anciently <note>original: "of Antiquitie"</note> counted as the Gospels of *Saint Peter* and *Saint Paul* themselves.

<margin>In the Catalog of Ecclesiastical Writers <note>original: "In Catal. Script. Ecclesiast."</note></margin>
*Mark*, the disciple and interpreter of *Peter* (says *Saint Jerome*), according to that which he heard from *Peter's* mouth, wrote at *Rome* a brief Gospel at the request of the Brethren (*about 10 or 12 years after our Lord's Ascension.*) Which when *Peter* had heard, he approved it, and with his authority did publish it to the Church to be read, as *Clement of Alexandria writes in book 6 of his "Outlines" <note>original Greek: "hypotyposeon"</note>.*

In the same place *Saint Jerome* adds how he went into *Egypt* to preach, and was the first Bishop of the chief city there, named *Alexandria*: and how *Philo*
<margin>Philo on the Suppliants <note>original: "de Supplicibus," referring to his work "On the Contemplative Life."</note></margin>
<margin>In the Catalog <note>original: "In Catalogo"</note></margin>
*the Jew* at the same time, seeing and admiring the life and conversation of the Christians there under *Saint Mark*, who were Monks, wrote a book thereof, which is extant to this day. And not only *Saint Jerome (in his entries on Mark and Philo)* but also *Eusebius in History, book 2, chapters 15, 16, 17; Epiphanius in Sect 29 regarding the Nazarenes, book 1, volume 2; Cassian in "On the Institutes of the Monasteries," <note>original: "de Instit. Cœnobiorum"</note> book 2, chapter 5; Sozomen, book 1, chapter 12; Nicephorus, book 2, chapter 15;* and diverse others, do make mention of the said Monks out of the same Author. Finally, he died (says *Saint Jerome*) in the 8th year of *Nero*, and was buried at *Alexandria, Anianus* succeeding in his place. But from *Alexandria* he was translated <note>In this context, "translated" refers to the ceremonial moving of a saint's relics from one location to another.</note> to *Venice, In the Year of our Lord 830.*
<margin>* Nauclerus, generation 28 <note>Referring to the "Chronica" of Johannes Nauclerus.</note></margin>

It is also to be noted, that in respect of *Saint Peter*, who sent *Saint Mark* his scholar to *Alexandria*, and made him the first Bishop there, this See <note>The "See" refers to the seat of a Bishop's authority or his diocese.</note> was esteemed next in dignity to the See of *Rome*, and the Bishop thereof was accounted the chief Metropolitan or Patriarch of the East, and that by the first Council of *Nicaea.* Regarding this, see *Saint Leo, epistle 53; Saint Gregory, book 5, epistle 60, and book 6, epistle 37.*

->A N N O T A T I O N S<-
->C H A P T E R. 1.<-

<margin>Confession.</margin>
5. *Confessing their sins.*] A certain confession of sins existed even in that penance <note>The term "penance" here refers to the act of repentance and outward expression of contrition preached by John the Baptist.</note> which John preached, and which was made before men were baptized. By this it is clear that John prepared the way for the Sacrament of Penance <note>The Catholic sacrament involving confession to a priest, which the authors argue is foreshadowed here.</note> which was later instituted by Christ, just as he prepared the way for Christ’s baptism by his own baptizing.

<margin>Particular confession.</margin>
5. *Their sins.*] He does not say that they confessed themselves generally to be sinners—which can be done in a general confession—but that they confessed their *sins*, which refers to a particular confession <note>The authors are emphasizing the practice of naming specific sins rather than making a vague statement of sinfulness.</note>.

<margin>John's example of penance.</margin>
6. *Clothed.*] The Holy Spirit thought it worthy of special reporting how strictly this Prophet lived, and how he abstained from delicate foods and fine clothing. *See Matthew, chapter 3.*

<margin>
Calvin, Institutes, book 4, chapter 16.
Baptism in Water.
</margin>
8. *With Water.*] John baptized with Water only, but Christ with the Holy Spirit; not only in the way the Heretics <note>A reference to Reformers, like John Calvin, who the authors argue downplayed the necessity of the physical element of water in the sacrament.</note> hold, who say water is not necessary, but with Water and the Holy Spirit, as it is plain in *John 3: 'Unless a man be born again of Water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven.'*

9. *Baptized by John.*] The humility of Christ, who did not disdain his servant's baptism. This serves as an example for all the faithful not to disdain Christ’s Sacraments when administered by any Priest, no matter how simple he may be, provided he is lawfully called by the Catholic Church. *Augustine, Book 5 on Baptism, chapter 9.*

# ANNOTATIONS
## CHAPTER II

4. *Uncovered.*) The same kind of diligence should be used to bring sinners to Christ through his <term>Sacraments<note>The sacred rites of the Church, such as Baptism or Penance, which are believed to convey God's grace to the soul.</note></term> as was used by this man and others to obtain physical health from Christ for their bodies.

<margin>St. Augustine, *On Pastors*, chapter 6, volume 9.</margin>
5. *Sick of the paralysis.*) Just as this man was physically paralyzed by the loosening of his limbs, he was also paralyzed in his soul by the harmful desires of the world occupying his heart and drawing him away from all good works.

<margin>The Sacraments should be requested during illness.</margin>
5. *Your sins.*) From this, it appears that Christ healed this sick man’s soul first, before he removed his physical infirmity. This serves as an instruction for all people suffering from physical disease: first, call for the Sacraments, which are medicines for the soul. It may also be gathered from this that many diseases are caused by sin, and therefore cannot be fully healed until the sins are forgiven.

<margin>Man has the power to forgive sins.</margin>
10. *The Son of man.*) Christ proves to them that he himself, as a man and not only as God, has the power to forgive sins. He demonstrates this in the sight of everyone by performing a miracle and making the sick man suddenly stand up. Likewise, since the Apostles were granted power from God to perform miracles, they—though they are not God—may in the same manner have authority from God to forgive sins; not as God, but as God’s ministers.

<margin>Christ forgives sins through the ministry of Priests.</margin>
<margin>Matthew 16:19; Matthew 18:18; St. Jerome to Heliodorus, epistle 1; St. Ambrose, book 2, chapter 18.</margin>
10. *On earth.*) This power that the Son of man has to forgive sins on earth was never taken from him. It continues still in his Sacraments and through his ministers, by whom he forgives sins in the Church, and not in heaven only. Regarding sin, there is one court of conscience on earth and another in heaven; the judgment in heaven follows and approves the one on earth. This is clear from the words of our Savior first to Peter, and then to all the Apostles: *Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven; whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.* Regarding this, St. Jerome says, *“That Priests, having the keys to the kingdom of heaven, judge in a sense before the day of judgment.”* St. John Chrysostom writes more extensively on this in book 3, *On the Priesthood*, shortly after the beginning.

25. *In necessity.*) In times of necessity, many things may be done without sinning that otherwise would not be allowed. For example, even the <term>chalices<note>The cups used to hold the wine during the Eucharist.</note></term> and consecrated treasures of the Church may, in cases of necessity, be turned to common use by lawful authority. To otherwise take these for a person's private profit is considered <term>sacrilege<note>The violation or misuse of what is regarded as sacred.</note></term>.

# ANNOTATIONS
## CHAPTER III.

<margin>Sermons, Service, and prayer of Heretics.</margin>
13. *Thou art the Son.*) The confession of the truth is not pleasing to God when it proceeds from just any person. The devil, acknowledging our Savior to be the Son of God, was commanded to hold his peace; Peter’s confession of the same was highly approved and rewarded. <note>original: "Aug. tract. 10 in ep. Ioan. Ser. 30. 31. de verb. Apostoli." — Augustine, Tractate 10 on the Epistle of John; Sermons 30 and 31 on the words of the Apostle.</note> Therefore, even the sermons of heretics <note>In this 16th-century context, "heretics" refers to Protestants and others outside the Catholic Church.</note> must not be heard, even if they preach the truth. The same applies to their prayer and service, which, though it may be good in itself, is not acceptable to God coming from their mouths; indeed, it is no better than the howling of wolves. <note>original: "Hiero. in 7 Osee." — Jerome's commentary on Hosea, chapter 7.</note>

<margin>The number of Twelve is mystical.</margin>
<margin>Acts 1.</margin>
14. *Twelve.*) This number of twelve Apostles is mystical <note>Having a hidden, symbolic meaning.</note> and of great importance (as is shown * by the choosing of Matthias to take Judas's place to complete the number again). It was prefigured by the 12 Patriarchs in Genesis 49, the 12 Princes of the children of Israel in Numbers 1, the 12 fountains found in Elim in Exodus 15, the 12 precious stones in the <term>Rational</term> <note>The high priest's breastplate.</note> of Aaron in Exodus 39, the 12 spies sent by Moses in Numbers 13, the 12 stones taken out of the Jordan where the Altar was made in Joshua 4, and the 12 <term>loaves of Proposition</term> <note>The showbread or "Bread of the Presence" in the Tabernacle.</note> in Leviticus 24, and so on. <note>original: "Anselm. in Mt. c. 10." — Anselm's commentary on Matthew, chapter 10.</note> And these are the 12 foundations of the heavenly Jerusalem in Revelation 21.

<margin>Peter's preeminence.</margin>
<margin>Matthew 16.</margin>
16. *Peter.*) In the numbering of the Twelve, Peter is always listed first, and his name was given to him to signify his calling to be the * Rock or Foundation of the Church under Christ. Similarly, here the name BOANERGES <note>A Hebrew/Aramaic term translated as "Sons of Thunder."</note> is given to two other Apostles for symbolic meaning, as names were given elsewhere in the Old and New Testaments.

<margin>Dissension of Heretics.</margin>
<margin>Gregory, book 7, epistle 3.</margin>
24. *Kingdom against kingdom.*) Just as this is true in all kingdoms and commonwealths where civil strife reigns, it is especially proven in heresies and among heretics, who always have divisions among themselves as a punishment from God for dividing themselves and others from the Church.

<margin>Venial sins forgiven after death.</margin>
<margin>Matthew 12:32.</margin>
29. *Eternal sin.*) That which is called "eternal" here is (as *St. Matthew* expresses it) that which shall neither be forgiven in this life, nor in the life to come. From *St. Mark* we learn that there are also sins that are not eternal; and from *St. Matthew*, we learn that these are such as shall be forgiven either here, or in the life to come <note>This is a classic Catholic argument for the existence of Purgatory—that some sins are cleansed after death.</note>.

<margin>Spiritual kindred and business preferred before carnal and worldly.</margin>
<margin>The Blessed Virgin without sin.</margin>
33. *Who is my mother?*) It is not said here that he had no mother (as some falsely conclude from these words), nor is ingratitude to our parents taught to us by this answer. Instead, we are admonished to prefer our spiritual mother, the faithful Catholic Church, and our brothers within her, and their spiritual good, above our physical parents or kin. For our Master, being occupied here with heavenly things, accounted all those his mother and brothers who did the will of his Father. In this number, our Lady his mother was also included, for she did his Father’s will. <note>original: "Aug. ep. 38." — Augustine, Epistle 38.</note> Indeed, she is included above all others, because she was given so much grace that she never sinned, not even <term>venially</term> <note>Committing a minor or "pardonable" sin.</note>, in all her life. <note>original: "Aug. de nat. & grat c. 36." — Augustine, On Nature and Grace, chapter 36.</note>

## ANNOTATIONS
### CHAP. IIII.

<margin>Matthew 13. Acts 28.</margin>
<margin>God is not the author of sin, but man’s own will.</margin>
12. *Lest they should be converted.*] These speeches here and elsewhere, we must understand as though he spoke in parables on purpose and to this end: that the hearers might not understand, lest they should be converted. This would be as much as to say that he did not want them to understand, nor be converted. But we must learn the true sense of this very place in Saint Matthew and in the Acts, where our Savior and Saint Paul speak thus: *They have heard heavily, and have shut their eyes, lest perhaps they may see, and understand, and be converted, and I heal them.* Whereby it is evident, that the speaking in parables was not the cause (for many besides the Apostles heard and understood) but they themselves would not hear, and understand, and be converted: and so were the cause of their own willful and obstinate infidelity. And therefore also he spoke in parables because they were not worthy to understand, unlike the others to whom he expounded them.

<margin>2 Corinthians 3.</margin>
27. *And sleep.*] The Church, and Christ’s doctrine (whether we sleep or wake), increases by the great providence of God; only the preachers must sow, and plant, and water, and God will give the increase, nourishing the seed in men’s hearts. And therefore we must not give up, or be impatient and <term>solicitous: anxious or overly concerned</term>, if we do not always have good success: but doing our duty, commit the rest to God.

<margin>The Church visibly increasing.</margin>
31. *Mustard seed.*] If the Church and Truth had more and more decayed and been <term>obscured: hidden or darkened</term> after the Apostles' time until ours, as the Heretics hold: then it would have been great in the beginning and small afterward. However, this Parable says the contrary: that it was a mustard seed first, and afterward a great tree. <note>original: "vide Chryf. to. 5 contra Gentiles in vita S. Babyla Mart."; See Chrysostom, volume 5, "Against the Gentiles," in "The Life of Saint Babylas the Martyr."</note>

<margin>Christian religion wonderfully spreading.</margin>
32. *The birds.*] Of all sects or doctrine, Christ’s religion at the beginning was the smallest and most <term>contemptible: seen as worthless or lowly</term>: but the success thereof far passed all man's doctrine: insomuch that afterward all the wisest and greatest of the world made their residence and rest therein.

# THE GOSPEL CHAPTER VI.

Immediately the young girl rose up and walked; and she was twelve years old. And they were astonished with great astonishment. <margin>43</margin> † And he commanded them earnestly that no one should know it; and he directed that something should be given her to eat.

->ANNOTATIONS<-
->CHAPTER V.<-

<margin>Profane and natural men.</margin>
3. **Could bind him.**] We see here that madmen who possess extraordinary strength are often possessed by the devil. Just as there is also a deaf and a dumb devil, and unclean spirits which work these effects in men by possessing their bodies. All these things infidels <note>those without faith</note> and carnal <note>fleshly or worldly</note> men—following only nature and reason—attribute to natural causes. The less faith a man has, the less he believes that the devil performs such things.

<margin>The touch of Relics. *Basil on Psalm 115.*</margin>
28. **If I shall touch.**] So says the good Catholic faith: "If I might but touch one of his Apostles, or even one of his Apostles' napkins, or even the shadow of one of his Saints, I should be better for it." *See Acts 5 and 19. See St. Chrysostom, volume 5, Against the Gentiles, at the beginning; and in the Life of Babylas.* Indeed, St. Basil says, "He that touches the bone of a martyr receives, in some degree, holiness from the grace or virtue <note>miraculous power</note> that is within it."

30. **Virtue,**] Virtue—the power to heal this woman's malady—proceeded from Christ, even though she touched only his coat. So when the Saints perform miracles through their relics or garments, the grace and force of it comes from our Savior; the objects are merely the means or instruments of that power.

<margin>Scripture inappropriately applied to prove "faith alone." *V. 5.*</margin>
36. **Only believe.**] It is a common way of speaking when we require one thing especially, even though other things are just as necessary, or even more necessary. As a physician might say to his patient, "*Only have a good heart*" <note>meaning: just stay positive</note>, when the patient must also keep a diet and take medicines, which are even more requisite. So Christ, amidst this great lack of faith among the Jews, required only that they would believe he was able to perform such a cure or miracle, and then he did it. Otherwise, as it says in the next chapter, *He could not do miracles there because of their unbelief.* Furthermore, for this faith, he gave them here (and in all similar places) health of body which they desired; therefore he does not say, "Thy faith has justified thee," but, "has made thee safe" or "whole." Additionally, this was the father's faith, which could not justify the daughter. Therefore, it is most evident that this Scripture and others like it are foolishly abused by heretics <note>a 16th-century reference to Protestant reformers</note> to try to prove that faith alone justifies a person.

<margin>The three people raised from the dead signify three kinds of sinners. *Augustine, On the Words of the Lord, sermon 44.*</margin>
41. **Young girl, arise.**] Christ's miracles, besides being wonders and ways to show his power, are also significant symbols. Just as he physically raised these people from death, he reminds us of how he raises our souls from sin. The Scripture makes special mention of only three people raised by our Savior: this young girl (inside the house); another, the widow’s son in Naim (being carried out toward the grave); and the third, Lazarus (who had been in the grave four days and was already stinking). These different states of the dead bodies signify different states of dead souls—some more desperate than others, some beyond all human hope, yet all able to be revived and reclaimed by the grace of Christ.

## ANNOTATIONS
### CHAPTER 6.

3. *The carpenter.*) Just as his fellow countrymen—seeing him not only to be a poor man, but also 
knowing (as they thought) his whole parentage to be common, not realizing his Godhead 
and divine generation—took offense or scandal at him: so do the heretics <note>The author is likely referring to Protestant reformers of the 16th century who rejected the Catholic doctrine of the Real Presence.</note> take similar offense 
at his person in the Blessed Sacrament <note>The Eucharist.</note>, saying, "Why, this is not God: for it is bread made of grain by 
such a baker, from the same mold as any other loaf." They do not notice that he was not made Christ by 
baking, but by Consecration, and the power of Christ's words.

<summary>This page recounts Jesus walking on water and the healing of the sick at Gennesaret, followed by a theological commentary defending the Real Presence in the Eucharist.</summary>
<keywords>Feeding of the Five Thousand, walking on water, Bethsaida, Gennesaret, miracles, healing, Transubstantiation, Consecration, Eucharist, St. Mark</keywords>

<meta>This page continues from the end of Mark chapter 6, providing commentary on the miracles and instructions given there, before beginning the text of Mark chapter 7. It addresses the rejection of Jesus in his hometown and the ritual traditions of the Pharisees.</meta>

<page-num>104</page-num>
<header>THE GOSPEL CHAPTER 7</header>

<margin>St. John Chrysostom, Homily 49 on Matthew.</margin>
3. **They were offended.**] This offense rose partly from the envy of those who were his equals by birth, who, considering themselves as good as he, felt it was an insult to be taught by him. For this reason Christ says, *A Prophet is not without honor except in his own country*: signifying (as is clear in Luke) the malice and envy of the Jews, his own countrymen, in rejecting him (<note>original: "Io. 1."; John 1</note>) and that the Gentiles would hold him in higher esteem.
<margin>Luke 4:25.</margin>

5. **He could not.**] It is said that he could not work miracles there, not meaning that he lacked the power, but that on their part there was no proper readiness to receive them. Therefore, out of a sense of fitness, he would not work there where their disbelief was so great that it would not have benefited them. For this reason he says elsewhere to those who wish to see and enjoy his miracles, *Only believe.*
<margin>Mark 6:36; Matthew 10:9.</margin>

8. **Not two coats.**] He forbids excess and overly anxious provision for physical needs when they are engaged in God’s service of saving souls. Regarding the apparent contradiction between this passage and St. Matthew, understand that here he forbids them to carry a rod or staff for self-defense, but here he permits a walking rod or staff to lean upon and stay themselves; there he forbids shoes that cover the entire foot, such as we wear, while here he permits sandals—that is, those which had soles only, which the poor commonly wore in Judea, and which some religious orders wear now. See the opinion of St. Augustine in <note>original: "li. 2 c. 30 de confenfu Euang. to. 4."; Book 2, chapter 30 of "On the Harmony of the Evangelists," volume 4.</note>

13. **With oil.**] In the words of the commission, oil is not mentioned, and yet it is certain from their use of oil that either Christ appointed them to use it then, or they took it up themselves by virtue of the general commission.

13. **With oil.**] From this it is clear that not only the Apostles or others may have the power to work miracles through their word alone and the invocation of Christ’s name, but also through the application of physical objects; these objects also possess a miraculous medicinal power to heal diseases.

### CHAPTER 7.

->*The masters from Jerusalem, coming from so far to criticize him, are charged by him for their traditions—some of which are trivial, and some actually contrary to God’s commandments. He explains to the people the reason for the things they criticized, and again to his disciples, showing that the basis of the Jewish washing traditions (namely, that certain foods otherwise defile the soul) is false. Shortly after, among the Gentiles, he finds wonderful faith in a woman, and therefore grants her the "crumb" she requested. He then returns to the Jews with the "loaf" (because the time for the Gentiles had not yet come). There he shows his compassion toward mankind, so deaf and dumb, and is greatly praised by the people.*<-

### A N N O T A T I O N S
### C H A P T E R VII.

**2. Common.]** Common and unclean are the same thing. For the Jews were commanded by the Law to eat only certain kinds of food, and not all indiscriminately. Because these were separated from other foods and, as it were, sanctified for their use, they called the others "common" and profane. And because the Law calls those clean and these unclean, it follows that "unclean" and "common" mean the same thing, as seen often in this chapter and in *Acts 10.*

<margin>Commandments of men.</margin>
<margin>Traditions.</margin>
**7. Precepts of men.]** Human ordinances that are contrary to God’s commandments are condemned here. All observations that are neither edifying nor profitable for fulfilling God’s commandments are vain and superfluous, just as many observations of the Pharisees were then, and as similar traditions of heretics are now. For however much they boast of the Scriptures, their entire manner of administration and ministry is their own tradition and invention, lacking Scripture and the warrant of God’s word. But we are commanded to keep the traditions of the Apostles and the ancient fathers, and all the precepts of the holy Church, as things prescribed not by man, but by the Holy Spirit. *Acts 15:28, 41; 2 Thessalonians 2:15.*

<margin>Duty to parents.</margin>
**11. Gift.]** Giving to the Church or the Altar is not forbidden, but it is impious and unnatural to forsake one's parents in their need while pretending or making an excuse that the money which should have helped them was given to God or the Altar. These Pharisees were wicked for teaching children to neglect their duties to their parents in this way.

<margin>Abstinence from certain foods.</margin>
**15. Nothing entering into a man.]** Just as these words of our Savior did not mean that the Jews of that time could eat foods that God had forbidden them, they do not mean now that we Christians may eat foods that the Church forbids us. Yet both then and now, all foods are clean, and nothing entering into a person defiles them. For neither they then, nor we now, abstain because any foods are inherently abominable or defile the eater; rather, they abstained for symbolic reasons, and we abstain for obedience and the discipline of our bodies.

<margin>Christ's spittle works miracles.</margin>
**33. Spitting.)** Miracles are performed not only by Christ's word and will, but also by ceremony and the use of external physical things made holy. This is seen here with Christ's spittle, which—though not a permanent part of his person but a bodily fluid—was nonetheless most holy. <note>original: "Theophyl. in 7 Marci" — referring to the commentary by Theophylact of Ohrid on Mark chapter 7.</note>

The Church most godly imitates and uses these very words and ceremonies of our Savior in the Exorcisms before Baptism, for the healing of the souls of those who are to be baptized, just as Christ here healed the bodily infirmity and the disease of the soul together. *Ambrose, Book 1 of "On the Sacraments," chapter 1.*

# ANNOTATIONS
## CHAPTER VIII.

<margin>6. Gave to his disciples.]</margin> He serves the people not immediately himself, but by the Apostles' ministry: to teach us that we must receive Christ’s Sacraments and doctrine, not at our own hand, but from his Priests and our Pastors.

<margin>Luke 9:16.</margin> <margin>7. Blessed them.]</margin> <margin>Having blessed them <note>original Greek: "εὐλογήσας αὐτὰ"</note>. The blessing of created things works an effect in them.</margin> So it is in some ancient Greek copies, agreeing with our Latin, and in Saint Luke expressly in the common Greek text, that he blessed the five loaves and the two fishes: which must be always noted against the heretics <note>A reference to Protestant reformers who viewed "blessing" merely as a prayer of thanks rather than a transformative act.</note>, who deny this blessing to pertain to the created things, but pretend it is always referred to God for thanksgiving. For if it were so, he would have said grace but once for that whole meal <note>original: "refection"</note>: but he did separately bless both the bread first, and afterward the fishes also, multiplying them by his said blessing (as *he did mankind and other creatures <margin>Gen. 1:22, 28.</margin> in the beginning by blessing them) and so working effectively some change or alteration in the very creatures themselves.

<margin>Luke 9.</margin> <margin>35. For me and the Gospel.]</margin> <margin>What it means to suffer for the Gospel.</margin> By "the Gospel" is signified not only the four Evangelists, but all Scriptures, and whatsoever Christ said that is not in Scripture: for he says in this very place, *He that shall be ashamed of my words, the Son of man will be ashamed of him* etc. Neither his own words only, but whatsoever the Apostles taught in word or writing: for our Savior says, *He that despises you, despises me.* For the defense of any or all of these and of every Article of the Catholic faith, we ought to die, and this is to lose our life for Christ and his Gospel.

<margin>36. Gain the whole World.]</margin> <margin>Acting against our own conscience.</margin> Let those note this, who for fear or flattery of the world condescend to obey the unjust laws of men regarding religion, against their own consciences: and are content for the rest of a few days of this life, and for saving their temporary goods, to lose their soul and the joys of heaven.

### ANNOTATIONS
#### CHAPTER 9.

<margin>
Elijah.
Moses.
</margin>
*4. Elijah with Moses.*) Moses represents the persons of all the Saints who shall have departed this life when Christ comes in his Majesty to judgment. And Elijah (who was then living <note>Elijah was traditionally believed to have been taken up to heaven alive in a whirlwind.</note>) figures the holy men who shall then be found alive when he comes in glory. Both shall then begin to reign with Christ in glory. <note>Bede on Mark chapter 9.</note>

<margin>
Elijah and John the Baptist as Hermits.
</margin>
*13. Elijah also is come.*) Elijah was zealous for God’s Law, a great rebuker of sin, and an <term>Eremite<note>A religious hermit living in isolation.</note></term>, and shall be the precursor of Christ in his second Advent. So was John before his first Advent: a zealot, a corrector, a hermit, and his precursor. <note>Theodoret in Thomas’s chain of commentary on this place.</note> See *St. Jerome* in the life of Paul the Hermit, that both Elijah and John the Baptist were counted the principal professors of that life.

<margin>
The name of JESUS works miracles.
</margin>
*38. In your name.*) Miracles are sometimes performed by the name of JESUS, regardless of the character of the men, when it is for the proof of a truth or for the glory of God. This was so much the case that *Julian* the Apostate <note>A Roman emperor who rejected Christianity and returned to paganism.</note> himself drove away devils with the sign of the Cross, as *St. Gregory Nazianzen* writes <note>Oration 1 against Julian; Theodoret, Book 3, Chapter 3 of his History.</note>. And so also heretics may perform miracles among the Heathen to prove any article of the Christian faith; but they never did, nor ever shall, work any miracle to prove any of their erroneous opinions—for instance, to prove that Christ is not really present in the Blessed Sacrament.

<header>HOLY WEEK. THE GOSPEL CHAPTER 11.</header>

# ANNOTATIONS
# CHAPTER 10.

<margin>Toleration and permission of evil.</margin>
4. *Permitted.*) Some things are permitted, though not approved or allowed, to avoid greater inconveniences. No man may do evil for any cause, but he may permit other men’s evils for various reasons: just as God himself does, who can do no evil. So does the Prince and Commonwealth permit lesser evils to avoid greater ones, and so may the Holy Church do much more (as St. Augustine says she does) <margin><note>original: "Aug. ep. 119 c. 19."</note> Augustine, Letter 119, chapter 19.</margin> being placed among much chaff and many weeds <note>original: "cockle"</note>, tolerate many things: and yet whatever is against faith and good life, she neither approves, nor ignores with silence, nor commits.

<margin>Marriage after divorce unlawful.</margin>
11. *And marries another.*) That which St. Matthew expressed more obscurely, and is mistaken by some—as though he meant that because of fornication a man might put away his wife and marry another—is here by this Evangelist (as also by St. Luke) put out of doubt, generally declaring that <margin>Luke 18:18.</margin> whoever puts away his wife and marries another commits adultery <note>original: "aduoutrie"</note>. <margin><note>original: "Aug. li. 1 de adult. coniug. c. 11 & ſequentibus."</note> Augustine, Book 1 on Adulterous Marriages, chapter 11 and following.</margin>

18. *None is good.*) None is entirely, substantially, and of himself good, but God: though by participating in God's goodness, men are truly also called good.

23. *A rich man.*) He is here called a rich man who places his confidence (as is expressed here) in his treasure, and would rather forsake his faith and duty to God than lose his riches—as do all those who live in Schism or Heresy <note>Refers to being outside the established Church</note> to save their goods.

<margin>Their reward in this life that forsake anything for God's sake.</margin>
30. *An hundred times so much.*) Sometimes God does so bless men also with worldly benefits who have forsaken all for him—such as St. Gregory, St. Augustine, and St. Paulinus. But the principal meaning <margin><note>original: "Hiero. in 19 Mat."</note> Jerome on Matthew 19.</margin> is that he will give to such men in this life an abundance of grace and spiritual comfort, and contentment <note>original: "contentatiō"</note> and joy of conscience (as those who have experienced it feel). These spiritual gifts exceed temporal comforts more than an hundred fold, so much so that he who has fully forsaken even small things for religion would not forsake religion to have all the world.

## A N N O T A T I O N S
## C H A P T E R  11.

<margin>Profaning of God's Church.</margin>
16. *Vessel through the temple.*] He could not abide to see the Temple of God profaned, no nor suffered those things to be done in it, which otherwise were not unlawful but honest, if they had been done in due place. How much less can he abide the profaning of Churches now with Heretical service and preaching of heresy and blasphemy?

17. *Den of thieves.*] If the Temple was then a den of thieves, because of profane and secular merchandise: how much more now, when the house appointed for the Holy Sacrifice and Sacrament of the Body of Christ, is made a den for the <term>Ministers of Calvin's bread|A derogatory term used by the Catholic translators for Protestant clergy who rejected the doctrine of the Real Presence of Christ in the Eucharist</term>?

---

## C H A P T E R  12.

> *He foretells to the Jews in a parable their most worthy <note>meaning "well-deserved"</note> reprobation, and the vocation of the Church of the Gentiles in their place. 10 himself being the headstone thereof. 13 He defeats the snare of the Pharisees and Herodians, about paying tribute to Caesar: 18 answereth also the invention of the Sadducees against the Resurrection: 28 also the opposition of a Scribe. 35 And so having put all the busy sects to silence, he turns and poses <note>challenges</note> them on the other side, because they imagined Christ should be no more but a man. 38 Bidding the people to beware of the Scribes, being ambitious and hypocrites. 41 He commends the poor Widow for her two mites, above all.*

---

<margin>

## ANNOTATIONS
### CHAPTER 12.

<margin>God is to be served first, and then the Prince.</margin>
17. *To God.*] These men were very circumspect and cautious to do all duties to Caesar, but for their duty to God they had no regard. So <term>Heretics|In this context, a term used by the Catholic authors to refer to Protestant reformers</term>, to flatter temporal Princes and use them to uphold their heresies, do not only insist upon men's duty to the Prince while hiding what is due to God, but also give to the Prince more than what is due, and take from God His right and duty. But Christ, while allowing Caesar his right, warns them also of their duty toward God. And that is what Catholics insist upon: Obey God, do as he commands, serve Him first, and then the Prince.

<margin>Leviticus 18:16. Deuteronomy 25:5.</margin>
<margin>Marrying the brother’s wife.</margin>
19. *His brother shall take.*] Note well here that the Law which says, "Thou shalt not marry thy brother's wife," is not the kind of law that allows no <term>dispensation|An exemption from a rule or usual requirement</term>, as if this marriage were against nature. For here the same Law says that in some cases, the brother not only might, but was then bound to marry his brother's wife.

<margin>Many truths are deduced from scripture which Heretics do not see.</margin>
24. *Not knowing the Scriptures.*] Who would have thought that the Resurrection was proved by this passage of Scripture cited by Christ? And yet we see that Christ deduces it from this, and charges these great Doctors and Masters (who claimed the knowledge of Scriptures for themselves) that it is their ignorance that they did not know how to deduce it so. It is no marvel, then, if the Holy Doctors and the Catholic Church sometimes make similar deductions and proofs where the Heretic does not or will not see as much; this is undoubtedly because he does not know the Scriptures (which he boasts of so much) nor the intent of the Holy Ghost in them. For example, when ancient fathers deduce from that passage—*It shall not be forgiven in this world nor in the world to come*—that there are sins remitted after this life in <term>Purgatory|A state of suffering or purification believed by Catholics to exist for those who die in God’s grace but still require cleansing from venial sins</term>. *See Matthew 12:32.*

<margin>Heretics are ignorant and without faith.</margin>
24. *The power of God.*] Even so do Heretics err in two ways: because they do not know the Scriptures, which they interpret contrary to the sense of the whole Church and of all the ancient fathers; and because they do not know the power of God—that just as He is able to raise the very same bodies again, so He can make His body present in many places. But being altogether faithless and not believing in His power, they dispute all such matters only by reason and their own imaginations.

---

# CHAPTER 13.

> *To his Disciples (prompted by the destruction of Jerusalem and the Temple) he foretells what things shall happen before the end of the world, specifically the Church's full preaching to all nations. 14 Then, what shall happen at the very end—namely, Antichrist with his massive persecution and deception, though only for a short time. 24 Then immediately the day of Judgment, 28 to our great comfort during those miseries under Antichrist. 32 As for the exact moment, it is not for us to know it, 33 but rather for every man to watch, so that we are not unprepared when he comes to each person particularly at death.*

## ANNOTATIONS
### CHAPTER 14.

<margin>Religious expense dedicated to Christ and his Church.</margin>
4. *This waste.*] Religious acts performed for Christ for the sake of symbolism, devotion, or honor—both during his life and now in the Holy Sacrament—are unjustly condemned by some (under the excuse of better spending such things on the poor).

6. *Leave her alone.*] Christ speaks up for the devout woman and defends her actions, just as we must answer the ignorant and malicious when they criticize good people for giving their property to the Church.

<margin>The real presence through Consecration.</margin>
22. *Bread.*] This is bread before the Sacramental Words <note>The words spoken by a priest to effect the transformation of the bread and wine.</note>, but once the Consecration is performed, the bread is made the flesh of Christ. <note>Ambrose, *On the Sacraments*, book 4, chapter 4.</note>

<margin>True blood under the appearance of wine.</margin>
23. *Chalice.*] Wine and water are put into the chalice, but are made into blood by the consecration of the heavenly word. Although you receive that which has the likeness and resemblance of wine (to avoid the revulsion that would come from the sight of blood), it is truly his blood. <note>Ambrose, ibid.</note>

<margin>Faith necessary in the Blessed Sacrament.</margin>
23. 24. *My body, My blood.*] Whoever does not believe what is said to be true falls from grace and salvation. <note>Epiphanius, in *The Well-Anchored* (*Ancoratus*).</note> Let us always trust God and never resist him, even if what he says seems absurd to our imagination or far surpasses our senses and understanding. For his words cannot mislead us, though our senses are easily deceived. Since he said, *This is my body*, let us never doubt the matter. <note>John Chrysostom, *Homily 83 on Matthew*, near the end.</note>

<margin>Peter.</margin>
71. *He began to curse.*] In this one Apostle, Peter—the first and chief in the order of Apostles, who represents the Church—both strengths and weaknesses were shown. This is because the Church consists of both the strong and the weak. <note>Augustine, *Sermon 13 on the Words of the Lord*.</note> Furthermore, our Savior wanted to show through the example of the chief Apostle that no man should be overconfident in himself, since not even Saint Peter could avoid the danger of being inconsistent. <note>Augustine, *Tract 66 on the Gospel of John*; Leo, *Sermon 9 on the Passion of the Lord*.</note>

<margin>The Priesthood of the New Testament.</margin>
...the Prophet saying, *The Law shall perish from the Priest and counsel from the Elders.* <note>Original: "Ancients."</note> But the Priesthood of the New Testament is to continue unto the end of the world, and has (as being the principal part of the Church) the assistance of the Holy Ghost forever promised, to teach it all truth: and for Peter, the chief Priest thereof under Christ, our Savior prayed, *That his faith should not fail*: and to the rest he said, *He that hears you, hears me.*

<margin>Execution of laws against innocents.</margin>
15. *To satisfy the people.*] Pilate should have suffered death, rather than by other men's provocation or commandment have executed an innocent: just as a Christian judge should rather suffer all extremity, than give sentence of death against a Catholic man for his faith.

<margin>Religious duty toward the bodies of Christ and his Saints.</margin>
46. *Buying a linen shroud.* <note>Original: "sindon."</note>] This duty done to Christ's body after his departure was exceedingly meritorious, and is therefore by holy Writ so often commended as an example to faithful men, to use all honor and devotion towards the bodies of Saints and holy persons.

### ANNOTATIONS
#### CHAPTER XVI.

<margin>The women’s devotion toward Christ’s body now dead. Mark 16:9; Matthew 28:9.</margin>
1. *Bought spices.*] Just as she <note>Mary Magdalene.</note> bestowed and used a costly ointment upon his body while he was still alive (Chapter 14:3)—with Christ himself defending and highly praising the act <note>Original: "fact." In this context, it refers to a deed or action.</note> against Judas and others who considered it wasteful and better spent elsewhere—so too, with great devotion and merit, she and these other women seek to anoint his dead body. This they did even though heretics <note>A term likely referring to Protestant reformers who criticized certain physical devotions.</note> or other simple people might claim such things are better given to the poor. Therefore, she was the first of all, and the others next, to see him after his Resurrection.

<margin>Christ's body under various forms.</margin>
12. *In another shape.*] Although Christ has only one physical shape natural to his person, through his omnipotence <note>The quality of having unlimited or sovereign power.</note> he may exist in any form and appear in the likeness of any other man or creature as he chooses. Therefore, let no one think it strange that he may be present under the form of bread in the Blessed <note>Original: "B."</note> Sacrament <note>The Eucharist or Holy Communion.</note>.

<margin>Not only faith. Matthew 28:20.</margin>
16. *He who believes.*] Take careful note: while this Evangelist mentions only faith and baptism, as though believing and being baptized were enough, St. Matthew adds these words of our Savior: *teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you*. This includes all good works and the complete righteousness of a Christian.

<margin>The gift of miracles.</margin>
17. *These signs shall follow.*] This does not mean that all Christians or true believers should perform miracles, but rather that some should have that gift to prove the faith for everyone. This is a grace or gift given to the entire Church, carried out by certain individuals for the improvement and benefit of all.

# THE ARGUMENT OF
## ST. LUKE'S GOSPEL.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut headpiece with a repeating pattern of scrolls and fleur-de-lis motifs.</image-desc>

St. Luke’s Gospel may be divided into five parts.
*The first part is of the Infancy both of the precursor <note>The "precursor" refers to John the Baptist, who preceded Jesus.</note> and of Christ himself: chapters 1 and 2.*
*The second, of the Preparation that was made for the manifestation of Christ: chapter 3 and a portion of chapter 4.*
*The third, of Christ’s manifesting himself by preaching and miracles, especially in Galilee: the other portion of chapter 4 until the middle of chapter 17.*
*The fourth, of his coming into Judea <note>Original: "Iurie."</note> towards his Passion: the other portion of chapter 17 until the middle of chapter 19.*
*The fifth, of the Holy Week of his Passion in Jerusalem: the other part of chapter 19 until the end of the book.*

<margin>Jerome in the Catalog <note>Referring to Jerome's *De Viris Illustribus* (On Illustrious Men).</note></margin>
<margin>2 Corinthians 8:18.</margin>
<margin>Luke 1:2.</margin>
<margin>Colossians 4:14.</margin>
<margin>2 Timothy 4:11.</margin>
<margin>Jerome in the Catalog.</margin>
<margin>* Constantius</margin>
<margin>Jerome against Vigilantius, book 2.</margin>
<margin>The Heretic <note>Vigilantius, a 4th-century priest who opposed the veneration of relics.</note> so considered the Catholics for their honoring of Saints and Relics.</margin>
<margin>* Constantius</margin>
*St. Luke was a follower <note>Original: "sectator." This implies a dedicated disciple or constant attendant.</note> (says St. Jerome) that is, a disciple of the Apostle Paul, and a companion of all his travels <note>Original: "peregrination."</note>. And we see the same in the Acts of the Apostles: where, from the 16th chapter, St. Luke puts himself in the company of St. Paul, writing thus in the history:* Forthwith we sought to go into Macedonia. *And in like manner, in the first person, commonly through the rest of that book. Of him and his Gospel, St. Jerome understands this saying of St. Paul:* We have sent with him the brother, whose praise is in the Gospel through all Churches. *Where he also adds: Some suppose that as often as Paul says in his Epistles,* According to my Gospel, *he means Luke's book. And again: Luke learned the Gospel not only from the Apostle Paul, who had not been with our Lord in the flesh, but from the other Apostles: which he himself also declares in the beginning of his book, saying,* As they delivered to us who themselves from the beginning saw, and were ministers of the word. *It follows in St. Jerome: Therefore he wrote the Gospel as he had heard, but the Acts of the Apostles he compiled as he had seen. St. Paul writes of him by name to the Colossians:* Luke the Physician salutes you. *And to Timothy:* Luke alone is with me. *Finally, of his end, St. Jerome writes: He lived eighty-four years, having no wife. He is buried at Constantinople; to which city his bones, with the relics of Andrew the Apostle, were moved <note>Original: "translated." In a religious context, this refers to the formal movement of holy relics from one place to another.</note> out of Achaia in the twentieth year of Constantius. And of the same translation <note>The movement of relics.</note> also in another place against Vigilantius the Heretic: It grieves him that the relics of the Martyrs are covered with precious coverings, and that they are not either tied in rags or thrown to the dunghill. Why, are we then \*sacrilegious when we enter the Churches of the Apostles? Was Constantius the Emperor sacrilegious, who moved to Constantinople the holy relics of Andrew, Luke, and Timothy, at which the devils roar, and the followers of Vigilantius confess that they feel their presence?*

*His sacred body is now at Padua in Italy, where it was again moved from Constantinople.*

<meta>This page transitions from the narrative of the Gospel text (the birth of John the Baptist and the Annunciation) into the scholarly and polemical annotations provided by the translators. These notes defend Catholic doctrine and traditional Latin Vulgate renderings against the Protestant translations of the 16th century.</meta>

138 THE GOSPEL CHAPTER 1.

# ANNOTATIONS
## CHAPTER 1.

<margin>Sacred Writers and holy Councils.</margin>
3. *Having diligently attained.*] By this we see that, although the Holy Spirit <note>original: "Holy Ghoft"</note> ruled the pen of the holy writers so that they might not err, they still used human means to search out and find the truth of the things they wrote about. Even so do Councils, and the President of them—God’s vicar <note>The Pope</note>—discuss and examine all causes by human means, with the assistance of the Holy Spirit concurring and directing them into all truth, according to Christ’s promise in *John 16:13*: as is manifest in the very first Council of the Apostles themselves at Jerusalem in *Acts 15:7 and 28.* Again, here we have a familiar preface by the Author to his friend, or to every godly Reader (signified by the name Theophilus <note>The name Theophilus means "Lover of God."</note>) concerning the cause, purpose, and manner of his writing; and yet this same preface is confessed Scripture, along with the whole book following. Do not marvel then if the Author of the second book of the Maccabees <margin>2 Maccabees 2 & 15.</margin> uses similar human speech both at the beginning and at the end; do not therefore reject that book as "no Scripture," as our Heretics <note>The translators are referring to Protestant reformers who removed the Deuterocanonical books (like Maccabees) from the biblical canon.</note> do, or think him anything less than a sacred writer.

6. *Just before God.*] Against the Heretics of this time, it is evident here that holy men are just, not only in the estimation of men, but in deed and before God.

<margin>True justification by observing the commandments.</margin>
6. *In all the commandments.*] Three things are to be noted here directly against the Heretics of our time. First, that good men do keep all of God's commandments; which the Heretics say are impossible to be kept. Again, that men are justified not by the mere "imputation" of Christ’s justice, nor by faith alone, but by walking in the commandments. Again, that the keeping and doing of the commandments is properly our justification.

<margin>Corrupt translation of Heretics. Justifications <note>original: "δικαιώματα"</note>.</margin>
6. *Justifications.*] This word is so common in the Scriptures (namely in *Psalm 118* <note>Psalm 119 in modern bibles.</note>) to signify the commandments of God, because the keeping of them is justification. The Greek is always so perfectly correspondent to this that the Heretics in this place (otherwise pretending to value the Greek highly) do not blush to say that they avoid this word on purpose to oppose the "justification of the Papists." And therefore one <note>Likely referring to Theodore Beza.</note> uses Cicero's word, *constituta* <note>original Latin: "constitutions" or "decrees"</note> in Latin, and his scholars in their English Bibles say, *Ordinances.* <margin>Beza in Annotations on the New Testament, 1556</margin>

14. *Joy and exultation.*] This was fulfilled, not only when he was born, but now also through the whole Church forever, in the joyful celebrating of his Nativity <note>The Feast of the St. John the Baptist.</note>.

<margin>The continence of priests.</margin>
23. *He departed.*] In the old Law (says St. Jerome), those who offered sacrifices for the people not only stayed out of their houses, but were purified for a time by being separated from their wives; they drank neither wine nor any strong drink, which are known to provoke lust. Much more must the Priests of the new Law, who must always offer sacrifices, be always free from marriage. *Against Jovinian, Book 1, chapter 19; and Epistle 50, chapter 3.* See also St. Ambrose in *1 Timothy 3.* Therefore, if there were any religion in Calvin’s "Communion," they would at least show as much reverence in this point as those in the old Law did for their sacrifices and the loaves of proposition <note>The Showbread (1 Samuel 21).</note>.

<margin>Often saying of the HAIL MARY <note>original: "AVE MARIE"</note>.</margin>
28. *Hail full of grace.*] Holy Church and all true Christian men much and often use these words brought from heaven by the Archangel, as much to honor Christ and our Blessed Lady, as also because they were the words of the first glad tidings of Christ's Incarnation and our Salvation. They are the very abridgement and sum of the whole Gospel. So much so <margin>Liturgy of James and Chrysostom; St. Athanasius on the Holy Mother of God; St. Ephrem in his prayer praising the Blessed Virgin; Ambrose in Luke, book 2; Jerome, epistle 140, explaining Psalm 44.</margin> that the Greek Church used it daily in the Mass.

<margin>Corrupt translation of Heretics. Full of grace <note>original Greek: "κεχαριτωμένη"</note>. Endued with grace <note>original Greek: "ἐχαρίτωσε"</note>. Full of sores <note>original Greek: "ἠλκωμένος"</note>.</margin>
28. *Full of grace.*] Note the excellent prerogatives of our Blessed Lady, and abhor those Heretics who make her no better than other common women. To take away her fullness of grace, they say here, *Hail freely beloved*, contrary to all meanings of the Greek word, which is at the least, *endued with grace*, as St. Paul uses it in *Ephesians 1* according to St. Chrysostom's interpretation; or rather, *full of grace*, as both Greek and Latin fathers have always understood it here. The Latins also read it so, namely St. Ambrose: *Well is she alone called "full of grace," who alone obtained the grace, which no other woman deserved, to be replenished with the author of grace.* And if the Heretics knew the nature of these Greek words as well as they claim, they might easily observe that they signify fullness; just as when they themselves translate a similar word in *Luke 16:20* as *full of sores.* Beza translates it as *ulcerosus* <note>original Latin: "ulcerous" or "full of ulcers"</note>.

<margin>Our Blessed Lady vowed virginity.</margin>
34. *I know not man.*] These words declare (says St. Augustine) that she had now vowed virginity to God. For otherwise, she would not have asked, *How shall this be done?* nor added, *because I know not man.* Indeed, if she had only said the first words, *How shall this be done?*, she would not have asked such a question about how a woman should bear a promised son if she intended to have sexual intercourse in marriage. *Chapter 4, On Virginity.* As if he should say: If she intended to know a man and thus have a child, she would never have asked, *How?*; but because the ordinary way was excluded by her vow of virginity, therefore she asks, *How?* And in asking *How?*, she plainly declares that she could not have a child by knowing man, because of her vow. See St. Gregory of Nyssa's sermon *On the Holy Nativity of Christ.*
