36. *Elizabeth thy Cousin.*] Because Elizabeth and our Lady <note>A traditional title for the Virgin Mary.</note> were cousins—one from the tribe of Levi and the other from the tribe of Judah—it is concluded that Christ descended from both tribes: Judah and Levi, the tribes of kings and priests. He himself is both a king and a priest, and the "Anointed One" (that is to say, the Messiah) by spiritual grace, just as those kings and priests were materially and physically anointed with oil. <note>original Latin: "August. 2 de Consens. Evang. c. 1." refers to St. Augustine’s work *On the Agreement of the Evangelists*, Book 2, Chapter 1.</note>

<margin>The blessed virgin MARY.</margin> 42. *Blessed art thou.*] At the very sound of our Lady's voice, the infant <note>John the Baptist in Elizabeth's womb.</note> and Elizabeth herself were filled with the Holy Spirit. She sang praises not only to Christ, but for his sake to our Blessed Lady, calling her blessed and her fruit <note>Jesus</note> blessed, just as the Church does by her words and example in the **HAIL MARY** <note>original Latin: "AVE MARIE".</note>.

<margin>Her excellence.</margin> <margin>Jerome's Preface to Zephaniah.</margin> 43. *Mother of my Lord.*] Although Elizabeth was an exceedingly just and blessed woman, the worthiness of God's mother so far exceeds her and all other women as the great light of the sun exceeds the little stars.

48. *Shall call me blessed.*] This prophecy is fulfilled when the Church keeps her feast days and honors her, and when the faithful in all generations say the **HAIL MARY** and other holy anthems of our Lady. Therefore, the Calvinists <note>The translators here criticize Protestant reformers who removed traditional Marian devotions.</note> are not among those generations who call our Lady blessed.

<margin>Mystery and significance in names.</margin> 63. *John is his name.*] We see that names are of great significance and importance, as God himself changed or gave names in both the Old and New Testaments: such as Abraham, Israel, Peter, and the most important of all, **JESUS**. Here we have **JOHN**, which signifies "God’s grace or mercy," or "God will have mercy." For he was the precursor and prophet of the mercy and grace that followed through **CHRIST JESUS**.

<margin>What names to be given in Baptism.</margin> Note also that just as names were given during circumcision then, so they are now given in Baptism (which corresponds to it). And as we see here and throughout the Old Testament, great respect was shown for names; therefore, we must avoid strange, profane, and secular names—which are too common nowadays—and instead, according to the <margin>* Council of Trent on Baptism, at the end.</margin> * Catechism of the holy Council of Trent, we should take the names of saints and holy people to remind us of their virtues.

<margin>True justice, not imputed.</margin> 75. *Justice before him.*] Here we also see that we may possess true justice <note>In this context, "justice" means righteousness or being "right" with God.</note>, not only in the eyes of men or by God "counting" it to us <note>The translators are arguing against the Protestant doctrine of "imputed righteousness," where a believer is declared righteous without an internal change.</note>, but in actual fact before him and in his sight; and that the purpose of Christ’s coming was to give men such true justice.

<margin>The Heretics criticize both the Greek and Latin text.</margin> <margin>Hebrew v.</margin> <margin>Beza.</margin> 78. *The orient.*] Do not wonder if the Heretics <note>The Protestant translators.</note> criticize the old authentic translation <note>The Latin Vulgate.</note> as if it differed from the Greek. Here they make a great fuss to criticize not only all the Greek interpreters of the Old Testament but also St. Luke himself for using the word <term>anatole <gloss>rising sun or dawn</gloss></term>, claiming it differs from the Latin text.

# ANNOTATIONS
## CHAPTER 2

<margin>Free will.</margin>
<margin>*Augustine, Questions to Simplician, book 1, question 2, volume 4.*</margin>
14. *Men of good Will.*] The birth of Christ gives peace of mind or salvation only to those who possess a good will, because he does not work our good against our wills, but rather with our wills concurring.

<margin>Our Blessed Lady full of deep contemplations.</margin>
19. *Kept all.*] Although little is spoken of our Lady regarding such matters in the Scriptures—because she was a woman and not admitted to teach or dispute in public about high mysteries—yet she knew all these mysteries. She wisely noted and meditated on all those things that were done and said concerning Christ, from the first hour of his Conception until the end of his life and his Ascension.

<margin>Humanity's ruin and damnation comes from themselves.</margin>
<margin>1 Peter 2:8.</margin>
<margin>2 Corinthians 2:16</margin>
34. *To the ruin.*] Therefore, he is for the ruin of some because they would not believe in him, and so they were the cause of their own ruin; as he is called elsewhere, *A stumbling stone, because many would stumble at him and so fall by their own fault.* Others he raised by his grace from sin to justice <note>meaning righteousness</note>, and so he was the resurrection of many. The Apostle uses similar speech, saying: *We are to some the odor of life, unto life: to others, the odor of death, unto death.* Not that their preaching was intended to cause death, but because those who would not believe their preaching willfully incurred deadly sin and damnation.

<margin>Holy widowhood.</margin>
<margin>1 Corinthians 7.</margin>
38. *A widow.*] Note that widowhood is mentioned here in praise of that state, even in the Old Testament. The fruit and, as it were, the "profession" of widowhood is commended here—namely, fasting, praying, and being continually in the Temple. This is just as St. Paul speaks more extensively regarding the era of the New Testament about widowhood and virginity, as these states are more suitable and convenient for the service of God.

<margin>Fasting as an act of religion.</margin>
37. *By fastings and prayers serving.*] "Serving" in the Greek is *latreuousa* <note>original: λατρευουσα</note>, which means performing divine worship to God, both by prayer and by fasting. Thus, fasting is *latreia* <note>original: λατρεια</note>, that is, an act of religion by which we worship God, just as we do by prayer. It is not used only to subdue our flesh, and certainly not (as the Reformers <note>original: "Heretikes"</note> would have it) merely as a matter of civic policy.

<margin>Dutiful obedience to parents.</margin>
51. *Subject to them.*] All children may learn from this how great their subjection and obedience to their parents ought to be, when Christ himself, being God, chose to be subject to his parents, who were but his creatures.

## CHAPTER 3

<margin>THE SECOND part: The preparation that was made for the manifestation of CHRIST.</margin>
> *John, to prepare all for Christ (as Isaiah had prophesied of him), baptizes them for penance, hinting at their rejection and the calling of the Gentiles. He also teaches and exhorts each group to do their duty. He shows that he himself is not Christ by explaining the difference between their two baptisms, and says that Christ will also judge those he has baptized. John’s imprisonment is noted. Christ, being himself also baptized by John, receives testimony from heaven, as the one whose lineage brings us back to God.*

# ANNOTATIONS
## CHAPTER III.

**20. *He added this above all.***] The fault of Princes and other great men—who not only cannot endure to hear of their faults, but also punish with death or imprisonment those who rebuke <note>original: "reprehend"</note> them for those same sins (especially if they are warned by Prophets and Priests on behalf of God)—is exceedingly great.

<margin>The reconciliation of Matthew and Luke in our Savior’s pedigree.</margin>
**23. *Of Heli.***] Although in St. Matthew, Jacob is listed as the father to Joseph, and here Heli is named, the situation was as follows: Mathan (named in St. Matthew), by his wife called Escha, fathered Jacob. After Mathan’s death, Melchi (named here in St. Luke) had a son named Heli by the same woman. Thus, Jacob and Heli were half-brothers sharing the same mother. When this Heli married and died without children, his brother Jacob married Heli’s widow according to the Law <note>This refers to Levirate marriage, a Jewish custom where a man was required to provide an heir for a deceased brother.</note> and fathered Joseph, thereby "raising up seed" for his brother Heli. Because of this, Jacob was the natural, biological father of Joseph (as St. Matthew writes), while Heli was his legal father according to the Law (as St. Luke signifies).
<note>Citations: Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 1, Chapter 7; Jerome, *Commentary on Matthew*, Chapter 1; Augustine, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, Book 2, Chapters 2 and 3.</note>

### -> A N N O T A T I O N S <-
#### -> CHAPTER 4 <-

<margin>The devil's temptations.</margin>
13. *Departed until a time.*) It is no wonder if the devil is often or always busy with Christian men, seeing that even after he was plainly overcome by Christ, he still did not give up on him entirely, but only left him for a time.

<margin>Miracles in one place and not in another.</margin>
<margin>Augustine, Letter 137.</margin>
23. *Done in Capernaum.*) God chooses the specific persons and places where he works miracles or grants benefits, even though he could do the same elsewhere if it suited his wisdom. He does the same when performing miracles through Saints—not in all places, nor toward all persons, but as it pleases him.

<margin>Christ's body is held in place above the laws of nature.</margin>
30. *Passing through the midst of them.*) Either by making himself invisible, or even more wonderfully, by passing through the crowd, just as he did through the door <note>This refers to Jesus's ability to pass through physical barriers, such as when he appeared to the disciples in a locked room after the Resurrection.</note>, his body being either without physical space or occupying the same space as other bodies. By all these actions mentioned in the Gospel, it is clear that he can change and govern his body as he desires, beyond the natural conditions of a physical body.

38. *Simon's wife’s mother.*) It is clear that Peter had a wife, but after being called to be an Apostle, he left her, as Saint Jerome writes in many places <note>original: "ep. 34 c. 2 ad Iulianum. Li. 1 adu. Iouin." Referring to Jerome’s Epistle 34 and his first book Against Jovinianus.</note>. See the Annotations for Matthew 8:19.

->A N N O T A T I O N S<-
->C H A P T E R 5<-

<margin>Peter’s ship.</margin>
3. *One ship Simon's.*) It is purposely expressed that there were two ships, and that one of them was Peter’s, and that Christ went into that one, and sat down in it, and that sitting he taught out of that ship: no doubt to signify the Church resembled by Peter’s ship, and that in it is the chair of Christ, and only true preaching.

<margin>Peter’s fishing.</margin>
6. *A great multitude of fishes.*) Likewise by this significant miracle wrought regarding Peter’s fishing, it is evidently shown what wonderful success Peter should have in converting men to Christ, both Jews and Gentiles. As when at one draught—that is to say, * at one Sermon—he drew into his ship, which is Christ’s Church, a great number of men, just as he did now with fishes: and so continually by himself and his Successors unto the world’s end. <margin>*Acts 2, 41. 4, 4.*</margin>

<margin>Peter’s coadiutors.</margin>
7. *Beckoned to their fellows.*) Peter had so much work that he called for help and joined unto him the other ship, representing to us his partners in the preaching of the Gospel, and the con-
junction of the Synagogue and the Gentile people unto Peter’s ship, that is, to the Church of Christ. <note>original: "Ambro. li. 4. in Luc. c. ult." — Reference to Saint Ambrose’s commentary on Luke, Book 4, final chapter.</note>

<margin>Peter’s preeminence in fishing for men’s souls.</margin>
10. *Thou shalt be taking men.*) That all this aforesaid did properly mean Peter’s labors to come, in the conversion of the world to Christ, and his prerogative before all men therein, it is evident by Christ’s special promise made to him severally and apart in this place, that he should be made the taker of men, though to others he gives also, as to Peter’s collaborators and assistants, the like office. *Matthew 4, 19.*

<margin>Zeal of souls.</margin>
19. *Went up upon the roof.*) A strange diligence in procuring bodily health from and by Christ: and an example for us of the like or greater diligence, to obtain salvation from him either for ourselves or our friends, and to seek his Church and Sacraments with whatever extraordinary effort.

<margin>The intercession of others.</margin>
20. *Whose faith.*) Great is God (says Saint Ambrose) and he pardons one group through the merits of others. Therefore, if you doubt your ability to obtain forgiveness for your great offenses, join to yourself intercessors; use the Church’s help, which may pray for you and obtain for you that which our Lord might deny to yourself. <note>original: "Amb. li. 5 in Luc." — Reference to Saint Ambrose, Book 5 on Luke.</note>

<margin>Priests do forgive sins.</margin>
24. *The Son of man on earth.*) By this act (says St. Cyril) it is clear that the Son of man has power on earth to forgive sins; which he said both for himself and for us. For he, as God being made man and Lord of the Law, forgives sins. And we also have obtained through him that wonderful grace. For it is said to his Disciples, *Whose sins you shall forgive, they are forgiven them.* And how should he not be able to forgive sins, who gave others the power to do the same?

<margin>Jerome on Matthew 9. Athanasius in the Life of St. Anthony. Augustine, Confessions, book 8, chapter 12. Bonaventure in the Life of St. Francis.</margin>
<margin>Forsaking all, and following Christ.</margin>
28. *Leaving all, he followed him.*) The <term>profane Julian</term> <note>Julian the Apostate, a 4th-century Roman Emperor who rejected Christianity and criticized the Gospels.</note> accused Matthew of too much lightness for leaving everything to follow a stranger at a single word. But indeed, here is seen the marvelous power of Christ’s word and internal working, which in a moment can change the heart of a man and cause him to value nothing—even the things most dear to him. This he did not only then in person, but he also does daily in the Church. For thus St. Anthony, St. Francis, and others, by hearing only the word of our Savior read in the Church, forsook all and followed him.

### ANNOTATIONS
->CHAPTER VI.<-

<margin>Heretics do not understand the Scriptures.</margin>
3. *Have you not read even this?*] The Scribes and Pharisees boasted most of their knowledge of the Scriptures: but our Savior often shows their great ignorance. Just so the <term>heretics</term> <note>In the context of this 16th-century commentary, "heretics" refers to Protestant reformers.</note> that nowadays boast most of the Scriptures and of their understanding of them, may soon be proved to understand little or nothing.

9. *Save a soul.*] By this it seems that Christ (as he almost always did at other times) did not only heal this man in body, but of some corresponding disease in his soul.

<margin>The Church's prayers at the times of giving holy Orders.</margin>
12. *The whole night.*] Our Savior prayed instantly, alone on the mountain outdoors, all night long, as a preparation for the appointment of his Apostles the day after: to give an example to the Church of praying urgently when priests are to be <term>ordained</term> <note>original: "ordered" — referring to the Sacrament of Holy Orders.</note>, and a lesson to us all what we should do for our own necessities, when Christ did so for other men's.

<margin>The name and dignity of Apostles</margin>
<margin>Calvin's Institutes book 4, chapter 8.</margin>
<margin>Psalm 108:8</margin>
<margin>Acts 1:20</margin>
<margin>Ephesians 2:20</margin>
<margin>Acts 14</margin>
<margin>1 Corinthians 12</margin>
<margin>Ephesians 4.</margin>
<margin>1 Corinthians 9:1</margin>
<margin>Philippians 2:25</margin>
<margin>Luke 4:18</margin>
<margin>Hebrews 3:1</margin>
13. *Whom he named Apostles.*] Here it is to be noted against our adversaries who deceitfully measure for the simple-minded the whole nature and quality of certain sacred functions, by the original meaning and scope of the names or words by which they are called. According to them, a Priest is but an "elder," and a Bishop, a "watchman" or "superintendent," so an Apostle is nothing but a "legate" or "messenger," and therefore (as they argue) <note>Referring to the marginal note for John Calvin's *Institutes of the Christian Religion*.</note> can make no laws nor prescribe or teach anything not expressed in his <term>mandate</term> <note>original: "mandatum" — the formal instructions or authority given to a representative.</note>. Know therefore against such deceivers, that such things are not to be ruled by the common meaning of the word or calling, but by the use and application of the holy writers, and in this point by Christ's own express naming. And so this word, *Apostle*, is a calling of Office, government, authority, and most high dignity given by our Master, especially to the College of the Twelve: Whom he endowed beyond what the common <term>etymology</term> <note>The study of the origin and historical meaning of words.</note> of their name requires, with power to bind and loose, to punish and pardon, to teach and rule his Church. Out of which position and dignity, which is called in the Psalms and in the Acts, a "Bishopric," when Judas fell, Matthias was chosen to supply it, and was numbered among the rest, who were as founders or foundations of our religion, as the Apostle terms them. Therefore to that college this name belongs by special assignment and prerogative, though afterward it was by use of the Scriptures extended to St. Paul and St. Barnabas, and sometimes to the Apostles' successors: as also (by the like use of Scriptures) to the first converters of countries to the faith, or their assistants in that function. In which sense St. Paul claims to be the Corinthians' Apostle, and names Epaphroditus the Philippians' Apostle: as we call St. Gregory and his disciple St. Augustine, our Apostles of England. In all which uses, it ever signifies dignity, rule, fatherhood, leadership, and primacy in the Church of God: according to St. Paul in 1 Corinthians 12: "He has placed in his Church, first indeed Apostles," etc. Whereby we may see that St. Peter's dignity was a wonderful eminent prerogative and sovereignty, when he was the head not only of other Christian men, but the head of all Apostles, yes, even of the College of the Twelve. And if our adversaries wished to have learned any profitable lesson by the word Apostle, more profitably and truly they might have gathered, that Christ called these his principal officers, *Apostles*, or *The Sent* (he himself also specially and above all others being <note>original: "Missus"</note> *The Sent*, and called also Apostle in the Scriptures) to warn us by the nature of the word, that none are true Apostles, Pastors, or Preachers, that are not specially sent and called, or that cannot show by whom they be sent, and that all heretics therefore be rather <term>apostates</term> <note>Those who have abandoned their religious faith or principles; a play on the word "Apostle."</note> than Apostles, because they are not sent, nor duly called, nor chosen to preach.

<margin>Peter's preeminence.</margin>
14. *Simon.*] Peter in the numbering of the Apostles, is always first named and preferred before Andrew his elder brother and senior by calling. See the *Annotation for Matthew 10, 2.*

<margin>All persecution for Christ, is a blessing.</margin>
23. *Be glad.*] The common miseries that fall to the true preachers and other Catholic men for Christ's sake, such as poverty, famine, mourning, and persecutions, are indeed the greatest blessings that can be, and are meritorious of the reward of heaven. Conversely, all the felicities of this world without Christ, are indeed nothing but woe, and the entrance to everlasting misery.

<margin>The vanity of Heretical preachers.</margin>
26. *Shall bless you.*] This woe pertains to the heretics of our days, that delight to have the people's praises and blessings and shouts, preaching pleasant things on purpose for their <term>itching ears</term> <note>A biblical reference to those who seek out teachers who tell them only what they want to hear.</note>.

<summary>This page concludes Jesus's teachings on building one's life on a solid foundation and begins the commentary on Chapter 6. The annotations focus on defending the specific authority and divine "sending" of the Apostles and the primacy of St. Peter against Protestant interpretations.</summary>
<keywords>Apostles, St. Peter, primacy, Holy Orders, ordination, John Calvin, heretics, persecution, St. Augustine of Canterbury, Sermon on the Plain</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the annotations for Chapter 6, specifically regarding the ethics of lending, and begins Chapter 7 of the Gospel of Luke. The text continues the narrative of Jesus’s ministry in Capernaum.</meta>

...ears: as did the false prophets, when they were praised and commended for it by the worldly-minded Jews. <note>original: "carnal Ievves" — those focused on physical laws and rewards rather than spiritual truth.</note>

<margin>Against usury.</margin>
*35. Lend, hoping for nothing back.)* In this passage, we may seem to be encouraged to lend to those whom we think are unable or unlikely to ever repay us; this should be considered a piece of advice rather than a strict command, except in cases of extreme necessity. However, it can also be taken as a rule against <term>usury</term> <note>Lending money with the expectation of profit or interest, a practice long debated in Church history.</note>, which is to say, the expectation of receiving back more than the money lent. This is forbidden just as it is condemned in other parts of Scripture and is considered a violation of natural law and international justice. It is a great shame and pity that it is so widely practiced or tolerated among Christians, often hidden or disguised under the appearance of other types of contracts.

->ANNOTATIONS<-
### CHAPTER VII.

<margin>Building of Churches, Monasteries, etc.</margin>
5. *Built a Synagogue.*] Just as at that time building a synagogue was acceptable to God and earned the prayers of the faithful people for whose use it was made, so now—much more so in the <term>New Testament</term><note>The era of the Christian covenant following the life of Jesus.</note>—to build a church, monastery, college, or any similar work for the honor and service of God is pleasing to him and earns the prayers of the good people for whose use such things are established.

<margin>External signs of more than common devotion.</margin>
44. *Into thy house.*] This is a strong approval of extraordinary works and signs of outward devotion, which seem to worldly men (though otherwise faithful) to be often unnecessary or unacceptable. This Simon was perhaps of good will, and therefore (as various others did elsewhere) invited Christ to his house, not out of curiosity or a desire to trap him, as some others did, but out of affection, as it seems from Christ’s familiar talk with him. Nevertheless, his duties toward him were only ordinary; but the anointing, washing, kissing, and wiping of his feet in the way the woman did were further signs of more than common love. This is like the devotion of men or women who go on a pilgrimage and devoutly kiss the holy <term>memories</term><note>Relics or shrines associated with Christ and the saints.</note> of Christ and his Saints. This is nothing more than an outward expression of their affection and proof that they love much, in a way that the average Christian man does not.

<margin>Justification is not attributed to faith alone.</margin>
50. *Thy faith.*] The forgiveness of her sins, which was previously attributed to <term>charity</term><note>Active love and good works.</note>, is now also said to come from her faith. By this, you may know that it commonly proceeds from both—and from hope as well—even though only one is named. Because when there are several causes working together toward one effect, the scriptures commonly name only one, especially that which is most suited to the purpose and time, without excluding the others. Therefore, his working of miracles upon any person is attributed to the faith of those on whom or at whose desire they are done. Because he performed his miracles to lead all men to believe in him, he specifically required faith from them—namely, before other things—asking whether they believed he was able to do what they requested. Without this, it would have been a mockery or a testing of him rather than a true desire for a benefit at his hands.

## ANNOTATIONS
### CHAP. VIII.

<margin>Holy women that followed Christ.</margin>
3. *That did minister.*] It was the custom of the Jews that women of their substance did minister meat and drink and cloth to their teachers, going about with them. Which because it <margin>1 Corinthians 9:5, 12.</margin> might have been <term>scandalous</term><note>In the biblical sense, "scandalous" refers to something that might cause others to stumble in their faith or misunderstand the nature of the ministry.</note> among the gentiles, Saint Paul makes mention that he used it not. And they ministered to our Lord of their substance for this cause, that he whose spiritual benefits they reaped, might reap their <term>carnal things</term><note>Meaning their material or physical goods, such as food and clothing.</note>.

<margin>The brethren of Christ.</margin>
20. *Thy brethren.*) These brethren of our Lord, were not the sons of the <term>B. Virgin MARIE</term><note>The Blessed Virgin Mary.</note> the mother of God, as Helvidius wickedly taught: neither are they to be thought (as some others <margin>Jerome, *Against Helvidius*, chapter 9. <note>original: "Hiero. cōt. Heluid. c. 9."</note></margin> say) the sons of Joseph by another wife: for (as Saint Jerome writes) not only our Lady was a virgin, but by reason of her, Joseph also: that our Savior might be born of a virginal matrimony. <margin>Ibid, chapter 8.</margin> But they are called his brethren (according to the usual speech of the Scriptures) because they were his cousins, either the sons of Joseph’s brother, or (as the more received opinion is) the sons of our Lady’s sister called MARY of James, which James therefore is also called the brother of our Lord.

<margin>A third place after this life.</margin>
55. *Her spirit returned.*) This returning of the souls again into the bodies of them whom CHRIST and his Apostles raised from death (especially Lazarus who had been dead four days) does evidently prove a <term>third place</term><note>A reference to Purgatory or the "Bosom of Abraham" (Limbus Patrum), arguing that if a soul returns to a body, it must have been in a temporary state rather than in the finality of Heaven or Hell.</note> against our adversaries, who say every one goes straight to Heaven or to Hell. For it cannot be thought that they were called from the one or the other, and therefore from some third place.

->ANNOTATIONS<-
->ON CHAPTER IX.<-

<margin>The Transfiguration.</margin> 27. *Until they see.*) To the Apostles, who were to preach the kingdom of God and to suffer so much misery for the same in this world, he will show his glory, and give them a taste of his own joyful state and of his Saints in heaven, calling there Moses and Elias <note>The Greek form of Elijah</note>, that the Law and Prophets might be witnesses of the same. See the annotation upon St. Matthew chapter 17, 2.

<margin>Schismatics.</margin> 53. *Face to go to Jerusalem.*) The Samaritans were <term>Schismatics</term> <note>Those who create a division or "schism" in the church, separating themselves from the main body of believers</note> from the Jews, and had a <margin>John 4:9; 1 Kings 12:27; Tobit 1.</margin> schismatical temple on mount Gerizim, for the purpose of drawing men there from God’s temple in Jerusalem, where alone was the true and, as it were, the Catholic service and Sacrifice unto God. Therefore they did not gladly receive our Savior, because they perceived he was going to Jerusalem.

<margin>Desire of revenge.</margin> 53. *He rebuked them.*) Neither justice nor all rigorous punishment of sinners is here forbidden, nor is the act of Elias <note>Referring to Elijah calling down fire from heaven in 2 Kings 1</note> reprimanded, nor the Church or Christian Princes blamed for putting <term>Heretics</term> <note>In this historical context, "heretics" referred to those holding beliefs contrary to established Church doctrine</note> to death:

<margin>The Church’s severity.</margin> but that none of these should be done for desire of our particular revenge, or without discretion, and regard for their amendment, and as an example to others. Therefore St. Peter used his power upon <margin>Acts 5.</margin> Ananias and Sapphira, when he struck them both down to death for defrauding the Church.

<margin>Looking back.</margin> 62. *No man looking back.*) It is a dangerous temptation for a man that has lost or left his goods for Christ, to look much back at them, and to remember with delight the pleasures and eases of this world; for it breeds in him discontent with the troubles and crosses that are incident to the state of such as fully follow Christ. In which case a man should ever look forward towards heaven, and never backward to the world.

<meta>This page continues the annotations for the Gospel of Luke, chapter 10. # ANNOTATIONS
## CHAPTER 10

<margin>The humble, unlearned Catholic knows Christ better than the proud, learned heretic.</margin>
21. *To little ones*) By this passage, a common craftsman should not assume that God has revealed all truth to him and therefore refuse to be taught by the learned. For Christ did not later endow fishermen and common men, or any others, with the gifts of wisdom and tongues without their own industry, study, and teaching. Though at the beginning, through great providence, he did so, so that it might be clear to the world that all nations were converted to him not by the persuasion of cunning orators or subtle debaters, but by the plain force of his grace and truth—which Saint Augustine considers greater than all other miracles. Furthermore, we are taught by this passage that the poor, humble, obedient children of the Church know by their faith the high mysteries of Christ's Divinity, and his presence in the Blessed Sacrament, and such things, more than Arius, Calvin, and other similar proud Scribes and Pharisees. <note>Arius was a 4th-century priest whose teachings on the nature of Christ were declared heretical; John Calvin was a primary leader of the Protestant Reformation.</note>

<margin>The commandments are possible to be kept.</margin>
28. *This do.*) Not by faith alone, but by keeping God's commandments we obtain life everlasting; not only by believing, but by doing. The heretics <note>Referring to Reformers who taught that human nature was too fallen to fulfill the Law.</note> say that it is impossible to keep this commandment of loving God with all our heart. But the Scriptures give us examples of many who have kept and fulfilled it, as far as is required in this life. *1 Kings 14:8; 2 Chronicles 15:15; Psalm 118:10; Ecclesiasticus 47:9, 10; 2 Kings 20:3; Luke 1:5.* <note>The original cites "3. reg." and "4 Reg." which are the Vulgate titles for 1 and 2 Kings; "2. Par." is 2 Chronicles.</note> And if it were impossible to keep it, and yet Christ proposed it as the means to obtain life everlasting, he would have been mocking this lawyer and others, not teaching them.

<margin>Second Council of Orange, chapter 25; Council of Trent, Session 6, chapter 1.</margin>
<margin>The parable of the wounded man, explained.</margin>
30. *Half dead.*) Here is symbolized man, wounded very severely in his understanding and free will, and all other powers of soul and body, by the sin of Adam. Yet, neither understanding, nor free will, nor the rest, were extinguished in man or taken away. The Priest and Levite signify the Law of Moses; this Samaritan is Christ, the Priest of the New Testament; the oil and wine are his Sacraments; the host <note>original: "host," here meaning the innkeeper</note> signifies the priests, his ministers. By this it is shown that the Law could not recover the spiritual life of mankind from the death of sin—that is, justify man—but Christ alone. Through his passion and the grace and virtue of it, administered in and by his Sacraments, Christ justifies and increases the justice of man, healing and enabling free will to do all good works.

<margin>The Contemplative or Religious life is better than the Active and secular life.</margin>
<margin>Vows and those who take them.</margin>
42. *Mary the best part.*) Two notable examples: one of the Active life in Martha, the other of the Contemplative life in Mary. These represent to us that in the Holy Church there should always be some to serve God in both of these distinct ways. The contemplative life is preferred here over the active. The "Religious" <note>Members of monastic orders like monks and nuns.</note> of both sexes are in that more excellent state. Therefore, our Protestants have wholly abandoned them from their commonwealth, which the true Church never lacked. But to tell the truth, they have neither Martha nor Mary. May our Lord give them grace to see their misery. If ours <note>The Catholic monastics.</note> were not living up to their profession, or had degenerated, why have the Protestants not created new ones? If our Church’s "Votaries" <note>Those bound by religious vows.</note> vowed unlawful things—Chastity, Poverty, Obedience, Pilgrimage—what other Votaries or lawful vows do the Protestants have? For, to offer voluntarily by vow (besides the keeping of God’s commandments, to which we are bound by precept and promise in our Baptism) our souls, bodies, goods, or any other acceptable thing to God, is an act of sovereign worship belonging to God alone. There was never a true religion without such vows and Votaries. If there are none in their whole church who profess contemplation, or who vow anything at all to God voluntarily, neither in their bodies nor in their goods: God and the world know they have no Church or religion at all.

## CHAPTER 11

->He teaches a form of prayer, and exhorts us to pray insistently, assuring us that God will thus give us good things. The Jews blaspheme his casting out of Devils and ask for a miracle from heaven; he defends his actions, also foretelling the Devil’s expulsion by him out of the world (that is, the calling of the Gentiles) and his re-entry into their nation, along with their rejection though he is of their flesh, and also their final, most deserved damnation. Again, to the Pharisees and Scribes he cries "Woe," as they are the authors of the said rejection now at hand.<-

## ANNOTATIONS
### CHAPTER 11.

<margin>Bede upon this place.</margin>
27. **Blessed is the womb.**) Let us also (says Venerable Bede) lift up our voice with the Catholic Church, of which this woman was a figure: let us lift up our hearts among the people, and say to our Savior, *Blessed be the womb that bore thee, and the breasts which thou didst suck*. <note>Original Latin: "Beatus venter qui te portavit, et ubera quae suxisti."</note> For blessed indeed is the mother which bore the King that rules heaven and earth for ever.
<margin>Our Blessed Lady.</margin>

29. **The sign of Jonah.**) Of all miracles, his Resurrection—after he had been, according to his body, in the grave, and according to his soul, in Hell for three days—was the greatest, and most convinces the incredulous Jews: and therefore he says he will not give them a greater or more evident sign than that.
<margin>The sign of Jonah.</margin>

<margin>Sirach 3, 33.</margin>
<margin>Daniel 4, 24</margin>
<margin>Tobit 4, 12,</margin>
<margin>11, 9.</margin>
<margin>Matthew 25, 35, 42.</margin>
41. **Give alms.**) The great force of alms is signified here and in various places of holy scripture. In one place, they extinguish sin; in another, they redeem sins; in another, they deliver from death; in another, our judgment to heaven or hell is attributed to them being given or omitted; and here they make clean and satisfy for the Jews' former offenses. For (as St. Augustine says in chapter 70 of his *Enchiridion* <note>A handbook on Christian faith, hope, and love.</note>) alms-deeds do not profit a man who has a will to continue in his sins, but they are to be done as a propitiation to God for former offenses. Now, how well the Protestants like this doctrine, so evidently set forth in Scripture, let the impartial judge, and how well it agrees with their "faith alone" <term>Sola Fide: the Protestant doctrine that salvation comes through faith without the necessity of good works.</term> doctrine.
<margin>The force of alms.</margin>

46. **Woe to you Lawyers.**) These were <term>Lawyers: Doctors of the Mosaic Law</term>, otherwise called Scribes. Shall we therefore cry out against all lawyers now, or should the name of lawyer be hateful to us because of these naughty lawyers among the Jews? Much less should the name of Priests be hateful (as heretics would have it) because of the Jewish priests who were so busy against our Savior.
<margin>The Lawyers and Priests of the old Testament.</margin>

## ANNOTATIONS
### CHAPTER 12.

<margin>Open confession of our faith.</margin>
8. *Everyone who confesses.*] A Catholic is bound to confess their faith when called to account or examined by a Jew, a non-believer, or a heretic concerning the same. It is not enough to keep Christ in one's heart; one must also acknowledge him in words and deeds. And to deny Christ, or any article of the Catholic faith, out of shame or fear of any earthly creature, carries no less a punishment than being denied, refused, and forsaken by Christ at the hour of death before all his angels. This is a far more significant presence and <term>Consistory<note>A 'consistory' is a formal council or court, usually of a religious nature.</note></term> than any earthly court or session where people can be called for their faith in this world.

<summary>This page contains Jesus' teachings on the responsibility of those with knowledge of God's will, the divisions the Gospel brings to families, and the importance of resolving spiritual debts. It also includes a significant Catholic annotation on the necessity of publicly confessing one's faith under trial.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Chapter 12 of Luke's Gospel, specifically focusing on how the faithful should conduct themselves under interrogation and how they should view earthly wealth, before transitioning into Chapter 13's warnings about repentance and the fate of Jerusalem.</meta>

### CHAPTER 13. ACCORDING TO ST. LUKE.

<margin>The Holy Ghost teaches every unlearned Catholic to give a sufficient reason for their faith.</margin>
11. **Be not careful.**] This is intended so that the poor, unlearned Catholic should not be discouraged or make the excuse that they are a simple person, unable to answer cunning <term>Heretics</term><note>In this 16th-century context, "heretics" refers to Protestant reformers who challenged Catholic doctrine.</note>, or to give a reason for their belief, and therefore must suffer or say anything rather than appear before them. Our Master gives them comfort, promising that the Holy Ghost shall always put into their hearts at the time of their appearance that which shall be sufficient for the purpose. This does not mean that everyone called before the adversaries of faith will always be endowed with extraordinary knowledge to dispute and refute, as the Apostles and others in the early Church were; rather, it means that God will always give to the simple person who trusts in Him sufficient courage and words to confess their belief. For such a person, when called before the Commissioners, says enough and defends themselves sufficiently when they answer that they are a Catholic, and that they will live and die in that faith which the Catholic Church throughout all Christian countries has taught and continues to teach, and that this Church can provide a reason for all the things they demand of him.

<margin>The involvement of Clergy in worldly affairs.</margin>
<margin>In the Life of Augustine, chapter 19. Book on the Work of Monks, chapter 29.</margin>
14. **Who hath appointed?**] Christ refused to meddle in this temporal matter, partly because the demand came from greed and ill intentions, and partly to give an example to Clergymen that they should not be withdrawn by secular affairs and controversies from their primary duties of praying, preaching, and spiritual leadership. However, this does not wholly forbid them from all actions pertaining to worldly business, especially where and when the honor of God, the increase of religion, the peace of the people, and the spiritual benefit of the parties require it. In such cases, St. Augustine (as <term>Possidius</term><note>Possidius was a friend of St. Augustine who wrote his biography.</note> writes) was often occupied for whole days in ending worldly controversies, and he wrote of this himself, not doubting that he would have a reward for it in heaven.

<margin>Meritorious works.</margin>
21. **Rich toward God.**] A person is rich toward God when, through goods bestowed upon the poor, they have a store of <term>merits</term><note>The theological idea that good deeds, performed through grace, are rewarded by God.</note> and the prayers of many who received their charity, which procure mercy for them at the day of death and judgment. This is what is called "treasure laid up in heaven," where the barns are large enough. The necessity of such charity is shown here by Christ himself to be so great, and so acceptable to God, that rather than lacking its fruit, they should sell all they have and give to the poor.

<margin>Charity (Alms).</margin>
34. **Where your treasure is.**] If a rich man, distracted by his worldly treasure, cannot set his heart upon heaven, let him send his money there before him by giving it as charity to those who will pray for him; then his heart will follow his purse there.

# CHAPTER XIII.

->*He threatens the Jews that they will soon be forsaken unless they perform penance, and he shames them for speaking ill of him for his miraculous good deeds on the Sabbath. He describes the heartache they will feel at the last day to see themselves excluded from the glory of this kingdom while the Gentiles are admitted in their place. He foretells that he does not fear Galilee, but that the obstinate and rejected Jerusalem will insist on murdering him, just as it did his messengers before and will do after him.*<-

## ANNOTATIONS
### CHAP. XIII

<margin>Numbers 16, 1 Maccabees 3, Acts 5.</margin>
<margin>Some are punished as an example.</margin>
2. *These Galileans*.) It is God’s mercy that he does not immediately punish all offenders, but only a few as a warning to all: just as for <term>Schism</term><note>A formal split or division within the church.</note> he does not strike down all those who have forsaken the Church and the lawful priests, as he did to <term>Korah</term><note>original: "Core," the leader of a rebellion against Moses in Numbers 16.</note> and his accomplices: or as he does not take revenge on all who rob churches, as he did to Heliodorus: or all who vow and then take back their gifts to God, as Ananias and Sapphira. A few, therefore, because of their just deserts, are handled this way as an example, to provoke all others guilty of the same crimes to do <term>penance</term><note>Repentance or acts of reparation for sin.</note>. If they do not do so in this life, they shall all assuredly perish in the next world. <note>original Latin: "Optatus li. 1 cont. Parmen. sub finem" — referring to the writings of St. Optatus against the Donatist Parmenian.</note>

### ANNOTATIONS
### CHAPTER 14.

<margin>Free will.</margin>
<margin>Heretics may be compelled to the Catholic faith by penal laws.</margin>
<margin>Letter 50, a little after the beginning; Letter 204; and Book 1 against the letter of Gaudentius, chapter 25.</margin>
23. *Compel them.*) The powerful persuasion that God uses—both externally through the force of his word and miracles, and internally by his grace to bring us to him—is called "compelling." This does not mean he forces anyone to come to him against their own will, but that he can change and soften a hard heart, making one willing who previously was not. Saint Augustine also applies this "compelling" to the penal laws <note>Laws that impose punishments for non-conformity</note> which Catholic Princes justly use against Heretics and Schismatics. He proves that those who are subject to the Catholic Church by their prior profession in Baptism, but have since departed into Sects, may and ought to be compelled back into the unity and society of the universal Church. Therefore, in this sense, according to the first two parts of the parable, the Jews (first) and the Gentiles (secondly)—who never before believed in Christ—were invited only by fair and sweet means. But by the third part, those are invited whom the Church of God has power over because of their promise in baptism; therefore, they are to be called back not only by gentle means, but by just punishment as well.

### ANNOTATIONS
### CHAPTER 15.

<margin>Joy in heaven for every penitent.</margin>
7. *Then upon ninety-nine just.*) Neither God, nor the Saints in heaven, nor men on earth, for all that, value penitent sinners more than they do those who continue to be just and godly. However, because of the sudden emotion and present feeling of joy that a person takes and expresses in such a change and new-found goodness, it is signified here that the conversion of every sinner is exceedingly acceptable to God. It gives his Saints a new cause for joy and thanksgiving to God in a different way than the continued righteousness of the just does.

<margin>The Angels and Saints know our hearts.</margin>
10. *Before the Angels.*) The Angels and other celestial spirits in heaven rejoice at every sinner’s conversion. They know about us then and care for us; indeed, our hearts and inward repentance are open to them. How then can they not hear our prayers? And between Angels and the blessed souls of Saints, there is no difference in this case, the one being as highly exalted as the other and <margin>Matthew 22:30</margin> as near to God—in whom and by whom alone they see and know our affairs—as the other.

<margin>The Blessed Sacrament and Sacrifice of the Altar.</margin>
23. *The fatted calf.*) This feasting and festivity (says Saint Augustine in <note>original: "li. 2, qu. Euang. c. 33 to. 4."</note> *Book 2, Questions on the Gospels, chapter 33, volume 4*) is now celebrated throughout the whole world as the Church is enlarged and spread. For that calf, in the body and blood of our Lord, is both offered to the Father and also feeds the whole house. And as the calf signifies the Blessed Sacrament of the body and blood of Christ, so the first robe <note>referred to in earlier verses as the "first stole"</note> may signify our innocence restored in baptism, and the rest signify other graces and gifts given to us in the other Sacraments.

-> ## A N N O T A T I O N S <-
-> ### C H A P. XVI. <-

<margin>Good works.</margin>
**8. *The lord praised.***) This man's deceiving of his master is not praised, nor are we authorized by his deed to gain wealth unjustly in order to have the means to give alms. Rather, his **prudence** is commended—in that he provided so substantially for himself while his master's goods were in his hands. This is noted not as a virtue, but as a worldly policy; it is proposed as an example of the careful provision that rich men (who are God's <term>stewards</term> on earth) should make for their souls before they are removed from their <term>bailiffship</term> <note>an old term for the office of a steward or manager</note> and called to account, which is the day of their death. It also serves as a condemnation of the folly and negligence of faithful men, who, knowing they will eventually leave their offices and knowing they might gain salvation through their money, have so little regard for it.

<margin>Alms are meritorious.</margin>
**9. *They may receive.***) A great comfort to all who give great alms, and a wonderful force and virtue in alms-giving; <margin>*Tobit 12:9; Matthew 25.*</margin> besides the merit of the work of mercy, which (as is said in other places of Scripture) purges sin and gains heaven, it also procures not only the prayers of their <term>beadsmen</term> <note>people who pray for a benefactor, often in exchange for alms</note> on earth

### CHAPTER 17. ACCORDING TO SAINT LUKE.

<margin>Jerome, Question 6 to Algasia, volume 3. Ambrose on Luke. Augustine, Sermon 35 on the words of the Lord, chapter 1. Gregory, Morals, book 21, chapter 14. Augustine, book 2 of Questions on the Gospels, question 31. Chrysostom, homily 33 to the people of Antioch, volume 5.</margin>
on earth, but also through their patronage in heaven. By this, the prayers of Saints for the living—<margin>The Saints pray for us.</margin> namely for those to whom they were indebted during their lives—are proven. Indeed, they are in such favor with God that they may and do receive their friends, who were once their benefactors, into their mansions in heaven, just as the farmers whom the steward helped might receive their friend into their earthly houses. This also suggests to us that alms given specifically to holy men—who, through their merits and prayers, are great in God's grace—may help us much more than our charitable deeds done for common people in need, although those are of exceeding great merit as well. See all this in the following Doctors <note>The "Doctors" refer to the authoritative Teachers and Church Fathers cited in the margin.</note>.

<margin>Marriage after divorce is unlawful.</margin>
18. *And marries.*) The good of Marriage among all nations and people lies in the offspring and the faithfulness of chastity; but among the people of God, it also consists in the holiness of the Sacrament. Because of this, it is a heinous crime to marry again as long as the parties live, even if a divorce has been made. Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage*, chapter 24, volume 6. See the Annotations upon Mark 10, 11.

<margin>Unmerciful rich men.</margin>
22. *Of the Angels.*) Angels carry the souls of good men to heaven now, just as they carried his <note>Lazarus's</note> to Abraham’s bosom then. See here the reward of poverty, affliction, and patience; and on the contrary, the end and reward of wealth joined with unmercifulness. Note also here that at the day of every person's death there is a particular judgment, and therefore the soul does not sleep nor hang in suspense until the general judgment.

<margin>Zechariah 9:11; Isaiah 42:7. Augustine on Psalm 85; Epistle 99.</margin>
<margin>Abraham's Bosom. Limbo of the Fathers. Christ descended into Hell and delivered the fathers.</margin>
22. *Abraham's Bosome.*) Abraham’s Bosom is the resting place for all those who died in a perfect state of grace before Christ's time, as heaven was previously shut to humanity. In Zechariah, it is called a "lake without water" <note>original: "lake vvvithout vvater"</note>, and sometimes a prison; but theologians most commonly call it the <term>Limbo of the Fathers (Limbus Patrum)</term>, because it is thought to have been the higher part or the edge of Hell. The places of punishment are much lower than it, which is why they are called *the lower hell* <note>original: "Infernum inferius"</note>. Where this mansion of the fathers stood, or whether it was a part of Hell, Saint Augustine is uncertain; but that such a place existed, neither he nor any Catholic ever doubted. All the Church Fathers state with certainty that our Savior, when descending into Hell, went there specifically and delivered those fathers from that dwelling. Irenaeus, book 4, ch. 39; Eusebius, *Demonstration of the Gospel*, book 10, ch. 8; Nazianzen, *Oration 2 on Easter*; Chrysostom, vol. 5; Epiphanius on the heresy of Tatian; Ambrose on the Paschal Mystery, ch. 4; Jerome on Zechariah 9; Augustine, Epistle 99 and *City of God* book 20, ch. 15; Paulinus; Cyril; Gregory. Although this truth and place are confessed by all ancient writers and proven by this and other Scriptures, our adversaries <note>A reference to Protestant reformers who rejected these concepts.</note> deny it (as they do Purgatory) most impudently.

<margin>Augustine, Epistle 99.</margin>
<margin>Purgatory.</margin>
26. *A great chaos.*) A great distance between Abraham's bosom and the lower hell. Some judge Purgatory to be located there, from where (without a doubt) Christ also delivered some during his descent into hell. For those in Abraham's bosom were not in pain; and Saint Augustine says the Scriptures are clear that he took some out of the places of punishment, yet none out of the hell of the damned. What other place can that be but Purgatory?

<margin>Genesis 32. Calvin, Institutes book 3, ch. 22, section 24.</margin>
<margin>Saints hear our prayers and care for us. Calvin's blasphemy.</margin>
28. *Lest they also.*) If the damned cared for their living friends—regardless of how or for what reason—the Saints and saved persons care much more. And if those in hell have the means to express their thoughts and desires and be understood by Abraham, who is so far distant in both place and condition, how much more may the living pray to the Saints and be heard by them? For between earth (that is, the <term>Church Militant</term> <note>The Church on earth</note>) and heaven, there is a continual passage of souls, and Angels are ascending and descending by Jacob’s ladder. Men must not, however, be overly curious in searching out how the souls of the deceased express their minds and hear one another, lest they fall into blasphemy as Calvin does. He mockingly asks whether their ears are so long as to hear from so far away, wickedly measuring all things by the coarse, physical way mortal men express ideas to one another. This communication was not done by the damned man or by Abraham using physical instruments like tongues, teeth, and ears; rather, to better explain the condition of the damned, Christ chose to speak in terms that suit our human understanding.

## ANNOTATIONS
### CHAP. XVII.

<margin>
How we are unprofitable and profitable servants.
</margin>
*10. Unprofitable servants.)* If our Savior had said that the keeping of God's commandments had been unprofitable and not available to ourselves, then might the Protestants have truly argued thereby that our works deserve not heaven or any reward at God's hand: but so he said not, but that our service is to God unprofitable, who calls for it as duty, and not as a thing needful to Him.

Aa iij
<meta>catchword: or</meta>

<summary>This page contains Jesus' teachings on the spiritual nature of the Kingdom of God and the sudden, unpredictable nature of his Second Coming, drawing parallels to the days of Noah and Lot. The annotations defend the merit of good works, arguing that while human service does not "benefit" an omnipotent God, it is still profitable and rewarded for the believer.</summary>

<header>THE GOSPEL CHAPTER XVIII.</header>

or profitable to himself. And though here our Master teaches us to conceive so humbly of our own doings toward him, yet he himself elsewhere calls not his servants unprofitable when they <margin>Matthew 25:21</margin> have finished their labor, but speaks thus: *Well done, good and faithful servant, because thou hast been faithful in a little, I will place thee over much: enter into the joy of thy Lord.* Indeed, of such as serve him in the grace of <margin>John 15:14</margin> the New Testament, he affirms that he will not now call them servants but friends, and even take them for his own children; and as his friends and sons, he counts us and our works <column-break/> toward heaven, though we in humility and truth must always confess that we are to him unprofitable servants. Indeed, and St. Paul says plainly, that by cleansing ourselves from sinful works, we shall be profitable vessels to our Lord. <margin>2 Timothy 2:21</margin>

<margin>Confession to the Priest.</margin>
14. *To the priests.*) This leprosy signifies sin, which although God may and can heal without any man’s means, yet he does it not ordinarily except by the Priests’ ministry: therefore let no man despise God’s ordinance nor say that it is enough to confess to God though he never comes to the priest. <note>original: "li. de visit. infirm. apud August." — *The Book on the Visitation of the Sick*, found among the works of Augustine.</note>

14. *As they went.*) A man may sometimes be so <term>contrite</term><note>Deeply and sincerely remorseful for one’s sins.</note> and penitent, that his sin is forgiven before he comes to the Priest, but even then he must nonetheless go to the Priest, as these lepers did: especially since we are never sure how contrite we are, and because there is no true contrition without the desire also for the <term>Sacrament</term><note>The outward sign of inward grace; here referring to the Sacrament of Penance or Confession.</note> in the proper time and place.

# ANNOTATIONS
## CHAPTER XVIII.

<margin>The Church does not err in faith.</margin>
<margin>Jerome, *Against the Luciferians*, ch. 6. Augustine, *On the Unity of the Church*, 15, and *On the Words of the Lord*, Sermon 88. <note>original: "Hier. con Lucif. c. 6. Aug. de unit. Ec. 15. & in verb. D. Ser. 88."</note></margin>
8. **Shall he find faith?**) The Luciferians and Donatists <note>The Luciferians and Donatists were early Christian groups that broke away from the mainstream Church, often claiming that the larger Church had become corrupt or lost its spiritual authority.</note> used this passage to excuse their departure from the Church, as our adversaries now do, saying that it was decayed in faith when they forsook it. To whom we answer as St. Jerome and St. Augustine answered them: that Christ does not say that there should be no faith left on earth, but by this manner of speech suggests that on the last day, during the great persecution of the Antichrist, faith shall be more rare, and the faithful among so many wicked people not so easily noticed. This specifically refers to that perfect faith containing devotion, trust, and affection toward God—which our Master so praised in certain people upon whom he performed miracles, and by the force of which mountains might be moved—which is rare even when the Church flourishes most.

### A N N O T A T I O N S
### C H A P T E R. XIX

<margin>
4. Went up.
External devotion.
</margin>
4. *Went up.*) Not only inward devotion of faith and charity toward Christ, but external acts of seeing, following, touching, receiving, and sheltering him are recommended to us in this example. Even so, our various outward devotions toward his Sacraments, Saints, and servants are pleasing to God. This specifically includes the effort of good people not only to be present at Mass or in the Church, but to be near the <term>Blessed Sacrament</term><note>The consecrated bread of the Eucharist, believed in Catholic tradition to be the literal body of Christ.</note>, and to see it with all reverence and devotion according to the order of the Church, and even more to receive it into the "house" of their own body.

<margin>
8. I restore fourfold.
Luke 21:3.
Restitution. Satisfaction.
</margin>
8. *I restore fourfold.*) That which we give of our own is considered alms and <term>satisfaction</term><note>An act to make amends for the temporal punishment of sin.</note> for our sins. But that which we return from ill-gotten goods—whether by extortion, <term>usury</term><note>Lending money at interest.</note>, <term>simony</term><note>The buying or selling of spiritual things or church offices.</note>, bribery, theft, or otherwise—is what is called here **Restoring**. This is a duty, not a matter of free alms, and must be returned not to whoever we choose, but to the injured parties if possible. Otherwise, it must be given to the poor or other good causes, according to the advice of our spiritual superiors. By yielding fourfold, Zacchaeus gave more than he was strictly bound to do, which was an act of great satisfaction for his former sins. We should note that it is not the giving of a penny, a <term>groat</term><note>A small silver coin worth four pence.</note>, or a <term>crown</term><note>A gold or silver coin of significant value.</note> from a rich man's excess that is recommended for redeeming faults; rather, it is this large-scale giving—selling all for alms, giving a <term>moiety</term><note>A half or a significant portion.</note> of our goods, or rendering four times what was stolen—that extinguishes sin. The poor widow’s copper penny was pleasing because it was all she had; but the rich man's pound from his excess, though good, is not nearly as pleasing.

## CHAPTER 20.

**AND** it happened that on one of those days, <margin>Matthew 21:23; Mark 11:27.</margin> 1 while he was teaching the people in the temple and preaching the good news <note>original: "euangelizing"</note>, the chief priests and the scribes, along with the elders, gathered together 2 and spoke to him, saying, <margin><note>See the annotations for Matthew 21:23.</note></margin> "Tell us, by what authority do you do these things? <margin>Isaiah 5:1; Matthew 21:33; Mark 12:1.</margin> <margin><note>See the marginal notes for Mark 12.</note></margin> 9 Then he began to tell the people this parable: "A certain <note>The "man" in this parable represents God the Father.</note> man planted a vineyard and leased it out to tenant farmers; and he went abroad for a long time. 10 And at the proper season, he sent a servant to the farmers so that they might give him some of the fruit of the vineyard. But they beat him and sent him away empty-handed. 11 And again he sent another servant. But they beat him also, and after treating him shamefully <note>original: "reproachfully abusing him"</note>, sent him away empty-handed. 12 And again he sent a third; and they wounded him also and threw him out. 13 Then the lord of the vineyard said, 'What shall I do? I will send my beloved son; perhaps when they see him, they will respect him.' 14 But when the tenant farmers saw him, they reasoned among themselves, saying, 'This is the heir; let us kill him, so that the inheritance may be ours.' 15 And casting him out of the vineyard, they killed him. What, therefore, will the lord of the vineyard do to them? 16 He will come and destroy these farmers, and will give the vineyard to others." ->ANNOTATIONS<-
->CHAPTER 20.<-

<margin>To be worthy of heaven, or to deserve and merit it.</margin>
<margin>To be accounted worthy. To be worthy. <note>original Greek: καταξιωθῆναι (kataxiōthēnai) and ἀξιωθῆναι (axiōthēnai)</note></margin>
35. *Shall be counted worthy.*) This truth and speech—that good men are worthy of heaven—is according to the Scriptures. It signifies that man's works, done by Christ's grace, do condignly <note>"Condignly" means "worthily" or "fittingly," suggesting a direct proportion between the effort and the reward.</note> or worthily deserve eternal joy. As seen in Wisdom 3: *God proved them, and found them worthy of himself.* And Matthew 10: *He that loves his father more than me, is not worthy of me.* And Colossians 1: *That you may walk worthy of God.* And most plainly in Apocalypse 3 <note>The Book of Revelation.</note>: *They shall walk with me in white, because they are worthy.* Just as it is said of Christ (chapter 1): *You are worthy, O Lord, to receive glory* etc. And it is plain by the Greek word that "to be counted worthy" and "to be worthy" are the same thing here. Saint Paul uses it this way, as the adversaries' <note>This refers to contemporary Protestant translations, which the author is critiquing.</note> own English Testaments testify, reading thus in Hebrews 10: *Of how much sorer punishment shall he be worthy, who* etc. It must necessarily signify this, because men are not only "counted" but are indeed worthy of punishment for sins, as they themselves grant. Therefore, they greatly forget themselves, are ignorant of the Scriptures, and do not know the force or the value of the grace of God, which does not only make our labors pleasing to God, but worthy of the reward which he has provided for those who love him. See the Annotations for 2 Thessalonians 1:5.
<margin>The New Testament, year 1580.</margin>

<margin>The dignity of Saints.</margin>
36. *Equal to Angels.*) Saints of our kind—presently in their souls, and after their resurrection in both body and soul—shall be equal to Angels in all things. Regarding the degree of bliss, many Saints of greater merit shall be above various Angels: such as Saint John the Baptist, the Apostles, and others; and our Blessed Lady is above all the orders of holy spirits in dignity and bliss. This is no marvel, as our nature has been so highly exalted above all Angels through Christ.

### ANNOTATIONS
### CHAPTER 21.

4. *Of her penury.*) To offer or give alms from our surplus <note>original: superfluities</note> is not as acceptable or meritorious as to bestow some of that which is part of our necessary provisions, and which we can hardly spare for ourselves: for that proceeds from greater zeal, will, and intention, which are more respected by God than the actual value <note>original: substance</note> of the gift.

# A N N O T A T I O N S
## C H A P T E R  X X I I.

<margin>The old Passover ceases and a new one is instituted.</margin>
15. *With desire I have desired.*] This great desire he had to eat this <term>Paschal lamb</term> <note>the lamb eaten during the Jewish Passover feast.</note> was not for itself, which he had celebrated many years before: but because he meant immediately after the Passover of the Law was sacrificed and eaten, to institute the other new Passover in the <term>oblation</term> <note>an offering made to God.</note> and eating of his own body, by which the old Passover should end and be fulfilled, and in which the old Testament and Law ceasing, the Kingdom of God (which is the state of the new Testament and of his Church) should begin. For, the very passage from the old Law to the new was in this one supper.

<margin>Two cups or chalices at Christ's last supper.</margin>
<margin>Matthew 26:29</margin>
17. *Taking the chalice.*] This chalice, according to the very evidence of the text itself also, is not the second part of the Holy Sacrament, but that solemn cup of wine which belonged as a <term>libament</term> <note>original: "libament"; a ritual drink offering poured out in honor of a deity.</note>, to the offering and eating of the Passover lamb. Which being a <term>figure</term> <note>a symbolic foreshadowing or type.</note> specially of the holy Chalice, was there drunken by our Savior, and given to the Apostles also, with declaration that it should be the last cup of the Law, not to be drunken any more, until it should be drunken new in the kingdom of God, that is to say, in the celebration of the Blessed Sacrament of his blood of the new Testament. And by this place it seems very likely that the words in St. Matthew, *I will not drink of the fruit of the vine etc.* were pertaining to this cup of the old Law, and not to the Holy Sacrament, though they be there by repetition or <term>recapitulation</term> <note>a summary or retelling of earlier events.</note> spoken after the holy Chalice.

<margin>The real presence.</margin>
19. *This is my body.*] Although sense tells thee it is bread, yet it is the body, according to his words. Let faith confirm thee, judge not by sense. After the words of our Lord let no doubt rise in thy mind. <note>original: *Cyril. mystag. 4.* Referring to Cyril of Jerusalem’s fourth Mystagogical Catechesis.</note> Of the verity of flesh and blood there is left no place to doubt: by the profession of our Lord himself and by our faith it is flesh and blood indeed. Is not this truth? To them be it untrue, who deny JESUS CHRIST to be true God. <note>original: *Hilar. li. 8. de Trinit.* Referring to Hilary of Poitiers, *On the Trinity*, Book 8.</note>

<margin>Christ sacrificed his body and blood in Sacrament at his supper.
The Sacrifice of the Altar.</margin>
<margin>*which is given* <note>original Latin: "quod datur"; original Greek: "τὸ διδόμενον"</note></margin>
<margin>Cyril of Alexandria, Book 11 on John, chapters 32 and 34.</margin>
19. *Which is given.*] As the former words make and prove his body present, so these words plainly signify, that it is present, as given, offered or sacrificed for us: and being uttered in the present tense, it signifies not only that it should afterward be given or offered on the Cross, but that it was then also in the Sacrament given and offered for us. Whereby it is <term>invincibly</term> <note>unconquerably or undeniably.</note> proved that his Body is present as a <term>host</term> <note>original: "hoſt"; from the Latin *hostia*, meaning a sacrificial victim.</note> or Sacrifice: and that the making or consecrating thereof must needs be Sacrificing. And therefore, the holy Fathers in this sense call it a Sacrifice. <note>original: The author lists a vast array of historical authorities to support this, including Gregory the Great, Ignatius of Antioch, Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, Tertullian, Cyprian, Chrysostom, Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, and several Church Councils including Nicaea and Trent.</note>

<margin>The Apostles are made Priests, & the Sacrament of holy Orders instituted.</margin>
19. *Do this*] In these words the holy Sacrament of <term>Order</term> <note>Holy Orders; the sacrament by which men are ordained as priests.</note> is instituted, because power and commission to do the principal act and work of Priesthood is given to the Apostles: that is, to do that which Christ then did concerning his body: Which was, to make and offer his body as a sacrifice for us and for all that have need of Sacrifice, and to give it to be eaten as Christ's body sacrificed, to all faithful. For as the Paschal lamb was first sacrificed, and then eaten: so was his body: and thus to do he here gives commission and authority to the Apostles, and to all Priests which be

be their successors in this matter. <note>Citations from the Early Church Fathers: Dionysius the Areopagite, *Celestial Hierarchy*, ch. 3; Irenaeus, book 4, ch. 32; Cyprian, *Epistle to Caecilius*; Chrysostom, homily 17 on the Epistle to the Hebrews; Ambrose on Psalm 38 and on ch. 10 of Hebrews.</note>

<margin>Ambrose on Hebrews 10. Chrysostom, homily 17 on the Epistle to the Hebrews.</margin>
<margin>A commemorative sacrifice is a true sacrifice, no less than the prefigurative sacrifices <note>Sacrifices in the Old Testament that "prefigured" or foreshadowed Christ.</note> were true sacrifices.</margin>
19. **For a commemoration.**] This Sacrifice and Sacrament is to be performed perpetually in the Church for the commemoration of Christ, especially of his Passion: that is to say, that it may be a lively representation, <term>exemplar</term> <note>a model or pattern to be copied.</note>, and form of his Sacrifice upon the cross. Of which one <term>oblation</term> <note>offering</note> on the cross, not only all other sacrifices of the Law were figures, but this also: though this in a more near, high, mystical, and marvelous sort than any other. For in them Christ’s death was signified as by resemblance and similitudes of external creatures and bodies of brute beasts. But in this of the new Testament, his body visibly sacrificed on the cross, in and by the self-same body sacrificed and <term>immolated</term> <note>offered as a sacrifice</note> in Sacrament and under the shapes of bread and wine, is most nearly and perfectly resembled: and therefore this is most properly commemorative, as most nearly expressing the condition, nature, efficacy, sort, and substance of that on the cross. For which the holy fathers call it the very self-same sacrifice (though in another manner) which was done on the cross, as it is the self-same thing, that is offered in the Sacrament, and on the cross. Whereby you may see the perversity of the Protestants or their ignorance, that think it therefore not to be Christ’s body, because it is a memory of his body or a figure of his body upon the cross: nor to be a true sacrifice, because it is a commemorative sacrifice. For as the thing that more lively, nearly, and truly resembles or represents, is a better figure than that which shadows it from afar: so this his body in the Sacrament, is more perfectly a figure of Christ’s body and sacrifice, than any other. Christ himself the Son of God is a figure and character of his father’s person, being yet of the self-same substance. And Christ’s body transfigured on the holy Mount, was a figure and resemblance of his person glorified in heaven. Even so is his body in the Sacrament to a faithful man that knoweth by his belief grounded on Christ’s own word, that in the one form is his body, in the other his blood, the most perfect representation of his death that can be. As for the sacrifice, it is no less a true Sacrifice, because it is commemorative of Christ’s Passion: than those of the old Testament were the less true, because they were prefigurative. For that is the condition annexed to all Sacrifice of every Law, to represent Christ’s Passion.
<margin>To be a figure of a thing, and yet the thing itself, is not a contradiction.</margin>

<margin>Hebrews 9, verse 20.</margin>
<margin>Both testaments dedicated in blood.</margin>
20. **The new Testament in my blood.**] Moses took the blood of the first sacrifice that was made after the giving of the Law (*Exodus 24*) and with blood confirmed the covenant and compact between God and his people, and so dedicated the old Testament, which without blood (says St. Paul) was not dedicated. Moses put that blood also into a standing piece, and sprinkled all the people etc. with the same, and said these formal words, *This is the blood of the covenant etc.* (as it is read in St. Paul) *of the Testament which God has delivered unto you.* Unto all which, Christ in this action about the second part of this his sacrifice, in every of the Evangelists most clearly alludes, expressing that the new Testament is begun and dedicated in his blood in the Chalice, no less than the old was dedicated, begun, and ratified in that blood of calves contained in the goblet of Moses. With which his own blood he sprinkled inwardly his Apostles as the first fruits of the new Testament, imitating the words of Moses, and saying, *This is the Chalice the new Testament etc:* Which the other Evangelists spoke more plainly, *This is my blood of the new Testament.* By all which it is most certain, that Christ’s blood in the Chalice, is the blood of Sacrifice, and that in this sacrifice of the altar consists the external religion and proper service of the new Testament, no less than the sovereign worship of God in the old Law did consist in the sacrifices of the same. For though Christ’s sacrifice on the Cross and his blood shed for us there, be the general price, redemption, and satisfaction for us all, and is the last and perfectest sealing or confirmation of the new law and Testament: yet the service and Sacrifice which the people of the new Testament might resort unto, could not be that violent action of the Cross, but this on the Altar, which by Christ’s own appointment is and shall be the eternal office of the new Testament, and the continual application of all the benefits of his Passion unto us.
<margin>The external religion of the new Testament principally in the sacrifice of the altar.</margin>

<margin>The chalice which... <note>original: "calix qui / τὸ ποτήριον τὸ ἐκχυνόμενον"; the cup that is poured out.</note></margin>
<margin>The chalice shed for us, must necessarily signify the blood therein, not wine, and the same sacrificed.</margin>
20. **Which shall be shed.**] It is much to be observed that the relative, *Which*, in these words is not governed or ruled (as some would perhaps think) by the noun "blood," but by the word "chalice" <note>the cup</note>. This is most plain by the Greek. This takes away all <term>cavillations</term> <note>frivolous objections</note> and shifts from the Protestants, both against the real presence and the true Sacrificing. For it shows evidently, that the blood as the contents of the chalice, or as in the chalice, is shed for us (for so the Greek reads in the present tense) and not only as upon the cross. And therefore as it follows from this invincibly, that it is no bare figure, but his blood indeed, so it ensues necessarily, that it is a Sacrifice, and <term>propitiatory</term> <note>having the power to atone for sin</note>, because the chalice (that is the Blood contained in the same) is shed for our sins. For all that know the manner of the Scriptures' speech, know also that this, *Blood to be shed for sin*, is to be sacrificed for propitiation or for pardon of sins. And this text proves all this so plainly, that Beza <note>Theodore Beza, a prominent Protestant reformer and successor to John Calvin.</note> turns himself roundly upon the Holy Evangelist, charging him with <term>Solœcisme</term> <note>a grammatical error or absurdity</note> or false Greek, or else that the words (which yet he confesses to be in all copies Greek and Latin) are thrust into the text out of some other place: which he rather stands upon than that St. Luke should speak incongruously in so plain a matter. And therefore he says plainly, that it cannot be truly said neither of the chalice itself nor of the contents thereof: which is indeed to give the lie to the blessed Evangelist, or to deny this to be Scripture. So clear is the Scrip-
