# THE GOSPEL CHAPTER XXII.

...nature for us; falsehood is forced into such miserable dodges and excuses, God be thanked.

<margin>Ambition.</margin>
**24. Contention.**] The Apostles, perceiving Christ’s departure from them and his kingdom to be near, acting as frail men not yet filled with the Spirit of God, began to feel envy and had thoughts of superiority over one another. Our Master restrains this in them by encouraging humility and by his own example—for though he was their Lord, he had only recently served them. He does not forbid seniority or authority among them, but rather pride, tyranny, and the looking down on those below them.

<margin>Peter’s faith shall never fail.</margin>
<margin>S. Leo, *Sermon 3 on the Anniversary of his Elevation to the Pontificate*; *Book of Questions on the New Testament*, question 75, volume 4.</margin>
**31. Simon, Simon.**] Finally, to remove any doubt, he calls Peter twice by name. Telling him that the Devil desires to sift and test them all to the limit (as he did that night), Jesus says that he has specially prayed for Peter, to the end that his faith should never fail. He adds that once Peter is converted, he should forever after strengthen, establish, or uphold the rest in their faith. This is to say that Peter is the man whom he would make superior over them and the whole Church. From this we may learn that it was deemed fit in the providence of God that the one who would be the head of the Church should have a special privilege through Christ's prayer and promise: never to fail in faith. No other Apostle, Bishop, or priest may claim any such unique or special prerogative for his office or person, except by joining with Peter and holding to his authority. 

The danger (says St. Leo) was common to all the Apostles, but our Lord took special care of Peter so that the state of all the rest might be more secure if the head were invincible. God dispensed the aid of his grace so that the assurance and strength which Christ gave to Peter might overflow through Peter to the rest of the Apostles. St. Augustine also writes: *Christ, praying for Peter, prayed for the rest, because in the Pastor and Prelate the people are corrected or commended.* <note>Original Latin: "in Pastore et Praelate populus corrigitur aut commendatur."</note> And St. Ambrose writes that Peter, after his temptation, was made Pastor of the Church because it was said to him, *You, being converted, confirm your brethren.* This was not the privilege of Saint Peter’s person, but of his Office, ensuring he should not fail in faith but always confirm all others in their faith. For the Church—for whose sake that privilege was deemed necessary in Peter, its Head—was to be preserved no less afterward than in the Apostles' time. 

Whereupon all the Church Fathers apply this privilege of not failing and of confirming others in faith to the Roman Church and Peter’s successors in the same. To this Church (says St. Cyprian) infidelity or false faith cannot come. And St. Bernard says, writing to Pope Innocent II against Abelard the Heretic: *We must refer to your Apostleship all the scandals and perils which may occur, especially in matters of faith. For there the defects of faith must be helped, where faith cannot fail. For to what other See was it ever said, I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith do not fail?* So say the Fathers.

<margin>The Roman faith of Peter’s successors cannot fail.</margin>
<margin>Cyprian, *Epistle 55, number 6*; Bernard, *Epistle 190*.</margin>
<margin>Popes may err personally, not judicially or definitively.</margin>
This does not mean that no one in Peter’s seat can err in their personal understanding, private doctrine, or writings. Rather, it means they cannot and shall not ever judicially conclude or give a definitive sentence for falsehood or heresy against the Catholic faith in their official courts, councils, decrees, or consultations kept for the decision and determination of such controversies or questions of faith. This is because Christ’s prayer and promise protect them therein for the strengthening of their brethren. And it is no marvel that our Master would have his Vicar’s <term>Consistory</term> <note>a formal council or administrative body of the Church</note> and Seat be infallible, seeing as even under the Old Law, the high priesthood and the "Chair of Moses" did not lack great privilege in this regard—though it was nothing like the prerogatives of the Church and Peter. 
<margin>Deuteronomy 17.</margin>
In both cases, any man of sense may see the difference between the person and the Office, in both doctrine and life. Pope Liberius under persecution might yield; Marcellinus out of fear might commit idolatry; Honorius might fall into heresy; and more than all this, some Judas might creep into the Office. 
<margin>Augustine, *Epistle 166*, at the end.</margin>
*And yet all this occurs without prejudice to the Office and Seat, in which (says St. Augustine) our Lord has placed the doctrine of truth.* Caiaphas, by the privilege of his Office, prophesied correctly about Christ, but according to his own personal knowledge and faith, he did not know Christ. The Evangelists and other writers of Holy Writ had the assistance of God for the execution of that function, and so far as that went, they could not possibly err; but we do not say that Luke, Mark, Solomon, or the rest might not have erred in their other private writings. 

<margin>The learned fathers sought out the Vicars; this made St. Bernard seek Innocent III, and St. Augustine seek the Bishop of Rome for resolution of doubts.</margin>
<margin>Bernard, *Epistle 190*; Chrysostom, *Epistles 1 and 2*.</margin>
It was not the personal wisdom, virtue, learning, or faith of Christ’s Vicars that made St. Bernard seek out Innocent III; or St. Augustine and the Bishops of Africa seek out Innocent I and Celestine (*Epistles 90, 92, 95*); or St. Chrysostom to seek the same Innocent; or St. Basil to seek the Pope in his time (*Epistle 52*); or St. Jerome to seek Damasus (*Epistles 57, 58, volume 2*). Rather, it was the prerogative of their Office, the higher degree of <term>Unction</term> <note>the ceremonial act of anointing with oil, symbolizing divine authorization</note>, and Christ’s ordinance that required all Apostles and Pastors in the world to depend on Peter for their strengthening in faith and church government. The lack of knowledge and humble acceptance of this divine plan—namely, that one leader is not honored and obeyed by the whole brotherhood—is the cause of all <term>Schisms</term> <note>formal splits or divisions within a religious body</note> and Heresies, as St. Cyprian says. This is a point of such importance that although all Twelve were equal in their Apostleship, Christ still willed that one should be the head of them all, so that by appointing a head, the occasion for division might be removed, as St. Jerome says. 
<margin>Cyprian, *Epistle 55, number 4*; *Against Jovinianus*, book 1, chapter 14.</margin>

<header>THE GOSPEL CHAPTER 24.</header>

<margin>The good thief.</margin>
*43. In Paradise.)* You must not use this example to delay your conversion or amendment of life, presuming you will receive grace at the last hour of your life. Nor should you expect to achieve salvation by faith and confession of Christ alone without good works, nor to go straight to heaven without making satisfaction, doing penance, or receiving punishment for your former sins and ill-spent life. You also cannot claim security or certain knowledge of your own salvation. This "good thief’s" case is not a common one, but a rare example of mercy and special privilege. Regarding the first point, learn only not to despair, even if you have lived poorly until the final moment of your life. Regarding the second, understand that faith, hope, charity, repentance, and good will are sufficient—and good works are not strictly required—in cases where time and opportunity are lacking. Regarding the 
<margin>Pardon of due penance and satisfaction.</margin>
third point, Christ gave this happy man—because of his zealous confession and his defense of Jesus against his fellow thief—not only the forgiveness of his sins, but also, by extraordinary grace, a pardon for all penance and satisfaction due either in this life or the next <note>A reference to the Catholic doctrine of Purgatory, suggesting that even forgiven sins may require temporal punishment.</note>. Just as the holy Church, by his example and commission, also grants pardons <note>This refers to the practice of Indulgences, where the Church remits the temporal punishment due to sin.</note> to some of her zealous children, remitting all punishment due for their offenses so they may go straight to heaven. Finally, realize that not everyone receives a direct revelation of their salvation as this man did, and therefore one cannot be as certain as he was.

*53. Wherein never.)* Just as no one was conceived in the womb of **MARY** before or after him, so in this monument <note>The word "monument" here refers to the tomb or sepulcher.</note> no one was laid before or after him. This privilege was undoubtedly part of God’s providence; just as the other Joseph <note>Joseph of Nazareth, Mary's husband.</note> abstained from sexual relations with the mother of our Lord, this Joseph <note>Joseph of Arimathea.</note> likewise refrained from being buried in this tomb later. *St. Augustine.*

<margin>Visiting the Sepulcher, or Tombs.</margin>
*55. Saw the monument.)* These devout women of great devotion observed the Sepulcher out of honor for the holy body. Following this, the devotion of the faithful who watch and visit the "sepulcher" made in every Church on Good Friday and Easter Eve—in memory of our Lord’s burial—is an exceedingly good and godly practice, especially when the Blessed Sacrament <note>The consecrated bread of the Eucharist.</note> is present in that Sepulcher for greater symbolic meaning.

<margin>Author of the *Imperfect Work* <note>An early Christian commentary on Matthew once attributed to St. John Chrysostom; original: "Author operis imperf."</note> homily 17. <margin>The Catholic or universal Church.</margin>
46. *Penance to be preached.*) He showed unto them out of the Scriptures, not only the things that were now accomplished in himself, but also those things that were yet to come concerning his Church: such as, where it should begin, namely, at Jerusalem: and how far it should go, namely, to all nations: so that he might not permit us (says St. Augustine) to err regarding either the bridegroom <note>Christ</note> or the bride <note>The Church</note>. For this stands clearly against all Heretics and Schismatics, who set up new churches in particular countries, drawing the people away from the aforementioned only true Church, which from Jerusalem grows * over all nations, until the end of the world comes.

<margin>* Hebrews 7:6, 10, 20, 21, 26. Mark 10:16. Genesis 48:14. * Tertullian, *On the Soldier’s Crown* <note>original: "de coron. milit."</note>, number 3. Basil, *On the Holy Spirit* <note>original: "de Sp. sanct."</note>, chapter 27.</margin>
<margin>Christ blessed in various ways.</margin>
<margin>Blessing with the sign of the cross.</margin>
50. *Blessed them.*) Christ our high priest, * prefigured specifically in that role by Melchizedek, often gave his blessing to his followers: sometimes by words, such as, *Peace be to you*: sometimes by the laying on of his hands: and now here by lifting up his hands over his Disciples as if for his farewell. In what form the Scripture does not express, but it is very likely it was in the form of the cross, just as Jacob the Patriarch blessed his nephews to signify Christ's blessing. For by this time the cross began to be glorious among the faithful, and it is most certain * by the fathers (who call it an ancient tradition) that they used that sign as an external mark of blessing. Indeed, St. Augustine says (<note>original: "in Ps. 30 Conc. 3"</note> *On Psalm 30, Sermon 3*) that Christ himself, not without cause, wanted his sign to be fixed on our foreheads as the seat of modesty, so that a Christian should not be ashamed of the "reproach of Christ" <note>His suffering and death on the cross.</note>. And what form can a Christian use to bless himself or others rather than that which was dedicated in Christ's death, and is a suitable memorial of the same? However it may be, the fact that the Bishops and Priests of God’s Church bless with an external sign, no man can criticize, as it is authorized by Christ’s own example and action.

THE HEADER: THE ARGUMENT

<image-desc>A rectangular decorative woodcut headpiece featuring symmetrical scrolling strapwork and stylized floral elements.</image-desc>

# THE ARGUMENT OF
## ST. JOHN’S GOSPEL.

St. John’s Gospel may be divided into four parts.

The first part concerns the acts of Christ before his solemn manifestation of himself, while John the Baptist was still baptizing: Chapters 1, 2, 3, and 4.

<margin>
* This phrasing, which is very common in this Gospel as shown by the places marked here, declares that he writes to the Gentiles.
</margin>
The second part concerns his Acts in Judea <note>original: "Iurie"</note> (having now begun his solemn manifestation in Galilee, Matthew 4:12) during the second <term>Pasch</term> <note>From the Greek 'pascha,' meaning Passover.</note> or Passover of his preaching: Chapter 5. Regarding the first Passover, we saw that in the first part, chapter 2:13: *And the Passover of the Jews was at hand.* And that feast mentioned in <margin>Irenaeus, book 2, chapter 39.</margin> this second part, chapter 5:1: *After this there was a festival day of the Jews,* is thought by good Authors to be the feast of the Passover.

The third part concerns his Acts in Galilee and in Judea, around the third Passover and after it: chapters 6 through 12. For we have it in chapter 6:4: *And the Passover, the festival day of the Jews, was at hand.*

The fourth part concerns the fourth Passover (which we find at the end of chapter 11:55: *And the Passover of the Jews was at hand*); that is to say, it concerns the Holy Week of his Passion in Jerusalem: chapter 12 until the end of the book.

By this division, it is clear that the intent of this Evangelist, writing after the other three, was to omit the Acts of Christ in Galilee because the other three had written about them at length, and instead to report his Acts done in Judea, which they had omitted.

And he does this because Judea, along with Jerusalem and the Temple, being the principal part of the country, was where the leaders of the Jews resided, both for authority and for learning in the law or knowledge of the Scriptures. Therefore, that was the place where our Lord JESUS—finding in the leadership and the elders such willful obstinacy and desperate resistance as the Prophets had foretold—took the opportunity, much more plainly than in Galilee, to both say and prove at various times (even every year of his preaching) that he himself was the CHRIST who had been so long promised to them and expected by them. He also proved the same CHRIST to be not only a man, as they imagined, but also the natural, <term>consubstantial</term> <note>Sharing the same substance or essence; a key theological term defining the relationship between the Son and the Father.</note>, and co-eternal Son of God the Father, who had now sent him. Therefore, these were the words and deeds that best served the purpose of this Evangelist, which was to show the glory and excellence of this person, JESUS. By this, the Gentiles might see how rightly Jerusalem and the Jews were rejected <note>original: "reprobated"</note> for having refused and even crucified such a person, and how well they might do for their own salvation to receive him and believe in him. That this was his purpose, he himself declares at the end, saying: <margin>John 20:31.</margin> *These are written, that you may believe that JESUS is CHRIST the Son of GOD: and that believing, you may have life in his name.*

<margin>
Jerome, in the *Catalog of Ecclesiastical Writers* <note>original: "Hier. in Catal." referring to De Viris Illustribus.</note>.
a. John 21:20.
b. Matthew 4:21.
c. Acts 12:2.
</margin>
And hereupon it is that St. Jerome writes thus in his life: John the Apostle, a whom JESUS loved very much, the b son of Zebedee and the brother of James the Apostle c whom Herod, after our Lord’s Passion

...[pas]sion <note>The OCR begins mid-word, likely "passion," referring to the martyrdom of the other Apostles.</note> and were beheaded, John was the last of all to write his Gospel, at the request of the Bishops of Asia. He wrote against Cerinthus <note>An early Gnostic teacher who claimed Jesus was a mere man upon whom the "Christ" descended at baptism.</note> and other heretics, and especially against the rising movement of the Ebionites <note>A Jewish Christian sect that denied the divinity of Jesus and his pre-existence.</note>, who claim that Christ did not exist before Mary <note>The original OCR reads "who say that Christ was before MARIE," but the context of "against the assertion" and the following sentence suggests they denied his pre-existence. Jerome’s original text confirms they believed Christ began his existence at his human birth.</note>. Because of this, John was compelled to declare Christ's Divine Nativity. *Regarding his three Epistles and his Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note>, more will be said in their proper places.*

It follows in St. Jerome’s writings that during the second persecution under Domitian, fourteen years after the persecution of Nero, John was exiled to the island of Patmos. But after Domitian was killed and his decrees were repealed by the Senate due to his extreme cruelty, John returned to Ephesus under the Emperor Nerva. He continued there until the time of the Emperor Trajan, founding and governing all the Churches of Asia. Worn out by old age, he died sixty-eight years after the Passion <note>The suffering and death</note> of our Lord and was buried near that same city.

The same holy Doctor <note>St. Jerome</note> briefly describes John’s excellence as follows:

<margin>
a John 13:23, 24; 21:20.
b John 20:4.
c John 21:7.

<image-desc>Decorative initial I featuring scrolling foliage and vines.</image-desc> *John the Apostle, one of our Lord’s Disciples, who was the youngest among the Apostles and whom the faith of Christ found to be a virgin, remained a virgin. Therefore, he is more loved by our Lord, and he a reclined upon the chest of Jesus. That which Peter did not dare to ask, a John asks of him. And after the resurrection, when Mary Magdalene had reported that our Lord had risen again, both of them ran to the Sepulcher, b but John arrived there first. When they were in the ship fishing in the Lake of Gennesaret, Jesus stood on the shore, and the Apostles did not know whom they saw; c only the virgin recognizes the virgin <note>In this context, Jerome means the pure Apostle recognizes the pure Lord.</note> and says to Peter, "It is our Lord." This John was at once an Apostle, an Evangelist, and a Prophet. He was an Apostle because he wrote to the churches as a Master; an Evangelist because he compiled a book of the Gospel, which (except for Matthew) no other of the twelve Apostles did; and a Prophet, for while banished to the island of Patmos by the Emperor Domitian for his testimony of our Lord, he saw the Apocalypse, which contains infinite mysteries of things to come.* 

*Tertullian also reports that at Rome, after being cast into a vat of hot boiling oil, he emerged more pure and more full of life than when he went in. Indeed, his Gospel itself differs greatly from the rest. Matthew begins writing of Christ as a man; Mark begins with the prophecy of Malachi and Isaiah; Luke begins with the priesthood of Zechariah. Thus, the first has the face of a man because of the genealogy; the second the face of a lion because of the voice of one crying in the desert; the third the face of a calf <note>Or an ox, symbolizing sacrifice.</note> because of the priesthood. But John, like an eagle, flies to the highest things and mounts to the Father himself, saying:* In the beginning was the WORD, and the WORD was with God, and God was the WORD. *Thus far St. Jerome.*

Regarding this Gospel, there are the famous commentaries of St. Augustine called *Treatises on the Gospel of John*, volume 9, and the twelve books of St. Cyril’s commentaries.

<margin>
How God the Son is called the WORD.
</margin>
1. *Was the Word,*] The second Person in the Trinity, who is the natural, only, and eternal Son of God the Father, is called the WORD: not in the same way as the holy Scriptures or the speeches of the Prophets and Apostles (written and spoken by God's commandment for the uttering of his divine will toward man) are called his word, but in a more divine, eminent, and inexpressible way, to express to

<meta>This page continues the theological commentary and annotations for the first chapter of the Gospel of John, specifically focusing on the nature of the "Word" (Logos) and the establishment of the Church's hierarchy through the naming of Peter.</meta>

<page-num>219</page-num>
->### CHAPTER 1. ACCORDING TO ST. JOHN.<-

<margin>Augustine, *The City of God*, Book 10, Chapter 29.</margin>
<margin>The Platonists.</margin>
It is explained to us in a way suited to our understanding, that the Son of God is, and from eternity is born of God the Father, just as our primary concept (which is our internal and mental word) is and proceeds from our intellect and mind. This **WORD** then—the Son, or second Person in the holy Trinity—was and already had his being when other creatures (of whatever kind) were only beginning. Therefore, he cannot be a creature, as many heretics <note>The translator refers here to early Gnostic and anti-Trinitarian groups.</note> thought before this Gospel was written, and as the Arians <note>Followers of Arius, who taught that Jesus was a created being rather than co-eternal with God.</note> taught later. Not only the faithful, but even the Platonists <note>Followers of the philosopher Plato, who shared similar concepts regarding the "Logos."</note> so admired this first sentence of the Gospel (as St. Augustine writes) that they wished it to be written in gold.

<margin>Calvin’s *Institutes*, Book 1, Chapter 13, Sections 23 and 25.</margin>
<margin>The **WORD** is co-eternal with the Father, distinct in person, and from the Father.</margin>
1. *With God.*] Because a man might ask: "If the **WORD** existed before anything was created, where or how could he be?" The Evangelist, preventing that physical concept, says first that he was with God, whose being does not depend on time, place, space, or any other creatures—all of which were made by him. Secondly, he gives us to understand that the **WORD** has his own proper existence or personality distinct from God the Father, by which Sabellius <note>An early heretic who taught that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were not distinct persons but merely different "masks" of one God.</note> the old heretic is refuted. Thirdly, the order of these two persons toward each other is suggested here: namely, that the Son is *with* and *from* the Father, and not the Father from the Son. Fourthly, you may here refute the blasphemy of Calvin, who holds that the second Person is God, not as being from God the Father, but as being from himself. <note>The author is criticizing Calvin's "autotheos" doctrine, which argued that Christ's divinity was not derived from the Father's essence.</note> And yet, these are the books that our youth now commonly read in England, and that by official command.

<margin>1 John 5:7, 20.</margin>
<margin>The **WORD** is true God by nature.</margin>
<margin>The Protestants are like the wrangling Arians.</margin>
1. *God was the Word.*] Lest anyone, based on the previous statements which set forth the relationship and distinction of the second Person from the first, might think that only the Father were God, the Evangelist expressly teaches the **WORD** to be God. For though the words seem to be arranged differently (because we have intentionally followed the elegance which the Evangelist himself observed in placing them so, and therefore they stand this way in both Greek and Latin), the actual meaning is this: *The **WORD** was God*, and (as the same Apostle writes in his first Epistle) *true God*. This is stated so that no one might say (as the Arians did) that he was God indeed, but not truly and naturally—only by adoption or title, just as good men in the church are called the "sons of God." We see in St. Augustine (*On Christian Doctrine*, Book 3, Chapter 2) the wonderful wrangling and excuses the Arians used to avoid the evidence of this passage—just as the Protestants do to avoid similar words, *This is my body*, concerning the Blessed Sacrament.

<margin>The **WORD** is not a creature but the creator.</margin>
3. *By him.*] Again, by this he signifies the eternity, divinity, omnipotence, and equality of the **WORD** or Son with God the Father, because all things were created by him. He says *all things*, both the visible things of this world and the invisible, such as Angels and all spiritual creatures. From this it is also evident that he himself is not a creature, being the creator of all. Neither is sin part of his creation, being a defect in a thing rather than a thing itself, and therefore it is neither from him nor by him.

<margin>Free will.</margin>
12. *He gave them power.*] Free will is given to receive or acknowledge Christ, and power is given to men—if they choose—to be made the sons of God through Christ; but they are not forced or drawn into it by any necessity.

<margin>Humble kneeling at the solemn words of Christ's incarnation.</margin>
14. *The Word made flesh.*] This is the high and divine testimony of Christ’s incarnation and the fact that he deigned to become man. For the acknowledgment of this inexplicable benefit and to give humble thanks for it, all Christian people in the world, by the tradition of the Fathers, prostrate themselves or kneel down when they hear it sung or said at the holy Mass, either in this Gospel or in the Creed at these words: AND HE WAS MADE MAN. <note>original: "ET HOMO FACTUS EST"</note>

<margin>How mortal men see God.</margin>
18. *No man hath seen.*] No man in this mortal life ever saw God in the actual shape and natural form of the divine essence; rather, men see him only in the shape of visible creatures, in or through which it pleases him to show himself to many in various ways in this world. But he never showed himself in such a way as when he showed himself in the person of the Son of God, having been made truly man and living among men.

<margin>The Blessed Trinity.</margin>
32. *The Spirit.*] Here is an evident testimony of the third Person in the Trinity, which is the Holy Spirit. So, in this one chapter, we find the truth of the Church's doctrine concerning the whole Trinity set forth expressly against all heretics, Jews, and Pagans.

<margin>Cephas. Peter. <note>original: "Petrus"</note> Book 2, Chapter 12 on John.</margin>
<margin>Peter, by his new name, is designated to be the Rock of the Church.</margin>
42. *Looking upon him.*] This gazing upon Simon suggests Christ's design and his preference for him to be the chief Apostle, the Rock of the Church, and his Vicar. And therefore, based on that Divine providence and intention, he changes his name accordingly—calling him *Cephas* instead of Simon, which is a Syriac <note>Aramaic</note> word meaning "Rock" or "Stone." St. Paul commonly calls him by this name, Cephas, whereas other Greeks and Latins call him entirely by the Greek word *Peter*, <note>original: "Petros"</note> which signifies the exact same thing. Regarding this, St. Cyril says that our Savior, by foretelling that his name would no longer be Simon but *Peter*, aptly signified by the word itself that he would build his Church upon him as upon a most firm rock and stone.

## ANNOTATIONS
### CHAPTER II.

<margin>Cyril on John 2, chapter 22.</margin>
<margin>Christ honors and approves of Marriage with his presence.</margin>
2. **JESUS also was called.**) By deigning to come with his followers to the Wedding, he approves of the custom of the Faithful meeting at honorable feasts and recreations to maintain love, peace, and friendship among themselves. He refutes the heresy of Tatian, Marcion, and others who condemn marriage <note>Tatian and Marcion were early Christian heretics who practiced 'Encratism,' a strict asceticism that rejected marriage as sinful.</note>. Finally (as St. Cyril says) he sanctifies and blesses the Marriage of the Faithful in the New Testament, making it a new creation in him, and freeing it from the many curses and disorders in which it existed before. By this blessing, frequent divorces, remarriages, and the practice of having multiple wives—as well as the woman's servant-like subjection and inequality—are corrected and returned to the original institution of marriage, thus making Christian marriage a Sacrament. See *St. Augustine, On Marriage and Concupiscence, book 1, chapters 10 & 21; and book 1, On Adulterous Marriages, chapter 8.*

<margin>Our Lady’s intercession.</margin>
3. **They have no wine.**) Our Lady understood in many ways that the time was now approaching for him to manifest himself to the world through miracles and preaching, and she did not doubt that he would begin now at her request. By this we learn that Christ ordinarily does not give his graces unless they are humbly asked and requested, and that his mother’s intercession is more than commonly effective, and that he denies her nothing.

<margin>Translators of holy Scriptures.</margin>
4. **What is to me and thee?**) Because this phrase <note>original: "Quid mihi et tibi?" A literal translation of the Greek "Ti emoi kai soi," a common idiom in the ancient world.</note> is subject to various meanings, we keep the exact words of our text. We fear that by turning it into any specific English phrase, we might limit the Holy Spirit's intention to one certain meaning that was either not intended, or not the only meaning intended. In this way, we avoid taking away the choice and neutrality from the reader, which all translators (especially of Holy Scripture) must be careful to do. Christ might mean here: "What is that to me and you, woman, since we are but guests, that they want wine?" as some interpret it. Or (which is the more proper use of that kind of speech in holy writing): "What have I to do with you?"—that is, why should I follow your desire in this case? In matters concerning my duties and the commission from my Father for preaching, performing miracles, and other graces, I must not be tied to flesh and blood. This was not a scolding of our Lady, nor a sign that he would not hear her in this or other things pertaining to God's glory or the good of men—for the outcome proves the opposite. Rather, it was a lesson to the company that heard it, and specifically to his Disciples, that family ties should not draw them to do anything against reason, nor be the primary reason they perform their duties, but rather God's glory.

<margin>Our Lady does not doubt that Christ will grant her petition.</margin>
5. **Whatever he shall say.**) By this you see that our Lady, through her divine wisdom and close familiarity with all his ways of speaking, knew it was not a rejection of her, but a teaching for others. She knew she had suffered no refusal, even though he seemed to say his time had not yet come.

<margin>Profaners of God's Church are to be punished in soul and body by the spiritual power.</margin>
**15. *Cast them out.***) By this corporal chastisement of those who defiled and abused the Temple, he shows not only his power—that being but one poor man he could by force execute his will upon so many sturdy fellows—but also his sovereign authority over all offenders. This authority extends not only to their souls, such as through excommunication and spiritual penalties, but also as far as is necessary for the exercise of spiritual jurisdiction, over their bodies and property as well. This serves as a lesson for the <term>Spirituality: The clergy or ecclesiastical authorities.</term> regarding how far and in what cases, out of just zeal for Christ's Church, they may use and exercise their forces and faculties, both spiritually and temporally, against offenders—especially against those who profane God's Church, according to the Apostle's allusion in 1 Corinthians 3: *If any man defile the Temple of God, him will God destroy.*

<margin>The Blessed Sacrament is not to be given to novices or beginners in the faith.</margin>
<margin>St. Augustine’s Tractates on John, 11.</margin>
**24. *JESUS committed not himself.***) Saint Augustine applies this—their initial faith and belief in Christ, which was suddenly raised by the admiration of his wonders but not yet fully formed or established in them—to the faith of Novices or <term>Catechumens: Individuals receiving basic instruction in the Christian faith before being baptized.</term> in the Church. Christ’s refusal to commit his Person to them yet is likened to the Church’s similar wariness and wisdom in not opening or giving our Lord in the <term>Blessed Sacrament: The Eucharist or Holy Communion.</term> to them, because not everyone was to be trusted with that high mystery without a full trial of their faith.

## ANNOTATIONS
### CHAP. III.

<margin>Baptism in Water is necessary for salvation.</margin>
5. *Born again of Water.*] Just as no man can enter into this world or have his life and being in it unless he is born of his physical <note>original: "carnal"</note> parents, no more can a man enter into the life and state of grace which is in Christ, or attain to life everlasting, unless he be born and baptized of water and the Holy Ghost. By this we see, first, that this Sacrament is called our regeneration or second birth, in relation to our natural birth that came before. Secondly, that this Sacrament consists of an external element of Water and the internal power of the Holy Spirit. In this, it excels the baptism of John the Baptist, which had the external element but not the spiritual grace. Thirdly, we see that no man can enter into the kingdom of God, nor into the fellowship of the Holy Church, without it. By this, <margin><note>original: "August haeref. 88." Referring to St. Augustine’s "On Heresies," section 88.</note></margin> the Pelagians <note>Followers of Pelagius who believed humans could achieve salvation without divine grace.</note> and Calvinists <note>Followers of the reformer John Calvin.</note> are condemned, as they promise everlasting life to young children who die without Baptism, and all others who think that faith alone is enough, or that the external element of water is superfluous or unnecessary—our Savior’s words being plain and universal. <margin>Baptism in two cases is not strictly necessary, but otherwise supplied.</margin> However, in this case, God (who has not bound his grace to any Sacrament in respect of his own freedom) may and does accept people as baptized if they are martyred before they could be baptized, or if they depart this life with the vow and desire to have that Sacrament but could not obtain it due to some unavoidable necessity. Lastly, it is proved that this Sacrament gives grace <term>ex opere operato</term> <note>Latin: "from the work performed." This is the Catholic doctrine that sacraments are effective by the very act of being administered, regardless of the qualities of the minister or recipient.</note> (which all Protestants deny) because it produces our spiritual life in God just as our physical birth gives us life in the world.

<margin>Every infidel, and specifically heretics, are judged already.</margin>
<margin>*Galatians 5:6*</margin>
18. *Is judged already.*] He who believes in Christ with faith "which works by charity" (as the Apostle Paul says) shall not be condemned at the last day nor at the hour of his death. But the Infidel—whether they be Jew, Pagan, or Heretic—is already (if they die in their disbelief) condemned by their own profession and sentence. They shall not come to judgment, either specific or general, to be examined according to their works of mercy done or omitted. In this sense, St. Paul says that the <margin>*Titus 3:11*</margin> obstinate Heretic is condemned by his own judgment, anticipating within himself, by his own free will, the sentence of both Christ and the Church.

<margin>The excellence of Christ’s power and graces.</margin>
31. *He that comes from above.*] It is as if John the Baptist were saying: It is no wonder that people flock to Christ so quickly and hold me in less account. For His baptism, His preaching, and His person are all immediately from heaven. He brings everything from the very bosom, mouth, and substance of God His Father. Whatever is in me is but a little drop of His grace. His spirit and graces are beyond all measure or human gifts, even according to His humanity <note>original: "Manhod"</note>; and all power—temporal and spiritual, the kingdom and the Priesthood, and all sovereignty in heaven and earth—is bestowed upon Him as He is man also.

Jacob: Whereas in truth that Patriarch, by worshipping there before the Temple was established or the Law given, did nothing to support their schism <note>A formal split or division within a religious body.</note>. This schism was begun by Manasses, a fugitive priest, solely to keep his unlawful wife and to obtain a position of superiority in his separation, which he could not do in unity with his brethren; this occurred long after the Temple of Jerusalem was built, from which they revolted. Therefore Christ gives judgment in favor of the Jews and the Temple of Jerusalem, affirming that they had a solid foundation for their worship, while the Samaritans had none at all.

<margin>
The true Temple prevails.

Josephus, *Antiquities*, Book 13, Chapter 6.
</margin>
Josephus also records how the Samaritans demanded from Alexander the Great the same privileges and immunities he had granted to the high priest and Temple of Jerusalem. They claimed their Temple was just as great and worthy, and that they themselves were Jews just like the others, worshipping the same God. But their schismatic hypocrisy was easily spotted, and they were dismissed with nothing. Another time, the Jews and Samaritans (as the same writer testifies) caused a great stir in Alexandria concerning the truth and antiquity of the schismatic temple and service at Mount Gerizim versus the true Temple of Solomon. The matter was put to arbitration by the command of King Ptolemy, specifically to determine which of the two came first. And the schismatics (as is their custom) *per saltum* <note>original: "per saltum" — meaning "by a leap" or "skipping steps."</note> claim their Church or service is as old as they wish, tracing it back to the Patriarchs, just as our modern schismatics <note>Likely referring to the Protestant Reformers from the author’s perspective.</note> do now with Christ and the Apostles. But when the trial was held, only those from Jerusalem could invincibly prove, by the continuous succession of their 

<margin>
The true Temple is proven by continuous succession.
</margin>
priests and by the precise historical record of when the schismatics left them, that theirs was the lawful temple and the other the false temple and false worship. Thus it was judged, and the Samaritans were silenced. Afterward, these same schismatics (which is typically the end of all schisms) revolted entirely from the Jewish religion and dedicated their temple at Gerizim to Jupiter Olympus. In the same way, Calvin's "Supper" and his bread and wine are likely, in the end, to turn into the sacrifices of Ceres and Bacchus <note>Goddess of grain and God of wine; the author is suggesting that without the true Church, religious rites eventually devolve into pagan or secular rituals.</note>.

Christian worship throughout all nations in every place, in spirit and truth: that is, in the Sacraments and service of the new law, full of spirit and grace: in the truth of things previously foreshadowed, especially the true sacrifice of Christ’s body and blood.
</margin>
23. *In Spirit and truth.*) Our Savior foretells to her that the end and ceasing of their sacrifice and worship in both Temples would soon come, and indeed was already beginning to be fulfilled. He instructs her in three things regarding that point. First, that the true Sacrifice would no 

<margin>
Malachi 1:11.
</margin>
longer be tied to that one place or nation, but that true worship would exist throughout all nations according to the prophecy of Malachi. Secondly, that the coarse and carnal worship involving the flesh and blood of beasts and other external earthly creatures—which do not contain grace, spirit, and life—would be taken away. In its place, another sacrifice would succeed, which would be in itself invisible, celestial, divine, and full of life, Spirit, and grace. And thirdly, that this worship and sacrifice would be the "truth" itself, of which all the former sacrifices and offerings <note>original: "hostes"</note> were but shadows and figures. And he 

<margin>
John 1:17.
</margin>
calls that "spirit and truth" here, which in the first Chapter is called "grace and truth." All of this is simply a prophecy and description of the Sacrifice of the faithful Gentiles in the body and blood of Christ. It is not that it is not given to us through external means (for otherwise we, being humans made of flesh and blood, could not receive it), but that it is spirit and life in itself, being the flesh of the WORD OF GOD. And if a man expands the word "Worship" (which here, as stated, refers properly to the worship of God by sacrifice) to all the Sacraments of the New Law, they likewise are spirit and grace, for the Holy Spirit works invisibly and internally upon our souls through each of them. Thus our Baptism is Water and the Holy Spirit; our Penance is the word of absolution and the Holy Spirit; our Confirmation is oil and the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands; finally, all the worship of the Catholic Church is properly spiritual, though certain external elements are joined to it for the sake of our human nature, state, and necessity. Take heed, therefore, that you do not conclude from Christ's words that Christian men should have no use for external ceremonies toward God; for that would do away with sacrifice, Sacraments, prayers, Churches, and the community of men in His service.

<margin>
1. The power of miracles given to created things.
</margin>
2. **Regarding the pond.** <note>The text refers to the Pool of Bethesda mentioned earlier in the chapter.</note> This is as great a wonder and work as any in the old Law, yet it was never recorded in the Scripture before. The conditions and circumstances of this event should be carefully weighed against the unbelievers <note>original: "Miscreants"</note> of this time for many reasons. First, that God—without any loss of His own honor, and indeed to its great praise—gives the power of miracles and healing to water or other created things. 
<margin>
2. The same power is given especially to sanctified creatures.
</margin>
Secondly, that He gives such powers specifically to those creatures which are sanctified through their use in sacred functions or otherwise. For this pond was the one in which the carcasses of sheep (therefore called <term>Probatica</term> <note>From the Greek word for sheep; referring to the Sheep Gate or Pool.</note>) and other beasts to be sacrificed were first washed. Because it was always red (as St. Jerome says) with the blood of the sacrificial victims <note>original: "hostes"</note>, this power was given to it for the
<margin>
3. Miracles are performed at one time more than another, especially during great festivals.
</margin>
honor of the sacrifices of the Law offered there. How much more should we recognize such miraculous works of God done in or around the Sacrifice or Sacraments of the New Testament, which faithless men completely reject and condemn as fables because they do not know the Scriptures or the power of God. Thirdly, that this operation occurred at certain times rather than others, and on great festival days rather than ordinary times (for this was the feast of Passover or Pentecost), as days more sanctified and when the people gathered in larger numbers. This
<margin>
4. Angels and Saints are patrons and workers in places of miracles.
</margin>
shows that we should not be surprised to see great miracles done at the memorials <note>original: "Memories"; referring to shrines or locations of relics.</note> and feasts of Martyrs or other great festivities, more than at other places and times. Fourthly, that the Angels or specific Saints are the overseers or patrons of such places of miracles, and are the workers, under God, of the effects that are extraordinarily performed there. This ought to make Christians less doubtful that the power of various waters in the world is rightly attributed by our ancestors and historical accounts to the prayers and presence of Saints—which profane and unbelieving men attribute only to nature, falsely pretending that God is more glorified by the works of nature (which belong to His ordinary providence) than by the graces of miracles given to His Saints or Angels (by His extraordinary providence). 
<margin>
5. Miracles happen in certain places and are performed upon those who physically visit them. See St. Augustine, letter 137.
</margin>
Fifthly, that miracles are not worked on men by their faith alone, nor through spiritual presence as much as physical presence, nor solely upon the person's desire or devotion—contrary to the heretics' excuse that God is equally present by His power and grace to every man and place. Therefore, men do need to travel from their own houses or countries to seek holiness or health at the places of Christ’s or His Saints’ birth, death, and memorials. ...that could get nobody to help him into the water, because he earnestly and long desired the remedy appointed by God, but was excluded by necessity: just as our Lord saves all those who die without Baptism, if they in their own persons earnestly intended, desired, and sought for the same. <note>The author is explaining the Catholic doctrine of "Baptism of Desire," where the intent to be baptized suffices when the physical act is impossible.</note>

<margin>Sin is the cause of sickness and infirmities.</margin>
14. **Sin no more.**) We may gather from this that this man's long infirmity was a punishment for his sins, and that men often attribute their sickness to other natural defects and seek for worldly remedies in vain, when the sin for which it was sent remains or is not repented of. Therefore, in all infirmities, men should first turn to God and go to their spiritual father <note>original: "Ghoſtly father"</note>, and only then call for worldly physicians afterward.

34. **I receive not.**) Our Master means that man's testimony is not necessary to him, nor does the truth of his Divinity depend on worldly witnesses or the commendations of men: though for us, such testimonies are agreeable and necessary. Thus, for our instruction, he deigned to accept the testimonies of John the Baptist, Moses, and the Prophets; and when departing from this world, he sent forth all his Apostles—and in them all Bishops and lawful Pastors—to be his witnesses from Jerusalem to the ends of the world.

<margin>Neither Jews nor Heretics find the truth because they do not search the Scriptures deeply, but read superficially.</margin>
39. **Search the Scriptures.**) He reprimands the Jews, who, despite reading the Scriptures daily and acknowledging that in them they should find life and salvation, nevertheless looked over them so superficially that they could not find him to be Christ, their King, Lord, Life, and Savior. For the prominent teachers and Scribes of the Jews then were like our heretics <note>The translator here refers to contemporary Protestant reformers.</note> now, who are always talking, turning, and shuffling the Scriptures, yet are of all men the most ignorant in the deep knowledge of them. Therefore, our Master refers them not merely to reading or memorizing them, nor to having the verses gloriously painted or written in their temples, houses, or coats, but to a deep search of the meanings and mysteries of the Scriptures, which are not so easily seen in the literal text.

<header>THE GOSPEL CHA. VI.</header>

# ANNOTATIONS
## CHAP. VI.

<margin>Why Christ is called bread: & believing, eating.</margin>
27. **Work not for the food.** By their greedy seeking after him for food <note>original: "meate"; in the 16th century, "meat" referred to any kind of solid food, not just animal flesh</note> for the body, he takes the opportunity to draw them to the desire of a more excellent food which he had to give them, and so by little and little to open unto them the great food and mystery of the Blessed Sacrament: which (as he proves) does not only far surpass their ordinary bread or his marvelous multiplied loaves, but Manna itself, which they thought came from heaven, and so much wondered at.

<margin>What it signifies, "The true bread." The Blessed Sacrament called bread.</margin>
<margin>Jeremiah 11, 19. Genesis 49, 11. Luke 24, 35. Acts 2, 42. 20, 7. 1 Corinthians 10.</margin>
32. **The true bread.** Though the person of Christ incarnate, even outside of the Sacrament also, be meant under the metaphors of bread and drink from heaven: and our belief in him be signified by eating and feeding: yet the reasons why they should be recommended unto us in such terms, were that he was to be eaten and drunken indeed in the forms of bread and wine: for which cause his body on the cross is called his bread <note>Jeremiah 11:19</note>: and his blood shed on the cross, the blood of the grape <note>Genesis 49:11</note>: no doubt because the same body and blood were in the Holy Sacrament to be eaten and drunken. In which speeches, either of Christ’s person generally, or particularly of the same as in the Blessed Sacrament, *the true bread* is not taken properly and specifically for that substance which is of corn, and called with us bread: but generally for food or nourishment, and therefore it has joined with it a term signifying a more excellent sort of sustenance: as, the true bread, the bread of heaven, the bread of life, Supersubstantial bread <note>original: "Supersubstantial bread"; a literal translation of the Latin "panis supersubstantialis" used in the Vulgate's version of the Lord's Prayer</note>, in which sort the holy Sacrament which is Christ’s body, is both here, and in St. Luke and St. Paul also, often called bread, even after consecration: not only because it was made of bread, but because it is bread more truly, and by more excellent property and calling, than that which ordinarily is named bread.

<margin>God draws us with our free will.</margin>
<margin>Augustine, *Against two Epistles of the Pelagians*, book 1 chapter 19. & *Sermon 2 on the words of the Apostle*, chapter 2.</margin>
44. **Draw him.** The Father draws us and teaches us to come to his Son, and to believe these high and hard mysteries of his incarnation and of feeding us with his own substance in the Sacrament: not compelling or violently forcing any against their will or without any respect of their consent, as Heretics <note>The author uses "Heretics" to refer to Protestant reformers who taught "total depravity" or "irresistible grace"</note> pretend: but by the sweet internal motions and persuasions of his grace and spirit he wholly makes us of our own will and liking to consent to the same.

<margin>The manifold preeminences of the Blessed Sacrament above Manna.</margin>
49. **Manna, and died.** The Heretics holding that the fathers of the old Testament ate the same food, and had as good Sacraments as we, are here refuted: Christ putting a plain difference in the very substance thereof, and in the graces and effects much more at large. Manna was only a figure <note>A "figure" is a symbolic foreshadowing in the Old Testament of a reality in the New Testament</note> of the Blessed Sacrament, though a very excellent figure thereof for many causes. It came in a sort from heaven, our Sacrament more: it was made by God miraculously, our Sacrament more: it was to be eaten for the time of their pilgrimage, our Sacrament more: it was to every man what he liked best, our Sacrament more: a little thereof served and sufficed as well as much, our Sacrament more: it was reserved for such days as it could not be gathered, and our Sacrament much more: it was kept for a memorial in the ark of the Testament, our Sacrament much more: the discontented and incredulous murmured and spoke against it, at our Sacrament much more: it sustained their bodies in the desert, our Sacrament both body and soul much more.

<margin>In the Blessed Sacrament, "How," is a Jewish word.</margin>
52. **How can this man.** It came not to their mind that nothing was impossible to God, they who wickedly said, *How can this man give us his flesh?* but we may make great profit from their sin, believing the Mysteries, and taking a lesson, never to say or once think, *How?* for it is a Jewish word and worthy of all punishment, so says St. Cyril <note>original: "li. 4 c. 13 in 10."; St. Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Book 4, Chapter 13</note>. Nevertheless if one asked only out of a desire to learn in humility, as our Lady did regarding her having a child in her virginity, then he must take the Angel's answer to her, That it is of the Holy Ghost, so says St. Damascene <note>original: "li. 4. c. 14."; St. John Damascene, On the Orthodox Faith, Book 4, Chapter 14</note>.

<margin>The real presence.</margin>
<margin>*Sermon 6 on the fast of the 7th month*.</margin>
53. **unless you eat.** Christ commending the Sacrament of the faithful unto us, said, *Except you eat etc. you cannot have life in you.* So the life says of life, and to him that thinks the life to be a liar, this food shall be death and not life to him. Augustine, *Sermon 2 on the words of the Apostle*, chapter 1. And St. Leo thus: *Because our Lord says, Except you eat etc. let us so communicate that we nothing doubt of the truth of Christ’s body and blood: for that is received with the mouth, which is believed in heart: and they answer "Amen" in vain, that dispute against that which they receive.*

<margin>Receiving in both kinds not necessary.</margin>
53. **And drink.** This the Protestants allege for the necessity of receiving in both kinds <note>the "kinds" refer to both the bread and the wine</note>: but in respect of themselves (who lightly hold all this chapter to pertain nothing to the Sacramental receiving, but to spiritual feeding on Christ by faith only) it can make nothing for one kind or the other. And in respect of us Catholics, who believe Christ's whole person both humanity and Divinity, both flesh and blood to be in either form, and to be wholly received no less in the first, then in the second or in both, this place commands nothing for both the kinds.

<margin>The Sacramental receiving of Christ's body, not always necessary to salvation.</margin>
<margin>*On the merits and forgiveness of sins*, book 1, chapter 20</margin>
53. **You shall not have life.** Though the Catholics teach these words to be spoken of the Sacrament, yet they mean not (no more than our Saviour here does) to exclude all from salvation, that receive not actually and Sacramentally under one or both kinds. For then children that die after they be baptized and never received Sacramentally, should perish: which to hold, were heretical. Neither did St. Augustine mean, applying these words to infants also, that they could not be saved without receiving sacramentally, as not only the Heretics, but Erasmus did unlearnedly.

<meta>The catchword at the bottom is "nedly," which is the end of the word "unlearnedly" on the following page.</meta>

<header>CHAPTER VI. ACCORDING TO ST. JOHN.</header>
<sig>Gg iij</sig>
<meta>catchword: 62. If</meta>

<margin>Council of Trent, session 21, chapter 4.</margin>
...taken as a mistake: but his meaning is that they were, by the right of their Baptism, joined to Christ's Mystical body, and thereby spiritual partakers of the other Sacrament also of Christ's body and blood. Just as all Catholic men who are in prison, joining with the Church of God in heart and desire <unclear>making up for the lack</unclear> of receiving and being partakers with the Church of this Sacrament—and those especially who devoutly, during the hearing of Mass, adore in person the body and blood of Christ, joining in heart with the Priest—all such receiving these receive the life and fruit of the Sacrament, even though they do not receive the Blessed Sacrament in one or both kinds <note>original: "kinds"; referring to the forms of Bread and Wine</note> every time. And although in the Primitive Church the holy Sacrament in the second kind <note>the consecrated wine</note> was often given even to infants to sanctify them, yet (as the holy Council has declared) it was never administered to them with the belief that they could not be saved without it. Therefore, the Heretics <note>Protestant reformers</note> untruly charge the Church and the Fathers with that error.

<margin>Cyril of Alexandria, book 4, chapters 14, 15.</margin>
<margin>Tertullian, On the Resurrection of the Flesh, number 7.</margin>
<margin>Irenaeus, Book 4, chapter 34.</margin>
<margin>Gregory of Nyssa, in the Great Catechetical Oration.</margin>
<margin>The effects of the Blessed Sacrament both in our body and soul.</margin>
54. *I will raise him.*) As the Son lives by the Father, *even so do we live by his flesh*, says St. Hilary <note>original: "li. 8. de Trin."; referring to his work On the Trinity, Book 8</note>. And St. Cyril again says: *Though by the nature of our flesh we be corruptible, yet by participation in life we are reformed to the property of life. For not only our souls were to be lifted up by the Holy Ghost to life everlasting, but this rude, gross terrestrial body of ours is to be reduced to immortality, by touching, tasting, and eating this agreeable food of Christ's body.* And when Christ says, *I will raise him up*, he means that *this body which he eats, shall raise him.* *Our flesh* (says Tertullian) *eats the body and blood of Christ, so that the soul may also be fattened. Therefore they shall both have one reward at the Resurrection.* And St. Irenaeus: *How do they affirm that our bodies are not capable of life everlasting, which are nourished by the body and blood of our Lord? Either let them change their opinion, or else cease to offer the Eucharist.* St. Gregory of Nyssa also says, *That living body entering into our body, changes it and makes it like itself and immortal.*

<margin>The Blessed Sacrament is the true Manna and water of the rock.</margin>
55. *Meat indeed.*) <note>"Meat" here means food in general</note> Manna was not the true food: nor was the water from the rock the drink indeed: for they only drove away death or famine for a time and for this life. *But the holy Body of Christ is the true food nourishing to life everlasting, and his blood the true drink that drives death away utterly, for they are not the body and blood of a mere man, but of him who, being joined to life, is made life: and therefore we are the body and members of Christ, because by this blessing of the mystery we receive the Son of God himself.* So says St. Cyril <note>Cyril of Alexandria, Book 4, chapter 16 on John</note>.

<margin>Council of Trent, Session 21, chapter 1.</margin>
<margin>The whole grace and effect is in either kind, and therefore there is no difference in receiving in one or both kinds, according to the holy Church's appointment.</margin>
58. *He that eateth this bread.*) By this passage the holy Council proves that regarding the grace and effect of the Sacrament, which is the life of the soul, there is no difference whether a man receives both kinds or only one. This is because our Savior, who previously attributed life to the eating and drinking of his body and blood, also affirms here that the same effect—which is life everlasting—comes from eating only under one form <note>the Bread</note>. Therefore, the Heretics are seditious slanderers who would make the people believe the Catholic Church and Priests have defrauded them of the grace and benefit of one of the kinds in the Sacrament. On the contrary, it is they who have defrauded the world, by taking away both the real substance of Christ and the grace from one kind, from both kinds, and from all other Sacraments. The Church only (by the wisdom of God’s Spirit and by the instruction of Christ and his Apostles, according to time and place, for God’s greatest honor, the reverence of the Sacrament, and the people's greatest profit) disposes of the manner and order of how the people shall receive, and all other particular points. These points, St. Augustine says, Christ himself did not set an order for, so that he might commit that task to the Apostles, through whom he was to arrange his Church’s affairs. Nevertheless, both he and the Apostles and the Fathers of the primitive Church left us examples of receiving under one kind. Christ at Emmaus <note>Luke 24:35</note>; the Apostles in Acts 2:42; the primitive Church in giving the blood only to children <note>Cyprian, Book on the Lapsed, number 10</note>; in reserving most commonly the body only <note>Tertullian, To his Wife, book 2, number 4; Cyprian, Book on the Lapsed, number 10</note>; in administering the Sacrament to the sick therewith <note>original: "houseling"; Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, book 6, chapter 36</note>; in the holy Hermits also who received and reserved it commonly (and not the blood) in the wilderness <note>Basil, Letter to Caesaria the Patrician</note>; and in various other cases which would be too long to rehearse.
<margin>St. Augustine, Letter 118, chapter 6 to Januarius.</margin>
<margin>Luke 24, 35.</margin>
<margin>Authority of Scriptures and the Primitive Church for receiving in one kind.</margin>

<margin>The causes of the Church’s practice and ordinance concerning one kind.</margin>
The Church is warranted in this, and fully taught by God's spirit in the ruling of such things—both for the reproving of certain heresies (which claimed that Christ, God and man, was not whole and entire in every part of the Sacrament) and especially because the Christian population has now enlarged. The communicants are often so many at once that not enough wine could be conveniently consecrated, nor could it be received without many accidents of spilling or abuse <note>original: "sheading"; the Church feared spilling the wine, which they believed was literally the blood of Christ</note>. The Protestants have no regard for this because it is only common wine which they use; but the Church, knowing it to be Christ's own blood, must have all dreadful regard for it. Therefore, I say, she has decreed and for some hundreds of years put into practice, that the Priest saying Mass should always both consecrate and also receive both kinds, because he must vividly represent the Passion of Christ and the separation of his blood from his body in the same; and to imitate the whole action and institution in both sacrificing and receiving, as he is the one to whom it was properly said, *Do this*, for that was spoken only to such as have power thereby to offer and consecrate. But the Laymen, and the Clergy also when they do not celebrate or say Mass themselves, should receive in one kind, being thereby no less partakers of Christ's whole person and grace than if they received both. For as St. Paul says: *He that eats the hosts is a partaker of the altar.* <note>1 Corinthians 10:18</note> He says "he that eats": for although there were drink-offerings or liquid offerings <note>original: "libaments"</note> joined lightly to every sacrifice, yet it was enough to eat only of one kind to be a partaker of the whole.
<margin>Luke 22, 19.</margin>
<margin>1 Corinthians 11.</margin>
<margin>The Priests that say Mass must receive both kinds.</margin>
<margin>1 Corinthians 10, 18.</margin>

<summary>This page defends the Catholic practice of receiving the Eucharist in only one form (the bread), arguing that Christ is fully present in either kind. It cites the Church Fathers and Scripture to claim that this practice prevents the desecration of the Sacred Blood while still providing the full grace of the Sacrament to the laity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the detailed Catholic commentary on John Chapter 6 from the Rheims New Testament. Having discussed the necessity of eating Christ’s flesh, the text now addresses the objections of those who find this teaching "hard," specifically interpreting Christ's words about his Ascension and the "profit" of the flesh to defend the doctrine of the Real Presence against Protestant Reformers.</meta>

<page-num>238</page-num>
<header>THE GOSPEL CHAPTER VI.</header>

<margin>Christ hints that we shall not believe his presence in the Blessed Sacrament because he has ascended.</margin>
62. *If you shall see.*) Our Savior seems to hint that those who do not believe his words regarding the holy Sacrament, and think it impossible for him to give his Body to be eaten in so many places at once while he was still on earth, would be much more offended and tempted after they saw or knew him to have ascended into heaven. This is proven true in the <term>Capharnaites</term><note>The author uses "Capharnaites" to refer to the people of Capernaum who doubted Jesus, applying the name here to contemporary Protestants who deny the Real Presence.</note> of this time, whose principal reason against Christ’s presence in the Sacrament is that he has ascended into heaven; indeed, they are so bold as to interpret this very sentence for themselves thus: *It is not this body or flesh which I will give you, for that I will carry with me to heaven.* By this, if they meant only that the condition and qualities of his body in heaven would be different from those in the Sacrament, it would be tolerable—for St. Augustine sometimes speaks in that sense—but to deny the substance of the body to be the same is wicked.

<margin>The Capharnaites' crude understanding of Christ’s flesh being given or eaten. And, how his flesh profits, and does not profit.</margin>
63. *The flesh profiteth nothing.*) If this speech were spoken in the sense of the <term>Sacramentaries</term><note>A 16th-century term for Reformers, such as Zwingli, who believed the bread and wine were merely symbolic signs.</note>, it would take away Christ’s Incarnation, manhood, and death, no less than his corporal presence in the Sacrament. For if his flesh were not profitable, all these things were in vain. Therefore, CHRIST does not deny his own flesh to be profitable, but rather that their crude and carnal understanding of his words, of his flesh, and of the manner of eating it, was unprofitable. This is made plain by the sentence following, where he warns them that his words are spirit and life, having a high mystical meaning, and are not to be taken vulgarly and crudely as they took them. It is the custom of the Scripture to call man’s natural sense, reason, and carnal resistance to (or failure to reach) supernatural truths, "flesh or blood," as in: *Flesh and blood revealed not this to thee, etc.* (Matthew 16).

<margin>Christ’s flesh gives life because it is the flesh of God and man.</margin>
<margin>Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, book 3, chapter 13.</margin>
<margin>Cyril, book 4, chapter 23 on John.</margin>
<margin>Ignatius cited by Theodoret, dialogue 3.</margin>
This carnality of theirs consisted specifically in two points: first, they imagined that he would kill himself, and cut and mangle his flesh into parts, and so give it to them raw or roasted to be eaten among them. This could not have been his meaning, says St. Augustine, for that would have involved a heinous and barbarous act; therefore, they should have been certain that he would command no such thing. Instead, they should have realized there was some other sweet sense to his hard, mystical, or figurative words, to be fulfilled in a Sacrament, mystery, and a marvelous divine fashion, otherwise than they could comprehend. Secondly, they erred regarding his flesh by taking it to be the flesh of a mere man, and of a dead man as well, when it came to be eaten. Of that kind of flesh, Christ here pronounces that it profits nothing. Whereupon St. Cyril says: *This body is not that of Peter or Paul or any other like them, but of Christ JESUS who is life itself; and therefore this Body gives life, the very fullness of the Divinity dwelling in it.* And the holy Council of Ephesus, in the 11th <term>Anathematism</term><note>A formal ecclesiastical curse or condemnation of a specific heresy.</note> as explained by the same St. Cyril, says: *The Eucharist is not the body of any common person (for the flesh of a common man could not give life) but of the WORD itself.* But the heretic <term>Nestorius</term><note>A 5th-century bishop who was condemned for teaching that Christ's human and divine natures were separate persons.</note> dissolves the power of this Mystery, holding that only man’s flesh is in the Eucharist. Thus it is stated there. And St. Ignatius, cited by Theodoret, and many other Fathers say the same. By this we may see that it comes from the Divinity and Spirit (without which Christ’s flesh cannot be) that this Sacrament gives life.

<margin>Judas the leader of those who do not believe the real presence.</margin>
<margin>* verse 64</margin>
64. *That believe not.*) You see here that it is a lack of faith that causes men to kick against this high truth of the Sacrament. It may also be learned here that it is the great and merciful gift of God that Catholic men, contrary to their senses and carnal reasons, believe and submit themselves to the humble acknowledgment of this Mystery. Lastly, it may well be gathered by Christ’s hint regarding Judas (* verse 64) that he specifically kicked against our Master’s speeches concerning the holy Sacrament.

<margin>Heretics do not believe the real presence because they see bread and wine, just as the Jews did not believe his Divinity because of the form of a poor man.</margin>
66. *went back.*) It can be no marvel to us now that so many revolt from the Church, taking offense or scandal unjustly at Christ’s body and blood in the Sacrament, seeing that many of his disciples—who saw his wonderful life, doctrine, and miracles—forsook Christ himself upon the speech and promise of the same Sacrament. For the mystery of it is so supernatural and divine in itself, and yet so low and base for our sakes (by appearing in the forms of these earthly elements under which it exists and we eat it), that the unfaithful and weak stumble at Christ in the Sacrament just as the Jews and Gentiles did at Christ in his humanity. For the reasons for contradicting the Incarnation and <term>Transubstantiation</term><note>The Catholic doctrine that the substance of bread and wine changes into the substance of the Body and Blood of Christ.</note> are the same. It may be truly judged that whoever cannot now believe the Sacrament to be Christ because it is under the forms of bread and wine, and is eaten and drunk, would not then have believed that Christ was God because he was in the shape of a man and was crucified.

<margin>The disciples revolting at Christ’s words prove that he spoke not metaphorically, as at other times.</margin>
To conclude, it was not a figure nor a mystery of bare bread and wine, nor any metaphorical or allegorical speech, that could make such a troop of his disciples revolt at once. When he said he was a door, a vine, a way, a Shepherd, and such like (to which kind of speeches the Protestants ridiculously compare the words of the holy Sacrament), who was so mad as to mistake him, or to forsake him for the same? For the Apostles, at least, would have pulled them by the sleeves and said, "Do not go away, masters, he is speaking in parables." The cause, therefore, was their unbelief and the height of the Mystery; they neither knew how he could be present, nor would they believe that he was able to give his flesh to be eaten in many places. And such is the unbelief of the heretics regarding this matter today.

<margin>As Judas represents all unbelieving heretics, so Peter carries the person of the Church.</margin>
<margin>* Cyprian, epistle 55, number 3.</margin>
68. *Peter answered.*) Peter answers for the Twelve, not knowing that Judas in his heart was already wicked and did not believe Christ’s former words regarding the Blessed Sacrament, but was to revolt afterward as well as the others. In this, Peter carries the person of the Church and all Catholic men, who, despite any difficulty of his word or any revolt (be it ever so general) of

<header>CHAPTER 7. ACCORDING TO ST. JOHN.</header>

<margin><note>original: "Tract. 27 in Evang."</note> St. Augustine, Tractate 27 on the Gospel.</margin>
<margin>The resolution of all believing Catholics: namely in the Blessed Sacrament.</margin>
Schismatics, heretics, or apostates, whether because of this Sacrament or any other Article of faith, will always forsake Christ. And when the company of others draws us toward revolt, let us say this: "Lord, to whom or where shall we go, once we have forsaken you? To Calvin, Luther, or such men? And shall we forsake you and your Church along with the unfaithful multitude? No, you have the words of life, and we believe you; your Church will not and cannot deceive us." "You have," says St. Augustine, "everlasting life in the ministration of your body and blood." And a little after: "You are everlasting life itself, and you give nothing in your flesh and blood but that which you yourself are."

Why *Amen, amen* is not translated.

* In the exact words. <note>original Greek: *Autolexei*</note>

*34. Amen, amen.] What does it mean (asks St. Augustine regarding this passage) when our Lord says, "Amen, amen"? He is greatly commending and emphasizing the thing he utters by doubling the word. It is a kind of oath of his, if one may put it that way. For "Amen" in Hebrew signifies "truth" <note>original Latin: *verum*</note>. Yet it is not translated here, even though it could have been said, "Truly, truly I say to you" <note>original Latin: *verum, verum dico vobis*</note>. Neither the* Greek interpreter nor the Latin dared to translate it; the Hebrew word has remained as it was, so that it might be held in higher esteem. *Tractate 41 on John.* By these words and similar ones recorded elsewhere in this New Testament, the reader can see the great reason why we also say "Amen, amen," and did not dare to translate it or other similar words into our English tongue.*

# CHAPTER 9.

Yet they are so obstinate that because it was the Sabbath when he performed it, they argue he is not from God; they even throw the man out of their synagogue for confessing him. 35 But our Lord receives him, 39 and takes the opportunity to foretell the blinding <note>The original term "excecation" refers to the act of making someone blind, here used spiritually.</note> of the Jews (because of their willful stubbornness) and the illumination of the Gentiles who confess their own blindness.*

### ANNOTATIONS CHAPTER 9

<margin>6. Made clay.] External ceremonies.</margin>
6. **Made clay.]** Christ, who could have cured this man by his only will or word, nevertheless used certain created things as his instruments in working, and various circumstances and ceremonies: clay, water, anointing, washing, etc. It is no wonder then that he and his Church use such varieties of <term>Sacraments</term> <note>Visible rituals that are believed to convey God's grace to the soul.</note> and external ceremonies in curing our souls.

<margin>22. Put out of the Synagogue.] A heretical translation. Casting out of the Synagogue.</margin>
22. **Put out of the Synagogue.]** The Heretics <note>The Catholic authors are here criticizing Protestant translators (like those of the Geneva Bible) for using the word "excommunicate" instead of "put out of the synagogue."</note> untruly translate here (and in verse 35) as *Excommunicate*: to make simple people think the Church's Excommunication is no different, or no better, or no more rightly used against them, than this casting out of the Synagogue of those who confessed our Savior. They might as well have translated "Church" for Synagogue; "the New Testament" for the Old; "grace" for Law; "spirit" for flesh; or "Christ" for Moses. For there is no less difference between being cast out of the Synagogue and true Excommunication. Besides, not every person who was not part of the Jews’ Synagogue was therefore out of the communion of the Faithful, as many true believers existed in other parts of the world who were not subject to the Jews’ Synagogue, Law, or Sacraments. And therefore, it was not the same thing to be out of the Synagogue and to be excommunicated. Whereas now, whoever is out of the Church's communion—either by their own will or by being thrust out for their just deserts by the spiritual Magistrate <note>A term for church authorities who held the power to judge and discipline.</note>—is entirely abandoned by all the society of Saints in heaven and earth, so long as they remain in that state.

<margin>The Church’s Excommunication. See in the *Annotations on Matthew 18, 17.* The Heretics' ridiculous Excommunication. Numbers 16.</margin>
As for the cause of thrusting this poor man and others like him out of the Synagogue, and excommunicating Heretics, there is as great a difference as between heaven and hell: he was treated so for following Christ and his Church, while these are treated so for forsaking Christ and his Church. Some more similarity exists between that corrupt sentence of the Jews against the followers of Christ and the pretended excommunication executed against Catholic men by our Heretics—although, in truth, there is no great resemblance. For the Jews, though they sometimes abused their power, still had actual authority by God’s law to punish those who despised their Law, and therefore it was feared and respected even by good men. But the excommunication used by heretics against Catholics or any offenders is not to be respected at all, being nothing more than a ridiculous usurpation of the Church’s right and its customs. For all faithful men ought to flee from their "synagogues" and not wait to be thrust out, according to the warning given against <term>Korah and Dathan</term> <note>original: "Core and Dathan." This refers to the biblical figures who led a rebellion against Moses and were swallowed by the earth.</note>: *Be separated from their tabernacles, lest you be wrapped up in their sins.*
