<meta>This page concludes the annotations for John chapter 10 and begins the narrative of chapter 11. It focuses on the distinction between true pastors and "heretics," the legitimacy of church festivals not explicitly commanded in Scripture, and the beginning of the account of the raising of Lazarus.</meta>

# THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO JOHN. CHAPTER 11.

<margin>Arch-heretics especially are the thieves that climb in another way, not by the door.</margin>
1. *He who climbs another way.*) Whoever takes it upon himself to preach without being lawfully sent, to administer Sacraments, and is not canonically ordained by a true Catholic Bishop to be a curate of souls, a parson, a Bishop, or any other spiritual Pastor, and does not enter by lawful election and the Holy Church’s ordinance to that dignity, but breaks in against order by force or the favor of men and by human laws, he is a thief and a murderer. So entered Arius, Calvin, Luther, and all Heretics, and all who succeed them in position and doctrine. Generally, this applies to everyone who does not descend by lawful succession in the known ordinary line of Catholic Bishops and Pastors that have existed in all countries since their conversion. According to this rule, *St. Irenaeus (Book 3, Chapter 3)* distinguishes true shepherds from thieves and heretics. So do *Tertullian (On the Prescription of Heretics, number 11)*, *St. Cyprian (On the Unity of the Church, number 7)*, *St. Augustine (Letter 165 and Against the Letter of Mani, Chapter 4)*, and *Vincent of Lérins*.

11. *Good Pastor.*) The good Pastor is he whose special care is not for his own advantage, but for the safety of the flock. The hireling is he who does not respect the profit and good of the flock, but his own profit. The wolf is the Heretic, or any persecutor of the Church, which is Christ’s flock.

<margin>When the Pastor must stay, or may flee.</margin>
13. *Flees.*) Every Bishop and Pastor is bound to remain with his flock in times of danger and persecution even unto death, unless he himself is personally sought after rather than the flock, or the flock itself forsakes him. In such cases the Pastor may flee, as the Apostles did, and St. Athanasius, and others. <note>original: *St. Athan. Apol. de sua fuga. August. ep. 180.* (St. Athanasius’s *Apology for his Flight* and St. Augustine’s *Letter 180*).</note>

<margin>Judas Maccabeus. Dedication of Churches.</margin>
22. *The dedication.*) This is the feast of Dedication instituted by Judas Maccabeus <note>original: *li. 1 Mach. c. 4.* (1 Maccabees chapter 4)</note>. Christ deigned to honor and keep that feast instituted by him; yet our Heretics <note>The author is referring to Protestant reformers who rejected the books of Maccabees and certain church traditions.</note> do not deign to pray and sacrifice for the dead, which was practiced and approved by him. The Dedication of Christian Churches is also warranted by this, along with the annual memories of it. It proves that such things may be instituted without any express commandment in Scripture.
<margin>2 Maccabees chapter 10.</margin>

<margin>Christ’s essence and divine nature from the Father. Calvin’s autotheism.</margin>
29. *That which he gave me.*) This is how various Fathers also read the text, namely *St. Hilary (On the Trinity, Book 7, after the middle)*, *St. Ambrose (On the Holy Spirit, Book 3, Chapter 18)*, *St. Augustine (On John, Tract 48)*, and *St. Cyril (On John, Book 7, Chapter 10)*. They use it to prove that Christ had his essence and nature from the Father. Therefore, some Heretics of our time wickedly accuse the Council of Lateran of falsifying this passage and applying it to that same purpose. They can tolerate it less because it is against Calvin’s <term>Autotheism<note>The doctrine that the Son is "God of himself" (autotheos) rather than receiving his divine essence from the Father through eternal generation.</note></term>, which holds that Christ took his person from the Father, but not his substance. *See the second Annotation in 1 John verse 1.*

->### A N N O T A T I O N S<-
->#### C H A P. X I.<-

<margin>Luke 22, 33.</margin>
*51. Being the high Priest.]* Do not marvel that Christ preserves his truth in the Church as well by the unworthy as the worthy Prelates <note>High-ranking church officials</note> thereof: the gifts of the Holy Spirit following their Order and office, as we see here in Caiaphas, and not their personal merits. And if this man—being in many ways wicked, and in part an usurper, and the Law and Priesthood being about to decline and give place to Christ’s new ordinance—had yet some assistance from God for the speaking of truth which he himself did not mean, nor know: how much more may we be assured, that Christ will not leave Peter’s Seat <note>The Papacy</note>, *whose faith he promised should never fail, though the persons who occupy the same were as evil as the blasphemous and malicious mouths of Heretics <note>The author is referring to Protestant reformers who criticized the personal conduct of various Popes.</note> do affirm?*

### ANNOTATIONS
### CHAPTER 12.

<margin>Church ornaments.</margin>
5. *Why was.*) So wicked, covetous, and sacrilegious persons criticize <note>original: "reprehend"</note> good men for bestowing their goods upon Church ornaments and so forth, under the pretense of better bestowing them on the poor. Such people "provide" for the poor just as Judas did.

<margin>Toleration of the evil.</margin>
6. *A thief.*) Judas did not first perish when he sold our Lord, for he was a thief before: and being already lost, he yet followed Christ—not in heart, but in body only. Which our Master tolerated, to give us a lesson to tolerate the evil rather than divide the body. <note>original: "Aug. tract. 50 in Io."; referring to St. Augustine’s 50th Tractate on the Gospel of John</note>

<margin>Purity required for the receiving of the Blessed Sacrament.</margin>
5. *Began to wash.*) This washing <note>original: "lotion"</note> was not only out of courtesy, such as the Jews used toward their guests, nor only for an example of humility; but for a mystery and significance of the great purity that is required before we come to receive the holy Sacrament, which straight after this washing was to be instituted and given to the Apostles. *Ambrose, On the Sacraments, book 3, chapter 1; Bernard, Sermon 1 on the Lord's Supper.* <note>original Latin: "Ambr. li. 3 de Sacra. c. 1 Bernard. de cœna Domini Serm. 1."</note>

<margin>Venial sins taken away by sacred ceremonies.</margin>
10. *To wash his feet.*) The foulness of the feet, when all the rest is clean, signifies the earthly affections and remnants of former sins that have been forgiven; which are to be cleansed by devout acts of charity and humility, as *Saint Ambrose (On the Sacraments, book 3, chapter 1)* and *Saint Augustine (Epistle 108 and Tractate 56 on John)* note. And because this was only a ceremony, and yet had such force—both then and afterward used by the Apostles—that it purged smaller offenses <term>venial sins</term> <note>Minor sins that do not break one's relationship with God but require spiritual cleansing.</note> and the filthiness of the soul, as *Saint Ambrose* and *Saint Bernard* gather, it should not seem strange that holy water and such ceremonies may remit venial sins. <margin>Ambrose and Bernard, in the places cited.</margin>

# ANNOTATIONS
## CHAPTER 14.

<margin><note>original: "li. de Babyla mart. 10. 5."</note> Book on the Martyr Babylas, Chapter 10, Section 5. * Acts 5:15, 19:12. * See Annotations on Matthew 17:20.</margin>
<margin>We may and must easily believe the miracles of Saints and of their relics, when Christ himself foretells they shall do such wonderful things.</margin>
<margin>The <term>Heretics</term> <note>Referring here to the Protestant reformers of the 16th century.</note> are as faithless in this point as the ancient Pagans.</margin>
12. *Greater than these.*) St. Chrysostom, in a whole book written against the Pagans, proves that this was fulfilled not only in Peter’s shadow and Paul’s garments—which, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles, healed illnesses—but also by the **Relics** and monuments of Saints, namely of St. Babylas, whom he discusses there. By this, he infers that Christ is God, who could and did perform these wonderful words through the very ashes of his servants. The Protestants, quite to the contrary, acting as patrons of the Pagans' infidelity, act as though our Savior had promised these and similar miraculous works in vain, either not meaning to or not being able to fulfill them. Thus they discredit all the approved histories of the Church concerning miracles performed by Saints: namely, that St. Gregory <term>Thaumaturgus</term> <note>From the Greek 'Thaumatourgos,' meaning 'wonder-worker.'</note> moved a mountain; the miracles of St. Paul the Hermit and St. Hilarion written by St. Jerome; the miracles of St. Martin written by Sulpicius Severus; the miracles testified by St. Augustine in <note>original: "de Ciuit. Dei"</note> *The City of God*; the miracles approved by St. Gregory in his *Dialogues*; the miracles reported by St. Bede in his *Ecclesiastical History* and lives of Saints; and all other miracles, no matter how faithfully recorded by Church writers. In all these things, which are beyond their reach of reason and nature, they are as little persuaded and have no more faith than the Pagans did, against whom St. Chrysostom in the aforementioned book, and St. Augustine in *The City of God* (Book 22, Chapter 8), and other Fathers have written in the past. No one, therefore, needs to marvel that even the **Image of our Lady** <note>The Virgin Mary.</note> and similar things perform miracles, just as Peter’s shadow did; nor wonder if such things seem stranger and greater than those which Christ himself did; whereas our Savior, to remove any doubt, says expressly that his Saints shall do greater things than he himself did.

<margin>The HOLY GHOST is promised to the CHURCH for ever.</margin>
16. *For ever.*) If the Holy Ghost had been promised only to the Apostles, then their successors and the Church after them could not have claimed it. But it was promised to them forever. From this we may learn both that the privileges and promises made to the Apostles were not personal, but pertained to their offices perpetually; and also that the Church and its Pastors in all ages had and have the same Holy Ghost to govern them that the Apostles and the primitive Church had.

<margin>The Spirit of truth shall assist the CHURCH always.</margin>
17. *The spirit of truth.*) They had many particular gifts and graces of the Holy Ghost before, and many virtues by the same, as all holy men have at all times; but the Holy Ghost promised here to the Apostles and their successors forever is specifically promised for this use: to direct them in all truth and verity. It is the opposite of the spirit of error, heresy, and falsehood. Therefore, the Church cannot fall into <term>Apostasy</term> <note>The total abandonment of the Christian faith.</note> or Heresy, or fade away into nothing, as our adversaries claim.

<margin>The Arians allege plain Scriptures just as the Protestants do.</margin>
28. *Father greater than I.*) There is no place in Scripture that seems to support the <term>Sacramentaries</term> <note>A term used by Catholics for Protestants who denied the Real Presence of Christ in the Eucharist.</note> as much as this and others, in the outward appearance of the words, seemed to support the <term>Arians</term> <note>A 4th-century group who believed that Jesus was a created being and not equal to God the Father.</note>, who denied the equality of the Son with the Father. These words, however, when rightly understood according to the Church's sense, contribute nothing to their false sect. They only signify that Christ, according to his **Manhood**, was indeed inferior, and that according to his **Divinity**, he came from the Father. If the heresy or "disease" of this current time were Arianism, we would rely on these passages and similar ones against the Arians, just as we now rely on others against the Protestants, whose sect is the disease and ruin of this time.

***

### ANNOTATIONS
### CHAPTER XV.

<margin>No man is sure of perseverance.</margin>
4. *Unless you abide.*] These conditional speeches, *If you remain in the vine, If you keep my commandments*, and such like, give us to know <note>original: "vvit"</note> that we are not certain to persist or persevere, nor to be saved, except under conditions to be fulfilled by us. *See St. Augustine, On Rebuke and Grace, chapter 13.*

4. *Unless it abide.*] Whoever, by Heresy or Schism or for any other cause, is cut off or separated from the Church, can do no meritorious work leading to Salvation.

<margin>Not only faith.</margin>
10. *Keep my precepts.*] This careful and frequent admonition to keep his commandments proves that a Christian man’s life consists not only or principally in faith, but in good works.

24. *If I had.*] If the Jews had not sinned by refusing Christ, in the event that he had not performed greater miracles than any other: then it would be a great folly for Catholics to believe the new opinions of Luther or Calvin <note>Key figures of the Protestant Reformation</note> which are presented without any miracles at all.

26. *Whom I will send.*] The Holy Spirit <note>original: "Holy Ghost"</note> is sent by the Son, therefore he proceeds from him also, as from the Father: though the modern Schismatic Greeks <note>The Eastern Orthodox Church, who historically disagree with the "Filioque" clause—that the Spirit proceeds from both Father and Son</note> think otherwise.

27. *You shall give.*] He deigns to join together the testimony of the Holy Spirit and of the Apostles: so that we may see the testimony of truth jointly consists in the Holy Spirit and in the <term>Prelates</term> <note>High-ranking clergy, such as bishops, who hold authority in the Church</note> of the Church.

---

<margin>Christ left many things to be taught by the Church.</margin>
12. *Yet many things.*) This place convinces <note>shows or proves</note> that the Apostles and the faithful are taught many things which Christ omitted to teach them because of their weakness: and that it was the providence of God that Christ in person should not teach and order all things, so that we might be no less assured of the things that the Church teaches by the Holy Ghost, than of the things that he himself delivered.

<gloss>13 The Spirit of truth.) Always note that the Holy Spirit, in the context of being promised to the Church, is called the Spirit of truth. This Holy Spirit is given to various individuals and all good people for the purpose of making them holy (sanctification). However, to teach all truth and to preserve the faith from error, he is promised and provided only to the Church itself, its chief leader <note>Referring to the Pope</note>, and its general Councils.</gloss>

## ANNOTATIONS
### CHAPTER XVII.

<margin>True knowledge of God.</margin>
3. *Life everlasting.*) Both the life of glory in heaven, and of grace here in the Church, consist in the knowledge of God: that [in heaven], in perfect vision; this [on earth], in faith working by charity. For, knowledge of God without keeping his commandments, is not true knowledge, that is to say, it is an unprofitable knowledge. *1 John 2.* <note>original: "1 Io. 2." referencing the First Epistle of John, chapter 2</note>

<margin>The Church cannot err.</margin>
17. *Sanctify them.*) Christ prays that the Apostles, their successors, and all that shall be of their belief, may be sanctified in truth. Which is as much to say, as to desire that the Church may ever have the Spirit of truth, and be free from error. Which prayer of Christ had not been heard, if the Church might err. <note>This refers to the Catholic doctrine of Infallibility, suggesting that because Christ prayed for the Church to be kept in truth, it is divinely protected from teaching false doctrine.</note>

<margin>The Canon of the Mass.</margin>
20. *But for them.*) He expresses (and it is a great comfort) that he prays not only for the Apostles, but for the whole Church after them, that is, for all believers. And all this profound and divine prayer is resembled in the holy Canon of the Mass <note>The central, most solemn prayer of the Eucharistic liturgy</note> before the consecration, as here it was made before his visible Sacrifice on the cross.

<summary>In this conclusion to his prayer, Jesus asks for the protection and sanctification of his followers, extending his petition to all future believers. The accompanying notes argue that this prayer ensures the Church's infallibility and find its liturgical parallel in the Roman Catholic Mass.</summary>
<keywords>Sanctification, High Priestly Prayer, Church Unity, Infallibility, Canon of the Mass, Knowledge of God, Sacrifice, Eucharist</keywords>

<margin>The HOLY CROSS.</margin>
15. *His own cross.*] This cross—because it was the instrument of our redemption and, as it were, the altar of the supreme sacrifice, highly sanctified by the touching, bearing, and offering of the sacred body and blood of our Lord—is truly called the **HOLY CROSS**. It has been endowed with the power of miracles, both as a whole and in every small piece. For these reasons, and especially as a very close memorial of Christ’s Passion, it has been visited in pilgrimages, honored by feast days and otherwise, and preserved and revered by the ancient fathers with all devotion. Conversely, it has been abused by Pagans, <term>Apostates</term> <note>those who renounce their faith</note>, and Heretics who seek in vain to deface and destroy it. See *Saint Cyril, book 6 against Julian; Saint Jerome, letter 17; Saint Paulinus, letter 11; Ruffinus, book 1, chapters 7 & 8; Evagrius’ History, book 4, chapter 25; Saint Leo, letter 72 and Sermon 8 on the Passion; Paulus Diaconus, book 18.*

<margin>By this you see why in Catholic Churches MARY and John stand by the Rood.</margin>
26. *To his mother.*] The marvelous respect that Christ had for his mother, deigning to speak to her and to provide for her even from the cross in the middle of his infinite anguishes and the mysteries being worked for mankind. <note>The "Rood" refers to the large crucifix traditionally placed at the entrance of the church sanctuary, flanked by Mary and John.</note>

<margin>book 2 against Jovinian.</margin>
27. *To the Disciple.*] A great honor and responsibility for John to have that blessed jewel <note>Mary</note> in his care; and an unspeakable comfort that from 그날 forward they were to be mother and son to one another. *He commended the virgin to a virgin,* <note>original: "virginem virgini commendauit"</note> says Saint Jerome.

<margin>Exodus 18. Numbers 20. Tract 9 on John. Homily 84 on John. Genesis 2:21.</margin>
<margin>The Sacraments issued out of Christ’s side, and from there have their power.</margin>
<margin>The CHURCH built from Christ’s side, as Eve was from Adam’s.</margin>
34. *Blood and water.*] This piercing of Christ’s side, though done blindly and insolently by the soldier, contained great mysteries by God’s ordinance. It was prefigured by Moses striking the rock with his staff. This stream of blood and water, miraculously drawn out of his dead body and flowing through the Sacraments of the Church for God's people, was symbolized by the water from that same rock which followed the Israelites in the desert. "Out of this side," says Saint Augustine, "issued the Sacraments." "From here," says Saint Chrysostom, "the great mysteries have their beginning." He warns us that when we come to drink from the holy chalice, we should approach as though we are drawing the blood directly from Christ’s side. Both blood and water flowed forth separately to show us the source of the two primary Sacraments and their distinct elements: Baptism and the <term>Eucharist</term> <note>The Lord's Supper or Holy Communion</note>, springing toward eternal life in the Church. The Church fathers also say that the Church—who is Christ’s spouse and helper in applying the blood and water for the benefit of the faithful—was formed and built here, taken from this holy side of Christ as he "slept" on the Cross, just as *Eve was taken from Adam’s side* when he was cast into a deep sleep in Paradise.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Gospel of John, Chapter 20, specifically focusing on the theological implications of Christ's resurrection appearances and the institution of the Sacrament of Penance. It addresses the nature of Christ's glorified body and refutes various Protestant views on the Eucharist and the power of the priesthood.</meta>

### THE GOSPEL CHAPTER 20.
#### Sacrament, humanity, Penance, Priesthood, Heretics, Ubiquitarians, Brentians, St. Augustine, St. Ambrose, St. Cyril, St. Jerome, remission of sins, absolution, Confession, Contrition, Satisfaction.

<margin>The presence of Christ's body in the Blessed Sacrament <note>original: "B. Sacramēt"</note> without occupying space or quantity corresponding to it, is proved by other examples in Scripture.</margin>
The manner of the quantity, space, or place agreeable to the condition of his humanity is invincibly refuted by Christ's entering in among the Disciples while the doors were shut; and by the fact that his true natural body—whole and perfect in all its limbs, length, breadth, and thickness, distinct and different from the substance and thickness of the wood—was in the same proper place that the wood was in, and passed through it. Just as he also came out of his mother's womb, the closure not disturbed, and passed through the stone out of his Sepulcher. By all of which the Heretics being plainly reproved and convinced of infidelity, they boldly deny the plain Scriptures, or so foolishly shift themselves from the evidence thereof, that their impudence is especially to be noted in this point.

<margin>Heretical excuses <note>original: "shifts"</note> to avoid plain Scripture.</margin>
Some say that he came in through the window; some, that the door opened of itself to let him in; some, that "to come in, the doors being shut," signifies no more than that he came in late in the evening, at which time men usually shut their doors; and such other flights to defend falsehood against express Scriptures and against the Apostles' testimony, who therefore took him to be a Spirit because they saw him stand suddenly in the midst of them, all the house being closely shut. And the Church Fathers all confess that he went in while the doors were shut. See *St. Ambrose, Book 10 on Luke, chapter 24; St. Augustine, letter 3 to Volusianus & Book 22 of The City of God, chapter 8; and St. Cyril, on John, Book 12, chapter 53; and St. Jerome, Book 1 Against Jovinianus, chapter 21.* We know it is the natural course of God's ordinance that every body should have but one and its own proper place fitted to the lineaments, quantity, terms, and limits of the same; without which naturally the bodies were nowhere, and consequently not at all, as *St. Augustine says to Dardanus.* <note>Reference to Augustine's *Letter 187*, often titled "On the Presence of God."</note>

<margin>Christ can dispose of his own body and others above nature.</margin>
<margin>Augustine, letter 57. Matthew 19. Augustine, book 2, chapter 8 of The City of God <note>original: "de civ Dei"</note>.</margin>
But to say that God supernaturally and miraculously cannot by his omnipotence dispose otherwise of his own body than its natural form or quantity or quality require—that is great incredulity. For we must believe that he can do so with any other body of mere men or other creatures, the Scripture being plain that he can make a camel pass through a needle's eye, while still continuing in its natural figure and quantity. And *St. Augustine* tells of a woman whose ring fell from her girdle while both remained fast and whole; and *Rupertus* <note>Rupert of Deutz, a 12th-century theologian.</note> tells of a Religious man whose fast-buckled girdle fell down before him from his body. *On the Offices of the Church* <note>original: "De off. Eccl."</note>.

<margin>Ubiquitarians or Brentians.</margin>
Therefore it is too much unfaithfulness, by the rules of physical place, to bar Christ from his will or wisdom to be in the Sacrament however he himself pleases, and on as many altars or places as he likes. We detest, for all that, the wicked heresy of certain Protestants—holding quite contrary to the Zwinglians <note>Followers of Huldrych Zwingli, who believed the Eucharist was merely symbolic.</note>—who claim that Christ, according to his Humanity, is in every place where the Divinity is. This is called the "Ubiquitarian" heresy, and it is against faith and the common rules of nature and divinity. <note>The Brentiani or Brentians were followers of Johannes Brenz, a Lutheran who argued for the omnipresence of Christ's human nature.</note>

<margin>Christ shows his commission and so gives the Apostles power to remit sins.</margin>
21. *As my Father.*) As when he gave them commission to preach and baptize throughout the world, he made mention of his own power therein; so here, before he institutes the Sacrament of Penance and gives them authority to remit sins—lest the wicked should ask afterward by what right they do such great functions—he shows his Father's commission given to himself, and then in plain terms most amply imparts the same to his Apostles. Thus, whosoever denies the Apostles and their successors, the Priests of God's Church, the right to remit sins, must consequently deny that Christ as man has authority to do the same.

<margin>The Holy Ghost is here purposely given to the Apostles to remit sins.</margin>
<margin>Augustine, <unclear>note</unclear> on the Testament 93, Against Parmenianus, Book 2, chapter 11. Cyril, Book 12, chapter 56 on John <note>original: "Io."</note>.</margin>
22. *He breathed.*) He gives the Holy Ghost in and by an external sign to his Apostles—not visibly and for all such purposes as later at Pentecost, but for the grace of the Sacrament of Orders, as *St. Augustine* says. This is so that none may doubt the Priest's right in the remission of sins, seeing the Holy Ghost is purposely given to them to do this very thing. In which case, if any remain contentious, he must deny the Holy Ghost to be God, or deny that He has power to remit sins. It is not absurd (says *St. Cyril*) that they forgive sins who have the Holy Ghost. *For when they remit or retain, the Holy Ghost remits or retains in them, and they do that in two ways: first in Baptism, and then in Penance.* As *St. Ambrose* also (*Book 1, chapter 7 on Penance*) says when refuting the Novatians <note>An early Christian sect that denied the Church could forgive grave sins committed after baptism.</note>—a sect of old Heretics who, pretending God's glory as our new Sectaries do, denied that Priests could remit sins in the Sacrament of Penance. He asks why it should be more a dishonor to God, or more impossible or inconvenient for men, to forgive sins by Penance than by Baptism, seeing it is the Holy Ghost that does it through the Priest's office and ministry in both.

<margin>The Sacrament of PENANCE instituted.</margin>
<margin>Men are bound to confess all their mortal sins, and that in particular.</margin>
<margin>* Cyprian, on the lapsed <note>original: "Cy. de laps."</note>, <unclear>number</unclear> 11. * Here in 16 John.</margin>
23. *Whose sins.*) The power to offer Sacrifice, which is the principal function and act of Priesthood, was given to them at the institution of the Blessed Sacrament <note>at the Last Supper</note>. The second and next special faculty of Priesthood, consisting in remitting sins, is bestowed on them here. And with it, the holy Sacrament of Penance—implying Contrition, Confession, and Satisfaction on the part of the Penitent, and absolution on the Priest's part—is instituted. For in that express power and commission is given to Priests to remit or retain all sins; and in that Christ promises that whose sins soever they forgive, they are of God forgiven also; and whose sins they retain, they are retained before God; it follows necessarily that we are bound to submit ourselves to their judgment for the release of our sins. For this wonderful power would be given to them in vain if no one were bound to seek absolution at their hands. Neither can any rightly seek absolution from them unless they confess particularly at least all their mortal offenses, whether they be committed in mind, heart, will, and * thought only, or in word and work. For God's priests, being constituted in this Sacrament of Penance in Christ's stead as judges in causes of our conscience, cannot rightly rule our cases without full and exact cognition and knowledge of all our sins, and the necessary circumstances and * differences of the same. Which cannot otherwise be had by them, being mortal men, than
<meta>catchword: then</meta>

<summary>This page provides a theological defense of Christ's physical presence in the Eucharist and the institution of the Sacrament of Penance (Confession). It argues that Christ's ability to enter through locked doors proves his body can transcend natural physical laws, and that he explicitly delegated the power to forgive sins to his Apostles and their successors.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Gospel of John, Chapter 20. Having established Christ’s physical resurrection and his appearance to the disciples, the text now focuses on the "Commission of Remitting Sins"—the biblical foundation for the Catholic Sacrament of Penance (Confession).</meta>

### CHAPTER 20. ACCORDING TO ST. JOHN.

<margin>To retain sins.</margin>
...then by our simple, sincere, and clear speaking of our sins to them, with a humble and contrite heart, ready to accept and perform penance according to their instruction. For that authority to "retain sins" consists especially in ordering satisfaction and works of penance, such as prayer, fasting, almsgiving, and the like. Anyone who condemns or despises this ordinance of God—as the Heretics <note>The author refers to Protestant reformers who rejected the necessity of sacramental confession to a priest.</note> do—or neglects it, as some careless Catholics might do, let them be assured they cannot be saved.

<margin>The necessity of this Sacrament.</margin>
Neither must any such Christian person claim or expect to have his sins committed after Baptism forgiven by God alone, without this Sacrament. This was the ancient heresy of the Novatians <note>The Novatians were a 3rd-century sect that denied the Church had the power to forgive serious sins committed after baptism.</note> (*Ambrose, Book 1 on Penance, chapter 2; Socrates, Book 7 of Ecclesiastical History, chapter 25*). One might as well hope to be saved or have their original sin (or other sins committed before Baptism) forgiven by God without the Sacrament of Baptism itself.

<margin>Jerome to Demetrias, chapter 6, note 1.</margin>
Let no man deceive himself; this is the "second plank after a shipwreck" <note>original: "second table or borde after shipvvracke"</note>, as Saint Jerome calls it. Whoever does not take hold of it shall undoubtedly perish, because they despise God's counsel and his order for their salvation. Therefore, Saint Augustine (*Epistle 180*), joining both together, says it is a pitiful case when men depart this life in the absence of God's Priests, "either not born again, or bound" <note>original Latin: "aut non regenerati, aut ligati"</note>—that is, either not regenerated by Baptism, or fast bound in sin and not absolved by the Sacrament of Penance and reconciliation. This is because they shall be excluded from eternal life, and destruction follows them. Saint Victor (*Book 2 on the Vandal Persecution*) describes the miserable lamentation of the people when their Priests were banished by the Arian Heretics: "Who," they said, "shall baptize these infants? Who shall minister penance to us, and loose us from the bonds of sins?" Therefore, Saint Cyprian very often (specifically in *Epistle 54*) calls it a great cruelty—and something for which Priests shall answer on the Last Day—to allow any man who is penitent for his sins to depart this life without this reconciliation and absolution.

<margin>Matthew 18.</margin>
This is because, he says, the Lawmaker himself (Christ) has granted that things bound on earth should also be bound in heaven, and that those things might be loosened there which were first loosened here in the Church.

<margin>The Heretics struggling against plain Scripture.</margin>
And it is a sight to see how the Heretics struggle with this very plain commission of remitting sins, claiming it refers only to preaching, or to announcing God’s threats against sinners, and to who-knows-what else.

<margin>See the Book of Common Prayer <note>original: "cōmunion booke"</note>.</margin>
<margin>The English Ministers hear confessions and absolve.</margin>
Though to our English Protestants this authority seems so clear that in their order for visiting the sick, their Ministers acknowledge and claim the same, using a formal absolution according to the Church's order after the specific confession of the person. But to conclude the matter, let everyone who wishes to see the true meaning of Christ’s words—and the great power and dignity given to Priests by these and other words—carefully note these words of Saint Chrysostom.

<margin>Book 3 on the Priesthood.</margin>
<margin>Priests' power to forgive sins is above the power of Angels or worldly Princes.</margin>
For, he says, to those who dwell on the earth and live in it, a commission is given to distribute those things that are in heaven. To them it is given to have the power which God would not give to Angels or Archangels. For it was not said to them, *Whatsoever you shall bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatsoever you shall loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.* Earthly Princes indeed also have power to bind, but only the body; but that bond of Priests which I speak of touches the very soul itself and reaches even to the heavens. So much so, that whatever the Priests do here below, God himself ratifies above, and the Lord confirms the sentence of his servants. For indeed, what else is this but that the power of all heavenly things is granted to them by God? "Whose sins soever," he says, "you shall retain, they are retained." What power, I ask you, can be greater than this? The Father gave all power to the Son, but I see that same power delivered entirely by the Son unto them.

<margin>Confession to Priests.</margin>
And as this concerns the high authority of Priests to absolve, the ancient Fathers speak in this way regarding confession being made to them. Saint Cyprian (*On the Lapsed, number 11*): "Those," he says, "who have greater faith and fear of God, though they did not fall during the persecution, yet because they even thought of it in their minds, they confess this very thought to God’s Priests sorrowfully and plainly, opening their conscience, uttering and discharging the burden of their mind, and seeking healing medicine for their wounds, even though they be small." And a little later: "I beseech you, my brethren, let everyone confess his sin while he is yet alive, while his confession may be admitted, and while satisfaction and the remission granted by the Priests is acceptable before God." Saint Cyril (or as some think, Origen), in *Book 2 on Leviticus*, calls it a great part of penance when a man is ashamed and yet opens his sins to our Lord’s Priest. See also Tertullian (*On Penance*), Saint Jerome (*on chapter 10 of Ecclesiastes*), and Saint Basil (*Short Rules, question 229*). They compare sinners who refuse to confess to those who have a disease in their private parts and are ashamed to show it to the Physician or Surgeon who could cure it. This clearly means secret confession must be made to those who have the power to absolve.

<margin>Secret or auricular Confession.</margin>
Saint Leo (*Epistle 80*) most plainly (as Saint Cyril did before) expressly names Priests: "That confession is sufficient which is made first to God, then to the Priest also." And again, "It is sufficient that the guilt of men’s consciences be uttered to the Priests only through the secrecy of confession." Saint Jerome (on *Matthew 16*) says that Priests loose or bind "after hearing the variety of sins" <note>original Latin: "audita peccatorum varietate"</note>.

<margin>In the life of Saint Ambrose <note>original: "D. Ambr."</note> near the end.</margin>
Saint Paulinus writes of Saint Ambrose that whenever anyone confessed their sins to him to receive penance, he wept with such compassion that he caused the penitent to weep also. He adds, moreover, that this holy Doctor was so secretive in these cases that no man knew the sins confessed, except God and himself.

<margin>Matthew 18.</margin>
And Saint Augustine (*Sermon 49*) says this: "Perform penance such as is done in the Church. Let no man say, 'I do it secretly, I do it to God.' In vain then was it said, 'Whatsoever you shall loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.'" See Saint Ambrose (*On Penance*) throughout, Saint Cyprian (*On the Lapsed*), and the book *On True and False Penance* in Saint Augustine. All of antiquity is full of these discussions concerning absolution and confession.

Peter is here made the general Pastor, and the Church is built upon him.

17. **Feed my sheep.**] As it was promised to him in Matthew 16, that the Church should be built upon
him, and that the keys of heaven should be given to him: so here it is performed, and he is actually
made the general Pastor and Governor of all Christ's sheep. For though the other ten (as Matthias
and Paul also afterward) were Apostles, Bishops, and Priests, and had authority to bind and loose, to
remit and retain, to preach, baptize, and such like, as well as he: yet in these things and all other
government, Christ would have him to be their head, and they to depend on him as head of

<meta>This page continues the commentary on John 21, specifically focusing on the Catholic defense of the Primacy of Peter (the Papacy). It uses the "Feed my sheep" command to argue that Peter and his successors hold universal authority over the entire Church, citing various Church Fathers to refute Protestant and Puritan views.</meta>

# THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO ST. JOHN. CHAPTER 21.

<margin>The Protestants, while otherwise denying this preeminence of Peter, yet to uphold their Archbishops, do claim and prove it against the Puritans.</margin>
<margin>Peter’s successors succeed him in universal authority.</margin>
<margin>*Cyprian, On the Unity of the Church* <note>original: "Cypr. de vnit. Ec."</note></margin>
<margin>*Book 2, On the Priesthood* <note>original: "Li. 2 de Sacerd."</note></margin>
(if he acknowledges himself to be a sheep of Christ) is exempted from his charge. And that Christ makes a difference between Peter and the rest, and gives him some greater preeminence and governance <note>original: "regiment," meaning the act of ruling</note> than the rest, it is plain by the fact that he is asked whether he loves our Lord more than the other Apostles do: whereas, for an equal charge, no difference of love would have been required. To Peter (says St. Cyprian) our Lord after his Resurrection said, *Feed my sheep*, and built his Church upon him alone, and to him he gives the charge of feeding his sheep. *For although after his Resurrection he gave his power equally to all, saying, As my Father sent me, so I send you, take the Holy Ghost, if you remit to any their sins, they shall be remitted etc. Yet to manifest unity, he established one Chair, and so disposed by his authority that unity should have its origin from one. The rest of the Apostles were what Peter was, in equal fellowship of honor and power, but the beginning comes from unity: the Primacy is given to Peter, that the Church of Christ may be shown to be one, and one Chair.* St. Chrysostom also says this: *Why did our Lord shed his blood? Truly to redeem those sheep, the care of which he committed both to Peter and also to his Successors.* And a little after, *Christ would have Peter endowed with such authority, and to be far above all his other Apostles: for he says: Peter, do you love me more than all these do? Whereupon our Master might have inferred: If you love me Peter, use much fasting, sleep on the hard floor, watch much, be a patron to the oppressed, a father to the orphans, and a husband to the widows: but omitting all these things, he says, Feed my sheep. For, all the aforesaid virtues certainly may be done easily by many subjects, not only men but women: but when it comes to the government of the Church and committing the charge of so many souls, all womankind must needs wholly give place to the burden and greatness thereof, and a great number of men also.* So he writes.

<margin>St. Gregory, though he disliked the title of *Universal Bishop*, yet is most plain both in his writings and doings for the Pope’s Supremacy, as is also St. Leo the Great.</margin>
<margin>*Gregory, Book 4, Epistle 76* <note>original: "Grego. li. 4, ep. 76."</note></margin>
<margin>The title of universal Bishop refused, but universal jurisdiction always acknowledged and practiced.</margin>
<margin>*See Book 4, Epistles 72, 75; Book 2, Epistles 37, 45; Book 4, Epistle 95; Book 7, Epistle 63.*</margin>
<margin>The Pope is Pastor of all Pastors.</margin>
<margin>*Bernard, Book 2, Chapter 8, On Consideration* <note>original: "Bernard. li. 2, c. 8. de cõſider."</note></margin>
<margin><term>to shepherd/rule</term> <note>original: "ποιμαῖνε" [poimaine]</note></margin>
<margin>\* *2 Kings 6:5; Psalm 7* <note>The book of 2 Kings in the Vulgate is 2 Samuel in modern bibles.</note></margin>
And because the Protestants would make the unlearned think that St. Gregory deemed the Pope’s Supremacy to be wholly unlawful and Antichristian, because he condemns John of Constantinople for usurping the name of "universal Bishop," resembling his insolence therein to the pride of Antichrist: note well the words of this holy father in the very same place and Epistle against the Bishop of Constantinople, by which you shall easily see that to deny him to be "universal Bishop" is not to deny Peter or the Pope to be head of the Church, or supreme Governor of the same, as our adversaries fraudulently pretend. *It is plain to all men*, he says, *that ever read the Gospel, that by our Lord’s mouth the charge of the whole Church was committed to St. Peter, Prince of the Apostles. For to him it was said, Feed my sheep: for him was the prayer made that his faith should not fail: to him were the keys of heaven given and authority to bind and loose: to him the care of the Church and principality was delivered: and yet he was not called the universal Apostle.* This title indeed was offered, for the honor of St. Peter, Prince of the Apostles, to the Pope of Rome by the holy Council of Chalcedon: but none of that See did ever use it or consent to take it. Thus much St. Gregory. * Who though he both practiced jurisdiction throughout all Christendom, as others of that See have ever done, and also acknowledged the Principality and Sovereignty to reside in Peter and his Successors: yet he would not, for just causes, use that title which was subject to vanity and misconstruction. But both he and all the Popes since have rather called themselves, *Servants of the servants of God* <note>original: "Seruos feruorum Dei"</note>. Though the word "universal Bishop," in that sense wherein the holy Council of Chalcedon offered it to the See of Rome, was true and lawful. For that Council would not have given any Antichristian or unjust title to any man. Only in the Bishop of Constantinople and others, who in no sense had any right to it, and who usurped it in a very false and tyrannical meaning, it was insolent, unjust, and Antichristian. See also the Epistles of St. Leo the Great concerning his practice of universal jurisdiction, though he refused the title of universal Bishop. And St. Bernard (so that you may better perceive that the general charge of Christ’s sheep was not only given to Peter’s person, but also to his successors the Popes of Rome, as St. Chrysostom also previously cited testifies) writes thus to Eugenius, *You are he to whom the keys of heaven are delivered, and to whom the sheep are committed. There be other Porters of heaven, and other Pastors of flocks: but you have inherited in a more glorious and different sort. For they have every one their particular flock, but to you all universally, as one flock to one man, are credited: being not only the Pastor of the sheep, but the one Pastor of all the Pastors themselves. But you will ask me how I prove that? Even by our Lord’s word. For to whom of all, I say not only Bishops, but Apostles, were the sheep so absolutely and without limitation committed? If you love me Peter, feed my sheep. He says not, the people of this kingdom or that city, but, my sheep, without all distinction.* So St. Bernard. And hereunto may be added that the second "feed," is in Greek a word <note>original: ποιμαῖνε</note> that signifies as well "to govern and rule," as in *Psalm 2, Micah 5, Matthew 2, and Apocalypse 2.* And therefore it is spoken of David also and other temporal Governors (as the Hebrew word answering to it) in the \* Scriptures very often, and the Greek in profane writers also.

<margin>Peter crucified at Rome.</margin>
<margin>*Beza on this place* <note>Theodore Beza, a major Protestant reformer.</note></margin>
18. *Another shall gird you.*] He prophesies of Peter's Martyrdom, and of the kind of death which he should suffer, which was crucifying. This \* the Heretics <note>meaning the Protestants</note>, fearing that it were a step to prove he was martyred in Rome, deny: whereas the Fathers and ancient writers are as plain in this, as they are that he was at Rome. *Origen according to Eusebius, Book 3, Chapter 1; Eusebius, Book 2, Chapter 24, Ecclesiastical History; Tertullian, On Prescription, number 14; Augustine, Tractate 123 on John; Chrysostom; Bede on this place.*

It addresses historical nuances regarding the title "Universal Bishop" and affirms Peter's eventual martyrdom in Rome.</summary>

# THE ARGUMENT <note>In this context, "Argument" refers to a thematic summary or overview of the book's contents.</note> OF
## THE ACTS OF THE
### APOSTLES.

<margin>* Jerome in the Catalog <note>original: "Hier. in Catal." Refers to St. Jerome’s "De Viris Illustribus" (On Illustrious Men), a collection of short biographies of Christian figures.</note></margin>
<image-desc>An ornamental drop-cap "T" set within a square frame featuring a bird perched on a branch surrounded by foliage.</image-desc>

THE Gospel having shown *how the* Jews *most impiously rejected* Christ (*as also* Moses *and the* Prophets *had foretold of them:) and therefore deserved to be rejected themselves also by him: now follows this book of the* Acts of the Apostles (*written by Saint Luke in* Rome *the fourth year of* Nero, AD 61) *and shows, how notwithstanding their deserts,* Christ *of his mercy (as the* Prophets *also had foretold of him) offered himself unto that unworthy people, even after they had crucified him, sending unto them his twelve* Apostles *to move them to repentance, and so by* Baptism *to make them of his* Church: *and while all the* Twelve *were so occupied with the* Jews: *how out of a persecuting* Jew *he made an extraordinary* Apostle (*who was* Saint Paul) *and to avoid the scandal of the* Jews (*to whom only he himself likewise for the same cause had preached) sent him, and not any of his* Twelve *immediately, who were his known* Apostles, *unto the* Gentiles, *who never before had heard of* Christ, *and were worshippers of many* gods, *to move them also (for, that likewise the* Prophets *had foretold) to faith and repentance, and so by* Baptism *to make them of his* Church: *and how the incredulous* Jews *everywhere resisted the same* Apostle *and his preaching to the* Gentiles, *persecuting him and seeking his death, and never ceasing until he fell into*

*the hands of the* Gentiles: *that so (as not only he everywhere, but also the* Prophets *before him, and* Christ *had foretold) the* Gospel *might be taken away from them, and given to the* Gentiles: *even from* Jerusalem (*whose rejection <note>original: "reprobation"</note> also by name had been often foretold) the head city of the* Jews, *where it began, translated to* Rome *the head city of the* Gentiles. *All this will be evident by the parts of the book: which may be these six.*

*First, how* Christ *ascending in the sight of his* Disciples, *promised unto them the* Holy Ghost, *foretelling that from him they should receive strength, and so begin his* Church *in* Jerusalem: *and from there expand it into all that* Country, *that is into all* Judea <note>original: "Iurie"</note>: *yea and into* Samaria *also, yea into all* Nations *of the* Gentiles, *be they never so far off. You shall receive (says he) the virtue <note>meaning "power" or "strength"</note> of the* Holy Ghost *coming upon you: and you shall be witnesses unto me in* Jerusalem, *and in all* Judea, *and* Samaria, *and even to the utmost of the earth. Chapter 1.*

Gentiles, by the ministry of Saint Paul and Saint Barnabas. Chapter 13.

<margin>Acts 25:11; Luke 23:1</margin>
Sixthly, of taking it away from Jerusalem itself, the head city of the Jews, and sending it (*as it were*) to Rome, the head city of the Gentiles. This happened through their persecution of Paul to such an extent *that he appealed to Caesar, and so delivered himself, in a way, unto the Romans—just as they had previously delivered Christ himself to them.* Meanwhile, Saint Peter’s first arrival there occurred on another occasion, as shall be mentioned shortly. Regarding these Romans and Gentiles, therefore, the same Saint Paul <margin>Acts 28:28</margin>—having now arrived in Rome (as described in the last chapter of the *Acts*)—foretells to the obstinate Jews there, saying: *And they themselves shall hear.* <note>original Latin: "Et ipsi audient."</note> *You will not hear, but, they will hear.* This was so that the prediction of Christ previously mentioned might be fulfilled: "And even to the uttermost part of the earth." And there Saint Luke ends the book, not even bothering to tell of the fulfillment of what our Lord had foretold (Acts 27:24) to Saint Paul, *Thou must appear before Caesar.* This is because his purpose was nothing more than to show the "new Jerusalem" of the Christians, where Christ would place the chief seat of his Church. Indeed, the Church Fathers and all other Catholics have in all ages looked toward that place whenever they were in any great doubt—no less than the Jews <margin>Deuteronomy 17:8</margin> looked to Jerusalem, as they were commanded in the Old Testament.

<margin>Romans 11:25</margin>

<margin>Tertullian, *On Prescription against Heretics* <note>original: "Tertul. de pręsc." Refers to Tertullian’s work arguing that only the apostolic church has the right to use the Scriptures.</note></margin>

No. The intention of the Holy Ghost was not to write all the Acts of all the Apostles, nor even the preaching of Peter and his followers to the Gentiles, but only to the Jews—thereby to display to the world the great mercy of Christ toward those unworthy Jews.

# ANNOTATIONS
## CHAPTER I.
---

2. *Giving commandment.*] He means the power given to them to preach, to baptize, to forgive sins, and generally the entire commission and responsibility of governing the Church after him, in his name, place, and right. This leadership <term>Regiment; an archaic term for governance or rule</term> was given to them along with the Holy Spirit to assist them in that role forever.

<margin>The times and moments of things to come do not pertain to us.</margin>
7. *It is not for you.*] It is not for us, nor is it necessary for the Church, to know the specific times and moments of the world's end, the coming of the Antichrist, and other such secrets of God. In this case, it is enough to be assured that Christ's faith shall be preached and the Church spread throughout all nations, with the Holy Spirit working continually alongside the Apostles and their successors for that purpose.

<margin>Christ has ascended, and yet is truly in the Blessed Sacrament.</margin>
11. *Taken up <note>original: "Assumpted"</note> from you.*] Based on this visible ascending of Christ to heaven and his similar return from there for judgment, the Heretics <note>The author refers here to Protestant reformers who denied the Real Presence</note> argue incredulously that he is not present in the Sacrament. But let the faithful instead listen to Saint Chrysostom saying: *O miracle! He who sits with the Father in heaven above is handled by men beneath at that very same time. Christ, ascending to heaven, both has his flesh with him and left it with us below. Elijah, being taken up, left only his cloak to his disciple; but the Son of Man, ascending, left his own flesh to us.* (See: Book 3 *On the Priesthood*; Homily 2 *To the People of Antioch*; and the Homily *On the Rich and the Poor*).

<margin>Her ASSUMPTION.</margin>
14. MARY the mother of JESUS.] This is the last mention made in Holy Scripture of our Blessed Lady. For although she was full of all divine wisdom and undoubtedly revealed to the Evangelists and other writers of Holy Scripture various actions, speeches, and mysteries of Christ—of which she had both personal and revealed knowledge—yet because she was a woman, the humblest creature living, and the pattern of all order and obedience, it did not please God for there to be any further record of her life, deeds, or death in the Scriptures. She lived the rest of her time with the Christians (as she is specifically named and noted among them here) and especially with Saint John the Apostle, to whom our Lord entrusted her. He provided for all her necessities, as her spouse Joseph is thought to have died previously. The common opinion is that she lived sixty-three years in total. 

At the time of her death, as Saint Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite</note> first, and after him Saint John Damascene (in *On the Falling Asleep of the Mother of God*) wrote, all the Apostles then dispersed into various nations to preach the Gospel were miraculously brought together to Jerusalem to honor her divine departure and funeral—except for Saint Thomas, who arrived on the third day. The said Saint Dionysius witnesses this, stating that he himself, Saint Timothy, and Saint Hierotheus were present. He also testifies from his own hearing that both before her death and for three days afterward, not only the Apostles and other holy men present, but also the Angels and Powers of heaven sang most melodious hymns. They buried her sacred body in Gethsemane, but for the sake of Saint Thomas, who desired to see and reverence it, they opened the sepulcher on the third day. Finding it empty of the holy body but exceedingly fragrant, they returned, assuredly believing that her body was taken <note>original: "assumpted"</note> into heaven. The Church of God holds this to be true, as it is most consistent with the singular privilege of the Mother of God, and therefore celebrates it most solemnly on the day of her Assumption. This is consistent not only with the writings of Saint Dionysius and Saint Damascene, but also with Saint Athanasius, who affirms the same in his *Sermon on the Gospel concerning the Mother of God*. Saint Bernard also wrote five notable sermons on the Assumption of her body, which are found in his works.

<margin>The Protestants have no feast for her at all, though they have them for other saints.</margin>
But neither these holy fathers, nor the Church's tradition and testimony, carry any weight nowadays with the Protestants, who have abolished her greatest feast, the Assumption. By rights, they should at the very least celebrate it as the day of her death, as they do for other saints. For though they do not believe her body was taken up, they will not (we suppose <note>original: "we trow"</note>) deny that she is dead and her soul is in glory. They cannot demand "Scripture" for her death any more than they require it for the deaths of Peter, Paul, John, and others, which are not mentioned in the Bible and yet are still celebrated by Protestants. But concerning the Blessed Virgin MARY, they have also erased both her Nativity and her Conception. It may be thought that the Devil bears a special malice toward this woman whose "seed" crushed his head. As for the other two days, her Purification <note>Candlemas</note> and her Annunciation, these are not specific to our Lady, but rather to Christ's Conception and his Presentation in the Temple. Thus, she is left with no festival of her own at all.

<margin>How the Primitive Church and ancient fathers honored our Blessed Lady.</margin>
On the contrary, considering how the ancient Church and the Church Fathers esteemed, spoke, and wrote of this excellent vessel of grace may make us detest the impiety of these men. They cannot endure the praises of her *whom all generations shall call blessed*, and they consider honors shown to her to be a detraction <note>original: "derogatio"</note> from her son. We will set down some of their speeches so all men may see that we neither praise her nor pray to her more extensively than they did. Saint Athanasius, in the place previously cited, after declaring how all the angelic spirits and every order of them honored and praised her

<margin>St. Ephrem.</margin>
...praise you with a loud voice, saying, **"Hail, full of grace"** <note>original: *Ave gratia plena*</note> etc. Hail, full of grace, our Lord is with you; pray for us, O Mistress, and Lady, and Queen, and Mother of God. The most holy and ancient Ephrem, also in a special prayer made in praise of our Lady, says this in various places: **"Undefiled Mother of God"** <note>original: *Intemerata Deipara*</note> etc. Mother of God undefiled, Queen of all, the hope of those who despair, my lady most glorious, higher than the heavenly spirits, more honorable than the Cherubim, holier than the Seraphim, and without comparison more glorious than the heavenly hosts, the hope of the fathers, the glory of the Prophets, the praise of the Apostles. And a little after: **"A Virgin before birth, during birth, and after birth."** <note>original: *Virgo ante partum, in partu, & post partum*</note> By you we are reconciled to Christ my God, your son: you are the helper of sinners, you are the haven for those tossed by storms, the solace of the world, the deliverer of the imprisoned, the help of orphans, the redeemer of captives. And afterward: Vouchsafe me, your servant, to praise you. Hail, lady MARY, full of grace; hail, Virgin most blessed among women. And much more in that sense, which would be too long to repeat.

<margin>St. Cyril.</margin>
St. Cyril has similar wonderful speeches for her honor in his sixth sermon against **Nestorius** <note>Nestorius was a 5th-century archbishop who was declared a heretic for denying that Mary could be called the "Mother of God" (Theotokos).</note>. Praise and glory be to you, O holy Trinity: to you also be praise, holy Mother of God, for you are the precious pearl of the world, you are the candle of unquenchable light, the crown of Virginity, the scepter of the Catholic faith. By you the Trinity is glorified and adored in all the world; by you heaven rejoices, Angels and Archangels are glad, devils are put to flight, and man is called again to heaven, and every creature that was held by the error of Idols is turned to the knowledge of the truth. By you Churches are founded throughout the world; with you being their helper, the Gentiles come to repentance—and much more which we omit.

<margin>The Greek Liturgies of St. James, St. Basil, St. Chrysostom.</margin>
Likewise, the Greek Liturgies or Masses of St. James, St. Basil, and St. Chrysostom make most honorable mention of our Blessed Lady, praying to her, saluting her with the Angelic hymn, **"Hail Mary,"** <note>original: *Ave Maria*</note> and using these speeches: Most holy, undefiled, blessed above all, our Queen, our Lady, the mother of God, MARY, a virgin forever, the sacred ark of Christ’s Incarnation, broader than the heavens that did bear your creator, holy mother of unspeakable light, we magnify you with Angelic hymns. All things pass understanding, all things are glorious in you, O mother of God. By you the mystery previously unknown to the Angels is made manifest and revealed to those on the earth. You are more honorable than the Cherubim, and more glorious than the Seraphim; to you, O full of grace, all creatures—both men and Angels—express joy and rejoice. Glory be to you, who are a sanctified temple, a spiritual paradise, the glory of virgins, from whom God took flesh and made your womb to be his throne, etc.

<margin>St. Augustine. "Holy MARY, help the wretched," etc.</margin>

Receive our prayers, obtain our requests, for you are the* * **special hope of sinners**; by you we hope for pardon of our sins, and in you, O most blessed, is the expectation of our rewards.* And then follow these words now used in the Church’s service: *Holy Mary, help the wretched, assist the faint-hearted, comfort the sorrowful, pray for the people, intervene for the clergy, intercede for the devoted female sex. <margin>Peter begins to practice his Primacy.</margin>
<margin>Beza in the Greek New Testament, 1565.</margin>
15. **"Peter rising up."**) Peter in the meantime practiced his **superiority** <note>This refers to the Catholic doctrine of Papal Primacy, arguing that Peter acted as the head of the Church from the beginning.</note> in the company or Church, announcing that an election be made of one to supply Judas's place. This Peter did not upon a written commandment from Christ, but by the suggestion of God’s Spirit, and by understanding the Scriptures of the Old Testament for that purpose—the meaning of which Christ had opened to the Apostles before his departure, though in more full manner afterward at the sending of the Holy Ghost. And this act of Peter in prescribing to the Apostles and the rest this election, and the manner of it, is so evident for his **Supremacy**, that even the **adversaries** <note>Referring to Protestant scholars like Theodore Beza.</note> confess here that he was the <term>Antistes</term> <note>A leader, chief priest, or bishop presiding over a religious body.</note>, the chief and Bishop of this whole College and company.

<margin>Casting of lots.</margin>
26. **"Lots."**) When the outcome or fall of the lot is not expected from Devils, or the stars, or any force of fortune, but is looked for and prayed for to be directed by God and his holy Saints, then may lots be used lawfully. And sometimes, to choose between two things that are entirely indifferent, they are necessary, as St. Augustine teaches in his 180th letter to Honoratus.

## ->ANNOTATIONS<-
### ->CHAPTER II.<-

<margin>The feasts of Passover and Pentecost.</margin>
1. *The days of Pentecost.*) Just as Christ our Passover <note>original: "Paſche"</note>, to correspond to the prophetic figure, was offered at the Jews' great feast of Passover, so fifty days after (in Greek, *Pentecost*)—to fulfill the similar figure of the Giving of the Law on Mount Sinai—he sent down the Holy Ghost exactly on the day of their Pentecost, which was always on Sunday, as appears in *Leviticus 23:15.* Both of these days the Church keeps yearly in memory of Christ’s death and Resurrection, and the sending down of the Holy Ghost; just as they did the same for the record of their delivery out of Egypt and the aforementioned Giving of the Law. These feasts with us contain, besides the remembrance of past benefits, great Sacraments also of the life to come. <note>original: "Aug. ep. 119, C. 16." — Augustine, Letter 119, Chapter 16.</note>

<margin>Luke 24:49.</margin>
<margin>Acts 1:14.</margin>
<margin>t. in hoc</margin>
<margin>verse 1.</margin>
<margin>The sending of the Holy Ghost on Pentecost Sunday and its effects.</margin>
4. *All filled.*) Although the Apostles and the rest were baptized before, and had thereby received the grace of the Holy Ghost for sanctification and the remission of sins, as well as for various other purposes: yet as Christ promised them they should be further endowed with strength and power from above, so here he fulfills his promise, visibly pouring down the Holy Ghost upon all the company and upon every one of them. He thereby filled the Apostles especially with all truth, wisdom, and knowledge necessary for the government of the Church, and gave both to them and to all others present the grace and effect of the Sacrament of Confirmation, accomplishing, corroborating, and strengthening them in their faith and the confession of it. And lastly, as a visible token of God’s Spirit, he endowed them all with the gift of various strange tongues: all (I say) there present, including our Lady <note>The Virgin Mary.</note>, as well as other holy women and brothers, besides the Apostles. <margin>Our Blessed Lady.</margin> though the Heretics <note>A common term used in this period by Catholic translators to refer to Protestant reformers.</note> foolishly argue—out of their desire to dishonor Christ’s mother—that neither she nor the others were present, nor had the gift of tongues, which is contrary to the plain text that says, *They were all together*, specifically all the 120 mentioned before in chapter 1, verse 15.

<page-num>296</page-num>
<header>THE ACTS, CHAPTER 3.</header>
<meta>Catchword: temple.</meta>

<margin>God's determination that Christ should die does not excuse the Jews.</margin>
23. *By the determinate counsel of God delivered.*) God delivered him, and he delivered himself, out of love and the intention of our salvation; thus, the act was holy and according to God’s own determination. But the Jews and others who betrayed and crucified him did so out of malice and wicked purpose. Their act was damnable and not caused by God’s counsel, though he tolerated it because he could and did turn their abominable deed toward the good of our salvation. Therefore, abhor those "new Manichees" <note>The Manichees were an ancient sect that believed in two opposing forces of good and evil; here, the author uses the term as an insult against Reformers like Luther and Calvin, accusing them of making God the author of sin.</note> of our time—both Lutherans and Calvinists—who make God the author and cause of Judas's betrayal of Christ no less than of Paul’s conversion. This is aside from the false translation by Beza, who uses "God's providence" instead of "God's prescience" or "foreknowledge" (original Greek: προγνωσις, *prognosis*).

<margin>Beza <note>Theodore Beza was a major Protestant reformer and scholar.</note>.</margin>
<margin>* Book 12, chapter 13 of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*.</margin>
24. *Loosing the sorrows.*) Christ was not in pain himself, but he loosed other men from those sorrows of Hell, where it was impossible for him to be touched by them. See *St. Augustine.

<margin>Corrupt translation against the Article of Christ's descending into Hell.</margin>
<margin>Soul: נפש (*nephesh*), ψυχη (*psyche*) <br/>Hell: שאול (*sheol*), ᾅδης (*hades*)</margin>
<margin>* English Bible, 1579</margin>
<margin>* New Testament, year 1556.</margin>
<margin>Annotations on Acts 2 and 1 Peter 3:19</margin>
27. *My soul in Hell.*) All the faithful, according to the Creed, have always believed that Christ, in his soul, went down into Hell to deliver the Patriarchs and all just men held in bondage there until his death. The Apostle, citing the Prophet’s words, expresses this most clearly, distinguishing Christ's soul in Hell from his body in the grave. Yet the Calvinists—to defend the blasphemy of their master (Calvin), who claimed Christ suffered the actual pains of Hell only upon the Cross and did not descend there otherwise—most falsely corrupt the text. They wrest the Hebrew and Greek words from their proper meanings of "Soul" and "Hell" and turn them into "body" and "grave." Instead of "my soul in Hell," they say "my body," "life," "person," or even (as Beza did in his 1556 New Testament) "my carcass in the grave." This latter corruption they use almost throughout the Bible for that purpose. To refute these corruptions, it is enough to say: First, all who understand Hebrew and Greek know that those words are as specifically used to mean "soul" and "hell" as *anima* and *infernus* are in Latin, or "soul" and "hell" are in English. Using them to mean "body" or "grave" is as improper as calling a body a "soul" in English. Second, even other Reformers like Castalio <note>Sebastian Castellio, a French theologian who often disagreed with Calvin.</note> disliked this translation and corrected it; to be even more certain, he translated it as *in Orco* (in the underworld/Hell). Third, Beza himself partially recanted in a later edition, admitting that "carcass" was an unfit word for Christ's body. He claimed to change it to "soul" while still keeping the same meaning (that it referred to the dead body). Fourth, he plainly admits that he translated it as "Thou shalt not leave my carcass in the grave" specifically to oppose the doctrines of the *Limbus Patrum* (Limbo of the Fathers), Purgatory, and Christ's descent into Hell, which he calls "foul errors." He marvels that most of the ancient Church Fathers held this "error" of Christ delivering the old fathers from Hell. What more do we need? He opposes himself to both plain Scripture and the ancient Fathers, perverting the former and despising the latter to overthrow a truth that is an Article of our Creed. Thus, it is evidently false when some of them claim they never translated falsely on purpose. See the Annotation on 1 *Peter* 3:19.

<margin>Living in common.</margin>
44. *All things common.*) This living with communal property is not a rule or requirement for all Christians, as the Anabaptists falsely claim. Rather, it is a "life of perfection" and a "counsel" followed by those in religious orders (monks and nuns) in the Catholic Church. See *St. Augustine on Psalm 132 at the beginning, and Letter 109.*

<margin>The increase and perpetuity of the VISIBLE CHURCH.</margin>
<margin>προσετίθει τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ <note>original Greek: "he added to the church"</note></margin>
47. *Increased.*) More and more people were added to the Church (as the Greek expresses more clearly), so that *we may see its visible growth and spread.* From this time, a diligent person can trace this same visible society of men joined in Christ through the whole book of Acts, and afterward through Church history, down to our own days—contrary to the "invisible church" claimed by the heretics.

### ANNOTATIONS
#### CHAPTER III.

<margin>Saints perform miracles and the like, but by the power of God.</margin>
6. *That which I have.*] This power of working miracles was in *Peter*, and *Peter* properly gave this man his health, although he received that force and power from God, and executed the same in and through Him. Therefore he says, *That which I have, I give to thee.* The heretics <note>The translator here attacks Protestant reformers who argued that the Apostles were merely passive instruments rather than active participants in the miracles.</note> are ridiculous to note here that the miracle was done by Christ through the hands of the Apostles, merely to make simple people believe that the Apostles were no more than a dead instrument in the workman's hand.

12. *By our power.*] When the Apostles forgive sins, or perform any other miracles, they do not do it by any human, personal, or natural power within themselves: but by a supernatural power given to them from above, to prove that the faith of Christ is true, and that He whom the Jews crucified is God—in whose name and faith they work, and not in their own.

### CHAPTER 5. OF THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES.

<margin>Time and the obvious success of Christ’s Church and religion prove it to be from God. No violence from the Jews, no persecution from the Heathen Princes, no effort of domestic adversaries—heretics, schismatics, or wicked people—has prevailed against it. On the other hand, many attempts were made by Arius, Macedonius, Nestorius, Luther, and others who thought they were important. But after they played their parts for a while, their memory is buried or lives only in curses and infamy, and their followers come to nothing. Therefore, let no Catholic man be scandalized that this heresy <note>The author is referring to the Protestant Reformation as a temporary "heresy."</note> holds up for a time. For the Arians and others flourished much longer than these and were better supported by Princes and learning, and yet they had an end.</margin>

### ANNOTATIONS
#### CHAPTER 5.

<margin>Augustine, Sermon 9 in the appendix 'On Various Matters', volume 10. <note>original: "Aug. ser. 9 in append. de diuersis tom. 10."</note></margin>
<margin>Sacrilege.</margin>
2. *Defrauded.*) In that (says Saint Augustine), because he withdrew any part of what he had promised, he was guilty at once of both sacrilege and fraud. He committed sacrilege because he robbed God of what was His by promise; and fraud because he withheld a piece of the whole gift. Now let the Heretics come and say it was only for lying or hypocrisy that this deed was condemned—because they are loath to have sacrilege counted as such a sin. These are the same people who have taught men not only to take away from God some piece of what they themselves gave, but plainly to spoil and take for themselves all that other men gave.

<margin>Excommunication joined with physical punishments.</margin>
3. *Peter said.*) Saint Peter (as you see here) knew of this fraud and the thoughts of Ananias without any human reporting it. As head of the College <note>The College of Apostles</note> and of the whole Church—against which this robbery was committed—he executed this heavy sentence of Excommunication against both him and his wife, who consented to the sacrilege. For it was an excommunication, according to Saint Augustine's judgment (<margin>Against the Letter of Parmenian, book 3, chapter 1, volume 7 <note>original: "li. 3 cont. ep. Parm. c. 1 to. 7"</note></margin>), and it had this miraculous physical death joined with it, as the Excommunication...

The excommunication that Saint Paul issued against the incestuous man and others carried with it the physical affliction by Satan. <note>The author suggests that early Church excommunication resulted in literal physical suffering or demonic harassment as a divine punishment.</note>

<margin>Vow of Chastity, and the breaking thereof.</margin>
4. *In your power.*) If it displeased God (says Saint Augustine) to withhold the money which they had vowed to God, how angry is He when chastity is vowed and is not performed? For to such a person it may be said what Saint Peter said of the money: *While your virginity remained, did it not remain yours? And before you made the vow, was it not in your own power?* For, *Whoever has vowed such things and has not paid them, let them not think they will be condemned to physical deaths, but to everlasting fire.* Augustine, Sermon 10 <note>original: "de diuersis," meaning "On Various Subjects"</note>. And Saint Gregory writes to the same purpose, <margin>Gregory, Book 1, Epistle 33.</margin> *Ananias had vowed money to God, which afterward, overcome by devilish persuasion, he withdrew; but with what death he was punished, you know. If then he was worthy of 그 death, who took away the money he had given to God, consider what great peril in God's judgment you shall be worthy of, you who have withdrawn not money, but yourself from almighty God, to whom you had vowed yourself under the habit or garment of a Monk.* <note>"Weede" is an archaic term for clothing or a religious garment.</note>

4. *Not to men, but.*) To take from the Church or from its Governors those things dedicated to their use and the service of God, or to lie to God's Ministers, is judged before God as if the lie were made and the fraud committed against the Holy Spirit himself, who is the Church’s President and Protector.

<margin>Peter’s shadow and intercession.</margin>
15. *His shadow.*) Especially they sought Peter, the chief of all, who cured all diseases not only by touching, as the others did, but by his very shadow. Whereupon Saint Augustine says, *If then the shadow of his body could help, how much more now the fullness of power? And if a certain little wind of him passing by profited those who humbly asked, how much more the grace of him now being permanent and remaining?* Sermon 29 <note>original: "de Sanctis," meaning "On the Saints"</note>, speaking of the miracles performed by the Saints now reigning in heaven. <note>This is a defense of the Catholic doctrine of the Intercession of Saints, arguing that if they had power on earth, they have more in heaven.</note>
