->### ANNOTATIONS<-
->#### CHAPTER VI.<-

<margin>Complaining and rivalry.</margin>
1. *Murmuring.*] It arises from human weakness that in every society of men—no matter how holy—there is some cause given or taken by the weak for complaining and disagreement. This must always be managed and stopped at the beginning, lest it grow into further division or rebellion. The more the Church increases in number and in the diversity of people and regions, the more it is subject to such defects. In all these matters, the spiritual leaders, following the example and authority of the Apostles, must establish order as time and occasion require.

<margin>The 7 Deacons</margin>
3. *Seven men.*] We should not think that these Seven (appointed here as Deacons) were only chosen to serve at ordinary tables or to manage the Church’s purely secular finances, even though that specific need was the occasion for their election and no other duty is explicitly mentioned here. Various circumstances in this passage, as well as all ancient traditions, provide evidence that their office was not primarily concerned with secular things, but with the holy Altar. The persons to be elected had to be "full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom," and they had to be ordained and consecrated through public prayer and the Apostles' laying on of hands, just as Bishops and Priests were later ordained. <note>original: "ep. ad Tim," referring to Saint Paul’s Epistle to Timothy.</note> In that letter, Saint Paul requires almost the same qualifications for Deacons as he does for Bishops. None of these requirements would have been necessary for a simple secular stewardship. Indeed, immediately after their ordination here (undoubtedly by commission from the Apostles, which they did not have before their election), they preached, baptized, and debated. It is also clear from the descriptions of Saint Stephen—that he was "full of grace and fortitude"—that they received a great increase of grace through their Deaconship.

<margin>1 Timothy 3, verse 4. Acts 6:8. The office of Deacons.</margin>
<margin>Dionysius the Areopagite, *The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapter 3, article 2.</margin>
Saint Ignatius <note>original: "ep. 2 ad Tral." refers to his second letter to the Trallians.</note> provides the best testimony of their office and the Apostles' intent, writing: *It is also necessary to please the Deacons in every way, for they are ministers of the ministry of JESUS CHRIST. For they are not merely servants of food and drink, but ministers of the Church of God. For what are Deacons but imitators or followers of Christ, serving the Bishop as Christ served his Father, and performing for him a clean and spotless work, just as Saint Stephen served Saint James, etc.* Saint Polycarp says something similar in his letter to the Philippians. Saint Dionysius <note>Known as Dionysius the Areopagite.</note> writes that their office was centered around the Altar, placing the holy bread and chalice upon it. Saint Clement also <note>original: "Apost. Const. li. 2 c. 61" refers to the Apostolic Constitutions.</note> states that their office, among other things, is to assist the Bishops and read the Gospel during the service. Saint Cyprian in various places <note>original: "ep. 65. & ep. 49 ad Cornel." refers to his letters to Cornelius.</note> calls Deacons the "Ministers of the Church and the Apostles" and refers to their office as a "sacred administration" <note>original: "administrationem sacram"</note>. Saint Jerome affirms this in his commentary on the seventh chapter of Micah and in his 85th letter to Evagrius (volume 2), where...

-> A N N O T A T I O N S <-
-> C H A P T E R. VII. <-

<margin>The holy land. Holy places.</margin>
33. *Holy ground.*) If that apparition of God himself or an Angel could make the place and ground holy, to be used by Moses with all signs of reverence and fear: how much more the corporal birth, residence, and wonders of the Son of God in <term>Jewry</term> <note>The region of Judea</note>, and his personal presence in the <term>Blessed Sacrament</term> <note>The Eucharist or Holy Communion</note>, may make that country and all Christian Churches & altars holy? And it is the greatest blindness that can be, to think it superstition to reverence any things or places in respect of God's presence or wondrous operation in the same. *See St. Jerome, letters 17, 18, 27, regarding the holy land.*

<margin>God is not contained in place, yet he will be worshipped in one place more than in another.</margin>
48. *Not in houses.*) The common heretics <note>Likely referring to Protestants who criticized the Catholic focus on physical church buildings and the Real Presence</note> allege this place against the corporal being of Christ in the Blessed Sacrament & in Churches: by which reason they might have driven him out of all houses, Churches, and corporal places, when he was visible on earth. But it is meant of the Divinity only, & spoken to correct the carnal Jews: who thought God either so to be contained, compassed, and limited to their Temple, that he could be nowhere else, or at least that he would not hear or receive men's prayers and sacrifices in the Churches of the Gentiles, or elsewhere, out of the said Temple. And so as it makes nothing for the <term>Sacramentarians</term> <note>A term for those who denied that the bread and wine literally become the body and blood of Christ</note>, no more does it serve for such as esteem Churches and places of public prayer no more convenient nor more holy than any other secular houses or chambers. For though his person or power be not limited to any place, yet it pleases him, condescending to our necessity and profit, to work his wonders and to be worshipped by us in holy places rather than secular ones.

<margin>Relics.</margin>
58. *They stoned him.*) Read a marvelous narration in St. Augustine of one stone, that hitting the Martyr on the elbow, rebounded back to a faithful man that stood near. Who keeping and carrying it with him, was by revelation warned to leave it at Ancona in Italy: whereupon a Church or Memorial of St. Stephen was there erected, and many miracles done after the said Martyr's body was found out, and not before. *Augustine, Volume 10, Sermon 38 "On Various Subjects," Paris edition.*

## CHAPTER VIII.

*Persecution is so far from prevailing against the Church that it actually causes the Church to grow from Jerusalem into all of Judea and Samaria. 5 Philip, the second of the Deacons, converts the city of Samaria itself through his miracles and baptizes the inhabitants, including Simon Magus himself. 14 However, the Apostles Peter and John are the ministers who provide them with the Holy Spirit. 18 Simon Magus attempts to buy this ministry from them. 26 The same Philip is sent by an Angel to a high official from Ethiopia who had come on a pilgrimage to Jerusalem; Philip first instructs him in the faith 36 and then, after the official professes his faith and desires Baptism, Philip baptizes him.*

### ANNOTATIONS
#### CHAP. VIII.

---

<margin>The relics of St. Stephen.</margin>
2. *Devout men.*] Just as great devotion was shown here in burying his body, so it was later at the discovery <note>original: "Inuention"</note> and the transfer <note>original: "Tranſlation"</note> of his remains. And the miracles performed by them, and at every small memorial of the same, were infinite, as St. Augustine witnesses in *The City of God*, Book 22, Chapter 8, and in his *Sermon on St. Stephen* 10.

<margin>That Peter was sent is no argument against his Primacy.</margin>
14. *Sent Peter.*] Some Protestants use this passage to prove St. Peter was not the head of the Apostles, because he and St. John were "sent" by the Twelve. By this logic, they might as well conclude he was not equal to the rest, for commonly a master sends a servant, or a superior sends an inferior, when the word "sending" is used strictly. But it is not always used this way in the Scriptures; for if it were, the Son could not be sent by the Father, nor the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son. Nor is it so in common worldly use, seeing an inferior or equal may entreat his friend or superior to do his business for him. Specifically, a political body or corporation may, by election or otherwise, choose their Head and send him. For example, citizens may send their Mayor to the Prince or Parliament, even though he is the head of the city, because he may be more fit to handle their business. Also, a superior or equal may be sent by his own consent or desire. Lastly, the College of the Apostles, including Peter with the rest (as every such body implies both the head and the members), was greater than Peter their head alone—just as the Prince and Parliament together are greater than the Prince alone. And so Peter might be sent by the authority of the whole College, despite being its head.

<margin>The Sacrament of Confirmation, administered by Bishops only.</margin>
17. *Did they lay* <note>original: "impoſe"</note>] *If this Philip <note>This refers to Philip the Deacon, not Philip the Apostle.</note> had been an Apostle (says St. Bede), he might have laid on his hands so that they might have received the Holy Spirit; but no one can do this except Bishops. For though Priests may baptize, and also anoint the baptized with chrism <term>chrism: holy oil</term> consecrated by a Bishop, he cannot sign the forehead with that same holy oil, because that belongs only to Bishops when they give the Holy Spirit to the baptized. Thus he speaks regarding the Sacrament of Confirmation in Acts 8. This laying on of hands, therefore, together with the prayers specified here (which no doubt were the very same that the Church still uses for that purpose), was the administration of the Sacrament of Confirmation.*
<margin>St. Cyprian's Letter 73, number 3, to Jubaianus <note>original: "ep. 73. n. 3 ad Iubianum"</note>.</margin>
*Concerning which St. Cyprian says this: "Those in Samaria who were baptized by Philip, because they had received lawful and ecclesiastical Baptism, did not need to be baptized again. Only that which was lacking was done by Peter and John—namely, that through prayer and the laying on of hands, the Holy Spirit might be poured upon them. This is also done among us now: those who are baptized in the Church are presented to the Rulers of the Church, and by our prayer and the laying on of hands, they receive the Holy Spirit and are signed with the seal of our Lord." So says St. Cyprian.*

they have turned this holy Sacrament *into a Catechism.* <note>The author argues that Protestant reformers reduced the spiritual ritual of Confirmation to a mere educational session or "catechism."</note> There are also those who allow the baptized, upon coming to the age of discretion, to choose for themselves whether they will continue as Christians or not. Into such devilish and diverse inventions they fall, those who will not obey God's Church nor the express Scriptures, which tell us of prayer, of the imposition of hands, of the Holy Ghost, and of grace and virtue from above—not merely of instruction, which might and may be done as well before Baptism, and by others, as by Apostles and Bishops, to whom only this Holy function pertains; so much so that in our country <note>Referring to England.</note> it is called *Bishoping*. <note>An old English term for the Sacrament of Confirmation, emphasizing that only a Bishop can perform it.</note>

*Simony.*
</margin>
18. *Offered money.*] This wicked sorcerer Simon is noted by St. Irenaeus (Book 1, chapter 20) and others to have been the first heretic, and the father of all heretics to come in the Church of God. He taught that "faith alone" in him, without a good life and works, was enough for salvation. He made the attempt to purchase a spiritual function with his money—that is, to be made a Bishop. For, to have the power to give the Holy Ghost by the imposition of hands is to be a Bishop; just as to buy the power to remit sins or to consecrate Christ's body is to buy the office of a Priest, or to buy Priesthood. Likewise, to buy the authority to minister Sacraments, to preach, or to have the care of souls, is to buy a "benefice" <note>A church office that provides an income.</note>. In all other spiritual things, to either sell or purchase for money or anything of value is a great and horrible sin called **Simony**. In such people who think it is lawful (as Simon judged it here), it is named the *Simoniacal Heresy*, after this detestable man who first attempted to buy a spiritual function or office. (See St. Gregory in John the Deacon’s *Life of Gregory*, Book 3, chapters 2, 3, 4, 5).

<margin>
*Penance.*
</margin>
21. *Do penance.*] St. Augustine (Letter 108) understands this as the penance performed in the Primitive Church for heinous offenses. He teaches us to translate this and similar passages (2 Corinthians 12:21, Revelation 9:21) as we do, and as it is found in the Vulgate Latin. Consequently, he argues that the Greek *metanoein* <note>original: μετανοεῖν</note> signifies exactly this. Indeed, when he adds that even very good men do daily penance for "venial" <note>minor or pardonable</note> sins through fasting, prayer, and alms, he warrants this phrase and translation throughout the New Testament, especially since he himself read it as it is in the Vulgate Latin and as we translate it.

22. *If perhaps.*] You may see that great penance is required here for the remission of sin, and that men must stand in fear and dread lest they be not worthy to be heard or to obtain mercy. By this, all men who buy or sell any spiritual functions, dignities, offices, or livings may be specially warned that the sin is exceeding great.

<margin>
*Simon Magus more religious than the Protestants.*
</margin>
24. *Pray you for me.*] This Sorcerer had more knowledge of the true religion than the Protestants have, who do not see that the Apostles and Bishops can give the Holy Ghost in this Sacrament or others (which Simon plainly perceived and confessed). Surely he was more religious than they are; for after being sharply rebuked by the Apostle, he did not blaspheme as they do when they are corrected by the Governors of the Church, but instead desired the Apostles to pray for him.

<margin>
*Beza.*
</margin>
<margin>
*Notes on the Testament, 155.*

This is to accuse the holy Evangelist and to blaspheme the Holy Ghost himself. See Beza <note>Theodore Beza, a major Protestant Reformer and scholar.</note>, who is often very cheeky with St. Luke.

<margin>
*The ceremonies of Sacraments are performed, even if not mentioned.*

*On Faith and Works, chapter 9.*

38. *He baptized him.*] When the heretics of this time find mention in Scripture of any Sacrament administered by the Apostles or others in the Primitive Church, they imagine no more was done than what is expressly told, and they scarcely believe even that much. For example, if the "imposition of hands" in the Sacrament of Confirmation is the only thing expressed, they think there was no chrism <note>holy oil</note> or any other work or word used. Similarly, they think no more ceremony was used in the baptizing of this nobleman <note>The Ethiopian Eunuch.</note> than is mentioned here. Upon this, St. Augustine has these memorable words: *In that which is said, "Philip baptized him," he would have it understood that all things were done which—though they are not mentioned in the Scriptures for the sake of brevity—we know were to be done by the order of tradition.*

### CHAP. IX.

-> Saul, not content to persecute so cruelly in Jerusalem, is on the way to Damascus when he is told by our Lord JESUS of his vain attempt, and is miraculously converted to be an Apostle. After great penance, he is restored to his sight by Ananias and baptized. He presently deals mightily against the Jews, proving JESUS to be Christ, to their great admiration. But such is their obstinacy that they lie in wait at Damascus to kill him. From there, he goes to Jerusalem and joins with the Apostles, and again his death is sought by the obstinate Jews. The Church having now grown over all Judea, Galilee, and Samaria, Peter visits all; and in his visitation, by healing a lame man and raising a dead woman, he converts very many. <-

<margin>Good works done before faith are preparations for it, not strictly deserving of merit on their own.</margin>
2. *Doing many acts of charity.*] He <note>Cornelius</note> knew God as the creator of all, but he did not yet know that His almighty Son had become human. In that faith, he offered prayers and gave alms which pleased God; and by doing good, he earned the opportunity to know God perfectly, to believe in the mystery of the Incarnation, and to receive the Sacrament of Baptism. So says the Venerable Bede, citing Saint Gregory. And Saint Augustine says this in <note>original: "li. 1. de Bapt. c. 8."</note> Book 1 of *On Baptism*, chapter 8: because whatever goodness he had in prayers and alms could not profit him unless he were incorporated into the Church by the bond of Christian society and peace, he is told to send for Peter. Through Peter, he may learn of Christ and be baptized. This shows that such works as are done before justification, though they are not enough for salvation, are yet acceptable preparations for the grace of justification, and move God to mercy. This is also seen in God’s <margin>* Bede on this passage.</margin> similar provident mercy toward the Ethiopian Eunuch <margin>* Acts 8.*</margin>, though all such preparatory works also come from grace. Otherwise, they could never deserve anything from God by <term>congruity</term> <note>A theological term meaning "fitness" or "suitability"—an act that, while not strictly "earning" a reward, makes it appropriate for God to respond with grace.</note> or any other way toward justification.

<margin>The Canonical hours.</margin>
9. *To pray about the sixth hour.*] The hour is specified because there were certain appointed times for prayer used under the Old Law. Devout persons observed these privately, following the public service in the Temple; the Apostles and the Holy Church later both kept and increased these times. Saint Cyprian writes very notably of this in <note>original: "De Or. Dom. n 15."</note> *On the Lord's Prayer*, section 15: *In celebrating their prayers, we find <margin>* On the Lord's Prayer, section 15.*</margin> that the three children with Daniel observed the third, sixth, and ninth hours, as a mystery of the Holy Trinity.* And a little later: *the worshippers of God, spiritually determining these spaces of hours long ago, observed set times to pray. Afterward, it became clear that the just prayed this way for a mystery. For at the third hour, the Holy Spirit descended upon the Apostles, fulfilling the grace of our Lord’s promise <margin>Acts 2.</margin>; and at the sixth hour, Peter, going up to the higher room of the house, was instructed by both voice and sign from God <margin>Acts 10.</margin> that all nations should be admitted to the grace of salvation, whereas he had doubted the cleansing of the Gentiles before. And our Lord, being crucified at the sixth hour, at the ninth hour washed away <margin>Luke 23</margin> our sins with His blood. But for us, dearly beloved, besides the seasons observed of old, both the times and mysteries of praying are increased. For we must pray early in the morning, so that the Resurrection of our Lord may be celebrated by morning prayer; as of old the <margin>Matins. Evensong.</margin> Holy Spirit indicated in the Psalm, saying, "Early in the morning I will stand before you, early in the morning <margin>* Psalm 5.*</margin> you will hear my voice." Toward the evening also, when the sun departs and the day ends, we must of necessity pray again.*

<margin>Daniel 6</margin> Saint Jerome also, writing of Daniel praying three times a day, says: *There are three times when we must bow our knees to God. The ecclesiastical tradition well understands the third, sixth, and ninth hours. Moreover, at the third hour, the Holy Spirit descended upon the Apostles; at the sixth, Peter went up into a higher chamber to pray; at the ninth, <margin>* Acts 3.*</margin> Peter and John went to the Temple.* Again, writing to Eustochium, a virgin and nun, in Letter 22, chapter 16: *Though the Apostle tells us to pray always, and for holy persons their very sleep is prayer, yet we must have distinct hours of prayer, so that if we are otherwise occupied, the time itself may remind us of our duty. No one can be ignorant of the third, sixth, and ninth hours, the early morning, and the evening.* And to Demetrias in Letter 8, chapter 8, he writes that in psalms and prayer she must always keep the third, sixth, and ninth hours, evening, midnight, and morning. He says the same in Letter 7, chapter 5. And in Letter 27, chapter 10, he tells how Paula, the holy Abbess,

# CHAPTER 11. OF THE APOSTLES.

<margin>To adore. <note>original Greek: "proskunein"</note></margin>
25. *Adored.*] Saint Chrysostom, in *Homily 21 on Acts*, thinks Peter refused this adoration out of humility only, because every falling down to the ground for the sake of worship is not "Divine worship" or due only to God, the word for "adoration" and "prostration" being commonly used in the Scriptures <margin>Adoration of creatures.</margin> toward men. But Saint Jerome, in *Against Vigilantius, chapter 2, volume 2*, rather thinks that Cornelius, through the error of his pagan background and Peter’s personal holiness, intended to adore him with Divine honor, and therefore was lifted up by the Apostle, who added that he was but a man.

40. *Gave him.*] Christ did not reveal his Resurrection and other mysteries to everyone at once, nor immediately to the common people: but to a few chosen men who should be the governors of the rest, instructing us thereby to receive our faith and all necessary things for salvation from the hands of our Superiors.

<margin>Augustine, *Questions on Leviticus*, question 84, volume 4.</margin>
47. *Baptized, who have received.*] Such may be the grace of God sometimes toward men, and their charity and contrition so great, that they may have remission <note>forgiveness of sins</note>, justification, and sanctification <margin>They that are justified before, must not omit the Sacraments.</margin> before the external Sacrament of Baptism, Confirmation, or Penance is received. We see this in this example, where at Peter’s preaching they all receive the Holy Ghost before any Sacrament; but in the same, we learn one necessary lesson: that such people must nonetheless receive the Sacraments appointed by Christ, which whoever treats with contempt can never be justified. *Augustine, on...*

### A N N O T A T I O N S
### C H A P. XI.

<margin>The Church visible.</margin>
24. *Multitude added.*) As before (chapter 10) a few, so now great numbers of Gentiles are joined also to the visible Church, consisting before only of the Jews. Which Church has been ever since Christ’s Ascension, notoriously seen and known: their preaching open, their Sacraments visible, their discipline visible, their Heads and Governors visible, the provision for their maintenance visible, the persecution visible, their dispersion visible: the Heretics that went out from them, visible: the joining either of men or Nations unto them, visible: their peace and rest after persecutions, visible: their Governors in prison, visible: the Church prays for them visibly, their Councils visible, their gifts and graces visible, their name (Christians) known to all the world. Of the Protestants' invisible church we hear not one word.

<margin>Jerome, *Against the Luciferians*, 6. 7. at the end.</margin>
26. *Christians.*) This name, *Christian*, ought to be common to all the Faithful, and other new names of Schismatics and Sectaries must be abhorred. If you hear (says St. Jerome) anywhere, such as are said to be of Christ, not to have their names from our Lord JESUS CHRIST, but to be called after some other certain name, as Marcionites, Valentinians, (as now also the Lutherans, Calvinists, Protestants) know you that they belong not to the Church of Christ, but to the Synagogue of Antichrist. Lactantius also (Book 7 of the *Divine Institutes*, chapter 30) says thus, *When Phrygians, or Novatians, or Valentinians, or Marcionites, or Anthropomorphites, or Arians, or any other be named, they cease to be Christians, who <margin>Names of Sectaries and Heretics.</margin> having lost the name of Christ, have taken on the names of men.* Neither can our new Sectaries discharge themselves, for they take not to themselves these names, but are forced to bear them as given by their Adversaries. For, so were the names of Arians and the rest of old, imposed by others, and not chosen commonly by themselves: Which notwithstanding were callings that proved them to be Heretics. And as for the name of Protestants, our men hold themselves well content therewith. But concerning the Heretics' turning of the argument against the peculiar callings of our <margin>Protestants.</margin> Religious, as Dominicans, Franciscans, Jesuits, Thomists, or such like, it is nothing, except they could prove that the orders and persons so named, were of diverse faiths and Sects, or differed in any necessary <margin>Diverse religious orders are not diverse sects.</margin> point of religion, or were not all of one Christian name and Communion: and it is as ridiculous as if it were objected, that some be Ciceronians, some Plinians, some good Augustine men, <margin>Jeremiah 35. Numbers 6.</margin> some Hieronymians, some Oxford men, some Cambridge men, and (which is most like) some * Rechabites, some * Nazirites.

<margin>Papists, Catholics, and true Christians, all one.</margin>
Neither does their objection, that we be called Papists, help or excuse them in their new names. For, besides that it is by them scornfully invented (as the name Homoousians <note>original: "Homouſians"; a Greek term meaning "of the same substance," used by the Council of Nicaea to define Christ's divinity. The Arians used it as a mocking label for the orthodox.</note> was by the Arians) this name is not of any one man Bishop of Rome or elsewhere, known to be the author of any schism or sect, as their callings be: but it is of a whole state and order of governors, and that of the chief Governors, to whom we are bound to cleave in religion and to obey in all things. So to be a Papist, is to be a Christian man, a child of the Church, and subject to Christ’s Vicar <note>The Pope, acting as the representative of Christ on earth.</note>. And therefore against such impudent Sectaries as compare the faithful for following the Pope, to the diversity of Heretics bearing the names of new Masters, let us ever have in readiness this <margin>Not to be with the Pope, is to be with Antichrist.</margin> <margin>Epistles 57 & 58 to Damasus.</margin> saying of St. Jerome to Pope Damasus, *Vitalis I know not, Meletius I refuse, I know not Paulinus, Whosoever gathers not with thee, scatters: that is to say, Whosoever is not Christ’s, is Antichrist’s.* And again, *If any man joins with Peter’s Chair, he is mine.*

<meta>This page concludes the annotations for Chapter 11, specifically focusing on the theological importance of the names "Christian" and "Catholic" as markers of the true Church. It then transitions into Chapter 12, detailing the martyrdom of Saint James the Greater and the miraculous rescue of Saint Peter from prison during the reign of Herod Agrippa I.</meta>

<margin>The name of CHRISTIANS.</margin>
We must further observe here that this name, "Christian," given to all believers and to the whole Church, was specifically chosen to distinguish them from the Jews and Heathens who did not believe in Christ at all. The same name now separates and identifies all Christian men from Turks <note>In the 16th century, "Turk" was often used as a general term for Muslims.</note> and others who do not follow Christ at all. But when Heretics began to rise from among the Christians—who professed Christ's name and various Articles of faith just as true believers do—the name "Christian" was too common to separate the Heretics from truly faithful men. Thereupon the <margin>The name of CATHOLICS.</margin> Apostles, by the Holy Ghost, imposed this name *Catholic* upon the Believers who were obedient to the Church’s doctrine in all points. *When heresies had arisen* (says Saint Pacian in his *Letter to Symphorian* <note>original: "ep. ad Symphorianum"</note>) *and endeavored by various names to tear apart the dove of God and Queen, and to rend her in pieces, the Apostolic people required their surname, whereby the incorrupt people might be distinguished, etc. And so those who before were called Christians, are now surnamed also Catholics. Christian is my name, says he, Catholic my surname.* And this word, "Catholic," is the proper mark by which the holy <margin>I BELIEVE IN THE CATHOLIC CHURCH <note>original: "CREDO ECCLESIAM CATHOLICAM"</note></margin> Apostles in their Creed taught us to discern the true Church from the false heretical congregation of whatever kind. And not only the meaning of the word—which signifies the universality of times, places, and persons—but the very name and word itself, by God’s providence, has always and only been appropriate for the true believers. Although it was sometimes challenged at the beginning of various Sects, it was never obtained by Heretics. It provides such a plain mark and evidence that Saint Augustine said, *In the lap of the Church the very name of Catholic keeps me.* (In his *Against the Fundamental Epistle, chapter 4* <note>original: "cont. ep. fund. c. 4"</note>). And again in his *Tractate 32 on John* <note>original: "tract. 32 in IO."</note>: *we receive the Holy Ghost if we love the Church, if we be joined together by charity, if we rejoice in the Catholic name and faith.* And again in *On True Religion, chapter 7, volume 1* <note>original: "de ver. rel. c. 7. to. 1."</note>: *We must hold the communion of that Church which is named Catholic, not only by her own people, but also by all her enemies. For, whether they like it or not, the Heretics and Schismatics themselves, when they speak not with their own fellows but with strangers, call the Catholic Church nothing else but the Catholic Church; for they could not be understood unless they identified it by this name by which she is called by all the world.* The Heretics, <margin>The Protestants deride the name CATHOLIC.</margin> when they see themselves deprived of this name "Catholic," then plainly reject it and deride the name—as the Donatists <note>A 4th-century schismatic group in North Africa that argued only they were the true, pure Church.</note> did, calling it a human forgery or fiction, which Saint Augustine calls "words of blasphemy" (*Against Gaudentius, book 1, chapter 33* <note>original: "li. 1 c. 33 cont. Gaudent."</note>). Some Heretics of this time scornfully call them "Catholics" and "Cacolics" <note>A derogatory pun combining "Catholic" with the Greek "kakos," meaning bad or evil.</note>. Another calls it the "most vain term Catholic" (*Beza in his preface to the New Testament, 1565* <note>Theodore Beza was a major Protestant reformer and successor to John Calvin.</note>). Another calls the Catholic religion a "Catholic Apostasy or defection" (*Humphrey <margin>* In the Catechisms of the Lutherans.</margin> in the Life of Jewel, page 213* <note>Laurence Humphrey was an English Puritan theologian.</note>). Indeed, some have even taken the word out of the Creed, <insert>*</insert> putting "Christian" in its place. But against these "good fellows," let us follow that which Saint Augustine (*On the Utility of Believing, chapter 8, volume 6* <note>original: "de vtil. cred. c. 8. to. 6."</note>) gives as a rule to direct a man in the right and sure way through the diversity and doubt of all error, saying: *If after these troubles of mind you seem to yourself sufficiently tossed and vexed, and want an end to these molestations, follow the way of Catholic discipline, which from Christ himself has proceeded through the Apostles even unto us, and shall proceed from here to posterity.* See the Annotation for 1 Timothy 3:15.

->ANNOTATIONS<-
->CHAPTER 12.<-

5. *Prayer was made.*] The Church prayed incessantly for her chief Pastor, and was heard by God: and all Christian people are warned by this to pray for their Bishops and Pastors when they are in prison.

<margin>Saint Peter’s chains.</margin>
6. *Two chains.*] These chains are famous for miracles and were brought from Jerusalem to Rome by the Empress Eudoxia, wife to Theodosius the Younger. There, they were matched and placed with another chain that the same Apostle was bound with by Nero, and a Church was founded upon them, named *Petri ad vincula* <note>Latin: "Peter in Chains." This church, San Pietro in Vincoli, still houses the relics today.</note>, where they are religiously kept and revered until this day. There is a Feast in the whole Church for the same on the first of August, which we call Lammas Day. <note>Lammas Day was an old English festival of the wheat harvest, but in the liturgical calendar, it coincides with the Feast of St. Peter’s Chains.</note>

<margin>Patronage of Angels.</margin>
15. *His Angel*] If particular Angels (says Saint Chrysostom) are assigned by our Lord to those who have only charge of their own life (as <margin>Genesis 48, 16</margin> one of the righteous said, *The Angel which hath delivered me from my youth upward*), how much more are heavenly Spirits at hand to help those to whom the charge and burden of the world is committed. <note>Original: *Chrysostom in laudem Pauli, homily 7, volume 3.* John Chrysostom was a 4th-century Church Father known for his eloquent preaching.</note>

<margin>Public prayer for Saint Peter the head.</margin>
17. *Tell James.*] He wishes them to show this to Saint James, the Bishop of Jerusalem, and to the Christians, so that they might see the effect of their prayers for him and give thanks to God. For Saint James, no doubt, organized public prayer for Saint Peter.

# ANNOTATIONS
## CHAPTER 13.

<margin>The Apostles' liturgy or Mass.</margin>
<margin><note>original Greek: λειτουργούντων αὐτῶν (leitourgountōn autōn)</note></margin>
2. *As they were ministering.*] If we should—as our adversaries do—boldly change whatever text we wish and flee from one language to another for the advantage of our cause, we might have translated *ministering* as *sacrificing*. For that is what <term>the Greek signifies</term><note>The word "leitourgountōn" is the root of "liturgy" and specifically refers to performing a priestly or public service.</note>, and so Erasmus translated it. Indeed, we might have translated it as *Saying Mass*, for so they did; and the Greek Fathers took the name for their service, "Liturgy," from this, which Erasmus translates as "Mass," saying, *the Mass of Chrysostom.* <note>original Latin: "Missa Chrysostomi"</note> But we keep our text as the translators of the Scriptures should do, most religiously.

<margin>Paul and Barnabas are consecrated by men.</margin>
<margin>Galatians 1.</margin>
2. *Separate for me.*] Though Paul was taught by God himself and specifically designated by Christ to be an Apostle, and here chosen by the Holy Ghost together with Barnabas, they were still to be ordered, consecrated, and admitted by men. This wholly condemns all these new, rebellious, and disordered spirits who challenge and usurp the office of preaching and other sacred actions "from heaven," without the Church's admission.

<margin>Ember days.</margin>
<margin>Prescribed times of fasts.</margin>
<margin>Leo, Epistle 8, chapter 1.</margin>
<margin>Epiphanius in the Compendium.</margin>
<margin>Leo, Sermon 4 on the fast of the 7th month.</margin>
3. *Fasting.*] Because of this, the Church of God uses and prescribes public fasts at the four solemn times of giving <term>Holy Orders</term><note>The sacrament by which men are ordained as deacons, priests, or bishops.</note> (which are our <term>Ember days</term><note>Quarterly periods of prayer and fasting in the liturgical calendar.</note>) as a necessary preparation for such a great work. Saint Leo declares this by referencing this passage, calling it an Apostolical tradition. See *Saint Leo, Sermon 9 on the fast of the 7th month, and Calixtus, Epistle 1, volume 1 of the Councils; Council of Mainz, chapters 34–35, volume 3.* And this fasting was not just "fasting from sin" or moral/Christian temperance—as the Protestants ridiculously claim, for such fasting they were always bound to keep—but it was abstinence for a time from all food or from certain kinds of food. This was joined with prayer and sacrifice, and done specifically at such seasons as the Church prescribed for everyone together (as in Lent, the Ember days, Friday, and Saturday), and not simply whenever every man felt like it, as Aerius and such heretics held. *Saint Augustine, Heresy 53.*

<margin>Imposition of hands.</margin>
<margin>Holy orders.</margin>
<margin>Acts 2.</margin>
<margin>Jerome on Isaiah chapter 58.</margin>
3. *Imposing hands.*] Because all blessings and consecrations were done in the Apostles' time by the external ceremony of <term>imposition of hands</term><note>The ritual act of placing hands on a person's head to confer a spiritual blessing or office.</note>, various Sacraments were named after the act itself—specifically Confirmation, as noted before, and the Holy Ordering or consecrating of Bishops, Priests, Deacons, and Subdeacons, as we see here and elsewhere. In these acts, though there were many holy words and ceremonies and a very solemn action, whatever is done in those Sacraments is collectively called the "Imposition of hands," just as whatever was done in the whole divine mystery of the Blessed Sacrament is named the "breaking of bread." For the Apostles (as Saint Dionysius writes in *The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, chapter 1* at the end) purposely kept the sacred words and actions of the Sacraments hidden in their open speeches and writings, which might come to the hands or ears of infidels. And Saint Ambrose says, *on 1 Timothy chapter 4: The imposition of the hand consists of mystical words wherewith the elected is conformed and made fit for his function; receiving authority (his conscience bearing witness) so that he may be bold to offer sacrifice to God in our Lord's stead.* And Saint Jerome says, *The imposition of hand is the Ordering of Clergy, which is done by prayer of the voice and imposition of the hand.* And this exists in some inferior orders also, but Paul and Barnabas were ordered to a higher function than inferior priests, even to be Bishops throughout all nations.

<margin>Spiritual officers of our souls.</margin>
4. *Sent of the Holy Ghost.*] Whosoever is sent by the Church is sent by the Holy Ghost, even though it is not done in such an extraordinary manner as this. By this we see how far the officers of our souls in the Church surpass temporal magistrates; though magistrates are of God's ordinance, they are not of the Holy Ghost's special calling.

### C H A P T E R 14.

<margin>Divine Worship <note>original: Latria</note></margin>
12. *They would sacrifice.*) This is divine worship, consisting in external sacrifice and in acknowledging the parties worshipped to be gods. This <margin>Augustine, The City of God, book 10, chapter 1.</margin> may be done for no man nor creature; therefore the Apostles refuse it with all possible diligence, and all the Angels and Saints in heaven refuse that adoration by sacrifice. The Catholic Church allows no Priest or anyone else to worship any Saint in heaven or earth in this way. She has but one external Sacrifice, which is in the Holy Mass, of Christ’s body and blood; that she offers to God alone, and neither to Peter nor to Paul <margin>Augustine, The City of God, book 20, chapter 27.</margin> (as Saint Augustine says), even though the Priest who offers the sacrifice stands over their bodies and offers it in their memory. But other kinds of honors and duties—inferior without any comparison (no matter how great <margin>Veneration <note>original: Dulia</note></margin> they may be) to this—we do perform, as the Scriptures and Nature teach us, to all superiors in heaven and earth, according to the degrees of grace, honor, and blessedness that God has called them to, from our Blessed Lady, Christ’s own mother, to the least servant He has in the world. For this, the critics of the Church would never accuse Christian people of idolatry if they had either grace, learning, faith, or natural affection.

<meta>This page continues the theological defense of the term "Priest" (Presbyter) against Protestant translations ("Elder"), following the account of Paul and Barnabas ordaining leaders in the newly founded churches. It then begins the narrative of Chapter 15, focusing on the Council of Jerusalem and the dispute over whether Gentile converts must follow the Law of Moses.</meta>

### CHAPTER 15. OF THE APOSTLES.

<margin>Jerome on Isaiah, Chapter 58.</margin>
The meaning of the word is clear from Saint Jerome saying (as was previously cited) that *ordination* <note>original: "χειροτονία" (cheirotonia)</note> is the *Ordering of Clergy or Clergymen by the prayer of the voice and the imposition of the hand.*

<margin>22. Priests.</margin>
<margin>Heretical translation against Priesthood.</margin>
Even so here also, as before, fleeing from the proper, apt, and known word—which is most precisely correspondent to the very Greek in our tongue and all nations—they translate *Priest* as *Elder*. That is, they substitute a word indicating age for a word indicating a calling of Office. For a term of art, appropriated to holy Order by the consent of all the Church, Apostolic authority, and the Fathers, they substitute a vulgar, common, and profane term. They do this with as little grace as if they should translate *High Priest* <note>original: "Pontificem"</note> as "a bridge-maker," or the *Mayor* of London as the *Bigger* of London <note>The author is mocking the translators for using the literal root of words rather than their established titles; 'Mayor' comes from 'maior,' meaning 'greater' or 'bigger'.</note>. And thus you see within the compass of three words they flee guilefully from the Latin to the Greek, and again guilefully from the Greek to the common English. Such corruption of Scriptures their hatred of Priesthood drives them unto. 

If they had translated it so when the Scriptures were first written (at which time the word was but newly received into its special and Ecclesiastical meaning, and when it was yet taken sometimes in a common profane way, as in 1 *Timothy* 5, or only where our ancient Latin version turns *Presbyter* <note>Priest/Elder</note> into *Elder* <note>original: "Senior"</note>, because the word was not yet wholly and only appropriated to holy Orders, as afterward by the use of many hundred years it was and is), their dealing might have had some color of honesty and plainness. But now, it can be nothing but plain falsehood and corruption, intended for a purpose further than the simple can see. Which is to take away the office of Sacrificing and other functions of Priests, which in the New Testament are proper to those whom the Apostles often, and posterity almost altogether, call Priests <note>original: "Presbyteros"</note>. 

This word "Presbyter" so certainly implies the authority of sacrificing that by use it has also become the only English for *Priest* <note>original: "Sacerdos," the Latin term for a sacrificing priest</note>. Even our adversaries translate it this way throughout all the Old and New Testament, though they cannot be ignorant that "Priest" comes from "Presbyter" and not from "Sacerdos." Antiquity applied the meaning of *Presbyter* to *Sacerdos* for no other cause but to show that a *Presbyter* in the New Law is what a *Sacerdos* was in the Old. The Apostles abstained from this and other such old names at first, rather using the words Bishops, Pastors, and Priests, so they might be distinguished from the Governors and sacrificers of Aaron’s order, who in the Apostles' time still performed their old functions in the Temple.

<margin>If a "Sacerdos" is a Priest, much more is a "Presbyter."</margin>
The Heretics themselves, always calling a *Sacerdos* a "Priest," must be driven to confess that this is true: that to be a Priest is to be a man appointed to sacrifice. Although their folly is notorious in this: they willingly apply the word "Priest" to *Sacerdos*, yet take it away from *Presbyter*, from which it is properly derived—not only in English, but in other languages like French and Italian.

<margin>Presbyter. Priest. Prebstre. Preti.</margin>
This is to take away the name that the Apostles and Fathers gave to the Priests of the Church, and to give it wholly and only to the order of Aaron, which never had it before our Priesthood began. Never did Heretics stand so much upon doubtful derivations and the "descant" of words <note>Playing or improvising on the literal meanings of words.</note> as these Protestants do, and yet never did men behave themselves more foolishly in the same, as anyone who notices their distinctions of Elders, Ministers, Deacons, and such like, shall perceive.

# THE ACTS CHAPTER 15

<meta>catchword: Then</meta>

† They therefore being brought on their way by the Church, passed through Phoenicia and Samaria, reporting the conversion of the Gentiles: and they made great joy to all the brethren.

<margin>c "Ancients" here, and often in this chapter, are the same as Priests in verse 2, as Saint Jerome also understands it in 1 Peter 5. The Greek word is always one and the same: *presbyteroi* <note>original: πρεσβύτεροι</note>, meaning Priests. Jerome in his commentary on Titus chapter 1 and Galatians chapter 4.</margin>

## ANNOTATIONS
### CHAPTER 15.

<margin>The way to end dissension in religion is to commit it to a Council.</margin>
1. **Appointed**] We learn by this example what is to be done when any controversy arises in religion between the teachers or other Christian people. We see it is not enough to contend by allegations of Scriptures or other proofs seeming to favor either side: for if we rely only on contentious partisanship, there would be no end. Instead, the more writing, wrestling, and striving there were—each person following their own fancy and cloaking it with the title of God's word and Scripture—the more Schisms, Sects, and divisions would occur, as we see especially in the restless Heresies of our own time. Those who support such views, admitting no judges, will not stand for a trial by mortal men, nor submit to the tribunal of the Pope, Councils, Bishops, or Synods. Instead, each man relies on his own fantastical spirit, his own interpretation of the Scriptures, and his own willful, stubborn rebellion against God's Church and his Superiors within it. 

But here we see Saint Paul and Barnabas—men who were Apostles and full of the Spirit of God—and the other parties, who were quite partial to the ceremonies of the Old Law due to their long history and education in them. Yet they did not stand stiffly in their own opinions on either side. Instead, they condescended <note>condescended: in this historical context, to agree or stoop to a specific course of action for the sake of unity</note> to refer the whole controversy and its final decision to the Apostles, Priests, or Ancients of Jerusalem. That is to say, they committed the matter to be tried by the heads and Bishops and their determination in Council. This is God’s holy and wise providence among other judgments in his Church: to keep the Christian people in truth and unity, and to condemn sects, false teachers, and those who trouble the Church. By these judgments and this order, whoever will not or dare not have their doctrine and actions tried, shows themselves to mistrust their own cause and to flee from the light and the ordinance of God. Without this order for settling all differences in faith and interpretations of the Scriptures, the Church would have been more defective and insufficient than any Commonwealth or Society of men in the world; for no society lacks the means to decide the discords and dissensions arising among its subjects and citizens.

<margin>Of what persons a Council consists.</margin>
<margin>Deuteronomy 17.</margin>
<margin>Malachi 2, 7.</margin>
<margin>Haggai 2.</margin>
6. **Apostles and Ancients**.] The Heresies of our Protestants, which would have all men give a voice or be present in Councils, and of others who would have none but the "holy" or "elect" admitted, are refuted by this example. Here we see none but Apostles and Priests (Ancients) assembled to dispute the matter, though many devout people were in the city at the same time. Neither did any others in the Ancient Councils of the Church ever assemble to debate and define matters except for such leaders, though many others may be present for other reasons. Secular men or women, no matter how great their gifts, cannot be judges in causes of faith and religion. *If anything,* says God, *be hard and doubtful, you shall come to the Priests of the Levitical stock, and you shall follow their sentence* <note>original: *Deuteronomy 17*</note>. Again, *The lips of the Priest shall keep knowledge, and the Law you shall require from his mouth* <note>original: *Malachi 2:7*</note>. Again, *Ask the Law of the Priest* <note>original: *Haggai 2*</note>. Much more must we refer all to our Bishops and Pastors, whom God has placed in the governance of the Church with much larger privilege than he ever gave the old Priests over the Synagogue, to whom it is said, *He that despises you, despises me* <note>original: *Luke 10:16*</note>.
<margin>Luke 10.</margin>

<margin>A general Council represents the whole Church.</margin>
<margin>book 1, chapter 18, On Baptism.</margin>
And it is to be noted that the Bishops gathered in Council represent the whole Church, have the authority of the whole Church, and the Spirit of God to protect them from error, just as the whole Church does. Saints Paul and Barnabas come here for the definition of the whole Church. The sentence of a plenary <term>plenary: a full or absolute meeting of all members</term> or general Council (says Saint Augustine) is *the consent of the whole Church.* And it must be this way in the Church, because the Magistrates, Senate, Council, or deputies of all commonwealths represent the whole body. To have it otherwise (as the Church's Rebels wish) would be to bring all to hell and horror; they themselves would be perpetually upheld in their wickedness by seditious and popular persons against Law, reason, and religion.

<margin>The first Council at Jerusalem.</margin>
6. **Assembled**.] A Council was called to discuss the matter. This Council was more easily gathered because the Christian Bishops and countries were not yet so many; the principal Governors of the Church were not far dispersed, and as many learned men as were necessary could be in Jerusalem or easily called there. And it was not merely a Provincial Council or Synod, but a general Council, consisting of the chief Apostles and Bishops that then were,

# CHAPTER 15. OF THE APOSTLES.

though the number was not nearly as large as those that would later assemble when the Church had spread into all nations.

<margin>Peter is the head of the Council, and his successors follow him.</margin>
7. **Peter rising up.**] Saint Peter, as the head of the Church, speaks first. His successors have always held the primary voice in all general Councils—not only through their personal presence but, in their absence, through their representatives and substitutes. No council has ever been accepted as having authority or credit in the Church without their confirmation. Therefore, the Councils of the Arians and other heretics <note>The author refers to early Christian groups like the Arians and Nestorians whose views were declared heretical by the central Church.</note>, no matter how large they were, were shamefully in error because they lacked the Pope’s consent, assistance, or confirmation. Examples include the Council of Rimini for the Arians, the second Council of Ephesus for the Nestorians, and other such condemned assemblies.

<margin>Peter’s preeminence toward both Jews and Gentiles.</margin>
<margin>Romans 15:8, Galatians 2:7.</margin>
7. **Chose that by my mouth.**] Although Paul was specifically called and appointed to be the Apostle to the Gentiles, it was Saint Peter’s special privilege—by God’s own choice—that the first Gentiles should be called by his mouth. Peter was the first to declare to the Church the truth regarding the admission of the Gentiles, for he was Christ’s Vicar <term>Vicar: a representative or deputy acting with the authority of a superior</term>. Even so, he was (just as his Master was) a "Minister of Circumcision" <note>original: *Minister Circumcisionis*</note>, meaning the Apostle of the Jews; Christ granted him preeminence in that role as well.

<margin>Saint James and the rest follow Saint Peter’s judgment.</margin>
<margin>Jerome, volume 2, epistle 89 to Augustine, chapter 2.</margin>
<margin>The principal question.</margin>
<margin>Incident questions.</margin>
<margin>How later councils alter the former ones.</margin>
13. **James.**] Saint James, because he was an Apostle and also the Bishop of Jerusalem, gave his judgment next. The speeches of Saints Paul and Barnabas that came in between were only to provide better information for the decision and to confirm Saint Peter’s judgment. Although Paul and Barnabas were Apostles and Bishops and had voices in the Council, many others did as well, even if their opinions are not reported here. And where Saint James says in his speech, *I judge*, it does not mean that he gave the primary or final defining sentence. For he (like all the rest) followed and approved the sentence of Saint Peter, as is clear in the text: the whole assembly held their peace out of reverence for Peter’s person and approval of his sentence. "All the multitude," says Saint Jerome, "held their peace, and the Apostle James and all the Priests passed into his sentence together." For although Saint James specified certain points related to the debate—such as eating "strangled meats" <note>Meats from animals killed by strangulation rather than ritual slaughter, which retained the blood prohibited by Jewish law.</note>—the actual controversy for which the Council met was whether Gentile converts were bound to observe the Law of Moses. It was concluded that they were not bound, nor should they be burdened with Moses' Law or its sacraments and ceremonies. This is the substance and main purpose of this Council’s decree, which remains binding forever; and Peter (says Saint Jerome in the same place) was the leader or author of this decree. The matters of fornication and "foods offered to idols" <note>original: *Idolothytes*</note> were only incidental to the main resolution. The forbidding of eating blood and strangled meat was a temporary prohibition which was later abolished by the consent of the Church. The Church of God understands the difference between times, places, and persons, knowing when and how far such things should be observed. It is regarding such things—which require alteration based on circumstances—that Saint Augustine says (in Book 2 of *On Baptism*), "Former general or full Councils may be amended by later ones."

<margin>The Church’s authority in making Decrees.</margin>
20. **Fornication.**] Fornication and the contamination of Idols are, in themselves, mortal sins and can never be lawful. Yet, because the Gentiles were traditionally prone to both and thought very little of fornication, it pleased the Holy Spirit to forbid both specifically. Regarding the other points—abstaining from blood and strangled meats—these were matters of an indifferent nature. For a time, the Jews were to be accommodated in this, and the Gentiles were to be practiced in obedience. By this, we see the great authority of God’s Church and its Councils, which may command such things as are fit for the current state of nations and times, even without express Scripture, thereby making things necessary that were previously indifferent.

<margin>Leaving the Church: a mark of heretics.</margin>
24. **Going forth from us.**] This is a proper description or sign of heretics, schismatics, and rebellious teachers: they "go out" from their spiritual Pastors and Governors to teach without commission or approval, troubling the Catholic people with many words and sweet speeches, and finally overthrowing their souls.

<margin>God and our Lady, and similar expressions.</margin>
<margin>Genesis 48:15-16, Judges 7:18-20, Exodus 14:31, 1 Timothy 5:21.</margin>
<margin>IT SEEMED GOOD to the Holy Spirit and to us.</margin>
28. **To the Holy Ghost and to us.**] From this, we first note that it is not a fault (as heretics would suggest to the simple-minded) to join God and His creatures together in one speech—referring to the primary cause and the secondary cause—and to attribute a result to both. Good people commonly say, "God and you," or "God and our Lady," "Christ and Saint John," or "We confess to God and to Peter and Paul." Similarly, Scripture says: "God and his Angel," "To our Lord and Gideon," "The sword of the Lord and of Gideon," "Our Lord and Moses," "Christ and his Angels," "Our Lord and all Saints," and "Saint Paul and our Lord." All these phrases, being either directly from Scripture or modeled after it, are also justified by this Council, which boldly says—and has given the pattern to all other lawfully called Councils to say—**It has pleased the Holy Spirit and us.** <note>original: *VISVM EST Sp. sancto & nobis*</note> Saint Cyprian, reporting on a similar Synod held in Africa, says, "It has pleased us by the suggestion of the Holy Spirit." 
Secondly, we note that holy Councils lawfully held for the determination of doubts, the condemning of errors and heresies, the settling of schisms, or the reformation of life, always have the assistance of God’s Spirit, and therefore can

<margin>The Holy Ghost is an assistant in all lawful councils until the world’s end, and that is by Christ’s promise. John 16:13.</margin>

Thirdly, we learn that in the holy Councils especially (though otherwise and in other Tribunals of the Church it is also verified) Christ’s promise is fulfilled: *that the Holy Ghost should suggest to them and teach them all truth*, and that not in the Apostles' time only, but to the world’s end. For as long as there are either doubts to resolve, or Heretics to condemn, or truths to be opened, or evil men to be reformed, or schisms to be appeased, Councils, the Church, and her Pastors shall have this privilege of God’s assistance. For which cause Saint Gregory—in *Book 1, Epistle 24, near the end* <note>original: "li. 1 ep. 24 sub fin."</note>—reverences the four general Councils (Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus, Chalcedon) as the four books of the holy Gospel, alluding to the number. And of the fifth also, he says that he reverences it alike; and so would he have done for more, if they had been before his time. He says of them thus: *While they are concluded and made by universal consent, he destroys himself and not them, whosoever presumes either to loose whom they bind, or to bind whom they loose.*

<margin>St. Gregory’s reverence of General Councils.</margin>
<margin>The Protestants' foolish distinction between the first 4 and the later Councils.</margin>
<margin>Beza’s blasphemy against the first general Councils. Preface to the New Testament, year 1565.</margin>
<margin>What the Fathers attribute to Councils, and namely St. Augustine.</margin>
<margin>Provincial Councils.</margin>
Saint Gregory therefore reverencing all five alike, it may be wondered where the Heretics <note>The author uses "Heretics" to refer to Protestant Reformers who questioned the authority of later medieval Church councils.</note> found their foolish distinction between those first four and other later ones: attributing much to the first, and nothing to the rest. Whereas, in truth, the later can err no more than the first four, being held and approved just as they were, and having the Holy Ghost just as they had. But in those first councils also, when a man finds anything against their Heresies (as there are various things), then they say plainly that they also may err, and that the Holy Ghost is not tied to men’s voices, nor to the number of sentences. This is directly to reprove this first Council of the Apostles as well, and Christ’s promise of the Holy Ghost’s assistance to teach all truth. Indeed, so that you may know and thoroughly abhor these Heretics, hear what a principal Sect-Master <note>Likely referring to Theodore Beza, a major figure in the Reformation.</note> with his blasphemous mouth or pen utters, saying *that in the very best times, such was partly the ambition of Bishops, partly their foolishness and ignorance, that the very blind may easily perceive Satan, in truth, to have been president of their assemblies.* Good Lord, deliver the people and the world from such blasphemous tongues and books, and give men grace to attend to the holy Scriptures and Doctors. Let them see how much—not only Saint Augustine and other fathers attribute to all general Councils specially (to which they refer themselves in all doubts among themselves and in all their controversies with Heretics)—but even Saint Paul himself (so specially taught by God) and others also yielded themselves. Notorious is the saying of Saint Augustine concerning Saint Cyprian, who, being a blessed Catholic Bishop and Martyr, yet erred about the rebaptizing of such as were Christened by Heretics. *If he had lived*—says Saint Augustine in *Book 2, On Baptism, Chapter 4* <note>original: "li. 2 de bapt c. 4"</note>—*to have seen the determination of a plenary Council, which he saw not in his lifetime, he would, because of his great humility and charity, have straightway yielded, and preferred the general Council before his own judgment and his fellow Bishops in a Provincial Council only.* By this we also learn that Provincial Councils <term>Provincial Council: a meeting of bishops from a specific region or province, rather than the entire world</term> may err, though many times they do not; and being conformable to the general Councils, or confirmed and approved by them or the Apostolic See, their resolutions are as infallible as the others.

<margin>Notwithstanding the Holy Ghost’s assistance, yet human means must be used to search for the truth. Luke 1:3.</margin>
<margin>Though the Apostolic See itself has the same assistance, yet councils are also necessary for many causes.</margin>
If any here ask, what need is there for so much disputing, study, and labor in Councils to find out and determine the truth, if the Holy Ghost infallibly guides them? We answer that such is the ordinary providence of God in this case: to assist them when they do their endeavor and use all human means of industry, and not otherwise. And so (though somewhat otherwise) God assisted the Evangelists and other writers of the holy Scriptures, so that they could not err in penning the same; but yet they did and ought to use all possible human diligence to know and learn out the histories and truth of matters, as is plain in the beginning of Saint Luke’s Gospel; otherwise, the Holy Ghost would not have assisted them. Even so in this Council of the Apostles, though they had the Holy Ghost assistant, yet the text says, *when there was great disputation* <note>original: "cum magna conquisitio fieret"</note>, search, and examination of the case, then Peter spoke, etc. If again it be demanded, what need is there to wait for the Council’s determination, if the Pope’s or the Apostolic See's judgment be infallible and have the assistance of God also, as the Catholics affirm? We answer, that for the Catholic and peaceable obedient children of the Church, it is a comfort to have such various means of determination, trial, and declaration of the truth. It is also necessary for the recovery of Heretics and for the contentment of the weak, who, while not always giving in to one man’s determination, will yet either yield to the judgment of all the learned men and Bishops of all Nations, or else remain desperate and condemned before God and man forever. And as I said before, this assistance of the Holy Ghost promised to Peter’s See presupposes human means of searching out the truth, which the Pope always has used, and will, and must use in matters of great importance—by calling Councils—even as here you see Saints Peter and Paul themselves and all the Apostles, though endowed with the Holy Ghost, yet thought it notwithstanding necessary for further trial and clearing of truth and maintenance of unity, to keep a Council.

Lastly, it is to be noted that as Christ and the Holy Ghost are present by his promise to all such assemblies as gather in the obedience and unity of the Church, with full mind to obey whatsoever shall be determined—whereby the assembled, though of diverse judgments before, do most peaceably yield to truth and agree in one uniform determination of the same—so all such

31. **Rejoiced for the consolation.**] Immediately upon receiving news of the Council's determination, not only the Gentiles, but even the instigators of the previous troubles and dissension, were at rest; everyone took great comfort that the controversy was so ended. And so should all Christian men do when they see the sects of our time condemned by the same authority and the most grave judgment of the holy Council of Trent <note>A major ecumenical council of the Catholic Church (1545–1563) held to address the challenges of the Protestant Reformation.</note>. And so say all thieves against those who correct and punish them; they would say and do even more against secular tribunals, judges, justices, and juries, if they had as much license and liberty in those matters as men now have in religion.

37. **Dissension**] Such occasions of difference occur even among perfect men often, without any great offense. Indeed, this parting of ways resulted in the great increase of Christians. Therefore, it is quite ridiculous when this is used to excuse the disagreements among heretics regarding the principal points of religion—namely, the Sacrament.

## CHAP. XVI.

-> ANNOTATIONS <-
-> CHAPTER 17 <-

<margin>The people may not judge the meaning of the Scriptures.</margin>
11. *Searching the Scriptures.*) The <term>Heretics<note>In the context of this 16th-century Catholic text, "Heretics" refers to Protestant Reformers who advocated for "Sola Scriptura" (Scripture alone).</note></term> use this passage to prove that listeners must test and judge by the Scriptures whether their teachers' and preachers' doctrine is true, and so reject that which they do not find in the Scriptures—as though here the sheep were made judges of their Pastors, the people of the Priests, and men and women of all sorts were judges even of Saint Paul’s doctrine itself. This would be the most foolish disorder in the world. And they did not read the Scriptures of the Old Testament (for none of the New were yet commonly available) to dispute with the Apostle, or to try and judge his doctrine, or whether they should believe him or not; for they were bound to believe him and obey his word, whether he cited Scripture or not, and whether they could read or understand the Scriptures or not. But it was a great comfort and confirmation for 
<margin>The comfort of Christian men by hearing or reading the Scriptures.</margin>
the Jews who possessed the Scriptures to find, just as Saint Paul said, that Christ was God, crucified, risen, and ascended to heaven. Through his preaching and explanation, they understood these things for the first time, even though they had read them and heard them read every Sabbath. Likewise, it is a great comfort to a Catholic man to hear the Scriptures declared and cited most clearly for the Church's truth against Heretics, in sermons or otherwise. It does Catholics good and greatly confirms them to view diligently the passages cited by Catholic preachers. Yet they must not be judges, for all that, over their own Pastors, whom Christ commands them to hear and obey, and from whom they hear the true sense of the Scriptures.

<margin>The Protestants call devotion "superstition."</margin>
22. *Superstitious.*) Saint Paul does not call them superstitious for adoring the true and only God with much devotion or many ceremonies or in a comely, prescribed order; or for doing reverence to holy Sacraments, to Saints and their memories, Images, or Monuments; or for keeping the prescribed laws, days, and fasts of the Church; or for fulfilling vows made to God; or for blessing with the sign of the Cross; or for <term>capping<note>Removing or touching one's hat as a sign of respect.</note></term> and kneeling at the name of JESUS; or for religiously using objects sanctified in the same name, or any other Christian observation for which our new Masters condemn the Catholic people as superstitious. These critics are themselves wholly void 
<margin>The Apostle speaks of the Heathens' superstition.</margin>
of that vice in the judgment of all wise men, because they have in a manner taken away all religion and have become Epicureans and Atheists. Such people are never troubled with superstition, because it is a vice consisting of an excess of worship or religion, of which they are void. But the Apostle calls the Athenians superstitious for worshipping the Idols and gods of the Heathen, and for the fear <margin><note>original: "δαίμονι" (daimoni); referring to a spirit or deity.</note></margin> they had lest they should leave out any God that was unknown to them. For their Altar was inscribed: <note>original Latin: "Dijs Asiæ, Europæ, & Lybiæ, Deo ignoto & peregrino."</note> *To the gods of Asia, Europe, and Libya: to the unknown and foreign God.* This superstition (says Saint Augustine) is wholly taken 
<margin>The Catholic Church allows no superstition.</margin>
<margin>Augustine, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, book 1, chapter 2.</margin>
away from the Church by Christ's incarnation, by the Apostles' preaching, and by the Martyrs' holy lives and deaths. Neither does the Catholic Church allow this or any other kind of superstitious observation. Only we must take heed that we do not believe her adversaries' definition of superstition, for they would imply that all true religion is included within it.

29. *The Divinity to be like.*) Nothing can be made by man’s hand, of whatever form or sort it may be, that is like to God's essence, or to the form or shape of his Godhead or Divinity. Therefore, however the Heathens painted or engraved their Idols, they were nothing like God. This is also impertinently cited by Heretics against the Church’s images, which are not made either...

<margin>How there may be images or representations of the three persons in the Trinity, and of Angels.</margin>
<margin>Daniel 7:22.</margin>
<margin>Genesis 18:2.</margin>
<margin>Genesis 32:24.</margin>
<margin>Exodus 37:7.</margin>
<margin>Isaiah 6:2.</margin>
<margin>Images are for the people’s instruction.</margin>
<margin>Gregory, book 9, epistle 9.</margin>
...to be worshipped with divine honor, or to be any resemblance of the Divinity or any of the three persons in the Godhead, but only of Christ as he was in the form of man—who in that respect may be truly expressed, as other men are by their portraits—and of the Holy Ghost, not as he is in himself, but as he appeared in fiery tongues or in the <term>likeness of a dove<note>The Holy Spirit is traditionally depicted as a dove or as tongues of fire, based on the descriptions in the Gospels and the Book of Acts.</note></term>, or such like. And so to paint or engrave any of the three persons as they appeared visibly and physically is no more inconvenient or unlawful than it was improper for them to appear in such forms. And therefore to paint or portrait the Father also, being the first person, as he has shown himself in vision to any of the Prophets of the Old or New Testament (namely to Daniel as an old man <note>The "Ancient of Days" in Daniel 7.</note>), or the three Angels representing the three Persons to Abraham, or the one Angel that wrestling with Jacob bore our Lord’s Person—no such thing is anywhere forbidden, but is very agreeable to the people's instruction. In which manner the Angels were commonly portrayed (and namely the Cherubim over the <term>Mercy Seat<note>original: "Propitiatorie"; the gold cover of the Ark of the Covenant.</note></term>) as they are now in the Church, not in their natural form, but with physical wings (as the Seraphim appeared to Isaiah the Prophet) to express their quality and office of being God’s Angels, that is, *Messengers*: and God the Father with the world in his hand, to signify his creation and government of the same, and such like. Of which the people, being well instructed, may take much good, and no harm at all, being now through their faith in Christ far from all <term>foolish imagination<note>original: "fond imagination"; in this period "fond" meant foolish or trivial.</note></term> of the false gods of the Pagans. And therefore Saint Gregory says of the Church’s Images, *“What scripture or writing does for the readers, the same does the picture for the simple who look upon it, for in it even the ignorant see what they ought to follow; in it they do read, who know no letters.”* Where he calls it a matter of antiquity and very convenient that in holy places Images were painted for the people's instruction, provided they be taught that they may not be adored with divine honor; and in the same place he sharply rebukes Serenus the Bishop of Marseille, who out of indiscreet zeal would take away Images rather than teach the people how to use them.

<margin>Saint Dionysius the Areopagite is entirely on the side of the Catholics.</margin>
34. *Dionysius the Areopagite.*) This is that famous <term>Denis<note>The text conflates Dionysius the Areopagite from Acts 17 with Saint Denis, the 3rd-century martyr and patron saint of France—a common belief in the 16th century.</note></term> that first converted France, and wrote those notable and divine works *On the Ecclesiastical and Celestial Hierarchy* <note>original: "de Ecclesiastica & caelesti hierarchia"</note>, *On Divine Names* <note>original: "de diuinis nominibus"</note>, and others, in which he confirms and proves plainly almost all things that the Church now uses in the administration of the holy Sacraments, and affirms that he learned them from the Apostles, giving also testimony for the Catholic faith in most things now contested, so plainly, that our <term>Adversaries<note>Refers to Protestant Reformers who questioned the authenticity of the Dionysian corpus.</note></term> have no choice but to deny this Denis to have been the author of them, pretending that they are by another of a later age. This is an old trick of Heretics, but most typical of these above all others, who, seeing all antiquity against them, are forced to be more bold or rather impudent than others on that point.

### CHAPTER 19.

*How Paul established the Church at Ephesus, first with twelve men who had been baptized only with John's baptism; then preaching for three months in the Synagogue of the Jews until, because of their stubbornness and blasphemy, he left them. He then held discussions in a certain school for two years, resulting in a marvelous increase of the Church, especially through his great miracles, such as healing diseases with the touch of his clothes and driving out devils, who nevertheless mocked the Jewish exorcists. How the Christians there confessed their deeds and burned their unlawful books; and how he foretold that after being in Jerusalem, he must see Rome. Also, the great riot raised against him at Ephesus by those who earned their living making shrines for the idolatrous Temple of Diana <note>The Greek goddess Artemis, known to the Romans as Diana.</note>.*
