## ANNOTATIONS
### CHAPTER 19.

<margin>Touching of Relics, and miracles performed by the same. Acts 5:15.</margin>
12. **Napkins.**] The napkins that had touched St. Paul’s body worked miracles, and it was no superstition to attribute that virtue to them which God gave to them in deed; nor was seeking to touch them for health any dishonor to God. Rather, it greatly proved Christ’s religion to be true, and him to be the only God, whose servants, staffs, books, or anything that belonged to them, performed such wonders. St. Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD) was an influential Church Father and Archbishop of Constantinople.</note> (*volume 5, Against the Gentiles, that Christ is God, in the Life of Babylas* <note>original Latin: *to. 5. cont. Gentiles, quod Christus sit Deus, in vit. Babylæ*</note>) shows this in a whole book for that purpose against the Pagans, proving by this and by the similar virtue of other Saints and their Relics that Christ their Lord and Master is God. For it is all the same concerning the bodies of Saints, relics, garments, staffs, books, or anything that belonged to them—all of which may and have done, and yet do (when it is necessary for our edification), similar wonders to God’s great honor: not only in their lifetime, but much more after their death. For St. Paul’s napkins had as great force when he was dead as when he lived—and even more so, as his grace and dignity with God is greater than before. St. Chrysostom, in the place cited, proves this at length by the shrine of St. Babylas the Martyr <note>Babylas was a 3rd-century Bishop of Antioch who died in prison; his relics were famous for silencing a nearby oracle of Apollo.</note>; and to think the contrary is the Heresy of Vigilantius <note>Vigilantius was a 4th-century priest who opposed the veneration of relics and was famously refuted by St. Jerome.</note>, condemned so long ago as St. Jerome’s time and abundantly refuted by him.

<margin>The name, presence, or Relics of Saints and holy men confound the Devil. In the Life of Hilarion. Chrysostom, in the place cited.</margin>
16. **Paul I know.**] Both the said napkins taken from St. Paul’s body, and his name also, were dreadful and able to expel devils. By this we learn that not only Christ’s name, which is the principal one, but his servants' names also, when invoked over the possessed, have power over devils. This is a marvelous honor to Saints and in no way diminishes the glory of Christ; rather, it exceedingly increases his fame that not only he himself, but his servants also, are able to do such things and to be stronger than any Devil in Hell. So we read in St. Jerome <note>original Latin: *S. Hierom*</note> that many invoked the name of St. Hilarion <note>An early Christian anchorite and miracle-worker in Palestine.</note> over the possessed, and the Devils immediately departed. So did the Devil know St. Babylas and other Saints, even after they were dead, when they could not speak because of the presence of their Relics, and when they were tormented and expelled by them; of this all antiquity is full of testimonies. But our Heretics, Luther and Calvin and their scholars, attempting to cast out Devils, succeeded much like these "good fellows" <note>A sarcastic reference to the sons of Sceva mentioned in the biblical text, who were beaten by the demon they tried to exorcise.</note> did.

<margin>Superstitious, heretical, and hurtful books must be put away.</margin>
19. **Curious things.**] Curious and unlawful sciences, such as Witchcraft, Necromancy, and other means of divination by soothsaying, horoscope-casting <note>original: "figure-casting"</note>, interpretation of dreams, or any way not allowed by God and his Church, must be much more abhorred by long-time Christians, seeing that these newly converted people were so zealous and diligent to leave them. And by this example, all who are newly reconciled to the Church are taught that the first thing they should do is to burn their heretical and wicked <note>original: "naughtie"</note> books.

<margin>Decrees and penal laws against heretical books.</margin>
19. **Books.**] A Christian man is bound to burn or deface all wicked books of whatever sort, especially Heretical books. Even though they may not always infect the person who keeps them, they remain available and may be harmful and destructive to others who might have them and read them after his death or otherwise. Therefore, the Church has taken order for condemning all such books and against the reading of them where danger may follow. The Christian Emperors—Constantine the Great, Valentinian, Theodosius, Marcian, and Justinian—made penal laws for the burning or defacing of them. (*Sozomen, book 1, chapter 20; book 2, chapter 31; Council of Chalcedon, act 3, at the end, chapter "Ample" and at the end of the whole Council, chapter "Imperator"; Second Council of Constantinople, session 5, chapter "Debitam" and Act 1, chapter 1 and chapter "Rem."*) See *Eusebius, book 3 on the life of Constantine, chapters 61, 62, 63, 64.* The danger of reading them is manifest, as signified by *Eusebius, book 7, chapter 6; St. Augustine, book 3 on baptism, chapter 14; St. Gregory, book 5, epistle 64.*

### ANNOTATIONS
### CHAPTER 20.

<margin>The Christian Pentecost.</margin>
16. *Pentecost.*] Though the Apostles might desire to come to the Jewish festivities because
of the general gathering of people to the same—the better to work for their salvation and to spread
the Gospel of Christ—yet it is likely that they now solemnly kept the Christian Pentecost or <term>Whitsuntide</term> <note>An English name for Pentecost, referring to the white garments worn by those newly baptized.</note>, in memory of the Holy Ghost; and that *St. Paul* went to that feast of the Christians rather
than the other of the Jews. And <term>Venerable Bede</term> <note>An 8th-century English monk and scholar.</note> says here, *The Apostle makes haste to keep the fiftieth
day, that is, of remission and of the Holy Ghost.* <note>original: "Apostolus festinat quinquagesimam celebrare, id est, remissionis et Spiritus Sancti."</note> For, that the Christians already kept the eighth day, that
is, the Sunday or our Lord’s day, and had already altered the ordinary <term>Sabbath</term> <note>The Jewish seventh day of rest.</note> into the same, is
<margin>It is Sunday.</margin>
plain by the Scriptures (*1 Corinthians 16:2, Revelation 1:10*) and by antiquity. *Justin Martyr, Apology 2 to Antoninus Pius, at the end.* <note>original: "Iustin. Mart. Apolog. 2 ad Anton. Pium in fine."</note> And it is just as likely that they changed the Jewish <term>Pascha</term> <note>Passover or Easter.</note> and Pentecost as they did that, especially
<margin>Augustine, Letter 118, chapter 1.</margin>
when it is evident that these festivities are kept by <term>Apostolic tradition</term> <note>Practices passed down from the Apostles not explicitly detailed in scripture.</note>, and approved by the use
of all ancient Churches and Councils.

<margin>Ravenous wolves are the heretics of all ages.</margin>
29. *Ravenous wolves.*] The governors of the Church are forewarned of the great danger that
should fall to the people by "wolves," that is to say, by heretics, whose cruelty toward the 
Catholics is noted by this term. They are known by their forsaking of the unity of the Church where-
of they were members before, by going out and drawing many disciples after them, and by their perverse
doctrine. Such wolves came afterward indeed in various ages: *Arius, Macedonius, Nestorius, Eu-
tyches, Luther, Calvin*—great bloodsucking wolves and wasters of the flock of Christ.

<margin>Christ's sayings not written in the Gospel.</margin>
35. *More blessed to give.*] Among many other infinite good things and speeches which Christ
spoke and are not written in the Gospels, this sentence is one: which *St. Paul* heard from some of the
Apostles who were daily in conversation with Him, or else learned from Christ himself, or from the Holy Ghost. And
it signifies that whereas the world commonly counts him happy who receives any benefit—
as alms, either temporal or spiritual—yet in deed he that gives or bestows is more happy.
<margin>Great almsgivers are blessed.</margin>
If the world considered this well, men would give alms faster than they do, if only
for their own benefit.

## ANNOTATIONS
### CHAPTER 21.

<margin>Virgins.</margin>
9. *Virgins.*] Saint Luke specifically notes that his daughters were virgins, meaning (without doubt) that they were of the state, profession, or purpose of perpetual virginity, and not simply that they were young unmarried women. It is also suggested that they were endowed with the gift of prophecy for that reason, as Saint Jerome says in his first book *Against Jovinianus*, chapter 24. See also Oecumenius, chapter 29 on this passage.

<margin>Avoiding scandal in things not unlawful.</margin>
24. *Keeping the Law.*] All the rituals and observations of the Jewish Law were now, in themselves, dead and unprofitable. Yet, until the Gospel was spread further, they were not damnable to those who kept them, nor offensive to God; rather, they could be observed even by Christian Jews. For fear of scandalizing the weak members of that nation—those newly converted or inclined toward the faith—the Apostles, by God’s guidance, thought it good to observe them as the occasion required.

---

<header>CHAPTER 24. OF THE APOSTLES.</header>

<margin>*See Annotations 10. verses 11, 51.*</margin> [The Jews] had both crucified our Lord, and which had now also lost their God and Christ, Temple and Priesthood; but though in false and spoiled Priests, yet considering the very bare shadow of the name of Priests, he said, *I knew not brethren that he was high Priest.* By which words of the Apostle, either it may be thought he knew not indeed that he was in that function, because he had not been of long time in those parts: or else that he so said in respect of the abrogation <note>The formal abolishing of a law or office.</note> of the high Priesthood of the Jews, whereby he knew this man not to be truly any Priest, as also because at this time they came not orderly to it by succession of Aaron and Law of Moses, but by the Roman Emperor’s favor, * as is said before, though (as it is lawful in such a case) the less to irritate them, he frames his speech so as they might not take occasion of further accusation against him.

<margin>2 Maccabees book 2, chapter 6, 12, 43. <br/> The Sadducees (as it seems) denied prayer for the dead.</margin> 8. *The Sadducees.*] This was the worst Heresy among the Jews, denying that there be any Angels, or spirits, the Resurrection also of the bodies: and consequently (as it may very well be gathered by the book of the Maccabees) they denied prayer for the dead; for to offer or pray for the dead, and to think rightly and religiously of the Resurrection, are made there sequels <note>Logical consequences.</note> one of another. Of this sect of Sadducees was (as Eusebius writes in <note>original: "li. 2 c. 22. Ec. hist.", referring to the *Ecclesiastical History*.</note> Book 2, Chapter 22) this Ananias the High Priest, that caused Paul to be smitten; for their Priesthood had now no more the protection of God to preserve it in truth and right judgment, the Christian Priesthood being then established.

<margin>Unlawful oaths and vows must not be kept. <br/> Matthew 14:9.</margin> 12. *Vowed themselves.*] Such vows, oaths, or execrations <note>Curses or solemn protests.</note> as this, bind no man before God; indeed, they must in no wise be observed. It is a great offense either to vow voluntarily, or to take any such thing upon a man, for fear or by commandment. For example, if thou have rashly by promise, vow, or oath, appointed to be revenged upon any man, thou bindest not thy self thereby, neither must thou keep thy promise. If thou be put to an oath to accuse Catholics for serving God as they ought to do, or to utter any innocent man to God's enemies and his, thou oughtest first to refuse such unlawful oaths: but if thou have not constancy and courage so to do, yet know thou that such oaths bind not at all in conscience and Law of God, but may and must be broken under pain of damnation. For to make or take such vows or oaths, is one sin, and to keep them, is another far greater, as when Herod, to keep his oath, killed John Baptist. And such vows and oaths to God as these, are unlawful and must be broken: and not the vows of Chastity and Religion, as our new Ministers <note>A reference to Protestant clergy during the Reformation.</note> teach by their words and works.

### CHAPTER 25.

*After two years of imprisonment, the Jews continue their lawsuit against Paul, petitioning the new Governor <note>original: "President," the Roman official in charge of a province</note> Festus, first at Jerusalem and then at Caesarea. There, because of the Jews' biased influence, Paul is forced to appeal to the Emperor. In the meantime, he is brought before King Agrippa and his Queen Bernice by Festus, who gives a favorable report of him despite the outcries of the Jews.*

# THE ACTS CHAPTER 28.
<meta>catchword: receiving</meta>

<margin>God’s providence for the <term>See<note>The "See" refers to the seat of authority and jurisdiction of a bishop; here it specifically refers to Rome as the center of the Catholic Church.</note></term> of Rome.</margin>
23. *An Angel.*] St. Paul had many visions, specifically to assure him that he should go to Rome and stand before Caesar. Our Lord himself appeared to him previously (23:11), and here an Angel appeared for that purpose. By this we plainly see the special providence of God toward that See, where his two principal Apostles <note>St. Peter and St. Paul.</note> were designated to preach, plant the faith, live, die, be buried, and be honored until the world’s end.

<margin>God’s predestination and appointment do not take away man’s free will and efforts.</margin>
31. *Unless these stay*] When God reveals anything to us, or assures us of any event to come, he does not thereby discharge us of our required efforts and labors for achieving the same. He does not ordinarily execute his designs toward men except through their own free will and actions. St. Paul did not say here, "Let us do what we like; whether we work or sit still, whether the sailors go out or stay inside, we are all sure to be saved, for so God has revealed to me, and he cannot lie, nor can it happen otherwise." But on the contrary he says, *If these sailors leave the ship, you cannot be saved.* So say all true Catholic preachers to Christian people: Whatever providence, <term>predestination<note>The doctrine that God has foreordained all things, especially the salvation of souls.</note></term>, or foresight God may have regarding your salvation, you are not thereby constrained in any way; you still have free will and cannot be saved (even if you are predestined) unless you keep God's commandments, repent of your sins, believe, and live and die well. And if it were revealed to any man that he was one of God's elect, and that he should finally die in grace and be saved, yet he would be bound to work out his salvation with fear and trembling, as <margin>1 Corinthians 9. Philippians 2.</margin> St. Paul both did and taught, lest he become a <term>reprobate<note>Someone who is rejected by God and excluded from salvation.</note></term>. This is no different than the Apostle here and his companions; though their lives were promised to them by God, they were still bound to labor and use all possible diligence so that they might not be drowned.

## A N N O T A T I O N S
### CHAPTER 28

<margin>Malta has Saint Paul's blessing and grace until this day.</margin>
<margin>God’s miraculous power in certain countries and creatures, by his Saints.</margin>
<margin>Tommaso Fazello, *Concerning Sicilian Affairs*, Decade 1, Book 1, Chapter 1.</margin>
5. *Shaking of the beast.*] The promise of Christ (*Mark 16*) that venomous serpents should not hurt them that believe in him, is fulfilled not in all believers, but in such as had the gift of miracles, as Saint Paul had. Whom here a viper—by nature so venomous that the people thought he should have died immediately—did not annoy at all: he extinguishing by the power of Christ all the poison of the beast. Yea and (as the Christian people there until this day believe) by Saint Paul's prayers the Island was delivered for ever from all such venomous serpents, in so much that children there play with scorpions ever since that time, and Pilgrims daily carry with them pieces of stones out of the place where Saint Paul stayed, by which they affirm that they heal them which in other countries adjoining are bitten of scorpions; the medicine therefore being called, *Saint Paul’s grace*. The Heretics <note>In this context, "Heretics" refers to Protestant reformers who were often skeptical of post-biblical miracles and the veneration of relics.</note> that know not the power of God, nor the miraculous virtues given to his Saints, marvel and blaspheme, when they hear such things as be proper to certain countries, attributed sometimes to God's miracles done by his Saints: as though that were not possible, or were not as much to God's honor, and more, than things proceeding only of natural causes. Such profane men would not have attributed the wholesomeness of the waters of Jericho to Elisha's virtue and miracles, amending them by casting salt into them, if the Scripture had not expressly testified the same. <margin>4 Kings 2 <note>In modern Bibles, this is 2 Kings 2.</note></margin> It is the part of all faithful men to refer such things to God, when any just occasion is given thereunto, rather than to nature: though the incredulous do always contrary, for fear of superstition and dishonoring God. As though this escape of drowning, might better and more to God’s glory, be referred to chance and the mariners’ industry, than to Saint Paul's prayers and extraordinary working.

<margin>Saint Paul's chains honored.</margin>
20. *Chain.*] I would wish now (says Saint Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, a 4th-century Church Father known for his eloquent preaching.</note>) to be for a time in the place where these chains remain, and to see the fetters which Devils fear, and Angels reverence. *Homily 5 to the people of Antioch.* See also Saint Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great (6th century).</note> *Book 3, Epistle 30*, of the miracles done by Saint Paul's chains, and that he sends to the Empress Constantia some dust thereof filed off, for a great Relic and holy gift.

# CHAPTER 28: OF THE APOSTLES.

<margin>
Isaiah 6:9; Matthew 13; Luke 8
The name "Nazarenes": just as the term "sect" is properly applied to all heresies, the Christian religion was falsely called by this name at first.
</margin>

22. *Concerning this sect.*] <note>Referring to Acts 28:22, where the local Jewish leaders in Rome ask Paul about the "sect" of Christianity.</note> Heretics of all kinds take great comfort whenever they find the Christian faith called a "sect" or a "heresy" by Jews or unbelievers, here or elsewhere. They also take comfort when, out of contempt for Christ the Master, it is called the "Sect of the Nazarenes." They act as if the Church of God might be just as mistaken in labeling their own doctrines as "heresy" as the Jews and Pagans were in mistakenly condemning the Christian religion as a heresy. Or, they act as if the Protestant doctrine were as well-proven and tested to be "no heresy"—by the Prophets, other Scriptures, miracles, and the consensus of all nations and ages—as the blessed doctrine of Christ is. The Christian religion is proven to be the only true doctrine of salvation, and not a heresy. And anyone who can trace the Christian faith from Adam to this day, through all the Fathers, Patriarchs, Prophets, Priests, Apostles, and Bishops—by the descent and succession of all laws and states of true worshippers and believers (which is the only or special way to prove the Christian faith is not a heresy)—will, by that same process, prove all at once that the Protestant doctrine is a heresy and a false sect. Therefore, although the Jews and wicked men in all places contradicted the Christian religion, calling it a "heresy" or a "sect" as if it had begun with some specific leader other than God himself, they were deceived. Nevertheless, the Church of God is acting rightly and most justly when it calls the Protestant doctrine "heresy" in the most negative sense possible, and as the worst kind of heresy that has ever existed.

# THE SUMMARY OF THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES, CONTAINING ESPECIALLY THE DEEDS OF THE TWO PRINCIPAL

<margin>
See the annotations for Romans 16:15 and Galatians 1.
</margin>

*Apostles, Saints Peter and Paul, in the order of time and the years of the Emperors, and from Christ's Birth and Ascension, as they were done: so far as can be gathered by holy Scriptures or Ecclesiastical writers. Although it is not possible to establish the precise and certain time or year of every event—because neither Saint Luke nor others record every moment of every action of the said Apostles in a particular and orderly way—we nevertheless follow the most probable and clear plan found in holy Scripture and ancient writers. By this, the studious reader may easily reveal the error of the Protestants, who claim there was no time in which Peter could have possibly come to Rome, served as Bishop, and died there. Various things in Saint Paul’s acts are no less difficult to reconcile with Saint Luke’s narrative than anything regarding the history of Saint Peter—namely, his three years of preaching in Arabia. All of these things must necessarily be true, whether we hit upon the exact time or not, and regardless of how authors differ regarding the same.*

# OF THE OTHER APOSTLES.

<margin>
Gilbert Génébrard <note>A 16th-century French Benedictine scholar.</note>, citing various authors.
</margin>
<margin>
Rufinus, in *Explanation of the Apostles' Creed*; Ambrose, *Sermon 38*; Jerome, *Epistle 61, chapter 9, Against the Errors of John of Jerusalem*.
</margin>
THE Acts of the rest of the twelve Apostles are not recorded extensively in this book <note>The Book of Acts.</note>: but as *other Church writers testify*, they preached specifically in these nations, as follows. *Andrew in Achaia <note>A province in Roman Greece.</note>, John in Asia. Philip in Phrygia <note>An ancient region in modern-day Turkey.</note>, James in Judea, Bartholomew in Scythia <note>A vast region in Eurasia covering parts of modern Ukraine and Russia.</note>, Thomas in India, Matthew in Ethiopia, Simon in Persia, Thaddaeus in Mesopotamia, the other James in Spain, Matthias in Palestine.* Thus, they distributed themselves throughout the world to gather one Catholic <note>Meaning "universal."</note> Church from all nations, just as Christ gave them the commission in *Matthew 28:19*: and as it was prophesied of them before in *Psalm 18: Their sound has gone out into every country, and their words into the ends of the whole world.* But before they departed from one another (the exact time of which is not known for certain), all Twelve assembled together and, being full of the Holy Spirit, each contributed his own sentence. They agreed upon twelve principal articles of the Christian faith and established them as a rule for all believers: which is therefore called, and is, THE APOSTLES' CREED: Not written on paper, like the Scriptures, but delivered from the Apostles by tradition. *Rufinus and Jerome, in the places cited above.* This Creed, as in ancient times (Jerome, *Against the Luciferians*), so today all people solemnly profess at their Baptism, either by themselves or through others <note>Referring to godparents answering for infants.</note>: and all those of age and capacity are bound to know and believe every article of the same. These are the articles that follow.

# THE ARGUMENT OF THE
## EPISTLES IN GENERAL.

<image-desc>A large decorative drop cap 'A' set within a square frame, embellished with intricate floral and scrollwork designs.</image-desc>
After the Gospels, which are a story of Christ himself, and after the Acts of the Apostles, which is a story of Christ's Church: now follow the Epistles of the Apostles, which they wrote regarding such matters as they had occasion to write about at that time. For being the founders and the Doctors <note>In this context, "Doctors" refers to the great authoritative teachers of the early Church.</note> of the Church, they did in their time as the Doctors that succeeded them did after them: who from the beginning until this day have written Epistles and Books against heresies, whenever they arose, and regarding all other ecclesiastical matters, as the occasion required. Of this practice, the Apostles first gave the example: just as Saint Luke, in the Acts of the Apostles, led the way for all the writers of Ecclesiastical History after him. For although there is no comparison between them in terms of authority—inasmuch as these are **Canonical Scripture**, while the writings of their successors are not—the occasions and subject matters (as I have said) are similar.

<margin>Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 2, chapter 22.</margin>
Most of these Epistles are Saint Paul’s Epistles; the rest are called ★ *Catholic Epistles* <note>original: "Catholicæ Epistolæ"</note>. For Saint Paul did not write any Epistle to everyone (although every one of them is intended for the whole Church), but rather some to particular Churches of the Gentiles, such as to the Romans, the Corinthians, the Galatians, the Ephesians, the Philippians, the Colossians, and the Thessalonians; some to particular persons, such as to Timothy and Titus (who were Bishops among the Gentiles, namely, of Ephesus and of Crete) and to Philemon; and then one to the Hebrews, who were the Jews of Jerusalem and Judea <note>original: "Iurie"</note>. But the Epistles of the other Apostles—that is, of Saint James, Saint Peter, Saint John, and Saint Jude—are not addressed to any one specific Church or person (except Saint John’s two later short Epistles, which nonetheless might not be separated from his first, because they were all by the same Author), and therefore they are termed *Catholic*, that is, *universal*. For so writes Saint James: *To the twelve tribes that are in dispersion, greeting.* And Saint Peter in his first Epistle, thus: *To the elect strangers of the dispersion of Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia.* In his second, thus: *To them that have obtained equal faith with us.* Likewise Saint Jude: *To them that are in God the Father beloved, and in Jesus Christ preserved, and called.* Saint John’s first Epistle is without a title.

Now, regarding the reasons for their writing, by which we shall perceive the matters or arguments that they handle: it must be remembered (as the story of that time in the Acts of the Apostles declares at length) that when the Church began, it was planted by the Apostles not only among the Jews, but also among the Gentiles—indeed, especially among the Gentiles. This thing offended the Jews in many ways. For they could not bear to see even their own country receive Him as **CHRIST** whom they had rejected and crucified; much less could they bear to see Him preached to the Gentiles as well. This offended even those Jews who—

<keywords>Epistles, Catholic Epistles, Saint Paul, Saint Luke, Acts of the Apostles, Jews, Gentiles, Church history, Eusebius, Canonical Scripture, Universal Church</keywords>

--- Page 410 ---
<meta>This page continues the general introduction to the Epistles, specifically focusing on the historical context of Saint Paul’s writings. It addresses the tension between Jewish converts, Gentile converts, and those who refused to accept Christ, establishing the theological foundation for the necessity of grace over the Old Law.</meta>

...believed him to be Christ. However, those among them who were Catholics—and therefore not stubborn—were satisfied when they understood from the Apostles that it was God's pleasure, as we read in **Acts 11**. But others among them became heretics and preached to the Christian Gentiles that it was necessary for them to also adopt the Jewish religion. We read of such people in **Acts 15**: *“Unless you are circumcised, you cannot be saved.”*

And just as these people preached against the truth, the non-Christian Jews not only persecuted the Christians themselves but also stirred up the idol-worshipping Gentiles everywhere to persecute them. By such stubbornness, they provoked God to reject their nation. Yet, they thought this was impossible because they were the descendants of Abraham, were circumcised, and had received the Law through Moses. Because of such worldly reasons, they trusted in themselves, as if God and Christ were inseparably bound to them. They also attributed so much to their own works (which they thought they performed by themselves, aided only by their knowledge of the Law) that they would not acknowledge the death of Christ as necessary for their salvation. Instead, they looked for a Messiah who would be like the other princes of this world and make them great men in a temporal, earthly sense.

Because of this, Saint Paul wrote his Epistles to show both the calling of the Gentiles and the rejection of the Jews. Furthermore, he wrote to warn the Christian Gentiles not to accept circumcision or the other ceremonies of Moses's law under any circumstances. He also warned the Jews not to put their trust in those same things, but rather to understand that now that Christ has come, those old ways must end. 

Again, he wrote to show the necessity of Christ’s coming and of His death: that without it, neither the Gentiles nor the Jews could be saved by any works they could do on their own, even if they were helped by the Law telling them what was good and what was bad. This is because all were sinners, and therefore also powerless or weak. The Law could not take away sin and weakness, nor give the strength to fulfill the very things it taught. Only God was able to do this, and He would only do it for Christ's sake. 

Therefore, it is necessary for everyone to believe in Christ and to be made His members by being incorporated into His Body, which is His Catholic Church. By doing so (even if they had never yet done a good work, but only evil), they shall have remission of their sins and a new strength as well. This strength makes them able to fulfill the commandments of God's Law. Indeed, their works after this shall be so pleasing in God's sight that He will give them everlasting life because of them. This is the necessity, and this is also the fruit of the Christian religion. Therefore, he encourages everyone, both Gentiles and Jews, to receive it humbly and to persevere in it constantly until the end, against all the deception of heresy and the terror of persecution. He exhorts them to walk all their lives in good works, as God has now made them able to do.

<margin>The doctrine of the Catholic Church concerning good works.</margin>
The Catholic Church teaches this exact same doctrine to this day: namely, that no works of the unbelieving or the unbaptized—whether they be Jews or Gentiles—can save them. Nor can the works of any heretic or schismatic, even if he is baptized, because he is not a member of Christ. Furthermore, no work of anyone who is not a "living" member <note>A "living member" refers to someone who is not only a member of the Church but is also in a "state of grace" rather than "mortal sin."</note> of Christ is meritorious or able to save him, even if he is baptized and remains within the Church, because he is in mortal sin.

<margin>St. Paul's doctrine concerning faith and good works.</margin>
This is the very same doctrine held by Saint Paul: he denies that the works of those who do not have the Spirit of Christ have any power to justify or to save. He does not require a man to have had knowledge of the Law or to have kept it in the past as a condition for being saved by Christ. However, once a person is "Christened" (baptized), Paul requires as a necessity that he keep God's commandments by avoiding all sin and doing good works. To the good works of such a man, Paul attributes as much virtue as any...

<summary>This page explains Saint Paul’s theological mission to reconcile Jewish and Gentile converts, emphasizing that salvation and the ability to perform "good works" come only through Christ's grace and membership in the Church. It clarifies that while the Old Law is obsolete, the New Covenant requires active moral obedience and perseverance.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous page regarding the necessity of both faith and good works, countering the claim that the Apostles taught "faith alone" as sufficient for salvation. It transitions from general biblical interpretation to the specific historical context of the Epistle to the Romans.</meta>

...any Catholic of this time.

<margin>2 Peter 3</margin>
Nevertheless, there were certain people at that time (as also all the heretics of this our time) whom Saint Peter terms unlearned and unstable, who, reading Saint Paul's Epistles, misconstrued his meaning, as though he required good works no more after Baptism than before Baptism; instead, they held that only Faith did justify and save a man. Thereupon the other Apostles wrote their Epistles, as Saint Augustine notes in these words: <margin>Augustine, *On Faith and Works*, chapter 14. And preface to Psalm 31.</margin> "Therefore, because this opinion (<note>original: *Ad salutem obtinendam sufficere solam fidem*</note> that faith alone is sufficient to obtain salvation) had then arisen, the other Apostolic Epistles—those of Peter, John, James, and Jude—specifically direct their intention against it: to vehemently avouch <note>original: *fidem sine operibus nihil prodesse*</note> that faith without works profits nothing." Just as Paul himself did not define it to be <note>original: *quamlibet fidem, quæ in Deum creditur*</note> any kind of faith whatever, by which we believe in God, but that wholesome and express Evangelical faith, whose works proceed from love; and <margin>Galatians 5</margin> "the faith," says he, "that works by love." Whereupon that faith, which some think to be sufficient for salvation, he so affirms to profit nothing, that he says: <margin>1 Corinthians 13</margin> *If I should have all faith so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing.*

<margin>1 Timothy 3</margin>
He therefore that will not err in this point, nor in any other, while reading either Saint Paul’s Epistles or the rest of the Holy Scriptures, must stick fast to the doctrine of the Catholic Church, which Church Saint Paul terms the <term>pillar and ground of the truth</term><note>A famous scriptural metaphor (1 Timothy 3:15) used by Catholic theologians to argue that the Church is the divinely protected guardian of correct biblical interpretation.</note>: assuring himself that if anything found there seems contrary to this, he fails to grasp the right sense. He should always bear in mind the <margin>2 Peter 3</margin> admonition of Saint Peter, saying: *As also our most dear brother Paul, according to the wisdom given to him, has written to you; as also in all his Epistles, speaking in them of these things, in which are certain things hard to understand, which the unlearned and unstable distort <note>The original text uses "deprave," meaning to twist or pervert the meaning.</note>, as they do also the rest of the Scriptures, to their own perdition. You therefore, brethren, foreknowing this, take heed lest you be led astray by the error of the unwise, and fall away from your own steadfastness.*

# THE TIME WHEN THE EPISTLE
## TO THE ROMANS WAS WRITTEN,
### and the Argument thereof.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial T featuring scrolling foliage and floral patterns.</image-desc>
<margin>Galatians 2</margin>
THE history of Saint Paul, until he came to Rome, was written exactly by Saint Luke in the Acts of the Apostles. Although he does so without any mention of Paul's Epistles, yet it is certain that he wrote some of them before he arrived there—namely, the two to the Corinthians, and this one to the Romans—and (as it seems) before them all, the Epistle to the Galatians. In that letter, because he mentions the fourteenth year after his conversion, it appears that he preached for that long without any writing.

And this order may thus briefly be gathered: First, he preached to the Galatians <margin>Acts 16</margin> while passing through Phrygia and the country of Galatia. Of this he makes mention himself also in <margin>Galatians 1</margin>: "We preached the Gospel to you," and <margin>Galatians 4</margin>: "I preached the Gospel to you heretofore." After this, the false apostles came and persuaded them to receive circumcision. Whereupon he says in <margin>Galatians 1</margin>: "I marvel that you are so soon transferred from him that called you to the grace of Christ, unto another Gospel," and wishes therefore...

So then, the Epistle to the Romans was not the first that he wrote. But yet it is \* and always was set first in the New Testament, because of the primacy of that Church. For which cause also he handles in it such matters as pertained not to them alone, but to the universal Church, and specially to all the Gentiles: to wit, the very frame (as it were) of the Church of Christ. *For as though he were acting as an ambassador for the Lord himself—that is, for the cornerstone—he binds together both peoples, the Jews as well as the Gentiles, in Christ through the bond of grace.* <note>original Latin: *Tanquam enim a pro ipso Domino legatione fungens, hoc est, pro b lapide angulari, vtrumque populum tam ex Iudæis quàm ex Gentibus connectit in Christo per vinculum gratiæ.*</note> So says Saint Augustine, giving us briefly the argument of the book. In English, it means that Paul, representing Christ (the "cornerstone" that joins two walls), shows that neither the Jews nor the Gentiles had anything to brag about regarding their lives before Christ. Neither their previous pagan lives nor their adherence to Jewish law gave them a right to claim justification or salvation. Instead, they both had sins to be sorry for. They needed to humble themselves to the faith of Christ so they could receive forgiveness and the strength to do meritorious works <note>The author distinguishes between "works of the law" (done by human strength) and "meritorious works" (done through the help of God's grace after becoming a Christian).</note> afterward. In this way, because the Gentiles did humble themselves, they found mercy, even though they never knew the Law of Moses.

<margin>
The works of the Law.
</margin>
But the Jews missed out on mercy because they relied on their own works, which they performed by their own strength while simply having knowledge of the Law (which is why these are called the *works of the Law*). Because they would not humble themselves to believe in Christ crucified, they became reprobate, <note>In this context, "reprobate" means those who have been rejected or have fallen away from God’s favor.</note> except for a few "Remnant" <note>original: *Reliquiæ*</note> that God in his goodness had reserved for himself. However, in the end, when the full number of the Gentiles has entered the Church, then shall the full number of the Jews also open their eyes, acknowledge their error, and submit themselves to Christ and his Church in the same way. In the meantime, he exhorts those who have found the grace to be Christians to persevere (as was especially necessary in those times of persecution) and to lead their whole life after Baptism in good works. He also urges them to be careful of unity, bearing with one another—both Jew and Gentile—as much as they <meta>catchword: may,</meta>

## ->ANNOTATIONS<-
### ->CHAPTER I.<-

<margin>Apostolic salutation or blessing. The same used by Heretics.</margin>
<margin>Epiphanius, *Against Heresies*, 66. <note>original: "Epiph. hæ. 66."</note></margin>
7. *Grace to you and peace.*] This is a kind of blessing rather than a common greeting; it is specific to the Apostles and carries greater power than the blessings of the fathers in the Old Testament. The holy fathers of the Church seemed to refrain from using it out of their reverence for the Apostles. * The Manichees (*Augustine, Against the Fundamental Letter, chapters 5 and 6* <note>original: "Auguſt. cont. ep. funda. c. 5. 6."</note>) and other Heretics (including those of our own time) often use it because they wish to be considered Apostles.

<margin>The Roman faith highly commended. It cannot fail, nor be corrupted.</margin>
<margin>Luke 22. <note>original: "Luc. 22."</note></margin>
8. *Your faith renowned.*] Based on these words of the Apostle, and especially by our Master’s promise * made to Peter that his faith should not fail, the holy Doctors of the Church give great testimony to God’s providence in preserving the Roman faith. Saint Cyprian says: *Letter 55, number 6. <note>original: "ep. 55. nu. 6."</note> They are so bold as to carry letters from profane Schismatics <note>Those who cause a split in the Church.</note> to the chair of Peter and the principal Church where priestly unity began: not considering that the Romans are those whose faith (praised by the Apostle) cannot be reached by misbelief.* So too Saint Jerome *Apology against Ruffinus, book 3, chapter 4, volume 2. <note>original: "Apolog. adu. Ruff. li. 3 c. 4. to. 2."</note> Know you, that the Roman faith commended by the Apostle's mouth will receive no such deceits, nor can it possibly be changed, even if an Angel taught otherwise, being protected by Saint Paul’s authority.* Again, in *Letter 63 to Pammachius and Oceanum, chapter 4, volume 2. <note>original: "ep. 63 ad Pammach. & Oceanum. c. 4. to. 2."</note> Whoever you are that promotes new sects, I pray you have respect for Roman ears; spare the faith which was praised by the Apostle's voice.* And in another place: *Will you know, O Paula and Eustochium, how the Apostle has noted every province with their traits? The faith of the people of Rome is praised. Where else is there such a great crowd at the Churches and the tombs of the Martyrs? Where does "Amen" sound like thunder from heaven, or where are the temples (emptied of idols) so shaken as there?* 
<margin>The Roman stations, a token of greater faith and devotion.</margin>
<margin>Preface to book 2 of the Commentary on Galatians. <note>original: "Proœm. l. 2. Com. in ep. ad Gal."</note></margin>
This does not mean the Romans have a different faith than the rest of the Christian Churches, but that there is in them more devotion and simplicity of faith. In another place, the same holy Doctor indicates that it is the same thing to say "the Roman faith" and "the Catholic faith." *Apology 1 against Ruffinus, chapter 1.* <note>original: "Apolog. 1 adu. Ruſſ. c. 1."</note> So does Saint Cyprian *Letter 52, number 1, to Antonianus:* <note>original: "ep. 52. num. 1. ad Antonianum:"</note> and Saint Ambrose *On the death of his brother, in the middle.* <note>original: "de obitu fratris, in med."</note> 
<margin>The Catholic and Roman faith are all one.</margin>
Therefore, the word "Roman" is added to "Catholic" in many countries where Sects abound, to better distinguish true believers from Heretics—who in all ages hated and abhorred the Roman faith and Church, just as all criminals hate their judges and correctors.

<margin>How God is served in spirit.</margin>
9. *Serve in spirit.*] Various Heretics, when they hear that God is a spirit and must be served and adored in spirit, imagine that he must be honored only inwardly, without ceremonies or external works. You see this is not the case, for the Apostle served God "in spirit" by the outward act of preaching the Gospel. To serve God in spirit, then, is to serve him with faith, hope, and charity, and with all works proceeding from them; just as to serve him "carnally" is to perform external works without those internal virtues.

<margin>Prayer for conversion of souls.</margin>
9. *A memory of you.*] A great example of charity for all men, especially for Bishops and Pastors: not only to preach, but to pray continually for the conversion of people to the faith of Christ. The Apostle did this even for those he never knew, out of respect for God’s honor and a zeal for souls.

<margin>The Gospel is not only the Written word.</margin>
15. *To evangelize.*] The Gospel is not only the life of our Savior written by the four Evangelists, nor only what is written in the New Testament: it is the entire course of preaching and teaching the faith. This faith normally comes from preaching and hearing, not just from writing or reading. Therefore, Saint Paul did not think he had finished his duty by writing to the Romans; his desire was to preach to them, for that was the specific commission given to the <meta>Apostles.</meta>

# CHAPTER II. TO THE ROMANS.

<margin>Matthew 28.</margin>
<margin>How the Apostles wrote and preached.</margin>
The Apostles * were to preach to all nations. The writing of the books of the Testament is another part of God's providence, necessary for the Church in general, but not necessary for every man in particular: just as being taught and preached to is for everyone of age and understanding. And therefore Saint Peter (who was the chief of the Commission) wrote little; many of them wrote nothing at all; and Saint Paul, who wrote most, wrote but little in comparison to his preaching; nor did he write to anyone except those who were already converted to the faith by previous preaching.

<margin>(Habakkuk 2)</margin>
<margin>The Catholic or Christian faith with good works justifies; and without this faith, no works whatever justify.</margin>
17. *Lives by faith.*] In the 10th chapter to the *Hebrews*, he shows by this passage from the Prophet that the just man, though he lives here in pilgrimage <note>referring to our temporary life on earth</note> and does not presently see or enjoy the everlasting life promised to him, yet holds fast the hope of it by faith. In this place, he applies the Prophet's words further to this sense: That it is our faith, that is to say, *the Catholic belief* (says Saint Augustine in *Against the Two Epistles of the Pelagians, Book 3* <note>original: "li. 3. cont. 2 ep. Pelag."</note>), which makes a man just and distinguishes between the just and unjust, and that is by the law of faith, and not by the law of works. From this, it arises that the Jew, the Heathen Philosopher, and the Heretic, though they excelled in all works of moral virtues, could not yet be just; and a Catholic Christian man living even an ordinary honest life—either not sinning greatly or making up for his faults through penance—is just. And this difference arises by faith. Not that faith can save any man without works—for it is not a "reprobate faith" that we speak of (as the holy Doctor <note>Saint Augustine</note> says), but that *which works by charity* <note>love in action</note>, and therefore remits sins and makes one just. See Saint Augustine’s passage.

<margin>Not only faith.</margin>
18. *Is revealed.*] By all the passage following, you may see that the Gospel and Christ’s law consist not only in preaching faith (though that is the foundation and is always to be done first), but also in teaching a virtuous life and good works, and in denouncing damnation to all those who commit deadly sins and do not repent. And again, we see that not only a lack of faith is a sin, but all other acts done against God’s commandments are as well.

<margin>God is not the author of sin.</margin>
<margin>God punishes sin by permitting men to fall further and further.</margin>
26. *Has delivered them up.*] As he says here, "God delivered them up," so to the Ephesians (chapter 4, verse 19), he says of the same persons and things, "They delivered themselves up to all uncleanness." So it is not meant here that God drives, forces, or causes any man to sin—as various blasphemous Heretics <note>likely referring to Reformers' views on predestination</note> hold—but only that by His just judgment, because of their own deserving and as a due punishment for their former grievous offenses, He withholds His grace from them, and so suffers them to fall further into other sins. For example, for their crime of Idolatry, He allowed them to fall into unnatural abominations; just as now for heresy, He takes His grace and mercy from many, and so they fall headlong into all kinds of depravity. Conversely, for an evil life, He allows many to fall into heresy. And for Christ’s sake, let everyone who is entangled with the "idolatry" of this time—that is to say, with these new sects—look well into his own conscience, whether his forsaking of the true God may not have come to him as a punishment for the former or present evil life he lives.

<margin>Sins mortal and venial.</margin>
32. *Worthy of death.*] Here you see why the Church considers some sins to be deadly and calls them "mortal": namely, because all who do them are worthy of damnation. Others are "venial," that is to say, pardonable by their own nature and not worthy of damnation.

# CHAPTER II. TO THE ROMANS.

<margin>** <term>Uncircumcision<note>original: "Prepuce"</note></term> is the foreskin not circumcised, and therefore signifies the Gentiles, or the state and condition of the Gentiles: as circumcision signifies the Jews and their state.</margin>
<margin>25</margin> ...[if you be a] <term>transgressor<note>original: "prevaricator"</note></term> of the Law, your circumcision has become <term>uncircumcision<note>original: "prepuce"</note></term>. † <margin>26</margin> If then the uncircumcised keep the <term>just decrees<note>original: "justices"</note></term> of the Law: shall not his uncircumcision be reputed for circumcision? † <margin>27</margin> And shall not that which by nature is uncircumcised, fulfilling the Law, judge you, who by the letter and circumcision are a transgressor of the Law? † <margin>28</margin> For he is not a Jew who is one in outward appearance, nor is that circumcision which is in outward appearance in the flesh: † <margin>29</margin> but he is a Jew who is one in secret: and the circumcision of the heart, in the spirit, not in the letter: whose praise is not of men, but of God.

---

->A N N O T A T I O N S<-
->C H A P T E R. II.<-

<margin>Judging other men.</margin>
*1. You who judge.*) Those who by public authority, either spiritual or temporal, have the duty to punish offenders, are not forbidden to judge or condemn anyone for their offenses, even though they themselves are sometimes guilty in their own conscience of the same or greater sins. Yet it may be a matter of aggravating their sins before God when they will not repent of those offenses themselves for which they punish others. But if they are public offenders themselves, in the same way for which they judge others, they give scandal, and thereby greatly aggravate their sins. Properly here he forbids charging another, whether falsely or truly, with those crimes of which he himself is just as guilty or more so than the other, as the Jews especially did to the Gentiles, to whom he speaks here.

<margin>God's long-suffering is for our repentance.</margin>
*4. Do you despise?*) This proves that God offers his grace and mercy to many, and by long patience and sufferance expects their repentance, delaying their punishment on purpose so that they may amend, and that he is not delighted in their perdition, nor is he the cause of their sin. But on the contrary, that they harden their own hearts, and of their own free will reject his grace and despise his <term>kindness<note>original: "benignity"</note></term>.

<margin>Good works are meritorious.</margin>
<margin>*Augustine, Book on Grace and Free Will, chapter 8.*</margin>
*6. According to his works.*) Although the holy Apostle's special purpose in this Epistle is to commend to the Gentiles (who trusted so much in their moral works) the faith in Christ, yet lest any man should think or gather untruly from his words that Christian men's works were not meritorious or the cause of salvation, he expressly writes that God gives everlasting life and glory to men for and according to their good works, just as he gives damnation for the contrary works. And however much heretics <term>foolishly<note>original: "fondly"</note></term> flee from the evidence of these places, yet St. Augustine says: *Life everlasting is to be rendered for good works according to this manifest Scripture: "God shall render to every man according to his works."*

<margin>The first justification is without works; the second is by works. St. Paul speaks of the first especially, St. James of the second.</margin>
<margin>*Augustine, On the Spirit and the Letter, chapter 26.*</margin>
*13. Not the hearers.*) This same sentence, which is also agreeable to Christ’s words (*Matthew 7:21*), is the very ground of St. James's argument: that not faith alone, but good works also justify. Therefore St. Paul (however some perversely <term>interpret<note>original: "conster"</note></term> his words in other places) means the same as St. James. And here he speaks not properly of the **first justification** (when an unbeliever or evil man is made just, who had no acceptable works before to be justified by—of which kind he especially means in other places of this Epistle), but he speaks of the **second justification** or the increase of former justice, in which he who is in God's grace daily proceeds by doing all kinds of good works, which are <term>just acts<note>original: "justices"</note></term>. For doing these, he is truly just before God, and it is this kind of justification that St. James specifically treats. This is directly against the heretics of our time, who not only attribute nothing to works done in sin and infidelity, but value nothing at all of any Christian man's works toward justification and salvation, condemning them as unclean, sinful, hypocritical, and Pharisaical. This is directly against these and other Scriptures, and is plain blasphemy against Christ and his grace, by whose spirit and cooperation we perform them.

<margin>Against "imputative" justice.</margin>
*13. Shall be justified.*) Of all other Articles deceitfully handled by heretics, they use the most guile in this one regarding Justification. They especially use the <term>ambiguity<note>original: "equivocation"</note></term> of certain words, which is common to all contentious wranglers, and specifically this word: *Justify*. Because they find it sometimes signifies the acquitting of a guilty man of some crime of which he is indeed guilty, and for which he ought to be condemned (as by human judgment, either from ignorance or purpose, a criminal is often deemed or declared and pronounced innocent), they falsely make it mean that in this place and similar ones, wherever a man is said to be "justified" by God for his works or otherwise. They act as though it were said that God justifies man—that is to say, only <term>credits<note>original: "imputes"</note></term> to him the justice of Christ...

# THE EPISTLE OF ST. PAUL CHAPTER III.

<margin>True inherent <term>justice<note>In this historical context, "justice" is used to mean "righteousness"—not just fairness, but a person's actual moral standing before God.</note></term> is more for God's glory and for the praise of Christ's merits.</margin>
...even if he is not actually just; or out of favor, considers him as just when he is actually wicked, ungodly, and unjust. This is a most blasphemous doctrine against God, making him seem either ignorant of who is truly just (and thus prone to error in his judgment) or not good, by suggesting he could love and save someone whom he knows to be evil. It is a wonderfully pitiful blindness in the Church's adversaries that they should think it more to God’s glory, and more to the praise of Christ’s justice, merits, and mercy, to call and count a wicked man "just" while he continues in his sin, rather than to actually make him just by His grace and mercy. To truly justify him—or as the word signifies here, to esteem and approve as truly just—is to see him by grace keeping the law and commandments. For it is plain that those who keep or do the commandments are just and are considered such, as seen in the earlier words: *Not the hearers are just, but the doers.* Regarding this, St. Augustine <margin>On the Spirit and the Letter, chapter 26, volume 3 <note>original: "de sp. & lit. c. 26. to. 3."</note></margin> wrote these words: *When it is said, "The doers of the Law shall be justified," what else is being said than, "The just shall be justified"? For the doers of the Law are truly just.*

<margin>True justice in both Jew and Gentile comes by keeping the Law.</margin>
26. *Keep the <term>justices<note>original: "iustices"; here referring to the righteous requirements or decrees of the Law.</note></term>.*] If a Gentile—either now since the time of Christ by his grace and faith, or any other before Christ who was not of the lineage of Abraham—keeps the righteous requirements of the Law through the Spirit of God, he is no less just than if he had been outwardly circumcised. Indeed, he shall condemn those who are circumcised but do not keep the Law. Without keeping the Law, the outward <term>Sacrament<note>Here referring to circumcision as a sacred sign or rite.</note></term> cannot help a person; rather, it will lead to their condemnation. This is because, despite having the Law and the specific signs of God, they did not keep the Law or inwardly practice in their heart what the outward sign represented. All of this is meant to suggest that true justice does not consist in faith alone, or knowledge of the Law, or in simply having the name of "Jew" or "Christian," but in doing good works and keeping the Law through God's grace.

<margin>The letter and the spirit. The carnal and spiritual Jew.</margin>
29. *In spirit, not letter.*] The outward ceremonies, Sacraments, threats, and commandments of God in the Law are called the *letter*. The inward working of God in a person's heart—endowing them with faith, hope, charity, and with the love, desire, will, and ability to keep His commandments by the grace and merits of Christ—is called the *spirit*. In this sense, the "carnal Jew" was a Jew according to the letter and was circumcised according to the letter. But the true believing Gentile, who observes in his heart and in God’s sight what was meant by that physical sign, is a Jew according to the spirit and is justified by God. Regarding the spirit and the letter, St. Augustine <margin>On the Spirit and the Letter, volume 3 <note>original: "de sp. & lit. to. 3."</note></margin> wrote a famous work, which is very necessary for understanding this Epistle.

<page-num>390</page-num>
<header>THE EPISTLE OF SAINT PAUL CHAPTER III.</header>

<margin>The meaning of the passages that sound as if God caused sin.</margin>
...had taught that the Jews' and Gentiles' ill life and incredulity had been directly the cause of God’s more mercy, and that therefore sin comes from God for the advancement of his glory, and consequently that men might or should do ill, that good might ensue thereof. Which blasphemous constructions they took of these and the like words: <margin>Romans 5:20. Romans 3:4.</margin> *where sin abounded, there did grace more abound.* and, *the Law entered in, that sin might abound.* and out of the Psalm 50. *That thou mayest be justified in thy words, and overcome when thou art judged.* As though he meant that men do sin, to the end that God may be justified. And at all these and the like places of the Apostle—though forewarned by Saint Peter, and by the Apostle’s own defense and Protestation, that he never meant such horrible things—yet the wicked also of this time do stumble and fall. But the true meaning is in all such places, that God can and does when it pleases him, convert those sins which man commits against him and his commandments, to his glory: though the sins themselves stand not with his will, intention, nor honor, but be directly against the same, and therefore may not be committed that any good may fall. For, whatever good accidentally falls, it proceeds not of the sin, but of God’s mercy that can pardon, and of his omnipotence that can turn evil to good. And therefore against those carnal interpretations, Saint Paul very carefully and diligently gives reason also in this place (verse 6), that it is impossible: because God could not justly punish any man, nor sit in judgment at the latter day for sin without plain injury, if either he himself would have sin committed, or man might do it to his glory. Therefore let all sincere readers of the Scriptures, and especially of Saint Paul’s writings, hold this for a certainty, as the Apostle’s own defense (whatever he seems to say hereafter sounding in their sense, that sin comes from God, or may therefore be committed that he may work good thereof) that the Apostle himself condemns that sense as slanderous and blasphemous.

<margin>How it is said, none are just.</margin>
10. *Not any just*] These general speeches, that both Jew and Gentile be in sin, and none at all just, are not so to be taken that none of either sort were ever good: the Scriptures expressly saying <margin>Job 1. * Luke 1.</margin> that Job, Zachary, Elizabeth, and such like, were just before God, and it were blasphemy to say that these words alleged out of the 13th Psalm <note>original: "13 Psalme." In the Vulgate numbering; this is Psalm 14 in modern Bibles.</note> were meant in Christ's mother, in Saint John the Baptist, in the Apostles, etc. For, this only is the sense: that neither by the law of nature, nor law of Moses, could any man be just or avoid such sins as here be reckoned, but by faith and the grace of God, by which there were a number in all ages (especially among the Jews) that were just and holy, whom these words touch not, being spoken only to the multitude of the wicked, which the Prophet makes as it were a separate body conspiring against Christ, and persecuting the just and godly, of which ill company he says, that none was just nor feared God.

<margin>No works avail without faith and grace.</margin>
20. *By the works of the Law.*] Saint Jerome and Saint Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an influential Early Church Father known for his powerful preaching.</note> expound this of the ceremonial works only, and in that sense the Apostle specially prosecutes this proposition in his Epistle to the Galatians. But it is true also of all man’s moral works done without faith and the grace of God: which cannot be acceptable or available in God’s sight to justify any man. And so Saint Augustine takes it in *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapters 8, 10, and 3. <note>original: "de Sp. & lit. c. 8. 10. 3." Refers to Augustine's treatise *De Spiritu et Littera*.</note>

<margin>The Heretics' fantastical or imputative justice.</margin>
22. *Justice of God.*] Beware of the wicked and vain commentary of the Calvinists, <term>glossing<note>To "gloss" here means to provide a misleading or superficial interpretation.</note></term> the justice of God to be that which is resident in Christ, apprehended by our faith: and so that imputed to us which we indeed have not. Wherein at once they have forged for themselves against God’s manifest word, a new "no-justice," a fantastical apprehension of that which is not, a false faith and untrue imputation. Whereas the justice of God here is that with which he endows a man at his first conversion, and is now in a man, and therefore man’s justice: but yet God’s justice also, because it is of God. Of this justice in us, whereby we be truly justified and indeed made just, Saint Augustine speaks thus: <margin>True inherent justice.</margin> <margin>On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins, book 1, chapters 9 and 10.</margin> <note>original: "De pec. mer. li. 1 c. 9. 10." refers to Augustine's *De peccatorum meritis et remissione*.</note>
> *The grace of Christ does work our illumination and justification inwardly also.* And again, *He gives to the faithful the most secret grace of his Spirit, which secretly he pours into infants also.* And again, *They are justified in Christ that believe in him through the secret communication and inspiration of spiritual grace, whereby every one leans to our Lord.* And again, *He makes just by renewing by the Spirit, and regeneration by grace.*

<margin>What works are excluded from justification.</margin>
28. *By faith, without works.*] This is the place whereon the Protestants gather falsely their "only faith," and which they commonly <term>avouch<note>To assert or claim positively.</note></term>, as though the Apostle said, that only faith does justify. Where he both in words and meaning excepts only the works of the Law done without Christ before our conversion: neither excluding the Sacraments of Baptism or Penance, nor hope and charity, or other Christian virtues, all which be the justice of faith, as the good works proceeding thereof be likewise the law and justice of faith. All which the Adversaries would exclude by foisting in the term, "only." Of which kind of men Saint Augustine upon this place <margin>On Grace and Free Will, chapter 7</margin> <note>original: "de grat. & lib. arb. c. 7." refers to Augustine's *De gratia et libero arbitrio*.</note> says thus: *Men not understanding that which the Apostle says (we count a man to be justified by faith without the works of the Law) did think that he said, faith would suffice a man though he lived ill and had no good works.* Which God forbid the <term>vessel of election<note>A traditional title for Saint Paul, based on Acts 9:15.</note></term> should think: who in a certain place <margin>Galatians 5.</margin> after he had said, *In Christ JESUS neither circumcision nor prepuce <note>original: "prepuce." Referring to the state of being uncircumcised (Gentiles).</note> availeth any whit, he straight added, but faith which worketh by love.*

->ANNOTATIONS<-
->CHAPTER 4.<-

<margin>Abraham's Works before faith.</margin>
1. **Abraham.**] The Apostle, disputing in this chapter as he did before against those who thought they might be justified by their works done without the grace of Christ and faith in him, proposes Abraham as an example. He proves that Abraham had no righteousness, nor estimation of righteousness before God, by any works done before he had faith, or that did not proceed from faith and God's grace.

<margin>Righteousness before men, and righteousness before God.</margin>
2. **By works.**] If Abraham did any commendable works before he believed in Christ—as many Philosophers did—men might count him righteous for them. However, in God's sight (who accepts nothing without faith in him, or that does not proceed from his grace), he would never have had the status of a righteous man. Therefore, when God in the Scriptures regards him as a righteous man, he gives the cause, saying: *Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness.*

<margin>Not works, but mere grace is the cause of our first justification.</margin>
4. **To him that works.**] That is to say: He who presumes his own works are done by himself without faith, God's help, and grace, and claims that grace or justification were given to him because of his works—this man claims his justification as a debt, and not as a matter of favor and grace.

5. **To him that works not**] In this context, "he who works not" refers to one who either has no works or does not cite his works done in his time of unbelief as the cause of his justification. Instead, he relies on faith in Christ, which proceeds from pure grace. On this point St. Augustine says: <note>original Latin: "Scias quia fides te iniustum invenit. Et si fides data tibi, fecit te iustum, invenit te impium quem faceret iustum. Si invenit te impium, & de tali fecit iustum, quae opera habebas tunc impius? Nulla habere potuisti (nec habere potes) antequam crederes. Crede ergo in eum qui iustificat impium, ut bona opera tua sint bona opera re vera."</note> *Know that faith found you unjust. And if the faith given to you made you righteous, it found you a wicked person to make righteous. If it found you wicked, and from such a state made you righteous, what works did you have while you were wicked? You could have none (nor can have any) before you believed. Believe then in him who justifies the ungodly, so that your good works may be good works indeed.* —Augustine on Psalm 31.

<margin>Heretical translation.</margin>
<margin><note>original Greek: λέγει (legei)</note></margin>
6. **As David terms.**] The <term>Protestants</term><note>The author is writing from a Catholic perspective, critiquing the English translations used by the Reformers.</note> translate the word <note>original: "λέγει", meaning "says" or "speaks"</note> as "describe" instead of "termeth." They do this because they want the unlearned to believe that the whole nature and definition of Justification is nothing other than the forgiveness of sins, and that no grace or inherent righteousness is given by God at all. However, the Apostle means nothing else except that in the first justification, God finds no good works or merits to reward, but only sins to forgive for those who have faith in him.

<margin>What it means for sins to be "covered" or "not imputed."</margin>
7. **Covered. 8. not imputed.**] You must not conclude (as the Heretics do) from these terms—"covered" and "not imputed"—that the sins of men are never truly forgiven, but only hidden. To say they are only hidden takes away from the power of Christ's blood and the grace of God, by which our offenses are truly...

24. **For us, to whom it shall be reputed.**] By this it is most plain against our Adversaries, that the faith which was reputed for justice to Abraham, was his belief of an Article revealed to him by God, that is to say, his assent and credit given to God's speeches: as in us his posterity according to the spirit, it is here plainly said, that justice shall be reputed to us by believing the Articles of Christ's death and Resurrection, and not by any fond special faith, <term>trust <gloss>original: "fiducia"</gloss></term> or confidence of each man's own salvation. To establish the which fiction, they make no account of the faith Catholic, that is, wherewith we believe the Articles of the faith, which only justifieth, but call it by contempt, an historical faith: so as they may term Abraham's faith, and our Lady's faith, of which <margin>Luke 1, 45.</margin> it was said, <note>original: "Beata quæ credidisti"</note> *Blessed art thou that hast believed.* And so in truth they deny as well the justification by faith, as by works.

# ANNOTATIONS
## CHAPTER 5.

<margin>Against the Heretics' "special faith" and "security."</margin> 1. *Let us have.*) Whether we read, *Let us have peace*, as various of the Greek Doctors <margin>Let us have <br/> We have</margin> <note>original: "ἔχωμεν" (let us have) and "ἔχομεν" (we have)</note> (Chrysostom, Origen, Theodoret, Oecumenius, Theophylact) do, or, *We have peace*: it makes nothing for that vain "security" and infallible certainty which our Adversaries <note>The Protestants.</note> say every man ought to have upon his presumed justification by faith—that he himself is in God's favor and sure to be saved. Peace toward God, being here nothing else but the sincere rest, tranquility, and comfort of mind and conscience, based on the hope he has that he is reconciled to God. Sure it is that the Catholic faith, by which (and none other) men are justified, neither teaches nor breeds any such absolute security of salvation. And therefore they have made for themselves another faith which they call *Confidence* <note>original: "Fiduciam"</note>, which is quite outside the scope of the Creed and the Scriptures.

<margin>Justification is attributed much to faith.</margin> 2. *Access through faith.*) Justification implies all grace and virtues received by Christ's merits, but the entrance and access to this grace and happy state is by faith, because faith is the ground and

<margin>to faith as the foundation.</margin>
and the first foundation to build on, and the port to enter into the rest. This is the reason that our justification is attributed to faith, specifically in this Epistle, even though faith itself is also a gift of grace.

<margin>Our hope is strengthened by well-doing.</margin>
4. **Testing produces hope.**) This also refutes the error of the Protestants, who would have our hope depend only on God’s promises and not at all on our own actions. Here we see that hope stands (and is also strengthened) upon patience, constancy, and the good testing and trial of ourselves in adversities; and being so grounded upon God’s promises and our own actions, it never leads to shame <note>The original uses "confoundeth," meaning to be put to shame or disappointment by a hope that fails.</note>.

<margin>Charity is a quality within us.</margin>
5. **Charity is poured.**) Charity is also given to us in our first justification. It is not merely "imputed" to us <note>A reference to the Protestant view that righteousness is credited to a person's account rather than changing their nature.</note>, but indeed is inwardly poured into our hearts by the Holy Spirit, who is bestowed upon us along with His gifts and grace. For this Charity of God is not that which is in God, but that which He gives to us, as Saint Augustine explains: <note>original: "li. de Sp. & lit. c. 32."</note> *Book on the Spirit and the Letter, chapter 32.* He also refers this passage to the grace of God given in the Sacrament of Confirmation. <note>original: "de bapt. cont. Donat. li. 3 c. 16."</note> *On Baptism against the Donatists, book 3, chapter 16.*

<margin>Council of Trent, session 5, decree on original sin. <note>original: "Conc. Tri. sess. 5 decr. de pec. orig."</note></margin>
<margin>All are born in original sin through Adam.</margin>
12. **By one man sin entered.**) By this passage specifically, the Church of God defends and proves against the old heretics, the Pelagians <note>Followers of Pelagius, who argued that humans could achieve salvation without divine grace and denied original sin.</note>—who denied that children have any original sin or need to be baptized for its remission—that in and by Adam, all are conceived, born, and established as sinners. This likewise argues against the Calvinists, who claim that the children of Christian parents are holy from their mother's womb. The same reasoning which St. Augustine uses <note>original: "li. 1 c. 8. 9. de pec. meritis."</note> (*Book 1, chapters 8 and 9, On the Merits and Remission of Sins*) out of this text to prove against the Pelagians—that the Apostle does not mean a general imitation of Adam in actual sins, but an inherited state—serves against Erasmus and others who incline toward that new interpretation rather than the Church's and the fathers' grave judgment in this matter. <note>original: "Conc. Mileuitanum c. 2."</note> *Council of Mileve, canon 2.*

<margin>Only Christ was not conceived in sin, and (as is believed) our Blessed Lady.</margin>
14. **Until Moses.**) Even in the time of the Law of Nature <note>The period before the written Law was given to Moses.</note>, when men did not fully recognize sin and therefore it could not be judged or imputed by man's standards; and in the time of Moses’ Law, when the commandment taught them to recognize it but gave them no strength or grace to avoid it, sin reigned. Consequently, death and damnation reigned even until Moses (inclusive), which is to say, even until the end of his Law. And this applied not only to those who actually sinned as Adam did, but also to infants who never actually offended, but were born and conceived in sin. That is to say, their natures were defiled, lacking justice, and turned away from God in Adam and by their descent from him. Christ alone is excepted, being conceived without man's seed; and his mother, for his honor and by his special protection (as many godly, devout men judge), was preserved from the same <note>An early reference to the doctrine of the Immaculate Conception.</note>.

<margin>The Law did not cause more sin, though that was the result of it.</margin>
20. **That sin might abound.**) The word "That" here does not imply causality, as if the Law were given for the purpose of making sin abound; rather, it notes the result. Because of the prohibition of sin, sin increased; by occasion of which, the power of Christ's grace is more amply and abundantly bestowed in the New Testament.
