# ANNOTATIONS
## CHAPTER 6.

<margin>Not only faith.</margin>
3. *We that are baptized.*) That which he previously attributed to the Law of Moses regarding faith is now credited to baptism, which is the first Sacrament of our faith and the entrance into the Christian religion. By this, it is plain that he does not mean that faith alone justifies, but that the Sacraments and the whole of the Christian religion—which he calls the Law of the spirit, grace, and faith—are also necessary. <term>justify: to be made righteous or right in the eyes of God</term>

<margin>The old man and the new.</margin>
6. *Old man, body of sin.*) Our fallen state, subject to sin and disordered desires [concupiscence] inherited from Adam, is called the *Old man*. Conversely, our person reformed in and by Christ is named the *New man*. The collective mass of sins that once ruled us is called the corpse or "body of sin."

<margin>Dying to sin. Living to God.</margin>
10. *To sin he died.*) Christ died to sin when his death destroyed the power of sin. We die to sin when we are discharged from its power, which previously acted as the "life" of our persons and commanded every part of our soul and body. On the other hand, we live to God when his grace rules and works within us, just as the soul rules our physical bodies.

<margin>How concupiscence is called sin.</margin>
12. *Sin reign.*) Disordered desire (concupiscence) is called "sin" here because it is the effect, the occasion, and the material of sin. It is like a disease or infirmity within us that inclines us toward evil. It remains even after Baptism in its substance, but it is not properly a "sin" in itself, nor is it forbidden by commandment, until it reigns over us and we obey its desires. <note>original citations: "August. li. de nupt. & concupisc. c. 23" refers to St. Augustine's *On Marriage and Concupiscence*; "Cont. 2 epist. Pelag." refers to his work *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*; "Conc. Trident. Sess. 5" refers to the Council of Trent’s decree on original sin.</note>

<margin>The doctrine of our first Apostles.</margin>
17. *Form of doctrine.*) When a nation is first converted to the Catholic faith, a standard rule of belief is established. Once the people have been entrusted to this rule by their Apostles, they must never allow any human persuasion to change it. They must not accept from any man or angel any new doctrine or "Analogy of Faith," as the Protestants call it. <note>The "Analogy of Faith" was a term used by Reformers to suggest that Scripture should be interpreted according to a specific framework of Protestant doctrine.</note>

<margin>Life everlasting a stipend, and yet grace.</margin>
23. *The grace of God, life everlasting.*) The logic of this passage suggests that just as death or damnation is the "stipend" (wages) of sin, so eternal life is the stipend of righteousness. Indeed, he spoke this way in the last chapter: that *as sin reigned unto death, so grace reigns through righteousness to eternal life*. But here he changes the phrasing slightly, calling eternal life "grace" rather than a "reward." He does this because the merits by which we attain life are themselves entirely the gift and grace of God. <note>original: "August. Ep. 105 ad Sixtum" refers to St. Augustine’s Letter 105 to Sixtus, which discusses grace and merit.</note>

# ANNOTATIONS
## CHAPTER 7.

<margin>Actual disordered desire is forbidden, not the habitual inclination.</margin>
7. *Thou shalt not covet.*) It is not the habitual disordered desire <term>concupiscence: the natural inclination toward sin</term> or the weakness of our nature, nor the sensual desire or inclination to evil that struggles against the spirit, which is properly forbidden in this commandment. Rather, it is the consent of our reason and mind to it—to obey and follow those lusts—that is a sin and prohibited.

<margin>Sudden involuntary impulses are not sin.</margin>
15. *That which I work.*) When this is understood as referring to St. Paul himself or any other righteous person, the meaning is that the flesh and the lower nature stir up various disordered motions, passions, or agitations against the mind. These sometimes invade the mind so suddenly that before a person can pay attention, or before reason can collect itself to deliberate, a man is in a sense (though unknowingly) entangled. As soon as this is perceived, if the righteous person condemns, rejects, and resists it, it never makes him a sinner.

<margin>Galatians 5:17.</margin>
<margin>Disordered desire does not take away free will.</margin>
15. *Not that which I will.*) He does not mean that he can do no good that he wills or desires, or that he is always forced to do what his will does not agree to. Instead, he means that because of the strength of disordered desire <note>concupiscence</note>, which he cannot be rid of during this life, he cannot fully accomplish all the desires of his spirit and mind. As he says to the Galatians: *The flesh lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, so that you cannot do whatever you will.*

<margin>Letter to Asellicus, 200.</margin>
<margin>Sin is intentional; otherwise, it is not sin.</margin>
19. *Not the good which I will.*) Likewise, a righteous person may be pressured by the rage of disordered desire or sensual appetite to do or suffer many things in his lower nature or physical members which his will does not consent to. As long as this is the case, it is so far from being a sin that (as * St. Augustine says) he never needs to say to God, *forgive us our sins*, for that reason. For sin is voluntary <note>intentional</note>, and these sudden passions are not.

19. *Which I will not.*) It does not count against free will when the Apostle says that good men sometimes do or suffer in their bodies things that the will does not agree to. In fact, it plainly proves free will, because the proper act of the will—that is, to will or not to will, to consent or to dissent—is always (as you can see here) free in itself. This remains true even if there is internal or external force preventing a man's physical members from obeying everything the will commands or prescribes. Therefore, nothing is ever attributed to a person which is done in his external or internal faculties when the will does not concur. Indeed, afterward (verse 20) the Apostle says, *It is not I who work* <note>original Latin: *Non ego operor*</note>, meaning man does not do what is not done by his will; this most evidently proves free will.

<margin>Disordered desire does not defile a righteous man’s actions, as the Lutherans claim.</margin>
25. *With the mind, with the flesh.*) Nothing done by disordered desire (which the Apostle here calls "sin") can make a person guilty before God if the spirit, reason, or mind of the man does not consent to it. Neither can the impulses of the flesh in a righteous man ever defile the workings of his spirit, as the <note>The translators here are arguing against the Protestant reformers (Lutherans) who believed that all human actions are tainted by sin.</note> Lutherans hold. On the contrary, these struggles often make his actions more deserving of reward because of the continual combat he has against them. For it is plain that the operations of the flesh and of the spirit do not combine to make a single act, as they imagine; the Apostle concludes the exact opposite, saying: That in his mind he serves the Law of God, but in his flesh the law of sin, which is to say, disordered desire.

->A N N O T A T I O N S<-
->C H A P T E R 8.<-

<margin>The testimony of the Spirit.</margin>
16. *The Spirit gives testimony.*) This passage does not support the "special faith" of the Heretics <note>The author refers to the Protestant doctrine of the "assurance of salvation," where an individual feels certain they are saved.</note>, or their arrogant certainty that every one of them is in a state of grace. The testimony of the Spirit is nothing else but the internal good impulses, comfort, and peace which the children of God feel daily more and more in their hearts by serving Him. Through these, they have something like a confirmation of His favor toward them, which greatly strengthens their hope of justification and salvation.

<margin>Notwithstanding Christ's satisfaction and Passion, our own is also required.</margin>
17. *Yet if they suffer.*) Christ's pains or passions did not satisfy God for everyone in such a way that Christian men are excused from their own particular suffering or making satisfaction for their own part. Our pains are not worthless for reaching heaven just because Christ has done enough. Quite the contrary: He was exalted to the glory of heaven by His passion; therefore, we shall attain to be companions with Him in His kingdom by "compassion"—that is, by sharing with Him in similar sufferings.

<margin>All suffering in this life is nothing compared to the heavenly glory; and yet it is meritorious and worthy of the same.</margin>
<margin>Heretical translation.</margin>
<margin>The source of the merit of works.</margin>
<margin>to the glory <note>original Latin: *ad gloriam*</note></margin>
<margin>to the glory <note>original Greek: πρὸς τὴν δόξαν</note></margin>
<margin>them <note>original Greek: αὐτὰς, referring to the sufferings</note></margin>
<margin>2 Corinthians 4:17</margin>
18. *Condign.* <note>The term "condign" means "worthy" or "deserved." The author is arguing against the idea that human works have no value toward salvation.</note>) Our adversaries <note>Protestant Reformers</note> base their argument here that the works or sufferings of this life are not meritorious or worthy of life everlasting. However, the Apostle says no such thing, any more than he says that Christ's Passions were not meritorious of His glory—which I think they would not dare to claim regarding our Savior's actions. He only explains that the afflictions are, by their own nature, short-lived, momentary, and of no account when compared to the reward we shall have in heaven. Indeed, Christ's pains were not comparable to His glory by their own nature either; yet they were meritorious and worthy of heaven, and so are ours. Therefore, to express this comparison, he says here: *They are not condign to the glory* <note>original: *ad gloriam* / πρὸς τὴν δόξαν</note>. He does not say "of the glory," as the Heretics falsely translate; though the Scripture does speak that way elsewhere when it implies only a comparison, as in *Proverbs 3* in the Greek: *Nothing precious is worthy of it*—meaning wisdom, or to be compared with it. See the same in *Sirach 26:20* <note>original: Ecclesiasticus</note> and *Tobit 9:2*. But when the Apostle wants to express that they are "condign," worthy, or meritorious of glory, he says plainly: *Our tribulation, which is presently momentary and light, works for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all measure.* (2 Corinthians 4:17). The value of Christ's actions does not come from their length or physical greatness—though they surpassed all human deeds—but from the worthiness of His person. Similarly, the value of our actions comes from the grace of our adoption, which makes those actions—which by their own nature are not meritorious or equal to the joys of heaven—to be worthy of heaven. These critics might as well try to prove that sinful works do not deserve damnation; for sin, in the quantity and nature of the act, does not equal the pain of Hell in pleasure. However, because it involves a turning away from God, no matter how brief, it deserves damnation because it always comes from God's enemy, just as good works that are meritorious come from a child of God.

<margin>Just as sometimes faith alone is named, so elsewhere only hope or only charity are cited as the cause of our salvation.</margin>
24. *Saved by hope.*) What is attributed to faith in other places is here attributed to hope. Whenever there are many causes for one thing, the holy writers—as the subject and occasion require—sometimes refer to one cause and sometimes to another. They do not name one alone to exclude the others, as our adversaries captiously and ignorantly argue, but at different times and in various places to express things that could not, or did not need to be, stated in every single discourse. In one discussion, faith is emphasized; in another, charity; in another, hope; sometimes alms and mercy; and elsewhere, other virtues. At one time it is said, *Everyone who believes is born of God* (1 John 5:1). At another time, *Everyone who loves is born of God* (1 John 4:7). Sometimes faith purifies the heart (Acts 15:9). At another time, charity removes sins (1 Peter 4:8). Of faith it is said, *The just lives by faith* (Romans 1:17). Of charity, *We know that we have passed from death to life because we love the brothers* (1 John 3:14).

<margin>Scripture misused against the Divinity of the Holy Spirit.</margin>
27. *The Spirit desires.*) Arius and Macedonius <note>Ancient heretics who denied the full divinity of the Son and the Spirit.</note>, those ancient heretics, also had passages they used to argue against the Church’s interpretation, just as our new masters now do. They misused this text to prove the Holy Spirit is not God, arguing that He would not need to pray or ask if He were God, but could instead command. Therefore, Saint Augustine explains it this way: *The Spirit prays*, meaning He *causes and teaches us to pray, and tells us what to pray for or ask.* (Augustine, *On the Soul and Its Origin*, Book 4, Chapter 9, and *Letter 121*, Chapter 15).

<margin>The doctrine of predestination, how it should be re-</margin>
30. *Whom he has predestinated.*) God's eternal foresight, love, purpose, predestination, and election of His dear children—and in time their calling, justifying, and glorifying by Christ—as well as all other acts and intentions of His divine will and providence toward their salvation, ought to be revered by all people with fearful humility. They should not be investigated or debated with presump- <note>The text cuts off mid-word, continuing on the next page.</note>

# CHAPTER 9. TO THE ROMANS.

<margin>Predestination is to be reverenced, and what it teaches us.</margin>
...tuous boldness and audacity. For it is the gulf in which many proud persons, both in this age and always, have perished by God’s just judgment, founding upon it most horrible blasphemies against God’s mercy, nature, and goodness, and various damnable errors against man’s free will, and against all good life and religion. This high conclusion is set down here for us so that we may learn to know upon whom we ought to depend in all our life, from whom we expect our salvation, and by whose providence all our graces, gifts, and works stand; by what an everlasting, gracious determination our redemption, which is in Christ JESUS, was designed; and to give God unceasing thanks for our calling and preferment to the state we are in, before the Jews, who deserved no better

<margin>God’s predestination does not take away free will.</margin>
than they, before the light of His mercy shining upon us accepted us and rejected them. But this aforementioned eminent truth of God’s eternal predestination stands (as we are bound to believe under pain of damnation, whether we understand how or not) and so St. Augustine in all his divine works written on the same (<note>Latin: *De gratia & lib. arb. De corrept. & gratia. Ad articulos falso impositos.* These titles refer to "On Grace and Free Will," "On Rebuke and Grace," and "Against the Articles Falsely Imposed."</note>) defends, declares, proves, and convinces us that it does stand (I say) with man’s free will and the true liberty of his actions. It forces no man to be either evil or good, to sin or virtue, to salvation or damnation, nor does it take away the means or nature of merits, and cooperation with God toward our own and other men's salvation.

<margin><term>pepeismai</term> <note>Greek: πεπεισμαι, meaning "I am persuaded" or "I am convinced."</note> I trust. <note>Latin: *Confido*. Jerome, question 9 to Algasia.</note></margin>
<margin>No man ordinarily is sure of his salvation, but only in hope.</margin>
38. *I am sure.*) This speech is common in St. Paul according to the Latin translation, even when he had no other assured knowledge but by hope: as in Romans 15:14, 2 Timothy 1:5, and Hebrews 6:9. In these places, the Greek word signifies only a "probable persuasion." Therefore, unless he is speaking of himself by special revelation, or of the predestined in general (in which two cases it may stand for the certainty of faith or infallible knowledge), otherwise, for every particular man to be infallibly assured that he himself is justified—and not only that, but sure also never to sin, or to have the gift of perseverance and certain knowledge of his predestination—that is a most damnable false illusion and presumption, condemned by the Fathers of the holy Council of Trent (<note>Session 6, chapters 9, 12, and 13. The Council of Trent was the 16th-century ecumenical council that defined Catholic doctrine in response to the Protestant Reformation.</note>).

## A N N O T A T I O N S
### CHAP. IX.

<margin>Anathema.</margin>
<margin>In what sense St. Paul wishes to be anathema.</margin>
<margin>Exodus 32:32.</margin>
3. **Anathema.**] <term>Anathema<note>original: "Anathema," a Greek word (ἀνάθεμα) used in the New Testament to signify something set apart, either for God's glory or for destruction.</note></term>, by use of Scripture is either that which by separation from profane use, and by dedication to God, is holy, dreadful, and not vulgarly to be touched: or contrariwise, that which is rejected, severed, or abandoned from God, as cursed and detested, and therefore is to be avoided. And in this later sense (according as St. Paul takes it 1 Corinthians 16. *If any love not our Lord JESUS CHRIST, be he Anathema*, that is to say, Away with him, Accursed be he, Beware you company not with him) the Church and holy Councils use the word for a curse and <term>excommunication<note>The formal exclusion of a person from the sacramental life of the Church.</note></term> against Heretics and other notorious offenders and blasphemers. Now how the Apostle, wishing himself to be Anathema from Christ to save his Countrymen's souls, did take this word, it is a very hard thing to determine. Some think, he desired only to die for their salvation. Others, that being very loath to be kept from the fruition of Christ, yet he could be content to be so still to save their souls. Others, that he wished what malediction or separation from Christ soever that did not imply the disfavor of God towards him, nor take away his love toward God. This only is certain that it is a point of unspeakable charity in the Apostle's breast, and a pattern to all Bishops and Priests, how to love the salvation of their flock. As the like was uttered by Moses when he said, *Either forgive this people, or blot me out of thy book.*

<margin>God's promise not made to carnal Israel.</margin>
6. **Not all of Israel.**] Though the people of the Jews were many ways honored and privileged, and namely by Christ's taking flesh of them: yet the promise of grace and salvation was neither only made to them, nor to all them that carnally came of them or their fathers: God's election and mercy depending upon his own purpose, will, and determination, and not tied to any nation, family, or person.

<margin>Isaac preferred before Ishmael.</margin>
7. **But in Isaac.**] The promise made to Abraham was not in Ishmael, who was a son born only by flesh and nature: but in Isaac, who was a son obtained by promise, faith, and miracle: and was a figure of the Church's children born to God in Baptism.

<margin>Jacob before Esau.</margin>
10. **Of one copulation.**] It is proved also by God's choosing of Jacob before Esau (who were not only brethren by father and mother, but also twins, and Esau the elder of the two, which according to carnal count should have had the preeminence) that God in giving graces follows not the temporal or carnal prerogatives of men or families.

<margin>By the example of Jacob and Esau, is showed God's mercy in the elect, and justice in the reprobate.</margin>
11. **Not yet born.**] By the same example of those twins, it is evident also, that neither nations nor particular persons be elected eternally, or called temporally, or preferred to God's favor before others, by their own merits: because God, when he made choice, and first loved Jacob, and refused Esau, respected them both as ill, and the one no less then the other guilty of damnation for original sin, which was alike in them both. And therefore where justly he might have reprobated both, he saved of mercy one. Which one therefore, being as ill and as void of good as the other, must hold of God's eternal purpose, mercy, and election, that he was preferred before his brother which was elder than himself, and no worse than himself. And his brother Esau on the other side has no cause to complain, for that God neither did nor suffered any thing to be done towards him, that his sin did not deserve. for although God elect eternally & give his first grace without all merits, yet he does not reprobate or hate any man but for sin, or the fore-sight thereof.

<margin>That God is not unjust, or an accepter of persons, is declared by familiar examples.</margin>
14. **Is there iniquity?**] Upon the former discourse that of two persons equal, God calls the one to mercy, and leaves the other in his sin, one might infer that God were unjust and an accepter of persons. To which the Apostle answers, that God were not just nor indifferent indeed, so to use the matter where grace or salvation were due. As if two men being Christened, both believe well, & live well: if God should give heaven to the one, & should damn the other, then were he unjust, partial, & forgetful of his promise: but respecting or taking two, who both be worthy of damnation (as all are before they be first called to mercy) then the matter stands on mere mercy, and of the giver's will and liberality, in which case partiality has no place. As for example.

<meta>This page continues the "Annotations" or commentary on Romans Chapter 9. The previous page defined "Anathema" and began discussing St. Paul's sorrow for the Jews. This page uses a legal analogy to explain the relationship between God's mercy, justice, and human free will.</meta>

->THE EPISTLE OF ST. PAUL CHAPTER 9.<-
406

<margin>Saint Augustine's example <note>original: "li. de predest. & gra. cap. 4." referring to St. Augustine’s *Book on Predestination and Grace*, Chapter 4.</note> is of two debtors: the one forgiven all, and the other made to pay all, by the same creditor.</margin>
1. Two criminals being condemned both for one crime, the Prince pardons the one, and lets the law proceed on the other.

2. The thief that is pardoned cannot attribute his escape to his own deservings, but to the Prince's mercy.

3. The thief that is executed cannot challenge the Prince for not being pardoned also: but must acknowledge that he has his deserving.

4. The bystanders must not say that he was executed because the Prince would not pardon him; for that was not the cause, but his offense.

5. If they ask further, why the Prince pardoned not both, or executed not both: the answer is, that as mercy is a beautiful virtue, so justice is necessary and commendable.

6. But if it be further demanded why John rather than Thomas was executed: or Thomas rather than John pardoned: answer, that (the parties being otherwise equal) it hangs merely and wholly upon the Prince's will and pleasure.

<column-break/>

1. So likewise, God seeing all mankind and every person of the same in a general condemnation, and a mass of sin, in and by Adam, delivers some, and not others.

2. All that are delivered out of that common damnation are delivered by grace and pardon, through the means and merits of Christ.

3. Such as are left in the common case of damnation cannot complain, because they have their deserving for sin.

4. We may not say that such are damned because God did not pardon them, but because they had sin, and therefore deserved it.

5. That some should be damned, and not all pardoned, and others pardoned rather than all condemned, is agreeable to God's justice and mercy: both of which virtues in God's providence towards us are recommended.

6. That Saul <note>Saul refers to the Apostle Paul before his conversion.</note> should be pardoned rather than Caiaphas <note>The High Priest who presided over the trial of Jesus.</note> (I mean where two are equally evil and unworthy) that is only God's holy will and appointment, by which many an unworthy man gets pardon, but no good or just or innocent person is ever damned.

---

<margin><term>Predestination</term> and <term>reprobation</term> <note>Predestination refers to being chosen for salvation; reprobation refers to being left in a state of sin leading to damnation.</note> take not away <term>free will</term>, neither must any man be reckless and desperate.</margin>
In all this mercy of God towards some, and justice towards others, both the pardoned work by their own **free will**, and thereby deserve their salvation: and the others no less by their own free will, without all necessity, work wickedness, and themselves and only of themselves procure their own damnation. Therefore no man may without blasphemy say, or can truly say, that he has nothing to do towards his own salvation, but will live, and thinks he may live without care or thought of his end one way or the other, saying, "If I am appointed to be saved, let it be so: if I am one designed for damnation, I cannot help the matter: come what may." All these speeches and thoughts are sinful and come from the enemy, and are rather signs of reprobation than of election. Therefore the good man must, without searching into God's secrets, work out his own salvation and (as St. Peter says) *make his election sure* by <margin>2 Peter 1:10</margin> **good works**, with continual hope of God's mercy, being assured that if he believes well and does well, he shall have well. For example, if a husbandman <note>A farmer.</note> should say, "If God wills, I shall have enough corn: if not, I cannot make it," and so neglects to till his ground: he may be sure that he shall have none, because he worked not for it. Another man uses his diligence in tilling and plowing, and commits the rest to God; he finds the fruit of his labors.

<margin>Our election or conversion is not of ourselves, but of God's grace and mercy.</margin>
16. **Not of the willer.**] If our election, calling, or first coming to God, lay wholly or principally upon our own will or works: or if our willing or endeavoring to be good would serve without the help and grace of God, as the <term>Pelagians</term> <note>A group following Pelagius, who taught that humans could achieve salvation through their own efforts without divine grace; this view was condemned as heresy.</note> taught, then our election would be wholly in ourselves, which the Apostle denies. And then might Pharaoh and other <term>indurate</term> <note>Hardened in heart.</note> persons (whom God has permitted to be obstinate, to show his power and just judgment upon them) be converted when they themselves pleased, without God's help and assistance: whereas we see the contrary in such obstinate offenders, whom God, as punishment for former sins, visits not with his grace, so that by no threats, miracles, nor persuasion, can they be converted. Whereupon we may not with Heretics infer that man has not free will, or that our will works nothing in our conversion or coming to God: but this only, that our willing or working of any good for our salvation comes from God's special motion, grace, and assistance, and that it is the secondary cause, not the principal.

17. **To this purpose have I raised.**] He does not say that he has of purpose raised or set him up to sin, or that he was the cause of the same in Pharaoh, or that he intended his damnation directly or absolutely, or any otherwise but in respect of his demerits: but rather (as the Apostle says straight after in his chapter of such hardened and obstinate offenders) that he with long patience and toleration expected his conversion, and (as St. Chrysostome <note>An influential Early Church Father and Archbishop of Constantinople known for his eloquent preaching.</note> interprets)

<meta>Catchword: interprets</meta>

# CHAPTER 10. TO THE ROMANS.

<margin>Exodus 9:16.</margin>
...interprets this word <note>original: "Excitavi," meaning "I have raised up" or "awakened"</note> as having preserved him alive to repent, whom He might justly have condemned before. In the 9th chapter of *Exodus*, from which this citation comes, we read, *I have put or set you up* <note>original: "Posui te"</note>, as it says here, *I have raised you*, which is to say: I have purposely advanced you to be so great a king, and chosen you to be a notorious example both of the stubborn obstinacy found in those whom I have forsaken for their great sins, and also to show the world that no obstinacy of even the mightiest offenders can resist me in doing anything that shall not ultimately serve my glory. This is no more than to say that God often, as punishment for nations and to show His justice and glory, gives them wicked Princes and endows them with power and all prosperity; then, withdrawing His grace from them because of their deserts, He hardens their hearts so that they withstand and despise God and afflict His people. In their end and fall, whether temporal or eternal, God will always eventually be glorified. Neither would He raise or suffer such people, or give them power and prosperity in this life—knowing they will become worse because of it—unless He could work all of that to His honor and glory. Indeed, that He does not use such rigorous justice on all who deserve it is a sign of His great grace and mercy. And that He exercises His justice upon certain persons rather than others of equal desert lies wholly upon His will, in whose judgments there are many secret things, but nothing unjust.

<margin>In what sense God raised up Pharaoh, etc.</margin>

<margin>Heretical books concerning predestination.</margin>
20. *Who are you?*] Here the Apostle stops the rashness and presumption of such poor worms who take it upon themselves to question God about their election or reprobation. Certain impious heretics of our time <note>A reference to Protestant Reformers like Calvin, from the perspective of the original Catholic commentators.</note> have done this, publishing books stuffed <gloss>concerning</gloss> with the most blasphemous and erroneous doctrine regarding this high and hidden mystery. They have given the ignorant—who are always curious—the occasion to wrangle and to err perishably in these matters, which are impossible for anyone to understand or think well of, except for the obedient and humble.

<margin>The example of the pot and the potter.</margin>
21. *The potter.*] This example of the pot and the potter goes no further than to declare that the creature may not argue with God his maker about why He does not give one person as much grace as another, or why He does not pardon one as well as another. It is no different than a chamber pot challenging the Potter as to why it was not made into a drinking vessel. Therefore, the heretics who extend this metaphor to prove that man has no free will—no more than a piece of clay—apply the example untruly and deceitfully. This is especially clear when we see expressly in the book of Exodus that Pharaoh, despite his hardened heart, had free will; for it is said both, *He would not dismiss the people,* and, *He hardened his own heart himself.* Exodus 8:15 and (in the Hebrew) verse 32, and chapter 9:35, and 1 Samuel 6:6 <note>original: "1 Reg. 6, 6." Following the Vulgate numbering where 1 & 2 Kings are 1 & 2 Samuel.</note>. And this Apostle also writes that a man may cleanse himself from filth and so become a vessel of honor in the house of God.

## ANNOTATIONS
### CHAPTER 10.

<margin>God's righteousness and the Jews' own righteousness.</margin>
3. **The righteousness of God.**] <term>The righteousness of God</term> <note>original: "iusticia Dei"</note> is that which God gives us through Christ. The Jews' "own" or proper righteousness is that which they claimed to have of themselves and by their own strength, helped only by knowledge of the Law but without the help or grace of Christ.

<margin>Righteousness of faith.</margin>
6. **The righteousness of faith.**] The righteousness which comes from faith reaches toward the life to come, making a person certain of the truth of the Articles of Faith. These include Christ’s Ascension to heaven, his descent into <term>Hell</term> <note>In this context, referring to the "Limbo of the Fathers" or the state of the dead before the Resurrection</note>, his coming down to be incarnated, and his Resurrection and return to glory. By these actions of his, we are pardoned, justified, and saved, in a way the Law could never achieve.

# CHAPTER 11. TO THE ROMANS.

<margin>Open confession and declaration of our faith is sometimes necessary.</margin>
<margin>Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 6, Chapter 31.</margin>
8. *The word of faith.*] The "word of faith" refers to the entire Law of Christ, regarding both how we live and what we believe. It is based on the fact that Christ is our Savior and that He has risen again. This point (like all others) must be both believed in the heart and confessed with the mouth. For although a person is justified inwardly when they receive the virtues of faith, hope, and charity from God, they are also bound—if the occasion arises—to confess their faith with their mouth and through all their external actions. This must be done without shame or fear of the world, or else they cannot be saved. This stands against certain <note>The author is likely referring to early groups like the Gnostics or later groups who suggested outward conformity to other religions was acceptable.</note> old heretics who taught that a person might say or do whatever they wished out of fear or danger, as long as they kept their faith in their heart.

<margin>The passage cited against the invocation of Saints, answered.</margin>
14. *How shall they call upon him?*] This does not work against the <term>invocation of Saints</term> <note>The practice of asking saints in heaven to pray to God on one's behalf.</note> as the heretics <note>In this 16th-century context, "heretics" refers to Protestant reformers who rejected the practice of praying to saints.</note> claim. The Apostle is saying nothing more than that people cannot call upon Christ as their Lord and Master if they do not believe in Him or have never heard of Him. He is speaking of Gentiles or Pagans, who could not pray to Him unless they first believed in Him. To properly pray to Christ, we must know Him and our duties toward Him. Likewise, it is true that we cannot pray to our Blessed Lady or any Saint in heaven until we believe in and know their persons, dignity, and grace, and trust that they can help us. But if our opponents think we cannot pray to them because we cannot "believe" in them, let them understand that the Scripture also uses this phrasing for believing in men—a common Hebrew idiom they should know, given how much they brag about their knowledge of the language. <note>original: "Exod. 14, 31. They believed in God and in Moses. and 2 Paralipomenon 20, 20 [2 Chronicles] in the Hebrew. Epistle to Philemon verse 5."</note> Furthermore, the ancient Church fathers read the Creed interchangeably as "I believe in the Catholic Church" and "I believe the Catholic Church." <note>original: "Council of Nicaea, as found in Epiphanius at the end of the Ancoratus; Jerome, *Against the Luciferians*; Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechetical Lectures*, 17."</note>

<margin>Preachers who are not lawfully called or sent.</margin>
<margin>The Confession of the Churches of France.</margin>
15. *Unless they be sent.*] This passage from the Apostle undeniably condemns all the preaching, writing, laws, innovations, and seizures of churches and pulpits by our "new Evangelists." They have intruded and entered "by the window" <note>An allusion to John 10:1, referring to those who enter the sheepfold illegally rather than through the door.</note>, showing that every one of them, from the highest to the lowest, are false prophets, running to preach and usurping authority without ever being lawfully called. This is so obvious in the heretics of our days that even the Calvinists admit it about themselves, saying an exception must be made for them because they found the state of the Church "interrupted."

<margin>The first justification is by mere grace. Free will.</margin>
20. *That asked not.*] The fact that Christ was found by those who never sought Him proves that the first grace and our initial <term>justification</term> <note>The process by which a person is made righteous in the eyes of God.</note> happen without our own merits. However, the fact that God called so continually and earnestly to the Jews through His Prophets and other signs, yet they resisted Him, proves <term>free will</term>. It shows that God desires all men to be saved, and that those who are lost are the cause of their own damnation.

## ANNOTATIONS
### C H A P. XI.

<margin>2 Chronicles 17.</margin>
<margin>God's answer to Elijah concerning the 7,000 proves nothing for the Protestants' "invisible Church."</margin>
4. *Seven thousand*] The Heretics <note>In this context, the Catholic translators are referring to Protestant reformers.</note> allege this place and example very inappropriately to prove that the Church may be wholly secret, hidden, or unknown. For though the faithful were forced to keep hidden during that persecution by Ahab and Jezebel, which was only in the kingdom of the ten tribes (that is, of Israel), yet at the very same time, in Jerusalem and all the kingdom of Judah, the external worship and profession of faith was open to all the world, and well known to Elijah and the faithful—so many, in fact, that the soldiers alone were numbered at over one million. <note>original: "ten hundred thousand." This refers to the military strength of King Jehoshaphat described in 2 Chronicles 17.</note> Besides, there is a great difference between the Christian Church and the Jews, ours resting upon better promises than theirs. And we will not challenge the Protestants to prove that there were 7,000 of their Sect when their "new Elijah," Luther, began; but let them prove that there were even seven, or any one person, either then or in all the ages before him, who held all points of his belief. There were heretics before him, such as Jovinian, Vigilantius, Helvidius, Wycliffe, etc., and with him, Zwingli, Calvin, etc., who believed as he did in some things, but not in all.

<margin>What works are not, and what are, the cause of salvation.</margin>
6. *Not now of works.*] If salvation is attributed to good works done by nature alone without faith and God's help, then it cannot be by grace. For such works exclude grace, favor, and mercy, and claim salvation as a debt owed rather than a gift. Therefore, be careful here of the Heretics' interpretation, which untruly excludes the works of Christian men from the necessity or merit of salvation—works which are done with and by God's grace, and therefore clearly go hand-in-hand with grace and are joined with God's grace as causes of our salvation. Our adversaries are like bad apothecaries <note>An apothecary was a historical pharmacist.</note>, always taking one thing for another <note>original: "quid pro quo"</note> either out of ignorance or with the intent to deceive the simple.

# THE EPISTLE OF ST. PAUL CHAPTER 12.

<margin>God is not the author of sin.</margin>
8. **God has given.**] This does not signify God's active work or action, but rather His permission. As St. Augustine says, God does this not by putting malice into people, but by not imparting His grace to them. This is always due to their own past deserts, and it is their own wills that properly work the evil. See the annotations for Matthew 13:14 and Romans 1:24.
<margin><note>original: "Chrys. ho. 19 in ep. Ro."</note> St. John Chrysostom, Homily 19 on the Epistle to the Romans. <note>original: "Aug. Ep. 105. ad Sixtum."</note> St. Augustine, Letter 105 to Sixtus.</margin>

<margin>A simplified explanation of the text regarding the Jews and Gentiles, their standing, falling, and rising again.</margin>
20. **Because of unbelief.**] The Apostle describes the pride of the Gentiles who boast about being received while the Jews were rejected. Specifically, they thought the Jews were forsaken only so that the Gentiles could take their place. Paul declares that the direct and proper cause of the Jews being forsaken was their own unbelief. He exhorts the Gentiles to beware of the same, because they can fall just as easily as the others. God is just as likely to execute justice against them as He did against the Jews, as He has already done in many nations that have fallen into heresy.

28. **According to the Gospel.**] In terms of belief in Christ and receiving the Gospel, the Jews are currently treated as God’s enemies. It was through their unbelief that the Gentiles found mercy. However, in respect to God's special election of the Jewish nation and the promises made to the ancient Patriarchs, the Jews are still dear to Him. For God never promises something without performing it, nor does He change His mind regarding the privileges given to that nation.

30. **For as you.**] Just as the Gentiles, who previously did not believe, found mercy and came to the faith when the Jews fell away, so too the Jews—who do not believe now while the Gentiles have obtained mercy—shall at the end of the world, by God's ordinance, obtain grace and pardon just as the Gentiles have.

32. **Concluded all.**] In this way, God finds all nations and all men in a state of sin (which they fell into by their own free will, not by His causing). He may then, out of His mercy, call and convert whomever and in whatever order He wills. Therefore, no party has cause to brag about their own deserving. Both countries and individuals must credit their eternal election, their first calling, and their conversion to Christ and His mercy alone. No works they performed while in a state of unbelief deserved such a gift, though their works performed afterward, proceeding from faith and grace, do truly merit heaven.

<margin>How far one should deal with or seek to know the doctrine of predestination.</margin>
33. **O depth.**] The Apostle concludes that no one should search deeper into God’s secret and unsearchable counsels regarding the calling of the Gentiles and the rejection of the Jews beyond this: all who are rejected are justly rejected because of their sins, and all who are saved are saved by God’s great mercy and the grace of Christ. Whoever seeks to spread the "contagion of curiosity" among the people by searching into things beyond the reach of men and Angels will only overreach and destroy themselves. If you wish to be saved, believe, obey the Church, fear God, and keep His commandments—that is your responsibility and every other person's. You must not try to examine whether you are "predestined" or "reprobate" <note>A term for those rejected by God or destined for damnation.</note>, nor seek to know the ways of God’s secret judgment toward yourself or others. It is the common enemy of our souls who, in these unhappy times, has opened the blasphemous tongues and directed the proud pens of Calvin, Beza, Verone <note>Likely referring to Peter Martyr Vermigli, a prominent Reformer.</note>, and such outcasts to discuss these particulars. This leads to the ruin of many simple people, especially young scholars in Universities, who find it requires less study to become proud and curious than to be humble, wise, and obedient.
<margin>The writings of Heretics on predestination.</margin>

### C H A P T E R. XII.

<margin>
*The body disciplined by penance is a pleasing sacrifice.*
</margin>
**1. A living host.]** <note>The word "host" here comes from the Latin *hostia*, meaning a sacrificial victim.</note> Lest men should think, by the former discourse of God’s eternal predestination, that no reward was to be had for a good life and works, the Apostle now earnestly recommends to them holiness of life.

**1. A living host.]** Man makes his body a sacrifice to God by giving it to suffer for Him, by disciplining it with fasting, watching, and such like, and by occupying it in works of charity and virtue to God’s honor. By this it appears how acceptable these works are to God and pleasing in His sight, being compared to a sacrifice, which is a high service done to Him.

</margin>

This Rule existed before any of the books of the New Testament were written, and...

# THE EPISTLE OF ST. PAUL. CHAPTER 13.

...before the faith was preached among the Gentiles: by which not only every other inferior teacher’s doctrine was tested, but the preaching, writing, and interpreting (which is here called <term>prophesying</term><note>In this historical context, "prophesying" refers to the inspired interpretation and explanation of Scripture for the community, rather than predicting the future.</note>) of all the Apostles and Evangelists were approved and admitted, or disapproved and rejected by God's Church. This form, by word of mouth and not by Scripture, every Apostle delivered to the countries they converted. For keeping this form, the Apostle previously praised the Romans, and afterward earnestly warns them not to be drawn away from it by any man’s persuasive speech. This he commends to Timothy, calling it his <term>entrusted deposit</term><note>original: "Depositum". This refers to the core teachings of Christianity handed down from the Apostles.</note>. For not holding this fast and sure, he blames the Galatians, further denouncing even himself or an Angel that should write, teach, or explain against that which they first received as an <term>anathema</term><note>A formal curse or excommunication by the Church.</note>, and commanding always to beware of those who taught otherwise. For fear of missing this line of truth, even though he had the Holy Ghost, Paul went to confer with Peter and the rest, lest he might have preached in vain and lost his labor. For the firm keeping of this <term>Rule of Truth</term><note>A standard of doctrine used to evaluate all Christian teaching.</note>, the Apostles held Councils, as did their successors following their example. For the holding of this Rule, and by its measure, all the holy Scriptures were written; for and by the same, all the glorious doctors of the Church have made their sermons, commentaries, and interpretations of God's word. All writings and interpretations are admitted and deemed to be of God only if they are agreeable to this Rule.

<margin>The heretics' imaginary rule—or rather, rules of faith—are many and different from one another.</margin>
And this is the sure <term>Analogy</term><note>original: "Analogie". A Greek term meaning proportion or correspondence; here, it means interpreting Scripture in proportion to the established faith.</note> and measure of faith, set down and commended to us everywhere as the Apostles' tradition. It is not the imaginary rule or standard that every sect-leader claims to gather out of the Scriptures (which they misunderstand and twist to their own purpose), by which Luther had his false standards, and Calvin his own as well. According to the specific measure of each sect, they have their own expositions of God's word; and in England (as in other infected countries), they have recently kept a clumsy imitation of this prophesying which St. Paul speaks of here and elsewhere. This was an exercise in the early Church, measured not by every man's personal spirit, but by the aforementioned Rule of Faith first set down by the Apostles. Therefore, all this new imaginary prophesying and all other preaching in Calvin's school is justly condemned by this note of the Apostle, because it is not according to, but quite against, the Rule of Faith.

->ANNOTATIONS<-
->CHAPTER 13<-

<margin>Obedience to temporal rulers, and in what cases.</margin>
1. *Every soul be subject.*] Because the Apostles preached liberty through Christ from the yoke of the Law and the servitude of sin, and gave all the faithful both the example and commandment to obey God more than men—while also strictly charging them to be obedient and subject to their <term>Prelates</term><note>High-ranking church officials like bishops.</note> as those who cared for their souls and were placed over the Church of God by the Holy Spirit—there were many in those days, newly converted, who thought themselves free from all <term>temporal</term><note>Relating to worldly or civil authority, as opposed to spiritual authority.</note> powers, earthly lords, and human institutions or authorities. Consequently, the servant thought himself free from his servitude, and the subject from his Sovereign—whether Emperor, King, Duke, or any other secular magistrate—especially since the Princes of those days were heathens and persecutors of the Apostles and of Christ's religion. For this reason, and because the Apostles were falsely accused by their enemies of leading men away from order and obedience to civil laws and officers, St. Paul here (as St. Peter does in 1 Peter 2) clears his name. He expressly commands every man to be subject to his temporal Prince and Superior. This does not mean every man must obey everyone in office, but rather everyone should obey the one whom God has placed in authority over him, such as his master, lord, or king. Furthermore, this obedience does not extend to matters of religion or the governance of their souls (for most rulers were pagans, whom the Apostle would not tell men to obey in matters of faith), but only in those things that concern public peace and civil policy, or whatever other causes agree with God's holy will and ordinance. For against God, no power may be obeyed. <margin>Acts 4:19 and 29.</margin>

<margin>In what sense all power or superiority is from God.</margin>
1. *No power but of God.*] St. Chrysostom <margin>Chrysostom, Homily 23 on the Epistle to the Romans.</margin> notes here that the concept of power, rule, and superiority is ordained by God, but not necessarily every individual Prince. This is because many may <term>usurp</term><note>To seize a position of power illegally or by force.</note> power, reigning only by God's permission rather than by His appointment. Nor are all actions performed by a sovereign power necessarily from God—such as Julian the Apostate’s persecution of Catholics, Pharaoh's tyrannical oppression of the Israelites, Ahab’s persecution of the Prophets, Nero’s execution of the Apostles, or Herod and Pilate’s condemnation of Christ. God permitted these rulers to accomplish such things through the abuse of their power, but those actions were outside the scope of His divine cause and ordinance.

<margin>In things lawfully commanded, it is a mortal sin not to obey our superiors.</margin>
2. *They that resist.*] Whoever resists or does not obey his lawful superior in those matters where he is subject to him withstands God's appointment. Such a person commits a mortal sin and is worthy of punishment both in this world by his superior and by God in the next life. In matters of temporal government and civil causes, Christians were bound in conscience to obey their Heathen Emperors; though on the other hand, they were bound under pain of damnation to obey their Apostles and Prelates, and not to obey their kings or
Emperours

<header>THE EPISTLE OF SAINT PAUL CHAPTER 14.</header>

Emperors, in matters of religion. By this it is clear that when we are commanded to obey our superiors, it is meant always and only in such things as they may lawfully command, and regarding those matters where they are our superiors.

<margin>The Apostle speaks of temporal powers.</margin>
4. *Beareth not the sword.*] That the Apostle specifically means temporal powers here, we can see by the sword, tribute, and external force, which he attributes to them. And the Christian men then had no doubt whether they should obey their spiritual powers; but now the disease is quite the opposite. For all power is given to the secular authority, and nothing to the spiritual, which was expressly ordained by Christ and the Holy Ghost: and all the faithful are commanded to be subject to it, as to Christ’s own word and will.

<margin>Heresies against rule and superiority.</margin>
There were heretics called *Begardi* <note>The Beguards were a medieval lay group often accused by the Church of believing they were beyond the need for authority or moral law.</note>, who took away all rule and authority. The Wycliffites <note>Followers of John Wycliffe, whose 14th-century teachings were seen as precursors to the Reformation.</note> would obey neither Prince nor Prelate if he were in a state of deadly sin. The Protestants of our time (as we can see in all countries where the secular sword is drawn against their sects) care neither for one nor the other, though they praise only the secular power when it works in their favor.

<margin>The obedience of Catholics both to spiritual and temporal superiors.</margin>
The Catholics alone most humbly obey both, according to God’s ordinance: the one in temporal causes, and the other in spiritual. In this order, both these states have blessedly flourished in all Christian countries ever since Christ’s time, and it is the very way to preserve both, as one day all the world shall confess with us.

<margin>The Clergy exempted from tribute.</margin>
<margin>Jerome on Matthew 17 <note>original: "Hiero. i Mat. 17"</note></margin>
6. *You give tributes.*] Though every man ought to be ready to serve his temporal Prince with his goods, by tributes or whatever other lawful taxes and subsidies may be: yet they may exempt by privileges whomever they think good. As in all Christian countries: Priests, for the honor of Christ whose ministers they are, have been excepted and exempted by the grants and ancient charters of kings. Nevertheless, they were never unready to serve their sovereign voluntarily in all common causes with whatever they had. See *Annotations on Matthew 17, 26.*

<margin>Saint Augustine's conversion.</margin>
12. *Not in banquetings.*] This was the very place which Saint Augustine, that glorious Doctor <note>A title for a saint whose writings have significantly advanced Church doctrine.</note>, was directed to by a voice from heaven at his first miraculous and happy conversion—not only to the Catholic faith, but also to perpetual <term>continence</term><note>A commitment to celibacy and refraining from sexual relations.</note>. This voice came from heaven saying, **Take up and read: Take up and read** <note>original: "Tolle, lege: Tolle, lege."</note>, as he himself tells in *Book 8 of his Confessions, chapter 12.*

--- Page 450 ---
<meta>This page continues the commentary on Romans Chapter 14, moving from the biblical text itself into the "Annotations"—detailed scholarly and polemical explanations common in 16th-century Bibles. It focuses on the transition from Jewish dietary laws to Christian liberty, while defending Catholic fasting practices against Protestant critiques.</meta>

->THE EPISTLE OF SAINT PAUL CHAPTER 14.<-

<margin>The Apostle's meaning about eating or not eating certain foods.</margin>
The Jews were forbidden from eating many things, such as pork, hare, rabbit, and similar creatures, including a great number of fish, birds, and beasts. After his Passion, Christ released all those who became Christians from those observances and all other ceremonies of the Old Law. Nevertheless, because many who were raised in the Law had a religious scruple and conscience about suddenly forsaking their former ways, the Apostle here admonishes those who are stronger and better instructed in the matter to bear with the weaker sort. These were Christians who could not yet find it in their hearts to eat and use the foods forbidden by God in the Law. On the other side, he warns the weak who would not eat not to take offense or scandal at those who did eat without hesitation any of the irregular or forbidden foods in the Law, nor in any way to judge or condemn the eater, but to commit that to God; finally, he instructs that neither side should condemn the other for eating or not eating.

<note>The term "conny" refers to a rabbit. The "Old Law" refers to the Mosaic Law found in the Torah.</note>

<margin>The Heretics foolishly abuse this passage against the fasts of the Church.</margin>
Now the Protestants <note>The original text uses "Heretikes" to refer to Protestant reformers.</note> foolishly apply all of this to the fasts of the Church and the differences of foods within them—as if the Church forbade any food from being eaten or touched entirely, or made any creature "unclean," or prescribed abstinence for any reason other than the disciplining of men's bodies and the service of God. It is a great blindness that they can see no difference between Christ’s fast of forty days (*Matthew 4*); John’s abstaining from all delicate foods and drinks (*Matthew 3, 11*); the widow Anna’s fast (*Luke 2:37*); the Nazirites (*Numbers 6*); the Rechabites (*Jeremiah 35:14*); the Ninevites (*Jonah 3*); Saint Paul’s fasts (*2 Corinthians 11:27*); or Saint Timothy’s abstinence (*1 Timothy 5:23*).

<note>The Rechabites were a biblical group noted for their strict avoidance of wine. Nazirites were individuals who took a vow of holiness involving abstinence from grapes and wine.</note>

<margin>Foolish Heretics do not see the differences between things.</margin>
(Which he said they should keep after his departure from them) and the ceremonial distinction of creatures and foods as "clean" and "unclean" in the old Law. It is evident the Apostle treats this distinction in this entire chapter and nothing else at all. Therefore, when the Protestants use the words of this passage to try to prove that we are either made free from fasting and from obeying the Church's commandment, or from following Christ's example in that matter—or that those who observe Christian fasts are "weak in faith" and should not condemn the breaking of the prescribed fasts of the holy Church as a sin—they are abusing the Apostle's words and discourse, whether ignorantly or willfully.

<margin>Distinction of days.</margin>
5. **Between day and day.** By a similar deception, they abuse this passage against the Holy Days of Christ and his Blessed Mother and the Saints. However, this passage concerns only the Jewish festivities and their observation of times, which is also discussed in the Epistle to the Galatians (*Chapter 4:10*).

<margin>The text explained concerning every man's conscience in Jewish foods and drinks.</margin>
6. **Every one in his own sense.** The Apostle does not give freedom, as the Church’s enemies would have it, for every man to do or think whatever he pleases. Rather, in this matter of the Jewish observation of days and foods—and only for a time, until the Christian religion should be perfectly established—he wanted no restraint made. He intended for everyone to be tolerated in his own judgment, yet in such a way that they should not condemn one another, nor make the observation of Jewish rites (regarding foods, days, etc.) a necessity for salvation.

<margin>Not eating, but disobedience is damnable.</margin>
17. **Not food and drink.** The substance of religion or the kingdom of God does not consist in food or drink; therefore, they could better practice indifference and tolerance in that point for a time, for the sake of peace and to avoid scandal. But if the precept of Moses' Law had still been binding as before, then (not for the food's sake, but because of the disobedience) it would have been damnable to have eaten the unclean foods.

22. **Have it with thyself.** You who are perfect and believe or know certainly that you are free from the Law concerning foods and festivities: for the sake of the trouble and hindrance of the weak who cannot yet be brought so far, be discreet and do not reveal your freedom at an inappropriate time.

<margin>To act against our conscience is sin.</margin>
23. **He that discerneth.** If the weak person has a conscience about it, and should be driven to eat the things which in his own heart he thinks he should not, he commits a deadly sin, because he acts against his conscience or against his own supposed knowledge.

<margin>John Chrysostom, Homily 26 on the Epistle to the Romans.</margin>
<margin>What actions of infidels are sin, and what are not.</margin>
23. **All this is not of faith.** The proper sense of this speech is that everything a man does against his knowledge or conscience is a sin; in this context, "faith" must be understood as such. Although Saint Augustine sometimes applies this to prove that all the actions of infidels (meaning those works which directly proceed from their lack of faith) are sins. But by all means, take heed of the Heretics' commentary, who by this would try to prove that an infidel <note>In this context, "infidel" refers to a non-Christian.</note> sins in honoring his parents, fighting for his country, tilling his ground, and in all other works. And it is no wonder they hold this of <margin>Martin Luther.</margin> infidels, since they maintain that Christian men also commit deadly sin in every good deed.

## A N N O T A T I O N S
### CHAPTER XVI.

<margin>That Saint Peter was at Rome.</margin>
<margin>See the Annotations 1 Peter chapter 5, verse 13.</margin>
16. *Salute one another.*] Never have leaders of sects <note>original: "Sectmaisters"</note> made more foul or difficult shifts to prove or defend falsehood than the Protestants; but in two points, specifically regarding Saint Peter, they surpass even themselves in impudence. The first is that they hold he was not preferred before the other Apostles, which is most evidently against all Scriptures. The second is that he was never at Rome, which is against all the ecclesiastical histories, all the Greek and Latin Fathers, and against the very sense and sight of the monuments of his Seat, Sepulcher, doctrine, life, and death there. There is certainly greater evidence and more weighty testimony of this than of Romulus, Numa, Caesar, or Cicero being there; yet a man would be very brutish to deny this to the discredit of so many writers and the whole world. It is much more monstrous to hear anyone deny the other. Theodoret says he was there, writing upon this chapter. Prosper also in his poem *Concerning the Ungrateful* at the beginning <note>original: "carmine de ingratis in principio"</note>. Saint Leo in his sermon *On the Birthday of Peter* <note>original: "de natali Petri"</note>. Saint Augustine in volume 6, chapter 4, *Against the Fundamental Epistle* <note>original: "cont. ep. fund."</note>. Orosius in book 7, chapter 6. Saint Chrysostom on Psalm 48. Saint Epiphanius in *Heresy 27* <note>original: "hær. 27"</note>. Prudentius in his second hymn for Saint Lawrence, and hymn 12. Optatus in book 2 *Against the Donatists*. Saint Ambrose in book 5, in his *Epistle on Handing Over the Basilicas* <note>original: "ep. de Basilicis tradendis"</note>. Saint Jerome in his *Catalog*. Lactantius in book 4, chapter 21, *On True Wisdom* <note>original: "de vera sapientia"</note>. Eusebius in *Ecclesiastical History* <note>original: "hist. Eccl."</note> book 2, chapters 13 and 15. Saint Athanasius in his work *On His Flight* <note>original: "de fuga sua"</note>. Saint Cyprian in epistle 55, number 6. Tertullian in *On Prescriptions* <note>original: "de præscriptionibus"</note> number 14 and book 4 *Against Marcion* <note>original: "contra Marcionem"</note> number 4. Origen on Genesis as cited by Eusebius <note>original: "apud Euseb."</note> in book 3, chapter 1. Irenaeus in book 3, chapter 3. Hegesippus in book 3, chapter 2 *On the Destruction of Jerusalem* <note>original: "de excid. Hierofolym."</note>. Caius and Papias, the Apostles' own scholars, and Dionysius the Bishop of Corinth, alleged by Eusebius in book 2, chapters 14 and 24. Ignatius in his *Epistle to the Romans* <note>original: "ep. ad Romanos"</note>. <margin>Council of Chalcedon, acts.</margin> The holy Council of Chalcedon and many others affirm it. Yes, Peter himself (according to the judgment of the ancient Fathers) confesses he was at Rome, calling it Babylon in his first epistle, chapter 5. Eusebius book 2, chapter 14 of his *Ecclesiastical History*. Some of these tell the time and cause of his first going there; some, how long he lived there; some, the manner of his death there; some, the place of his burial; and all, that he was the first Bishop there. How could so many of such wisdom and spirit, so near the Apostles' time, deceive or be deceived? How could Calvin and his followers, after fifteen hundred years, know that which none of them could see?

<margin>The Protestants' great argument that Peter was never at Rome.</margin>
<margin>Epiphanius, Heresy 27.</margin>
They must need some great argument to override the credit of the whole world. This, in truth, is their argument here—nor do they have a better one in any place—namely: If Saint Peter had been at Rome, Saint Paul would have saluted him, just as he did others here at the end of his letter to the Romans. Is this not a high point from which to disprove all antiquity? Any man of discretion can immediately see that Saint Peter might have been known by Saint Paul to be out of the city, either due to persecution or business, when this epistle was written (for he went out often, as Saint Epiphanius declares); thus, the failure to salute him proves nothing more than that he was not in Rome at that moment. But it does not even prove that much, because the Apostle might, out of respect for Peter's dignity or other Church affairs, have written to him in separate letters, and so had no cause to salute him in his common Epistle. Or how do they know that this Epistle was not sent enclosed to Saint Peter, to be delivered by his means to the whole Church of the Romans in one of their assemblies? It is very likely it was recommended to some one principal man or other who is not named here; and there may be twenty causes unknown to us why he did not salute him. There is no cause why our adversaries, based on such frivolous reasons, should reject an approved truth. For they might just as well say that Saint John was never at Ephesus because Saint Paul, in his Epistle to the Ephesians, does not salute him. And it is plain that it is the Roman seat and the faith of Peter which they (like all heretics before them) [attack]

<margin>Kissing the Pax.</margin>
<margin>Origen, Commentary on Romans, Book 15.</margin>
16. *Holy kiss.*] From this, and by the common custom of the first Christians—who had special regard for unity and peace among themselves, and as a sign and public profession of it, kissed one another—came our holy ceremony of giving the <term>Pax</term><note>The Pax is a liturgical object or gesture (like the "Sign of Peace") used in the Mass to symbolize Christian unity.</note>, or kissing one another during the Sacrifice of the Holy Mass.

<margin>Against leaders of sects: how to examine our faith.</margin>
17. *To mark them.*] He carefully warns them to look out for those who stir up rebellion and sow seeds of sects and division in religion. This is always to be their identifying mark: if they should teach or move them toward anything that does not agree with what they learned at their initial conversion. We should not follow their demand to examine the case by the Scriptures alone, but rather by the first form of faith and religion delivered to them before they had even read any book of the New Testament. <note>The author argues that tradition and the initial "rule of faith" taught by the Apostles precede the written Bible as a standard for truth.</note>

<margin>Heretics given to physical pleasures.</margin>
18. *But their own belly.*] However much heretics pretend in words and the external appearance of "sheep's clothing," in reality they seek only their own profit and pleasure. By the Apostle’s own testimony, we are authorized to judge them as men who truly have no religion or conscience.

19. *Your obedience.*] Against heretics and their deceptions, there is no better way than to cling in simplicity to that which has been taught before; for this, the Roman obedience is greatly praised. *See the Annotations for the first chapter, verse 8.*

How Saint Paul established the Church at Corinth, staying there for a year and a half, we read in *Acts 18.* After that, while he was at Ephesus (*Acts 19*), near the end of the three years he stayed there, he wrote this first Letter to the Corinthians.

<margin>
Acts 19:21.

1 Corinthians 16:5.

*For just as Saint Luke writes there, when these things were finished, Paul determined in the Spirit—after he had traveled through Macedonia and Achaia—to go to Jerusalem. Likewise, Saint Paul himself writes here: "I will come to you in Achaia once I have passed through Macedonia, for I intend to travel through Macedonia. But I will remain at Ephesus until Pentecost."*

*The subject he writes about is not a single one, as in the Letter to the Romans, but varied. It concerns partly the faults reported to him by those from Chloe's household (1 Corinthians 1:11) and partly the questions they themselves wrote to him about:* "Now concerning the things you wrote to me" (*1 Corinthians 7:1*). *Therefore, we may (it seems) divide the Letter into these two parts. Or, to group them all together, he writes about eight things: 1. Concerning certain <term>schisms</term><note>A schism is a formal division or split within a religious body, often caused by differing loyalties to specific teachers.</note> starting among them because of certain preachers, whom he addresses more clearly in the Second Letter as "false apostles" (chapters 1, 2, 3, 4). 2. Concerning a man involved in incest, and those who took their legal disputes before non-Christian judges (chapters 5, 6). 3. Concerning marriage and <term>continency</term><note>Continency refers to self-restraint, specifically the choice to refrain from sexual relations for religious reasons.</note> (chapter 7). 4. Concerning food sacrificed to idols (chapters 8, 9, 10). 5. Concerning his traditions (chapter 11). 6. Concerning the gifts of the Holy Spirit (chapters 12, 13, 14). 7. Concerning the Resurrection (chapter 15). 8. Concerning the collection of money he gathered from the Gentiles to help the Jewish Christians in Jerusalem (chapter 16).*

<header>CHAPTER 2. TO THE CORINTHIANS. 427</header>

### ANNOTATIONS
#### CHAPTER 1.

<margin>Faith comes by hearing rather than reading.</margin>
5. *In all knowledge.*] Observe that the Apostles never wrote their letters except to those who were converted to Christ's faith beforehand. For men cannot easily learn the Christian religion by reading Scriptures, but by hearing, and by the presence of their teachers, who may instruct them at length and particularly on every Article, which they could not do as clearly and briefly by letters. Neither does any man now learn his faith first except by hearing from his parents and masters. For if we should, when we come to years of discretion, be set to pick our faith out of the Scriptures, there would be a mad work and many faiths among us. <note>The author is emphasizing the Catholic tradition of "Oral Tradition" and the teaching authority of the Church over the Protestant principle of *Sola Scriptura* (Scripture alone).</note>

<margin>Christ is made our justice, because he is the author of the justice in us.</margin>
30. *Who is made.*] He does not mean, as our <term>adversaries</term><note>A common 16th-century term for Protestant reformers.</note> captiously argue, that we have no justice, wisdom, nor sanctity of our own, other than Christ's <term>imputed</term><note>The theological concept that Christ's righteousness is credited to a believer's account, rather than being an internal change in the person.</note> to us. Rather, the sense is that he is made the author, giver, and meritorious cause of all these virtues in us. For the Apostle interprets himself plainly in the 6th Chapter following, when he writes: *You are washed, you are justified, you are sanctified in the name of our Lord JESUS CHRIST and in the Spirit of our God.*

# ANNOTATIONS
## CHAPTER 2.

<margin>How Angels, Saints, and mortal men know our thoughts.</margin>
11. *But the spirit of man.*] One man cannot naturally know another's secret thoughts <note>original: "cogitations"</note>: but God often gives to Prophets and others, even in this world, the extraordinary grace to know the secrets of men. He did this for St. Peter, so he could know the fraud of Ananias and Sapphira <margin>Acts 5</margin>; and for Elisha <note>original: "Eliseus"</note>, so he could know his servant’s bribery in his absence, and what was being done in the King of Syria’s bedchamber <margin>2 Kings 5 & 6</margin> <note>original: "4. reg." referring to the Fourth Book of Kings in the Vulgate, known today as 2 Kings.</note>. In the same way, He grants to all * Angels and Saints (as far as is necessary for our needs and their heavenly glory) the ability to understand not only our spoken prayers, but <margin>Luke 15:7</margin> our inward repentance and desires.

<margin>The Heretics' claim for their empty security, answered.</margin>
12. *That we may know.*] The Protestants, who claim that a "particular spirit" reveals to each individual person their own predestination, justification, and salvation, would try to twist this text for that purpose. However, this passage means nothing else (as is clear from the Apostle’s argument) than that the Holy Spirit has given to the Apostles, and through them to other Christians, the knowledge of God’s unspeakable gifts bestowed upon believers in this time of grace: that is, Christ’s Incarnation, Passion, presence in the <term>Sacrament</term><note>Specifically the Eucharist or Real Presence.</note>, and the incomprehensible joys of heaven, which Pagans, Jews, and Heretics mock.

<margin>The sensual man.</margin>
14. *The sensual man.*] The "sensual man" is specifically one who measures these heavenly mysteries by natural reason, human prudence, physical senses, and worldly affection—just as the Jew, Pagan, and Heretic do. Sometimes, both here and elsewhere, the weaker and more ignorant sort of Christians are called sensual or carnal as well; because they are occupied with secular affairs and given to physical joy and worldliness, they have no such sense or feeling of these great gifts of God as the more "perfect" sort of the faithful have. Those who test these high points of religion—not by reason and sense, but by grace, faith, and the Spirit—are therefore called "spiritual."

<margin>The spiritual man.</margin>
The spiritual man, then, is he who judges and discerns the truth of such things that the carnal man cannot reach. By the spirit of the Church (of which he is a part through its unity), he not only sees the errors of the carnal but condemns them and judges every power that resists God’s spirit and word. The carnal Jew, Heathen, or Heretic has no means or right to judge the aforementioned spiritual man.

<margin>How the spiritual man judges all, and is judged by none.</margin>
For when it is said that the spiritual man is "judged by none," the meaning is not that he should be exempt from being subject or obedient to his Pastors and spiritual Authorities or the whole Church—especially regarding the examination of his life, doctrine, and faith. Rather, it means that a Catholic man, and specifically a teacher of Catholic doctrine in the Church, should not be subject at all to the judgment of the Heathen or the Heretic, nor care what they say against him out of ignorance or infidelity. For such carnal men have no judgment in such matters, nor can they attain the Church’s wisdom in any ceremony, mystery, or matter which they condemn.
