## A N N O T A T I O N S
### CHAPTER III.

<margin>Good works are meritorious, and the rewards in heaven are different according to the same.</margin>
<margin>Reward <note>original: "μισθος" (misthos)</note>.</margin>
<margin>1 Tim. 5:18.</margin>
<margin>Apoc. 22:12. Mat. 16:27. Rom. 2:6.</margin>
<margin>according to works <note>original: "κατὰ τὰ ἔργα" (kata ta erga)</note>.</margin>
8. *Every man shall receive according.*] A most plain text for proof that men, by their labors and by the differences between them, shall be diversely rewarded in heaven: and therefore that by their works proceeding from grace, they do deserve or merit heaven, and more or less joy within it. For though the holy Scripture commonly does not use this word *merit*, yet in innumerable places of the Old and New Testament, the very true sense of merit is contained; and so often as the word "reward" <note>original: "merces"</note> and the like are used, they are always understood as correlatives or corresponding to it. For if the joy of heaven is retribution, repayment, hire, or wages for works (as in infinite places of holy Scripture), then the works can be nothing other than the value, desert, price, worth, and merit of the same. And indeed this word "reward," which in our English tongue may signify a voluntary or bountiful gift, does not so well express the nature of the Latin word, or the Greek <note>original: "μισθος" (misthos)</note>, which are rather the very stipend that the hired workman or day-laborer contracts to have from him whose work he does; it is a thing equally and justly answering to the time and weight of his travels and works. In this sense the Scripture says, *The worker is worthy of his hire* <note>original: "Dignus est operarius mercede sua"</note>, rather than a free gift. Though, because faithful men must acknowledge that their merits are the gifts and graces of God, they rather use the word "reward" than "hire," "stipend," or "repayment." Though indeed they are all one, as you may see by various places of holy writ: such as, *My reward is with me to render to every one according to his works.* And *Our Lord will render to me according to my justice.* (Psalm 17). And the very word "merit" itself (equivalent to the Greek) is used thus: *Mercy shall make a place for everyone according to the merit of works.* (Ecclesiasticus 16:15). And *If you do your justice before men, you shall not have reward in heaven.* (Matthew 6:1), where you see that the reward of heaven is a recompense for justice. And the excuse of the Heretics <note>The authors are likely referring to Protestant Reformers who denied the doctrine of merit.</note> is frivolous and evidently false, as the former and similar words prove; for they say heaven is our "reward" not because it is due to our works, but due to the promise of God. Yet the words are plain: *According to every man's works* or labors—upon which works, and for which works conditionally, the promise of heaven was made.

<margin>Building of gold, or stubble.</margin>
12. *Upon this foundation.*] The foundation is Christ, and faith in him working through charity. The upper building may be either pure and perfect matter of gold, silver, and precious stone—which (according to the most authentic and probable exposition) are good works of charity and all Christian justice done by God’s grace—or else, wood, hay, stubble, which signify the manifold acts of man’s infirmity and his venial sins <note>Venial sins are considered lesser sins that do not fully separate a person from God's grace but require purification.</note>. These, being more or less mixed and mingled with the better matter mentioned before, require more or less punishment or purgation <note>Purification, referring to Purgatory.</note> at the day of our death. At which

<meta>The catchword "day" indicates the next page continues the discussion of the "day of our death" or the day of judgment.</meta>

The commentary provides a robust Catholic defense of the doctrine of merit, arguing that heavenly rewards are justly earned through works performed under God's grace.</summary>

<page-num>431</page-num>
<header>CHA. III. TO THE CORINTHIANS.</header>
<meta>catchword: So</meta>

day, if by penance or other means in the Church, the said venial sins <note>In Catholic theology, venial sins are lesser sins that do not fully break a person's relationship with God but still require purification.</note> be beforehand cleansed, there shall need no purging at all, but they shall straight receive the reward due to them.

<margin>Our works shall be manifested by fire.</margin>
13. *Shall be manifest.*] Whether our life and works be pure and need no cleansing, now in this world is hard to judge: but the day of our Lord, which is at our death, will make it plain in what terms every man's life is towards God. For then Purgatory fire shall reveal and prove it. For, whosoever has any impure matter of venial sins or such other debts, payable and purgable to God’s justice, must into that fire, and after due payment and cleansing, be saved through the same. Where the works of the perfect men and such as died with all debts paid, cleansed, or forgiven, are quitted from the fire, and never incur damage, pain, or loss thereby. The places of the Church Fathers expounding this as Purgatory are very many and most evident, which are cited in the last Annotation following.

<margin>Calvin on this place.</margin>
<margin>the day <note>original Greek: ἡ ἡμέρα</note></margin>
<margin>What is signified by "the day of our Lord."</margin>
13. *The day of our Lord shall declare.*] That this purgation signifies the place of God's justice after our death, rather than any affliction in this life, is declared by the Apostle’s precise specifying of fire, and of revealing and notifying the difference of men's works by the same: which is not always done evidently in this life. Specifically, the phrase, *day of our Lord* <note>original Latin: "dies Domini"</note>: which commonly and properly signifies in Scripture and namely in this Apostle (1 *Cor.* 5:5, 2 *Cor.* 1:13, *Philip.* 1:10, 6, 1 *Thess.* 5:2, 2 *Thess.* 2:2) either the particular, or the general judgment. Therefore, the trial spoken of is not properly nor literally meant as any affliction or adversity of this life, as Calvin <note>John Calvin (1509–1564), a primary leader of the Protestant Reformation who rejected the doctrine of Purgatory.</note> also confesses, though coining a foolish new construction of his own. Where you may note also in that man’s Commentary, that this word, *day of the Lord*, was so prejudicial against him and all other interpretations of the trial being made in this world, that he would gladly have had (*Lord*) out, reading thus, *A day shall come which shall open* etc. Understand here, that if it were only *Day* (as it is in the Greek) <note>original Greek: ἡ ἡμέρα</note> yet thereby also the Scripture is accustomed to signify the selfsame thing: as in 2 *Tim.* 1:12, 18 and 2 *Tim.* 4:8, and *Heb.* 10:25, *the day*, as in this place, with the Greek article only, which is all one with *That day* <note>original Latin: "Dies illa"</note>, or *The day of our Lord*.

<margin>Two fires after this life: one eternal, the other temporal, that is, the purging or amending fire.</margin>
<margin>Purgatory fire exceeds all the pains of this life.</margin>
15. *As by fire.*] St. Augustine <note>A highly influential 4th-century bishop and theologian.</note> upon these words of the Psalm 37, *Lord rebuke me not in your indignation, nor amend me in your wrath.* For it shall come to pass (says he) that some are amended in the wrath of God, and are rebuked in his indignation. And not all perhaps that are rebuked shall be amended, but yet some there shall be saved by amending. It shall be so surely, because amending is named: yet so as by fire. But some there shall be that shall be rebuked, and not amended, to whom he shall say, "Go you into everlasting fire." Fearing therefore these more grievous pains, he desires that he may neither be rebuked in indignation by eternal fire, nor amended in his wrath. That is to say, "Purge me in this life, and make me such a one as shall not need the amending fire," being for those who shall be saved, yet so as by fire. Why? Because here they build upon the foundation wood, hay, and stubble? For if they did build gold, silver, and precious stones, they should be secure from both fires—not only from that eternal fire which shall torment the impious eternally, but also from that which shall amend them that shall be saved by fire. For it is said, "he shall be safe, yet so as by fire." And because it is said, "he shall be safe," that fire is often held in contempt. Yea, verily, though safe by fire, yet that fire shall be more grievous than whatsoever a man can suffer in this life. And you know how great evils the wicked have suffered, and may suffer: yet they have suffered such as the good also might suffer. For what has any criminal suffered by the laws that a Martyr has not suffered in the confession of Christ? These evils therefore that are here are much easier, and yet see how men, in order not to suffer them, do whatsoever you command. How much better do they do that which God commands, so that they may not suffer those greater pains? Thus far St. Augustine. See also St. Ambrose upon this place, 1 Cor. 3 and Sermon 20 on Psalm 118; Jerome, book 2, chapter 13 against Jovinian; Gregory, book 4 of the Dialogues, chapter 39, and on the 3rd Penitential Psalm at the beginning; Origen, homily 6 on Exodus chapter 15, and homily 14 on Leviticus chapter 24. <note>These citations are to the "Church Fathers," early Christian theologians whose writings the author uses to prove that the belief in Purgatory dates back to the early centuries of the Church.</note>

### ANNOTATIONS
### CHAPTER 4.

<margin>No man is certain of grace or justification.</margin>
*4. But not justified.]* The Reformers <note>original: "Heretikes"; referring to the Protestant view of assurance of salvation</note> are certain that they are in God’s grace, but Saint Paul, though guilty of no crime in his conscience, dared not assure himself that he was justified, nor could he take it upon himself to be the judge of his own heart and thoughts, whether they were pure or not; instead, he left the trial of such matters only to God’s day of judgment.

<margin>Spiritual power to punish or pardon.</margin>
*21. With a rod.]* The Apostles possess the power of discipline and the ability to issue censures against offenders, as well as the power of gentleness, meekness, and indulgence. They may use either punishment or pardon according to their wisdom and the requirements of time and place.

->A N N O T A T I O N S<-

3. *I absent.*] Saint Paul here uses his Apostolic power of binding this incestuous person, excommunicating him by his letters and *Mandatum* <note>an official command or mandate</note>, even though he is absent.

<margin>The authority of Church censures resides in the Clergy only, and is executed in the name of Christ.</margin>
4. *You being gathered,*] Though he commanded the act should be performed in the presence of the Church—just as such sentences and censures are executed today—nevertheless, the judgment and the authority to give the sentence was in himself, and not in the whole multitude, as the Protestants and the popular Sectaries <note>radical groups advocating for congregational rule</note> claim. For the power of binding and loosing was not given to the whole Church, but to the persons of the Prelates <note>high-ranking clergy</note>, and to them for the benefit of the whole body. Whereupon Saint Chrysostom, commenting on those words, *Dic Ecclesiæ* <note>original: "Tell the Church"; Matthew 18:17</note>, says: "Complain to the Church, that is," he says, "to the Prelates and Presidents thereof."

4. *With the power.*] All such great power over sinners is held and exercised in the name and power of CHRIST JESUS. And whoever treats it lightly despises our Lord’s name and power.

<margin>The terrible sentence of excommunication.</margin>
5. *To Satan,*] This is to assure us that all excommunicated persons are in the power and possession of the Devil, and entirely outside of Christ's protection as soon as they are separated by the Church’s sentence from her body, the Sacraments, and the fellowship of Christian Catholic men. It pleased God to give power to the Apostles and Prelates in the early Church to cause the Devil, immediately upon their sentence of excommunication, to invade the body of the excommunicated person and to torment him physically. So Christ excommunicated Judas, and the Devil entered into him, and he went out from the happy fellowship of the Apostles <note>original reference: "John 13:27"</note>. So this Apostle excommunicated Alexander and Hymenaeus, and Satan immediately took them <note>original reference: "1 Timothy 1"</note>. Indeed, it is thought that Saint Peter <margin>*Acts 5*</margin> excommunicated Ananias and Sapphira, and as a sign of his power and the terror of the sentence, struck them both stone dead <note>original reference: "On the Miracles of Holy Scripture, book 3 chapter 16, attributed to Saint Augustine"</note>. Although this miraculous power is not joined to that sentence now, yet as far as it concerns spiritual punishment—which it especially pertains to—it remains as before. According to the judgment of the holy Doctors <note>including Cyprian, Chrysostom, Ambrose, Jerome, and Augustine</note>, it is the most terrible and greatest punishment in the world, far surpassing all earthly pain and torment in this life, being a true resemblance of damnation. <margin>*Deuteronomy 17*</margin> *And by this spiritual sword* (says Saint Cyprian) *all must die in their souls who do not obey the Priests of Christ in the new law, just as those who were disobedient to the judges of the old law were slain with the physical sword.* Would to God the world knew what a marvelous punishment Christ has appointed the Priests to execute upon the offenders of his laws, and especially upon the disobedient, such as Heretics.

<margin>Purity in receiving the Blessed Sacrament.</margin>
8. *Let us feast.*] The Pascal lamb, which was the most perfect figure of Christ in every way, was first sacrificed and afterward eaten with *azymes* <note>unleavened bread</note>. So Christ our Passover, <margin>*Exodus 12*</margin> having been newly sacrificed on the Cross, is recommended to them as one to be eaten with all purity and sincerity in the holy Sacrament. These mysteries the holy Church commends to the faithful every year at the feast of Easter using these words.

<margin>We are bound to avoid, not all sinners, but</margin>
11. *Not to take meat.*] It is not meant that we should separate ourselves physically from all sinners, or that we might refuse to live in one Church or fellowship of Sacraments with them—which was the error and cause of the Donatists' <note>a schismatic group that argued the church must be a society of saints</note> great schism. Nor is it meant that every man is immediately excommunicated after he has committed any deadly sin, as some Lutherans hold; but that we should

### ANNOTATIONS
#### CHAPTER VI.

<margin>Going to law before non-Christian or heretical judges.</margin>
6. *Contends in judgment.* ] To be given much to quarreling <note>original: "brabling"</note> and litigiousness for every trifle—to spend a pound rather than lose a penny—the Apostle greatly rebukes in Christian men. For a Christian man to draw another to the judgment seats and courts of Heathen <note>non-Christian</note> Princes (who then alone reigned) and not to allow their controversies and quarrels to be settled among themselves brotherly and peaceably, was a great fault. Likewise, for one Catholic to draw another before secular or heretical officers for mere trifles is a very un-Christian act.

<margin>Going to law is not forbidden, but it is better to agree otherwise.</margin>
7. *A fault.* ] He did not forbid all judgments of controversies, but only indicated that it was a fault, and that it proceeded from some injuries done to one another and from imperfections, that they so troubled one another. It would have been more agreeable to Christian perfection and charity to instead tolerate and suffer a small injury rather than to drag a fellow believer to the judgment seats.

## ANNOTATIONS
### CHAPTER VII.

<margin>1 Corinthians 7 verse 2.</margin>
<margin>The Apostle does not bid all to marry, but to keep the wives they married before.</margin>
2. *His own wife.*—] He does not say, as the Protestants here pretend in order to excuse the unlawful joining of those under vows <note>This refers to monks or nuns who left their cloisters to marry during the Reformation</note>, *Let every one marry*: but, *let every one have, keep, or use his own wife* to whom he was married before his conversion. For the Apostle answers here to the first question of the Corinthians, which was not whether it were lawful to marry, but whether they were not bound upon their conversion to abstain from the company of their wives married before in their infidelity, as some did persuade them that they ought to do. <note>original: "Hiero. li. 1 cont. Iouin. c. 4. Chrys. in hunc locum ho. 19." — Jerome, Book 1 against Jovinian, chapter 4; Chrysostom, Homily 19 on this passage.</note>

3. *Let the husband render.*—] These words reveal the Apostle's intention and talk to be only of such as are already married, and to instruct them of the bond and obligation that is between the married couple for rendering the "debt" of sexual intimacy <note>original: "carnal copulation"</note> one to another: declaring that the married persons have yielded their bodies so to one another, that they cannot without mutual consent, neither permanently nor for a time, defraud one another.

<margin>Abstinence in married folks for the sake of prayer.</margin>
5. *Give yourself to prayer.*—] This current time, and the Heretics' <note>The Catholic translators here refer to the Protestant Reformers as heretics</note> doctrine and high estimation of matrimonial acts, are far from the purity of the Apostolic and primitive Church, when the Christians, to make their prayers and fastings more acceptable to God, abstained by mutual consent even from their lawful wives. Our new Masters <note>The Protestant leaders</note> do not much abstain (as it may be thought) from their wives for any such matter. And yet St. Augustine says the Prelate <note>A high-ranking member of the clergy</note> should surpass others in this case, and think that what might be endured in others is not lawful for him, because he must daily stand in Christ’s place, offer sacrifice, baptize, and pray for the people. So says he in <note>original: "li. 1. q. ex vtroque test. q. 127 in fine." — Book 1, Questions on both Testaments, question 127 at the end.</note> <note>See St. Jerome, Book 1, chapter 19 against Jovinian; St. Ambrose, Book 1 on Offices, last chapter.</note> But alas for the people, whose married Pastors are in this point far worse than the common folk, neither teaching self-control <note>original: "continencie"</note> nor giving a good example.

<margin>Perpetual abstinence in married folks is better than sexual intimacy.</margin>
6. *By indulgence, not commandment.*—] Lest some might misinterpret his former words, as though he had precisely commanded married persons not to abstain perpetually from sexual intimacy, or not to give their consent to one another for lifelong abstinence <note>original: "continencie"</note> but for a time only: he declares plainly that he gave no rule or precept absolutely therein, but that he spoke all the aforesaid, condescending to their weaknesses <note>original: "infirmities"</note> only, suggesting that abstinence from sexual intimacy is much better, and that he himself kept it continually. <note>original: "Aug. de bon. coniug. c. 10. Enchirid. c. 78." — Augustine, On the Good of Marriage, chapter 10; Enchiridion, chapter 78.</note>

<margin>* See St. Augustine, Book 2, chapters 19 and 20, On Adulterous Marriages, chapter 6.</margin>
<margin>Who are bound to live abstinently: and that God gives this gift to all who ask for it.</margin>
7. *A proper gift.*—] To such as may lawfully marry, or are already married, God does not always give that more high and special gift or grace of self-control <note>original: "continencie"</note>, though every one of them all that duly ask and labor for it might have it: but such are not bound to endeavor or seek for it always, and therefore cannot be commanded to abstain further than they like. But whenever a man is bound to abstain, either by vow or any other necessary occasion (as if one of the parties be in prison, war, banishment, sickness, or absent perpetually by lawful divorce), the other must necessarily, under pain of damnation, abstain, and cannot excuse the lack of the gift of chastity. For he is bound to ask it and to seek for it from God by fasting, praying, and disciplining <note>original: "chastising"</note> his body: and so laboring duly for it, God will give the grace of chastity. So Saint Paul had it, and so had all the holy men that ever lived chaste. Therefore detest the doctrine of the Protestants in this point, who, when they choose not to fast nor pray for it, say they do not have the gift. And it would be a great marvel why so few of the new Sects—or rather none nowadays—have that gift, except that we see it is obtained by those means which our forefathers used, and they use not at all. To live in marriage abstinently

<page-num>440</page-num>
<header>THE FIRST EPISTLE OF ST. PAUL CHAPTER VII.</header>

...without the breach of conjugal fidelity, is a gift of God also; but men must not break their marriage vows for lack of it, but must know that this gift is given to those who humbly ask it of Him. <note>Augustine, *On Grace and Free Will*, chapter 4; *On Continence*, chapter 1.</note>

<margin>
The Apostle permits marriage to those who are free, not to those who have taken religious vows.
</margin>
9. *If they do not contain.*] <note>original: "If they conteine not." In this context, "to contain" means to exercise self-control or remain continent.</note> He refers to those who are free: for if they marry after they have made a vow or promise of chastity to God, they are worthily damned; such persons are bound to remain continent, and can do so if they choose. <note>Augustine, *On the Good of Widowhood*, chapters 8 and 9; *On Adulterous Marriages*, book 1, chapter 15; *On Faith, to Peter*, chapter 3, at the end. Ambrose, *To a Fallen Virgin*, chapter 5.</note>

<margin>
Theodoret on this passage.
</margin>
9. *Better to marry.*] It is better to marry for the aforementioned persons who are free, than to be overcome and fall into fornication. For, *to burn*, or, *to be burnt*, does not mean simply to be tempted (as the Protestants think, who easily pick quarrels in order to marry), but it signifies to yield to <term>concupiscence</term> <note>strong sexual desire or lust</note> either in mind or through external actions. We say this also applies to those who are free. As for others who have been lawfully ordained as Priests, and those who have otherwise made a vow of chastity, they cannot marry at all; therefore, there is no comparison for them between marriage and fornication or "burning," for their marriage is merely a pretense, and is the worst sort of incontinence, fornication, or burning.

<margin>
No remarriage after divorce.
</margin>
11. *To remain unmarried.*] Neither party may dismiss the other and marry someone else for any cause; for even if they are separated due to fornication, neither may marry again. <note>Augustine, *On Adulterous Marriages*, book 1, chapters 8 and 9, and book 2, chapters 5 and 19. See the Annotations for Matthew 19, and St. Augustine in his entire books *On Adulterous Marriages*, volume 6.</note>

<margin>
The Apostle's precepts.
</margin>
12. *I say, not our Lord.*] By this we learn that there were many matters beyond the things that Christ taught or prescribed that were left to the Apostles' ordering and interpretation. In these matters they might, as the case required, either command or counsel, and we are bound to obey accordingly.

<margin>
How the unbeliever, or the children of unbelievers, are sanctified by the Christian spouse.
</margin>
<margin>
Jerome, book 1, chapter 5, *Against Jovinian*.
</margin>
14. *Sanctified.*] When the unbelieving party is said to be clean or sanctified by the faithful spouse, or the children of their marriage are said to be clean, we must not think that they are in a state of grace or salvation because of it. It only means that the marriage is an occasion for the <term>sanctification</term> <note>the process of being made holy</note> of the unbelieving party and the children. For St. Augustine (<note>*On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, book 3, chapter 12</note>) concludes against the Pelagians—as we may do against the Calvinists, who hold that the children of Christians are holy from their mother's womb and do not need Baptism—that whatever other sanctification is meant here, it cannot be enough for salvation without faith, Baptism, and so on.

19. *But the observation.*] Neither being a Jew nor a Gentile, enslaved or free, married or single, nor even the faith itself which is proper to Christians, will suffice for salvation without good works and keeping the commandments. <note>St. Jerome, *Against Jovinian*, book 1, chapter 16.</note>

<margin>
The difference between counsels and precepts.
</margin>
<margin>
Augustine, *On Virginity*, chapters 13 and 14.
</margin>
25. *Counsel I give.*] A <term>counsel</term> <note>a recommendation for a higher spiritual path, like celibacy</note> is one thing; a <term>precept</term> <note>a direct command or law</note> is another. To do what is counseled is not strictly necessary, because one may be saved regardless; but he who chooses to do what is counseled shall have a higher degree of glory. He who does not fulfill a commandment, unless he performs penance, cannot escape punishment. <note>Augustine, *On Virginity*, chapters 13 and 14.</note>

<margin>
A professed virgin may not marry.
</margin>
28. *If a virgin marry.*] He is not speaking of a virgin who has dedicated herself to God (for if any such person marries, she shall be damned for breaking her first vow), but only of young unmarried women living in the world. <note>Jerome, *Against Jovinian*, book 1, chapter 7; Chrysostom, Homily 20; Theodoret, Photius, and the other Greek Doctors on this place in the works of Oecumenius; Epiphanius, *Against Heresies*, 61.</note>

<margin>
Virginity counseled as more meritorious.
</margin>
28. *Tribulation of the flesh.*] They are marvelously deceived (says St. Augustine in *On Virginity*, chapter 13) who think the Apostle counsels virginity over marriage only because marriage has many miseries and troubles joined to it—which virginity avoids—rather than in respect of the greater reward in heaven. For the Apostle's prudent counseling of virginity is for the next life; he mentions these troubles of marriage specifically in the sense that they are a hindrance to the service of God here, and therefore an impediment toward the next life and its more ample joys.

<margin>
The self-control of married people.
</margin>
<margin>
Their perpetual self-control is best.
</margin>
29. *As though they had not.*] He exhorts those who have wives not to entirely devote themselves to the vain, transitory pleasures and voluptuousness of the flesh, but to live with such moderation that their marriage hinders them as little as possible from spiritual thoughts. This is best fulfilled by those who, by mutual consent, remain entirely continent—whether they have had children or none—valuing heavenly joys over physical offspring. These marriages are more blessed than any other, says <note>St. Augustine, *On the Lord's Sermon on the Mount*, book 1, chapter 14.</note>

<margin>
Virginity preferred, and why.
</margin>
<margin>
Why self-control is required of the clergy.
</margin>
32. *Careful for the things of our Lord.*] The Protestants might learn here, if they chose: first, that virginity is not only preferred over marriage because it is a more quiet state of life in this world, but because it is more suitable for the service of God. Secondly, that virginity has a pleasing purity and sanctity of both body and soul, which marriage does not have. Thirdly, they may learn the reason why the Church of God requires chastity in the clergy and forbids not only fornication but all sexual relations, even in lawful marriage. This is not only so that God’s Priests are not divided from Him by the burdens of marriage, but also so that they may be clean and pure from the physical acts of copulation.

### CHAPTER VIII.

->*He rebukes the learned who, in the pride of their knowledge, ate things offered to idols (<term>Idolothyta</term> <note>Greek: things sacrificed to idols</note>), exercising what they called their liberty. They failed to consider that the ignorant followed their example and ate such meats as they did before in their paganism, believing the meat itself carried some religious power.*<-

<margin>1. Knowledge without charity puffs up with pride and profits nothing at all; when it is joined with charity, then it <term>edifies</term> <note>builds up the faith of others</note>. <note>Augustine, *The City of God*, book 9, chapter 20.</note></margin>

<image-desc>An ornamental drop cap initial 'A' featuring a pastoral landscape with figures and foliage.</image-desc>
AND concerning those things that are sacrificed to idols, we know that "we all have knowledge." Knowledge puffs up, but charity edifies. † And if any man thinks that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know. † But if any man loves God, the same is known by Him. † But as for the meats that are sacrificed to idols, we know that an idol is nothing in the world, and that there is no God but one. † For although there are those called gods, whether in heaven or on earth (for there are many gods and many lords), † yet to us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and we unto Him; and one Lord, Jesus Christ, by whom are all things, and we by Him. † But not everyone has this knowledge. For "some, until this present time, with a <term>conscience</term> <note>an internal sense of religious obligation</note> of the idol, eat it as a thing sacrificed to idols; and their conscience, being weak, is defiled. † But meat does not bring us closer to God. For neither if we eat shall we abound, nor if we do not eat shall we lack. † But take heed lest perhaps this liberty of yours becomes a stumbling block to the weak. † For if a man sees him who has knowledge sitting at the table "in the idol's temple, shall not his conscience, being weak, be "edified" <note>This is used ironically here: the weak person is "built up" or encouraged to do something they believe is wrong.</note> to eat things sacrificed to idols? † And through your knowledge shall the weak brother perish, for whom Christ has died? † But sinning thus against the brethren, and wounding their weak conscience, you sin against Christ. † Wherefore, if meat <term>scandalizes</term> <note>causes to fall into sin</note> my brother, I will never eat flesh, lest I scandalize my brother.

<header>THE FIRST EPISTLE OF SAINT PAUL CHAPTER 9.</header>

<margin>The giving of <term>scandal</term> <note>original: "scandal"; here meaning a stumbling block that leads others into sin</note> is rebuked.</margin>
By nature and creation—as the <term>Manichaeans</term> <note>A dualist sect that believed physical matter was inherently evil</note> thought—meat is not evil; nor is it evil by any other pollution, such as being offered to idols. Therefore, they ate boldly of such meats that were sacrificed, look down upon and condemning their idols as mere nothing, and the worship of them as the honoring of imaginary things. However, the Apostle here rebukes this action because of their lack of discretion and charity, and for the use of their liberty to the offense and <term>scandal</term> of the weak.

7. *Some with a conscience.*] The fault of the more "perfect" men was that they caused offense to the weaker Christians by their eating. These weaker Christians, seeing those whom they considered wise and learned eating meats offered to idols, conceived that there was some virtue and sanctification in those meats derived from the idol to which they were offered; they thought that such things were, or might be, eaten with the same conscience and devotion as they had before their conversion.

<margin>The <term>Heretics</term> <note>Referring here to Protestant reformers</note> ridiculously apply Saint Paul’s words against the Church's fasts and abstinence.</margin>
Therefore, the case standing thus, and the Apostle’s discourse on eating or not eating meats being as has been declared (a thing so evident that it admits no other interpretation), if the Protestants apply any of this admonition against our fasts in the Catholic Church, they are being quite ridiculous.

<margin>Attending the Communion: what a sin it is for Catholics.</margin>
10. *In the idol’s temple.*] Just as now, some Catholics have said they know that <term>Calvin’s communion</term> <note>The Reformed service of the Lord's Supper</note> is nothing but ordinary bread and wine. Yet, when the ignorant see such people go to that Communion, they think it is a good act of religion. Indeed, whatever they may pretend, it must necessarily seem like an honor to Calvin’s communion when they are seen in the idol's temple solemnly sitting or communicating at that abominable table.

***

## CHAPTER IX.

> ->*To those who so boasted of their liberty regarding <term>Idolothyta</term> <note>Greek: things sacrificed to idols</note>, he brings his own example: namely, that he also had the liberty to live by the Gospel, yet he did not use it, so as to avoid the scandal of the weak and because it was more meritorious. He declaims against their sense of security, showing them through metaphors and examples—both of himself and of the Israelites—that salvation is not so easily attained. He then concludes again against the eating of food sacrificed to idols, because it is also an act of idolatry and not only a bad example to the weak.*<-

If others are partakers of this right over you, why not we rather? Nevertheless, we have not used this power; but we bear all things, lest we should give any offense to the Gospel of Christ.

13. Do you not know that those who work in the holy place eat the things that are of the holy place? And they that serve the altar, share with the altar? 14. So also our Lord ordained for them that preach the Gospel, to live of the Gospel.

<margin>The English Bible (1562) <note>Likely referring to the Great Bible or the Bishops' Bible used by Protestants</note> here and in the next chapter, says *temple* for *altar*: most falsely and heretically, against holy altars, which about the time of that translation were dug down in England.</margin>

15. But I have used none of these. Neither have I written these things, that they should be so done for me; for it is better for me to die, than that any man should make my glorying void. 16. For if I do this willingly, I have a reward; but if against my will, a charge is committed to me. 18. What is my reward then? That in preaching the Gospel, I may offer the Gospel without cost, so that I do not abuse my power in the Gospel.

19. For whereas I was free from all, I made myself the servant of all, that I might gain the more. 20. And I became to the Jews as a Jew, that I might gain the Jews. 21. To them that are under the Law, as though I were under the Law (whereas I myself was not under the Law) that I might gain them that were under the Law. To them that were without the Law, as though I were without the Law (whereas I was not without the law of God, but was in the law of Christ) that I might gain them that were without the Law.

<margin>Not by pretending or lying, but by compassion for the weaknesses of all sorts of people. Augustine, Letter 9.</margin>

24. Do you not know that they who run in a race, all run indeed, but one receives the prize? So run, that you may obtain it. 25. <header>THE FIRST EPISTLE OF ST. PAUL CHAPTER 9</header>

# ANNOTATIONS
## CHAPTER 9.

<margin>The Heretics' foolish pretense of God's honor.</margin>
1. *My work.*] Just as he previously called himself God's co-worker, so here he also boldly claims the conversion of the Corinthians as his own handiwork in our Lord. This takes nothing away from Christ, despite the crude accusations of the Protestants—who, under the pretense of protecting God's honor, charge Church Fathers and Catholic men for using such phrases or speech in the same sense as the Apostle when referring to the Saints or the Sacraments.

<margin>Heretical translation.</margin>
<margin>New Testament 1580.</margin>
<margin>Matthew 27.</margin>
5. *A woman a sister.*] The Heretics perversely (as they do in all other places to favor their own sect) explain this as the Apostles' wives, and translate "woman" as "wife," although it sounds like "wedding" to them. However, the Apostle clearly means the devout women who, following the custom of the Jewish people, served the preachers with necessities. Many such women followed Christ and supported him and his followers from their own resources. This is how St. Chrysostom, Theodoret, and all the Greek commentators understand it (<note>original: "Oecu. in collect super hunc lo." — Oecumenius in his collection of commentaries on this passage</note>). St. Augustine likewise in *On the Work of Monks*, chapter 4, and St. Jerome in his first book *Against Jovinian*, chapter 14, both argue and prove this by the very words of the text, as does St. Ambrose in his commentary on this place. The matter is quite plain: for why would he talk about the burden of the Corinthians supporting his wife when he himself clearly states (Chapter 7:7, 8) that he was single?

<margin>What is due to pastors and preachers.</margin>
7. *Who plays the soldier?*] He proves through the Scriptures and natural reasoning that preachers and pastors have a right to claim support from their flock, even though he himself, for specific reasons, did not use—and did not intend to use—his right and liberty in this matter.

<margin>Work of <term>supererogation</term> <note>The practice of doing more than what is strictly required by God's commandments; an act of voluntary devotion.</note>.</margin>
16. *If I preach the Gospel.*] If I were to preach out of compulsion and servile fear, or out of mere necessity because I had no other way to live and sustain myself in this world, I could not look for a reward in heaven. But now, doing it not only because it is commanded of me, but also out of love and charity—and doing it freely without putting any man to expense, voluntarily and out of a true desire to save my hearers—I shall have my reward from God. Indeed, I shall have a reward of Supererogation, which is given to those who, out of abundant charity, do more in the service of God than they are commanded, as St. Augustine explains (<note>original: "De op. Mon. c. 5." — Augustine's "On the Work of Monks," chapter 5</note>).

<margin>Doing well for the sake of reward.</margin>
23. *That I may be partaker.*] This is a remarkable passage to convict the Protestants, who do not want men to perform good works in hopes of a reward at God's hand. The Apostle expressly confesses that everything he does—whether out of duty or out of Supererogation beyond duty (such as preaching for free, working with his own hands to provide food for himself and his companions, and abstaining from many lawful things)—is all done specifically to attain the reward of heaven.

<margin>Running for the prize.</margin>
24. *So run.*] If those who run for a prize abstain from many foods and pleasures to make themselves faster and win the game, what should we not do or suffer to win the crown of glory? This crown is proposed and promised to none but those who run, labor, and strive for it.

<margin>Meritorious penance.</margin>
27. *I chastise.*] The goal of everlasting glory is not promised or set forth for "faith-only" men, for such people run at random. Rather, it is the prize for those who chastise and subdue their bodies and fleshly desires through fasting, vigils, voluntary poverty, and other afflictions. Lord, how far is the carnal doctrine of the Sectaries and the behaviors of these days from the Apostle's spirit! In this, even we who are Catholics—though we do not join the Protestants in condemning these voluntary afflictions as superfluous (much less as superstitious or injurious to Christ's death), but rather commend them highly—do not use the same zeal and diligence as our first Christian ancestors. Therefore, we are likely to be more subject to God's temporal punishments, at least in the next life, than they were.

<margin>St. Paul did not have the Protestants' security of salvation.</margin>
<margin>Augustine via Peter Lombard.</margin>
27. *Lest perhaps.*] "Here may we lambs tremble," says a holy father (<note>referring to St. Augustine as cited by Peter Lombard</note>), when the "ram," the leader of the flock, must labor so hard and punish himself (in addition to all the other miseries connected to preaching the Gospel) lest perhaps he miss the mark. A man might think St. Paul should be as sure and confident of God's grace and salvation as we poor wretched wretches are; but the Heretics' unhappy security, presumption, and faithless persuasion of their own salvation is not the *faith of the Apostles* (<note>original Latin: "fides Apostolorum"</note>) but the *faith of devils* (<note>original Latin: "fides dæmoniorum"</note>).

### ANNOTATIONS
#### CHAPTER X.

<margin>The old figures <term>symbolic types</term> of our Sacraments.</margin>
<margin>We receive greater benefits by our Sacraments than the Jews did by theirs.</margin>
<margin>Calvin on this place.</margin>
2. *the same.*] The Red Sea and the cloud were a figure <term>foreshadowing</term> of our Baptism: the Manna from heaven and water miraculously drawn out of the rock were a figure of the holy Sacrament of Christ’s body and blood. Our Sacraments contain the actual things and graces in truth, which theirs only signified. And it is an impudent forgery of the Calvinists to write upon this place that the Jews received no less the truth and substance of Christ and his benefits in their figures or Sacraments than we do in ours; and that they and we all eat and drink of the self-same meat and drink. The Apostle says only that they among themselves did all feed of one bread and drink of one rock, which was a figure of Christ—especially in that out of Christ’s side, pierced upon the Cross, gushed out blood and water for the matter of our Sacraments.

<margin>The Apostle and ancient fathers speak covertly of the Blessed Sacrament.</margin>
15. *As to wise men.*] To cause them to leave the sacrifices and meats or drinks offered to Idols, he puts them in mind of the only true Sacrifice and meat and drink of Christ’s body and blood: of which, and the sacrifice of Idols also, they might not be in any case partakers. Using this term, *as I speak to wise men* <note>original Latin: "ut prudentibus loquor"</note>, in the same sense (as it is thought) as the Fathers of the primitive Church did, giving a watchword to keep the mystery of this divine Sacrifice secret from the infidels and unbaptized. They used these words: *The faithful know, those who have been initiated know.* <note>original Latin: "Norunt fideles, norunt qui initiati sunt." This was a standard phrase used by St. Augustine and others to avoid describing the Eucharist in front of non-Christians.</note> (See Augustine on Psalms 39, 33, and 109; Origen on Leviticus; Chrysostom on Genesis and Timothy). Saint Paul says, "I speak to you boldly of this mystery as to those who are wiser and better instructed in the same."

<margin>The Apostles blessed the Chalice, and so consecrated it.</margin>
<margin>The cup which we bless. <note>original Latin: "Calix cui benedicimus"</note></margin>
<margin>Blessing <note>original Greek: "εὐλογία" (eulogia)</note></margin>
16. *Which we blesse.*] That is to say, the Chalice of Consecration which we Apostles and Priests, by Christ’s commission, do consecrate. By this speech, both the Calvinists (who use no consecration of the cup at all, blasphemously calling it "magical murmuring" and perversely referring the "blessing" only to thanksgiving to God) and the Lutherans are refuted. The Lutherans affirm Christ’s body and blood are made present only by the act of receiving. For the Apostle expressly refers the blessing to the chalice, and not to God; making the holy blood and the communion thereof the effect of the blessing.

<page-num>447</page-num>
<header>CHAPTER 10. TO THE CORINTHIANS.</header>

<margin>Our uniting to Christ by the Blessed Sacrament.</margin>
16. *The participation of the body.*] When we receive the holy Sacrament and Sacrifice of Christ’s body and blood, it joins us in soul and body and grafts us into Christ himself. This makes us partakers and, as it were, a piece of his own body and blood. *For not by love or spirit only (says Saint Chrysostom) but in very deed we are united in his flesh, made one body with him, members of his flesh and bones.* <note>original: "Chrysostom, Homily 45 on John, near the end." John Chrysostom was a 4th-century Church Father known for his eloquent preaching.</note> And Saint Cyril says, *such is the force of mystical benediction <term>the prayer of consecration</term> that it makes Christ corporally dwell in us by the communicating of his flesh.* <note>original: "Cyril, Book 10 on John, chapter 13." Cyril of Alexandria was a 5th-century theologian.</note>

<margin>Our union among ourselves by the Blessed Sacrament.</margin>
17. *One bread, one body.*] Just as we are first made one with Christ by eating his body and drinking his blood, so secondly we are joined together by this "one bread" (which is his body) and "cup" (which is his blood). This creates a perfect union and fellowship of all Catholic men in one Church, which is his Mystical Body. This name "Mystical Body" is specifically given to this community and society of faithful people because all its true members are marvelously knit together by Christ’s own body and by that same blood in this divine Sacrament. *See Saint Augustine, Book 21, chapter 25 of The City of God; Hilary, Book 8 on the Trinity, around the middle.*

18. *They that eat the hosts.*] It is also clear from the example of the Jews in their sacrifices that whoever eats any of the sacrificed victim <term>the "host" or "hostia"</term> is a participant in the Sacrifice. They are joined by duty and obligation to God, to whom the sacrifice was offered.

<margin>Participation in the Sacrament or sacrifice shows which society we belong to.</margin>
20. *I will not have you.*] The Apostle Paul concludes like this: when a Christian eats and drinks from the sacrifice or Sacrament of the altar, they participate in Christ’s body and are joined in fellowship with all Christian people who eat and drink the same. This is the "host" <term>sacrificial victim</term> of the New Law. Likewise, all who ate the sacrifices of Moses’ Law belonged to that state and were associated with the God to whom the sacrifice was made. Therefore, whoever eats the meat offered to Idols shows and professes that they belong to the communion and society of those same Idols.

<margin>The sacrifice of the altar is proved by the Apostle’s comparison with the sacrifices of Jews and Gentiles.</margin>
<margin>It is proved to be a sacrifice by the Church Fathers.</margin>
<margin>* Cyprian, Justin, Irenaeus, below.</margin>
<margin>* Malachi 1:11.</margin>
<margin>* Ambrose, Epistle 33.</margin>
<margin>The Fathers called this sacrifice the MASS.</margin>
21. *You cannot drink.*] Based on what he has already said, Paul warns them plainly: they must either abandon the sacrifice and fellowship of idols, or else give up the Sacrifice of Christ’s body and blood in the Church. In all this discussion, we should notice that our bread and chalice, our table and altar, and the participation in our sacrificial victim and offering, are compared point by point—in every effect and condition—to the altars, victims, and sacrifices of the Jews and the Gentiles. The Apostle could not have made this comparison with the Sacrament of the Altar (rather than with other sacraments or services) if it were not a true Sacrifice and the specific way Christians worship God, just as the others were for the Jews and Pagans. All the Church Fathers acknowledge this, calling it almost continually by terms they use for no other ceremony: *The lamb of God laid upon the table* <note>original: "Council of Nicaea"</note>; *the unbloody service of the Sacrifice* <note>original: "Council of Ephesus, Letter to Nestorius, page 605"</note>; *the Sacrifice of sacrifices* <note>original: "Dionysius, Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, chapter 3"</note>; *the quickening holy sacrifice*; *the unbloody host and victim* <note>original: "Cyril of Alexandria at the Council of Ephesus, Anathema 11"</note>; *the propitiatory <term>atoning</term> sacrifice both for the living and the dead* <note>original: "Tertullian, On the Soldier’s Crown; Chrysostom, Homily 41 on 1 Corinthians, Homily 3 to the Philippians, Homily 66 to the people of Antioch; Cyprian, Epistle 66 and On the Lord's Supper, number 1; Augustine, Enchiridion 109, Questions to Dulcitius, volume 4, Sermon 34 On the Words of the Apostle"</note>; *the Sacrifice of our Mediator*; *the sacrifice of our price* <term>the price of our redemption</term>; *the Sacrifice of the New Testament*; *the sacrifice of the Church* <note>original: "Augustine, Book 9, chapter 13 and Book 3 On Baptism, chapter 19"</note>; *the one and only indestructible victim without which there is no religion* <note>original: "Cyprian, On the Lord’s Supper, number 2; Chrysostom, Homily 17 to the Hebrews."</note>. It is also called: *The pure offering*; *the new offering of the New Law*; *the vital and unpolluted victim*; *the honorable and awesome Sacrifice*; *the Sacrifice of thanksgiving or Eucharistical*; and *the Sacrifice of Melchizedek*. Melchizedek, by his offering of bread and wine, specifically foreshadowed Christ’s eternal Priesthood and Christ sacrificing himself under the forms of bread and wine. This sacrifice shall continue in the Church throughout all Christian Nations in place of the offerings of the old Priesthood of Aaron, as the *Prophet Malachi foretold, and as Saint Cyprian, Saint Justin, Saint Irenaeus, and other ancient Doctors and Martyrs testify. <note>original citations for Cyprian, Justin Martyr, and Irenaeus are provided.</note> And Saint Augustine, Saint Leo, and others expressly state that this one Sacrifice has replaced and fulfilled all other types of sacrifices. It has the power and virtue of all others combined, to be offered for all persons and causes—for the living and the dead, for sins, for thanksgiving, and for any other necessity of body or soul. *These holy Fathers also call this sacred action the MASS in plain words.* <note>original citations for Augustine, the Councils of Carthage and Milevis, Leo, and Gregory are provided.</note> This is the doctrine of the Apostles and the Fathers. God grant that our opponents may find the mercy to see such an evident and invincible truth.

<margin>The distinction, and the rest, is by Catholics communicating with him.</margin>
21. *Partakers of the table.*] Although faithful people are known to be God’s own in many ways—being joined to Him and to each other, and separated from all others like Jews, Pagans, Heretics, and Schismatics by various signs like sacraments and doctrine—the most essential union or distinction lies in the Sacrifice and the Altar. Through these, God specifically communicates with his Church and <margin>communicating with the.</margin> binds it to himself, so that he acknowledges no one to be

...his [Christ's], he that is not a partaker of his one and only Table and Sacrifice in his Church. He [Paul] separates himself from all those who join in fellowship with any of the Heathens in their Idolatry, or with the Jews at their Sacrifices, or with Heretics and Schismatics at their profane and detestable table. Because this is the proper badge of their separation from Christ and his Church, and an altar purposely erected against Christ’s Altar, Priesthood, and Sacrifice, it is indeed a very sacrifice, or (as the Apostle here speaks) a table and cup of Devils; that is to say, one wherein the Devil is properly served, and Christ’s honor defiled (no less than by the altars of Jeroboam <note>Jeroboam was a king of Israel who led a schism and set up golden calves for worship to prevent his people from going to the Temple in Jerusalem.</note> or any profane superstitious rites of the Pagans). And therefore all Catholic men, if they hope to have fellowship with Christ and his members in his body and blood, must view it as Idolatry or sacrilegious superstition. They must abstain from it and from all society associated with it, just as the good Tobit did from Jeroboam’s calves and the altars in Dan and Bethel, and as the faithful did from the "High Places" and from the temple and sacrifices of Samaria. Now in Christian times we have no other Idols but heresies, nor <term>Idolothytes</term> <note>Food or meat that has been sacrificed to an idol.</note> but their false services shifted into our Churches instead of God’s true and only worship. *Cyprian, On the Unity of the Church, number 2. Jerome, on Hosea 11, Amos 8, and Habakkuk 2. Augustine, on Psalm 80, verse 10; The City of God, book 18, chapter 51.*

<margin>
How by participating with idolaters, idolatry is committed.

How to avoid scandal in things indifferent.
</margin>
22. **All things are lawful.**] Up to this point, the Apostle’s arguments and examples, by which he would turn them away from meats offered to Idols, seem plainly to condemn their actions as idolatrous, or as participating in and being accessory to Idolatry, and not only as a cause of "scandal" <note>In a religious sense, a "scandal" is an action that leads another person to stumble or sin.</note> given to the weak brothers. And so no doubt it was, in that they went into the very temple of the Idols, and—along with the rest who served the Idols—did eat and drink of the flesh and <term>libaments</term> <note>Drink offerings or liquid sacrifices.</note> directly offered to the Idol; yes, they even feasted together in the same banquets made to the honor of those Idols. This could not help but defile them and entangle them with Idolatry—not because the meat itself belonged to anyone other than God, or could be defiled or made unlawful to eat in itself, but in respect to the abuse of it and the detestable dedicating of that to the devil which belonged not to him, but to God alone. Of which sacrilegious act they ought not to be partakers, as they necessarily must be if they enter and eat with them in their solemnities. To this end has Saint Paul hitherto admonished the Corinthians. Now he declares that, otherwise, in secular feasts it is lawful to eat without excessive doubting or asking whether this or that were offered meats; and in markets to buy whatever is sold there without scruple and without seeking to know whether it be of the <term>Idolothytes</term> or not. This is with two exceptions: first, that if someone should invite him to eat, or buy this or that specifically as "sacred" and offered meats, then he should not eat it, lest he should seem to approve the offering of it to the Idol, or to like it better for that reason. Secondly, when the weak brother may take offense by it. For though it be lawful in itself to eat any of these meats without concern for the Idol, yet all lawful things are not expedient to be done in every time and place.

->CHAPTER 11.<-

2. *My precepts.*] Our Pastors and <term>Prelates</term> <note>High-ranking clergy such as bishops.</note> have authority to command, and we are bound to obey. And the Governors of the Church may take order and prescribe that which is comely in every state, as time and place require, though the things be not of the substance of our religion.

5. *Every woman.*] Whatever gifts of God soever women have, though supernatural, as some had in the Primitive Church, yet they may not forget their womanly modesty, but show themselves subject and modest, and cover their heads with a veil.

<margin>The Custom of the Church is a good answer against all wranglers.</margin>
16. *Custom.*] If women or others, to defend their disorder and <term>malapertness</term> <note>Impudence or bold disrespect.</note>, dispute or allege Scriptures and reasons, or require causes of their preachers why and by what authority they should be thus restrained in things indifferent, make them no other answer but this: "This is the custom of the Church, this is our custom." Which is a goodly rule to repress the sauciness of contentious <term>janglers</term> <note>People who argue pointlessly or noisily.</note>, who, being out of all modesty and reason, never want words and replies against the Church. Which Church—if it could then by <term>prescription</term> <note>A legal claim based on long-term use or tradition.</note> of twenty or thirty years, and by the authority of one or two of their first preachers, stop the mouths of the seditious—what should not the custom of fifteen hundred years, and the decrees of many hundred Pastors, gain of reasonable, modest, and humble men?

<margin>That heresies shall come, and wherefore.</margin>
19. *There must be heresies*] When the Apostle says, "Heresies must be," he shows the event, and not that God has directly so appointed it as necessary. For, that they exist comes from man's malice and free will; but that they be converted to the manifestation of the good and constant in faith and the Church's unity, that is God's special work of providence that works good out of evil. And because there should fall Heresies and Schisms, specially concerning the Article and use of the Blessed Sacrament of the Altar, whereof he now begins to treat, it may make us marvel the <margin>What advantage we may make of heresies.</margin> less to see so great dissensions, Heresies, and Schisms of the wicked and weak in faith concerning the same. Such things then will be, but woe to him by whom scandals or Sects do come. Let us use Heretics, says Saint Augustine, <note>original: *S. Augustinus*</note> not to that end to approve their errors, but that by defending the...

# CHAPTER 11. TO THE CORINTHIANS.

<meta>catchword: rubric</meta>

...Catholic doctrine against their deceits, we may be more watchful and wary: *because it is most truly written, There must be heresies so that those who are tested and approved may be revealed or discovered from among the hollow hearts among you.* <note>Reference to 1 Corinthians 11:19.</note> *Let us use this benefit of God’s providence. For Heretics are made of those who would err or be wicked even if they were in the Church; but being outside, they profit us exceedingly—not by teaching the truth, which they do not know, but by stirring up the carnal members in the Church to seek the truth, and the spiritual Catholics to clarify the truth. For there are innumerable holy and approved men in the Church, but they are not distinguished from others among us, nor made manifest, as long as we would rather sleep in the darkness of ignorance than behold the light of truth. Therefore, many are raised out of their sleep by Heretics to see the day of God, and they are glad for it.* Saint Augustine, chapter 8, *On True Religion* <note>original: *de vera relig.*</note>.

<margin>Council of Gangra, canon 11. Council of Laodicea, canons 27, 28.</margin>
<margin>Agapae or feasts of charity.</margin>
<margin>Whether the Apostle means the Blessed Sacrament by "our Lord’s supper."</margin>
20. **Our Lord’s supper.**] The Christians, at or about the time of the Church's only Sacrifice and their participating in it, held great feasts. These continued for a long time because they helped provide relief for the poor (funded by the wealthier members) and preserved charity and unity among all sorts of people. For this reason, the ancient Church Fathers called these feasts *Agapae* <note>original Greek: *Αγαπαι*, meaning "Charities"</note>. They were commonly held in church buildings, porches, or in the main body of the church (concerning this, see Tertullian’s *Apology, chapter 39*, Clement of Alexandria, Saint Justin, and Saint Augustine’s *Against Faustus, book 20, chapter 20*). These took place after the Sacrifice and Communion were finished, as Saint Chrysostom judges in his *27th Homily on 1 Corinthians*. Saint Paul calls these feasts *Lord's Suppers* <note>original Latin: *Cænas Dominicas*</note> because they were held in the churches, which were then called *the Lord's houses* <note>original Latin: *Dominicæ*</note>. Therefore, the Apostle seeks here to correct the disorder found among the Corinthians during these charitable church-feasts, specifically the foul abuses mentioned in the text. As Saint Ambrose notes on this passage, and as most good authors now believe, what he calls "the Lord’s supper" here does not refer to the Blessed Sacrament. The context of the text supports this: namely, the neglect of the poor, the rich privately devouring everything without waiting for others, and the gluttony and drunkenness involved—none of which can apply to the Holy Sacrament. Therefore, the Heretics <note>The author is referring to Protestant reformers.</note> have little reason to use this passage to name the Holy Sacrament "the Supper of the Lord" rather than using the terms of the primitive Church: the *Eucharist*, the *MASS*, or the *Liturgy*. It seems they prefer this name to bring it back to a literal supper or evening service where men are not fasting, primarily to diminish the ancient reverence for its holiness.

<margin>Tradition without writing.</margin>
<margin>Whether the Catholics or Protestants better imitate Christ's institution of the Blessed Sacrament.</margin>
23. **I have delivered.**] Just as all other parts of religion were first delivered through preaching and word of mouth to every nation that was converted, so too this holy order and use of the Blessed Sacrament was first given to the Corinthians by Saint Paul through tradition. He calls them back to this tradition (as something received from our Lord) through this Epistle. He does not put every specific detail regarding the order, use, and institution into writing, as he says later: *but repeating the sum and substance of it, and leaving the rest until his return.* However, we will specifically examine his words and the account written here, because the Heretics claim to follow them in their so-called reformation of the MASS.

<margin>Matthew 26; Mark 14; Luke 22.</margin>
<margin>Not all circumstances of our Savior’s actions regarding the Blessed Sacrament need to be imitated.</margin>
23. **In the night.**] First, our adversaries may be convinced here that not all circumstances of time, person, and place noted in Christ’s actions need to be imitated. For example: that the Sacrament should be administered at night, only to men, only to twelve people, during or after a supper, and similar details. As Saint Cyprian <note>Epistle 63, number 7</note> and Saint Augustine <note>Epistle 118, chapter 6</note> note, there were specific reasons for those circumstances in Christ’s time that do not apply to us now. He instituted this holy act; we do not. He made his Apostles Priests—that is to say, gave them the commission to perform and administer it; we do not. He intended this to be the final act of his life and within the context of his Passion; that is not the case for us. He intended to eat and conclude the Passover <note>original: Paschal</note> to fulfill the old Law; that cannot be part of our action. Therefore, he had to do it after supper and at night; we must not do so. He excluded all women, all his other disciples, and all laypeople; we invite all the faithful, both men and women. In many circumstances, then, neither we nor the Heretics imitate Christ’s original action. Though they seem inclined to call it "Supper" to justify having it at night or after a meal, they have no just cause to do so based on Christ’s actions. The Evangelists clearly show that the Sacrament was instituted *after* supper, as the Apostle himself records here. Most believe a long sermon and the washing of the Apostles' feet occurred in between—indeed, that the supper was entirely finished and grace had been said. In all these matters, only the Catholic Church, guided by Christ’s Spirit, can determine which actions are to be imitated and which are not.

<margin>Matthew 26; Mark 14; Luke 22.</margin>
<margin>The Protestants do not imitate Christ in blessing the bread and wine.</margin>
23. **Took.**] Christ took bread into his hands, applying this ceremony, action, and blessing to it. He blessed the very element itself, using power and an active word upon it, *just as he did over the bread and fishes which he multiplied*. The Church of God does the same. The Protestants do not, if they follow their own books and doctrine; instead, they let the bread and cup stand at a distance and use Christ’s words only as a report or a story, not applying them at all to the physical elements provided. Therefore, even though the simple people are deceived by the rehearsal of the same words Christ used, the Protestants themselves profess to perform no consecration, blessing, or sanctification of the bread and wine at all. At the first change of religion <note>referring to the English Reformation</note>, there was a sign of the Cross at the word *He blessed*; and at the word *He took*, there was a marginal note or instruction <note>original: gloss or rubrike</note>...

# THE FIRST EPISTLE OF ST. PAUL Chapter 11.

...rubric <note>A liturgical instruction, traditionally written in red ink.</note> that appointed the Minister to imitate Christ's action and to take the bread into his hands; afterward, that was reformed and Christ's action abolished, and His blessing of the bread turned into a thanksgiving to God.

<margin>
They do not imitate Him by using unleavened bread and mixing water with wine.
</margin>
23. **Bread.**] Christ made the holy Sacrament using unleavened bread, and all the Latin Church <note>The Roman Catholic Church and those following the Western rite.</note> imitates Him in this. This is considered much more agreeable to the spiritual meaning, both in itself and in our lives, than leavened bread. Yet our adversaries <note>A term used here for Protestant Reformers.</note> follow neither Christ, St. Paul, nor the Western Church in this; instead, they purposely choose a kind of bread that is in itself less seemly and less agreeable to the original institution. In the other part of the Sacrament, they hold Christ and His Church in even more impudent and damnable contempt. For Christ, all the Apostles, and all Catholic Churches in the world have always mixed their wine with water for its great mystery and significance—specifically because water gushed out together with blood from our Lord's side. Our Lord did this (says **St. Cyprian, Letter 63 to Caecilius, numbers 4, 7**), and no one offers the sacrifice correctly who does not follow Him in this. **Irenaeus (Book 5, chapter 2)**, **Justin (Apology 2, at the end)**, and all the Fathers testify that the Primitive Church did this. It is performed in this way in all the **Masses** of the Greeks: those of St. James, St. Basil, and St. Chrysostom. And yet our Protestants, while pretending to return everything to Christ’s original way, will not do as He did, nor as the Apostles and all historical Churches have ever done.

<margin>
The words of consecration must be said over the bread and wine, which the Protestants do not do.
</margin>
<margin>
*Tract 80 on John.*
</margin>
24. **This is.**] These words are set down not as a report by the Evangelists or Apostles, but expressed as if in Christ's own person to be said over the bread (and similarly over the wine). These are the "forms" of the Sacrament and the words of consecration. It is not a Sacrament unless (as **St. Augustine** says) the words are applied; that is to say, actively and presently applied to the physical elements. Therefore, because the Protestants never apply these words as anything more than a general narration of the institution—nor do they recite the whole narrative except in a historical manner—they make no Sacrament at all. It is as if someone were to administer Baptism but never actually apply the words to the child, only reading Christ's speech about Baptism. That these specific words are the only form of this Sacrament, and are to be spoken over the bread and wine, **St. Ambrose** writes plainly and precisely. He records how far the Evangelist's narrative words go, and where Christ's own peculiar mystical words of consecration begin. The rest of the Fathers agree. (**Ambrose, Book 4 on the Sacraments, chapters 4 and 5; On the Initiated into Mysteries; Justin, Apology 2, at the end; Cyprian, On the Supper of the Lord, numbers 1, 2; Augustine, Sermon 28 on the Words of the Lord according to Matthew; Tertullian, Book 4 against Marcion; Chrysostom, Homily 2 on 2 Timothy, at the end, and the Homily on the Betrayal of Judas, volume 3; Gregory of Nyssa, in his Catechetical Oration; John of Damascus, Book 4, chapter 14.**)

<margin>
The Protestants have taken away the Blessed Sacrament altogether.
</margin>
24. **My body.**] When the words of Consecration are removed from the elements by this Protestant impiety, it is no wonder that Christ's holy body and blood are not present, or that it is now no more than a common snack of bread and wine rather than a Sacrament. So, those who unjustly charge the Catholic Church with defrauding the people of "one piece" of the Sacrament <note>A reference to the Protestant critique of withholding the cup from the laity.</note> have, in truth, left no part or trace of the Sacrament remaining. They follow neither Christ, as they pretend, nor St. Paul, nor any Evangelist, but rather their own detestable sect. They have boldly defaced the entire institution, not just in accidental or indifferent details, but in its very substance. The right name is gone, the proper elements are gone, and there is no blessing, consecration, or other ritual action over them. The forms are gone, and consequently, the body, the blood, the Sacrament, and the Sacrifice are all gone.

<margin>
The power to consecrate is given to Priests only.
</margin>
24. **This do.**] By these words, authority and power are given to the Apostles, and by similar words in the Sacrament of Holy Orders, to all lawful Priests only. It is no wonder then that the new "heretical ministers," being laymen, give the people nothing but bare bread and wine—profane, naked, and natural elements devoid of the Sacrament and all grace. See the Annotation upon St. Luke, chapter 22, verse 19.

<margin>
The Sacrament does not consist solely in the act of receiving it.
</margin>
<margin>
Why the Protestants call it the Communion.
</margin>
<margin>
Communion, which is a part of the...
</margin>
24. **Take and eat.**] This refers to the receiving of those things which, through consecration, are already present and have been sacrificed. Just as when the people or Priests in the Old Law ate the sacrifices offered to God, they were made partakers of a sacrifice that had already been performed. This "eating" is not the substance, the being, or the making of the Sacrament or Sacrifice of Christ's body and blood; rather, it is the use and application of the things that were made and offered to God previously. There is a difference between the making of a medicine (its substance and ingredients) and the act of taking it. Now, since receiving is merely a consequence or one of the goals for which the Sacrament was made—the means to apply it to us—our adversaries unlearnedly make the "eating" the entire thing. Therefore, they improperly name the whole Sacrament and its administration "the Communion." They prefer this name over any other to make the ignorant believe that many people must receive it together, as if it were called "Communion" simply because it is common to many. By this deception, they do away with the Priest receiving alone, the sick receiving alone, and the practice of reserving the consecrated Host. Against this deceit, know that this part of the **MASS** is not called *Communio* because many people must always participate together in the external Sacrament, but because we communicate...
