# CHAPTER 11. TO THE CORINTHIANS.

<margin>MASS, what it signifies.</margin>
<margin>St. John of Damascus, Book 4, Chapter 14, *On the Orthodox Faith* <note>Original: "de orthod. fide"</note>.</margin>
...nicate or join in unity, and perfect fellowship of one body, with all Christian men in the world; with all (we say) that eat it through the whole Church, and not with them only which eat with us at one time. And this fellowship rises from that: that we are, every time we receive—either alone or with company—partakers of that one body which is received throughout all the world. It is called communion (says St. Damascene) and so indeed it is, because by it we communicate with Christ and are partakers of his flesh and divinity; and by it, we do communicate and are united one with another. Only let us take heed that we do not participate with heretics <note>In this 16th-century context, "heretics" refers specifically to Protestant reformers.</note>. And when the Apostle says that all are one bread and one body who are partakers of one Bread, he means not only those that communicate at one time and place, but that all are so who communicate in unity through the whole Church. Thus, the name "Communion" is as ignorantly used by them <note>The Protestants</note> as the name "Supper."

<margin>How Christ's death is shown by the Blessed Sacrament itself without a sermon or otherwise.</margin>
26. *You shall show.*] Upon this word, the Heretics foolishly ground their false supposition that this Sacrament cannot rightly be administered or performed without a sermon on the death of Christ; and that this and other Sacraments in the Church are not profitable when they are administered in a strange language <note>Referring to the use of Latin in the Catholic Mass.</note>. As though the grace, force, operation, and activity—together with the instruction and representation of the things which they signify—were not in the very substance, matter, form, use, and work itself of every one of the Sacraments. It is as though preaching were not one way to show Christ’s Passion, and the Sacraments another way: namely, this Sacrament, containing in the very kinds of the elements and the action a most lively representation of Christ’s death. As wisely might they say that neither Abel’s sacrifice nor the Paschal lamb could signify Christ’s death without a sermon.

<margin>The wicked receive the body and blood. The real presence is proved by the heinous offense of receiving.</margin>
27. *Guilty of the body.*] First, mark well upon this that evil men receive the body and blood of Christ, whether they be infidels or evil-livers. For in this case, they could not be "guilty" of that which they do not receive. Secondly, it could not be so heinous an offense for any man to receive a piece of bread or a cup of wine, even if they were a true Sacrament. For it is a deadly sin to receive any Sacrament with the will and intention to continue in sin, or without repentance of former sins; yet, by the unworthy receiving of no other Sacrament is a man "guilty of Christ's body and blood" except here, where the unworthy (as St. Chrysostom says) does villainy to Christ's own person—just as the Jews or Gentiles did who crucified it. <note>St. Chrysostom, *Homily on not despising the Church*, etc. Homilies 60 & 61 *To the people of Antioch*.</note> This forcefully proves against the Heretics that Christ is really present.

<margin>St. Cyprian, *On the Lapsed*, number 7. St. Augustine, *Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, chapter 53.</margin>
<margin>Confession before receiving the Blessed Sacrament.</margin>
28. *Let him prove.*] A man must examine his life diligently to see whether he be in any mortal sin, and must confess himself of every offense which he knows or fears to be deadly before he presumes to come to the holy Sacrament. For so the Apostle’s doctrine here—along with the continual custom of the Catholic Church and the example of the Church Fathers—binds him to do. <note>Citations: St. Cyprian, *On the Lapsed*, number 7; St. Augustine, *Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, chapter 53.</note>

<margin>Adoration of the Blessed Sacrament.</margin>
29. *Not discerning the body.*] That is, because he puts no difference nor distinction between this high meat <note>A term for "spiritual food."</note> and others. Therefore, St. Augustine says in Letter 118, chapter 3, that it is he who *shall be damned, that does not by singular veneration or adoration make a difference between this meat and all others.* And again in Psalm 98: *No man eats it before he adores it.* And St. Ambrose in Book 3, chapter 12, *On the Holy Spirit*: *We adore the flesh of Christ in the Mysteries.* St. Chrysostom in Homily 24 on 1 Corinthians: *We adore him on the altar, as the Sages <note>The Magi or Three Wise Men.</note> did in the manger.* St. Nazianzen in his *Funeral Oration for Gorgonia*: *My sister called on him which is worshipped upon the altar.* Theodorete, Dialogue 2, *The Unconfused*: *The mystical tokens are adored.* St. Denis <note>Dionysius the Areopagite.</note>, this Apostle’s scholar, made solemn invocation of the Sacrament after Consecration <note>*The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapter 3, part 3, at the beginning.</note>. And before receiving, the whole Church of God cries 

<margin>* See the Annotation for Matthew 8:8.</margin>
<margin>The manifold honor and discerning of Christ's body in the Catholic Church.</margin>
upon it, * *Lord, I am not worthy, God be merciful to me a sinner.* <note>Original: "Domine non sum dignus, Deus propitius esto mihi peccatori."</note> Lamb of God that takest away the sins of the world, have mercy on us. And for better discerning of this divine meat, we are called from common profane houses to God’s Church; for this, we are forbidden to make it in vulgar apparel, and are appointed sacred, solemn vestments <note>St. Jerome, *Funeral Oration for Nepotian* and Book 2 *Against the Pelagians*, chapter 9; Paulinus, Letter 12 to Severus; Joannes Diaconus, *The Life of St. Gregory*, Book 3, chapter 59.</note>. For this is the hallowing of Corporals <note>The linen cloths upon which the bread and wine are placed during Mass.</note> and Chalices <note>St. Ambrose, *On Duties*, Book 2, chapter 28; St. Nazianzen, *Oration to the Arians*; Optatus, Book 6 at the beginning.</note>. For this, profane tables are removed and altars consecrated <note>St. Augustine, *Sermon on the Seasons* 255.</note>. For this, the very Priests themselves are honorable, chaste, and sacred <note>St. Jerome, Letter 1 to Heliodorus, chapter 7; Book 1 *Against Jovinian*, chapter 19; St. Ambrose on 1 Timothy 3.</note>. For this, the people are forbidden to touch it with common hands <note>St. Nazianzen, *Oration to the Arians* at the beginning.</note>. For this, great care and solicitude is taken that no part of either kind <note>The species of bread and wine.</note> fall to the ground <note>St. Cyril of Jerusalem, *Mystagogical Lecture* 5, at the end; Origen, Homily 13 on Exodus 25.</note>. For this, sacred provision is made that if any hosts or parts of the Sacrament do remain unreceived, they be most religiously reserved with all honor and diligence possible. <header>THE FIRST EPISTLE OF SAINT PAUL CHAPTER 12.</header>

<margin>Holy bread.</margin>
<margin>St. Augustine, *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, book 2, chapter 26 <note>Original Latin: *Aug. de pec. merit. li. 2. c. 26.*</note>.</margin>
<margin>Epistle of Jude.</margin>
(and therefore is no more holy by your own judgment than the rest of his meats) but from all other either common or sanctified meats, such as the <term>Catechumens' bread</term> <note>Bread given to those studying to become Christians but not yet baptized.</note>, and our usual <term>holy bread</term> <note>The "Eulogia," or blessed bread distributed in some traditions, which is distinct from the consecrated Eucharist.</note>. If this be plain and true, and you have nothing agreeable to the Apostles' nor Christ's institution, but all clean contrary: then may God rebuke you <note>Original Latin: *imperet vobis Deus*</note> and confound you for not discerning his holy body, and for trampling upon the blood of the New Testament.

<margin>Unworthy receiving.</margin>
30. **Many sleep.**] We see here by this, it is a fearful case and crime to defile by sin (as much as in us lies) the body of Christ in the Sacrament, seeing God struck many to death for it in the Primitive Church, and punished others by grievous sickness. No marvel that so many strange diseases and deaths fall upon us now in the world.

<margin>Penance and satisfaction.</margin>
31. **Judge yourselves.**] We may note here that it is not enough, only to sin no more, or to repent lightly of that which is past: but that we should punish ourselves according to the weight of the faults past and forgiven: and also that God will punish us by temporal <term>scourges</term> <note>Physical or spiritual hardships intended for discipline.</note> in this life or the next, if we do not make ourselves very clean before we come to receive his holy Sacrament. We may escape his heavy hands by punishing ourselves through fasting and other penance.

33. **Expect one another.**] Returning now to their former fault and disorder for which he took this occasion to talk of the holy Sacrament, and how great a fault it is to come unworthily to it: he exhorts them to keep their said suppers or feasts in unity, peace, and sobriety, the rich waiting for the poor, etc.

<margin>The Mass is agreeable to the Apostles' use and tradition: the Communion is not.</margin>
<margin>St. Augustine, Letter 118, chapter 6.</margin>
<margin>St. Augustine, Tractate 84 on John.</margin>
<margin>St. Chrysostom, Homily 21 on Acts.</margin>
34. **I will dispose.**] Many particular orders and decrees—more than are here or in any other book of the New Testament expressly written—did the Apostles set down by tradition, as we see here, and namely Saint Paul to the Corinthians. Our whole administration of the **MASS** is agreeable to these traditions, as the substance of the Sacrifice and Sacrament is proved by the preceding arguments to be most consistent with them. Calvin’s supper and Communion are in all points wholly <term>repugnant</term> <note>Directly opposed or contradictory.</note> to the same. And that it agrees not to these other unwritten traditions, they easily confess: The Apostles delivered to the Church the practice of taking it only while fasting: they <note>The Reformers</note> care not for it. The Apostles taught the Church to <term>consecrate</term> <note>To make holy through prayer and ritual.</note> by the words and the sign of the Cross, without which (says Saint Augustine in his *Tractate on John 118* and *Sermon 75 in the appendix*, and Saint Chrysostom in his *Homily 55 on Matthew 16*) no Sacrament is rightly perfected: the Protestants have taken it away. The Apostles taught the Church to keep <margin>Bread.</margin> a Memory or <term>invocation</term> <note>A prayer calling upon someone for help.</note> of Saints in this Sacrifice: the Calvinists have none. The Apostles decreed that in this Sacrifice there should be special prayers for the dead (as seen in Saint Chrysostom, *Homily 3 on the Epistle to the Philippians*, and Saint Augustine, *On the Care for the Dead, chapter 1*): they have none. Likewise that water should be mixed with the wine, and so forth. *See Annotations in chapter 11, verse 23.* Therefore if Calvin had made his new administration according to all the Apostles' written words, yet not knowing how many things besides, the Apostle had to prescribe in these words, *The rest I will set in order when I come* <note>Original Latin: *Cætera cum venero disponam*</note>, he could not have satisfied any wise man in his new change. But now seeing they are fallen to such palpable blindness, that their doing is directly opposite to the very Scripture also, which they pretend to follow only, and have quite destroyed both the name, substance, and all good characteristics of Christ’s principal Sacrament, we trust all the world will see their folly and impudence.

### -> A N N O T A T I O N S <-
### -> C H A P T E R XIII. <-

<margin>Charity.</margin>
1. **Not Charity.**] Without Charity, both toward every particular person and especially toward the common body of the Church, none of the gifts and graces of God are profitable.

<margin>False Martyrs.</margin>
3. **Deliver my body.**] Believe (says St. Augustine) assuredly and hold for certain, that no *heretic or schismatic who does not unite himself to the Catholic Church again—no matter how great an amount of alms he gives, or even if he sheds his blood for Christ’s name—can possibly be saved.* For many heretics, under the cloak of Christ’s cause, deceive the simple and suffer much. *But where true faith is not, there is no justice <note>original: "iustice," here meaning righteousness or a state of grace</note>, because the just man lives by faith.* So it is also with schismatics, *because charity is not there, justice can be none: which if they had, they would never tear to pieces the body of Christ, which is the Church.* <note>Augustine (or perhaps Fulgentius), *On the Faith, to Peter*, chapter 39.</note> St. Augustine says this in various places, not only regarding heretics who died directly for the defense of their heresy—as the Anabaptists and Calvinists do nowadays (for that is more damnable)—but even of some heretics and schismatics who might die among the Heathen or Turks in defense of the truth or some Article of Christ’s religion. <note>Augustine, *On the Words of the Lord*, sermon 50, chapter 2; and *On Psalm 34*, second discourse near the end; Cyprian, *On the Unity of the Church*, number 8.</note>

<margin>The three theological virtues. Charity is lost by mortal sin, but not faith.</margin>
13. **These three.**] These are the three theological virtues, each one distinct from the other by nature and definition. Faith is by nature the first, and can often exist before and without Charity; it truly remains in many people after they have lost Charity through deadly sin. Beware, therefore, of the heretics' opinion, which claims that faith is lost by every mortal sin just as much as charity is.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on 1 Corinthians 14, transitioning from the scriptural text to detailed scholarly annotations. It focuses on the distinction between the "gift of tongues" and the "gift of prophecy" (preaching/interpretation), specifically defending the use of the Latin liturgy against Protestant criticisms of the time.</meta>

# ANNOTATIONS
## CHAPTER 14.

<margin>A summary explanation of this Chapter regarding unknown tongues.</margin>
1. *Rather prophesy.*] The gift of <term>prophesying</term> <note>In this context, "prophesying" refers to the inspired ability to explain and interpret difficult points of religious doctrine, rather than simply foretelling the future.</note>, that is, of expounding the hard points of our religion, is better than the gift of foreign tongues, though both are good.

2. *Not to men.*] To talk in a foreign language, unknown even to the speaker himself, does not benefit the hearers—even though before God, who understands all languages and things, there is no difference in the mysteries he utters in his spirit or in his own spiritual growth. However, the Prophet or Expositor, treating the same matters so the whole assembly can understand, builds up not only himself but all his listeners.

6. *If I come.*] That is, if I, your Apostle and Teacher, should preach to you in an unknown tongue and never use any kind of exposition, interpretation, or explanation of my foreign words, what profit could you take from it?

8. *If the trumpet.*] Just as the trumpeter cannot give a warning to advance to or retreat from the fight unless he uses a distinct and intelligible sound known to the soldiers; even so the preacher who encourages a good life or warns against sin cannot achieve his purpose or do the people any good unless he speaks in a language his hearers understand.

13. *Let him pray that.*] He who has only the gift of foreign tongues should pray to God for the gift of interpretation, so that the one gift may be made more profitable by the other. For to encourage or preach in a foreign tongue was not unlawful or unprofitable—indeed, it was glorious to God—provided that the speech was afterwards explained, either by the speaker or by another.

14. *My spirit prays.*] Also, when a man prays in a foreign tongue which he himself does not understand, it is not as fruitful for his own instruction as it would be if he knew specifically what he prayed. Nevertheless, the Apostle does not forbid such praying either, acknowledging that the person's spirit, heart, and affection pray well toward God, even though his mind and understanding are not improved by instruction as they might have been if he understood the words. Nor does he command such a person to have his foreign prayer translated into his <term>vulgar tongue</term> <note>The "vulgar tongue" refers to the common, everyday language spoken by the local people, such as English or German, as opposed to a sacred or scholarly language like Latin or Greek.</note> to obtain that instruction. See the Explanation following this Chapter.

22. *A sign.*] The extraordinary gift of tongues was a miraculous sign in the early Church, to be used especially among the Heathen nations for their conversion.

23. *Unbelievers.*] In the early Church, when unbelievers lived near or among Christians and often came to their public preaching and exercises—such as exhortations, explanations of Scripture, and the like—it was both unprofitable and ridiculous to hear many people talking, teaching, and singing Psalms all at once in different languages. It sounded like a <term>black sanctus</term> <note>original: "blacke-faunts." This refers to a "Black Sanctus," which was a term for a discordant, noisy, or nonsensical cacophony or a burlesque hymn.</note>, where one person was not understood by another (sometimes not even by themselves), and certainly not by strangers or the simple people standing by. Otherwise, if they had spoken in known languages or in an orderly way with an interpreter, the unbelievers might have been convinced.

<margin>Concerning what spiritual exercises the Apostle speaks.</margin>
26. *A Psalm.*] We see here that those spiritual exercises consisted especially of: first, singing or providing new Psalms, prayers, and praises; second, Doctrine, teaching, or reading lectures; third, Revelation of secret things, either present or to come; fourth, speaking the Tongues of foreign nations; and lastly, translating or Interpreting what was said into some common known language, such as Greek, Latin, etc. All these gifts they possessed among them by miracles from the Holy Ghost.

<margin>The disorders in the same.</margin>
27. *In turn.*] They were doing all these things without order; out of pride and contention they preached, prophesied, prayed, and blessed without any respectful regard for one another or observing turns. Even women, without head coverings or veils and without regard for their sex, the Angels, the Priests, or their own husbands, boldly spoke in tongues, taught, or prophesied with the rest. This was the disorder among the Corinthians which the Apostle corrects in this whole chapter, utterly forbidding women from that public exercise and teaching the men the proper order and turn for speaking in tongues, interpreting, and prophesying.

# A MORE DETAILED EXPLANATION OF THE
## sense of this 14th Chapter.

<margin>That Saint Paul's passage makes no argument against the service in the Latin tongue.</margin>
Since this was the scope and direct intent of the Apostle—as is most clear from his whole discourse and the records of all antiquity—let the godly, grave, and discreet reader take note of one point: the deceitful dealing of the Protestants, who abuse the simplicity of the common people by perverting God’s holy word based on a small similarity and the misuse of certain terms, against...

<meta>This page continues the detailed annotations on 1 Corinthians 14, specifically addressing the controversy over the use of Latin in the liturgy versus local "vulgar" languages. The text defends the traditional Catholic practice against Protestant reformers by arguing that St. Paul’s warnings against "strange tongues" referred to miraculous, unintelligible utterances, not the established sacred languages of the Church.</meta>

# CHAPTER 14. TO THE CORINTHIANS.

<margin>By strange tongues the Apostle does not mean Latin, Greek, or Hebrew.</margin>
...against the approved godly use and truth of the universal Church; regarding the service in the Latin or Greek tongue: which they ignorantly, or rather willfully, pretend to be against this discourse of St. Paul touching strange tongues. Know therefore, first, that here is no word written or meant of any other tongues but such as men spoke in the Primitive Church by miracle; and that nothing is meant of those tongues which were the common languages of the world or of the Faithful, understood by the learned and civilized people in every great city, and in which the Scriptures of the Old or New Testament were written, such as Hebrew, Greek, and Latin. For though these also might be given by miracle and without study, yet being known to the Jews, Romans, or Greeks in every place, they are not counted among the differences of "barbarous" and "strange" tongues spoken of here, which could not be interpreted commonly, except by the miraculous gift of interpretation. And therefore this Apostle (as the Evangelists and others also did with their books) wrote his Epistles in Greek to the Romans and to all other Churches. When he wrote them, though he did not pen them in the <term>vulgar language</term> <note>The "vulgar" language refers to the common, everyday speech of the local people, as opposed to a learned or liturgical language.</note> peculiar to every people, yet he wrote them not "in Tongue"—that is, in any strange tongue unintelligible without the gift of interpretation, of which he speaks here—but in a notable, known, and learned speech interpretable by thousands in every country.

<margin>St. Augustine, our Apostle, introduced the Service in the Latin tongue.</margin>
No more did <term>St. Augustine, our Apostle</term> <note>This refers to St. Augustine of Canterbury, sent by Pope Gregory the Great in 597 AD to convert the Anglo-Saxons, often called the "Apostle to the English."</note>, speaking in Latin and bringing in the Scriptures and Service in Latin, preach and pray in "Tongues" according to the Apostle's meaning here. For Latin was not, and is not, in any part of the West, either miraculous or strange, though it is not the national tongue of any one country today. And therefore St. Bede says (<note>original: *li. 1 hist. Angl. c. 1.*</note> *Book 1 of the History of the English People, chapter 1*) that although there were then four different vulgar languages in our country, Latin was made common to them all.

<margin>The Latin service is one and the same in all countries and strange to none.</margin>
<margin>The service in a vulgar tongue is strange and barbarous to every stranger.</margin>
And indeed, of the two (though in truth neither sort is forbidden by this passage of St. Paul), the <term>barbarous</term> <note>In this context, "barbarous" means foreign, localized, or unrefined, rather than "savage."</note> languages of every individual province, in respect to the whole Church of Christ, are more truly the "strange tongues" spoken of here than the common Latin tongue. Latin is universally learned, more or less, by the entire Western Church, and pertains much more to the unity and orderly conjunction of all nations in one faith, service, and worship of God, than if it were in the various barbarous speeches of every province. In the Latin system, all Christians who travel about this part of the world (or the Indies as well) shall find the self-same Mass, Mattins, and Service wherever they go, just as they had at home. Whereas now, if we go to Germany, or the Germans or Genevans come to us, each other’s service shall be thought "strange and barbarous." Yea, and the service in our own language within a few hundred years (or rather every age) shall wholly become barbarous and unknown to ourselves, because our tongue (as all vulgar tongues do) changes so often.

<margin>Whether the service in vulgar tongues provides more edification.</margin>
<margin>See Annotation 1 Cor. 10:53.</margin>
And as for <term>edification</term> <note>Edification refers to the spiritual building up or improvement of the believer.</note>—that is, for the increase of faith, true knowledge, and a good life—the experience of a few years has given the whole world a full demonstration of whether our forefathers were not as wise, as faithful, as devout, as fearful of breaking God's laws, and as likely to be saved as we are with all our various tongues, translations, and English prayers. Much vanity, curiosity, contempt of superiors, disputes, emulations, contentions, schisms, horrible errors, and the profanation and commonizing of the secret mysteries of the dreadful Sacraments—which were purposely hidden from the vulgar (as <note>original: *S. Denys Eccl. Hier. c. 1.* and *S. Basil de Sp. Sanct. c. 27.*</note> *St. Dionysius the Areopagite and St. Basil* testify)—have resulted from this change, but virtue or sound knowledge has not increased at all.

<margin>The virtue of the Sacraments and service does not consist in the people's understanding.</margin>
In this also there is a gross illusion and untruth: that the force and efficacy of the Sacraments, Sacrifice, and common prayer depends upon the people's understanding, hearing, or knowledge. The principal efficacy of such things, and of the whole ministry of the Church, consists especially in the very virtue of the work itself and the public office of the Priests, who are appointed on Christ's behalf to dispense these mysteries for our greatest good. The infant, the innocent, the <term>idiot</term> <note>In the 16th century, "idiot" referred to an unlearned person or a layman, not a person with a mental disability.</note>, and the unlearned take no less fruit from Baptism and all other divine offices suited to their condition than the most learned clerk in the Realm—and even more, if they be more humble, charitable, devout, and obedient than the other who has more learning but less of those qualities.

<margin>The people are to be taught the meaning of Sacraments and ceremonies, and they are taught in all Catholic countries.</margin>
We say this not as though it were inconvenient for the people to be well instructed in the meaning of the Sacraments and holy ceremonies and Service of the Church. (For, to their comfort and necessary knowledge, Christian people do learn these things through preaching, catechizing, and reading good Catholic books in all nations—much more so in those countries where the Service is in Latin than in our own nation, God knows.) But we say that there are other ways to instruct them, which are less subject to danger and disorder than turning the liturgy into vulgar tongues. We say that the simple people (and many who think themselves important) understand as little of the sense of various Psalms, Lessons, and Orations in the vulgar tongue as if they were in Latin; yea, and they often take them in a wrong, perverse, and pernicious sense, which they could not easily have done in Latin. We say that those who would learn in devotion and humility may and must rather diligently learn the tongue in which such divine things are written, or use diligence in hearing sermons and instructions, rather than altering the holy universal order of God's Church for the sake of a few men’s non-essential knowledge. For if in the kingdom of England alone it is not convenient, necessary, nor almost possible to accommodate their service book to every province and people of different dialects, how much less should the whole Church do so, consisting of so many differences? Neither does the Apostle in all this Chapter appoint any such thing.

<meta>This page continues the defense of the Latin liturgy, arguing that St. Paul's instructions in 1 Corinthians 14 regarding "speaking in tongues" do not apply to the established use of Latin in the Catholic Church. The author distinguishes between miraculous spiritual gifts in the early Church and the formal, structured prayers and services of the 16th-century Church.</meta>

# THE FIRST EPISTLE OF ST. PAUL. CHAPTER 14.

<margin>Catholic people in every country understand every ceremony and can behave themselves accordingly.</margin>
...thing to be done, but admonishes them to pray and labor for the grace of understanding and interpretation, or to get others to interpret or expound for them. And we may do much more concerning the Service in Latin, which is not a strange or miraculously acquired or understood tongue, but common to most of the principal churches of the world. Since the time of the Apostles, it has been expounded daily with all diligence throughout all these parts of Christendom in every house, school, church, and pulpit. It is so well known for every necessary part of the divine Service that, through the diligence of parents, masters, and <term>curates</term> <note>In this context, a curate is a parish priest or member of the clergy responsible for the care of souls.</note>, almost every Catholic of age can tell the meaning of every ceremony of the **Mass**: what to answer, when to say **Amen** at the Priest’s blessing, when to confess, when to adore, when to stand, when to kneel, when to receive, what to receive, when to come, when to depart, and all other duties of praying and serving, sufficient for salvation. And thus it is evident that St. Paul does not speak of the common languages of the Church's service.

<margin>That he [Paul] does not speak of the Church's service is proved by invincible arguments.</margin>
<margin>St. Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, book 2, chapter 13.</margin>
Secondly, it is just as certain that he does not mean, nor does he write any word in this place about, the Church’s public Service, prayer, or the administration of the holy Sacrament—wherein the Office of the Church specially consists. Rather, he speaks only of a certain exercise of mutual conference, wherein people shared with one another and the assembly the miraculous gifts and graces of the Holy Ghost: such as canticles, psalms, secret mysteries, different languages, and other revelations as it pleased God to give to certain men and women in that first beginning of His Church. In doing this, the Corinthians committed many disorders, turning God's gifts toward pride and vanity—specifically that "gift of tongues." This was indeed the least of all gifts, yet it most puffed up those who had it, just as it now commonly puffs up those who claim such knowledge, according to what St. Augustine writes about it. This specific exercise and the disorder associated with it has not been in the Church (for anything we can read in antiquity) for these fourteen hundred years; therefore, neither the use nor the abuse, nor St. Paul’s correction of it, can concern the Service of the Church at all. Furthermore, it is evident that the Corinthians had their Service in Greek at this same time, and it was not performed in these miraculous "tongues." Therefore, nothing here refers to the Church Service. Again, the public Service used only one language; in this exercise, they spoke in many tongues. In the public Service, every man did not have his own special tongue, his own special interpretation, his own special revelation, or his own proper psalms; but in this exercise, they did. Again, the public Service principally included the administration of the holy Sacrament, which was not done during this time of conference. For into this exercise were admitted <term>Catechumens</term> <note>Those receiving basic instruction in Christianity before being baptized.</note> and <term>Infidels</term> <note>Non-believers or those outside the faith.</note> and whoever wished; in this exercise, women—before St. Paul’s order—spoke and prophesied, which they never did during the administration of the Sacrament. These, along with many other plain differences, show that by no means can the Apostle's words be rightly and truly applied to the Corinthians' Service then, or ours now. Therefore, it is either great ignorance on the part of the Protestants, or great guilt, to apply them so untruly and perversely.

<margin>The Apostle does not speak of the people's private prayers in Latin, such as from prayer books, beads, or otherwise.</margin>
Neither is anything meant here regarding the private prayers which devout persons of all sorts and sexes have always used, especially in Latin, both in their <term>Primers</term> <note>A "Primer" was a popular medieval and Renaissance book of private devotions.</note> and <term>Beads</term> <note>A reference to the Rosary.</note>. For the private prayers spoken of here were psalms or hymns and songs newly inspired to them by God, uttered in this conference or prophesying for one another's comfort, or to themselves and God alone. But the prayers, psalms, and holy words used privately by Christian people are not composed by them, nor diversely inspired to them, nor are they now to be approved or examined in the assemblies. Instead, they are those given and written by the Holy Ghost and prescribed by Christ and His Church for the faithful to use: namely, the **Our Father** <note>original: "Pater noster"</note>, the **Hail Mary** <note>original: "Aue Marie"</note>, and the **Creed**, the **Morning Prayers of our Lady**, the **Litanies**, and the like. Therefore, the Apostle prescribes nothing here concerning them, condemns nothing in them, and does not touch upon them at all. But the devout people, in their ancient right, may and ought still to use their Latin prayer books, beads, and prayers, as they did before. The wisdom of the Church, for great reasons, has better liked and allowed these than that they should be in <term>vulgar tongues</term> <note>The common, everyday languages of the people (like English or German) as opposed to the sacred/learned language of Latin.</note>. However, she does not wholly forbid them, but sometimes grants permission to have them translated, and would gladly have all faithful people in order and humility learn the contents of their prayers as they are able. The Church has also commanded in some Councils that those who cannot learn distinctly in Latin (especially the **Our Father** and the **Creed**) should be taught them in the vulgar tongue. Therefore, as we do not doubt that it is acceptable to God and helpful in all necessities—and more agreeable to the practice of all Christian people ever since their conversion—to pray in Latin rather than in the vulgar tongue (even if every individual does not understand exactly what he says), so it is plain that such people pray with just as much consolation of spirit, with as little boredom, and with as much devotion and affection (and often more) than the others. And they always pray with more devotion than any <term>Schismatic</term> <note>Someone who promotes a split or division within the Church.</note> or <term>Heretic</term> does in his known language. Such holy prayers are, in a way, consecrated...

<margin>Latin prayers translated, or the people taught the contents thereof.</margin>
<margin>The people's devotion is not at all lessened by praying in Latin.</margin>

# CHAPTER 14. TO THE CORINTHIANS.

<margin>Matthew 24.</margin>
<margin>* Gregory, book 27 of the *Morals*, chapter 6.</margin>
<margin>The service has always been in Latin throughout the Western Church.</margin>
...consecrated and sanctified in and by the Holy Ghost that first inspired them. There is a reverence and majesty in the Church’s tongue, dedicated upon our Savior’s Cross, which gives more force and value to prayers said in the Church’s obedience than to others. The children cried *Hosanna* <note>A Hebrew expression of adoration meaning "Save, we pray."</note> to our Savior and were approved, even though they did not know what they said. It has been nearly a thousand years since *our people—who could do nothing else but *gnash out barbarian sounds* <note>original: "barbarum frendere"</note>—sang *Hallelujah* <note>original: "Alleluia"</note>, and not "Praise ye the Lord." It was even longer ago that poor farmers sang the same at the plow in other countries. (*Jerome, Epistle 58.*) Furthermore, the *Lift up your hearts* <note>original: "Sursum corda"</note>, the *Lord have mercy* <note>original: "Kyrie eleison"</note>, and the Psalms of David sung in Latin in the Service of the Primitive Church have the ancient and solid testimonies of St. Cyprian, St. Augustine, St. Jerome, and other Fathers. (*Gregory, book 7, epistle 63; Cyprian, Exposition on the Lord's Prayer, number 13; Augustine, On the Gift of Perseverance, chapter 13, and On the Good of Widowhood, chapter 16, and Epistle 178; Jerome, Preface to the Psalms for Sophronius; Augustine, On Catechizing the Uninstructed, chapter 9, and On Christian Doctrine, book 2, chapter 13. See also Augustine’s Epistle 10 regarding St. Jerome’s Latin translation being read in the Churches of Africa.*) Prayers are not made to teach, to make people learned, or to increase knowledge—though they sometimes instruct us by occasion—but their special use is to offer our hearts, desires, and wants to God, and to show that we depend on Him in all things. Every Catholic does this according to his condition, whether he understands the words of his prayer or not.

<margin>It is not necessary to understand our prayers.</margin>
The simple sort of people cannot understand all the Psalms, and neither can the learned, even if they are translated or read in known languages; yet men must not cease to use them for all that, when they are known to contain God’s holy praises. When simple people desire anything specifically from God's hand, they are not bound to know, nor can they tell, to which petition or part of the *Our Father* <note>original: "Pater noster"</note> their request belongs, even if it is in English. They can tell no more what *Thy kingdom come* means than *May your kingdom come* <note>original: "Adueniat regnum tuum"</note>. Nor can they tell whether their petition for their sick children or any other necessity pertains to this part, or to *Thy will be done* <note>original: "Fiat voluntas tua"</note>, or *Lead us not* <note>original: "Ne nos inducas"</note>, or to any other part. It is enough that they can tell that this holy prayer was appointed for us to call upon God in all our desires.

<margin>How much it is sufficient for the people to understand.</margin>
More than this is not necessary. And the translation of such holy things often breeds manifold danger and irreverence among the common people (such as thinking God is the author of sin when they read, *Lead us not into temptation*) and seldom provides any edification at all. For, though when the prayers are translated and read in English, the people know the words, they are still not edified in the instruction of their mind and understanding unless they also know the sense of the words and the meaning of the Holy Ghost.

<margin>How the mind or understanding is edified.</margin>
<margin>1 Corinthians 13.</margin>
For if any man thinks that St. Paul, when speaking of the edification of a man’s mind or understanding, means the understanding of the words only, he is foully deceived. For how is a child of five or six years old edified or increased in knowledge by saying his *Our Father* in English? It is the sense, therefore, which every man cannot have—neither in English nor Latin—the knowledge of which properly and rightly edifies for instruction. The knowledge of the words alone often edifies not at all, and sometimes builds toward error and destruction, as is plain in all heretics and many curious persons besides. Finally, both the one and the other, without charity and humility, make the heretics and schismatics—with all their English and whatever other tongues and intelligence they have—to be as *sounding brass and a tinkling cymbal* <note>original: "sonans & cymbalum tinniens"</note>.

<margin>1 Corinthians 11, 16.</margin>
<margin>A notable rule of St. Augustine.</margin>
To conclude, regarding praying either publicly or privately in Latin—which is the common sacred tongue of the greatest part of the Christian world—this is thought by the wisest and godliest to be most expedient, and is certainly seen to be in no way repugnant to St. Paul. If any will still be contentious in the matter, we must answer them with this same Apostle: *The Church of God has no such custom.* And with this notable saying of St. Augustine, *Epistle 118, chapter 5*:
> Anything that the whole Church practices and observes throughout the world, to dispute thereof as though it were not to be done, is most insolent madness.

<margin>Women may have any temporal sovereignty, but no ecclesiastical function.</margin>
34. *Let women hold their peace.*] There are, or were, certain heretics in our country (for such people always interpret the Scriptures differently to suit the advantage of the time) who denied that women could lawfully hold any kingdom or temporal <term>sovereignty</term> <note>Supreme power or authority, such as that of a Queen.</note>. But that is false and against both reason and the Scriptures. This alone is true regarding that sex: it is not capable of <term>holy orders</term> <note>The sacrament by which men are ordained as priests or bishops.</note>, spiritual government, or the care of souls. Therefore, they cannot perform any function proper to priests and bishops: they may not speak in the church, and so cannot preach, nor dispute, nor have or give a voice—either deliberative or definitive—in Councils and public assemblies concerning matters of religion. They cannot make ecclesiastical laws concerning the same, nor bind, nor loose, nor excommunicate, nor suspend, nor degrade, nor absolve, nor minister <term>Sacraments</term> <note>Sacred rites of the Church, such as the Eucharist or Penance.</note> (other than Baptism in cases of mere necessity when neither a priest nor another man can be found). Much less can they prescribe anything to the clergy on how to minister them, or give any man the right to rule, preach, or execute any spiritual function as if under her and by her authority; no creature is able to impart that of which it is itself incapable by both nature and Scripture. This government is expressly given to the Apostles, Bishops, and <term>Prelates</term> <note>High-ranking members of the clergy, such as bishops or abbots.</note>: they alone have authority to bind and loose (*Matthew 18*); they alone are set by the Holy Ghost to govern the Church (*Acts 20*); they alone have the care of our souls directly and must give an account to God for the same (*Hebrews 13*).

## ANNOTATIONS
### CHAPTER 15.

<margin>Free will working with grace.</margin>
<margin>Heretical translation.</margin>
10 *With me.*] God does not use man like a mindless beast or a block of wood. Instead, He works in man and through man so that **free will** may cooperate in every action with His **grace**, which is always the primary mover. The heretics <note>The translator refers here to Protestant reformers whose translations might imply that grace acts alone without human cooperation</note>, to avoid this idea of cooperation in working and laboring, translate this as "which is with me," whereas the Apostle actually says, "**which labors with me.**"

<margin>Fasting is meritorious.</margin>
32 *Let us eat and drink.*] Saint Ambrose applies these words to our "Christian Epicureans" <note>A term for those who prioritize physical pleasure over spiritual discipline</note> who do away with fasting and deny its spiritual merit. *How can we be saved,* he asks, *if we do not wash away our sins by fasting, seeing that the scriptures say, "fasting and alms deliver from sin"? Who are these new teachers then who exclude all merit from fasting? Is this not the very voice of the heathens saying, "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die"?* (Book 10, Epistle 82).

## THE ARGUMENT OF THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS.

<margin>2 Corinthians 11:2. Galatians 2:1.</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'F' featuring a seated figure in classical or biblical dress, possibly a scholar or apostle, surrounded by intricate floral and architectural scrollwork.</image-desc>
FOR the time when this *Epistle was written*, look at the *Argument of the epistle to the Romans: that is, about the eighteenth year after his conversion, and our Lord's passion. Because in the 11th chapter he mentions 14 years, not only after his Conversion (as in the letter to the Galatians), but also after his "rapture" <note>An experience of being "caught up" into heaven; see 2 Corinthians 12.</note>, which seems to have happened when he was at Jerusalem (Acts 9:26) four years after his Conversion (Galatians 1:18) in a trance or "excess of mind" <note>A state of spiritual ecstasy; original: *excessus mentis*.</note>, as he calls it in Acts 22:17. It was written at Troas (it is thought) and sent by Titus, as we read in chapter 8.*

It is for the most part against those false Apostles whom, in the first part of the first letter to the Corinthians, he noted—or rather spared—but now is constrained to deal openly against them. He does this to defend both his own person (which they sought to bring into contempt, making a way thereby to corrupt the Corinthians) and at the same time to maintain the excellence of the Ministry and Ministers of the new Testament. These false teachers magnified the Ministry of the old Testament above the new, carrying themselves very high because they were Jews.

Against these, therefore, Saint Paul asserts the preeminent power of his Ministry. By this power, he also gives a pardon to the incestuous fornicator <note>Referring to the man punished in 1 Corinthians 5.</note> whom he excommunicated in the last Epistle, seeing now his penance; and again he threatens to come and excommunicate those who had grievously sinned and remained impenitent <note>Unrepentant.</note>. He also interposes two chapters regarding the contributions to the church of Jerusalem (mentioned in his last letter), exhorting them to give liberally and also to have everything ready for his arrival.

## ANNOTATIONS
### CHAPTER I.

<margin>All our afflictions are Christ’s afflictions, because of the union between the head and the body.</margin>
5. *Passions of Christ.*] All the afflictions of the faithful are called Christ’s own passions, not only because they are suffered for him, but because there is so straight a union and communion between him, being the head, and every one of the living members of his body, which is the Church. Therefore, whatever is suffered by any one member is counted as a piece of his own Passion. Likewise, whatever good works are done to any of them or by any of them, are accepted as done to or by Christ himself. If the Protestants carefully considered this, they would not <note>The text likely continues to argue that this union justifies the Catholic doctrine of the "merits of saints" or the "treasury of the Church," which Protestants rejected.</note>

<summary>Paul defends his integrity and the consistency of his message, explaining that his delayed visit to Corinth was out of pastoral concern rather than indecision. He emphasizes that all of God's promises are fulfilled ("Yes") in Christ and describes the Holy Spirit as a "seal" or pledge in the believer's heart.</summary>
<keywords>fickleness, Silvanus, Timothy, Judea, seal of the Spirit, conscience, Godly sincerity, Yes and No, Passions of Christ</keywords>

--- Page 503 ---
<meta>This page continues the commentary on the first chapter of Second Corinthians. The previous page discussed Paul’s sincerity and his defense against charges of being indecisive. This page focuses on the theological implications of suffering, the intercession of saints, the stability of Church teaching versus the "instability" of the Reformers, and the nature of the sacraments.</meta>

<page-num>471</page-num>

### CHAPTER 1. TO THE CORINTHIANS.

<margin>Merit and satisfaction.</margin>
...it is no wonder that the Catholic Church attributes such force of merit and <term>satisfaction|The concept that good works or suffering can make amends for the temporal punishment due to sin</term> to the works of holy people.

<margin>Worldly people do not feel the comfort of afflicted Catholics.</margin>
5. **The comfort abounds.**] Worldly people who see only the outward miseries and afflictions that Catholics suffer when persecuted by heathens or heretics consider them exceedingly miserable. But if they could feel or even conceive of the abundance of consolation which Christ always gives in proportion to the measure of their afflictions, they would never wonder at the voluntary endurance of whatever torments are faced for Christ’s sake. Instead, they would wish to be in any dungeon in England <note>This refers to the imprisonment of Catholic recusants during the reign of Elizabeth I.</note> with the comfort such people receive from God, rather than to live outside the Church with all the wealth of the world.

<margin>The intercession of Saints or holy people for us does not take away from Christ’s role.</margin>
<margin>Jerome, *Against Vigilantius*.</margin>
11. **You helping in prayer.**] Saint Paul knew that the help of other people’s prayers was in no way derogatory to Christ’s office as mediator or intercessor for him, nor to the hope he had in God. Therefore, he craves the aid of the Corinthians as a support and help for himself in the sight of God. With what reason or Scripture, then, can the Protestants say that the prayers of Saints are injurious to Christ, or inconsistent with the confidence we have in Him? As though it were more dishonor to God for us to use the aid of Saints in heaven than of sinners on earth; or as if the intercession of these fellow-beings below were more effective than the prayers of those who are in the glorious sight of God above.

<margin>Public prayers and fasts.</margin>
11. **By many men's.**] He means that just as the prayers of many joined together for him shall be heard more readily than those of one person alone, so their common thanksgiving to God for granting their request shall be more acceptable and glorious to God than any one man’s thanks alone. This greatly commends the holy Church’s public prayers, processions, <term>stations|Devotional visits to specific churches or shrines</term>, and pilgrimages, where so many meet and uniformly join their prayers and praises together to God.

<margin>The glory in heaven of those who convert others.</margin>
24. <note>original: "Your glorie." This likely refers back to verse 14.</note> **Your glory.**] The Apostles, teachers, and preachers who convert countries or specific persons to Christ—and the people or parties converted by them—shall, on the day of judgment, have much mutual joy and glory from and for each other. One gives to the other great matter of merit in this life and reward in the next. See 1 Thessalonians 2:19.

<margin>The inconsistency of Protestants in changing their writings, translations, and service books.</margin>
18. **It is, it is not.**] Just as he clears himself of any other lightness regarding his promise or purpose of coming to them, he clears himself even more of any inconstancy in preaching Christ’s doctrine and faith. In that ministry, to affirm one day and deny the next, to disagree with his colleagues or himself, to change the form of his teaching every year or in every letter, or to come daily with new devices that contradict his own rules, would not be appropriate for an Apostle and true teacher of Christ. Such things are characteristic of false prophets and heretics. We see notorious examples of this in the Protestants: being destitute of the spirit of peace, concord, constancy, unity, and truth, they vary from their own writings (which they continually retract, reform, or ruin). Both in their preaching and their form of Service, they are so restless, changeable, and self-contradictory that if they were not kept in check with much effort by temporal laws or by the shame and rebuke of the world, they would coin for us every year or every Parliament new Communions, new faiths, and new Christs, as seen in the various efforts of the <term>Puritans|A reform movement seeking to "purify" the Church of England from Catholic practices</term>. To see that this is the proper sign of false Apostles and heretics, see Saint Irenaeus, book 1, chapter 18; Tertullian, *On the Prescription of Heretics*; and Saint Basil, epistle 82.

<margin>Ephesians 4:30.</margin>
<margin>The indelible character of Baptism, Confirmation, and Holy Orders.</margin>
<margin>Council of Tarragona.</margin>
22. **Has sealed.**] Learned theologians prove by this passage, and by a similar one in the fourth chapter of Ephesians, that the Sacrament of Baptism does not only give grace but also imprints and seals the soul of the baptized with a spiritual sign, mark, badge, or token. This <term>character|A permanent spiritual mark</term> can never be blotted out—not by sin, heresy, apostasy, or any other way—but remains forever in a person as the recognition of their Christianity and as a distinction from others who were never part of Christ’s fold. By this, he is also, as it were, consecrated and assigned to God, made capable and a participant in the rights of the Church, and subject to her laws and discipline. See Saint Jerome on Ephesians 4; Saint Ambrose, book 1, *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 6; Saint Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechism 17* at the end; and Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapter 2. These Fathers express that spiritual sign by various agreeable names, which the Church and most theologians, after Saint Augustine, call the *character* of Baptism. By the truth and force of this spiritual note or mark of the soul, Augustine specifically convinced the <term>Donatists|A schismatic group that believed the validity of sacraments depended on the moral purity of the priest</term> that the said Sacrament, even if given and administered by heretics or schismatics or anyone else, can never be repeated. See epistle 57, and book 6, *Against the Donatists*, chapter 1, and book 2, *Against Parmenianus*, chapter 13. Similarly, the indelible characters given also by the Sacraments of Confirmation and Orders make those also unrepeatable and never to be received more than once. Whereas all other Sacraments, except these three, may be often received by the same person. For the fact that Holy Orders cannot be repeated, see Saint Augustine, book 2, *Against Parmenianus*, chapter 13; *On the Good of Marriage*, chapter 24; and Saint Gregory, book 2, *Register*, epistle 32. A similar rule for Confirmation was decreed in the very ancient Council of Tarragona, chapter 6. Finally, that this character is given only by these three Sacraments, and is the reason none of them can be repeated in any person, see the decrees of the Councils of Florence and Trent. This is no new invention of theirs, as the heretics falsely claim, but is consistent (as you see) both with the Scriptures and with the ancient Fathers and Councils.

24. **Not because we overrule.**] Calvin and his seditious sectaries, along with others who despise authority...

### A N N O T A T I O N S
### C H A P T E R  I I.

<margin>The Apostle excommunicates, enjoins penance, and afterward pardons and absolves.</margin>
<margin>2 Corinthians 5:5. he delivers <note>original: "tradit"</note>.</margin>
6. **This rebuke is enough.**] This Corinthian man was excommunicated for incest and assigned penance by the Apostle, as seen in the first Epistle, chapter 5. Here, orders are given for his absolution and pardon. In this, we first have a clear example and proof of Apostolic power: of binding and loosing, of punishing and pardoning, of retaining and remitting sins. Secondly, we can prove from this that mere amendment, stopping one's sin, or internal repentance before God alone is not always enough to obtain full reconciliation. We see here his separation from the faithful, the Sacraments, and all company or dealings with other Christians, along with physical affliction. All of this was called by the Apostle the "destruction of the flesh" <note>original: "interitus carnis"</note>, and named here "Rebuke" or—as the Greek word also implies—a fine, penalty, correction, or chastisement. These were enjoined on him by the Apostle's command in the presence of the Church, and the offender patiently endured them for a long time. <margin>Pardon or remission of assigned penance.</margin> Thirdly, we see that it is within the authority of Apostles, Bishops, and spiritual leaders to determine the duration of such penance or discipline. This is based not only on the severity of the offense but also on the weakness of the person being punished and other circumstances of time and place, as their wisdom deems best for the individual's good and the building up of the Church. <margin>Penance and satisfaction clearly proven against the Protestants.</margin> Lastly, by this entire handling of the offender's case, we may refute the wicked heresy of the Protestants, who would make simple people believe that no personal punishment for sins committed, no penance required by the Church, nor any temporal pains or satisfaction for one's past life are necessary. They claim such things are superfluous because Christ satisfied enough for all. <margin>Joel 2:12. Matthew 3 and 4. Acts 2 and 26.</margin> This Epicurean <term>Epicurean|A philosophy often associated with the pursuit of pleasure and avoidance of pain; here used as a derogatory term for a doctrine that avoids the "pain" of penance</term> doctrine is refuted not only here, but also by the preaching of the Prophets, John the Baptist, Christ, and the Apostles regarding penance and worthy works or fruits of repentance for every man in his own person, and not only in Christ's person. It is also refuted by the whole history and clear words of the Church's penitential laws <note>original: "canons"</note>.

<summary>This page discusses the Apostle Paul's authority to grant absolution to a repentant sinner in Corinth, emphasizing that the Church has the power to both impose penance and provide pardon. The annotations argue against Protestant views by asserting that personal penance and Church-mandated satisfaction are necessary components of reconciliation.</summary>

<margin>Zeal against the excommunicated.</margin>
8. **I beseech you.**] Those who at the beginning were too lenient with the offender, and seemed reluctant to have him excommunicated in such an austere manner, yet through their obedience to the Apostle became, on the other hand, so rigorous and so far detested the evildoer after he was excommunicated, that the Apostle—now intending to absolve him—was glad to entreat and command them also to accept him into their company and grace again.

<margin>The Apostle claims their obedience to his ecclesiastical authority.</margin>
9. **Obedient.**] Although in the last chapter he cleared himself of exercising tyrannical dominion over them, yet he claims their obedience in all things as their Pastor and Superior, and consequently in this matter of receiving the penitent Corinthian back into mercy. By this we see that just as the power and authority of excommunicating belongs to St. Paul's person, so does the power of absolving, even though both were to be done in the presence of the Church; otherwise, he would not have commanded or required their obedience.

<margin>The authority of indulgences and upon what it is grounded.</margin>
<margin>Matthew 18:18. Cyprian, letters 13, 14, 15. I have forgiven <note>original: "κεχάρισμαι"</note>. See Theodoret on this place, 10:8, 11.</margin>
10. **I also.**] The heretics and others not well-founded in the Scriptures and antiquity marvel at the Pope’s pardons, counting them either fruitless or unlawful, or no older than St. Gregory <note>St. Gregory the Great, Pope from 590–604 AD.</note>. But indeed, the authority, power, and right of them comes from Christ’s own word and commission, principally given to Peter, and so afterward to all the Apostles, and in their persons to all the chief Pastors of the Church, when it was said, *Whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.* By this commission, the holy Bishops of old cut off large portions of penance enjoined to offenders, and granted peace, grace, or indulgence <note>Indulgence here refers to the remission of the duration or severity of a required public penance.</note> *before* they had accomplished the measure of their appointed or deserved punishment; and that is what it means to give a pardon. And so St. Paul did here toward the Corinthian, whom he absolved out of mere grace and mercy, as the word *to give* or *to pardon* <note>original: "donare" or "condonare"</note> signifies, when he could have kept him longer in penance and temporal affliction for his offense. Although he had already inwardly repented before God, yet he was justly held under this correction for some satisfaction of his past fault, during the Apostle's pleasure.

<margin>What is a pardon or indulgence.</margin>
To remit, then, the temporal punishment or chastisement due to sinners after the offense itself and the guilt of it are forgiven by God, is an indulgence or pardon. This is something the principal magistrates of God's Church, by Christ’s warrant and the Apostle’s example, have always done, being no less authorized to pardon than to punish. By imitation of our Master (who forgave the adultress <note>original: "aduouteresse"</note> and various other offenders, not only their sins but also often the temporal punishments due for them), they are as much inclined to mercy as to justice.

<margin>Indulgences or pardons in the early Church.</margin>
<margin>Cyprian, in the places cited. 2 Corinthians 1. Colossians 1:24.</margin>
10. **For you.**] Theodoret <note>A 5th-century bishop and theologian.</note> says regarding this passage that the Apostle gave this pardon to the Corinthian at the intercession of the blessed men Timothy and Titus. And we may read in various places, specifically in St. Cyprian, that indulgences or remissions were given in the early Church through the mediation of holy Confessors or Martyrs, and by communicating the satisfactory works of one to another. To this end, they gave their letters to Bishops on behalf of various Christian brothers, a practice most agreeable to the mutual exchange that exists between the members of Christ’s mystical body, and very consistent with God's justice, which stands firm by the supply of one sort who abound in favor of another sort who lack. In this way, the Apostle confesses that he himself, through his suffering and tribulations, supplies the lack of such sufferings as Christ has to endure—not in his own person, but in his body, which is his Church. Upon this, we infer most certainly that the satisfactory and penal works of holy Saints suffered in this life are communicable and applicable to the use of other faithful men, their fellow members in our Lord, and are to be dispensed according to everyone's necessity and merit by those whom Christ has placed over his family and made the dispensers of his treasures.

<margin>All pardon and remission is in the power and name of Christ. Heretical translation.</margin>
<margin>In the person of Christ <note>original: "ἐν προσ-ωπω χυ"</note>. 1 Corinthians 5.</margin>
10. **In the person of Christ.**] Because many, out of ignorance or pride, might reprove the practice of God’s Church and her officers, or deny the Apostle’s authority to be so great over men's souls as to punish and pardon in this way, St. Paul purposely and precisely tells them that he gives pardon as Christ's Vicar, or as representing his person in this case. Therefore, no man should marvel at his power in this, unless he thinks that Christ’s power, authority, and commission are not sufficient to release temporal punishment due to sinners. And this is the proper meaning of these words, **In the person of Christ**, and not as the Protestants would have it (the better to avoid the previous conclusion of the Apostle giving indulgence), **In the face or sight of Christ**. You may easily understand this by the Apostle's similar appeal to Christ’s power when he committed this offender to Satan, affirming that he gave that sentence in the name and with the virtue or power of **our Lord JESUS CHRIST.** In all these cases, the Protestants' blindness is exceedingly great, who

Who cannot see that it is not the way to extol Christ's power to deny it to His Priests, seeing the Apostle claims it by the fact that Christ has such power, and that he himself does it in His name, virtue, and person? <margin>All binding and loosing must be used for the party's salvation.</margin>
We may see by this that the administration of such discipline, and the releasing of the same, are put into the power and hands of God's ministers. They may deal more or less rigorously, pardon sooner or later, and punish for a longer or shorter time, as shall be thought best by their wisdom. For the end of all such correction or pardoning must be the salvation of the party's soul, as the Apostle noted in 1 Corinthians 5:5. For some people, and at certain times, this may be better procured by the rigor of discipline than by <term>indulgence</term> <note>In this historical context, "indulgence" refers to leniency or the relaxing of required penance.</note>, and for others by lenity and humane

dealing (for so the pardoning of penance is called in the old Councils) rather than by too much chastisement. In those times, there was less pardoning and fewer indulgences because, in that voluntary use and acceptance of punishment, and through great zeal and fervor of spirit, every man fulfilled his penance and few asked for pardon. Now, in the decline of devotion and the loathing that men commonly have for doing great penance—though the sins are

Therefore, she enjoins small penance and seldom uses extremity with offenders as the holy Bishops of the primitive Church did. Instead, condescending to the weakness of her children, she pardons exceedingly often and much, not only all enjoined penance, but also all or great parts of whatever temporal punishment is due or deserved, either in this world or in the next.
<margin>Matthew 11:18.</margin>

They truly neither know nor like Christ's ordinance and commission in <term>binding or loosing</term> <note>The authority given to the Apostles to forgive or retain sins.</note>, nor His providence in the government of the Church.

<margin>17. Adulterating.]</margin>
<margin><note>original Greek: καπηλεύοντες (kapēleuontes)</note> Peddling or corrupting for profit.</margin>
<margin>The Heretics' corrupting of the Scripture.</margin>
The Greek word signifies to make a commodity of the word of God, as common wine merchants do with their wine. By this is expressed the peculiar trade of all Heretics, and it is exceedingly characteristic of the Protestants, who so corrupt the Scriptures by a mixture of their own fantasies, by false translations, glosses, and deceptive and pleasant commentaries. They do this to deceive the taste of the simple, just as tavern-keepers and tapsters do, making their wines salable by many artificial deceits. The Apostles, on the contrary—as do all Catholics—deliver the Scriptures and utter the word of God sincerely and entirely, in the same sense and manner as the fathers left them to the Church, interpreting them by the same Spirit by which they were written or spoken.

#### ->CHAPTER III.<-

<margin>The Apostles wrote the Gospel in men's hearts much more than on paper.</margin>
3. *the Epistle of Christ.*] St. Paul and other holy writers of Scriptures did set down many things in writing, by pen, ink, and paper, all of which are of the Holy Ghost; but the special and proper book of Christ's truth and Gospel, is not the external writing in those dead creatures <note>The author refers to physical materials like paper and ink as "dead creatures."</note>, but in the hearts of the faithful, being the proper subject of these truths and graces preached in the new Testament, and the dwelling-place of the Holy Ghost. In the which book of faithful men’s hearts St. Paul wrote diverse things not uttered in any Epistle: as sundry of the Apostles wrote the Christian religion in the hearts of their hearers only, and in other material books not at all. Whereof St. Irenaeus <note>original: "li. 3. c. 4." referring to his work *Against Heresies*</note> says, *What if the Apostles also had left no Scriptures, ought we not to follow the order of the tradition, which they delivered unto them to whom they committed the Churches? to which ordinance many nations of those barbarous people that have believed in Christ do consent, without letter or ink, having salvation written in their hearts, and keeping diligently the tradition of the elders.* And St. Jerome, (<note>original: "cont. Io. Hierof. c. 9. ad Pam." referring to his work *Against John of Jerusalem*</note>) *In the Creed of our faith and hope, which being delivered by tradition from*
<margin>Scripture written, and Tradition unwritten.</margin>

And this is the Church's book also, whereby and wherein she keeps faithfully all truth written in the hearts of those to whom the Apostles did preach, with the same diligence as she keeps and preserves the other book which is of Holy Scriptures, from all corruption by heretics and other injuries.

<margin>God's grace and free will must both work together.</margin>
5. *Of ourselves.*] This argues first against the heretics called Pelagians <note>A 5th-century group that believed humans could achieve salvation through their own efforts without divine grace.</note>, who hold that our meritorious actions or thoughts come from free will alone, and not from God's special grace. Secondly, it argues against the Protestants, who on the contrary refer everything to God and take away man's freedom and personal initiative in his thoughts and doings. The Apostle confesses our good thoughts to be our own, but not as coming from ourselves, but from God.

<margin>The letter kills both Jew and Heretic.</margin>
6. *The letter killeth.*] Just as the "letter" of the Old Law—when not truly understood or referred to Christ—killed the carnal Jew by commanding things without giving the grace and spirit to fulfill them; so the "letter" of the New Testament—when not truly understood or explained by the Spirit of Christ (which is only found in His Church)—kills the heretic. The heretic, being also carnal and void of spirit, gains nothing from the external commands or good lessons of the Scriptures, but rather takes harm from them. See Saint Augustine, <note>original: "to. 10. Ser. 70 & 100 de tempore. & li. de Sp. & lit. c. 5. 6. & seq."</note> Volume 10, Sermons 70 and 100 regarding the Church seasons; and the book *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapters 5, 6, and following.

<margin>The superiority of the New Testament, Sacraments, etc.</margin>
9. *Much more.*] The superiority of the New Testament and of its priesthood or ministry over the Old is this: the New, through all her Sacraments and Priests acting as immediate ministers of grace and the forgiveness of sins, does—by the very act performed <note>original: "ex opere operato," a technical term meaning the sacraments are effective by the power of the rite itself when properly administered.</note>—give the spirit of life and charity into the hearts of the faithful, just as the Old Law gave the letter or external act of the Law.

<margin>Heretics are more blind regarding the Church than the Jews are regarding Christ.</margin>
<margin>Augustine, on Psalm 30, discourse 2.</margin>
14. *The selfsame veil.*] Just as the Jews reading the Old Testament cannot see Christ in the Scriptures due to their blindness (which God allows to remain as a cover over their eyes and hearts as punishment for their disbelief), but shall perceive everything spoken of Him in their Law and Scriptures once they believe and have that cover removed; even so heretics have a far greater cover of blindness and disbelief over their hearts regarding the Catholic Church which they attack (as Saint Augustine notes). They cannot see the marvelous evidence of the Catholic Church and the truth in all points, no matter how much they read the Scriptures. But when they return to the obedience of that same Church, they shall find the Scriptures most clear in favor of her and her doctrine, and shall wonder at their former blindness.

<margin>True Christian liberty.</margin>
<margin>1 Peter 2, verses 14 and following.</margin>
17. *Liberty.*] The Spirit and grace of God in the New Testament releases us from the bondage of the Law and sin, but it is not a warrant for us to engage in "fleshly license" <note>An excuse for sinful behavior or lack of self-restraint.</note> as Saint Peter writes. Nor does it release Christians from their obedience to the order, law, and power of Magistrates, whether spiritual or temporal, as some heretics of these days seditiously teach.

->### ANNOTATIONS<-
->#### CHAPTER 5.<-

<margin>The objection against prayers for the dead, answered by St. Augustine.</margin>
10. *The proper things of his body.*] St. Augustine <note>original: "Enchiridion chapter 110"</note> objects to this speech of the Apostle, as if spoken by those who deny that the prayers, alms, and sacrifices of the living are available <note>meaning effective or helpful</note> for the dead, and he answers as follows: *This practice (he says) of God's Church in the commendation of the dead is in no way repugnant to the sentence of the Apostle, where he says that we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ, that every one may receive according to his deserts in the body, either good or evil. For, in his life and before death he deserved this: that these works after his death might be profitable unto him. For indeed they are not profitable for all men. And why so? Only because of the difference and diversity of men's lives while they were in the flesh.* He has the same argument in various other places. <note>Augustine, Book on the Predestination of the Saints, chapter 12; and To Dulcitius, question 2. See also St. Dionysius, chapter 7, Ecclesiastical Hierarchy.</note>

<margin>Works meritorious and demeritorious.</margin>
10. *Either good or evil.*] Heaven is as much the reward of good works as Hell is the stipend <note>wages or payment</note> for evil works. Neither is faith alone sufficient to procure salvation, nor lack of faith the only cause of damnation: by good deeds men merit the one, and by evil deeds they deserve the other. This is the Apostle’s doctrine here and in other places, however the adversaries of good life and works <note>A reference to Protestant reformers who taught salvation by faith alone.</note> teach otherwise.

<margin>Bishops and Priests under Christ are ministers of our reconciliation.</margin>
18. *The ministry of reconciliation.*] Christ is the chief Minister, according to his manhood, of all our reconciliation to God: and for him, as his ministers, the Apostles and their successors—the Bishops and Priests of his Church—are placed. In them is the word of reconciliation, both by the ministering of the Sacrifice <note>The Mass</note> and Sacraments for the remission of sins, and by preaching and governance of the world toward salvation. And therefore their preaching must be to us as if Christ himself preached: their absolution and remission of sins as Christ’s own pardon: their whole office being nothing else (as we see by this passage) but the Vicarship <term>Vicarship: acting in the person or place of Christ</term> of Christ.

21. *The justice of God.*] Even as (says St. Augustine) when we read, *Salvation is our Lord’s*, it is not meant that salvation whereby our Lord is saved, but whereby they are saved whom he saves: so when it is said,

### A N N O T A T I O N S
### C H A P T E R VI.

<margin>God’s Ministers are his co-workers.</margin> 1. *Helping.*] Because he declared before that the Ministers of the New Testament are Christ’s deputies, and that when they preach or perform any function, God as it were speaks or acts through them, he now boldly says, *Helping therefore:* that is to say, joining or working together with God, we exhort you. <gloss>working together</gloss> <note>original: συνεργοῦντες (*synergountes*)</note>

<margin>God’s grace forces no man against his will. Voluntary penance.</margin> 1. *Grace in vain.*] The grace of God does not work in man against his will, nor does it force anything without his acceptance and consent; therefore it lies within man’s will to frustrate or to follow the movement of God, as this text plainly proves.

5. *In Watchings.*] When in the midst of many miseries and persecutions, the Apostles yet of their own accord added and required voluntary vigils, fastings, and chastity, we may well perceive these works to be wonderfully pleasing to God, and especially necessary for the Clergy.

<margin>Not to communicate with Heretics in any act of religion.</margin> 14. *What society.*] Generally here is forbidden conversation and dealing with all Infidels, and consequently with Heretics, but especially in prayers, or meetings at their Schismatical Service, preaching, or any other divine office whatsoever. Which the Apostle here utters in more particular and different terms, so that Christian people may take better heed of it. No society (he says) nor fellowship, no participation nor agreement, no consent between light and darkness, Christ and Baal <note>Baal: here used as a general term for false gods or the devil</note>, the temple of God and the temple of Idols: all Service—the pretended worship of God set up by Heretics or Schismatics—being nothing else but the Service of Baal and plain Idolatry, and their conventicles <note>conventicles: secret or unauthorized religious meetings</note> nothing but conspiracies against Christ. From such people, therefore, we must especially sever ourselves always in heart and mind, and regarding any act of religion, in body also, just as the children of Israel were commanded by God to separate themselves from the Schismatics <margin>Numbers 16:26</margin> Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, and their tabernacles, by these words: *Depart from the tabernacles of the impious men, and touch not those things which belong to them, lest you be wrapped up in their sins.*
