### A N N O T A T I O N S
### C H A P T E R. VIII.

<margin>Temporal benefits upon spiritual persons. One may satisfy and perform works of supererogation for another.</margin>
14. *Abundance supply.*] He means that those who abound in worldly riches should share them to supply the needs of their other brothers, in whatever way they can. On the other hand, those whom they help with material things may share with the wealthy some of their spiritual riches, such as prayers and other holy works and graces—which is a happy exchange and interaction for wealthy men, if only they could see it. And this passage proves plainly that the fastings and satisfactory deeds <note>Acts of penance intended to make "satisfaction" for the temporal punishment of sin.</note> of one man are beneficial to others; yes, and that holy Saints or other virtuous persons may, in measure and proportion to other men's necessities and deservings, allot to them the <term>supererogation</term> <note>The Catholic doctrine that saints can perform "works of supererogation"—good deeds beyond what is strictly required by God's commandments—which form a "treasury of merit" that can benefit others.</note> of their spiritual works, just as those who abound in worldly goods may give alms from their surplus to those who are in need. The Apostle sets down this exchange and proportion of things quite clearly.

## ANNOTATIONS
### CHAPTER IX.

<margin>Proctors for Catholic prisoners.</margin> 1. *Toward the Saints.*] By the Apostle’s earnest and often calling upon the Corinthians to give alms for relieving the faithful in distress, the Pastors of God’s Church may learn, that it specially pertaineth to their office to be <term>proctors</term> <note>An agent or representative who acts on behalf of another; in this context, someone who advocates for and manages aid.</note> for holy men in prison, poverty, and all other necessity, specially when their want cometh for confession of their faith.

<margin>Cheerful giving.</margin> 5. *Not as avarice.*] The covetous man that parteth with his penny painfully and with sorrow as though he lost a limb of his body, is noted; and cheerful, ready, voluntary, and large contribution is commended.

<margin>The greater alms, the greater merit and reward.</margin> 6. *Soweth sparingly.*] Alms is compared to seed. For as the seed thrown into the ground, though it seem to be cast away, yet is not lost, but is laid up in certain hope of great increase: so that which men give in alms, though it seem to be cast away and to perish in respect of the giver, yet in deed it is most fruitful, the benefit thereof manifoldly returning to him again. Whereupon the Apostle’s conclusion is clear, that according to the measure of the alms or feeding or harvest, that is, of grace and glory shall ensue. See St. Augustine in *Psalm 49 near the middle, and question 4 to Dulcitius.* <note>original: "Psal. 49 circa med. & q. 4. ad Dulcitium."</note>

<meta>The text cuts off at the start of a new annotation for verse 8, likely discussing "sufficiency" or "notion."</meta>

<summary>In this passage, St. Paul encourages the Corinthians to give generously and cheerfully to the collection for the poor, using the metaphor of sowing and reaping to describe spiritual rewards. The annotations emphasize the role of church leaders as advocates for those imprisoned or impoverished for their faith.</summary>

<margin>Alms result in God’s honor.</margin>
12. *Does not only supply.*] When alms are given, especially to holy men <note>In the early Church, "holy men" often referred specifically to the "saints" or the poor Christians in Jerusalem for whom this collection was gathered.</note>, not only do the givers obtain a great benefit thereby, and the needs of others are supplied, but God is also exceedingly honored by the receivers' continual prayers and thanksgivings. Thus, charity bestowed in this manner is an act of God’s worship and of religion.

## ANNOTATIONS
### CHAPTER X.

<margin>Punishing of Heretics.</margin>
<margin>Their pride.</margin>
4. *Weapons.*] He means the ample spiritual and Apostolic power given by Christ for the punishment of false Apostles, Heretics, and rebels against God’s Church. These are noted here specifically by their pride and insolence (which is the defining mark of such individuals), as they exalt themselves above the knowledge of God, which consists in humble obedience to the faith and to its preachers.

<margin>The spiritual power of Bishops against Heretics.</margin>
<margin>Calvin upon this place.</margin>
6. *To revenge.*] You may see by this that the spiritual power of Bishops consists not only in preaching the Gospel—and thus only by persuasion and exhortation (as some Heretics hold) to forgive or retain sins—but that it also has the authority to punish, judge, and condemn Heretics and other such rebels. <note>The author is defending the judicial authority of the Catholic Church against Protestant reformers.</note> This power is acknowledged by one of the principal rebels of this time <note>A reference to John Calvin</note>, who, being convinced by the evidence of this passage, admits it is grounded upon Christ's word: *Whatever you bind on earth, shall be bound in heaven (Matthew 18:18).* He also applies the words spoken to Jeremiah (Chapter 1:10)—*Behold, I appoint you over Nations and kingdoms, to plant, pluck up, build, and destroy*—to confirm and explain the Apostolic power cited here by St. Paul. <margin>Heretical Consistories.</margin> However, they would gladly take this power away from the lawful successors of the Apostles and give it to themselves, their ministers, and their consistories <note>administrative councils in Protestant churches</note>, which are nothing but the workshops and councils of sedition and all the conspiracies of this time against the lawful Princes of the world.

<margin>Ecclesiastical censures (namely Excommunication) when and where to be executed.</margin>
8. *Unto edification.*] This great power of the Church’s censures—especially Excommunication—was given for the good and salvation of the people. Therefore, it must not be used against the innocent. Furthermore, it should not even be used against Heretics or other offenders unless it is likely to benefit the individuals or the people, or can be executed without hurting or disturbing the whole Church—which is often not possible due to the sheer number of offenders. This caused the Apostle to signal here that he would not use his full authority against the false Apostles who disturbed the Corinthians until the people themselves were in perfect obedience to him. He feared that by punishing the principal offenders too soon, a greater disturbance and revolt might occur among the people if they were not first firmly settled in obedience.

## ANNOTATIONS
### CHAPTER 11.

<margin>Just as Eve was seduced by the Serpent, so the people are seduced by Heretics.</margin>
3. *From the simplicity.*] People fall from their first faith, purity, and simplicity in Christ, not by a sudden revolt, but little by little, by listening to the subtle persuasion of the Serpent. He speaks to them through the sweet words and allurements of Heretics. The Apostle gives the example of Eve, who was drawn away from her natural simplicity and obedience to God by her greedy desire for knowledge and the Devil's promise of the same. Likewise today, the promise and pretense of "secret" knowledge drives many a poor soul away from the sure, true, sincere, and only belief of God's Church.

<margin>Heretics are sometimes eloquent.</margin>
<margin>Knowledge is better than fancy words.</margin>
<margin>Young orators among heretics are preferred over the ancient Doctors of the Church.</margin>
6. *Unskilled in speech.*] By this we see that seditious and false teachers often have the gift of eloquence, by which simple people are easily deceived. Such were Korah and Dathan, as Josephus writes in *Antiquities of the Jews, Book 4, Chapter 2.* For this same reason, St. Augustine (in *Confessions, Book 5, Chapters 3 and 13*) calls the heretic Faustus the Manichaean <note>Faustus was a prominent 4th-century Manichaean bishop who was known for his rhetoric but lacked theological depth.</note> "a great snare of the Devil" <note>original: "magnum laqueum Diaboli"</note>. Augustine says that Faustus surpassed the glorious Doctor St. Ambrose in the outward show of words, but was far inferior to him (beyond all comparison) in substance and matter. In this way, the Apostle is content here to compare himself with the false apostles. The Corinthians followed and praised those men far above Paul because of their eloquence; Paul grants them that gift but claims for himself superiority in knowledge, which all wise men prefer over empty words. It is the ruin of our poor country that people nowadays give credit to new orators and foolish youngsters for their sweet speeches, rather than to the glorious Doctors of Christ's Church for their singular knowledge and more serious eloquence.

<meta>catchword: CHAP.</meta>

<summary>Paul lists his extensive physical sufferings and escapes as evidence of his apostleship, while the commentary warns that heretics use smooth speech to lead the faithful away from the Church's simple truths.</summary>

->C H A P T E R XII.<-

<margin>
*Visions have no credit with heretics.*
</margin>
1. *Visions.*] St. Cyprian (*Letter 69, number 4*) complains that the adversaries of God’s Church and priests give no credit to visions. But their incredulity is much greater in our days, as they condemn all such revelations, even though they are reported and recorded as most certain by holy St. Gregory, St. Bede, or whosoever else. Yea, they are so wicked in this case, that the vision which the holy author of the book of Machabees calls <note>original: fide dignum</note> *worthy of credit*, is one reason why they deny the whole book to be <term>Canonical<note>Considered part of the official, authoritative list of books in the Bible.</note></term>. And they might just as well deny all of St. Paul’s Epistles for this vision, and for similar reasons, the Acts of the Apostles (*Acts 9, 10, 11, 12, 27*) and the Gospel itself (*Matthew 1:20, 2:13, 19*). <margin>2 Machabees 15:11.</margin>

<margin>
*The Apostles: some greater than others.*
</margin>
11. *Above measure Apostles.*] Although all were equal in that they were Apostles of one and the same order, yet we may see that some had marvelous great preeminence and privilege above others in the same office: especially St. Peter and St. John, whom St. Paul often calls *great Apostles, above measure* or *passing Apostles, the pillars*, etc. (2 Corinthians 11:5, 12:11; Galatians 2:9).

<margin>
*We must stick to the faith first planted by miracles.*
</margin>
12. *In signs.*] Miracles are necessary, and are great signs of truth when it is first newly taught. And therefore let all Catholic men hold fast that faith which was first preached and confirmed by miracles—as in England by St. Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Canterbury, the 6th-century missionary to the English.</note>, and in other nations by other holy Apostolic men. And let the Heretics—who preach extraordinarily, newly, and otherwise than we received at our first conversion—show their calling and doctrine by miracles, or else let them be taken for false Apostles, as they are.

## A N N O T A T I O N S
### C H A P T E R XIII.

<margin>We may know that we have faith, but not that we are in a state of grace.</margin> 5. *Test yourselves.*] The <term>Heretics<note>Likely referring to Protestant reformers who taught the "assurance of salvation."</note></term> argue from this, that every man may know himself certainly to be in a state of grace. However, the Apostle speaks expressly and only of faith. A man may know and feel the act of faith within himself because it is an act of the understanding (the mind). Yet, he cannot be assured that he has had his sins remitted, or that he is in all points in a state of grace and salvation. This is because every man who holds the Catholic faith does not always live a good life agreeable to that faith; nor are the acts of our will so subject to our understanding that we can know for certain whether we are good or evil. See St. Augustine *Volume 7, On the Perfection of Justice, Chapter 15; Book on Rebuke and Grace, Chapter 13;* and St. Thomas Aquinas *Summa Theologiae, Part 1-2, Question 112, Article 5.*

<summary>This page concludes the Second Epistle to the Corinthians with Paul’s final warnings of disciplinary action and his famous Trinitarian blessing. The annotations defend the Catholic view that while one can be sure of their faith, they cannot have absolute certainty of being in a state of grace.</summary>

# THE ARGUMENT OF THE
## EPISTLE OF ST. PAUL TO
### THE GALATIANS.

<image-desc>An ornamental drop-cap letter 'T' set within a square frame decorated with foliage.</image-desc>

THAT this Epistle may seem to be the first that St. Paul wrote, was declared in the <term>Argument<note>A summary or introductory explanation of a book's contents and purpose.</note></term> of the Epistle to the Romans; notwithstanding that in the second chapter it is evident to have been written at least 14 years after his Conversion, and (as it is said) from Ephesus, likely at that time of his being there which is mentioned in Acts 18.

*The occasion of it was such False apostles as we read of in Acts 15: <note>original: "Et quidam descendentes, &c."</note> "And certain men coming down from <term>Jewry<note>Judea.</note></term>, taught the brethren (that is, the Christian Gentiles at Antioch) that unless you be circumcised according to the manner of Moses, you cannot be saved." Such newcomers also came to the Galatians (whom St. Paul had converted in Acts 16, as he himself mentions in Galatians 1 and 4) and did seduce them, saying that all the other Apostles—to whom they should listen rather than to Paul (who came they knew not from where)—practiced Circumcision: yes, and that Paul himself, when he was among them, dared do nothing else. And to win them over more easily, they did not lay upon them the burden of the whole Law, but of Circumcision only.*

*Against these deceivers, St. Paul declares that he received his Apostleship and learned the Gospel that he preaches from Christ himself after his Resurrection: and that the other Apostles (although he learned nothing from them) received him into their society, and approved well of his preaching to the Gentiles, even though they themselves, being Jews and living among the Jews, had not yet left the ceremonies of the Law. However, they did not place in those ceremonies any hope of <term>justification<note>The process by which a person is made righteous or "right" in the eyes of God.</note></term>, but in Christ alone without them. He declares moreover, that the said False apostles lied about him in saying that he also preached Circumcision sometimes. Again, he argues that they themselves, in preaching nothing more than Circumcision, acted against the nature of Circumcision, because it is a profession to observe the whole Law. Finally, he states that whatever they pretended, they actually did it only to please the Jews, by whom they would otherwise be persecuted.*

*So it is that in this Epistle he handles the same matter as in the Epistle to the Romans, but here less exactly and more briefly, because the Galatians were very <term>rude<note>In this context, meaning uneducated, simple, or lacking in spiritual maturity.</note></term>, and the Romans, on the contrary, were <note>original: "repleti omni scientia"</note> replenished with all knowledge (Romans 15).*

<summary>This page introduces the Epistle to the Galatians, explaining that Paul wrote it to counter "False Apostles" who insisted that Gentile converts must be circumcised. Paul defends his divine authority and argues that salvation comes through Christ rather than Jewish ceremonial law.</summary>
<keywords>St. Paul, Galatians, Circumcision, False Apostles, Justification, Law of Moses, Ephesus, Acts of the Apostles</keywords>

## ANNOTATIONS
### CHAPTER 1.

<margin>St. Paul sent to preach by the ordinary laying on of hands.</margin>
1. *Neither by man.*] Although he was not first chosen to be an Apostle by human election, nomination, or assignment, but by God's own special appointment: yet by the same express ordinance of God, he took orders or the <term>imposition of hands</term><note>the traditional ritual for ordination</note> from men, as is clear in *Acts 13.* Let us be wary then of such false Apostles as nowadays intrude themselves into the office of Ministry and preaching, being neither called by God, nor rightly ordained by men.

<margin>No show of learning or virtue must move us from the faith.</margin>
8. *Or an Angel.*] Many worthy observations are made in the writings of the Church Fathers regarding this earnest 
admonition of the Apostle, and we may gather much from the text itself. First, that the credit of any man or Angel—regardless of their learning, eloquence, appearance of grace, or virtue, or even if they worked miracles—should not move a Christian man from that truth which he has once received in the Catholic Church. Vincent of Lérins treats this point excellently in his <note>original: "li. cont. profan. hæreſ. Nouitates"; *Book against the profane novelties of heresies*</note>. From this we may see that it is a great pity and shame that so many follow Luther and Calvin and such other <term>unlearned</term><note>original: "leude"; in this period, the word meant unlearned, common, or wicked</note> fellows into a new Gospel; they are so far from being Apostles or Angels that they are not at all comparable with the ancient Heretics in gifts of learning or eloquence, much less in a good life.

<margin>Preaching contrary to the faith received is forbidden, not other preaching.</margin>
<margin><note>original: "Tract. 98 in Ioā."; *Tract 98 on the Gospel of John*</note></margin>
Secondly, St. Augustine notes upon the word, *Beside*, that not all other teaching, or preaching more than what was first given, is forbidden, but only such as is contrary to and disagreeing with the rule of faith. The Apostle did not say, he says, "If any man preaches to you *more* than you have received," but, "*beside* that you received." For if he had said that, he would be doing a disservice to himself, who desired to come to the Thessalonians so that he might supply that which was lacking in their faith. Now, he who supplies,
<meta>The catchword at the bottom of the page "addeth" indicates that the text continues on the next page with the thought: "he who supplies, adds to what was there, but does not take away from the foundation."</meta>

<summary>Paul details his transformation from a persecutor of Christians to a divinely commissioned Apostle, emphasizing that his authority came directly from Christ rather than the other Apostles. The commentary uses Paul's words to attack Protestant reformers like Luther and Calvin, arguing that they lack the proper ordination and continuity of faith found in the Catholic Church.</summary>

# CHAPTER 1. TO THE GALATIANS.

...addeth that *which was lacking*, taketh not away that *which was*, etc. By which we see how frivolously and calumniously the Heretics charge the Church with addition to the Scriptures.

<margin>The Gospel is not only in the written word of scripture, but in unwritten tradition also.</margin>
Thirdly, as well by the word *we evangelize* <note>original Latin: "euangelizamus"</note> as the word *you have received* <note>original Latin: "accepistis"</note> we may note that the first truth, against which no second "Gospelling" or doctrine may be admitted, is not that only which he wrote to the Galatians, or which is contained either in his or any other of the Apostles' or Evangelists' writings, but that which was by word of mouth also preached, taught, or delivered to them first, before he wrote to them. Therefore the Adversaries of the Church that measure the word of God or Gospel by the Scriptures only, thinking themselves not to incur St. Paul's curse, except they teach directly against the written word, are foully beguiled. As therein also they shamefully err, when they charge the Catholics with adding to the Gospel, when they teach anything that is not in express words written by the Apostles or Evangelists; not marking that the Apostle in this Chapter, and elsewhere, commonly calls his and his fellows' whole preaching "the Gospel," be it written or unwritten.

<margin>After-preaching and "over-sowing" of novelties argues false doctrine.</margin>
Fourthly, by the same words we see condemned all "after-preachings," later doctrines, new sects and authors of the same: that only being true, which was first by the Apostles and Apostolical men (as the lawful husbandmen of Christ's field) sown and planted in the Church: and that false, which was later and as it were "over-sown" by the enemy. By which rule not only Tertullian (*On Prescription against Heretics, numbers 6 & 9*) but all other ancient Doctors, and specially St. Irenaeus (*Book 3, chapters 2, 3, 4*) tried truth from falsehood, and condemned old Heretics, proving Marcion, Valentine, Cerdon, Menander, and such like, to be false Apostles, because they came in with their novelties long after the Church was settled in former truth.

<margin>Book against the profane novelty of heresies <note>original Latin: "Li. cont. proph. hær. nouit."; a reference to the work of Vincent of Lérins</note></margin>
<margin>The Apostle's curse upon all that teach new doctrine, and draw men from the Catholic Church.</margin>
Sixthly, this curse or <term>execration</term><note>A formal and religious denunciation or curse</note> pronounced by the Apostle, touches not only the Galatians, or those of the Apostle's time that preached otherwise than they did, but it pertains to all times, preachers, and teachers, unto the world's end. And it concerns them (as <term>Vincent of Lérins</term><note>A 5th-century monk and theologian famous for his guide on how to distinguish true Catholic teaching from heresy</note> says) that preach a new faith, or change that old faith which they received in the unity of the Catholic Church. *To preach anything to Christian Catholic men (says he) besides that which they have received, never was it lawful, never is it, nor never shall it be lawful. To say <term>anathema</term><note>A formal curse or excommunication</note> to such, it has been, and is, and shall be always beneficial.* So St. Augustine by this place holds all accursed, 
<margin>St. Augustine, Epistle 165.</margin>
that draw a Christian man from the society of the whole Church, to make him a separate part of any one sect; that call people to the hidden <term>conventicles</term><note>Secret or illegal religious meetings</note> of Heretics, away from the open and known Church of Christ; that allure to the private, away from the common: finally all that draw with chatting curiosity
<margin>St. Augustine, Epistle 48; Psalm 103, Sermon 2.</margin>
the children of the Catholic Church, by teaching anything besides what they found in the church. *Mentioning also that a <term>Donatist</term><note>A member of a schismatic sect in North Africa that claimed only they were the true, pure church</note> feigned that an Angel had admonished him to call his friend out of the Communion of the Catholic Church into his sect. And he says, that if it had been an Angel indeed, yet should he not have heard him.* Lastly St. Jerome uses this
<margin>Zeal against heretics.</margin>
place, wherein the Apostle gives the curse or anathema to all false teachers not once but twice, to prove that the zeal of Catholic men ought to be so great toward all Heretics and their doctrines, that they should give them the anathema, though they were never so dear unto them. In which case, says this holy Doctor, I would not spare my own parents. *To Pammachius, chapter 3, against John of Jerusalem.*

<margin>to visit for the purpose of getting to know <note>original Greek: ιστορησαι</note></margin>
<margin>St. Paul does visit St. Peter out of honor and reverence toward him.</margin>
18. *To see Peter.*] In what estimation St. Peter was with this Apostle, it appears: seeing that for respect and honor of his person, and out of duty (as Tertullian says in *On Prescription*), notwithstanding his great ecclesiastical affairs, he went so far to see him. Not in a vulgar manner, but (as St. Chrysostom notes the Greek word to import) to behold him as men behold a thing or person of name, excellence, and majesty. For which cause, and to fill himself with the perfect view of his behavior, he stayed with him fifteen days. See St. Jerome (*Epistle 103 to Paulinus, volume 3*), who makes also a mystery of the number of days that he tarried with St. Peter. See St. Ambrose in his *Commentary on this place*, and St. Chrysostom upon this place, and *Homily 87 on John*.

**2. Conferred with them.]** Though St. Paul were taught his Gospel of God and not of man, and had an extraordinary calling by Christ himself, yet by revelation he was sent to Jerusalem to confer the said Gospel which he preached, with his elders the ordinary Apostles and Rulers of the Church, to put both his vocation and doctrine to their trial and approbation, and to join in office, teaching, and society or communion with them. For there is no extraordinary or miraculous vocation, that can sever or separate the person so called, in doctrine or fellowship of Christian life and religion, from the ordinary known society of God's people and Priests. Therefore whosoever he be (upon what pretence so ever) that will not have his calling and doctrine tried by the ordinary Governors of God's Church, or disdaineth to go up to the principal place of our religion, to confer with Peter and other pillars of the Church, it is evident that he is a false teacher, a Schismatic, and a Heretic. By which rule you may try all your new teachers of Luther's or Calvin's school: who never did nor ever durst put their preaching to such conference or trial of holy Council or Bishops, as they ought to do, and would do, if it were of God, as St. Paul's was.

<margin>
The approbation of St. Paul's doctrine by Peter and the rest, was very requisite.

<margin>
No absurdity that the Scriptures be approved by the Church's testimony.

**2. Wherein we see, this holy Apostle did not as the seditious proud Heretics do nowadays, which refusing all man's attestation or approbation, will be tried by Scriptures only. As also we may learn that it is no such absurdity as the Adversaries would make it, to have the Scriptures approved by the Church's testimony. Seeing the Gospel which St. Paul preached (being of as much certainty and of the same Holy Ghost that the Scriptures be) was to be put in conference and examination of the Apostles, without all derogation to the truth, dignity, or certainty of the same. <margin>All Catholic preachers and pastors must communicate with Peter and his successors.</margin>
9. *Gave the right hands of society.*] There is, and always ought to be, a common fellowship and fraternity among all pastors and preachers of the Church. Into which society whoever does not enter, but stands in <term>Schism</term> <note>A formal division or separation within a church or religious body.</note> and separation from Peter and the chief Apostolic pastors—no matter what pretense he has or from where he claims his authority—he is a wolf and no true pastor. This union and communion together was so necessary even in St. Paul’s case that, despite his special calling from God, the Holy Ghost still caused him to go up to the senior Apostles to be received into their fellowship or brotherhood. For it should be noted that St. Peter, James, and John were not sent to St. Paul to join with him or to have their doctrine and calling tested by him; but on the contrary, he was sent to them as the chief, well-known, and ordinary Apostles. They, therefore, gave Paul their hands—that is to say, took him into their society—and not he them. And St. Jerome’s rule concerning this shall be found true until the world's end, speaking of St. Peter's successor: *He that gathers not with you, scatters.* <note>original: *He that gathereth not vvith thee, scattereth. Ep. 57.*</note> And in another place, for the same cause, he calls Rome the *most safe and sure haven of communion* or society. <note>original: *tutissimum Communionis portum. Ep. 16. c. 3.*</note>

<margin>The heretics' ridiculous argument against Peter’s preeminence.</margin>
Furthermore, when the <term>Heretics</term> <note>In this context, the author refers to Protestant reformers who challenged the Pope's authority.</note> try to use this passage to prove that Peter had no preeminence over Paul (since they were fellow Apostles), it is ridiculous. It is as if they think all members of one fellowship or brotherhood must always be equal, or as if there were no order, government, superiority, and inferiority in every well-appointed society. They might perceive from this whole passage that Peter was, in a special and more singular way, the Apostle of the Jews, even though James and John were as well; just as St. Paul is called the Apostle and teacher of the Gentiles in a more singular way than St. Barnabas, even though they were both taken into this society here, just as they were both set apart for this ministry and ordained together in *Acts 13*. It is a poor reason, then, to say or think that St. Peter is not above St. Barnabas either, simply because of this society and fellowship into which he was received along with St. Paul.

<margin>The heretics maliciously disparage St. Peter.</margin>
<margin>Paul’s rebuke of Peter teaches us the zeal of the one and the humility of the other.</margin>
11. *I resisted him.*] The wicked Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote a famous treatise against Christianity.</note> (as St. Jerome writes) charges St. Paul with envy and impudent boldness, and St. Peter with error. <note>original: *Proœm. Comment. in Galat.* (Preface to the Commentary on Galatians)</note> Even so, the similar impious "sons of Ham" <note>A biblical reference to Ham, who mocked his father Noah's nakedness; used here to describe those who gleefully point out the faults of Church fathers.</note> gladly charge St. Peter for this and other things, as though he had committed the greatest crimes in the world. It is the property of heretics and evil men to be glad to see the Saints rebuked and their faults discovered, as we may learn in the writings of St. Augustine against Faustus the Manichee, who collected all the acts of the holy Patriarchs that might seem worthy of blame to the people. The faithful Doctor (Augustine) defends them at length against him, just as he and St. Cyprian before him find much reason here to praise the virtues of both Apostles: St. Paul’s great zeal and St. Peter’s wonderful humility. They praise that the one, for the cause of God, would not spare his superior, and that the other, in his excellent dignity, would not take it poorly, nor by claiming his supremacy disdain or refuse to be corrected by his junior. Of these two traits, the Fathers count Peter's humility the greater grace and more worthy of imitation.

"For neither did Peter," says St. Cyprian, "whom our Lord chose first and upon whom he built the Church, when Paul disputed with him about circumcision, claim anything to himself insolently or arrogantly, saying that he held the <term>Primacy</term> <note>The state of being first in rank or authority; the office of the Pope.</note> and therefore the later disciples ought rather to obey him." <note>original: *ep. 71 ad Quintum. nu. 2.*</note> And St. Augustine says: "That which was done by Paul profitably through the liberty of charity, the same Peter took in good part through the holy and kind godliness of humility. And so he gave to posterity a more rare and holy example—if at any time they perhaps did wrong, to be content to be corrected by their juniors—than Paul did by being bold and confident; indeed, it shows that inferiors may resist their betters to defend the truth of the Gospel, provided brotherly charity is always preserved." <note>original: *ep. 19 c. 2 in fine.*</note>

<margin>It proves nothing against Peter’s superiority that he was rebuked.</margin>
<margin>The superior may be rebuked or admonished by the inferior.</margin>
By these notable speeches of the Doctors, we may also see how frivolously the heretics argue that St. Peter could not be superior to St. Paul because he was rebuked by him. On the contrary, the Fathers make it an example for superiors to bear the correction or control of their inferiors with humility. Specifically, by this example, St. Augustine excellently declares that the Blessed Martyr St. Cyprian—who went astray regarding the rebaptizing of those christened by heretics—could not, and would not, have been offended to be admonished and reformed on that point by his fellows or inferiors, and much less by a whole Council. "We have learned," says Augustine, "that Peter the Apostle, in whom the Primacy of the Apostles is so preeminent by excellent grace, when he acted otherwise concerning circumcision than the truth required, was corrected by Paul, the later Apostle. I think (without any reproach to him) Bishop Cyprian may be compared to Peter the Apostle; however, I ought rather to fear lest I be insulting to Peter. For who does not know that the principal rank of the Apostleship is to be preferred before any dignity of Bishop whatsoever? But if the grace of the Chairs or <term>Sees</term> <note>The seat of authority of a bishop.</note> differ, yet the glory of the martyrs is one." <note>original: *li. 2 de bapt. c. 1.*</note> And who is so dull that they cannot see that the inferior—though not by office and jurisdiction, yet by the law of brotherly love and fraternal correction—may rebuke his superior? Did any man ever wonder that a good priest or any virtuous person should tell the Pope, or any other great prelate or greatest prince on earth, their faults? Popes may be rebuked and are justly admonished of their faults, and they ought to take it in good part.

<margin>The heretics' criticism of Catholic Bishops is more like verbal abuse.</margin>
...and so they do and ever have done, when it comes from zeal and love, as in the cases of St. Paul, Irenaeus, Cyprian, Jerome, Augustine, and Bernard. But as for Simon Magus, Novatus, Julian the Apostate, Wycliffe, Luther, Calvin, and Beza, who do it out of malice and rail no less at the virtues of <term>Prelates</term> <note>High-ranking church officials, such as bishops.</note> than at their vices—I say that God's leaders must not be taught or corrected by such as these. However, they must patiently endure it, just as our Savior endured similar reproaches from the malicious Jews, and as David endured the cursing of Shimei. <margin><note>original: "2 Reg. 16"</note> 2 Samuel 16</margin>

<margin>St. Peter's error was not in matters of faith, but in his conduct or behavior.</margin>
11. *Reprehensible.*] The heretics use this passage to argue again that Peter then erred in faith, and therefore that Popes may fail in faith as well. To this we answer that, however other Popes may err in their private teachings or writings (which we have discussed before in the annotation on the words, *That thy faith fail not* <margin>Luke 22:32</margin>), it is certain that St. Peter did not fail in faith here, nor did he err in doctrine or knowledge. For it was <note>original: "conuersationis non predicationis vitium"</note> "a fault of conduct, not of preaching," as Tertullian says (*Against Heretics*, number 7). It was a default in behavior, life, or administration—which may be committed by any man, no matter how holy—and not an error in doctrine. St. Augustine and others who emphasize the severity of the incident think no differently. But St. Jerome and many other holy fathers deem it to have been no fault at all, but rather the same thing St. Paul himself did on similar occasions; they believe this entire conflict was a staged event agreed upon between them. It is a <term>school point</term> <note>A topic of debate among academic theologians (Scholastics).</note> much debated between St. Jerome and St. Augustine. <margin><note>original: "ep. 9. 11. 19. apud Auguft."</note> See Letters 9, 11, and 19 in Augustine's works. See also St. Chrysostom, Theophylact, etc.</margin>

<margin>...are truly just, and may keep the commandments.</margin> (quoting Deuteronomy, from where he recites this text) but only such as commit great and damnable crimes, and so by grievous and <term>mortal transgressions</term> <note>Sins that are considered grave enough to sever one's relationship with God's grace.</note> wholly break God’s precepts, and thereby incur the curse of the Law, from which the said Law could not deliver them of itself, nor by any other means, but by the faith and grace of JESUS CHRIST.

<margin>Not only faith. James 2.</margin> 11. *Lives by faith.*] It is neither the <term>heretics'</term> <note>A reference to the Protestant Reformers, who argued for "faith alone."</note> special presumption and confidence, nor the faith of Devils, nor faith without works which is dead in itself (as St. James says), that can give life to the just. For that which is dead cannot be the cause of life. But it is the Catholic faith, as St. Augustine writes, which works by <term>charity</term> <note>Love in action.</note> (according to the Apostle's own explanation of this whole passage) by which the just person lives. <note>original: "Li. 3 c. 5. cont. duas ep. <margin>Baptism gives grace and justification, not faith only.</margin> 27. *Have put on Christ.*] Here the adversaries <note>The opponents of the Catholic Church’s teachings on sacraments.</note> might have seen, if they were not blinded by contentious striving against God’s Church, that when Justification is attributed to faith without mention of good works or other Christian virtues and Sacraments, it is not meant to exclude any of the same from the working of justice or salvation. For here we learn that by the Sacrament of Baptism also we put on Christ, which is to put on faith, hope, charity, and all Christian justice. By the same we prove also that the Sacraments of the new law give grace, because the receivers of them "put on Christ." And the adversaries' evasion—that it is faith which works in the Sacrament, and not the Sacrament itself—is plainly false: Baptism gives grace and faith itself even to the infant who had none before.

->THE EPISTLE OF ST. PAUL CHAPTER 4.<-

# A N N O T A T I O N S
## CHAPTER 4.

<margin>External worship of God by use of creatures is necessary: and how the Heathen, Jews, and Christians differ in the same. The use of external elements in the Sacraments.</margin>
3. *Serving.*] There can be no external worship of God nor association of men in religion, either true or false, without the use of corporal things or elements <note>Paul uses the Greek word *stoicheia*, translated here as "elements," referring to the physical components used in religious rites.</note>. The Heathen so used the creatures of elements that they served them as their gods. The Jews, of whom the Apostle here speaks, served not the creatures themselves which they occupied in their ceremonies, but they served the only true God under the elements: that is to say, being servilely clogged, yoked, kept occupied and in awe, with innumerable fleshly, gross, and cumbersome offices about creatures. The Christians neither serve elements, as the one, nor are kept in servile thraldom thereby, as the other: but occupy only a few exceedingly easy, sweet, seemly, and significant, for an agreeable exercise both of body and mind. *Whereof St. Augustine says thus, in Book 3, Chapter 9 of On Christian Doctrine <note>original: "de doct. Christ."</note>: A few for many, most easy to be done, most honorable for significance, and most clean and pure to be observed and kept, has our Lord himself and the Apostolical discipline delivered. And in On True Religion <note>original: "de ver. relig."</note> Chapter 17: From the wisdom of God itself, human nature being taken, whereby we were called into liberty, a few Sacraments most wholesome were appointed and instituted, which might contain the society of Christian people, that is, of the free multitude under one God. And again, Against Faustus <note>original: "cont. Faust."</note> Book 19, Chapter 13: The Sacraments are changed, they are made easier, fewer, wholesomer, happier. The same he has in the 118th Epistle, Chapter 1, and many other places besides.* By which you may see, it is not all one to use elements, visible Sacraments or ceremonies, and to serve them as the Pagans do, or to serve under them as the Jews did, wherewith the <term>Heretics</term> <note>The author refers here to Protestant Reformers who criticized Catholic rituals as being too similar to Jewish or Pagan legalism.</note> calumniously charge the Christians. And as touching the small number, facility, efficacy, and significance, wherein the said holy father puts the special difference: who sees not that for so many busy sacrifices, we have but one; for Sacraments well near infinite, but seven: all so easy, so full of grace, so significant, as can be possible, as of every one in their several places is proved?

<margin>Our Sacraments are few and easy in respect of the Jews.</margin>
<margin>St. Augustine falsely alleged by the Heretics for two Sacraments only.</margin>
<margin>The other Sacraments proved out of St. Augustine.</margin>
<margin>Epistle 118, Chapter 1 & in Psalm 103, Sermon 1.</margin>
<margin>\* Augustine, Sermon 215 On the Time & On Rectitude of Catholic Conversation <note>original: "de temp & de rectitud. Cath. conversat."</note>.</margin>
Here, let the good Readers take heed of a double deceit used by the Adversaries about St. Augustine’s places alleged. First, in that they say he made but two Sacraments, which is untrue. For, although treating of the difference between the Jewish Sacraments and ours, he namely gives example in Baptism and the Eucharist (as sometimes also for example he names but one) yet he has no word nor sign at all that there should be no more. But contrariwise in the aforesaid Epistle 118 he insinuates, that besides those two, there are others of the same sort in the Scriptures. Yea, with water and bread, which are the elements of the two aforesaid Sacraments, he expressly names oil also (Book 2 Against the Letters of Petilian <note>original: "cont. lit. Petil."</note> Chapter 104) the element or matter of the Sacrament of Confirmation: which in the same place he makes to be a Sacrament as Baptism is. So does he affirm of the Sacrament of Orders in Book 1 On Baptism <note>original: "de bapt."</note> Chapter 1, and also of Matrimony in On the Good of Marriage <note>original: "de bono coniug."</note> Chapter 24. Of Penance likewise, he speaks as of Baptism, which he calls Reconciliation, in Book 1 On Adulterous Marriages <note>original: "de adult. coniug."</note> Chapter 28. Lastly, by the book On the Visitation of the Sick <note>original: "de visitatione infirmorum"</note> in St. Augustine, Book 2, Chapter 4; by Prosper in On Predictions <note>original: "de praedictionibus"</note> part 2, Chapter 29; St. Innocentius to Eugubinus <note>original: "ad Eugubinum"</note> volume 1, Council Epistle to Eugubinus, Chapter 8; St. Cyril Book 2 on Leviticus; and St. Chrysostom Book 3 On the Priesthood <note>original: "de Sacerdotio"</note>, \* *Extreme Unction* is proved to be a Sacrament. It is false then what the Heretics affirm of St. Augustine, by whose doctrine it is plain, that though the elements or Sacraments of the new law be but few and very few in comparison of those in the old law, yet there are no fewer than seven specified by him. Which number of seven the holy Councils of Florence and Trent do expressly define to have been instituted by Christ, against these late Heretics. See more of these Sacraments in their places: Acts 8, 1 Timothy 4, John 20, James 5, Ephesians 5.

<margin>St. Augustine falsely alleged against the ceremonies of the Church.</margin>
The other forgery of the Adversaries concerning the elements or ceremonies, is, that St. Augustine (Epistle 119, Chapter 19) should affirm, that the Church and Christian people in his days (whereupon they infer that it is so much more now) were so laden with observation of unprofitable ceremonies, that they were in as great servility and subjection to such things as the Jews. He says so indeed of some particular <term>presumptions</term> <note>In this context, unauthorized or superstitious customs practiced by individuals rather than the official Church.</note>, inventions, and usages of certain persons, as that some made it a heinous matter to touch the ground with their bare feet within their own octaves <note>The eight-day period following a major feast day.</note>, and such like vanities. Whereby some simple folks might be infected, which this holy Doctor specially disliked, and wishes such things (as they may, without scandal) to be taken away. But that he wrote or meant so of any ceremony that the Church uses, either appointed by Scripture, or Council, or custom of the Catholic Church, himself denies it in express terms in the same place, and in sundry others: where he allows all the holy ceremonies done in the ministration of the Sacraments and elsewhere. Whereby it is clear, that the Church's most comely orders and significant rites pertain not to the yoke of the old law, much less to the superstition of Gentility, as Heretics affirm: but to the sweet yoke of Christ and light burden of his law, to order, decency, and instruction of the faithful, in all liberty, love, faith, grace, and spirit.

9. *Weak and poor.*] Whether he means of the creatures which the Gentiles served (as it may seem by the words before of serving strange gods) so the elements were

<margin>
The Heathen and Jewish observation of days compared with the Christian observation of festivals and holy days, etc.
</margin>
10. *You observe days.*] That which St. Paul speaks against the idolatrous observation of days, months, and times, dedicated by the Heathen to their false gods, and to wicked men or spirits, as to Jupiter, Mercury, Janus, Juno, Diana, and such like, or against the superstitious differences of days—regarded as fatal, fortunate, or dismal—and other observations of times for good or ill luck in human actions, gathered either by personal fancy, popular observation, or curious and unlawful arts, or (lastly) of the Jewish festivals that were then ended and abolished, to which certain Christian Jews nevertheless wished to return the Galatians against the Apostle's doctrine: all that (I say) do the Heretics of our time falsely and deceitfully interpret against the Christian holidays, and the sanctification and necessary keeping of the same. This is not only contrary to the Church Fathers' exposition, but against the very Scriptures, and the practice of the Apostles and the whole Church. *See St. Augustine, Against Adimantus, chapter 16; Letter 118, chapter 7; and St. Jerome on this passage.* In Revelation chapter 1, verse 10, there is plain mention of Sunday, that is, our Lord’s day <note>original: "Dominicus dies"</note> unto which the Jewish Sabbath was altered, their Passover into our Easter, their Pentecost into our Whitsuntide <note>Whitsuntide is the traditional English name for Pentecost, seven weeks after Easter.</note>: which were ordained and observed by the Apostles themselves. And the antiquity of the feasts of Christ’s Nativity <note>Christmas</note>, Epiphany, and Ascension is such that they can be referred to no other origin but the Apostles' institution: who (as St. Clement testifies in *Apostolic Constitutions, book 8, chapter 39*) gave order for celebrating their fellow Apostles, St. Stephen's, and other Martyrs' days after their death: and much more no doubt did they give order for Christ’s festivals. According to which, the Church has kept not only his, but St. Stephen's and the Holy Innocents', even on the same days they are now solemnly kept, and his Blessed mother’s, and other Saints', (as the adversaries themselves confess) for above 1300 years, as appears in the harsh debates between Westphalus the Lutheran and Calvin, and by the writings between the Puritans and Protestants.

In this we cannot but wonder at the new Church of England, which (though against the pure Calvinists' will and doctrine) keeps other Saints' and Apostles' days of their death, and yet has abolished this special feast of our Lady's departure. They might keep it even if they did not believe in her bodily Assumption (to which St. Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite</note> gives such great testimony), being assured she has departed at the least: unless they either hate her, or think her worthy of less remembrance than any other Saint, * she herself prophesying the contrary of all Catholic generations, that they should bless her. And indeed the Assumption is her proper day, as also the feast of her Nativity: the others, the Purification and the Annunciation, which they keep in England, being not so unique to her, but belonging rather to Christ’s Presentation in the Temple and his Conception. To conclude, we may see in St. Cyprian (Letter 34), Origen (Homily 3 on various subjects), Tertullian (*On the Soldier's Crown* <note>original: "de cor. mil."</note>), St. Gregory Nazianzen (*On Love for the Poor* <note>original: "de amore pauperum"</note>), the Council of Gangra, and even in the Council of Nicaea itself giving order for Easter and the certain celebrating thereof, that Christian Festivals be holy, ancient, and to be observed on prescribed days and times. This is not "Jewish observation of days," as Aerius taught, for which he was condemned of Heresy, as St. Epiphanius witnesses. But regarding holidays, St. Augustine shows both the reason and his approval in these memorable words. First, for the feasts belonging to our Lord:
> We dedicate and consecrate the memory of God’s benefits with solemnities, feasts, and certain appointed days, lest by the passage of time there might creep in ungrateful and unkind forgetfulness.

<header>THE EPISTLE OF ST. PAUL CHAPTER 5</header>

<margin>The Scriptures have an allegorical sense besides the literal.</margin>
24. **By an allegory.**] Here we learn that the holy Scriptures have, besides the literal sense, a deeper spiritual and more fundamental meaning. This meaning is found not only in the holy words themselves, but in the actual events and people described; both the speeches and the actions signify something beyond the literal letter. If St. Paul himself had not indicated this richness of multiple meanings in certain places, the <note>The author is referring to Protestant Reformers who favored a strictly literal interpretation.</note> Heretics would have been less wicked and arrogant in their near-total condemnation of the holy fathers' allegorical explanations. These critics now show themselves to be merely brutish and worldly men, having no sense or feeling for the depth of the Scriptures which our holy fathers, the Doctors of God's Church, perceived.

<margin>True Christian liberty.</margin>
31. **Freedom.**] He means the liberty and release from the old ceremonies, sacraments, and the entire burden of the Law, as well as from the slavery of sin and the Devil for those who obey him. He does not mean liberty for every man to do whatever he pleases, or to be exempt from obeying spiritual or temporal laws and governors. It is not a license to never pray, fast, keep a holiday, or a workday except when and how it suits a man’s own imagination. Such a lawless and unrestrained state is far from the true liberty which Christ purchased for us.

### CHAPTER V.

6. *Faith.*] This is the faith working through charity, which St. Paul means elsewhere when he says that faith justifies. And note well that by these terms—circumcision and uncircumcision being of no value for justification—it is plain that in other places he means the works of Circumcision and Uncircumcision (that is, of the Jews and the Gentiles) done without faith, which are of no value. Rather, he means faith working through charity: as if to say, faith and good works, not works without faith.

<margin>
Justification by faith alone, disproved by comparing Scriptures.
</margin>
Again, note here that if the Protestants—who claim that comparing different passages is the best or only way to explain difficult parts of the Holy Scriptures—had followed their own rule, this one text would have interpreted and cleared up for them all others where justice and salvation might seem to be attributed to faith alone. The Apostle here so expressly sets down that the faith he commends so much before is not alone, but with charity: not idle, but working through Charity: as St. Augustine notes. <note>original: "de fid. & op. c. 14." — From St. Augustine's work 'On Faith and Works', chapter 14.</note>

<margin>
How the Protestants admit charity and good works to justification.
</margin>

Instead, they view them only as fruits and effects of faith alone, which they say does everything, even though the others are present. <margin>
Duty to our spiritual teachers.
</margin>
6. *Communicate*] The great duty and respect that we ought to have for those who preach or teach us the Catholic faith. This is not only because of the hard work they do for us and how they deserve well of us through their doctrine, but so that we may be sharers in their merits. We ought especially to do good to such people, or (as the Apostle speaks) communicate <term>communicate: to share resources or participate in</term> with them in all our temporal <term>temporal: earthly or material</term> goods, so that we may be partakers of their spiritual goods. See St. Augustine, book 2. *Questions on the Gospels, question 8.* <note>original Latin: "Euang. quaest. q. 8."</note>

<margin>
Whom to prefer when giving alms.
</margin>
10. *Especially.*] In giving alms <term>alms: charitable gifts for the poor</term>, though we may do well in helping all who are in necessity as far as we can, yet we are more bound to help Christians than Jews or Infidels, and Catholics rather than Heretics. See St. Jerome, *question 1 to Hedibia.* <note>original Latin: "q. 1. ad Hedibiam."</note>

<margin>
Justice is a quality that lives within us.
</margin>
<margin>
Faith, along with the other virtues, is the formal cause of justification.
</margin>
15. *A new creature.*] Note well that the Apostle calls that a "new creature" here, which in the last chapter he termed "faith working by charity," and in 1 Corinthians 7:19 "the observation of the commandments of God." From this we may learn that under the name of faith is contained the entire reformation of our souls and our new creation in good works. It also shows that Christian justice <term>justice: righteousness or being right before God</term> is a real quality, condition, and state of virtue and grace resident within us, and not an imaginary <note>original: "phantastical"</note> apprehension of Christ's justice merely credited <term>imputed: a theological term meaning to attribute something to someone legally rather than inherently</term> to us. Lastly, that the faith which justifies, when joined with the other virtues, is properly the "formal cause" <term>formal cause: the essential nature that makes a thing what it is; here, it means the grace that actually changes the person</term>, and not merely the "efficient" or "instrumental" cause of justification. That is to say, these virtues put together, being the effect of God’s grace, are our "new creature" and our justice in Christ.

# THE ARGUMENT <note>In this context, "Argument" means a summary or introduction to the themes and history of the book.</note> OF THE
## EPISTLE OF ST. PAUL TO
### THE EPHESIANS.

<image-desc>A large square ornamental initial 'O' containing a central human face (possibly a personification of the sun or wind) surrounded by decorative strapwork and floral flourishes.</image-desc>

Of St. Paul’s first coming to Ephesus, and his short stay there, we read in *Acts 18.* And immediately in *Acts 19,* we read of his return there according to his promise. At that time, he stayed there for three months, speaking to the Jews in the Synagogue (*Acts 19:8*), and afterward apart from them (because they were stubborn) for two years in a certain school, so that all who lived in Asia heard the word of our Lord, both Jews and Gentiles (*Acts 19:10*). The whole time he himself calls "three years" in his exhortation at Miletum <note>The ancient city of Miletus.</note> to the Clergy of Ephesus (*Acts 20:31*).

<margin>Eph. 3:1 & 4:1. Eph. 6:20.</margin>
After all this, he writes this Epistle to them from Rome (as it is said) being then a prisoner and in chains. This seems not to be from the first time he was in bonds there (of which we read in *Acts 28*), but the second time, which we read about in the Ecclesiastical Histories afterward. This is because he says in this Epistle (*Chapter 6:21*): *Tychicus will inform you of all things, whom I have sent to you.* Of whom again in the *2nd to Timothy (Chapter 4:12)* he says: *Tychicus I have sent to Ephesus.* And the said 2nd Epistle to Timothy was (no doubt) written very shortly before his death; for in it he says: *I am even now to be sacrificed, and the time of my resolution <note>Original: "resolution," meaning his departure from life or death.</note> is at hand. (2 Tim. 4:6).*

<margin>* See Act. 20:25, 32.</margin>
In the first three chapters, he commends to them the grace of God in calling the Gentiles no less than the Jews, and making one blessed Church of both. In this, his intention is to move them to persevere (for otherwise they would be exceedingly ungrateful) and especially not to be unsettled by his troubles, since he was their Apostle. He likely knew that it would be a great temptation <note>A trial of faith or a cause for discouragement.</note> to them if they should hear soon after that he had been executed; therefore, he also arms them at the end of the Epistle as if in complete harness <note>Armor.</note>.

In the other three chapters, he exhorts them to a good life in all points and all states, as becomes Christians. Above all other things, he urges that they be most diligent to continue in the unity of the Church and obedience to its pastors, whom Christ has given to continue and to be our support against all heretics, from his Ascension even to the full building up of his Church at the end of the world.

<summary>This page provides the historical and theological introduction to the Epistle to the Ephesians, explaining Paul's history with the city and his motivation for writing while a prisoner in Rome.</summary>
<keywords>Ephesians, St. Paul, Ephesus, Tychicus, Church Unity, Gentiles and Jews, Imprisonment, Spiritual Armor, Pastors, Heresy</keywords>

# ANNOTATIONS
## CHAP. I.

<margin>Nine orders of Angels.</margin>
**21. All Principality.]** The Fathers <note>Early Christian theologians and bishops</note> upon this, and other places of the old and new Testament, where they find the orders of holy Angels or spirits named, agree that there be nine orders of them. Of which some be here counted and called, as we see: in the Epistle to the Colossians, the order of Thrones is specified, which makes five: to which if we add these four, Cherubim, Seraphim, Angels, and Archangels, which are commonly named in holy writ, in all there be nine. *S. Dionysius, The Celestial Hierarchy, chapters 7, 8, 9, and The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, chapter 1; S. Athanasius, book on the Common Essence, near the end; Gregory, Moralia, book 32, chapter 18.* Therefore, good Reader, make no <margin>Calvin upon this place.</margin> account of * Calvin’s and others' infidelity, which blasphemously blame and condemn the holy doctors' diligence in this point, calling it curiosity and impiety. The whole endeavor of these heretics is, to bring all into doubt, and to corrupt every Article of our Religion.

<margin>As Christ is king, and yet men are kings also: so Christ is head of the Church, yet he may have a vice-regent.</margin>
**22. Head.]** It makes a high proof among the Protestants, that no man can be head of the Church, because it is a calling and dignity proper to Christ. But in truth by as good reason there should be no king nor lord, because, *He is king and lord.* neither should <margin>Rev. 19. 1 Pet. 2, 25.</margin> there be Bishop or Pastor, because he is the Bishop and Pastor of our souls: nor Pontifex <note>High Priest</note> nor Apostle, for by those titles S. Paul terms him *Hebrews 3:* none should be pillar, foundation

right in the same) to be given and shared with the Princes and Magistrates of the earth, both spiritual and temporal. This is true even though Christ, in a more divine, ample, absolute, excellent, and superior way, has all these things attributed or assigned to himself. So then, though he be the head of the Church, and the only head in such a sovereign and principal manner as no earthly man or mere creature ever is or can be, and is joined to the Church in a more excellent kind of union than any king is to his subjects or country, or any Pope or Prelate to the Church of which he is governor—even so far that it is called his Mystical Body: life, motion, spirit, and grace issuing down from him to it and its members, as from the head to the natural body. Though in this way (we say) no man can be head but Christ, nor the Church be a body to any but to Christ; yet the Pope may be the ministerial head <note>A "ministerial head" acts as a deputy or servant-leader rather than the ultimate source of authority</note>, that is to say, the chief Governor, Pastor, and Prelate of the same, and may be his Vicar <note>A "Vicar" is a representative or deputy acting in the place of a higher authority</note> or representative in the government of that part which is on earth. As Saint Jerome calls Pope Damasus *the chief and highest Priest* <note>original Latin: "Summum Sacerdotem"</note>; 
<margin>
Jerome, epistle 123.
1 Corinthians 12:21.
</margin>
and the Apostle says of this ministerial head, *The head cannot say to the feet, you are not necessary for me.* For therein also is a great difference between Christ and every mortal Prelate: that (as the Apostle here says) he is head of the whole Church, meaning of the triumphant Church in heaven (and of all Angels also, though in another way) no less than of the Church militant on earth. So Peter was not, nor any Pope, nor any man can be. Where you must observe that because of this sovereign preeminence of Christ in this case, the Church is not called the mystical body of any Governor, Peter, Paul, or whatever Prelate or Pope soever.

### ANNOTATIONS
->CHAPTER II.<-

<margin>Our first justification is of mere grace, and faith is the foundation of it.</margin>
8. *By grace you are saved through faith.*] Our first <term>justification</term> <note>The process by which a person is made righteous in the eyes of God.</note> is of God's grace and not of our own deserving, because none of our actions performed before our justification could merit or justly obtain the grace of being made right with God. Again, he says, *through faith*: because faith is the beginning, foundation, and root of all justification, and the first of all other virtues, without which it is impossible to please God.

<margin>The Church is built upon Christ, and yet upon the Apostles also.</margin>
20. *Built upon the foundation.*] Note, against the <term>Heretics</term> <note>In this context, a reference to Protestant reformers who questioned Catholic traditions regarding Church authority.</note> who think it is dishonorable to Christ to attribute his titles or roles to mortal men, that the faithful (though built first, principally, and properly upon Christ) are nevertheless said here to be built upon the Apostles and Prophets. Why, then, may the Church not also be said to be built upon Peter?

<summary>This page contains the text of Ephesians 2, emphasizing that salvation comes through grace rather than human works, and describes the reconciliation of Jews and Gentiles into one "holy temple." The accompanying commentary defends the Catholic view of "first justification" and the legitimacy of describing the Church as being built upon the foundation of the Apostles (and by extension, the Pope/St. Peter).</summary>

# CHAP. IIII.

*He exhorts them to keep the unity of the Church most carefully with all humility: bringing them many motives thereunto: 7 and answering that even the diversity itself of offices is not for division, as being the gift of Christ himself, but to build up the Church, and to hold all in the unity thereof against the subtle circumventions of Heretics: that under Christ the head, in the Church being the body, every member may prosper. 17 Neither (as touching life) must we live like the Heathen, but as it becomes Christians, laying aside our old corrupt manners, and increasing daily in all goodness.*

# THE EPISTLE OF ST. PAUL CHAPTER 4.

<margin>
Detestable schism.
</margin>
<margin>
Ephesians 4.
</margin>
one hope, one faith, one baptism, one head, one body. Regarding which St. Cyprian (in his *Book on the Unity of the Church, number 3* <note>original: "li. de vnit. Ec. nu. 3."</note>) says this: *One Church the Holy Spirit in the person of our Lord designates and says, "One is my dove" <note>A reference to Song of Solomon 6:9, used to symbolize the singular nature of the Church.</note>. This unity of the Church, he that holds not, does he think he holds the faith? He that withstands and resists the Church; he that forsakes Peter’s chair upon which the Church was built, does he trust that he is in the Church?* When the blessed Apostle St. Paul also shows this Sacrament of unity, saying, *One body and one spirit* etc. Which unity we Bishops especially, who rule in the Church, ought to hold fast and maintain, so that we may prove the Bishoply function itself also to be one and undivided, etc. And again, *There is one God, and one Christ, and one Church, and one Chair, by our Lord’s voice founded upon Peter. To set up another altar, or to make a new Priesthood, besides one altar and one Priesthood, is impossible. Whosoever gathers elsewhere, scatters. It is adulterous, it is impious, it is sacrilegious, whatsoever is instituted by man’s fury to the breach of God’s divine disposition. Get yourselves far from the contagion of such men, and flee from their speeches as a cancer and pestilence, our Lord having premonished and warned beforehand: They are blind, leaders of the blind, etc.* By which we learn that this unity of the Church, so much commended to us, consists in the mutual fellowship of all Bishops with the See of Peter <note>The "See of Peter" refers to the authority and office of the Pope in Rome.</note>. St. Hilary also (*in his book to Constantius Augustus* <note>original: "li. ad Constantium Augustum"</note>) thus applies this same passage of the Apostle against the Arians <note>A 4th-century sect that denied the full divinity of Christ.</note>, as we may do against the Calvinists <note>Followers of the reformer John Calvin.</note>.

<margin>
Among heretics, as many faiths as there are wills.
</margin>
*It is perilous and miserable*, he says, *that there are now as many faiths as there are wills; and as many doctrines as there are manners; while either faiths are written as we will, or are understood as we will. And whereas according to one God, and one Lord, and one Baptism, there is also one faith, we fall away from that which is the only faith; and while more faiths are made, they begin to come to the point that there is none at all.*

<margin>
The heretics' foolish negative argument against the Pope answered. The Pope’s office is called an Apostleship.
</margin>
11. *Some Apostles.*] Many functions that were present even in the Apostles' time are not named here. This must be noted against the Adversaries <note>A term often used in these texts to refer to Protestant reformers.</note> who demand to see the name of "Popes" here, as though the names of Bishops, Priests, or Deacons were not also left out; yet they cannot deny these were in use in St. Paul’s days. And therefore they have no more reason to use this passage to argue against the Pope than against the rest of the ecclesiastical functions. Neither is it necessary to reduce those functions not specified here to those that are named; though indeed both other Bishops and Prelates, and especially Popes, may be contained under the names of Apostles, Doctors, and Pastors. Certainly the office and dignity of the Pope is a very continual Apostleship, and St. Bernard calls it an *Apostleship* <note>original: "Apostolatum." St. Bernard of Clairvaux, writing to Pope Eugenius III, *Book 4, chapters 4 and 6 at the end*.</note>.

<margin>
Continual succession of Bishops: an evident argument for the true visible Church.
</margin>
<margin>
The Fathers refuted heretics by the succession of the Bishops of Rome.
</margin>
13. *Until we meet.*] The Church of God shall never lack these spiritual functions, or others answerable to them according to the time and state of the Church, until the world’s end. By this you may prove the Catholic Church—that is to say, that visible company of Christians which has ever had, and by good records can prove they have had, a continual ordinary succession of Bishops, Pastors, and Doctors—to be the only true Church. And these other fellows who, for many worlds or ages together, cannot show they had any one Bishop, or ordinary (or even extraordinary) officer for them and their sect, are shown to be an adulterous, heretical generation. And this passage of the Apostle, assuring to the true Church a perpetual visible continuance of Pastors and Apostles or their successors, warranted the holy Fathers to test all heretics by the most famous succession of the Popes of Rome. So did St. Irenaeus (*Book 3, chapter 3*), Tertullian (in *The Prescription against Heretics*), Optatus (*Book 2 against Parmenianus*), St. Augustine (in his *Psalm against the party of Donatus*, and *Against the letter of Mani, chapter 4*, and *Letter 165*), Epiphanius (*Heresy 27*), and others.

<margin>
Heretical blasts carry away only the inconstant.
</margin>
14. *With every wind.*] The special use of the spiritual Governors is to keep us in unity and constancy of the Catholic faith, so that we are not carried away with the blast or wind of every heresy. This is a very characteristic trait of sects and new doctrines that trouble the weak members of the Church during certain seasons of diverse ages: as at one time the Arians, then the Manicheans, another time the Nestorians, then the Lutherans, Calvinists, and such like—who at diverse times in diverse places have blown diverse blasts of false doctrine.

->**A N N O T A T I O N S**<-
->**C H A P T E R V.**<-

<margin>No salvation out of the Catholic CHURCH.</margin>
23. *Saviour of his body.*] No one has salvation or benefit by Christ who is not of his body, the Church. And what Church that is, Saint Augustine expresses in these words: "The Catholic Church alone is the body of Christ, of which he is head. Outside of this body the Holy Ghost gives life to no man." <note>original Latin: 'Ecclesia Catholica sola est corpus Christi, cujus ipse est caput. extra hoc corpus neminem vivificat Spiritus Sanctus.'</note> And a little after, "He that will have the Spirit, let him beware he remain not outside the CHURCH, let him beware he enter not into it feignedly." Saint Augustine's Letter 50 to Count Boniface, at the end.

<margin>The CHURCH never errs.</margin>
24. *Subject to Christ.*] The **CHURCH** is always subject to Christ—that is, not only under him, but ever obedient to his words and commandment. This is an evident and invincible demonstration that she never rebels against Christ, never falls from him by error, idolatry, or false worship, as the <term>Heretics<note>A reference to contemporary Protestant reformers.</note></term> now, and the <term>Donatists<note>A 4th-century schismatic group in North Africa who claimed the Church had become corrupted.</note></term> of old, did teach.

<margin>Christ's love toward his Church.</margin>
<margin>The Church triumphant without spot and wrinkle.</margin>
25. *Loved the Church.*] Behold Christ's singular love for the **CHURCH**, for which alone and its members he effectively suffered his Passion, and for whose continual cleansing and purifying in this life he instituted holy Baptism and other Sacraments; so that at length in the next life it may become without spot, wrinkle, or blemish. For, in this world, by reason of the manifold infirmities of various members, she cannot be wholly without sin, but must say always, "Forgive us our debts" <note>original Latin: 'Dimitte nobis debita nostra'.</note>. Augustine's *Retractions*, book 2, chapter 18.

<margin>The manifold dignity of the Church.</margin>
<margin>The Church is the principal creature.</margin>
<margin>The Church cannot err.</margin>
29. *As Christ the Church.*] It is an unspeakable dignity of the **CHURCH**, which the Apostle expresses often elsewhere, but especially in this whole passage: to be that creature only for which Christ effectively suffered; to be washed and <term>embrued<note>Soaked or stained.</note></term> with water and blood issuing out of his holy side; to be nourished with his own body (for so does Saint Irenaeus explain in Book 5, at the beginning); to be his members; to be so joined unto him as the body and members of the same flesh, bone, and substance are to the head; to be loved and cherished by him as a wife by a husband; indeed, to be his wife and most dear spouse, taken and formed (as Saint Augustine often says) out of his own side upon the Cross, just as Eve, our first father Adam's spouse, was made from his rib. See Augustine *On Psalm 126*, *On Psalm 127*, *Tract 9 on John*, and *Tract 120*. In respect of which great dignity and excellence, the same holy father affirms the **CHURCH** to be the principal creature, and therefore named in the Creed next after the Holy Ghost. He also proves against the <term>Macedonians<note>A group that denied the divinity of the Holy Spirit.</note></term> that the Holy Ghost is God, because he is named before the Church in the confession of our faith. If the Heretics of our time had any sense or consideration of this incomparable excellence of the Church—so beloved by Christ and so inseparably joined in marriage with him—they would neither think their contemptible company or "congregation" to be the glorious spouse of our Lord, nor teach that the Church may err (that is to say, be divorced from her spouse for idolatry, superstition, heresy, or other abominations). Whereupon one of these absurdities would ensue: that either
