<header>CHAPTER VI. TO THE EPHESIANS.</header>

<margin>Absurdities that follow, if the Church may err.</margin>
Christ may sometimes be without a Church and spouse on earth (as he was all the while there were no Calvinists, if their Church be the spouse of Christ) or else if the Catholic Church only is and has been his wife, and the same have such errors as the heretics falsely pretend, then his wife so dear and so praised here, is notwithstanding a very whore. Which horrible absurdities prove and convince to any man of common sense, both that the Catholic Church always is, and that it teaches truth always, and to honor God truly and sincerely always: whatsoever the adulterous generation of heretics think or blaspheme.

32. *This is a great Sacrament.*] <margin>MATRIMONY a Sacrament.</margin> Marriage a great <term>Sacrament<note>original: 'Sacramentum'. The author is arguing that marriage is one of the seven formal sacraments that confer grace, not just a sacred 'mystery'.</note></term> of Christ and his Church prefigured in the first parents. *Adam* (says St. Augustine <note>original: 'tract. 15 in Io.' — Tractate 15 on the Gospel of John.</note>) *who was a form or figure of him that was to come—yea rather God in him—gave us a great token of a Sacrament. For both he deserved while sleeping to take a wife, and of his rib his wife was made unto him: because out of Christ sleeping on the Cross the Church was to be made out of his side.* In another place he makes Matrimony a Sacrament of Christ and his Church: in that, as the married man must forsake father and mother and cleave unto his wife, so Christ as it were left his father, <term>emptying himself<note>original: 'exinaniting'. A technical term for Christ's self-emptying during the Incarnation, from the Latin 'exinanivit'.</note></term> by his incarnation, and left the Synagogue his mother, and joined himself to the Church. <note>original: 'Li. 12 c. 8. cont. Faustum' — Against Faustus the Manichaean, Book 12, Chapter 8.</note> In diverse other places he makes it also a Sacrament, especially in that it is an inseparable bond between two, and that can never be dissolved but by death: signifying Christ’s perpetual and indissoluble <term>conjunction<note>union</note></term> with the Church his one only spouse. <note>The author cites several works of Augustine: 'On the Literal Meaning of Genesis', 'Against Pelagius on Original Sin', 'On Faith and Works', and 'On the Good of Marriage'.</note> And in another place, *The good of Marriage* (says he) *among the people of God is in the holiness of a Sacrament. <note>original: 'De bono coniugali c. 24' — On the Good of Marriage, Chapter 24.</note>*

Who would have thought such mysteries and Sacraments to be in Marriage, that the joining of man and wife together should represent so great a mystery, if the Apostle himself, and after him this holy father and others, had not noted it? Or who can marvel that the holy Church takes this to be a Sacrament, and to give grace of sanctification to the parties married, that they may live together in mutual fidelity, bring up their children in faith and fear of God, and possess their <margin>1 Thessalonians 4.</margin> vessel (as the Apostle speaks) in sanctification and honor, and not in passion of lust and ignominy, as the Heathen do which know not God, and as our brutish new Masters seem to do <margin>The grace given by this Sacrament.</margin> that commend marriage above all things so far as it feeds their <term>concupiscences<note>strong sexual desires or lusts</note></term>, but for grace, Sacrament, mystery, or sanctification thereby, they care no more than the Heathen or brute beasts do? And thus we gather that matrimony is a Sacrament, and not of the Greek word <margin>The Protestants' fleshly estimation of marriage.</margin> <margin>mystery, sacrament <note>original: 'μυςήριον Sacramentum'</note></margin> *Mystery* only, as Calvin falsely says, nor of the Latin word *Sacrament*, both which we know have of their nature a more general signification, and that in the Scriptures also: but whereas these names are here given to Matrimony by the Apostle, and are not given in the Scriptures to Baptism and the Eucharist, let them tell us why they also apply these words from their general signification to signify specially and peculiarly those two Sacraments never so named expressly in Scripture, and do not likewise follow the Catholic Church in calling matrimony by the same name, which is here so called of the Apostle, especially whereas the signification in it, is as great as in any other of the Sacraments, and rather greater.

# THE ARGUMENT OF THE EPISTLE OF ST. PAUL TO THE PHILIPPIANS.

<image-desc>Decorative initial H containing an illustration of a man (likely Saint Paul) seated at a desk with books and writing implements.</image-desc>

How St. Paul was called by a vision into *Macedonia*, we read in *Acts 16*, and how he came to *Philippi*, being the first city of that region, and of his preaching, miracles, and suffering there. And again in *Acts 19*, Paul purposed in the Spirit—when he had passed through *Macedonia* and *Achaia*—to go to *Jerusalem*, saying: "After I have been there, I must see *Rome* also." This purpose he executed in *Acts 20*, taking his leave at *Ephesus*. And being afterward come into *Achaia*, he was advised to return through *Macedonia*, and so at length from *Philippi* he began his voyage toward *Jerusalem*. From *Jerusalem*, being carried prisoner to *Rome* (*Acts 28*), he wrote from there this Epistle to the Philippians—or rather during his second <term>apprehension<note>original: 'apprehension'. Here meaning his second period of imprisonment or arrest.</note></term>, about 10 years after the first.

<margin>Ephesians 3</margin>
In this letter, he strengthens them (*as he also did the Ephesians about the same time*) against the temptation they might face upon hearing that he might be executed. Therefore, he first says: <margin>Philippians 1, verses 12, 23, 26</margin> *And I will have you know, brethren, that the things concerning me have turned out to the further advancement of the Gospel, so that my imprisonment became well-known in Christ throughout the whole Court,* etc. Secondly, he signifies that his desire is to be <term>dissolved<note>original: 'dissolued'. A poetic way of referring to death; to be released from the body to be with God.</note></term> and to be with Christ; but yet (lest they should be discouraged), he hopes to come to them again. Concerning this, although he does not yet have certainty, he signifies by saying: <margin>Philippians 2, verses 23, 24, 17</margin> *I hope to send Timothy to you immediately, as soon as I see how things go with me.* Thirdly, therefore, he prepares them for the worst, saying: *I hope to come to you again; but even if I am <term>immolated<note>original: 'immolated'. In this context, it means to be offered up as a sacrifice, referring to his potential martyrdom.</note></term> upon the sacrifice and service of your faith, I rejoice and congratulate you all; and for this same reason, you also should rejoice and congratulate me.*

Moreover, he partly warns them (*as he had done before*) of those *Jewish False-apostles who preached circumcision and the Law of Moses to the Christian Gentiles*. He also partly exhorts them to suffer persecution, to live uprightly, and especially to humble themselves toward one another, rather than breaking the peace and unity of the Church through pride.

<margin>Bishops and Priests have always been distinct roles.</margin>
2. *Bishops and deacons.*] <note>This refers to verse 1 of the first chapter.</note> Wycliffe and other heretics would try to prove by this passage—since priests are not named here and there could not be many Bishops in this one town—that there is no difference between a Bishop and a Priest. This was the old heresy of Aerius <note>A 4th-century priest who argued that bishops and presbyters were of equal rank.</note>, which is discussed in other places <margin>See Annotations on Titus 1:5.</margin>. For now, it is enough to know that in the Apostles' time, the specific distinct names for either office were not always used as strictly as they were shortly afterward. However, they were always diverse degrees and distinct functions. See St. Chrysostom, Oecumenius, Theophylactus, and the rest of the Greek scholars <note>original: "Gracians"</note> on this passage.

# ANNOTATIONS
## CHAP. II.

<margin>Calvin's blasphemy against Christ’s own merits.</margin>
9. *For the which.*] Calvin so abhors the name of "merit" in Christian men toward their own salvation that he wickedly and unlearnedly denies that Christ himself deserved or merited anything for himself. However, these words—which he shamefully distorts <note>original: "writheth"</note> from their proper and plain sense to suggest a sequence of events rather than a cause of his exaltation—and various other passages in Holy Scripture prove that he merited for himself, according to the judgment of all learned men. As in Revelation 5 <note>original: "Apoc 5"</note>: *The Lamb that was slain is worthy to receive power and Divinity.* And Hebrews 2: *We see Jesus, for the suffering of death, crowned with glory and honor.* See St. Augustine on these words of Psalm 109: *Therefore he shall lift up his head* <note>original: "propterea exaltabit caput"</note>.

<sig>Xxx</sig>
<meta>catchword: 10. Name</meta>

<summary>Paul expresses his willingness to be martyred for the Philippians' faith and commends his companions Timothy and Epaphroditus. The concluding annotation attacks John Calvin’s rejection of the doctrine of merit, asserting that Christ earned his own exaltation through his suffering.</summary>
<keywords>Timothy, Epaphroditus, sacrifice, martyrdom, John Calvin, merit, salvation, exaltation of Christ, St. Augustine</keywords>

--- Page 562 ---
<meta>This page continues the commentary on Paul's Letter to the Philippians, concluding Chapter 2 and beginning Chapter 3. The notes transition from a defense of Catholic practices regarding the name of Jesus and free will into Paul’s warnings against "false apostles" and his reflections on his own Jewish heritage.</meta>

<page-num>530</page-num>
<header>THE EPISTLE OF ST. PAUL CHAPTER III.</header>

<margin>Protestants refuse to show reverence at the name of JESUS.</margin>
10. *Name of JESUS.*] With similar wickedness, they accuse faithful people of tipping their caps or kneeling when they hear the name of JESUS, as if they were not worshipping our Lord God in that act, but rather the syllables, letters, or other material elements of which the written or spoken word consists. All of this is done through sophistry to draw people away from the honor and devotion due to CHRIST JESUS. This is Satan's goal: to plant doubts in the minds of simple people <margin>How Catholics honor the name of JESUS and other things pertaining to him.</margin> regarding his Sacraments, his Saints, his Cross, his name, his image, and such things, in order to abolish all true religion from the world and make them plain Atheists. But the Church knows Satan’s thoughts, and therefore, by the authority of Scripture and reason, she warrants and teaches all her children to show reverence whenever JESUS is named. This is because Catholics do not honor these things or consider them holy for their physical matter, color, sound, or syllables, but because of the respect and relationship they have with our Savior, bringing us to remember and understand Christ through sight, hearing, or the use of these signs. Otherwise, why would we not show reverence at the name of Jesus the son of Sirach <note>The author of the Book of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, in the Old Testament</note>, as well as at the name of JESUS CHRIST? It is a pitiful situation to see these profane tricks of Heretics take hold in religion, which would be ridiculous in any other area of life. When we hear our Prince or Sovereign named, we may show respect without these doubts, yet toward Christ, it is considered superstitious.

<margin>The empty security of salvation.</margin>
12. *With fear and trembling.*] Against the empty presumption of Heretics who make men feel secure in their predestination and salvation, he tells the Philippians to work out their salvation with fear and trembling, according to that other Scripture, *Blessed is the man who is always fearful. (Proverbs 28:14).*

<margin>St. Augustine answers the objection against free will.</margin>
13. *Works in you.*] Regarding this, St. Augustine says: *Just because the Apostle says it is God who works in you both to will and to work, we must not think he takes away our free will. For if that were the case, he would not have told them a little earlier to work out their own salvation with fear and trembling. For when they are commanded to work, their free will is being called upon; but "with trembling and fear" is added, lest by attributing their good work to themselves, they might become proud of their good deeds as if they came from themselves. (Augustine, On Grace and Free Will, chapter 9).*

<margin>Martyrdom.</margin>
17. *The sacrifice.*] The obedience of faith and martyrdom are such acceptable acts to God, when they are voluntarily dedicated to his honor, that by a metaphor they are called a "sacrifice" and "pleasant offerings" <note>original: "hosts," referring to a sacrificial victim</note> to God.

---

### CHAPTER III.

->He warns them about the False Apostles, showing that he himself had much more to boast about in Judaism than they did; however, he values nothing but Christ, Christian justice, and suffering with him (verse 12, in which he still acknowledges his own imperfection), exhorting them to bear Christ’s Cross with him and not to imitate those who make a god of their bellies.<-

<margin>By a play on words, he calls the carnal Christian Jews who still boasted in the circumcision of the flesh "the concision" (the mutilation), while calling himself and the rest who spiritually circumcised their hearts and senses "the true circumcision." St. Chrysostom, Theophylact.</margin>

<margin>Double perfection: here, and in the life to come.</margin>
12. *Not that now.*] No man in this life can attain the absolute perfectness either of justice or of that knowledge which shall be in heaven: but yet there is also another perfectness, such as according to this state a man may reach unto, which in respect of the perfection in glory, is small, but in respect of other lesser degrees of man's justice and knowledge in this life, may be called perfectness. And in this sense the Apostle in the next sentence calleth himself and others perfect, though in respect of the absolute perfectness in heaven, he saith here, he is not yet perfect nor hath yet attained thereunto.

<margin>The heretics' foolish defense of their dissensions and divisions among themselves.</margin>
15. *Otherwise minded.*] When Catholic men nowadays charge Heretics <note>The term "Heretics" here refers to the Protestant Reformers, as this commentary was written during the height of the Counter-Reformation.</note> with their horrible divisions, dissensions, combats, contentions, and diversities among themselves, as the Catholics of all other ages did challenge their adversaries most truly and justly for the same, (both because where the Spirit of God is not, nor any order or obedience to Superiors, there can be no peace nor unity, and especially for that it is, as St. Augustine saith <note>Original Latin: *On the Christian Combat*, chapter 29</note> the just judgment of God that they which seek nothing else but to divide the Church of Christ, should themselves be miserably divided among themselves) therefore (I say) when men charge the Protestants with these things, they flee for their defense to this: that the old Fathers were not all of one judgment in every point of religion; that St. Cyprian stood against others; that St. Augustine and St. Jerome wrote earnestly in a certain matter one against another; that our Dominicans and Franciscans, our Thomists and Scotists <note>These represent different schools of theological and philosophical thought within the Catholic Church that disagree on technical points but remain in communion.</note> be not all of one opinion in diverse matters, and therefore divisions and contentions should not be so prejudicial to the Zwinglians and Lutherans, as men make it.

<margin>The difference between the disagreeing of ancient fathers or other Catholics, and the Heretics' dissensions among themselves.</margin>
Thus they defend themselves: but ridiculously and against the rule of St. Paul here, acknowledging that in this imperfection of man's science in this life, every one cannot be free from all error, or think the same that another thinketh: whereupon may rise differences of understanding, opinion, and judgment, in certain hard matters which God hath not revealed or the Church determined, and therefore that such diversity is tolerable and agreeable to our human condition and the state of the way that we be in: always provided, that the controversy be such and in such things, as be not against the set known rule of faith, as he here speaketh, and such as break not mutual society, fellowship, and communion in prayer, service, Sacraments, and other offices of life and religion. For such divisions and differences come never but of Schism or Heresy, and such are among the Heretics, not only in respect of us Catholics, but among themselves:

<margin>The spiteful writings of Heretics, one Sect against another.</margin>
as they know that be acquainted with the writings of Luther against Zwingli, or Westphalus against Calvin, or the Puritans against the Protestants, not only charging one another with Heresy, Idolatry, Superstition, and Atheism, but also condemning each other's ceremonies or manner of administrations, until it comes to excommunication and banishment, yea sometimes burning one of another. Thus did not St. Cyprian, St. Augustine, St. Jerome, the Dominicans, Franciscans, Thomists, Scotists, who all agree in one rule of faith, all of one communion, all most dear one to another in the same, all (thanks be to God) come to one holy Mass, and receive the same Sacraments, and obey one head throughout all the world. St. Augustine <note>Original Latin: *On Baptism*, Book 2, chapter 5.</note> shall make up this matter with this notable sentence:

<margin>A notable place of St. Augustine.</margin>
> We are men (he says) and therefore to think somewhat otherwise than the thing is, is a human temptation: but by loving our own sentence too much, or by envying our betters, to proceed unto the sacrilege of dividing the mutual society and of making schism or heresy, is devilish presumption: in nothing to have other opinion than the truth is, that is Angelical perfection.

And a little after,

> If you be any otherwise minded, this God will reveal: but to them only (he says) that walk in the way of peace, and that stray aside into no division or separation.

Which saying would God all our dear countrymen would mark, and come into the Church, where only God reveals truth.

# THE INTRODUCTION TO THE
## EPISTLE OF ST. PAUL TO
### THE COLOSSIANS.

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial 'T' within a square frame, decorated with floral motifs and a seated figure.</image-desc>

*THE Epistle to the Colossians is not only similar in its meaning, but almost in its very words, to the Epistle to the Ephesians; it was also sent by the same messenger, Tychicus (Colossians 4:7). In it, Paul makes similar mention of his chains and sufferings (Colossians 1:24 and 4:3, 18). Therefore, there is no doubt it was written at Rome at the same time—namely, during his last imprisonment, yet before he knew of his impending martyrdom.*

*The difference is this: Paul had personally preached to the Ephesians, but he had never been among the Colossians, as he indicates in chapter 2, verse 1. Therefore, although he is briefer here than in his letter to the Ephesians regarding matters of exhortation, he is more detailed in matters of doctrine. Generally, he assures them that the truth is what their Apostle Epaphras had taught them. Specifically, however, he warns them both against the Judaizing <term>False-apostles</term><note>Early Christian teachers who insisted that converts must still follow the old laws of Moses, such as circumcision and dietary restrictions.</note>, who sought to corrupt them with certain ceremonies of the Law of Moses, and also against the <term>Platonic Philosophers</term><note>Followers of the Greek philosopher Plato; here, the text refers to those blending Greek philosophy with Christian teaching in ways the author considers heretical.</note>. These philosophers rejected Christ (who is truly the head of the Church and the Mediator who brings us to God) and instead introduced certain Angels as being more excellent than He. They called these "lesser gods" <note>original: "Minores dij"</note>, teaching the people to offer sacrifices to them—calling this "humility"—so that they might bring them to the great God. With this falsehood, the heresy of Simon Magus deceived many for a long time, as we read in <term>Epiphanius</term><note>A 4th-century Church Father known for his "Panarion," a massive work detailing and refuting various heresies.</note> (Heresy 21).*

*Against such people, therefore, St. Paul tells the Colossians that Christ is the Creator of all the Angels, God in person, the head of the Church, and the most important in all respects. He is the Redeemer, Mediator, and peacifier between God and men; therefore, through Him we must go to God. Thus, whether we pray ourselves or ask anyone else on earth or in heaven to pray for us, all must be done—as the Catholic Church does in every <term>Collect</term><note>A short, formal prayer used in the liturgy of the Western Church that follows a specific structure.</note>—"Through Christ our Lord" <note>original: "Per Christum dominum nostrum"</note>, or "through our Lord Jesus Christ your Son, who lives and reigns with you, etc." <note>original: "per Do. nostrum Iesum Christum filium tuum, qui tecum viuit & regnat, &c."</note>. By this, the Church continually professes, against such deceptions, both the Mediatorship and the Divinity of Christ.*

### CHAPTER I.

*He states that he thanks God for their excellent faith and charity, and continually prays for their growth. At the same time, he gives testimony to the preaching of their Apostle, Epaphras, and praises the grace of God in bringing them to Christ—who is supreme over all and a peacemaker through his blood. This is the Gospel not only of Epaphras but of the universal Church and of Paul himself, who also suffers for its sake.*

<header>THE EPISTLE OF ST. PAUL CHAPTER 1</header>

# ANNOTATIONS
## CHAPTER 1.

<margin>There is no lack in Christ's passions which he suffered in himself as the head: but there is a lack in those passions of Christ which he daily suffers in his body, the Church, and its members.</margin>
<margin>Romans 8:17. St. Leo, Sermon 19 on the Passion.</margin>
24. **Do accomplish that which is lacking.**] Just as Christ the head and his body make one mystical person and one full Christ—the Church therefore being his plenitude, fullness, or completion <note>Original: *Ephesians 1*</note>—so the passions of the head and the afflictions of the body and its members make one complete mass of passions. There is, however, a difference between the two, as the preeminence of the head (especially such a head) above the body requires and grants. It is not only those passions which he suffered in himself—which were fully ended in his death and were in themselves fully sufficient for the redemption of the world and the forgiveness of all sins—but all those which his body and members suffer are his also. From him, they receive the status, quality, and power to be meritorious and <term>satisfactory</term><note>Acts that "satisfy" or make up for the temporal punishment due to sin.</note>. For though there is no insufficiency in the actions or passions of Christ the head, yet his wisdom, will, and justice require and ordain that his body and members should be partners in his passions, just as they hope to be partners in his glory. Thus, by suffering with him and following his example, they may apply to themselves and others the general medicine of Christ’s merits and satisfactions, just as it is effectively applied to us through Sacraments, sacrifice, and other ways. The one way is no more insulting to Christ's death than the other, despite the empty protests of the <term>Protestants</term><note>The author is writing during the Counter-Reformation and is defending Catholic doctrine against Reformers like Luther and Calvin.</note>, who would use the pretense of Christ’s Passion to take away the value of all good deeds.

<margin>How Christ's merits are applied to us without any injury to his death.</margin>
<margin>The works of one may satisfy for another.</margin>
<margin>2 Corinthians 1:6. Romans 9:3. Philippians 2. 2 Timothy 4. Job 6.</margin>
From this it is plain now that this completion of the "lacking" of Christ's Passions, which the Apostle and other Saints fill up in their flesh, refers to the painful and satisfactory works of Christ in his members. Every good man (and especially Martyrs) adds continually to accomplish the full measure of these works. These constitute the fullness of his passions and satisfactions, just as the Church is the fullness of his person. Therefore, through the <term>Communion of Saints</term><note>The spiritual union of all members of the Christian Church, living and dead.</note> and the bond that exists not only between the head and the body, but also between one member and another, these works are not only satisfactory and profitable for the sufferers themselves, but also for their fellow members in Christ. For though one member cannot strictly "merit" for another, one may bear the burden and discharge the debt of another, both by the law of God and of nature. It was a ridiculous <term>heresy of Wycliffe</term><note>John Wycliffe (c. 1320–1384), an English theologian whose views prefigured the Reformation.</note> to deny this. Indeed, as we see here, the passions of Saints are always suffered for the common good of the whole body, and sometimes they are even applicable to specific persons by special intention. For instance, here the Apostle rejoices in his passions for the Colossians; in another place, his afflictions are for the salvation of the Corinthians. Sometimes he even wishes to be <term>Anathema</term><note>Greek: *Anathema*, meaning "set apart" or accursed. Here interpreted as a sacrificial offering.</note>—that is, according to Origen's exposition <note>Original: *in librum Numerorum homilia 10 & 24* (In the Book of Numbers, Homilies 10 and 24)</note>—a sacrifice for the Jews. He often speaks of his death as a <term>libation</term><note>A drink offering poured out to a deity.</note>, a host, or an offering, as the Church Fathers do regarding all the passions of the Martyrs. All these, dedicated and sanctified in Christ's blood and sacrifice, make up the fullness of his Passion and have a powerful cry, intercession, and satisfaction for the Church and its particular needs. In this treasury, as some abound in good works and satisfactions—such as St. Paul, who lists his afflictions and glories in them <note>2 Corinthians 11</note>; and Job, who declared his penalties far exceeded his sins; and <term>our Lady</term><note>The Virgin Mary.</note> much more, who never sinned and yet suffered such great sorrows—so others are in need and are to be helped by the abundance of their fellow members.

<margin>The ground of Indulgences or pardons.</margin>
This exchange of spiritual offices, and the balancing of the needs of one part by the abundance of another, is the foundation for the old "letters of Indulgence" (discussed previously regarding St. Cyprian; see the Annotations for 2 Corinthians 2:10) and of all <term>indulgences</term><note>Remissions of temporal punishment for sins that have already been forgiven.</note> or pardons which the Church daily dispenses with great justice and mercy. These are granted by the hands of those to whom Christ has given the word of reconciliation, the keys to keep and use, his sheep to feed, his mysteries and goods to dispense, his power to bind and loose, his commission to remit and retain, and the stewardship of his family to give everyone their food in due season.

## ANNOTATIONS
## CHAPTER 2

<margin>Philosophy and other human sciences: how profitable or hurtful to the Church of God.</margin>
**8. By Philosophy.]** Philosophy and all human science, so long as they are subject and obedient to Christ (as they are in the Schools of Christian Catholic men), are not forbidden, but are greatly commended and are very profitable in the Church of God. Otherwise, where secular learning is made the rule of religion and commands faith, there it is pernicious and the cause of all heresy and infidelity. For this reason, St. Jerome and, before him, Tertullian call philosophers *the Patriarchs of Heretics*, and declare that all the old heresies rose only by too much admiring of profane philosophy. <note>See Jerome, *Letter to Ctesiphon against Pelagius*, chapter 1; and Tertullian, *On the Prescription of Heretics*, *Against Hermogenes*, and *Against Marcion*, book 5.</note>

<margin>The Protestants abuse Philosophy against the Blessed Sacrament.</margin>
And so do these new sects, no doubt, in many things. For they have no other arguments against the presence of Christ in the Blessed Sacrament <note>The Eucharist</note> but such as they borrow from Aristotle and his like, concerning quantity, accidents, place, position, dimensions, senses, sight, taste, and other limits of reason to which they bring Christ’s mysteries. All philosophical arguments, therefore, against any article of our faith are here condemned as deceitful, and are also called here *the tradition of men, and the elements of the world*.

<margin>School learning.</margin>
To better resist these fallacies and traditions of Heathen men, "School learning" <note>This refers to Scholasticism, the systematic theological and philosophical method used in universities.</note> is necessary. It keeps philosophy in awe and under the order of faith, using it to withstand the philosophical and sophisticated deceits of the heretics and the Heathen. Thus, the great philosophers St. Dionysius, St. Augustine, Clement of Alexandria, Justin Martyr, Lactantius, and the rest used it to the great honor of God and the benefit of the Church. So also came St. Cyprian, St. Ambrose, St. Jerome, and the Greek fathers, furnished with all secular learning, to the study of Divinity; concerning which, see St. Jerome’s *Letter 84 to Magnus the Orator*.

<margin>Scriptures abused by the Protestants against Christian fasting and holidays.</margin>
<margin>Augustine, Letter 59 to Paulinus, question 7.</margin>
**16. In meat.]** The Protestants willfully or ignorantly apply all these kinds of forbearing meats to Christian fasts. But it is plain from the context (as St. Augustine also teaches) that the Judaic observation and distinction of certain clean and unclean meats is what is forbidden to the Colossians. They were in danger of being seduced by certain Jews who, under a pretense of holiness, wanted them to keep the Law regarding meats, festivities, and the like, which the Apostle shows were only shadows of things to come. Those things have now come, and therefore the said shadows must cease. Since he names the Sabbaths and feasts of the new moon, no one should doubt that he speaks only of Jewish days and types of fasts and feasts, and not of Christian holidays or fasting days at all.

<margin>St. Paul’s passage concerning the religion of Angels explained: and that the Jews defended their superstition toward Angels by claiming that the Law was given through them.</margin>
**18. Religion of Angels.]** By a similar false application of this text as with the one before, the heretics abuse it against the invocation or honor of Angels used in the Catholic Church. Here, the Apostle notes the wicked doctrine of Simon Magus and others (See St. Chrysostom, homily 7 on this passage, and Epiphanius, heresy 21), who taught that Angels were our mediators and not Christ, *not holding the head* <note>original Latin: *non tenens caput*</note>, as the Apostle says here. They prescribed sacrifices to be offered to them, meaning both the evil angels and the good. The said heretic took this doctrine from Plato, who taught that spirits (which he calls *demons* <note>original Latin: *dæmones*</note>) were to be honored as mediators next to God. Against this, St. Augustine disputes in *The City of God*, books 8, 9, and 10, just as he also condemns that same undue worship in his *Confessions*, book 10, chapter 42. St. Jerome (in his *10th question to Algasia*) also explains this as referring to evil spirits or devils, whom he proves (from St. Stephen’s sermon in Acts 7) the Jews worshipped, claiming they still serve them as often as they observe the old Law. Theodoret also speaks of this idolatry toward Angels in this passage, declaring that deceitfully...

The annotations specifically target Protestant interpretations, arguing that Paul’s warnings apply to ancient Jewish rites and heretical innovations, not to Catholic fasting or the veneration of angels.</summary>

<header>CHAPTER 2. TO THE COLOSSIANS. 541</header>

<margin>18.</margin>
<margin>
The Protestants wickedly abuse this passage against the due honor and invocation of Angels.
</margin>
...deceitfully at once inducing the Colossians, both to keep the law, and to the honoring of the Angels as the givers of the same. Whereby many of the faithful were so seduced, that they forsook Christ and his Church and service, and committed idolatry to the said Angels. Against which abominations the Council of Laodicea, Canon 35 <note>The Council of Laodicea (c. 363 AD) famously condemned the "angel-worship" practiced by certain sects as a form of idolatry that diverted honor away from Christ.</note> took order, accursing all that forsook our Savior and committed idolatry to Angels, and contemning Christ, kept secret assemblies in the name of spirits and Idols. Of which kind of worship of Angels and Devils see **Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* Book 3.** **Tertullian (Book 5 against Marcion)** expounds this place as referring to the false teachers that feigned themselves to have revelations from Angels, claiming that the Law should be kept regarding the difference between clean and unclean meats. This is very much in agreement with that <gloss>*</gloss> in the Epistle to Timothy, where St. Paul calls abstaining from meats after the Jewish or heretical manner, *the doctrine of Devils:* whereof see more in <margin>* 1 Timothy 4:1.</margin> the annotation upon that place. **Haimo** <note>Haimo of Halberstadt was a 9th-century monk and scholar.</note> a godly ancient writer, upon this place, says further, that some Philosophers of the Gentiles and some of the Jews also taught that there were four Angels presiding over the four elements of the human body, and that in feigned hypocrisy (which the Apostle here calls humility) they pretended to worship the said Angels by sacrifice. **Theophylact** <note>An 11th-century Byzantine archbishop who wrote influential commentaries.</note> expounds this feigned humility as referring to certain Heretics who, pretending that having a mediator would be a derogation to Christ's majesty, worshipped Angels as the only mediators. All of which we set down with more diligence so that the Heretics <note>Referring here to the Protestant Reformers of the translator's own time.</note> may be ashamed to abuse this place against the due reverence and respect or prayers made to the holy Angels. Whom the Scriptures record so often to offer our prayers up to God, and to have been lawfully reverenced by the Patriarchs—never as gods, but as God's ministers and messengers. Joshua 5:14; Tobit 12:12; Genesis 48:16: *The Angel who delivered me* <note>original: "Angelus qui eruit me"</note>; 1 Timothy 5:21. And that they may be prayed unto, and can help and hear us, see **St. Jerome on chapter 10 of Daniel**; **St. Ambrose on Psalm 118, sermon 1**; **St. Augustine, *The City of God*, Book 10, chapter 12**; **Bede, Book 4 on the Canticles, chapter 24.**

19. *Not holding the head.*] Because he has much to do with such false preachers as taught the people to prefer the Angels who gave the Law, or any others whatsoever, before Christ: in this Epistle, and to the Ephesians, he often affirms Christ to be our head, yes, and to be exalted far above all creatures, Angels, Powers, Principalities, or whatever else.

<margin>Why are you subject to decrees? <note>original: δογματίζεσθε (*dogmatizesthe*)</note></margin>
<margin>Heretical translation.</margin>
20. *Why do you.*] A marvelous impudent translation of these words in the English Bibles <note>Refers to early Protestant versions like the Great Bible or Bishops' Bible.</note> thus: *Why are you burdened with traditions?* Whereas the Greek does not have that significance; but to make the name of "Tradition" odious, they put it here on purpose, though it is not in the Greek. Yet in other places where Traditions are commended (1 Corinthians 11 and 2 Thessalonians 2) and where the Greek is most flatly "traditions" <note>original: παραδόσεις (*paradoseis*)</note>, there they translate it as *instructions, ordinances, etc.*

<margin>Scripture abused against the Church's fasts.</margin>
<margin>* Will-worship / Voluntary worship <note>original: ἐθελοθρησκεία (*ethelothreskeia*)</note></margin>
21. *Touch not.*] The Heretics (as before and always) very vainly allege this against Catholic fasts. However, it is most clear that the Apostle is reprimanding the aforementioned false teachers who thought to make the Christians subject to the observation of the ceremonies of the old Law—such as not eating pigs, rabbits, or hare's flesh, not touching a dead corpse, nor any place where a woman in her period had sat, and other infinite doctrines of touching, tasting, washing, eating, and the rest. These were either commanded to the ancient people by God, or (as many things were) voluntarily taken up by themselves, sometimes clearly against God's ordinance, and often frivolous and superstitious. Which sort, as Christ did in the Gospel, so here St. Paul calls the "precepts and doctrines of men," and "superstition," and (as the Greek word signifies) <gloss>*</gloss> voluntary worship. That is, worship invented by Heretics of their own head without the warrant of Christ in the Scriptures, or the Holy Ghost in the Church, or any lawful authority of those whom Christ commands us to obey. Against such Sect-Masters, therefore, who would have yoked the faithful again with the Jewish or heretical fasts of Simon Magus and the like, St. Paul speaks, and not of the Church's fasts or doctrines.

<margin>The hypocritical abstinence of old Heretics makes nothing against true and sincere fasting, but commends it.</margin>
<margin>1 Corinthians 9:27. 2 Corinthians 11:27.</margin>
23. *Having a show.*] Again, the Heretics of our time object that these aforementioned false teachers pretended to holiness, wisdom, and the chastisement of their bodies (for so St. Paul says) by forbidding certain meats according to the Jewish observation, even as the Catholics do. It is true they did so, and so do most vices imitate virtues. For if chastising men’s bodies and repressing their concupiscence and lusts were not godly, and if abstinence from some meats were not laudably and profitably used in the Church for that same purpose, no Heretics (to introduce the abolished observations and differences of meats of the Jews, or the condemnation of certain meats and creatures as abominable according to others) would have falsely pretended the chastisement of their flesh, or made other shows of wisdom and piety to found their unlawful heretical or Judaical superstition concerning the same. The Catholic Church and her children, by the example of Christ, St. John the Baptist, the Apostles, and other blessed men, do that lawfully, godly, religiously, and sincerely in deed to the end aforesaid, which these false Apostles only pretended to do. So <gloss>*</gloss> St. Paul did chastise his body in deed, by watching, fasting, and many other afflictions, and that was lawful and was true wisdom and piety in deed. The aforementioned Heretics did not so; but to induce the Colossians to Judaism and other abominable errors, they only pretended these things in hypocrisy.

### C H A P T E R. III.

<margin>Heretical and foolish translation.</margin>
9. *Avarice, which is the service of idols.*] Here is a marvelous impudent and foolish corruption in the vulgar English Bible printed the year 1577 and (as it seems) most authorized <note>The author is likely referring to the Bishops' Bible or a similar Protestant version of that era.</note>. Where for their error against the Images of Christ and his Saints, and to make image and idol all one: the translator, for that which the Apostle says in Greek, *Covetousness is idolatry*, makes him to say in English, *Covetousness is worshipping of images*: as also Ephesians 5, 5 he translates thus, *The covetous person is a worshipper of images*: for that which the Apostle says, *The covetous man is an idolater*, meaning spiritual idolatry, because he makes money his God. In which sense to call this spiritual idolatry "worshipping of images" is too ridiculous, and must needs proceed from blind heresy.

<margin>Justice an inherent quality in us.</margin>
9. *Putting on the new.*] By this and the whole discourse of this chapter containing an exhortation to good life, and to put on the habit of the new man with all virtues: we may see, our justice <note>In this context, "justice" refers to "righteousness" or being made right before God.</note> in Christ to be a very quality and form inherent in our soul, adorning the same, and not an imputation only of Christ's righteousness, or a hiding only of our sins and wickedness, which the Heretics falsely affirm to remain in us after baptism and always during life. See St. Augustine *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins, book 2 chapter 7* <note>original Latin: "de pec. mer. & remif. li. 2 c. 7."</note> and *Against Julian, book 6 chapter 7* <note>original Latin: "cont. # THE ARGUMENT OF THE FIRST EPISTLE OF ST. PAUL TO THE THESSALONIANS.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut drop-cap initial 'H' containing an illustration of a bearded figure, likely Saint Paul, seated at a writing desk with a book or manuscript.</image-desc>

*How Saint Paul, with Silas (also called Silvanus) and Timothy—following a vision calling him out of* Asia *and into* Macedonia—*came to* Philippi, *which was the primary city of that region, as we read in Acts chapter 16. And how again from* Philippi, *after being scourged and imprisoned there, he came to* Thessalonica, *the capital city of that country, as we read in Acts chapter 17. There, after three weeks of preaching, the* Jews *stirred the city against them and pursued them even to* Beroea. *Consequently,* Paul *was escorted from there to* Athens, *where he waited for the arrival of* Silas and Timothy *from the aforementioned* Beroea *in* Macedonia, *but he finally met them (as we find in Acts chapter 18) at* Corinth *in* Achaia.

*Having therefore left the* Thessalonians *in the midst of such persecution, and being anxious to know how they were faring, he desired to return to them, as he indicates in the second chapter of this* Epistle, *verse 17. But (as he adds there),* Satan *hindered us. Therefore, while staying at* Athens *himself, he sent* Timothy *to them. Upon Timothy’s return, having learned of their steadfastness, Paul was greatly comforted, as he declares in chapter 3. Thus, all three were together at the writing of this* Epistle, *as we see in its opening title:* Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy to the Church of the Thessalonians. *It therefore appears to have been written at* Corinth, *rather than Athens; because after Timothy was sent to* Thessalonica, *they did not meet again in* Athens, *but in* Corinth.

*The first three chapters are intended to confirm and comfort them against the temptations brought by those persecutions. The other two chapters consist of exhortations to live according to his teachings: specifically, in the sanctification of their bodies and avoiding sexual immorality; to love one another; and to comfort one another regarding their deceased friends with the doctrine of the* Resurrection, *and with constant readiness for death. He also instructs the laity* <note>The general congregation of believers, as distinct from the ordained leaders.</note> *to be obedient, and the* Clergy *to be diligent in every aspect of their office.*

<summary>This page provides the "Argument," or historical and thematic introduction, to St. Paul's first letter to the Thessalonians. It contextualizes the letter within Paul's missionary journeys in Macedonia and outlines the book's dual focus on encouraging a persecuted church and providing moral guidance.</summary>
<keywords>St. Paul, Thessalonians, Macedonia, Silas, Timothy, Acts of the Apostles, Persecution, Resurrection, Church Leadership, Sanctification</keywords>

### ANNOTATIONS
### CHAPTER I.

<margin>Religious persons' imitation of various holy men is the imitation of Christ himself.</margin>
**6. *Followers of us.***] Saint Paul is bold to commend them for the imitation of him, and even to join himself in that point with Christ, to be their pattern to walk after. In this, without curiosity, he names himself first and our Lord afterward, because he was a more near and ready object than Christ, who was not—and could not be—followed except through the preaching and conversation <note>In this context, "conversation" refers to one's way of life or social conduct.</note> of the Apostle, who was in their sight or hearing. And this imitation of some holy man or other has made so many Religious men <note>The author is referring to members of Catholic religious orders (like Franciscans or Dominicans) who follow the "rule" of a founder as a way of following Christ.</note> of various orders and rules, all tending to the better imitation of Christ our Lord. See the similar words of the Apostle in 1 Corinthians 11:1 and Philippians 3:17.

->ANNOTATIONS<-
->CHAPTER II.<-

<margin>Not only the written word is the word of God.</margin>
12. *The word of God.*] The Adversaries <note>The Protestant reformers, whom the Catholic translators of this Bible often argued against.</note> will have no word of God but that which is written and contained in the Scripture: but here they might learn that all Paul's preaching before he wrote to them, was the very word of God. They might also learn that whatsoever the lawful Apostles, Pastors, and Priests of God's Church preach in the unity of the same Church, is to be taken for God's own word, and ought not to be reputed by them as doctrines of men or Pharisaical traditions, as they falsely call the canons, precepts, and decrees of the holy Church.

# THE ARGUMENT OF THE
## SECOND EPISTLE OF SAINT PAUL
### TO THE THESSALONIANS.

<image-desc>Decorative historiated woodcut initial 'T' featuring a seated figure in classical robes holding a book, possibly an apostle, within a square frame decorated with foliage and floral motifs.</image-desc>

<margin>* Acts 18:11.</margin>
The second letter to the *Thessalonians* has the same title as the first: Paul and Silvanus and Timothy, etc. And therefore it seems to have been written in the same place—to wit, at Corinth—where they remained * a year and six months, and written immediately upon receiving their answer to the first epistle.

First, he thanks God for their growth and perseverance (comforting them again during those persecutions) and prays for their completion. Secondly, he assures them that the Day of Judgment is not at hand, reminding them of what he told them by word of mouth when he was present. Therefore, he bids them afterward * to hold his unwritten Traditions <note>The "unwritten Traditions" refer to oral teachings passed down by the Apostles that were considered as authoritative as their written letters.</note> no less than those that were written—namely, that all those persecutions and heresies raised then, and afterward against the Catholic Church, were but the mystery of Antichrist, and not Antichrist himself. But he explains that there should come at length a plain Apostasy <note>original: "Apostasie"; a total desertion or departure from the faith.</note>, and then (the entire preceding mystery being once perfectly finished) there should follow the revelation of Antichrist himself in person (just as after all the mysteries of the Old Testament, Christ JESUS our Lord came himself in the fullness of time). And then at length, after all this, the Day of Judgment and the second coming of Christ shall be at hand, and not before—regardless of any pretended vision, or any speech of mine (says Saint Paul) that anyone might use to seduce you, or even references to my former letter. For this reason, at the end of this epistle, he tells them to recognize his handwriting, which is a distinguishing sign in every letter.
<margin>* Chapter 2, verse 15.</margin>

Lastly, he requests their prayers and requires them to keep his commandments and Traditions—namely, that the poor who are able-bodied should earn their own living through work, as he also gave them an example, even though he was not bound to do so.

## ANNOTATIONS
### CHAP. II.

<margin>The day of judgment is unprofitable to be left to God's secrets.</margin>
2. *As though the day.*] The curiosity of man, fed by Satan’s deceits, has sought to know and to announce to the world such things as God will not impart to him, nor are they necessary or profitable for him to know. It has gone so far that, both in the Apostles' days and often afterward, some have feigned revelations, some have falsely gathered theories out of the Scriptures, and some have presumed to calculate and conjecture by the stars, giving out to the world a certain time for Christ’s coming to judgment. All such deceivers are noted here in the person of some who were about to deceive the Thessalonians therein. And St. Augustine (in his 80th Epistle to Hesychius) proves that no man can be assured by the Scriptures of the day, year, or age that the end of the world or the second Advent shall be.

<margin>Two special signs before the latter day: a general apostasy, and the coming of Antichrist.</margin>
3. *Unless there come a revolt first.*] Though we cannot be assured of the moment, hour, or any certain time of our Lord’s coming, yet he warrants us that it will not be before certain things are fulfilled, which must come to pass by the course of God’s providence and permission beforehand. These are various, and we are forewarned of them in other places of the Scriptures. Here he warns us of two specifically: of a revolt, defection, or an apostasy, and of the coming or revelation of Antichrist. These two pertain in effect to the same thing, one depending on the other, and shall fall (as it may be thought) near together; and therefore St. Augustine considers them but one thing.

<margin>Calvin <note>John Calvin (1509–1564), a major French Protestant reformer.</note> on this place.</margin>
This apostasy or revolt, by the judgment of nearly all ancient writers, is the general forsaking and fall of the Roman Empire. So says Tertullian in his book *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*; St. Jerome in question 11 to Algasia; St. Chrysostom in homily 4; St. Ambrose upon this place; and St. Augustine in *The City of God*, book 20, chapter 19. All these fathers and the rest are * presumptuously condemned of error and folly here by Calvin, <margin>The heretics' interpretation of this apostasy, and their condemning of the fathers.</margin> because their exposition does not agree with his and his fellows' blasphemous fiction that the Pope should be Antichrist. To establish which false impiety, they interpret this revolt or apostasy to be a general revolt of the visible Church from God, whose house or building (they say) was suddenly destroyed, and lay for many years ruined, and ruled only by Satan and Antichrist. So says the foresaid arch-heretic <note>referring to Calvin</note> here, though for the advantage of his defense and as the matter elsewhere requires, he seems (as is all their fashion) to speak in other places quite the contrary: but with such color and collusion of words that neither other men nor he himself can tell what he would have or say. And his predecessors Wycliffe <note>John Wycliffe (c. 1320s–1384), an English precursor to the Reformation.</note> and Luther <note>Martin Luther (1483–1546), the primary figure of the Protestant Reformation.</note>, his fellows and followers Illyricus <note>Matthias Flacius Illyricus (1520–1575).</note>, Beza <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605).</note>, and the rest, are (regarding the time of the Church's falling from Christ) so various among themselves, and so contrary to him, that it is horrible to see their confusion, and a pitiful case that any reasonable man will follow such companions to evident perdition.

<margin>There can be no apostasy of the visible Church from God.</margin>
But concerning this error and falsehood of the Church's defection or revolt, it is refuted sufficiently by St. Augustine against the Donatists <note>A North African sect that claimed the mainstream Church had fallen into apostasy.</note> in many places. There he proves that the Church shall not fail until the world's end, no, not in the time of Antichrist: affirming that those who teach that the Church may fail or perish actually deny Christ and rob him of his glory and inheritance bought with his blood. (*On the Unity of the Church*, chapters 12 and 13; *The City of God*, book 20, chapter 8; On Psalm 85 at the phrase, *You alone are the great God.* <note>original Latin: "Tu solus Deus magnus."</note>)

<header>THE SECOND EPISTLE OF ST. PAUL CHAP. II.</header>

<margin>St. Jerome's Dialogue against the Luciferians, chapter 6.</margin>
...great. <note>original: "magnus"</note> Psalm 70, Consideration 2; and Psalm 60. *On the Advantage of Believing*, chapter 8. St. Jerome refutes the same wicked heresy in the *Luciferians*, <note>The Luciferians were a 4th-century schismatic group named after Lucifer of Cagliari.</note> proving against them that they make God subject to the Devil and imagine a poor, miserable Christ who would allow the Church (His own body) to either perish or be driven into some hidden corner of the world. Both of these saints answer the heretics' arguments—which are grounded on Scriptures falsely understood—though those arguments would be too long to rehearse here. It is enough for the Christian reader to know that it is an old deceit and excuse used by all heretics and schismatics to justify their forsaking of God's Church: they claim the Church has perished, or remains hidden, or exists only within themselves and in those places where they and their followers dwell. Know also that this claim is rejected by the holy Doctors of the early Church, and that it is an insult to Christ’s honor, power, providence, and promise.

---

<margin>
It is very likely the Apostle speaks of a great apostasy from the See of Rome, and from most articles of the Catholic faith.
</margin>
<margin>1 John 2:18.</margin>
If the adversaries <note>The "adversaries" refers to Protestant reformers like Luther or Calvin.</note> had said that this revolt—which the Apostle foretells shall come before the world's end—refers to great numbers of heretics and apostates revolting from the Church, they would have told the truth about themselves and others like them, whom St. John calls "Antichrists." And it is very likely (to be spoken under the correction of God's Church and all learned Catholics) that this great defection or revolt shall not only be from the Roman Empire, but specifically from the Roman Church, and along with it, from most points of Christian religion. This does not mean that Catholic Christians, either in the time of Antichrist or before, shall refuse to obey the Church; rather, it means that near the time of Antichrist and the end of the world, there is likely to be a great revolt of kingdoms, peoples, and provinces from the open, external obedience and communion with Rome. This revolt, having been begun and continued by heretics of various ages—who resist and hate the <term>Seat of Peter</term> <note>The Papacy, or the office of the Pope in Rome.</note> (which they called "the chair of pestilence" <note>original Latin: "cathedram pestilentiæ"</note> in St. Augustine's days) because it is Christ’s fortress erected against the gates of Hell and all heretics—and being now wonderfully increased by those of our days (who seem to be the next precursors of Antichrist), shall be fully achieved a little before the end of the world by Antichrist himself. Even then, although for the few days of Antichrist's reign the external state of the Roman Church and public interaction of the faithful with it may cease, the due honor and obedience of Christians toward it—and their communion in heart with it, and its practice in secret, and open confession of it if occasion requires—shall not cease, any more than it does now among the Christians of Cyprus and other places where open religious interaction is forbidden.
<margin>St. Augustine, Book 2 against the letters of Petilian, chapter 51.</margin>

---

<margin>
The wonderful providence of God in preserving the See of Rome more than all other states, notwithstanding manifold dangers and scandals.
</margin>
This is certain and wonderful in all wise men's eyes, and must surely be of God’s providence and a singular prerogative: that this Seat of Peter stands even when all other <term>Apostolic Sees</term> <note>Ancient church centers founded by Apostles, such as Antioch, Alexandria, and Constantinople, which had largely fallen under non-Christian rule.</note> are gone. It stood there for certain ages alongside the secular seat of the Empire; the Popes stood without wealth, power, or human defense, while the Emperors knew of them and sought to destroy them, putting to the sword more than thirty of them one after another. Indeed, the Emperors were as much afraid of the Popes as if they had been "rivals of their empire," <note>original Latin: "æmuli imperij"</note> as St. Cyprian notes in his 52nd epistle to Antonianus regarding Pope St. Cornelius and the Emperor Decius. Furthermore, the Emperors afterward yielded the city of Rome to the Popes while still continuing in their Imperial dignity elsewhere. The successors of those who persecuted the Church later laid down their crowns before the Pope’s seat and tombs, honoring the very memories and relics of the poor men whom their predecessors had killed. For nearly 1,600 years now, this Seat has stood—beginning in continual misery, and now for a long time mostly in prosperity—without any change in its essence, which no other kingdom or state in the world has done, as every one of them has been manifoldly altered in that time. It stands (to use St. Augustine’s words from *On the Advantage of Believing*, chapter 17) while "the heretics bark about it in vain." <note>original Latin: "Frustra circumlatrantibus hæreticis"</note> Neither the first Heathen Emperors, nor the Goths and Vandals, nor the Turks, nor any sacks or massacres by Alaric, Genseric, Attila, Bourbon, <note>Charles III, Duke of Bourbon, whose troops sacked Rome in 1527.</note> and others; nor the jealousy of secular Princes (be they kings or Emperors); nor the Popes' own internal divisions and the many difficulties and dangers in their elections; nor the great vices which have been noted in some of their persons—none of these, nor any other effort or scandal, could yet prevail against the See of Rome. Nor is any ever likely to prevail until the end of the world draws near, at which time this revolt (spoken of here by the Apostle) may occur in the manner described before, as will be further discussed in the following annotations.

Many Antichrists, as forerunners of the great Antichrist.

The great Antichrist shall be one special and notorious man.

3. **The man of sin.**] There were many even in the Apostles' time (as we see by the 4th chapter of St. John’s first epistle and in the writings of the ancient fathers) who were forerunners of Antichrist. For attacking Christ’s truth and Church, they were called "antichrists," whether they did it by force and open persecution (as Nero and other Heathen or heretical Emperors did) or by false teaching and other deceits (as the heretics of all ages). In this common and general sense, St. Jerome says that all who were not in communion with Damasus, then Pope of Rome, belonged to Antichrist (*Jerome, Epistle 57 to Damasus*). In another place, he says all who take new names after the peculiar calling of heretics—such as Arians, Donatists (and as we say now, Calvinists, Zwinglians, etc.)—all such are Antichrists (*Dialogue against the Luciferians, chapter 9*). Indeed, these later ones of our time are much more so than any of the former, for various reasons which shall afterward be set down. Nevertheless, neither they nor any of them are that *great* Adversary, enemy, and attacker of Christ, who is distinguished by a peculiar and special name as **the Antichrist** (1 John 2) and **the man of sin**, the...

...the son of perdition, the Adversary, described here and elsewhere as opposing himself directly against God and our Lord JESUS CHRIST. The Heathen Emperors were many, Turks are many, Heretics have been and now are many; therefore they cannot be that one great Antichrist which is spoken of here, and which—by the article always added in the Greek—is signified to be one special and singular man. Evidence includes his peculiar and direct opposition to Christ’s person in the 5th chapter of St. John’s Gospel, verse 43; the hint of the particular lineage and tribe he should be born from, namely the Jews (for he shall be received by them as their Messiah, *John 5:43*) and from the tribe of Dan (*Irenaeus, book 5; Jerome’s commentary on Daniel 11; Augustine, questions on Joshua, question 22*); the mention of his proper name in *Revelation 13*; the time of his appearance so near the world’s end; his short reign; his extreme destruction of God’s honor and all religion; his fake miracles; and the figures of him in the Prophets and Scriptures of both the New and Old Testaments. All these and many other arguments prove him to be but one specific, notorious Adversary in the highest degree, to whom all other persecutors, heretics, atheists, and wicked enemies of Christ and his Church are merely members and servants.

And this is also the most common opinion of all the ancient fathers. Only heretics claim without doubt that Antichrist is a whole order or succession of men. They hold this against the previous clear Scriptures and reasons only to establish their foolish and wicked paradox: that Christ’s chief Minister <note>Referring to the Pope.</note> is Antichrist, or even the whole order of the Papacy. In this, Beza <note>Theodore Beza, a major Protestant Reformer and successor to Calvin.</note> especially aims so high that he claims Antichrist (even this great Antichrist) was active in St. Paul’s days, though he was not yet revealed to the world. Who this should be (unless he means St. Peter, because he was the first of the order of Popes), God knows. And certainly, unless Peter were Antichrist, neither the whole order nor any of that order can be Antichrist, as they are all his lawful successors in both dignity and the truth of Christ’s religion. Nor can all the heretics alive prove that they or any of them used any other church government or jurisdiction, or forced the people to any other faith or worship of God, than Peter himself preached and established. Therefore, if the rest are Antichrist, let Beza boldly say that St. Peter was so as well, and that many of the ancient Catholic fathers served and worked (though unaware) toward the setting up of the great Antichrist. For so does that blasphemous pen boldly write in his annotations upon this passage. An English book recently published from that same school of thought has these words: *As for Leo and Gregory, Bishops of Rome, although they had not reached the full pride of Antichrist, yet the mystery of iniquity had been working in that See nearly five or six hundred years before them, and having then greatly increased, they were deceived by the long-standing nature of the error.* Thus writes a disrespectful student of that impudent school, placing the "mystery of Antichrist" as working in the See of Rome even in St. Peter’s time, and making these two holy fathers <note>Pope Leo the Great and Pope Gregory the Great, doctors of the Church.</note> great workers and promoters of the same. Whereas another English "Rabbi" <note>A sarcastic term for a prominent Protestant teacher, likely referring to Bishop John Jewel.</note> did not hesitate at Paul’s Cross <note>A famous outdoor pulpit in London where sermons were delivered.</note> to speak of these same fathers as great Doctors and patrons of their new Gospel, saying: *O Gregory, O Leo, if we be deceived, you have deceived us.* We give the good Christian reader warning of this more diligently, to beware of such damnable books and ministers, who lead many unsuspecting people to ruin.

Antichrist shall permit no worship or adoration except of himself alone; therefore the Pope cannot be Antichrist.

4. ***Extolled.***] The great Antichrist, who must come near the world's end, shall abolish the public practice of all other religions, both true and false. He shall pull down both the Blessed Sacrament of the altar—in which consists especially the worship of the true God—and also all idols of the Gentiles and sacrifices of the Jews. He will end all kinds of religious worship, except that which must be done for himself alone. This was partially foreshadowed by kings who decreed that no God or man but themselves should be praised for a certain number of days, such as Darius and others like him. How then can the Protestants, for shame and without obvious contradiction, claim the Pope is Antichrist? The Pope (as we say) honors Christ the true God with all his power; or (as they say) honors idols, and claims no divine honor for himself—much less for himself alone—as Antichrist shall do. He humbly prays to God and lowly kneels down in every church at various altars erected to God in memory of His saints, and prays to them. He says or hears Mass daily with all devotion; he confesses his sins to a priest as other poor men do; he adores the holy Eucharist, which Christ affirmed to be his own body. (The heretics call it an idol; it is no wonder they make the Pope, His Vicar, into Antichrist, when they make Christ himself an idol!) These religious duties the Pope performs, whereas Antichrist shall worship no one, nor pray to any, at least not openly.

# THE SECOND EPISTLE OF ST. PAUL CHAPTER II.

<margin>The abomination of desolation consists chiefly in abolishing the sacrifice of the altar.</margin>
...worship of the true God by profanation of that Temple, specially by abrogating the daily sacrifice, which was a figure of the only sacrifice and continual oblation of Christ's holy body and blood in the Church. The abolishing of that former sacrifice was a figure of the abolishing of this one, which shall be done principally and most universally by Antichrist himself (as now in part by his forerunners) throughout all Nations and Churches of the world. Though even then, the Mass may be held in secret, just as it is now in nations where the secular force of some Princes prohibits it from being said openly. <note>The author is referring to the "Penal Laws" in England and other Protestant regions where Catholic Mass was illegal.</note> For although he may have his principal seat and honor in the Temple and city of Jerusalem, yet he shall rule over the whole world, and specially prohibit that principal worship instituted by Christ in his Sacraments, as being the proper Adversary of Christ’s person, name, law, and Church. The profanation and desolation of this Church by taking away the sacrifice of the altar is the proper "abomination of desolation," and the work of Antichrist alone.

<margin>How Antichrist shall sit in the Church.</margin>
<margin>Neither Antichrist nor his precursors are members of the Church.</margin>
<margin><gloss>Theodore Beza</gloss> <note>Beza was a major French Protestant Reformer.</note></margin>
<margin>* <term>as into the temple</term> <note>original Greek: ὡς εἰς τὸν ναὸν</note></margin>
St. Augustine therefore (in *The City of God*, book 20, chapter 19) and St. Jerome (in *Question 11 to Algasia*) do think that this "sitting" of Antichrist in the temple signifies his sitting in the Church of Christ, rather than in Solomon’s temple. This does not mean he should be a chief member of the Church of Christ, or a special part of his mystical body, being Antichrist while still continuing within the Church of Christ—as the Heretics <note>Meaning the Protestants.</note> pretend, in order to make the Pope out to be Antichrist. By doing this, they plainly confess and acknowledge that the Pope is a member of the Church, *and in the very bosom of the Church* <note>original Latin: "et in ipso sinu Ecclesiæ"</note>, they say. For it is ridiculous to suggest that all the Heretics whom St. John calls "Antichrists" as his precursors should go out of the Church, while the great Antichrist himself should be of the Church, in the Church, and continue in the same. Yet to those who make the whole Church revolt from God, this is no absurdity. But the truth is, that this Antichristian revolt spoken of here is a revolt *from* the Catholic Church; and Antichrist, if he ever were of or in the Church, shall be an apostate and a renegade out of the Church. He shall usurp it by tyranny and by challenging the worship, religion, and government of it, so that he himself shall be adored in all the Churches of the world which he chooses to leave standing for his honor. And this is what it means to "sit in the temple" or *against* the Temple of God, as some interpret. If any Pope ever did this, or shall do it, then let the Adversaries call him Antichrist.

<margin>Antichrist (by interpretation, "One against Christ") why so called.</margin>
And let the good Reader observe that there are two special causes why this great "man of sin" is called Antichrist. The one is for impugning Christ’s kingdom on earth—that is to say, his spiritual government which he constituted and appointed in his Church, and the form of government ordained therein—applying all to himself by singular tyranny and usurpation. In this sense, St. Athanasius (in his *Epistle to those living a solitary life*) is bold to call the Emperor Constantius (being an Arian Heretic) "Antichrist" for making himself *Prince over the Bishops and President of Ecclesiastical judgments, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Principem Episcoporum"</note> The other cause is for impugning Christ’s Priesthood, which is only or most properly exercised on earth by the sacrifice of the holy Mass, instituted for the commemoration of his death and for the external exhibition of godly honor to the Blessed Trinity. No lawful people of God ever lacked this kind of external worship by sacrifice. And by these two things, you may easily perceive that the Heretics of these days <note>Protestants</note> do more properly and nearly prepare the way for Antichrist and for extreme desolation than any before them, their special heresy being against the spiritual Primacy of Popes and Bishops, and against the sacrifice of the altar, in which two the sovereignty of Christ on earth consists.

<margin>Protestants and Calvinists are the near forerunners of Antichrist.</margin>
<margin>St. Augustine's humility in interpreting the scriptures</margin>
6. *What letteth.*] <note>Refers to 2 Thessalonians 2:6, "And now you know what is restraining him."</note> St. Augustine (*The City of God*, book 20, chapter 19) professes plainly that he understands not these words, nor those that follow regarding the "mystery of iniquity," and least of all that which the Apostle adds: *Only that he which holdeth now, do hold etc.* This should humble us all and stop the confident rashness of this time, namely of Heretics, who boldly invent whatever meaning is agreeable to their heresy and fantasy. The Apostle had told the Thessalonians before by word of mouth a secret point which he would not utter in writing, and therefore refers them to his former talk. The "mystery of iniquity" is commonly referred to Heretics, who work toward the same ends and do what Antichrist shall do—but not yet openly. They work in cover and under the cloak of Christ’s name, the Scriptures, the word of the Lord, and a show of holiness. Whereas Antichrist himself shall openly attempt and achieve the aforementioned desolation. Satan, now serving his turn by Heretics underhandedly, shall toward the very end utter, reveal, and bring him forth openly; and that is what is meant here by being *revealed*—that is, to appear in his own person.

<margin>The mystery of iniquity is the covert working of heretikes toward the manifest revelation of Antichrist himself.</margin>
These other words, *Only that he which now holdeth, hold:* Some explain this as referring to the Emperor, during whose continuance in power God shall not permit Antichrist to come. This suggests that the Empire itself shall be wholly desolate, destroyed, and taken away before or by his coming, which is more than a mere defection from the same (as was spoken of before). For there shall be a revolt from the Church also, but it shall not be utterly destroyed. Others say that it is an admonition to all the faithful to hold fast their faith and not be beguiled by such as seek to deceive them under the name of Christ or Scriptures, until those who now pretend religion and the Gospel end in a plain breach, revolt, and open apostasy by the appearance of Antichrist. All Heretics serve him in a "mystery"—that is, covertly and according to the Devil's meaning—even though the world does not see it, nor did they themselves think it at the beginning. Yet now, every day more and more, all men perceive they tend toward plain Atheism and Antichristianism.

# CHAPTER II. TO THE THESSALONIANS.

<margin>What kind of men shall follow Antichrist.</margin>
9. **In all power.** Satan, whose power to do harm is limited by Christ, shall then be released and shall assist Antichrist with all manner of signs, wonders, and false miracles. By these, many shall be led astray—not only the Jews, but all those who are deceived and carried away merely by the common talk of Heretics <note>The author uses "Heretics" to refer to the Protestant Reformers of the 16th century.</note> who cannot perform any miracles. How much more will people follow this "man of sin" when he performs such great wonders? Such people follow Heretics now, and they shall receive Antichrist then, because they deserve to be forsaken by God for abandoning the unity and blessed fellowship of the Saints in the Catholic Church. For it is only there that the **Love of the Truth** resides, as the Apostle says here.

I Corinthians 11
