<margin>Heretical translation.</margin>
<margin>Unwritten traditions.</margin>
15. **Traditions.** This refers not only to the things written and recorded in the Holy Scriptures, but to all other truths and points of religion spoken by word of mouth and delivered or given by the Apostles to their students through tradition. These are approved both here and elsewhere in the Scripture itself. Yet the Heretics, out of a guilty conscience (which likely rebukes them), purposely and guiltily refrain in their translations from using the standard ecclesiastical word *Tradition* whenever it is used in a positive sense, even though it most accurately translates the Greek word. However, when the word sounds to their foolish imagination like it goes against the traditions of the Church (as it never actually does in its true sense), they use the word most eagerly. Therefore, here and in similar places, to prevent the reader from easily accepting the unwritten traditions commended by the Apostle, they translate it as *Instructions, Constitutions, Ordinances*, or whatever else they can invent to hide the truth from the simple or unwary reader. Their translations have no other purpose but to deceive such people through cleverness and trickery.

<margin>Their authority and estimation, and examples of some specific traditions from the Church Fathers.</margin>
<margin>St. Chrysostom</margin>
<margin>St. Basil.</margin>
But St. Chrysostom (in Homily 4 on 2 Thessalonians <note>The source text says "I Thes. 2," but the context and quotation belong to the commentary on 2 Thessalonians.</note>) and the other Greek scholars and commentaries say that the Apostles gave both written and unwritten precepts by tradition, and both are worthy of being followed. St. Basil (*On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 29, at the beginning) says: *I consider it Apostolic to remain firm even in unwritten traditions.* To prove this, he cites this passage from St. Paul. In the same book, chapter 27, he says: *If we once attempt to reject unwritten customs as things of no importance, we shall, before we are aware, damage the principal parts of the faith and reduce the preaching of the Gospel to a mere name.* And as examples of these necessary traditions, he names the sign of the Cross, praying toward the east, the words spoken at the elevation or showing of the Holy Eucharist <note>The "Elevation" refers to the priest raising the consecrated Host during Mass.</note>, along with various ceremonies used before and after the consecration, the hallowing of the baptismal font, the blessing of the oil, the anointing of the baptized with that oil, the three immersions into the font, and the words of renunciation and the exorcisms of the person to be baptized, and so on. *What scripture,* he asks, *taught these and similar things? None, truly; they all come from secret and silent tradition, with which our fathers thought it proper to cover such mysteries.*

<margin>St. Jerome.</margin>
<margin>St. Augustine.</margin>
<margin>St. Epiphanius.</margin>
<margin>St. Irenaeus.</margin>
<margin>Tertullian.</margin>
<margin>St. Cyprian.</margin>
<margin>Origen.</margin>
St. Jerome (*Dialogue against the Luciferians*, chapter 4, and letter 28 to Licinius) lists several similar traditions, urging men to attribute to the Apostles those customs which the Church has received in various Christian countries. St. Augustine values Apostolic traditions so highly that he plainly states in several places that not only the observance of certain festivals, fasts, ceremonies, and other solemnities used in the Catholic Church are holy, profitable, and Apostolic (even if they are not written in the Scriptures), but he also often writes that many articles of our religion and points of the highest importance are to be proven by tradition rather than Scripture. Specifically, he asserts that we could in no way believe that children should be baptized in their infancy if it were not an Apostolic tradition (*On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book 10, chapter 23). Tradition caused him to believe that those baptized by heretics should not be rebaptized, despite the authority of St. Cyprian and the many scriptures he cited, which seemed very convincing (*On Baptism*, book 2, chapter 7). By tradition alone, he and others condemned Helvidius the heretic for denying the perpetual virginity of our Lady <note>Helvidius was a 4th-century writer who argued that Mary had other children after Jesus; he was famously refuted by St. Jerome.</note>. Without this tradition, no matter how plain the Scriptures may be, no Arian, Macedonian, Eutychian, Pelagian, or Zwinglian <note>These names refer to various groups throughout history whose doctrines on the Trinity, Christ, or the Sacraments were condemned by the Catholic Church.</note> will yield. *We must use tradition,* says St. Epiphanius (*Heresies*, 61, "Against the Apostolics"), *For the Scripture does not contain all things. Therefore, the Apostles delivered certain things in writing and certain things by tradition.* For this, he also cites this passage from St. Paul. And again (*Heresies*, 55, "Against the Melchizedekians"): *There are boundaries set down for the foundation and building up of our faith: the tradition of the Apostles, the Holy Scriptures, and the succession of doctrine, so that the truth is protected on every side.*

St. Irenaeus (*Book 3, chapter 4*) has one notable chapter stating that in all questions we must have recourse to the traditions of the Apostles. He teaches us that the way to test an Apostolic tradition and trace it to its source is through the Apostolic succession of Bishops, but especially through the Apostolic See of Rome. He declares in the same place that there are many "barbarous" people—simple in their learning but most wise in the constancy of their faith—who never had the Scriptures but learned only by tradition. Tertullian (*On the Soldier's Crown*, number 3) lists a great number of Christian observations or customs (as St. Cyprian does in many places) of which he concludes: *Of such things, if you require a rule from the Scriptures, you shall find none. Tradition shall be named as the author, custom the confirmer, and faith the observer.* Origen also writes on this matter in plain terms,

# THE SECOND EPISTLE OF ST. PAUL CHAPTER III.

...that there be many things done in the Church (which he there names) whereof there is no easier reason to be given than tradition from Christ and the Apostles. <note>original: "ho. 5. in Numer."; Origen’s 5th Homily on the book of Numbers.</note> Saint Dionysius the Areopagite refers the praying and offering for the dead in the Liturgy or Mass to an Apostolical tradition. <note>original: "in fine Ec. Hierarch. c. 7. parte 3."; referring to the end of *The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*.</note> So does Tertullian <note>original: "De coron. militis"; "On the Soldier's Crown."</note>, Saint Augustine <note>original: "De cura pro mortuis c. 1."; "On the Care to be Taken for the Dead."</note>, Saint Chrysostom <note>original: "ho. 3. in ep. ad Philip. in Moral."; Homily 3 on the Epistle to the Philippians.</note>, and Saint Damascene <note>original: "Ser. de defunctis in initio."; "Sermon on the Deceased."</note>

<margin>The Scriptures given to us by tradition, and the sense thereof.</margin>
<margin>The Creed is an Apostolical tradition.</margin>
<margin>An invincible argument for the credit of Traditions.</margin>
We might add to all this that the Scriptures themselves, even all the books and parts of the holy Bible, are given to us by tradition; otherwise we should not, nor could not, take them (as they are indeed) for the infallible word of God, any more than the works of Saint Ignatius, Saint Clement, Saint Dionysius, and the like. The true sense also of the Scriptures (which Catholics have and heretics have not) remains still in the Church by tradition. The Creed is an Apostolic tradition. <note>original references to Ruffin, Jerome, Ambrose, and Augustine regarding the Creed's origin.</note> And what Scriptures do they have to prove that we must accept nothing not expressly written in Scriptures? We have to the contrary: plain Scriptures, all the Fathers, and most evident reasons that we must either believe such and such things (which are not expressed in Scriptures) were taught and delivered by word of mouth from the Apostles, or not. If they say no, then they are impious for not trusting the Apostles' preaching; if they say they would believe if they were assured that the Apostles taught it, then to prove this point to them, we bring forward those who lived in the Apostles' days, the testimonies of so many Fathers named before who lived near those days, and the whole Church’s practice and affirmation descending down from man to man to our time. This is sufficient proof (at least for a matter of historical fact) in the judgment of all reasonable men. This is especially true when it is known that Saint Ignatius, the Apostles' contemporary, wrote a book on the Apostles' traditions, as Eusebius witnesses. <note>original: "li. 3. Ec. hist. c. 30."; Eusebius’s *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 3, Chapter 30.</note> And Tertullian’s book, *Prescription Against Heretics*, serves no other purpose but to prove that the Church has this advantage over Heretics: that she can prove her truth by plain Apostolic tradition, which none of them can ever do.

10. **Neither let him eat.**] It is not a general precept or rule that every man should live by his manual labor, as the Anabaptists <note>A radical 16th-century Protestant group that often argued for social equality and against the nobility.</note> argue falsely against Gentlemen, and the Calvinists apply it perversely against the quiet life of the Clergy, specially of Monks and other Religious men. But it is a natural admonition only, given to such as had not the means to live on their own, or any right or good cause why to claim their support from others; and to such as, under the color of Christian liberty, did pass their time idly, curiously, unprofitably, and scandalously, refusing to do such works as were agreeable to their former calling and upbringing. Such as these were not tolerable, especially there and then, when the Apostle and others (who might lawfully have lived off the altar and their preaching) yet to disburden their hearers, and for the better advancement of the Gospel, wrought for their living: protesting nevertheless continually, that they might have done otherwise, as well as Saint Peter and the rest did, who wrought not, but were supported otherwise justly and lawfully—as all types of the Clergy preaching or serving the Church and the altar are and ought to be, by the law of God and nature. Their spiritual labors far surpass all bodily toils, when the duties and functions of that vocation are done accordingly: as Saint Augustine affirms of his own extraordinary pains incident to Ecclesiastical affairs and government <note>original: "regiment"</note>: instead of which, if the use of the Church and his infirmity would have permitted it, he wishes he might have labored with his hands some hours of the day—as some of the Clergy did ever voluntarily occupy themselves in teaching, writing, engraving, painting, planting, sowing, embroidering, or such like seemly and innocent labors. *See Saint Jerome, Epistle 114, or the Preface to Job, and in the Life of Hilarion.* <note>original: "See S. # THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIANS. CHAPTER III.
### PAGE 562

<margin>Monks were shaven in the primitive Church, and Nuns had their hair clipped.</margin>
Members of religious orders do this (women especially) in many places, which is consistent with their vocation. And Saint Augustine writes a whole book (*On the Labor of Monks, volume 3*) against the error of certain disorderly monks who abused these words (“Do not be anxious” <note>original Latin: *Nolite esse soliciti*</note> and “Behold the birds of the air” <note>original Latin: *Respicite volatilia caeli*</note>) to argue that they should not work at all, but only pray and leave their upkeep to God. They used this not only to excuse their idleness, but also to claim they were holier than their companions who did work. They also incorrectly interpreted the Scriptures to argue they should not be shaven in the monastic fashion. Augustine strongly blames them for letting their hair grow. *See book 2 of the Retractions, chapter 21, and On the Labor of Monks, chapter 31*; and Saint Jerome (*letter 48, chapter 3*) regarding Nuns cutting their hair.

<margin>Saint Augustine’s opinion regarding whether members of religious orders should work or not.</margin>
By the way, you can see here that the religious were shaven even in Saint Augustine’s time; he reproaches them for their hair, calling them “the long-haired ones” <note>original Latin: *Crinitos*</note>, just as the heretics today mockingly call them “the shaven” <note>original Latin: *Rasos*, or “Shavelings”</note>. Thus, there is a great difference between the ancient Church Fathers and the modern Protestants. Regarding manual labor: while Saint Augustine, in the book cited, did not want religious folk to refuse work when necessity, physical strength, or the rules of the Church or Monastery required it, he also explicitly writes that not everyone is able or bound to work. He states that whoever preaches or administers the Sacraments to the people or serves the altar (as almost all religious men do now) may claim their livelihood from those they serve and are not bound to work <margin>On the Labor of Monks, chapter 21.</margin>—not even those who were raised as gentlemen and gave away their lands or goods to become poor for Christ’s sake. This should be noted because heretics claim that both the Scriptures and Saint Augustine condemn all such people as idle.

<margin>Church punishments against the disobedient.</margin>
14. *Obey not.*] Our Pastors must be obeyed, not just secular princes. For those who will not obey their spiritual governors, the Apostle (as Saint Augustine says) gives orders that they be corrected through rebuke or warning, by removal from office <term>degradation: a formal reduction in status within the clergy</term>, excommunication, and other lawful kinds of punishments. *Against the Donatists after the Conference, chapter 4. 20.* Read also this holy father’s answer to those who said, “Let our superiors only command us what we ought to do, and pray for us that we may do it: but let them not punish us.” He proves there that superiors must not only command and pray, but also punish if the command is not followed. *On Rebuke and Grace, chapter 3.*

<margin>Not to associate with excommunicated persons except in certain cases.</margin>
14. *Note him.*] This implies that disobedient persons should be excommunicated, and the excommunicated should be separated from the company of other Christians. The faithful are not to keep company or interact with excommunicated persons, whether in religious acts or the duties of daily life, except in cases of absolute necessity or others allowed by law. All of this is suggested here, showing that all Church punishments <note>original: “censures”</note> are grounded in the Scriptures and the examples of the Apostles.

# THE ARGUMENT OF THE FIRST EPISTLE OF SAINT PAUL TO TIMOTHY <note>In this context, "Argument" means a formal introduction or a summary of the main themes and purpose of the letter.</note>

<image-desc>A large historiated woodcut initial 'A' depicting a figure seated at a desk or table, possibly an evangelist or author portrait of St. Paul.</image-desc>

AFTER the Epistles written to the various Churches, now follow his Epistles to particular persons, such as to Timothy and Titus, who were Bishops, and to Philemon.

Regarding Timothy, we read in *Acts 16* how Saint Paul, during his travels, took him into his company at Lystra, having him circumcised beforehand because of the Jews in the area. At that time, he was a "disciple," which is to say, a Christian man. Afterward, the Apostle gave him holy Orders and consecrated him as a Bishop, as he testifies in both of these Epistles written to him (*1 Timothy 4:14* and *2 Timothy 1:6*).

<margin>1 Timothy 3</margin>
*He writes to him, therefore, as to a Bishop, and he himself expresses the purpose of this first Epistle, saying:* These things I write to you, so that you may know how you ought to conduct yourself in the House of God, which is the Church. *And so he instructs him (and through him, all Bishops) how to govern both himself and others. Regarding himself, he is to be an example and a spectacle of virtue to all people. Regarding others, he is to prohibit all those who attempt to preach anything other than what the Catholic <note>The word "Catholic" here is used in its historical sense to mean the universal and orthodox Christian Church.</note> Church has received, and to firmly instill the Catholic faith in the people. He is to preach to the young and old, men and women; to servants, to the rich, and to every group in a suitable manner. He also instructs him on how carefully he should grant holy orders and to which persons; for whom he should pray; and whom to admit to the vow of widowhood, and so forth.*

<margin>1 Timothy 3; 1 Timothy 1; Acts 20:25, 38</margin>
*This Epistle was written, it seems, after Paul's first imprisonment in* Rome, *when he was dismissed and set at liberty. It is because of this that he is able to say here,* I hope to come to you quickly—*meaning to* Ephesus, *where he had requested Timothy to remain. This is despite the fact that during his voyage to* Jerusalem, *before his time in* Rome, *he had said at* Miletum <note>Modern Miletus</note> *to the Clergy of* Ephesus *out of a well-founded fear:* And now behold, I know that you shall see my face no more.

<margin>Colossians 2:1</margin>
*Where the letter was written remains uncertain, though it is commonly said to have been at* Laodicea. *This seems unlikely, however, because it appears he was never there, as can be gathered from the Epistle to the* Colossians, *which was written at* Rome *during his final imprisonment before he was put to death.*

->ANNOTATIONS<-
->CHAPTER 1.<-

<margin>
<note>original Greek: ἑτεροδιδασκαλεῖν</note>
Teaching otherwise than what was received is a special mark of heretics.
</margin>
<margin>
Luther’s "teaching otherwise."

3. *Not to teach otherwise.*] The proper mark of heretics and false preachers is to teach "otherwise" or contrary to that which they found taught and believed generally in the unity of the Catholic Church before their time. All doctrine that is odd, singular, or new—doctrine differing from that which was first planted by the Apostles and descended down from them to all nations and ages following without contradiction—is assuredly erroneous. The Greek word which the Apostle uses here <note>original Greek: ἑτεροδιδασκαλεῖν (heterodidaskalein)</note> expresses this point so effectively that in one compound term he lets us know that a heretic is nothing else but an "after-teacher" or "teacher-otherwise." This in itself is the easiest rule even for simple people to discern a false prophet or preacher, especially when a heresy first begins. Luther found all Christian nations at rest and peace in one uniform faith, and all preachers of one voice and doctrine regarding the Blessed Sacrament and other Articles: so that whatever he taught against that which he found preached and believed must necessarily be "another" doctrine, a later doctrine, an after-teaching or "teaching-otherwise," and therefore consequently must be false. And by this admonition of St. Paul, all Bishops are warned to take heed of such, and especially to provide that no such odd teachers arise in their dioceses.

<margin>
All heretical doctrine is made of fables.
</margin>
4. *To fables.*] He speaks specifically of the Jews' later doctrines and human constitutions that are repugnant to the laws of God (of which Christ gives warning in Matthew 23 and other places) which are contained in their Cabala and Talmud. Generally, he speaks of all heretical doctrines, which indeed—however much the simple people are beguiled by them—are nothing but fabulous inventions. We see this in the Valentinians, Manichees, and others of old, and by the "Brethren of Love," Puritans, Anabaptists, and Calvinists of our time. For

<header>THE FIRST EPISTLE OF ST. PAUL CHAPTER II.</header>
<meta>catchword: who</meta>

For which cause Theodoret entitles his book against heretics, *Hereticarum fabularum*, which means *Of Heretical Fables*.

<margin>Curious questioning in religion.</margin>
4. **Questions.**] Let our loving brethren consider whether these contentious and curious questionings and disputes in religion, which these unhappy heresies have engendered, have brought forth any increase of good life, any devotion, or edification of faith and religion in our days. And then shall they easily judge of the truth of these new opinions, and the end that will follow from these innovations. In truth, all the world now sees they lead to Atheism and nothing else.

<margin>Charity the very formal cause of our justification.</margin>
5. **The end Charity.**] Here again it appears that Charity is the chief of all virtues, and the end, consummation, and perfection of all the law and precepts. And yet the adversaries <note>A term often used in this period by Catholic commentators to refer to Protestant reformers.</note> are so foolish as to prefer faith before it, even to exclude it from our justification. Such obstinacy there is in those who have once, in pride and stubbornness, forsaken the evident truth. Charity, doubtless, which is here commended, is justice itself, and the very formal cause of our justification, just as the works proceeding from it are the works of justice. <note>original Latin: "Charitas inchoata, inchoata iustitia: Charitas prouecta, prouecta iuſtitia: Charitas magna, magna iuſtitia: Charitas perfecta, perfecta iuſtitia est."</note> *Charity now beginning, is justice beginning: Charity grown or increased, is justice grown or increased: great Charity, is great justice: perfect Charity, is perfect justice.* (St. Augustine, *Book on Nature and Grace, chapter 70*).

<margin>Heretics great boasters, but unlearned.</margin>
7. **Desirous to be Doctors.**] It is the particular vice both of Jewish and of heretical false teachers to profess knowledge and great skill in the Law and Scriptures, while being indeed, in the sight of the learned, most ignorant of the word of God, not knowing the very principles of divinity, even to the amazement of the truly learned who read their books or hear them preach.

<margin>Libertines allege scripture.</margin>
9. **The law not made to the just.**] By this place and others like it, the Libertines <note>Radical groups who claimed that those "in the spirit" were free from all moral and legal constraints.</note> of our days would excuse themselves (whom they count just) from obedience to laws. But the Apostle's meaning is that the just man does well, not because he is compelled by law or for fear of punishment due to those who break it, but out of grace and pure love toward God and all goodness, most willingly, even if there were no law to command him.

<margin>Excommunication of Heretics, and the effect thereof.</margin>
20. **Delivered to Satan.**] Hymenaeus and Alexander are here excommunicated for falling from their faith and teaching heresy: an example for Bishops to use their spiritual power upon such people. In the primitive Church, physical affliction through the ministry of Satan was joined to excommunication. Here we see also the devil's readiness to invade those who are cast out by excommunication from the fellowship of the faithful, and the supreme power of Bishops in that case. Regarding this, St. Jerome (*Epistle 1 to Heliodorus, chapter 7*) has these memorable words:
<margin>The Priest's high authority of Excommunication.</margin>
> God forbid (says he) *I should speak unfavorably of those who, succeeding the Apostles in their rank, make Christ's body with their holy mouth <note>A reference to the consecration of the Eucharist.</note>, through whom we are made Christians: who, having the keys of heaven, judge in a certain way before the day of judgment: who in sobriety and chastity keep the spouse of Christ <note>The Church.</note>.*
And a little after,
> *They may deliver me up to Satan, for the destruction of my flesh, so that the spirit may be saved in the day of our Lord Jesus.*
<margin>The terrible effect thereof.</margin>
And in the old Law, whoever was disobedient to the Priests was either cast out of the camp and so stoned by the people, or, laying down his neck to the sword, paid for his offense with his blood: but now the disobedient person is cut off with the spiritual sword, or being cast out of the Church, is torn by the furious mouth of Devils. So says he. I wish every Christian man would weigh these words.

# ->A N N O T A T I O N S<-
## ->CHAPTER II.<-

<margin>The prayers and petitions in the Mass, deduced out of the Apostle's words by St. Augustine and other fathers.</margin>
<margin>Petitions <note>original Greek: δεήσεις (deēseis)</note></margin>
<margin>Prayers <note>original Greek: προσευχαί (proseuchai)</note></margin>
<margin>Intercessions <note>original Greek: ἐντεύξεις (enteuxeis)</note></margin>
<margin>Thanksgivings <note>original Greek: εὐχαριστίαι (eucharistiai)</note></margin>
<margin>Theophylact on this location.</margin>
1. **Obsecrations <note>Or "Supplications."</note>.**] This order of the Apostle, St. Augustine (*Epistle 59*) finds to be fulfilled specially in the holy celebration of the Mass, which has all these kinds, expressed here in four diverse words pertaining to four sorts of prayers. The difference of which he exactly seeks out from the proper signification and difference of the Greek words. And he teaches us that the first kind of prayers, which here are called *obsecrations*, are those that the Priest says before the consecration; that the second called *Prayers* are all those which are said in and after the Consecration, and about the Receiving, including specially the *Our Father* <note>original Latin: *Pater noster*</note>, wherewith the whole Church
<margin>OUR FATHER in the Mass.</margin>
(he says) in a manner ends that part, as St. Jerome also affirms, that Christ taught his Apostles to use the *Our Father* in the Mass. *Thus he taught, etc.* <note>original Latin: *Sic docuit, & c. Li. 3 cont. Pelag. cap. 5.*</note> where he alludes to the very words now used in the preface to the said *Our Father* in the said Sacrifice, *we dare to say, Our Father* <note>original Latin: *audemus dicere, Pater noster*</note>. The third sort called here in the text *Postulations* <note>Or "Intercessions."</note> are those which are used after the Communion, as it were for dismissing the people with a benediction, that is, with the Bishop’s or Priest’s blessing. Finally, the last kind, which is *Thanksgivings*, concludes all, when the Priest and people give thanks to God for so great a mystery then offered and received. Thus the said holy father handles this text in Epistle 59 to Paulinus.

<margin>Prayer in the Mass for kings and others.</margin>
St. Epiphanius also suggests these words of the Apostle pertain to the Liturgy or Mass, when he thus writes to John, Bishop of Jerusalem: *When we accomplish our prayers after the rite of the holy Mysteries, we pray both for all others, and for thee also.* <note>Epistle 60, chapter 2 to John of Jerusalem, found in the works of Jerome.</note> And most of the other fathers explain the aforesaid words as public prayers made by the Priest, which are said in all Liturgies or Masses, both Greek and Latin, for the good estate of all that be in high dignity, as kings and others. See St. Chrysostom, Homily 6 on 1 Timothy, and St. Ambrose on this location; also Prosper, *On the Call of All Nations*, Book 1, Chapter 4. So exactly does the practice of the Church agree with the precepts of the Apostle and the Scriptures, and so profoundly do the holy fathers seek out the proper sense of the Scriptures, which our Protestants do so profanely, popularly, and lightly skim over, that they can neither see nor endure the truth.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the First Epistle to Timothy, Chapter 2. The previous page discussed the requirement for Christians to pray for all people, including secular rulers. # THE FIRST EPISTLE OF SAINT PAUL CHAPTER II.

<margin>God wills no one's destruction but the salvation of all.</margin>
4 **Who will all men**] The perishing or damnation of men must not be blamed on God, who takes no delight in anyone's destruction. Rather, he has provided a general medicine and redemption to save everyone from perishing if they will accept it, or if they have it applied to them through his Sacraments and other means ordained by him. Thus, he would have all saved by his conditional will and ordinance: that is, if people themselves are willing, by accepting, doing, or having done for them all things required by God’s law. For God does not use his absolute will or power toward everyone in this matter. <note>The author distinguishes between God's "absolute will" (what He ordains to happen unconditionally) and His "conditional will" (salvation offered to all, but dependent on human response and the use of the Sacraments).</note> But for those who wish to see the various interpretations (all good and true) that these words may carry, let them see Saint Augustine, *Response to the articles falsely attributed to him, Response 2, volume 7; Enchiridion (Handbook), chapter 103; Letter 107; On Rebuke and Grace, chapter 15*, and *Saint John Damascene, Book 2 on the Orthodox Faith, chapter 29.*

<margin>How there is but one Mediator, Christ: and what it is to be such a Mediator.</margin>
<margin>
*Augustine, Book 9 of The City of God, chapter 15; On the Faith to Peter, chapter 2.*
</margin>
5 **One mediator.**] The Protestants are so stubbornly and pitifully blind that they charge the Catholic Church and Catholics with making more mediators than one (which is Christ our Savior) because they ask the Saints to pray for them, or to be their patrons and intercessors before God. We tell them, therefore, that they do not understand what it is to be a Mediator in the sense that Saint Paul uses the word, and in which it is properly and only attributed to Christ. For, to be a Mediator in this way is, by nature, to be truly both God and man; to be that one eternal Priest and Redeemer who, by his sacrifice and death upon the Cross, has reconciled us to God and paid his blood as a full and sufficient ransom for all our sins. He himself had no need of any redemption and was never subject to the possibility of sinning. Furthermore, he is the unique Advocate and Patron of mankind, who by himself alone and by his own merits procures all grace and mercy for mankind in the sight of his Father. No one makes intercession for him, nor gives any grace or force to his prayers, but he gives it to all. No one asks for or obtains either grace in this life, or glory in the next, except through him. In this way, then (as Saint Augustine truly says in *Against the Letter of Parmenian, Book 2, chapter 8*), neither Peter nor Paul, nor even our Blessed Lady, nor any creature whatsoever, can be our Mediator. Our adversaries think too lowly of Christ’s mediation if they imagine this to be his only prerogative—to pray for us—or if they think we make the saints our Mediators in the same way Christ is when we ask them to pray for us. This is so far inferior to his unique mediation that no Catholic ever can or would dare think or speak so lowly to him as to ask him to pray for us. 

<margin>The different manner of praying to Christ and to Saints.</margin>
<margin>*Lord have mercy. Christ have mercy.*</margin>
Instead, we say, "Lord have mercy upon us, Christ have mercy upon us," and not, "Christ pray for us," as we say to our Lady and the rest. Therefore, to invoke Saints in the manner the Catholic Church does cannot make them our Mediators in the way Christ is, whom we must not invoke in that manner. And by the logic of our adversaries’ arguments, we would be making the faithful who are still living our "mediators" when we ask for their prayers, just as much as we do with the departed Saints.

<margin>How there are many mediators, just as there are many saviors and redeemers, even in the Scriptures.</margin>
<margin>*Judges 3:9; 2 Esdras 9:27; Acts 7:35.*</margin>
But now, concerning the word *Mediator*: although in that unique sense proper to our Savior it applies to no mere creature in heaven or earth, yet when taken in a broader and more common sense—by the usage of Scripture, the Doctors of the Church, and common speech—not only the Saints, but good men living who pray for us and help us on the path to salvation, may be and are rightly called mediators. As Saint Cyril proves in *The Treasury, Book 12, chapter 10*, Moses, Jeremiah, the Apostles, and others are mediators according to the Scriptures. Read his own words, for they plainly refute all the adversaries' trivial objections in this case. And if the names of "savior" and "redeemer" are given to men in the Scriptures without taking away from Him who is, in a more excellent and incomparable manner, the only Savior of the world, what can they say against there being many mediators in an inferior degree to the one and only Mediator? Saint Bernard says: <note>original: "Opus est mediatore ad Mediatorem Christum, nec alter nobis utilior quam Maria."</note> *We have need of a mediator to Christ the Mediator, and there is none more profitable for us than our Lady.* (Bernard, Sermon beginning *A great sign appeared*, etc., after the 5th Sermon on the Assumption). Saint Basil also, in the same sense, writing to Julian the Apostate, asks for the mediation of our Lady, the Apostles, Prophets, and Martyrs to obtain God's mercy and the remission of his sins. His words are cited in the *Second Council of Nicaea, act 4, pages 110 and 111.* This is what all the holy fathers believed and practiced, most agreeably with the Scriptures, and this is what all children of the Church must do, no matter how persistent and willfully blind the adversaries are in these matters.

<margin>Women as great talkers of Scripture and promoters of heresy.</margin>
<margin>*Saint Chrysostom, Homily 9 on 1 Timothy.*</margin>
12 **I permit not.**] In times of licentiousness, liberty, and heresy, women are much given to reading, disputing, chatting, and bickering over the holy Scriptures—and even to teaching, if they were permitted. But Saint Paul utterly forbids it. The Greek Doctors <note>Early Greek-speaking theologians and commentators of the Church.</note> noting this passage observe that woman taught only once: that was when, after her reasoning with Satan, she persuaded her husband to sin, and so she undid all mankind. In the writings of Church historians, we find that women have been great promoters of every sort of heresy (on which see a notable discourse in Saint Jerome’s *Letter to Ctesiphon against the Pelagians, chapter 2*). They would not have done this if they had followed the Apostle’s rule: to pursue piety and good works, and to live in silence and subjection to their husbands.

<header>THE FIRST EPISTLE OF SAINT PAUL, CHAPTER 3</header>

<margin>The great responsibility and great merit of Church duties.</margin>
1. **A good work.**] *Nothing (says Saint Augustine) in this life, and especially at this time, is easier, pleasanter, or more acceptable to men than the office of a Bishop, Priest, or Deacon, if the thing be done only for fashion’s sake and to flatter: but before God, nothing is more miserable, more lamentable, or more damnable. On the other hand, there is nothing in this life, and especially at this time, harder, more laborious, or more dangerous than the office of a Bishop, Priest, or Deacon: but before God, nothing is more blessed, if they serve in such a way as our Captain commands.* <note>original Latin: "vvarre" or *militent*, meaning to serve as a soldier.</note> Augustine, Letter 148.

<margin>The Apostle, using the title of Bishop, gives instructions to Priests as well.</margin>
2. **A Bishop.**] What is said here regarding a Bishop (because the words "Bishop" and "Priest" in the New Testament are often used interchangeably for both or either of the two, as noted elsewhere) is meant for every Priest as well. However, the qualities required here ought to be more outstanding in the Bishop than in the Priest, according to the difference in their ranks, dignities, and callings.

<margin>The heretics' opinion concerning the marriage of Priests.</margin>
2. **of one wife.**] Certain Bishops of Vigilantius's sect <note>Vigilantius was a 4th-century priest who opposed clerical celibacy and the veneration of relics.</note> (whether based on a false interpretation of this text or through the filthiness of their fleshly lust) would admit no one to the Clergy unless they were married first. *They did not believe (says Saint Jerome in "Against Vigilantius," chapter 1) that any single man lives chastely, showing how "holily" they live themselves when they suspect evil in every man, and will not give the Sacrament of Holy Orders to the Clergy unless they see their wives have great bellies and children wailing at their mothers' breasts.* Our Protestants, though they belong to Vigilantius's sect, have yet to go so far as to command every Priest to be married. Nevertheless, they dislike those who will not marry even more, and they suspect evil of every single person in the Church, thinking the gift of chastity is very rare among them. Not only do they make the state of marriage equal to a chaste single life, following the heretic Jovinian, but they are bold enough to say sometimes that a Bishop or Priest may do his duty and charge better while married than single. <margin>1 Corinthians 7.</margin> This is expressly against Saint Paul, who affirms that the unmarried think of the things that belong to God, while the married are diversely distracted and entangled with the world.

<margin>Saint Paul’s passage "of one wife" excludes "bigamists" from Holy Orders.</margin>
The Apostle then, in this passage we are now treating, neither commands, nor counsels, nor wishes, nor would have Bishops or Priests marry, or only those who have been married to be received. Rather, he means that such a person who has been married (provided it was only once, and to a virgin) may be made a Bishop or Priest. This is nothing more than an inhibition that no one who has been twice married, or who is a <term>bigamus</term> <note>From the Latin *bigamus*, referring here to someone who has been married twice, even if sequentially (e.g., a widower who remarries).</note>, should be admitted to that holy Order. This interpretation alone agrees with the practice of the whole Church, the definitions of ancient Councils, the doctrine of all the Church Fathers without exception, and the Apostle's tradition. Saint Chrysostom follows this sense entirely in his commentary on the Epistle to Titus (though here he does not follow the same sense entirely). See Homily 2 on the Epistle to Titus. Saint Ambrose also comments on this place, and most plainly and at length in his 82nd Letter *after the middle*, giving the reason why a <term>bigamus</term> cannot be made a Bishop or Priest; finally, he affirms that not only the Apostle but the holy Council of Nicaea ordered that no one should be received into the Clergy who had been twice married. Saint Jerome (Letter 83 to Oceanus, ch. 2; Letter 2, ch. 18; Letter 11, ch. 2) expressly writes that the Clergy is made of those who have had but one wife, at least after Baptism; for he thought that if someone were married multiple times while still a pagan, he might nonetheless be ordained a Bishop or Priest. But Saint Ambrose (Letter 82), Saint Augustine (*On the Good of Marriage*, ch. 18), Saint Innocent I (Letter 2, ch. 5-6, volume 1 of the Councils), <margin>* Book 2, Letter 25.</margin> Saint Leo (Letter 87), Saint Gregory, and after them the whole Church, also exclude those who have been twice married at any time. Saint Augustine gives an excellent reason and example of this in the place cited. Saint Leo (Letter 87) adds further and proves that a man is counted as a "bigamist," and not the husband of one wife in respect to Holy Orders, not only if he has had two wives, but if his one wife was not a virgin. <margin>Leviticus 21.</margin> Since this was observed for the High Priests of the Old Law, it must certainly be kept much more strictly now. See also the book *On Church Doctrines*, chapter 72, in Saint Augustine’s works.
<margin>Who are counted as "bigami."</margin>

<margin>The heretical clergy completely ignore the Apostle’s rule of "one wife."</margin>
By these few examples, you may see how shamefully the state of the new heretical Clergy of our time has fallen from the Apostolic and Patristic practice and doctrine in this matter. They not only take men who were married once or twice before, but (something never heard of before in any person or part of the Catholic Church) they marry *after* they become Bishops or Priests—once, twice, and as often as their lusts require. However, it was never lawful in God's Church to marry after receiving Holy Orders. There is not one authentic example of this in the world. As for those of whom the Council of Nicaea speaks, they were married *before* ordination and were only tolerated to continue living with their wives. <margin>No one ever married after receiving Holy Orders.</margin> The Fathers in that same Council expressly provided at that time that none from then on should marry after entering Holy Orders, according to the ancient tradition of the Church, as Socrates and Sozomenus <note>Socrates Scholasticus and Sozomen were 5th-century Church historians.</note> declare in very plain words. See Suidas under the word *Paphnutius*. And in whatever country they have been permitted to have physical relations even with those wives <margin>Socrates, Book 1, ch. 8; Sozomen, Book 1, ch. 22</margin> <margin>Those married men who were made Priests abstained from their wives.</margin> whom they had before, it was not according to the exact rule of the Apostles and the Church's tradition. By that tradition, all who are in Holy Orders should wholly abstain, not only from marrying but even from the wives they married previously. Regarding this, Saint Epiphanius writes thus:

# CHAPTER III. TO TIMOTHY.

<margin>Saint Epiphanius.
Marriage of Priests is contrary to the ancient canons.</margin>
Saint Epiphanius in *Against Heresies, book 59, against the Cathars* <note>original Latin: "haeref. 59 cont. Catharos"</note> says: *The holy preaching of God does not receive, after Christ, those who marry again after their wives' departure, because of the great dignity and honor of the Priesthood. And this the holy Church of God observes with all sincerity. Indeed, she does not receive the once-married person who still uses his wife and fathers children; but only such a one she takes to be a Deacon, Priest, Bishop, or Subdeacon, who abstains from his one wife, or is a widower, especially where the holy canons are sincerely kept. But you will say to me, that in certain places Priests, Deacons, and Subdeacons still father children* (likely this holy father never heard of any Bishop who did so, and therefore he leaves out that order, which he named with the others in the former part of the sentence) *but that is not done according to order and rule, but according to man's mind, which slackens over time, and because of the great multitude (of Christian people) when there were not found sufficient men for the ministry, etc.* The rest of his words are excellent for that purpose.

<margin>Eusebius.
Saint Jerome.</margin>
Eusebius also, in *The Demonstration of the Gospel, book 1, chapter 9* <note>original Latin: "Euang. demonst. li. 1. c. 9"</note> says that such as are consecrated to the holy ministry should abstain wholly from the wives which they had before. Saint Jerome, in *Apology to Pammachius, chapter 8*, proves that such of the Apostles as were married did so, and that the Clergy ought to do the same by their example. Indeed, in his time he testifies (*Against Vigilantius, chapter 1*) that they lived single almost throughout the world, even in the Eastern Church also. *What,* he says, *shall the Churches of the East do, or those of Egypt, or of the Apostolic See: which take into the Clergy either virgins, or those who are continent and unmarried, or such as, if they have wives, cease to be husbands?* And again he says in *Apology to Pammachius, chapter 3* (See also chapter 8): *If married men do not like this, let them not be angry with me, but with the holy Scriptures, with all Bishops, Priests, Deacons, and the whole company of Priests and Levites, who know they cannot offer sacrifices if they use the act of marriage.*

<margin>Saint Augustine.
See Saint Leo, letter 92, chapter 3.</margin>
Saint Augustine, in *On Adulterous Marriages, book 2, chapter 20*, makes it so plain a matter that all Priests should live chaste, that he writes that even such as were forced (as many were in the primitive Church) to be of the Clergy, were bound to live chaste; yes, and did it with great joy and happiness, never complaining of these necessities and "intolerable burdens," or "impossibilities" of living chaste, as our carnal company of new Ministers and Superintendents <note>The author refers to Protestant reformers who rejected clerical celibacy.</note> do now, who think there is no life without women. This is much like Saint Augustine before his conversion, when he was still a Manichee, who (as he himself reports in *Confessions, book 6, chapter 3*) 

<margin>Saint Ambrose.</margin>
while admiring in Saint Ambrose all his other incomparable excellencies, yet counted all his happiness to be less because he lacked a woman, without which he thought (during the time of his infidelity) no man could live. But after his conversion, he said this to God concerning Saint Ambrose: *What hope he had, and against the temptations of his excellence what a fight he felt, or rather what a comfort and solace in tribulation, and his secret mouth which was within his heart, what savory and sweet joys it tasted of your bread, I could neither guess, nor had I tried.*

<margin>Tertullian.
Saint Cyprian.
Councils.</margin>
See Tertullian, *Book 1, To His Wife*; Saint Cyprian, *On the Singleness of Clerics*; the first Council of Nicaea, *canon 3*; the second Council of Toledo, *canon 3*; the third Council of Orleans, *canon 2*; the second Council of Carthage, *chapter 2*; the Council of Neocaesarea, *chapter 1*; and the Council of Ancyra, *chapter 10*. You shall find that this was generally the Church's order even from the Apostles' time, though in some places, due to the licentiousness of many, it was sometimes not so religiously observed. By this, you may easily refute the shameless cries of Heretics against Siricius, Gregory VII, and others, whom they falsely claim were the authors of the Clergy's single life.

<margin>No one is to be rashly admitted to the Clergy.
Heretics admit without exception.</margin>
6. **Not a Neophyte.**] That which is spoken here properly and principally of the newly baptized (for so the word <term>Neophyte</term> <note>From the Greek *neophytos*, meaning "newly planted."</note> signifies), the fathers extend also to all such as have only newly retired from profane occupations, civil government, warfare, or secular studies, of whom a good trial must be taken before they ought to be promoted to the high dignity of Bishop or Priest. Though for some special prerogative and excellence, it has been otherwise in certain persons, as in Saint Ambrose and some other notable men. Tertullian (*The Book of Prescriptions*) notes Heretics for their lightness in admitting everyone without discretion to the Clergy. *Their Orders (he says) are rash, light, and inconstant: now they appoint Neophytes, then secular men, then our apostates, so that they may bind them by glory and preferment, since they cannot bind them with the truth. Nowhere may a man sooner prosper and come forward than in the camp of rebels, where to be present is to deserve much. Therefore one is today a Bishop, tomorrow something else: today a Deacon, tomorrow a Lector (that is, a Reader): today a Priest, tomorrow a layman. For to laymen also they assign the functions of Priests.* And Saint Jerome (*Letter 83 to Oceanus, chapter 4*) says of such: *Yesterday a <term>catechumen</term> <note>A person receiving basic instruction in Christianity before baptism.</note> or newly converted person, today a Bishop; yesterday in the theater, today in the Church; at night in the place of games and mastery, in the morning at the altar; a while ago a great patron of stage-players, now a consecrator of holy virgins. And in another place: Out of the bosom of Plato and Aristophanes they are chosen to a Bishopric; their care is not how to suck out the marrow of the Scriptures, but how to soothe the people's ears with flourishing declamations.* (*Dialogue against the Luciferians, chapter 5*).

<margin>Leo, letter 92, chapter 3.
Gregory, book 1, letter 42.
The three holy orders, alone bound to chastity.</margin>
8. **Deacons.**] Under the name of Deacons are here contained Subdeacons, just as previously under the name of Bishop, Priests were also included. For to these four <note>Bishops, Priests, Deacons, and Subdeacons.</note> pertain the Apostle's precept and order regarding one wife, and regarding continence and chastity, as appears by the cited Councils and Fathers (namely by the words of Saint Epiphanius). For they alone are in holy Orders, as serving by their proper function at the Altar and the Blessed Sacrament: in respect of which...

# THE FIRST EPISTLE OF SAINT PAUL, CHAPTER 3.

<margin>The 4 inferior orders not bound to chastity.</margin>
Whereof, the law of chastity pertains to them, and not to the four inferior Orders of **Acolytes**, **Exorcists**, **Lectors**, and **Porters** <note>original Latin: "Acolyti, Exorciste, Lectores, and Ostiary"</note>. These are neither bound by precept nor vow to perpetual chastity, as the others of the holy and high Orders are bound, both by precept and promise or solemn assent made when they took the **Subdeaconship** <term>the first of the 'major orders' in the traditional hierarchy, requiring a commitment to celibacy</term>.

<margin>All the seven orders are ancient, even from the time of Christ and the Apostles.</margin>
That all these degrees and orders have existed since the time of Christ in the Church of God could be proved by all antiquity. However, because the Apostle’s purpose here is not to reckon up the entire **Ecclesiastical Hierarchy** <term>the ranked structure of church government</term>, it need not be treated in full in this place. But we wish the learned to read chapters 3 through 9 of the 4th Council of Carthage, at which Saint Augustine was present. There they shall see the express callings, offices, and manner of ordaining or creating all the said groups, and shall well perceive these things to be most ancient and venerable. Let them read also the history by **Eusebius** <note>an early Christian historian, often called the "Father of Church History"</note>, Chapter 35 of the 6th book, where for all these orders he recites the epistle of Cornelius to Fabius concerning **Novatus** <note>a 3rd-century scholar and priest who held rigorous views on penance and was considered a schismatic</note>. Likewise, Saint Cyprian in many places, namely Epistle 55, number 1 (see the notes upon that same letter). Saint Jerome, Epistle 2, chapter 6. Of the **Subdeacon** there is mention in Saint Augustine, Epistle 74, and Epistle 20 (number 22 in the Paris edition). See also Saint Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 59; Saint Cyprian, Epistle 24; Saint Ignatius, Epistle 9 *to the Antiochians* <note>original Latin: "ad Antiochenos"</note>; and in the 43rd canon of the Apostles. See also the Second Council of Toledo, canons 1 and 3; the Council of Laodicea, canon 21; and the Epistle of Epiphanius found in Jerome, book 60, chapter 1.

<margin>Saint Ambrose calls the Bishop of Rome the Rector of the whole Church.</margin>
13. *In the house of God.*] Although all the world belongs to God, yet the Church only is his house, the **Rector** <term>from the Latin for 'ruler' or 'guide'</term> or Ruler whereof at this day (says Saint Ambrose upon this passage) is **Damasus** <note>Pope Damasus I, who reigned from 366 to 384 AD</note>. Here, let our loving brethren note well how clear a case it was then, that the Pope of Rome was not the Governor only of one particular **See** <term>the jurisdiction or 'seat' of a bishop</term>, but of Christ’s whole house, which is the Universal Church, whose Rector today is **Gregory the Thirteenth** <note>the Pope at the time of this manuscript's writing (1572–1585), famous for the Gregorian calendar</note>.

<margin>The heretics say directly the contrary to the Apostle: that the Church is not the pillar of truth.</margin>
15. *The pillar of truth.*] This passage presses all Heretics wonderfully, and so it ever did. Therefore, they oppose themselves directly against the very letter and confessed sense of the same—that is, clean contrary to the Apostle. Some say the Church is lost or hidden; some, that it has fallen away from Christ for these many ages; some, that it is driven into a corner of the world only; some, that it has become a **stew** <note>an archaic term for a brothel; here used as a derogatory metaphor by Reformers to describe the Catholic Church</note> and the seat of Antichrist. Lastly, the Protestants say most plainly and directly that it may and does err, and has shamefully erred for many hundred years together. And they speak this way for the sake of their own doctrine, which cannot be true in very deed unless the Church errs—even the Church of Christ, which is here called the house of the living God.

<margin>That the Church is the pillar of truth and cannot err is proved by many reasons.</margin>
<margin>John 14, 16. Matthew 16. Matthew 28. Ephesians 4. 10. 17. Luke 22. Psalm 2. Ephesians 5.</margin>
But the Church, which is the house of God—whose Rector (says Saint Ambrose) in his time was Damasus, and now Gregory the Thirteenth, and in the Apostle’s time Saint Peter—is the pillar of truth and the establishment of all verity; therefore, it cannot err. It has the Spirit of God to lead it into all truth until the world’s end; therefore, it cannot err. It is built upon a rock, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it; therefore, it cannot err. Christ is in it until the end of the world; he has placed in it Apostles, Doctors, Pastors, and Rulers, for the consummation and full perfection of the whole body, so that in the meantime we are not carried about with every blast of doctrine; therefore, it cannot err. He has prayed for it, that it be sanctified in verity, and that the faith of its chief Governor fail not. It is his house, his spouse, his body, his lot, kingdom, and inheritance given him in this world; he loves it as his own flesh, and it cannot be divorced or separated from him; therefore, it cannot err. The New Testament, Scriptures, Sacraments, and sacrifice cannot be changed, being the everlasting dowry of the Church, continued and never rightly occupied in any other Church but in our Catholic Church; therefore, it cannot err. And therefore all those points of doctrine, faith, and worship, which the Arians, Manichees, Protestants, Anabaptists, and other old or new Heretics untruly think to be errors in the Church, are no errors indeed. Rather, they themselves are most shamefully deceived, and so shall they be still, until they enter again into this house of God, which is the pillar and ground of all truth. That is to say, not only is the Church itself free from all error in faith and religion, but it is the pillar and stay to lean upon in all doubts of doctrine, and to stand upon against all heresies and errors that evil times yield, without which there can be no certainty nor security.

<margin>The meaning of this article, "I believe the Catholic Church."</margin>
And therefore the holy Apostles, and the Councils of Nicaea and Constantinople, made it an article of our Creed to believe the **CATHOLIC AND APOSTOLIC CHURCH**. Which is not only to acknowledge that there is such a Church, as heretics falsely say, but that that which is called the Catholic Church—and is known to be so, and communicates with the **Apostolic See** <term>the authority of the Pope in Rome as successor to St. Peter</term>—is the Church. We must believe, hear, and obey the same as the touchstone, pillar, and **firmament** <term>a solid foundation or support</term> of truth. For all this is comprised in that principle: *I believe the Catholic Church*. And therefore the Council of Nicaea said, *I believe in the Church*, that is, I believe and trust the same in all things.

<margin>Into the Church <note>original Greek: "εἰς τὴν ἐκκλησίαν"</note></margin>
Neither can the Heretics escape by fleeing from the known visible Church to the hidden congregation or company of the **Predestinate** <term>those chosen by God for salvation from the beginning of time</term>. For that is but a false fantastical apprehension of...

# CHAPTER 4. TO TIMOTHY.

<margin>It is the visible Church that is the pillar of truth and cannot err.</margin>
This contradicts the understanding of **John Wycliffe** <note>an English reformer whose followers, the Lollards, argued the true Church was an invisible group of people predestined for salvation</note> and his followers. The company of the **Predestinate** <term>those chosen by God for salvation</term> does not make up a single society among themselves, as many of them are not yet born, and many are currently infidels or heretics. Therefore, they are not part of the one "house of God" which is called here "the pillar of truth." Those of the Predestinate who are already part of the Church do not form a separate group from the known **Catholic Church**, but are baptized, **houseled** <term>given the Sacrament of the Eucharist</term>, and taught; they live and die in the common, visible Catholic Church. Otherwise, they could receive neither the Sacraments nor salvation. Saint Paul does not instruct Timothy on how to teach, preach, correct, and live within an invisible society of the predestined, but within the visible house of God. So, it must necessarily be the visible Church which cannot err.

<margin>From where the Church has this privilege to never err.</margin>
<margin>Saint Augustine.</margin>
<margin>Lactantius.</margin>
<margin>Saint Cyprian.</margin>
<margin>Saint Irenaeus.</margin>
If anyone asks further how it can be that any society of men (as the Church is) can be free of error in faith, seeing that all men may err, he must know that it is not by human nature, but by the privilege of Christ’s presence, the assistance of the Holy Spirit, and our Lord’s promise and prayer. See Saint Augustine upon these words of the 118th Psalm, Sermon 13: *Do not take the word of truth utterly out of my mouth* <note>original Latin: "Ne auferas de ore meo verbum veritatis usquequaque"</note>. There he speaks beautifully on this matter. For the same purpose, these words of **Lactantius** <note>an early Christian author and advisor to Constantine I</note> are very notable: *“It is the Catholic Church only that keeps the true worship of God; this is the fountain of truth, this the house of faith, this the Temple of God. If any man does not enter here, or if any man goes out from here, he is an alien and stranger to the hope of everlasting life and salvation. No man should flatter himself through stubborn contention, for it is a matter of life and salvation,”* etc. Saint Cyprian says, *“The Church never departs from that which she has once known.”* (Epistle 55 to Cornelius, number 3). Saint Irenaeus says, *“The Apostles have laid up in the Church, as in a rich treasury, all truth. And she keeps with the most sincere diligence the Apostles' faith and preaching.”* (Book 3, chapters 4 and 40, and Book 1, chapter 3). It would be an endless task to recite everything the Church Fathers say on this matter, as they all count it a most destructive absurdity to claim that the Church of Christ could err in religion.

<margin>All Heretics are apostates from the faith.</margin>
<margin>to depart <note>original Greek: ἀποστῆναι (apostēnai)</note></margin>
<margin>* Chapter 1:19.</margin>
1. **Shall depart.**] It is the proper description of Heretics to forsake their former faith and to be Apostates, as the Greek word implies: to give ear to private spirits of error and deception, rather than to the Spirit of Christ in his Church; to follow in hypocrisy and the appearance of virtue the destructive doctrine of Devils, who are the suggestors and prompters of all Sects, and are lying spirits in the mouths of all Heretics and false preachers. These are men who have silenced their conscience and made it senseless to the holy Church’s admonition. The Apostle noted * once before also in this same Epistle, that Heretics have no conscience, which is the cause both of their fall and of their stubbornness <term>obduration</term> in heresy.

<margin>The old Heresies against marriage.</margin>
<margin>* Augustine, Heresies, 46.</margin>
3. **Forbidding to marry.**] He speaks (says Saint Chrysostom) of the Manicheans, Encratites, and Marcionites <note>early Christian sects that often viewed the physical world and marriage as evil</note>. Homily 12 on 1 Timothy. Saint Ambrose, upon this place, adds to these the Patricians also. See also Saint Irenaeus, book 1, chapter 30; Saint Epiphanius, heresies 45, 26, 61, 30; Saint Jerome, book 1 against Jovinian, chapters 1 and 3; and Saint Augustine, heresies 25 and 40. Generally, all antiquity assumes the same of them, and also of the Heretics called Apostolics, Ebionites, and the like. Their heresy about marriage was that to marry or to use the act of matrimony is of Satan, as Saint Irenaeus witnesses (book 1, chapter 22); and that the distinction of male and female and the creation of man and woman for generation came from an evil God. They taught their followers, * says Saint Augustine, that if they did use women, they should by all means ensure they did not conceive or bear children. Clement of Alexandria (book 3 of the *Stromata* <note>Miscellanies</note>, at the beginning) writes that such people admit no marriage nor procreation of children, lest they should bring into the world creatures to suffer misery and mortality. And this is the damnable opinion concerning marriage noted here by the Apostle.

<margin>The old Heresies about abstinence from foods.</margin>
For the second point, consisting in the prohibition of foods <note>original: "meates"</note> or the use of certain creatures made to be eaten, the said Heretics or various ones among them (for they were not all of one sect regarding these points) taught that men might not eat certain sorts of foods, especially of beasts and living creatures, because they were not made (they say) by the good God, but by the evil one. And wine they called the gall of the Prince of Darkness, saying it should not be drunk at all, and that the Vine from which it came was of the Devil's creation. Various other creatures they condemned as things by nature and creation polluted and abominable. *Augustine, Heresies of the Manicheans, 46, and Heresy 25 regarding Tatian; and throughout his book on the Morals of the Manicheans, volume 1.* Look, these were the Heretics and their heresies which Saint Paul here prophesies of—those who forbid marriage and foods as you have heard—for which they and their followers were condemned in various Councils.

<margin>The Catholics are shamelessly charged with the said old heresies.</margin>

### CHAPTER 4. TO TIMOTHY. 575

<margin>Abstinence from certain meats is no condemnation of the meats.</margin>
of Priests and Religious? As though either by appointing or using some days of abstinence from certain meats, the Church or any Catholic man condemned the said meats. Unless the Rechabites *Jeremiah 35* or the Nazarites *Numbers 6* or the Ninevites *Jonah 3* or Moses *Exodus 34* or Elias *1 Kings 19* <note>original: "3 Reg. 19"; the Douay-Rheims Bible follows the Vulgate numbering where 1 and 2 Samuel are 1 and 2 Kings, and 1 and 2 Kings are 3 and 4 Kings</note> or holy Anna the widow *Luke 2* or John the Baptist *Matthew 3 and 9* or Christ himself *Matthew 4*—commending, using, and following a prescribed number of fasting days—or God himself, who in the very beginning in Paradise prescribed abstinence from the fruit of one certain tree, and later appointed so many fasts in the Law; unless he, therefore, condemned his own creatures, and the rest condemned those creatures from which they abstained. No, there are many good and lawful causes to forbid some or to abstain from some meats: as for obedience, as in Paradise; for significance, as the Jews; for that they have been offered to Idols, as in the Epistle to the Corinthians; for chastening the body and penance; for health also; and only those causes are unlawful for which the Manichees <note>An ancient sect that believed physical matter was evil and created by a bad god</note> and other Heretics abstained.
<margin>Diverse good causes of abstinence.</margin>

<margin>Forbidding certain persons to marry is no condemnation of matrimony.</margin>
Concerning marriage likewise, they may as well charge God or the Church for forbidding the father to marry the daughter, or the brother the sister, or other prohibited persons in the Law: as well might they charge Christ and the Apostle for prohibiting the same to marry again during his wife’s life; and appointing widows that serve the Church to live unmarried, and not admitting a married woman as well as a widow, nor her that has had more husbands, as well as her that has been married but once: as they charge the Church for not admitting married persons to the altar <note>Referring to the requirement of clerical celibacy</note>, and for forcing them and Religious persons to keep their promise of chastity. No, the holy Church is so far from condemning wedlock that she honors it much more than the Protestants, accounting it an holy Sacrament, which they do not, who only use it for lust as the Heathen do, and not for religion.
<margin>Catholics esteem matrimony more than the Protestants do.</margin>

But it is an old deceitful practice of Heretics to charge Catholic men with old condemned heresies. The Eutychians slandered the Council of Chalcedon and Saint Leo to be Nestorians, and to make two persons in Christ, because they said there were two natures. *Vigilius, book 5, Against Eutyches.* Arius charged Alexander his Bishop with Sabellianism <note>An early heresy that denied the distinct persons of the Trinity</note> for avouching the unity of substance in the Trinity. *Socrates, book 1, chapter 3.* Julianus accused Saint Augustine of the heresy of Apollinaris. *Book 5, Against Julian, chapter 15.* Other Pelagians challenged him for condemning marriage. *Retractions, book 2, chapter 53.* And so that our Protestants brag not too much of their goodly invention, Jovinian the old Heretic, their Master in this point, ac-
<margin>* Augustine, book 2, chapter 5, On Marriage and Concupiscence.</margin>
<margin>The Protestants' objections answered long ago by Saint Jerome and Saint Augustine.</margin>
cused the holy doctors and Catholics upon this same place to be Manichees, and to condemn meats and marriage, as both Saint Jerome and Saint Augustine do testify. And they both answer to the Heretic that the Church indeed and Catholics do abstain from some for ever, and some for certain days, and every Christian man lightly <note>readily or commonly</note> all the 40 days of Lent fast: not because they think the meats unclean, abominable, or of an evil creation, as the Manichees do; but for punishment of their bodies and taming their concupiscences <note>worldly or physical desires</note>. *Jerome, book 2, Against Jovinian, chapter 11; Augustine, Against Adimantus, chapter 14; Book on the Morals of the Catholic Church; Jerome on chapter 4 to the Galatians.* And as for marriage, the said doctors answer that no Catholic man condemns it as unlawful, as the old Heretics did, but only prefers virginity and continence before it, as a state in itself more agreeable to God and more meet <note>suitable</note> for the Clergy. See *Saint Augustine* against Faustus the Manichee *book 30, chapters 5 and 6, and Heresy 25* in the name, *Apostolici.* *Saint Jerome, epistle 50, chapters 1 and 3.* All this the Catholics continually tell the Adversaries, and they cannot but see it. Yet by accustomed audacity and impudence they bear it out still.

4. *With thanksgiving.*] By the most ancient custom of the faithful both before Christ and since, men use to bless their table and meats by the hand and word of a Priest, if any be present, otherwise by such as can conveniently do it. And in husbandmen’s houses where they have no other means, they should at least bless God's gifts and themselves with a *Pater noster* <note>The Lord's Prayer</note> or the sign of the Cross: not only to acknowledge from whom they have their continual sustenance, but also to bless their meat and sanctify it. For the
<margin>Blessing of the table or of meats, especially by a Priest.</margin>
<margin>with thanksgiving <note>original: "μετὰ εὐχαριστίας"</note></margin>
Greek word used by Saint Paul, by Ecclesiastical use, when it concerns meats, signifies not only thanksgiving, but blessing or sanctifying the creatures <note>In this context, "creatures" refers to created things, like food</note> to be received, as being all one with *blessing* <note>original: "εὐλογία" (eulogia)</note>, and in English we call it grace, not only after meat, which is only thanks to God, but before meat, which is always a benediction of the creatures, as it is plain in the prescribed and usual forms of grace. For which cause a Priest should ever do it rather than a layman or any of inferior order in the Clergy. In so much that Saint Jerome (Epistle 85) reprehendeth certain Deacons whom he saw say grace or bless the meat and the company in the presence of a Priest. Who also records (in
<margin>To blesse is a preeminence of the better person.</margin>
the life of Saint Paul the holy Eremite) the great courtesy and humility of him and Saint Anthony, yielding one to the other the preeminence of blessing their poor dinner. For to bless is a great thing, and a Priestly prerogative, as the Apostle witnesses, declaring the
<margin>Hebrews 7.</margin>
preeminence of Melchizedek in that he blessed Abraham. Read the note following.

*2 Peter 1.*
</margin>
5. *Sanctified.* All creatures are created by God; none come from the Devil or any other source, as the Manicheans <note>A sect that believed physical matter was inherently evil and created by a malevolent god</note> blasphemously claimed. Therefore, no creature is evil, abominable, or unclean by its nature or condition; all are good and made for human use, though not all are equally holy or sanctified. God made seven days, but he sanctified only one of them. He made all places, but he sanctified only the Temple and similar things dedicated to his service—such as the Ark, the altar, and the rest. These were holy themselves because of their sacred use, and they also gave holiness and sanctification to things that touched them or were applied to them. So our Savior says that the Temple sanctified the gold, and the altar the gift <note>original: Matthew 23:17-19</note>, and generally all creatures set apart from common and worldly use for religion and the worship of God are made sacred by that purpose. Thus, the places and days where God appeared or performed special wonders or benefits for the people were holy, such as Bethel and Sinai. Even more holy are those times and places related to Christ’s Birth, Passion, burial, Resurrection, and Ascension. This is so clear a case that even the mountain where he was transfigured is called by St. Peter *the holy mount.*

<margin>
Creatures hallowed by the sign of the Cross.
</margin>
<margin>
The blessing of our food and the power it has.
</margin>
<margin>
*It is hallowed* <note>original: "ἁγιάζε- ται"</note>
</margin>
Therefore, these are holy memories and monuments of all sorts that have been sanctified. Additionally, creatures (as we see here) are also sanctified by the word of God and prayer—that is, by blessing and calling upon our Lord's holy name over them, especially by the sign of the Cross, as St. Chrysostom notes on this passage <note>original: "Homily 12 on 1 Timothy"</note>. By this blessing, the power of Satan—who unjustly seizes God’s creatures because of human sin and seeks to harm the human body or soul—is driven out, and the food is purified and made healthy. St. Gregory <note>original: "Book 1, Dialogues, chapter 4"</note> records that a devil entered a certain religious woman because she ate a piece of lettuce without blessing it. And St. Augustine <note>original: "City of God, book 18, chapter 18"</note> shows at length how the Devil uses food, drink, and other common creatures of God to harm people, though his power is much less than it was before Christ. Yet he still desires to bother the faithful by abusing the things most necessary to them, hurting them both physically and spiritually. As a remedy, this sanctification the Apostle speaks of is very powerful. It applies not only to the common blessing of our food and drink, but much more (as the specific Greek word used by the Apostle for sanctification implies) to the more precise hallowing and higher dedication of certain creatures, blessing them for Christ’s honor in the Church and for human spiritual and physical benefit.

<margin>
Holy bread.
</margin>
<margin>
*Augustine, epistles 31, 34, 35, 36.*
</margin>
For as St. Augustine writes <note>original: "On the merits and forgiveness of sins, book 2, chapter 26"</note>, besides the usual blessing of our daily food, the catechumens <note>Students preparing for Baptism</note> are sanctified by the sign of the Cross. He says the bread they receive, though it is not the body of Christ, is holy—more holy than the usual bread on the table. He means a kind of bread hallowed specifically for those not yet admitted to the Blessed Sacrament. This is either the same as or similar to the "holy bread" <note>The *eulogia* or *pain bénit*, blessed bread distributed after Mass but distinct from the Eucharist</note> used in the Church of England and France on Sundays. It was a common custom in the early Church to bless loaves and send them as sacred tokens from one Christian to another. This was not done just among the simple or superstitious (as our opponents might imagine), but among the holiest, most learned, and wisest. St. Paulinus sent such hallowed breads to St. Augustine and Alipius, and they sent them back to him, calling them "blessings." Read St. Jerome in his *Life of Hilarion* to see how princes, learned bishops, and others of all sorts came to that holy man for "blessed bread" <note>original: "panem benedictum"</note>. In the early Church, people commonly brought bread to the priests to be hallowed <note>original: "Author of the Imperfect Work, Homily 14 on Matthew"</note>. The Third Council of Carthage <note>original: "chapter 24"</note> mentions the blessing of milk, honey, grapes, and grain. See also the 4th Canon of the Apostles. Not only are various other creatures used at certain times in the Church service—such as wax, fire, palms, and ashes—but also holy oil, Chrism, and the water of Baptism are sanctified. Most importantly, the bread and wine in the high Sacrifice are sanctified, for without sanctification—and as St. Augustine affirms <note>original: "Tractate 118 on John"</note>, without the sign of the Cross—none of these things can be done rightly.

<margin>
The sign of the cross used in blessing.
</margin>
<margin>
The Church’s exorcisms.
</margin>
<margin>
Holy water.
</margin>
<margin>
*Luke 9.*
</margin>
Can anyone now wonder that the Church of God, following St. Paul’s words as explained by the long practice and tradition of the early Church fathers, uses different elements and blesses them for human use and God's service? By calling on Christ’s name, the Church expels the enemy's power from them, according to the authority given by Christ: *Over all demons* <note>original: "Super omnia demonia," Luke 9:1</note>. This is done through prayer, which, as the Apostle says here, implies a desire for help through Christ’s power to fight the Devil and expel him from God's creatures. This is done through holy exorcism, which always begins with: "Our help is in the name of the Lord" <note>original: "Adiutorium nostrum in nomine Domini"</note>, as we see in the blessing of holy water and similar sanctifications. Regarding these exorcisms—specifically those for children before they come to Baptism—see St. Augustine <note>original: "Against Julian, book 6, chapter 5; On Ecclesiastical Dogmas, chapter 31; and On Marriage and Desire, book 1, chapter 20"</note>. As for holy water, it has been used for 1,400 years in the Church, established by Alexander I <note>Pope from c. 107 to 115 AD</note> in all Christian countries. For its power against devils, see a famous account in Eusebius <note>original: "History, book 5, chapter 21"</note> and in Epiphanius <note>original: "Heresy 30, Against the Ebionites"</note>. See also St. Gregory’s letter to St. Augustine (our Apostle to the English) about using holy water to hallow pagan temples so they could become Churches of Christ <note>original: "recorded in Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English People, book 1, chapter 30"</note>. Remember how the Prophet Elisha <note>original: "Eliseus"</note> used salt to heal and purify the waters <note>original: "4 Kings 2," which is 2 Kings 2 in modern Bibles</note>, and how the Angel...

<summary>This page provides a theological defense of the practice of "sanctifying" physical objects, such as holy water, bread, and oil, through prayer and the sign of the cross. It argues that while all of God's creation is inherently good, specific items can be set apart for holy use to drive out demonic influence and benefit the faithful.</summary>

<margin>
Theodoret, Book 3, Chapter 3.
</margin>
<margin>
The power of Psalmody.
Sanctified creatures.
