</margin>
The Angel Raphael used the liver of the fish to drive away the Devil, *Tobit 6:8*; consider how David’s harp kept the evil spirit from Saul, *1 Kings 16* <note>In modern Bibles, this is 1 Samuel 16. Older translations grouped Samuel and Kings together as 1-4 Kings</note>; how a piece of the holy earth saved a man’s chamber from the infestation of Devils, *Augustine, The City of God, Book 22, Chapter 8*; how Christ himself, both in Sacraments and outside of them, used various sanctified elements, some for the health of the body, some for grace and remission of sins, and some to work miracles. See in St. Jerome’s work against Vigilantius, chapter 2, how holy Relics torment them <note>referring to demons</note>. In the history of Julian the Apostate <note>The Roman Emperor who attempted to revive paganism</note>, see how the sign of the Cross; and in the Acts (chapter 19), how the name of JESUS and even the name of Paul puts them to flight.

<margin>
James chapter 5.
</margin>
<margin>
Remission of venial sins attached to creatures.
St. Gregory.
</margin>
Furnish yourselves with such examples and grounds from the Scriptures and antiquity, and you shall despise the Adversaries' <note>The Protestant Reformers</note> quibbles and blasphemies against the Church’s practice in such things. Furthermore, you will find that these sacred actions and creatures do not only purge the impurity of our souls and procure remission of our daily infirmities by increasing faith, fervor, and devotion, but that the chief Ministers of Christ’s Church, by their sovereign authority granted by our Lord, may join to the same their blessing and remission of our venial sins <note>Lesser sins that do not fully separate a soul from God's grace</note> or spiritual debts. As we see in St. James, the remission of all sins is annexed to the anointing with holy oil, which to Catholics is a Sacrament, but to the Protestants was but a temporary ceremony, and to some of them not even of Christ’s institution, but only of the Apostles'. In their low view of creatures <note>The material world</note>, they should not marvel that such spiritual effects should proceed from the use of sanctified creatures, whereas venial trespasses are remitted in many ways, though mortal sins are ordinarily remitted by the Sacraments only. St. Gregory commonly sent his blessing and remission of sins in and with such holy tokens as were sanctified by his blessing and the touching of the Apostles' bodies and Martyrs' Relics, as his successors do now in the like hallowed remembrance of religion. See his 7th book, epistle 126; and 9th book, epistle 60. Thus, therefore, and for the effects aforesaid, the creatures of God are sanctified.

<margin>
The difference between the Church’s exorcisms and other conjurations.
</margin>
If any man objects that this use of creatures is like conjuration in Necromancy <note>Sorcery or communication with the dead</note>, he must know the difference: in the Church’s sanctifications and exorcisms, the Devils are commanded, forced, and tormented by Christ’s word and by prayers; but in the other wicked practices, they are pleased, honored, and entered into covenant with. Therefore, the first is godly and according to the Scriptures, but Necromancy is abominable and against the Scriptures.

<margin>
Grace given in the Sacrament of Orders.
</margin>
14. **The grace.** St. Augustine declares this grace to be the gift of the Holy Ghost given unto him by receiving this holy Order, whereby he was made fit to execute the office to his own salvation and that of other men. And note also that grace is not only given in or with the Sacraments by the receiver's faith or devotion, but by the Sacrament itself, *by imposition* <note>original Latin: "per impositionem"</note>, *by imposition of hands*, for so he speaks in *2 Timothy 1*, which is here said, *with imposition.*

<margin>
Consecration of Priests by imposition of hands.
</margin>
14. **With imposition.** St. Ambrose, upon this place, implies in the word *Imposition of hands* the holy action and sacred words done and spoken over him when he was made a Priest. Whereby (he says) he was designated to the work and received authority, so that he dared to offer sacrifice in our Lord’s stead unto God. Thus does the holy Doctor allude to the words that are said now also in the Catholic Church to him that is made a Priest: *Receive the power to offer for the living and the dead in the name of the Lord.* <note>original Latin: "Accipe potestatem offerendi pro vivis & mortuis in nomine Domini."</note> For this same reason, St. Jerome also (as is noted before) says that the ordaining of Priests is done by the imposition of hands and the invocation of the voice <note>original: "imprecation of voice." In this context, imprecation means a formal spoken prayer or calling down of blessing.</note>.

<margin>
In Isaiah chapter 58.
Council of Carthage IV, chapter 3.
Beza on chapter 6 of Acts.
</margin>
<margin>
Holy Orders a Sacrament.
</margin>
14. **Of Priesthood.** The practice of the Church gives us the sense of this place, which the ancient Council of Carthage sets down thus: "When a Priest takes orders, the Bishop blessing him and holding his hand upon his head, let all the Priests present lay also their hands on his head by the Bishop’s hands," etc. Who does not see now that holy Orders, giving grace by an external ceremony and work, is a Sacrament? So all the old Church counts it. And St. Augustine (*Against the Letter of Parmenian, Book 2, chapter 13*) plainly says that no man doubts but it is a Sacrament. And lest any man think that he does not use the word "Sacrament" properly and precisely, he joins it in nature and name with Baptism. Again, who does not see by this use of imposition of hands in giving Orders and other Sacraments that Christ, the Apostles, and the Church may borrow certain convenient ceremonies and Sacramental actions from the Jewish rites? For this same practice (as even the Heretics cannot deny) was received from the manner of Ordaining Aaron and the Priests of the old law or other heads of the people. See *Exodus 39* and *Numbers 27:23*.

<margin>
Men also are called saviors without derogation to Christ.
</margin>
16. **Save both thy self.** Though Christ is our only Savior, yet the Scriptures do not refrain from speaking freely and in common language <note>original: "vulgarly"</note> and in a true sense, that a man also may save himself and others. But the Protestants, notwithstanding this, follow such a captive kind of Divinity that if a man speaks any such thing of our Lady <note>The Virgin Mary</note> or any Saint in heaven, or any other means of procuring salvation, they make it a derogation to Christ’s honor. We have to deal with such hypocrites nowadays.

<margin>Ambrose on this passage. Luke 2:37.</margin>
<margin>widowhood.</margin>
3. *widows indeed.*] Saint Ambrose calls them widows and desolate indeed who might marry, but to make themselves better and more worthy of God, they refuse marriage—which they know to be blessed but once—imitating * holy Anne <note>Saint Anne the Prophetess, mentioned in Luke 2</note>, who served God night and day with fasting and prayers, never knowing more than one husband. Such professed widows, then, are to be honored and supported. Neither does he speak only of the Church’s widows (of whom he speaks specifically afterward) but of all who by profession kept their widowhood, exhorting them to spend their time in prayer and fasting (verse 5). This was an honorable and holy state much written about and commended in the early Church, namely by Saint Ambrose and Saint Augustine, who wrote books titled after it and ranked it next to virginity. *Ambrose, On Widows. Augustine, On the Good of Widowhood.* <note>original: "Ambr. de viduis. August. de bono viduitatis."</note>

8. *He has denied.*] Not that by this or any other deadly sin (except for unbelief or doubt in belief) they lose their faith: but that their actions are not consistent with their faith and with the Christian religion, which prescribes all such duties.

<margin>widows called Deaconesses and their office.</margin>
9. *Let a widow be chosen.*] Now he speaks more particularly and specifically of such widows as were maintained and supported by the offerings of the faithful and the alms of the Church. These widows also performed some necessary services for women who were to be confessed or baptized—for their instruction and preparation for that and other Sacraments—and also cared for the sick and the weak. Furthermore, they sometimes had charge of Church property or its distribution under the Deacons: because of this, they and those like them are called *Deaconesses* <note>original: "Diaconiſſæ"</note>. Eusebius (Book 6, Chapter 35) records from the Epistle of Cornelius that in the Church of Rome there is one Bishop, 46 Priests, seven Deacons, seven Subdeacons, 42 Acolytes, 52 Exorcists, Readers, and Doorkeepers, and 1,500 widows together with the poor, all of whom God nourishes in His Church. See *Acts of the Apostles, chapter 6*. Saint Chrysostom (Book 3, *On the Priesthood*, near the end). Saint Epiphanius (in *Heresy 79 of the Collyridians*). Now then, what kind of women should be taken into the fellowship of those supported by the Church, he further declares.

<margin>3, 2. 1 Corinthians 7:39. 1 Timothy 5:10.</margin>
<margin>These widows must have had but one husband: from which similar conclusions are deduced. 1 2 3</margin>
9. *the wife of one husband.*] If you wish to see a plain pattern of heretical fraud, corruption, and the distortion of the natural sense of God’s word—and an invincible demonstration that these new Commentators <note>A jab at Protestant reformers</note> have their consciences seared and hearts hardened, willingly perverting the Scriptures against what they know to be the meaning, for the maintenance of their sects—mark well their handling of this place regarding these widows of the Church. Saint Paul prescribes that only those be admitted who have been the wives of one husband—that is to say, married only once—not admitting any who have been twice married. By these words, Catholics prove, first: that the similar phrase used earlier regarding Bishops and Deacons (that they should be the husbands of one wife) must necessarily mean that they cannot be twice married, nor admitted to these and similar functions if they were married more than once before. Secondly, we prove by this passage against our adversaries that the state of widowhood is more worthy, honorable, decent, and pure in respect to the service of the Church, and more deserving of relief from its revenues, than the state of married folks. This is not only (as the adversaries may answer) because of their greater necessity, or more leisure, freedom, or speed to serve since they are not encumbered with a husband and household, but in respect to their widowly continence, chastity, and purity. Otherwise, those who were widows with the intention and freedom to marry afterward might have been admitted by the Apostle just as well as those who were never to marry again.

Thirdly, we prove that second marriage—not only after admission to the alms or service of the Church, but even before—is unsuitable and a sign of lack of restraint or more lust and fleshiness than is agreeable or comely for any person belonging to the Church: and consequently, that the

<meta>This page continues the commentary on 1 Timothy 5, specifically addressing the qualifications for widows and the discipline of the clergy. It transitions from the general requirements for widows to a sharp defense of clerical celibacy and the permanence of religious vows, contrasting Catholic tradition with Protestant interpretations.</meta>

<page-num>580</page-num>
<header>THE FIRST EPISTLE OF ST. PAUL CHAPTER 5.</header>

The Apostle, in the last chapter, treated the holy functions of Bishops, Priests, and Deacons, and the Church’s general refusal of <term>bigamos</term> <note>original: "bigamos"; refers to those who have been married twice</note> or twice-married persons. He must therefore mean, even more strongly, that no man who has been married twice should be received into Holy Orders. Furthermore, just as no women were admitted to be widows of the Church if they ever intended to marry again, so no one should ever be received to minister the Sacraments—which is a far greater thing and requires more purity and <term>continency</term> <note>self-restraint, specifically refraining from sexual relations</note> than the office or state of the said widows—if they intended to marry again. To receive the body of Christ (says St. Jerome in his *Apology for the books against Jovinian, epistle 50, chapter 6*) is a greater and holier thing than prayer; therefore, Priests, who must both pray continually and be occupied with receiving or administering the Holy Sacrament daily, must live continently.

<margin>4</margin>
Fourthly, we prove that it is not unlawful to attach—by precept or the party’s promise—a single life or chastity to a whole state or order of the faithful. This is because the Apostle and the entire Church in his time attached perpetual <term>continency</term> to the state of the Church’s widows.

<margin>5</margin>
Fifthly, we prove by this that refusing to accept the twice-married, or those who will not live a single life, into the state of widowhood or Holy Orders is not "condemning or forbidding marriage" (or once and often marrying) in the manner of the <term>Manichees</term> <note>an early Christian dualist sect that viewed marriage and procreation as evil</note> according to the "doctrine of devils." The Protestants (and before them the old, condemned <term>Jovinianists</term> <note>followers of Jovinian, a 4th-century monk who argued that virginity was not superior to marriage</note>) blaspheme the Church with this claim. If that were true, then St. Paul himself allowed and taught the "doctrine of devils," for he refuses a twice-married woman and binds others, by their entry into this state, never to marry again—as he undoubtedly did even more strictly for the Clergy in the third chapter before this. Thus, we Catholics compare and consider the Scriptures, and for this meaning, we have the support of all the Church <term>Doctors</term> <note>authoritative theologians of the Church</note> without exception. What shift or excuse do the Heretics have then? For they insist they must marry and remarry, even if the Scriptures and all the Doctors in the world say no to it. In truth, they do not explain the word of God, but flee from the evidence of it, some going one way and some another.

<margin>The Calvinists’ most absurd explanation of the Apostle’s words.</margin>
<margin>Their blasphemy against the plain text.</margin>
<margin>Beza on this passage.</margin>
And of all others, their most extreme and shameful evasion is the claim that the Apostle here does *not* forbid the admission of widows who have been twice married, but only those who have had two husbands *at the same time*. This was a very improbable and forced explanation before, when they applied it to Bishops and Deacons in chapter 3; as St. Jerome says (Epistle 83), "a bad wedge for a hard knot" <note>original Latin: "malo nodo malus cuneus"; a proverb meaning a harsh solution for a difficult problem</note>. But here, to suggest that an exception was made only against widows who had two husbands at once (a thing that was never lawful nor ever heard of) is a most intolerable impudence. It is a construction that never entered the mind of any wise man before. Yet these fancies of theirs must be called "God’s word," and <term>bigamus</term> or <term>bigamia</term> must, against their original nature and the usage of all writers, be made identical with <term>Polygamus</term> and <term>Polygamia</term> <note>having multiple spouses at once</note>. They give an example of such widows being women justly divorced from their husbands under the old Law. As though St. Paul here were only making rules for Jewish widows, or as if that had been such a common case among the Jews that the Apostle needed to make such careful rules for it! Finally, they do not hesitate to say that if the Apostle were understood to refuse a widow married twice at different times, it would be unreasonable and injurious to second marriages, which they claim have no more indecency or sign of <term>incontinency</term> than the first. Thus bold they are with the Apostle and all antiquity.

<margin>to grow wanton <note>original Greek: καταστρηνιᾶν (katastrenian)</note></margin>
11. *Wanton in Christ.*] Widows growing warm, idle, and well-fed by the Church, lust after husbands—just as Apostate-Priests and "Superintendents" <note>a term used by some Reformers for Bishops</note> marry, especially after they have obtained good Church livings. This is to "wax wanton" in Christ, or against Christ: <note>original Greek: καταστρηνιᾶν (katastrenian)</note>. The Greek word signifies casting off the reins or the bridle—that is, the bond or promise of <term>continency</term> which they had taken upon themselves.

<margin>The very will to break the vow of chastity is damnable.</margin>
11. *They will.*] Regarding the chastity of widowhood or Virginity, St. Augustine says (in *The Good of Widowhood*, chapter 9) that the excellence of a greater gift is sought. Once this gift has been desired, chosen, and offered to God by a vow, it is not only damnable to actually enter into marriage afterward, but even to have the *will* to marry is damnable.

<margin>judgment <note>original Greek: κρῖμα (krima)</note></margin>
12. *Having damnation.*] This does not mean mere blame, a check, or the reprimand of men—as some would have it to make the fault seem smaller—but judgment or eternal damnation <note>original Greek: κρῖμα (krima)</note>, which is a heavy sentence. God grant all married Priests and Religious may consider their lamentable case. To see what a grievous sin it is, see St. Ambrose’s *To a Lapsed Virgin*, chapters 5 and 8.

<margin>Breaking their "first faith" is (by the consent of all antiquity) when they break their vow of chastity.</margin>
12. *Their first faith.*] All the ancient fathers who ever wrote commentaries on this Epistle, both Greek and Latin—such as St. Chrysostom, Theodoret, Oecumenius, Theophylactus, Primasius, St. Ambrose, Venerable Bede, Haimo, Anselm, and the rest—and all others who occasionally use this passage—such as the 4th Council of Carthage (chapter 104), the 4th Council of Toledo (chapter 55), St. Athanasius (*On Virginity*), St. Epiphanius (*Heresy 48*), St. Jerome (*Against Jovinian*, book 1, chapter 7), and St. Augustine in exceedingly many places—all these explain the Apostle's words as referring to the vow of Chastity or the faith and promise made to Christ to live continently. "What is it to break their first faith?" asks St. Augustine. "They vowed, and performed it not" (on Psalm 75). Again in another place: "They break their first faith, who do not stand by that which they vowed" (*On Holy Virginity*, chapter 33). Again, he and all the fathers with him in the Council of Carthage named before: "If any widows, however young they were left by their deceased husbands, have vowed themselves to God, left their secular clothing, and under the testimony of the Bishop and Church have appeared in religious habit, and afterward go again to secular marriage, according to the Apostle’s sentence..."

<summary>This page presents a vigorous defense of the Catholic requirement for clerical celibacy and the permanence of religious vows for widows, refuting Protestant "Calvinist" interpretations through extensive citations of Church Fathers and Councils.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on 1 Timothy 5, focusing on verses 12 through 15. It defends the Catholic position that "the first faith" mentioned by St. Paul refers to a vow of chastity rather than baptismal faith, and argues that breaking such a vow to marry constitutes a spiritual betrayal.</meta>

<header>CHAPTER 5. TO TIMOTHY.</header>

they shall be sentenced to damnation, because they were so bold as to void the faith or promise of Chastity which they vowed to our Lord. So says he and 215 more fathers in that Council.

<margin>Why this vow is called faith or fidelity.</margin>
And this promise of chastity is called "faith" because the fidelity between married persons is ordinarily called "faith" by holy writers; and the vow of chastity made to God joins Him and the persons so vowing, as if in a marriage, so much so that if the said persons break their promise, they are counted and called in the last-cited Council "God’s adulterers." In the 3rd chapter to the Romans, and often elsewhere, "faith" is used to mean a promise or fidelity. And that it is used that way here, the words *irritum facere* <note>original: "irritum facere"; to frustrate or make void</note> prove, for that term is commonly used in matters of vows, promises, or contracts. *Genesis 17, Numbers 30.*

<margin>Why it is called the "first faith."</margin>
This promise is called here "the first faith" <note>original: *prima fides*</note> in respect to the later promise which vow-breakers make to those with whom they pretend to marry. So says St. Augustine in his book *On the Good of Widowhood, chapters 8 and 9*, and Pope Innocent I in his second epistle, chapter 13, volume 1 of the Councils. And this is the only natural, evident, and agreeable sense according to the context of the text.

<margin>The heretics' interpretation of this "first faith" is impossible and against the text.</margin>
And the empty excuse of the <term>Heretics</term> <note>Referring to Protestant reformers like Luther and Calvin who rejected monastic vows.</note> to save <term>Apostate</term> <note>An "apostate" is someone who has abandoned their religious vows or faith.</note> monks, friars, nuns, and priests from damnation for their pretended marriages is frivolous: namely, their claim that "first faith" here signifies the faith of Baptism or Christian belief, and not the promise or vow of Chastity. But we ask them if this baptismal faith is broken by marriage or not. For the text is plain that by intending to marry, they break their faith, and by breaking their faith they are damned, if they die without repentance. In truth, whichever way they twist themselves to defend their sacrilege or pretended marriages, they lose their labor and struggle against their own conscience and the plain Scripture.

<margin>$\star$ otherwise written to Geruchia, epistle 31.</margin>
<margin>St. Paul does not mean that widows who have already taken vows should marry.</margin>
<margin>It is better for the frailer sort, who are in danger of falling, to marry rather than to vow.</margin>
<margin>Young women may be accepted into religious life.</margin>
**14.** *I will the younger.*] He speaks of such young ones as were yet free. For those who had already made a vow could not marry without damnation, whether they were young or old, nor could he without sin command or counsel them to do it. Neither (as St. Jerome proves to $\star$ Gerontia <note>likely referring to Geruchia, a widow Jerome advised</note>, and St. Chrysostom on this passage) does he strictly command or counsel the young ones who were free to marry, or absolutely forbid them to vow chastity: "God forbid," they say. Rather, his speech contains only a wise admonition to the frailer sort, that it would be far better for them not to have vowed at all, but to have married again, than to have fallen into adultery and apostasy after their profession. This is nothing more than preferring a second marriage over <term>fornication</term> <note>sexual relations outside of marriage</note>; it is a good warning that those who are about to take a vow should look carefully at what they are doing. St. Paul’s experience with the fall of some young women into marriage caused him to give this admonition here: as also his previous rule that none should be received to the Church's alms under sixty years of age. He was not forbidding the Church forever from accepting any vows of widows or virgins until that age, as the heretics falsely affirm; rather, he was showing what was appropriate for that time and the beginning of Christianity, when there were as yet no monasteries built, no prescribed rule, and no exact order of obedience to Superiors. Instead, the professed (as St. Paul notes here) ran and wandered up and down idly—which our professed virgins or Nuns do not, and cannot, do today. Therefore, where discipline is observed, there is no cause for such danger. Besides, widows who have had the use of physical intimacy before are more dangerously tempted than virgins who are brought up from their tender age in piety and have no experience of such pleasures. See St. Ambrose in his book *On Widows*, proving by the example of holy Anna (who lived as a widow from her youth until eighty years of age in fasting and praying night and day) that the Apostle does not here, without exception, forbid all young widows from vowing; indeed, he esteems that profession in younger women as much more laudable, glorious, and meritorious. See the beginning of his book *On Widows*.

<margin>1 Corinthians 7.</margin>
<margin>To marry after the vow of Chastity is to follow Satan.</margin>
**15.** *After Satan.*] We may learn here that for those who have taken vows to marry is to turn back after Satan. For he speaks of such as were married contrary to their vow. And because of this, we call the Religious who marry (such as Luther, Bucer, Peter Martyr, and the rest) "Apostates." Furthermore, we learn that such young people have no excuse based on their age, or the fact that they are strongly tempted and "burn" in their desires, or that they do not have the gift of Chastity. For notwithstanding all these excuses, if these widows who have taken vows marry, they go backward after Satan, and are Apostates, and are damned, unless they repent. As for the Apostle’s words to the Corinthians, *It is better to marry than to burn*, we have previously explained this using the Church Fathers, and we add here that it pertains only to persons who are free and have not vowed to the contrary. St. Ambrose, St. Augustine, and St. Jerome all explain it this way.

<margin>The heretics' only remedy against desire is marriage.</margin>
The heretics of our time think there is no remedy for fornication or "burning" desire but marriage. St. Augustine thought so too when he was still a Manichee. "I thought," he says in Book 6 of his *Confessions*, chapter 11, "that I would be an unhappy and miserable man if I lacked the company of a woman; and the medicine of Your mercy to heal that same infirmity I did not think upon, because I had not tried it. I imagined that <term>continency</term> <note>refraining from sexual relations</note> was within a man’s own power and liberty, which I did not feel in myself; being so foolish as not to understand that no man can be continent unless You [give it]..."

give it; Truly you would give it, if with inward mourning I would knock at your ears, and with sound faith would cast my care upon you.

<margin>The vow of chastity is lawful, possible to be kept, and more pleasing to God.</margin>
By all which you may easily prove that chastity is a thing that may lawfully be vowed, that it is not impossible to be fulfilled by prayer, fasting, and the disciplining of human desires, and that it is a thing more pleasing to God than the condition of married persons: for otherwise it should not be required either in the <term>Clergy</term> <note>The body of people ordained for religious duties</note> or in the <term>Religious</term> <note>Those living under monastic vows</note>. Finally, it is most abominable to persuade poor virgins or others who have professed these vows to enter such sacrilegious marriages, which St. Augustine asserts is worse than adultery. *On the Good of Widowhood, chapter 11.*

<margin>Jovinian’s heresy in this point, condemned of old, is called by the Protestants "God’s word."</margin>
<term>Jovinian</term> <note>A 4th-century monk who opposed the idea that virginity was spiritually superior to marriage</note> was the first that ever made marriage equal with virginity or a chaste life, for which he was condemned of heresy. *Augustine in the argument of the book On the Good of Marriage; On the Merit and Forgiveness of Sins, book 3, chapter 7; On Heresies, heresy 82.* He was the first that persuaded professed virgins to marry, which St. Augustine says was so clearly and without question wicked that it could never infect any Priest, but only certain miserable Nuns. Indeed, for this strange persuasion he calls Jovinian a monster, saying of him thus in *Retractations, book 2, chapter 22*: "The holy Church that is there (at Rome) most faithfully and stoutly resisted this monster." St. Jerome calls the said Heretic and his accomplices <note>original: "Christianos Epicuros"</note> "Christian epicureans." *Against Jovinian, book 2, chapter 19.* See St. Ambrose’s *Epistle 82 to the Bishop of Vercelli*, at the beginning. But what would these holy doctors have said if they had lived in our sorrowful time, when the Protestants go quite away with this wickedness and call it God’s word?

<margin>Many good and worthy Bishops exist who do not have the gift of preaching and teaching.</margin>
17. **In word and doctrine.]** Such Priests especially, and <term>Prelates</term> <note>High-ranking clergy such as Bishops</note>, are worthy of "double honor"—that is, of more ample respect and support—who are able to preach and teach, and who labor therein. Here we may note that all good Bishops or Priests in those days were not as well able to teach as some others, and yet for the ministry of the Sacraments, and for wisdom and leadership, they were not unfit to be Bishops and Pastors. For though it is a high commendation in a Prelate to be able to teach, as the Apostle noted before, yet all cannot have the same grace in it, and it is often compensated by other singular gifts no less necessary. St. Augustine labored in "word and doctrine," but Alipius and Valerius were good Bishops and yet did not have that gift. *Possidius in the Life of Augustine, chapter 5.* And sometimes certain countries require preachers more than others. We note all this to expose the pride of <term>Heretics</term> <note>Here referring to the Reformers</note> who despise some of the Catholic Priests or Bishops, pretending that they cannot preach as they do with "meretricious" <note>showy or insincere</note> and painted eloquence.

23. **Water.]** You see how lawful and how holy a thing it is to fast from certain foods or drinks, either on certain days or always, as this Blessed Bishop Timothy did; he was hardly persuaded by the Apostle to drink a little wine with his water in respect of his illnesses. And mark as well what a slanderous and stale trick it is to say that abstaining from certain foods and drinks for the discipline of the body or for devotion is to "condemn God’s creatures." See a homily of St. Chrysostom upon these words, volume 5.

# ANNOTATIONS
## CHAPTER 6.

4. **Languishing.**] Even these are the typical disputes of our new Sect-masters <note>Referring to Protestant reformers</note>, and the world has for too long experienced the inconveniences named here, which are the fruits of such endless arguments in religion as these unhappy sects have brought forth.

<margin>The "Deposit" is the Catholic truth descending from the Apostles by the succession of Bishops, even unto the end.</margin>
<margin>The Protestants can show no such "Deposit."</margin>
20. **Depositum.** <note>The "Deposit of Faith"</note>] The whole doctrine of our Christianity, being taught by the Apostles and delivered to their successors, and coming down from one Bishop to another, is called the *Depositum*, as if it were a thing laid into their hands and committed to them to keep. Because it passes from hand to hand, from age to age, from Bishop to Bishop without corruption, change, or alteration, it is one and the same as Tradition; it is the truth given to the holy Bishops to keep, and not to laypeople. See the notable discourse of Vincent of Lérins <note>A 5th-century monk and theologian famous for his definition of "Catholic" as that which has been believed everywhere, always, and by all</note> upon this text in his *Book against the profane novelties of heresies* <note>original: "li. cont. profan. har. Nouationes"</note>. It is because of this great, old, and known treasure committed to the Bishops' custody that St. Irenaeus calls the Catholic Church the "rich treasury" <note>original: "Depositorium diues"</note> of truth (*Book 3, Chapter 4*). And as Clement of Alexandria writes in his second book of the *Stromata* <note>original: "li. 2 Strom."</note>, this passage makes so much of a case against all Heretics—who all change this *Deposit*—that for this reason alone, such men in his days denied this Epistle. The Heretics of our days also claim the truth and say it is the "old truth," but they leap over fourteen or fifteen hundred years of history to reach the Apostles. But we call for the *Deposit*, and ask them in whose hands that truth which they pretend to have was laid up, and how it came down to them. For it cannot be Apostolic unless it was a *Deposit* in some Timothy's hand, continuing from one Bishop to another until our time and to the end.

20. **Profane novelties.**] "He did not say ANTIQUITIES," says Vincent of Lérins; "he did not say ANCIENTNESS; but PROFANE NOVELTIES. For if novelty is to be avoided, antiquity is to be kept; if novelty is profane, ancientness is holy and sacred." <note>original: "Non dixit antiquitates... non dixit vetustates, sed prophanas nouitates. Nam si vitanda est nouitas, tenenda est antiquitas: si prophana est nouitas, sacrata est vetustas."</note> See his whole book against the profane novelties of heresies.

<margin>How profane novelties of words are to be tried and examined.</margin>
We should not measure the newness or oldness of words and terms used in religion by the holy Scriptures alone—as though all those, and only those, were new and to be rejected that are not expressly found in holy writ. Rather, we must evaluate them by their agreement or disagreement with the true sense of the Scriptures, the form of Catholic faith and doctrine, the phrasing of the ancient Christians, the Apostolic use of speech come to us by tradition of all ages and Churches, and the decrees of holy Councils and Schools of the Christian world. These bodies have provided (according to the time and questions raised by heretics and contentious persons) very fitting, precise, and significant words to discern and defend the truth against falsehood.

<margin>Catholic terms not expressly in the Scriptures, but in sense, are not "novelties" of words.</margin>
These terms—*Catholic, Trinity, Person, Sacrament, Incarnation, Mass*, and many more—are not (in the sense wherein the Church uses them) in the Scriptures at all. Several of them were spoken by the Apostles before any part of the New Testament was written, and some were taken up immediately after the Apostles' days in the writings and preachings of holy Doctors and in the speech of all faithful people; therefore, they cannot be counted as "Novelties of words." Others besides these, such as *Consubstantial, Mother of God* <note>original: "Deipara"</note>, *Transubstantiation*, and the like, are neither found in express terms in Scriptures, nor yet in sense, if we should follow the judgment of the specific sects against which those words were first invented. For instance, the Arians cried out against the Council of Nicaea for the first term; the Nestorians against the Council of Ephesus for the second; and the Lutherans and Calvinists against the Lateran and later Councils for the third. Nevertheless, these words—by the judgment of the holy Church and approved Councils—are found to be consistent with God’s word and made authentic among the faithful. They are sound and true words, and not the kind the Apostle calls "Novelties."

<margin>Heretical novelties of words.</margin>
The words forbidden here are the new profane terms and speeches invented or specifically used by heretics. St. Irenaeus records that the Valentinians had a number of most monstrous ones, as did the Manichees, as can be seen in St. Augustine. The Arians had their <margin>* Of similar substance. <note>original: "ὁμοιούσιος" (homoiousios)</note></margin> "Similar substance" and claimed Christ was "from things that do not exist" <note>original: "ex non existentibus"</note>. Other heretics after those days had their <margin>* Christ-bearer. <note>original: "Χριστοτόκος" (christotokos)</note></margin> "Christ-bearer," and such like, agreeable to their sects. But the

<margin>The Protestants' profane novelties of words.</margin>
Protestants surpass all in this kind, as they exceed most heretics in the number of new opinions. These include their *Slave-will* <note>original: "Seruum arbitrium," the idea that humans lack free will in salvation</note>, their *sole faith*, their *assurance* <note>original: "fiduce"</note>, their *apprehension of Christ’s justice*, and their *imputative righteousness* <note>The doctrine that God merely "credits" righteousness to a sinner without changing them</note>. They use horrible terms like *terrors, anguishes, distresses, distrust, fears, and the feeling of hell pains* in the soul of our Savior to express their blasphemous fiction of his temporary damnation, which they call his *descending to hell*. They use terms like *marks, tokens, and sacramental badges*, or *Companation, Impanation, Circumpanation* <note>Theological theories that Christ is present "with" or "inside" the bread, rather than the bread actually becoming his body</note>, to avoid the true conversion of the Eucharist. They speak of his *presence in figure, in faith, sign, spirit, pledge, effect.*

<meta>catchword: effect.</meta>

<summary>This page defines the "Deposit of Faith" as a sacred tradition preserved by a succession of bishops and critiques the use of "profane novelties" in religious language. It argues that while Catholic terms like "Trinity" are not in the Bible's literal text, they are valid, whereas Protestant theological terms are rejected as dangerous innovations.</summary>

effect, to avoid the real presence of Christ's body. These and such like innumerable terms which they occupy in every part of their false doctrine, are in the sense that they use them, all false, captious, and deceitful words, and are **"novelties of words"** <note>original: "novitates vocum"</note> here forbidden.

<margin>Catholics must abhor heretical phrases and words.</margin>
<margin>Psalm 132.</margin>
And though some of the said terms have been by some occasion mentioned in passing <note>original: "obiter"</note> without ill meaning spoken by Catholics before these Heretics arose, yet now knowing them to be the proper speeches of Heretics, Christian men are bound to avoid them. In this, the Church of God has ever been as diligent to resist novelties of words as her adversaries are busy to invent them. For this cause she will not have us communicate with them, nor follow their fashion and phrase newly invented, though in the nature of the words sometimes there be no harm. In St. Augustine’s days when Christian men had any good befallen them, or entered into any man’s house, or met any friend by the way, they used always to say, **"Thanks be to God"** <note>original: "Deo gratias"</note>. The Donatists and Circumcellions <note>Schismatic and violent extremist groups in 4th-century North Africa</note> of that time being fond of new things, forsook the old phrase and would always say, **"Praise be to God"** <note>original: "Laus Deo"</note>: from which the Catholic men did so abhor (as the said Doctor writes) that they would as soon meet a thief as one that said to them, "Praise be to God," instead of "Thanks be to God." As now we Catholics must not say, *The Lord*, but, *Our Lord*: as we say, *Our Lady*, for his mother, not, *The Lady*. Let us keep our forefathers' words, and we shall easily keep our old and true faith that we had from the first Christians. Let them say, *Amendment*, *abstinence*, *the Lord's Supper*, *the Communion table*, *Elders*, *Ministers*, *Superintendent* <note>A term used by some Reformers to replace the office or title of "Bishop"</note>, *Congregation*, so be it, *praise ye the Lord*, *Morning-Prayer*, *Evening-prayer*, and the rest, as they will: Let us avoid those novelties of words, according to the Apostle's prescription, and keep the old terms: *Penance*, *Fasting*, *Priest*, *Church*, *Bishop*, *Mass*, *Matins*, *Evensong*, *the Blessed Sacrament*, *Altar*, *Oblation* <note>An offering to God</note>, *Host*, *Sacrifice*, *Alleluia*, *Amen*, *Lent*, *Palm Sunday*, *Christmas*; and the very words will bring us to the faith of our first Apostles, and condemn these new apostates' new faith and phrases.

<margin>Heretics arrogate knowledge falsely so called.</margin>
20. **Falsely called knowledge.**] It is the property of all Heretics to claim for themselves great knowledge, and to condemn the simplicity of their fathers, the holy Doctors, and the Church. But the Apostle calls their pretended skill a "knowledge falsely so called," being in truth high and deep blindness. Such (says St. Irenaeus, **Book 5, chapter 17**) *as forsake the preaching of the Church, argue the holy Priests of unskillfulness, not considering how far more worth a religious simple person is than a blasphemous and impudent sophister, such as all Heretics be.* And again, Vincent of Lérins <note>A 5th-century monk known for his writings on the preservation of Catholic tradition</note> speaking in the person of Heretics says, *Come, O you foolish and miserable men, that are commonly called Catholics, and learn the true faith which has been hidden for many ages heretofore, but is revealed and shown of late, etc.* See his whole book concerning these matters.

---

# THE ARGUMENT OF THE
## SECOND EPISTLE OF ST. PAUL
### TO TIMOTHY.

<image-desc>Ornate decorative woodcut initial 'T' featuring foliage and a small landscape scene within a square frame.</image-desc>
*The chief scope of this second letter to Timothy is to open unto him that his martyrdom is at hand. Which yet he does not state plainly before the end: preparing first his mind with much circumstance, because he knew it would grieve him sorely, and also might be a temptation unto him. Therefore he talks of the cause of his trouble, and of the reward: that the one is honorable, and the other most glorious: and exhorts him to be constant in the faith, to be ready always to suffer for it, to fulfill his ministry to the end, as he himself now had done his.*

*By this it is certain that it was written at Rome, during his last apprehension and imprisonment there: as he signifies by these words in Chapter 1: "Onesiphorus was not ashamed of my chain, but when he was come to Rome, carefully sought me," etc. And of his martyrdom, thus: "For I am now ready to be offered, and the time of my resolution (or death) is at hand" in Chapter 4.*

### ANNOTATIONS
#### CHAP. I.

<margin>A great blessing, to have Catholic progenitors: and very commendable to cleave fast to their faith.</margin>
**5. *In thy grandmother.***] Though God show mercy to many that be of incredulous, heretical or ill parents, yet it is a goodly benediction of God to have good education and to have good faithful progenitors and Catholic parents. And it is a great sin to forsake the faith of our fathers that be Catholics, or contrary to our education in the Church to follow strange doctrines, abandoning not only our next natural parents' faith, but the ancient faith and belief of all our progenitors for many hundred years together. And if it to follow the faith of mother and grandmother only, the Christian religion being then but newly planted, was so commendable even in a Bishop, how much more is it now laudable to cleave fast to the faith of so many our progenitors and ages that continued in the same Christian religion which they first received?

<margin>Citations: Polycarp against the Ephesians, book 1. 8. <note>original: "pol. con. eff. li. 1. 8."</note></margin>
<margin>Deuteronomy 32. Psalm 43.</margin>
<margin>Acts 24. 1 Corinthians 11.</margin>
<margin>The people's speech of their fathers' faith, is very Christian and laudable.</margin>
Our Protestants in their great wisdom laugh at good simple men when they talk of their fathers' faith. But St. Jerome, *I am a Christian*, saith he, *and born of Christian parents, and carry the sign of the cross in my forehead.* And again epistle 65. chapter 3. *Until this day the Christian world hath been without this doctrine. That faith will I hold fast being an old man, wherein I was born a child.* And the holy Scriptures set us often to school to our fathers. *Ask thy fathers, and they will show thee, thy ancestors, and they will tell thee.* And again, *Our fathers have showed unto us.* And commonly the true God is called the God of the faithful and of their forefathers. *Daniel 2. 3.* And false Gods and new doctrines or opinions be named, *New and fresh, such as their fathers worshipped not. Deuteronomy 32.* Finally St. Paul both here and * often else alleges for his defense and commendation, that he was of faithful progenitors. And it is a case that Heretics cannot lightly brag of, no one sect commonly during so long without intermission, that they can have many progenitors of the said sect. Which is a demonstration that their faith is not true, and that it is impossible our Catholic faith to be false, supposing the Christian religion to be true.

<margin>All our good deeds are laid up with God, to be rewarded</margin>
**12. *Deposit.*** <note>original: "Depofitum."</note>] A great comfort to all Christians, that every of their good deeds and sufferings for Christ, and all the worldly losses sustained for confession of their faith, be extant with God, and kept as a **deposit** <note>original: "depofitum"</note>, to be repaid or received again in heaven. Which if the worldlings believed or considered, they would not so much marvel to see Catholic men so willingly to lose land, liberty, credit, life and all for Christ's sake and the Church's faith.

**13. *A form.***] The Apostles did set down a platform of faith, doctrine, and phrase of Catholic speech and preaching, and that not so much by writing (as here we see) as by word of mouth: to which he refers Timothy over and above his Epistles unto him. And how precisely Chris-

<margin>We must speak in Catholic terms, according to a certain rule of faith and form of words.</margin>
<margin>* Augustine, Book 10 of *The City of God*, chapter 23: Philosophers speak with freedom of words, etc., but we must speak according to a certain rule, lest a licentious liberty of words breeds an impious opinion of the things that are also signified by the same.</margin>
Christian Doctors <note>In this context, "Doctors" refers to learned teachers and theologians of the Church.</note> ought to keep the form of words anciently appropriated to the mysteries and matters of our religion, as Saint Augustine expresses in these words in Book 10 of *The City of God*, chapter 23. * **Trinity**, **person**, **essence**, **Consubstantial**, **Transubstantiation**, **Mass**, **Sacrament**, and such like, are <term>sound words</term> <note>original Latin: "verba sana"</note> (as the Apostle speaks), given to express certain high truths in religion. These were given partly by the Apostles and first founders of our religion under Christ, and partly very aptly invented by holy Councils and Fathers to express as nearly as possible the high, <term>ineffable</term> <note>too great or extreme to be expressed or described in words</note> or unspeakable truth of some points. This was done to stop the audacity of heretics and their invention of new words and profane speech in such things, which the Apostle warns Timothy to avoid (1 Timothy 6:20 and 2 Timothy 2:16). See the annotations there.

# ANNOTATIONS
## CHAPTER II.

<margin>What secular affairs do not agree nor consist with the function of spiritual men.</margin> 4. *No man being a soldier.*] First of all, the Apostle (1 Corinthians 7) makes marriage and the necessary cares, anxiety, and distractions ever depending upon it, special impediments for all such as should employ themselves wholly to God's service, as Bishops and Priests are bound to do. *He that is with a wife (he says) is careful for the world, how to please his wife, and is distracted or divided.* <note>Reference to 1 Corinthians 7:33.</note>

Secondly, the practice of medicine, trade, or any other profane faculty and way of life to gather riches—and much more to be given to hunting, hawking, gambling, shows, interludes <note>early theatrical plays</note>, or similar pastimes—is forbidden here.

<margin>How spiritual men may serve secular Princes, and deal in civil causes.</margin> <margin>Luke 12.</margin> Thirdly, the services of Princes and various lowly offices done for them to obtain dignities and promotions are disagreeable to Priestly functions; however, it is not so to be their chaplains for the purpose of preaching to them, hearing their confessions, administering the Sacraments to them, saying Divine service before them, and such other spiritual duties. For all such services done to principal persons, both of the Clergy and Laity, are godly and consistent with the Priestly vocation. As also is the serving of Princes and Commonwealths in civil causes and matters of state, for the purpose of making peace and quietness

<margin>Catholics only, right handlers of the Scripture.</margin>
<margin>2 Corinthians 2 and 4.</margin>
15. *Rightly.*] The Scriptures or claim of the word of God is common to Catholics and Heretics, but all is in the handling of them. These latter handle them guilefully, adulterating the word of God, as elsewhere the Apostle speaketh: the other sincerely after the manner of the Apostles and doctors of God's Church. Which the Greek expresses by a significant word of cutting a thing straight by a line, *orthotomounta* <note>original Greek: "ὀρθοτομοῦντα," meaning to cut straight or handle correctly</note>.

<margin>Heretical books and sermons are to be avoided.</margin>
17. *Their speech.*] The speeches, preachings, and writings of Heretics be pestiferous <note>dangerous or disease-spreading</note>, contagious, and creeping like a canker <note>a spreading sore or gangrene</note>. Therefore Christian men must never hear their sermons nor read their books. For such men have a popular way of talk whereby the unlearned, and especially women laden with sin, are easily beguiled. *Nothing is so easy (says Saint Jerome) as with a voluble and rolling tongue to deceive the rude people, which admire whatsoever they understand not. Letter 2 to Nepotian, chapter 10. <note>original Latin: "Ep. 2. ad Nepot. c. 10."</note>*

<margin>Who are out of the Church or within it.</margin>
20. *In a great house*] He means not that Hymenaeus and Philetus (of whom he spoke immediately before) or other heretics, be properly within the Church, as Catholic men are, though grievous sinners: but that evil men who for the punishment of their sins become heretics, were before they fell from their faith as vessels of contumely <note>dishonor or insult</note>, within the Church. Yes, and often also after they be severed in heart and in the sight of God, so long as they stand in external profession and use of the same Sacraments, and in the outward fellowship of Catholics, not yet either separated of themselves, nor cast out by the governors of the Church, so long (we say) they be after a sort in the Church: though properly and in deed they be out of the compass of God's house. Many of those that are openly severed in Sacraments, Service, and communion, there is no question but they are out of the Church.

<margin>Free will.</margin>
21. *Cleanse himself.*] Man then hath free will to make himself a vessel of salvation or damnation: though salvation be attributed to God's mercy principally, the other to his just judgment: neither of both being repugnant to our free will, but working with and by the same, all such effects in us as to his providence and our deserts be agreeable.

<margin>number 3.</margin>
2. *Men shall be.*] All these words Saint Cyprian explains as referring to such as by pride and disobedience resist God's Priests. Let no faithful man, he says, who keeps in mind our Lord's and the Apostles' admonition, marvel if he sees in the latter times some proud and stubborn fellows and the enemies of God's Priests, go out of the Church or attack the same: when both our Lord and the Apostle foretold us that such should be. *Cyprian, Epistle 55.*

<margin>Women easily seduced by heresy.</margin>
6. *Women loaded.*] Women loaded with sins are, because of such their deservings and through the frailty of their sex, more subject to the heretics' deceits than men: the enemy attempting (as he did in the fall of our first parents) by them to overthrow men. See Saint Jerome upon the 3rd chapter of Jeremiah. Where he adds that every heresy is first broached *for the sake of the gullet and the belly* <note>original Latin: "propter gulam & ventrem"</note>, meaning for gluttony and belly-cheer.

<margin>The folly of Heretics in time appears.</margin>
9. *Folly manifest.*] All heretics in the beginning seem to have some show of truth, God—for the just punishment of men's sins—permitting them for some while in some persons and places to prevail: but in short time God detects them, and opens the eyes of men to see their deceits: so much so that after the first brunt they are maintained by force only, all wise men in a manner seeing their falsehood, though for fear of troubling the state of such commonwealths where unluckily they have been received, they cannot be so suddenly rooted out <note>original: "extirped"</note>.

<margin>Persecution.</margin>
12. *All that will live.*] All holy men suffer one kind of persecution or other, being grieved and molested by the wicked, one way or another: but not all that suffer persecution are holy, such as all criminals <note>original: "malefactors"</note>. The Church and Catholic Princes persecute heretics, and are persecuted by them again, as Saint Augustine often declares. *See Epistle 48.*

<margin>The great profit of reading the Scriptures.</margin>
16. *All Scripture.*] Besides the Apostles' teaching and tradition, the reading of holy Scriptures is a great defense and help to the faithful, and especially to a Bishop—not only to avoid and condemn all heresies, but for the guiding of a man in all justice <note>meaning righteousness or moral uprightness</note>, good life, and works. This commendation is not given here to the books of the New Testament only (of which he does not speak here, as a great part was not yet written) but also to the Scripture of the Old Testament, and indeed to every book within it. For there is not one of them, nor any part of them, that is not profitable for the aforementioned purpose, if it be read and understood according to the same Spirit with which it was written.

<margin>The Heretics' foolish argument: "All Scripture is profitable, therefore only Scripture is necessary and sufficient."</margin>
The Heretics <note>Referring to Protestant reformers who held the doctrine of *Sola Scriptura* or "Scripture Alone"</note>, based on this commendation of holy Scriptures, pretend (quite simply, in truth) that therefore nothing is necessary for justice and salvation except the Scriptures. This is as if everything that is profitable or necessary for a certain result excluded all other help, and was sufficient on its own to achieve it. By that logic, a man might just as well prove that the Old Testament was enough, and so exclude the New; or that any one piece of the Old Testament was enough, and thereby exclude the rest. For Paul affirms every Scripture to have the aforementioned uses. They might also see in the very next line before this, that he requires Timothy’s constant perseverance in the doctrine which he had taught him *in addition* to what he had learned out of the Scriptures of the Old Testament. Timothy had read those since his infancy, but could not learn all the mysteries of the Christian religion from them alone. Neither does the Apostle affirm here that he gained his knowledge of Scriptures by reading alone, without the help of masters and teachers—as the adversaries suggest (in order to leave the holy Scriptures to every man's own presumption). Rather, he affirms only that Timothy knew the Scriptures because he had studied them by hearing good readers and teachers, just as Saint Paul himself did under Gamaliel and the like, and as all Christian students do who are trained from their youth in Catholic universities in the study of Divinity <note>theology</note>.

<margin>Isaiah 30:10</margin> **3.** *There shall be a time.*] If ever this time came (as it must needs be that the Apostle foresaw and foretold it), now it is undoubtedly. For the characteristics fall so exactly in every point upon our new Masters <note>Referring to Protestant Reformers</note> and their disciples, that they seem to be portrayed rather than prophesied of. The people are not so fast crying out, *Speak pleasing things* <note>original: "Speake placentia," from the Latin Vulgate</note>, *things that please:* but the Masters are just as fast guaranteeing them to do *pleasing things*.

**8.** *A crown of justice.*] This passage provides a convincing argument for Catholics that all good works done by God’s grace after the first justification <note>The initial movement into a state of grace</note> are truly and properly meritorious, and fully worthy of everlasting life. Based on this, heaven is the due and just stipend <term>stipend|A formal payment or reward for service</term>, crown, or recompense, which God by his justice owes to the persons so working by his grace. For he renders or repays heaven as a just judge, and not only as a merciful giver. And the crown which he pays is not only of mercy or favor or grace, but also of justice. It is his merciful favor and grace that we work well and merit heaven: it is his justice, for those merits, to give us a corresponding crown in heaven. Saint Augustine, upon these words of the Apostle, expresses both points briefly thus:

<margin>It is not from us, but from God's grace, that works are meritorious.</margin>
And when you hear or read anything in the Scriptures that may seem to diminish the value of human works in this case, it is always meant for works considered in their own nature and value, not involving the grace of Christ. It is by this grace—and not by the work in itself—that we have a right to heaven and deserve it worthily. The Apostle in the 6th chapter to the Hebrews more than suggests this, saying these words, *God is not unjust, to forget your work and love which you have showed in his name etc.* It is as though he would say that he would be unjust if he forgot to repay their works.<insert>*</insert>

<margin>Matthew 20.</margin>
<margin>To such good works heaven is due: to say the contrary is to diminish God's grace.</margin>
The parable also of the men sent into the vineyard proves that heaven is our own right, bargained for and worked for, and accordingly paid to us as our hire <term>hire: wages or payment for labor</term> at the day of judgment; for that is "reward" <note>original: *merces* (Latin) and *μισθὸς* (Greek)</note> by which the Scripture so often calls it. It is the goal, the mark, the price, the hire of all striving, running, and laboring, due both by promise and by covenant and as a rightful debt. See a notable passage in Saint Augustine at the end of *Psalm 83*, the beginning of *Psalm 100*, and in his *50 Homilies, homily 14, chapter 2*. See also Saint Cyprian, specifically the latter end of his book *On Works and Almsgiving*; there you shall easily despise the contrary falsehood, which does not so much diminish human works as it does God's grace, which is the cause and ground of all worthiness in human merits. Saint Augustine’s words are these: *Mark that he to whom our Lord gave grace, also has our Lord as his debtor. He found him a giver in the time of mercy; he has him as his debtor in the time of judgment.* <note>original: *In Psalm 100*</note> See that passage and the rest cited here, where he examines and explains the matter at length.

# THE ARGUMENT <note>The "Argument" is a traditional term for a summary or introductory explanation of a book's contents and context.</note> OF THE EPISTLE OF SAINT PAUL TO TITUS.

THAT Titus was a Gentile <note>a non-Jew</note> and not a Jew, and that he was in Saint Paul’s company at least fourteen years after Paul's conversion, if not before, we understand by the Epistle to the Galatians, chapter 2. And that he continued with him to the very end appears in the second epistle to Timothy, chapter 4, where he mentions that he sent him from Rome into Dalmatia, when Paul himself was shortly after to be put to death.

And therefore, although Saint Luke never names him in the *Acts of the Apostles* (nor does he name himself), yet no doubt he includes him generally when he speaks in the first person plural: *Forthwith we sought to go into Macedonia (Acts 16).* For Saint Paul also sent him to Corinth between the writing of his first and second epistles to the Corinthians (which time coincides with Acts 19), by occasion of which he makes much honorable mention of him in the said second epistle, chapters 2 and 7.

<margin>2 Corinthians 8.</margin>
And again <insert>*</insert> he sent him with the same epistle—both times regarding great matters—so that no doubt he was even then a Bishop, and received accordingly by the Corinthians with fear and trembling (2 Corinthians 7:15). But the same is clearer in this epistle to Titus himself (chapter 1:5), where the Apostle says: *For this cause I left thee at Crete, etc.* By these words it is also manifest that this epistle was not written during the history recorded in the *Acts* (since there is no mention there of Saint Paul being in the isle of Crete), but after his release at Rome from his first imprisonment, and before his second or last trouble there, as is evident by these words: *When I shall send to thee Artemas or Tychicus, make haste to come to me to Nicopolis, for there I have determined to winter (Titus 3).*

Therefore, he instructs him (and in him, all Bishops) much like he does Timothy: what qualities he must require in those he shall ordain as priests and Bishops; in what manner to preach and to teach all sorts of people; and to commend good works to them. Finally, he instructs Titus himself to be their example in all goodness.

### ANNOTATIONS CHAPTER 1.

<margin>
Priests must be consecrated by Bishops only.
</margin>
<margin>
The popular election of the Clergy taken away.
</margin>
5. *Ordain Priests.* Though Priests or Bishops may be nominated and elected by Princes, the people, or patrons of places—according to the custom of the time and the diversity of countries and fashions—yet they cannot be ordered and consecrated except by a Bishop who was himself rightly ordered or consecrated before, just as this Titus was by Saint Paul. And here it seems that he did not only consecrate those whom the people had previously elected, but he himself also made the choice of persons, as no mention is made here of any other popular election. Though this was long used in the primitive Church, it was justly taken away for various reasons, especially because of constant riots, partiality, and disorders which Saint Augustine complained of in his time, and other better means for their appointment were established. *See the Council of Laodicea, chapters 12 and 13; Saint Augustine, On Adulterous Marriages, book 2, chapter 20; Letter 110; and Possidius in the Life of Augustine, chapter 8.*

<margin>
The preeminence of a Bishop above a Priest.
</margin>
<margin>
To put no difference between them is the heresy of Aerius.
</margin>
<margin>
Heretical translation.
</margin>
And that the ordaining of Priests or the imposition of hands for that purpose belongs only to Bishops, and to no inferior Priests or other persons, is clear by the Apostolic practice set down in the Scriptures—namely in the Acts, and in the Epistles to Timothy and Titus. And Saint Jerome <note>original: "S. Hierom"</note>, who sometimes seems to say that in the primitive Church there was no great difference between a Bishop and a Priest, yet always excepts the giving of holy Orders, which preeminence he attributes to Bishops only. *Letter 85.* He does the same regarding the confirmation of the baptized by giving them the Holy Ghost through the imposition of hands and holy chrism <note>anointed oil</note>. *Dialogue against the Luciferians, chapter 4.* Note also that Aerius <note>a 4th-century priest who argued bishops and priests were equal</note> was of old condemned for heresy for holding that there was no difference between a Priest and a Bishop. *Epiphanius, Heresy 75; Augustine, Heresy 53.* Finally, note the fraudulent translation used by the Heretics <note>referring to contemporary Protestant translators</note> always, who turn *Priests* (which here is clearly a title of Order and office) into *elders*, saying, *That you ordain Elders.* In our common language, this signifies age and not the Office properly; and they do all this out of hatred for Priests.

<margin>
Bigamists excluded from holy Orders, and the causes thereof.
</margin>
6. *Of one wife.* To what is said regarding the similar words in *1 Timothy 3*, add this testimony of Saint Epiphanius, *Against Heresies, book 3, volume 2,* at the end: >*Holy Priesthood,* he says, *for the most part proceeds from Virgins; and if not from virgins, then from those who live a celibate or single life. But if single and celibate persons do not suffice for the Ministry, it comes from those who abstain from their wives or remain widowers after being married once. For it is not lawful to admit someone who has been married twice <note>The Church often barred "successive bigamists"—men who remarried after a first wife's death—from the priesthood</note> to the Priesthood, etc.*< 
If you wish to see the reasons why bigamy is forbidden to those who are to be Priests and why continence is required of the Clergy, see the same author, *Against Heresies, book 2, volume 1, heresy 59;* Saint Ambrose, *On Duties, book 1, chapter 50,* and on *1 Timothy 3;* Saint Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage, chapter 18;* Saint Jerome, *Letter 50, chapter 5, to Pammachius,* and *Against Jovinian, book 1, chapter 19;* Saint Leo, *Letter 87;* and other ancient authors.

<margin>
The notable men of both Testaments who lived continently from their wives.
</margin>
And if the studious reader examines all antiquity, he shall find that all notable Bishops and Priests of God’s Church have been single or lived in continence from their wives if they were married before entering the Clergy. Such was Saint Paul, who exhorts all men to the same: *1 Corinthians 7:7.* So lived all the Apostles in continence after they followed Christ, as Saint Jerome witnesses, affirming that our Lord loved...

## ANNOTATIONS
### CHAP. III.

<margin>The Life of Augustine, chapter 18. <note>Original: "vit. Aug. c. 18." refers to the biography written by Possidius.</note></margin>
<margin>Who is properly a Heretic, and who is not.</margin>
<margin>Descriptions or marks how to know a Heretic.</margin>
10. *A man that is an Heretic.*] Not every one that errs in religion is a Heretic, but he only that after the Church's determination willfully and stubbornly stands in his false opinion, not yielding to the decree of a Council or the chief Pastors of the Church therein. They (<note>Original: "saith S. Augustine ep. 162." refers to Augustine's 162nd letter.</note> *says Saint Augustine*) *who defend their opinion (though false and perverse) with no stubborn stomach or obstinate heart, especially if it be such as they themselves did not originate through bold presumption, but received from their deceived parents, and do seek the truth warily and carefully, being ready to be reformed if they find it, such are not to be counted among Heretics.* And again, in <note>Original: "li. 18 de Ciuit. c. 51." refers to Augustine's "The City of God," Book 18, Chapter 51.</note> *The City of God:* They that in the Church of Christ have any weak or perverse opinion, if being admonished to be of a sound and right opinion, they resist obstinately, and will not amend their poisonous opinions, but persist in defense of them, are thereby become Heretics, and going forth out of the Church, are counted for enemies that exercise us. Again in <note>Original: "li. 4 de Bapt. cont. Donat. c. 16." refers to Augustine's work "On Baptism against the Donatists," Book 4, Chapter 16.</note> *On Baptism against the Donatists: He is an Heretic that, when the doctrine of the Catholic faith is made plain and manifest unto him, had rather resist it, and choose that which he himself held etc.* And in diverse places he declares that Saint Cyprian, though he held an error, yet was no Heretic, because he would not have defended it after a general Council had declared it to be an error <note>Original: "li. 2 de bapt. c. 4." refers to Augustine's "On Baptism," Book 2, Chapter 4.</note>. So Possidius in the life of Saint Augustine reports how, after the determination of the See Apostolic <note>meaning: The Pope's authority in Rome</note> that Pelagius's opinion was heretical, all men esteemed Pelagius an Heretic, and the Emperor made laws against him as against an Heretic. Again Saint Augustine says, *He is an Heretic in my opinion, that for some temporal commodity, and especially for his glory and leadership, coins or else follows false or new opinions.* <note>Original: "de vtilit. credendi cap. 1." refers to Augustine's "On the Usefulness of Believing," Chapter 1.</note>

<margin>Epistle 52, number 7.</margin>
<margin>The former marks agree to the Protestants.</margin>
<margin>Their books, service, and preaching must be avoided.</margin>
Let our Protestants behold themselves in this glass, and withal let them mark all other properties that old Heretics ever had, and they shall find all definitions and marks of an Heretic to fall upon themselves. And therefore they must not marvel if we warn all Catholic men by the words of the Apostle in this place, to take heed of them, and to shun their preachings, books, assemblies, and companies. Neither need the people be curious to know what they say, much less to confute them: but they must trust God's Church, which does refute and condemn them. And it is enough for them to know that they be condemned, as Saint Augustine notes in the latter end of his book <note>Original: "de heręſibus" refers to Augustine's "On Heresies."</note> *On Heresies*. And Saint Cyprian says notably to Antonianus demanding curiously what heresies Novatianus did teach: *No matter, said he, what heresies he has or teaches, when he teaches without, that is to say, outside of the Church.*

<margin>The Church seeks the amendment of the most obstinate Heretics.</margin>
11. *Subverted.*] Heretics be often incorrigible, yet the Church of God ceases not by all means possible to recall them, therefore Saint Augustine says in <note>Original: "ep. 162."</note> *Epistle 162: The Heretic himself though swelling with odious and detestable pride, and mad with the forwardness of wicked contention, as we admonish that he be avoided lest he deceive the weaklings and little ones, so we refuse not by all means possible to seek his amendment and reformation.*

<margin>Heretics cut themselves from the Church.</margin>
11. *By his own judgement.*] Other grievous offenders be separated by excommunication from the communion of Saints and the fellowship of God's Church, by the sentence of their Superiors in the same Church: but Heretics—more miserable and unfortunate than they—run out of the Church of their own accord, and so give sentence against their own souls to damnation.

<meta>This page continues the introduction to the Epistle to the Hebrews. It explains the distinction between Saint Paul’s mission to the Gentiles and Saint Peter’s mission to the Jewish people (the "Circumcision"), and provides a structural overview of the letter's arguments regarding the superiority of Christ's new covenant over the old Law.</meta>

<page-num>602</page-num>

<margin>* Yet was Christ head of the Gentiles also. So likewise was his vicar Saint Peter, notwithstanding his more peculiar Apostleship over the Jews. 2 Timothy 1; 1 Timothy 2; 1 Peter 1; Romans 15; Matthew 15.</margin>

...his Epistles to the Churches and Bishops of the Gentiles. The most likely cause for this is that he was the preacher, Apostle, and Master of the Gentiles. And again, in another place, he says that he himself was appointed the Apostle of the Gentiles, just as Peter was of the Jews (Galatians 2). Only Saint Peter, therefore, writing to the Jews, uses this style: "Peter, an Apostle of JESUS Christ," etc., because he was more peculiarly their Apostle, being the <term>vicar of Christ<note>A title used here to denote Peter's role as the earthly representative or deputy of Christ in leading the Church.</note></term>, who was also himself <margin>*</margin> more specially the <term>minister of the Circumcision<note>A term referring to the Jewish people, who were defined by the ritual of circumcision.</note></term>—that is (as he himself says), "not sent but to the sheep which were lost of the house of Israel" (Matthew 15).

<margin>Hebrews 10; 1 Thessalonians 2:14.</margin>

Saint Paul himself tells us the <term>Argument of the Epistle<note>In this historical context, an "argument" is a summary of the main points and purpose of a piece of writing.</note></term> in two words, calling it <term>verbum solatii<note>Original Latin: "a word of solace."</note></term>, the word of solace and comfort. This is also plain throughout the course of the Epistle, namely in the tenth chapter, verse 32 and following, where he exhorts them to take great comfort and confidence in their many tribulations suffered at the hands of their own countrymen, the Jews—which the Apostle also mentions to the Thessalonians (1 Thessalonians 2:14). Those persecutions from the obstinate, unbelieving Jews, their own countrymen, were one great temptation for them. Another temptation was the persuasive arguments they brought to them from the Scriptures, trying to make them cling to the Law and not believe in JESUS, whom they regarded as a dead man.

And whereas the Jews magnified their Law because of the Prophets, and the Angels by whom it was given, and by Moses, and by their land of promise into which <term>Joshua<note>The original text uses "Iosue," the Latinized form of Joshua, the successor of Moses.</note></term> brought them, and by their father Abraham, and by their <term>Aaronical or Levitical priesthood<note>The traditional Jewish priesthood descended from Aaron and the tribe of Levi.</note></term> and sacrifices, by their Tabernacle, and by their Testament: Paul shows that our Lord JESUS, as the natural son of God, incomparably surpasses the Prophets, the Angels, and Moses. He shows that the Rest or peace which God promised was not in their earthly land, but in heaven; that his <term>figure<note>A "figure" or "type" is a person or event in the Old Testament seen as a foreshadowing of Christ.</note></term> <term>Melchizedek<note>The mysterious priest-king mentioned in Genesis, whom Paul uses as a symbol of Christ's eternal priesthood.</note></term> far surpassed Abraham; and that his priesthood, sacrifice, Tabernacle, and testament far surpassed theirs. In all of this, he often aims at these three marks: to remove the scandal of Christ's death by giving them various good reasons and testimonies for it; to lift their minds from visible and earthly promises (on which the Jews were solely focused) to invisible and heavenly ones; and to suggest that the Ceremonies should now cease, the time of their correction by Christ having now come.

The Epistle may be divided into these parts: the first, concerning Christ’s excellence above the Prophets, Angels, Moses, and Joshua (chapters 1, 2, 3, 4). The second, concerning his priesthood and its excellence above the priesthood of the Old Testament (chapter 5 through the middle of chapter 10). The last part consists of exhortation (chapter 10, verse 9, to the end of the Epistle).

<summary>This page outlines why Saint Paul addressed the Hebrews differently than the Gentiles and provides a theological roadmap of the Epistle, contrasting the temporary Old Law with the eternal superiority of Christ's priesthood.</summary>

# THE EPISTLE
## OF PAUL THE APOSTLE
### TO THE HEBREWS.

<margin>Heretical corruption.</margin>
<margin>* In the English Bible of the year 1579.</margin>
<margin>The Epistle to the Hebrews is Saint Paul’s.</margin>
Let the Christian reader note the corruption and shameless boldness of our <term>adversaries<note>A term used by the Catholic editors of this Bible to refer to Protestant Reformers, who often questioned the traditional authorship of certain books.</note></term>, who—based on a false, private persuasion of their own that Saint Paul was not the author of this Epistle—leave out his name in its title, contrary to the authentic copies in both Greek and Latin. In ancient times, there was some doubt as to who the writer was, but that was back when it was also doubted whether it was <term>Canonical Scripture<note>Books of the Bible officially recognized by the Church as divinely inspired and authoritative.</note></term> at all. Afterward, the whole Church (by which alone we know the true Scriptures from other writings) held it and delivered it, as she does now, to the faithful as Canonical and as Saint Paul’s Epistle. Notwithstanding, the adversaries would have rejected the Epistle as well as they do the Author, except that they falsely imagine certain places in it to work against the <term>Sacrifice of the Mass<note>The central act of worship in Catholic tradition; the editors argue that Protestants only accepted the book because they misinterpreted its verses to support their own theology.</note></term>.

### CHAP. I.

-> *God spoke to their fathers by the Prophets: but to themselves by his own Son, who incomparably surpasses all the Angels.* <-

<margin>1</margin>

The Blessed Sacrament is a figure, and yet the true body.
