3. *The figure.*] To be the figure of his substance signifies nothing else but that which Saint Paul speaks in other words to the Philippians chapter 2, verse 6: that he is the form and most express resemblance of his Father's <term>substance<note>In theology, "substance" refers to the essential nature or underlying reality of something, rather than its outward appearance.</note></term>. So Saint Ambrose and others expound it, and the Greek word *Character* is very significant to that purpose. Note also by this place, that the Son, though he be a figure of his Father's substance, is notwithstanding of the same substance. So Christ's body in the <term>Sacrament<note>Referring to the Eucharist or Holy Communion.</note></term> and his mystical death and sacrifice in the same, though called a figure, image, or representation of Christ's visible body and sacrifice upon the Cross, yet may be and is the selfsame in substance.

<margin>
The adoration of Christ in the Blessed Sacrament.
</margin>
6. *Let all the Angels adore.*] The <term>Heretics<note>The editors' term for Protestant reformers.</note></term> marvel that we adore Christ in the Blessed Sacrament, when they might learn by this place that wherever his person is, there it ought to be adored both by men and Angels. And where they say it was not made present in the Sacrament nor instituted to be adored, we answer that no more was he <term>incarnate<note>Taking on human flesh; becoming man.</note></term> purposely to be adored: but yet straight upon his descending from heaven, it was the duty both of Angels and all other creatures to adore him.

...admonished to come to him with confidence as to a most merciful Mediator and Bishop. But by that argument, they <note>The "Heretics" or reformers mentioned later.</note> might as well take away the help and prayers of the living for one another. And we do not require the help either of the Saints in heaven, or of our brethren on earth, because of any mistrust of God's mercy, but because of our own unworthiness: being assured that the prayer of a righteous man prevails more with him than the desire of a grievous sinner; and the prayers of many making intercession together are more effective than those of one man alone. This the Heretics cannot deny unless they reject the plain Scriptures. Neither do we come less to him, or with less confidence, when we come accompanied by the prayers of Angels, Saints, Priests, or righteous men joining with us, than if we prayed by ourselves alone.

# CHAPTER 5. TO THE HEBREWS.

13 as have need of milk, and not of solid food. † For every one who is a partaker of milk is unskillful in the word of justice: for he is a infant. 14 † But solid food is for the perfect, those who by habit have their senses exercised to the discerning of good and evil.

->ANNOTATIONS<-
->CHAPTER 5.<-

<margin>The description of a Priest, and his office.</margin>
1. **Every high Priest.**] By the description of a Priest or high Priest (for in this context both are the same matter) he proves Christ to be one in the most excellent manner. First then, a Priest must not be an Angel, or of any nature other than human. Secondly, every man is not a Priest, but such a one as is specially chosen out of the rest, and preferred before others of the community, set apart, assumed, and exalted into a higher state and dignity than the common people. Thirdly, the cause and purpose why he is so sequestered and picked out from the rest, is to take charge of Divine things, to deal as a mediator between God and the people, to be the Deputy of men in such things as they have to crave or to receive from God, and to present or give to him again. Fourthly, the most proper and principal part of a Priest's office is, to offer oblations, gifts, and sacrifices to God for the sins of the people: without which kind of most sovereign duties, no person, people, or Commonwealth can belong to God: and which can be done by none, of whatever other dignity or calling he may be in the world, who is not a Priest: as we read in the Scriptures, various Princes were 
<margin>3 Kings 13. 2 Chronicles 26. 1 Kings 13. <note>The book numbering follows the Vulgate; 3 Kings corresponds to 1 Kings in modern Bibles, and 1 Kings to 1 Samuel.</note></margin>
punished by God, and king Saul was deposed from his kingdom, specifically for attempting to do the same.

<margin>The temporal authority of Princes and how far it extends.</margin>
And generally we may learn here, that *in those things which pertain to God* <note>original: "in ys quæ sunt ad Deum"</note>, in all matters touching God, his service, and religion, the Priest alone has charge and authority: just as the temporal Prince is the people's governor, guide, and sovereign in things touching their worldly affairs: which must nonetheless be directed and managed by him in no other way than is agreeable to the due worship and service of God. If the earthly powers commit anything against this, the Priests ought to admonish them on behalf of God.

<margin>There is a peculiar order and calling of Priests of the New Testament.</margin>
We learn also by this, that everyone is not a Priest, and that the people must always have certain persons chosen out from among them to deal in their suits and causes with God, to pray, to minister Sacraments, and to sacrifice for them. And whereas the Protestants <note>The author uses "Protestants" to refer to the Reformers who rejected the sacrificial nature of the Mass.</note> will have no Priest, Priesthood, nor sacrifice, but Christ and his death—pretending these words of the Apostle to be verified only in the Priesthood and Service of the old law, and Christ’s person alone, and after him no others—in this they show themselves to be ignorant of the Scriptures and of the 
<margin>Priests and sacrifice are necessary in the New Testament, and are not derogatory to Christ's priesthood or sacrifice.</margin>
state of the New Testament, and they introduce a plain Atheism and Godlessness into the world. For, so long as man has to do with God, there must necessarily be some deputed and chosen out from among the rest to deal, according to this declaration of the Apostle, in things pertaining to God, and those must be Priests. For otherwise, if men need to deal no more except immediately with Christ, what do they do with their Ministers? Why do they not let every man pray and minister for himself, and to himself? What do they do with Sacraments, seeing Christ’s death is just as sufficient without them as without sacrifice? Why does his death not stand just as well with Sacrifice as with Sacraments: as well with Priesthood as with other Ecclesiastical functions? There is no other cause in the world, but that (Sacrifice being the most principal act of religion that man owes to God, both by his Law and by the law of nature) the Devil, through these his ministers, under the pretense of deferring or attributing more to Christ's death, would abolish it.

<margin>The difference and excellence of Christ's Priesthood.</margin>
This definition of a Priest and his function, with all the properties belonging to it, holds true not only in the law of Moses and the order of Aaron’s Priesthood, but it was true before, in the law of nature, in the Patriarchs, in Melchizedek, and now in Christ, and all his Apostles, and Priests of the New Testament: except that it is a peculiar excellence in Christ that he alone offered for other men's sins, and not at all for his own, as all others do.

<margin>All true priests and preachers must be lawfully called to the office.</margin>
4. **Taketh to him self.**] A special proviso for all Priests, preachers, and such as have to deal for the people in things pertaining to God, that they do not take that honor or office by their own hands, but by lawful calling and consecration, even as Aaron did. By which clause, if you examine Luther, Calvin, Beza, and the like, or if all such as nowadays intrude themselves into sacred functions look into their consciences, great and foul matter of damnation will appear.

<margin>The dignity and function of Priesthood is [passing high]</margin>
5. **Did not glorifie him self.**] The dignity of Priesthood must necessarily be surpassingly high and sovereign, when it was a promotion and preferment in the Son of God himself according to his manhood, and when he would not usurp, nor take the same upon himself, without his father's express...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Hebrews Chapter 5, focusing on Christ’s specific calling as a High Priest according to the order of Melchizedek. # THE EPISTLE OF SAINT PAUL CHAPTER 5.

<margin>The priesthood is not to be usurped.</margin>
...express commission and calling for that purpose. This serves as an eternal example of humility and an argument for the condemnation of all mortal men who unjustly claim for themselves any spiritual office or power that has not been given to them from above, through a lawful calling and the commission of their superiors.

<margin>Christ is both Priest and King: but his Priesthood is the more excellent of the two.</margin>
<margin>Christ is a Priest insofar as he is man, not insofar as he is God.</margin>
<margin>Psalm 2. 109.</margin>
<margin>Retention, page 89.</margin>
6. **A Priest for ever.**] In the 109th Psalm <note>Modern Bibles: Psalm 110</note>, from which this testimony is taken, both Christ's kingdom and Priesthood are set forth. However, the Apostle specifically emphasizes his Priesthood as the more excellent and preeminent state in him, because our Redemption was achieved and accomplished by sacrifice—which was an act of his Priesthood, and not of his kingly power. Although he was properly a king as well (just as Melchizedek was both Priest and King, being a resemblance of Christ in both roles), he was much more a Priest. Our Lord possessed this excellent double dignity from the very first moment of his conception or incarnation, as shown by Saint Paul’s discourse and his references to the Psalms. One must be wary of the wicked heresy of the Arians <note>An early Christian belief that denied the full divinity of Christ</note> and Calvinists (unless in the case of the latter it is an error proceeding from ignorance) who do not hesitate to say that Christ was a Priest, or offered sacrifice, according to his Godhead <note>his divine nature</note>. To say this is to make Christ the Priest of God the Father rather than his Son, and implies he performs sacrifice and homage to the Father as his Lord, rather than being his equal in dignity and nature. Therefore, Saint Augustine says in his commentary on *Psalm 109*: <note>original Latin: "Quod secundum quod homo erat, sacerdos erat: secundum quod Deus, non erat sacerdos."</note> **That insofar as he was man, he was a priest; insofar as he was God, he was not a priest.** And Theodoret <note>A 5th-century theologian</note> says on *Psalm 109*: **As man, he offered sacrifice; but as God, he received sacrifice. And again: Christ, touching upon his humanity, was called a priest, and he offered no other host <term>host: a sacrificial victim or bread</term> but his own body, etc.** (Dialogue 1, near the middle). Some of our "new masters" <note>A derogatory term for Protestant reformers</note>, not knowing this much, allowed the opposite view to fall from their pens; even after being warned of the error and told it was pure Arianism, they persist in it out of mere ignorance of the foundations of Divinity.

<margin>The sacrifice on the Cross was the principal act of Christ's priesthood.</margin>
<margin>Luke 23:46.</margin>
7. **With a strong cry.**] Although our Savior continually makes intercession for us in heaven according to his human nature, he does not perform sacrifice through external physical elements there, nor does he use sacrificial prayers as he did during his mortal life and during his Passion. Most importantly, he did this when he spoke with a loud voice and this prayer: <note>original Latin: "In manus tuas commendo spiritum meum"</note> **"Into your hands I commend my spirit,"** where he voluntarily laid down his soul, yielding it in the most proper way as a sacrifice. For in that final moment of his death consists specifically his high Priestly office, and the very work and completion of our redemption.

<margin>Priests' prayers are more effective.</margin>
<margin>Christ's Priestly actions.</margin>
Observe furthermore that although every faithful person commonly prays for themselves and others and offers their prayers to God, no one offers prayers by virtue of an official role or special appointment in the name of the whole Church and people, except for the Priest. Therefore, a priest's prayers are more effective in themselves because they represent the voice of all faithful men together, offered by one who is appointed and accepted by God as the people’s representative. All of Christ's prayers throughout his life and death were of this kind, as were all his other actions: his fasting, watching, preaching, instituting, and ministering or receiving Sacraments—every one was performed as a Priestly action.

<margin>A notorious Heretical translation used to maintain Calvin's horrible blasphemy.</margin>
<margin><note>original Greek: "ἀπὸ εὐλαβείας"</note></margin>
<margin>Flacius Illyricus on this passage.</margin>
7. **For his reverence.**] These words have been harmfully and most presumptuously corrupted by our English translators <note>Referring to Protestant translations like the Geneva Bible</note>, who turned them into: **"In that which he feared."** This is contrary to the version and sense of all antiquity, and to Erasmus as well, and contrary to the ordinary use of the Greek word, as Beza <note>Theodore Beza, a major Calvinist theologian</note> himself defines it in *Luke 2:25*. It is also contrary to the rules of the Greek phrase, as not only Catholics but even the best-learned Lutherans show and prove with many examples. They follow the singular presumption of Calvin, who was the first (as his fellow Beza confesses) that ever found this interpretation—one which neither Saint Chrysostom nor any other perfect Greek scholars could ever see. To have chosen the sense of that impious and arrogant sectarian over the Church Fathers and all other churches was shameful enough; but to set it down as the very Scripture of God’s blessed word is intolerable and surpasses all impiety. We see plainly that they have no conscience or fairness, but only the purpose of making poor readers believe their opinions are God’s own word, twisting the Scriptures to match their heretical fantasies. If the good reader knew for what specific doctrine they framed this translation, they would abhor them to the depths of Hell. They want this Scripture to mean that Christ was in a horrible fear of damnation, and that he was not only in physical pain on the Cross (which they hold was not sufficient for man's redemption), but that he felt the very sorrows and distress of the damned, with the only difference being that his was not everlasting.

<margin>Calvin's blasphemy that Christ suffered hell's pains on the cross, and that his death would otherwise be insufficient.</margin>
For the sake of this horrible blasphemy (which is their interpretation of Christ's "descending into Hell"), God's holy word must be corrupted. They suggest that the sacrifice of Christ's death (which they talk about so boastfully) was not enough for our redemption unless he was also damned for us in the pains of Hell. Woe to our poor country that must have such books and read such translations. See Calvin and Beza in their commentaries and annotations on this place, and you shall see that they have translated this text specifically to defend these blasphemies. See the earlier annotations on *Acts 2:27* and *Matthew 27:46*.

# CHAPTER 6. TO THE HEBREWS. 611

Christ himself did various things, and now does in heaven, and we ourselves also must use many means for the application of his work to our particular necessities. See the next Annotation.

<margin>Christ's Passion is sufficient for all, but profitable only to those who obey, not by faith alone, but by doing as he and his Church command.</margin>
9. **Was made to all.**] The Protestants, under the pretext of the sufficiency of Christ's Passion and his sole redemption, deceitfully oppose themselves—in the sight of the simple—against the invocation of Saints and their intercession and help for us. They also oppose our penitential works or suffering for our own sins, whether in this life or the next; the merits of fasting, praying, alms, and other things commended to us in Holy Scripture; and most things done in the Church regarding sacrifice, Sacrament, and ceremony. But this passage and many others show that Christ’s Passion—though it is in itself far more sufficient and powerful than the Protestants in their narrowness of understanding can consider—nevertheless benefits no one except those who both do his commandments and use such remedies and means to apply its benefit to themselves as he appoints in his word, or by the Holy Spirit in his Church. And the Heretics who say that faith alone is the thing required to apply Christ’s benefits to us are also easily refuted by this: for we do not obey him only by believing, but by doing whatever he commands. Lastly, we note in these same words that Christ does not appoint men to be partakers of the fruit of his redemption by his absolute and eternal election without any condition or respect for their own works, obedience, or free will: but always with this condition—if men will obey him and do that which he appoints. See Saint Augustine (or Prosper) in the *Response of Prosper, book 2, article 1, to the objections of Vincent* <note>original: "Responſ. Proſperi li. 2. articulo 1 ad obiectiones Vincentij"</note>, where he says regarding the cup of Christ’s passion, *“It has indeed in itself the power to benefit all: but if it be not drunken, it heals not.”*

<margin>The Apostle omits speaking of the Blessed Sacrament as a mystery then too deep for the Jews' capacity.</margin>
11. **Inexplicable.**] Intending to treat more largely and particularly of Christ's or Melchizedek's Priesthood, he forewarns them that the mystery of it far exceeds their capacity. Because of their feebleness in faith and weakness of understanding, he is forced to omit various deep points concerning the Priesthood of the new law. Among these (no doubt) the mystery of the Sacrament and Sacrifice of the altar, called the **MASS**, was a principal and pertinent matter. The Apostles and Fathers of the primitive Church did not usually treat this so largely and particularly in their writings, which might come into the hands of the unfaithful, who—above all things—were quickest to take offense at the Blessed Sacrament, as we see in John 6. He spoke to the Hebrews (says Saint Jerome in Epistle 126) <note>original: "S. Hierom ep 126"</note>, that is, to the Jews and not to faithful men, to whom he might have been bold to utter the Sacrament. And indeed, it was reasonable to talk much to them of that sacrifice which was the resemblance of Christ's death, when they did not even think correctly of Christ's death itself. Our adversaries wickedly abuse the Apostle's wisdom and silence on this matter against the holy Mass.

<margin>The Novatians <note>A 3rd-century sect known for their extreme rigorism, refusing to readmit those who had turned away from the faith under persecution</note> (as all heretics do) made Scripture the ground of their heresy.</margin>

4. *Impossible.*] How difficult the holy Scriptures are, and how dangerously they are read by the unlearned—or by the proud, no matter how well-learned they may be—this one passage might teach us. Here, the Novatians of old stumbled so badly that they thought, and heretically taught, that no one falling into any mortal sin after Baptism could be received to mercy or penance in the Church. Thus, to a contentious man who would follow his own sense, or the bare words without regard for the Church’s understanding and the rule of faith (according to which every Scripture must be interpreted), the Apostle’s speech here seems to sound that way. It is just as it is for the simple-minded or the heretic who does not submit his understanding to the Church’s judgment: certain places in this same Epistle seem, at first sight, to stand against the daily offering or sacrifice of the Mass. And let the good readers be wary here also of the Protestants' exposition, for they are even worse than the Novatians in this matter, especially those who strictly follow Calvin. They impiously hold that it is impossible for one who entirely forsakes his faith—that is, becomes an apostate or a heretic—to be received to penance or to God’s mercy. To establish this false and damnable sense, these men ignore the exposition of St. Ambrose, St. Chrysostom, and the other Fathers, which is the sense held by the Holy Church: That the Apostle is speaking of that penance which is performed before and during Baptism. This is simply to say that it is impossible to be baptized again, and thereby to be renewed and enlightened, to die, be buried, and rise again a second time in Christ through such an easy and perfect penance and cleansing of sins as that first sacrament of generation <note>The Sacrament of Baptism</note> provided. That sacrament applies Christ’s death in such an ample manner to the receivers that it takes away all punishments due for sins committed before it; therefore, it requires no further penance afterward for those prior sins, all being washed away by the power of that Sacrament when it is duly received. St. Augustine calls the remission in Baptism a "great pardon." <note>original Latin: "Magnam indulgentiam"</note> *Enchiridion*, chapter 64.

<margin>The Sacrament of penance is ready for all sinners whatsoever.</margin>
<margin>Jerome, epistle 8 to Demetrias, chapter 6.</margin>
The Apostle, therefore, warns them that if they fall from their faith, and from Christ’s grace and law which they once received in their Baptism, they may not look to have that first great and wide remedy applied to them again, nor may anyone else who sins after Baptism. However, the other form of penance—which is called the "Second plank after shipwreck" <note>A traditional theological term for the Sacrament of Penance, suggesting it is the only way to survive after losing the 'ship' of baptismal grace</note>—is a more painful medicine for sin than Baptism, requiring much fasting, praying, and other bodily afflictions. This remains open not only to other sinners, but to all who have been baptized, whether they be heretics or malicious opponents of the truth, or whatever else, during this life. See St. Cyprian, epistle 52; St. Ambrose on this passage; St. Augustine against the epistle of Parmenian, book 2, chapter 13, and epistle 50; and St. Damascene, book 4, chapter 10.

<margin>God’s justice in rewarding meritorious works.</margin>
10. *God is not unjust.*] It is a sight to see what twisting and writing the Protestants do to shift themselves away from the evidence of these words. These words make it most clear to all who are not blinded by pride and contention that good works are meritorious, and are the very cause of salvation—so much so that God would be unjust if he did not grant heaven for them. "Indeed, it would be a great injustice of God," <note>original Latin: "Reuera grandis iniustitia Dei"</note> says St. Jerome, "if he would only punish sins, and would not receive good works." <note>original Latin: "Si tantum peccata puniret, & bona opera non susciperet"</note> Book 2 against Jovinian, chapter 2.

## ANNOTATIONS
### CHAPTER VII.

1. *Melchizedek.*] The excellence of this person was so great that some of the ancient writers took him to be an angel, and some the Holy Spirit. This opinion is condemned not only by the Hebrews—who claim him to be Shem, the son of Noah—but also by the chief Fathers of the Christians. They do not doubt that he was a mere man, a priest, and a king, whoever he specifically was. For otherwise, he could not have been such a perfect type and resemblance of our Savior in office, order, and sacrifice, as is shown in this chapter and elsewhere.

<margin>The resemblance of Melchizedek to Christ in many points.</margin>
3. *Without father.*] Not that he was literally without a father and mother, says Saint Jerome in <note>original: "ep. 126"</note> Letter 126; for Christ himself was not without a father according to his divinity, nor without a mother in his humanity. Rather, it is because his pedigree is not set out in Genesis, as the genealogy of other Patriarchs is, but he is suddenly introduced into the holy history with no mention made of his stock, tribe, beginning, or ending. Therefore, in that case, he also resembles in a way the Son of God, whose generation was extraordinary, miraculous, and ineffable <note>ineffable: too great or extreme to be expressed or described in words</note> according to both his natures—lacking a father in one and a mother in the other. His person has neither beginning nor ending, and his kingdom and priesthood—especially in himself and in the Church—are eternal, both in respect of the time past and the time to come, as the said Doctor of the Church writes in the same letter.

<margin>By the various excellencies of Melchizedek's priesthood, the excellence of the priesthood and sacrifice of the New Testament is proved.</margin>
4. *Behold.*] To prove that Christ’s priesthood far surpasses the priesthood of Aaron, and that the priesthood of the New Testament surpasses the priesthood of the old law—and consequently that the sacrifice of our Savior and the sacrifice of the Church much excel the sacrifices of Moses' law—the author disputes profoundly regarding the preeminence of Melchizedek above the great Patriarch Abraham, who was the father of the Levites.

<margin>He received tithes from Abraham, and consequently from Levi and Aaron.</margin>
<margin>Tithes.</margin>
4. *Tithes.*] The first preeminence is that Abraham paid tithes—and those of the best and most chief things that he had—unto Melchizedek as a duty and homage. This was not for himself alone in person, but for Levi, who was not yet born, and so for the whole priesthood of Levi’s line, acknowledging thereby Melchizedek not only to be a priest, but *his* priest and superior, and thus superior to all the Levitical order. And it is to be observed here that whereas in the 14th chapter of Genesis, from which this holy narrative is taken, it stands indifferent or doubtful in both the Hebrew and the <note>original: "70"</note> Septuagint whether Melchizedek paid tithes to Abraham or took tithes from him; the Apostle here puts it all out of controversy, plainly declaring that Abraham paid tithes to the other as the inferior to his priest and superior. Regarding the payment of tithes, it is a natural duty that men owe to God in all laws, to be given to his priests on his behalf for their honor and livelihood. Jacob promised or vowed to pay them (Genesis 28); Moses appointed them (Leviticus 27, Numbers 18, Deuteronomy 12, 14, 26); Christ confirms that duty (Matthew 23); and Abraham specifically here gives them to Melchizedek.

<summary>This page argues that Jesus is the perfect and eternal High Priest, fulfilling the prototype of Melchizedek, whose priesthood is shown to be superior to the old Levitical order because even Abraham paid him tithes.</summary>

<page-num>616</page-num>
<header>THE EPISTLE OF ST. PAUL CHAPTER VII.</header>

[Melchi]sedek: plainly thereby approving them <note>tithes</note> or their equivalent to be due to Christ and the Priesthood of the New Testament, much more than either in the Law of Moses, or in the Law of Nature. Regarding these tithes due to the Clergy of Christ’s Church, see *St. Cyprian, letter 66; St. Jerome, letter 1, chapter 7, and letter 2, chapter 5 to Heliodorus and Nepotian; and St. Augustine, sermon 119 on time.*

<margin>He blessed Abraham.</margin>
<margin>Blessing is a great mark of superiority, especially in Priests.</margin>
7. *Is blessed by the superior.*] The second mark of superiority is that Melchizedek blessed Abraham. We see here that St. Paul considers this a great and sovereign holy act, basing our Savior’s prerogative above the entire order of Aaron upon it. We see that in this sense, it is the proper act of the Priesthood; and that without any controversy, as the Apostle says, the person who has the authority to bless is greater in dignity than the person who does not. Therefore, the Priest’s calling is, in this regard, far above any earthly king, who does not have the power to give a blessing in this sacred manner, neither to humans nor to any other creature. Just as Melchizedek did here, so Christ blessed much more, and the Bishops of his Church have done so and continue to do so. No one should wonder that our forefathers esteemed and sought this so highly, if they note the wonderful mystery and grace expressed here. This Patriarch <note>Abraham</note> who here receives a blessing from Melchizedek, also blessed his own sons (though in an inferior way), just as the other Patriarchs did, and as fathers bless their children by that example.

<margin>The full accomplishment of man's redemption was not through Aaron’s priesthood, but through Melchizedek’s.</margin>
11. *If perfection.*] The main proposition of the entire epistle and all the Apostle's discourse is inferred from and grounded upon the previous superiorities of Melchizedek over Abraham and Levi: that is, that the end, perfection, accomplishment, and fulfillment of all human duties and debts to God—by the general redemption, satisfaction, full price, and perfect ransom of all mankind—was not achieved by any or all the Priests of Aaron’s order. It was not achieved by any sacrifice or act of that Priesthood, nor by any part of the Law of Moses (which was grounded upon the Levitical Priesthood), but by Christ and his Priesthood, which follows the order and rite of Melchizedek.

<margin>The Apostle, to disprove the Jews' false belief in Aaron’s Priesthood and sacrifices, speaks entirely about the sacrifice of the Cross.</margin>
11. *What necessity.*] This argument regarding the superiority of Christ’s Priesthood over the Levitical order is directed against the mistaken belief of the Jews, who thought their law, priesthood, and sacrifices were everlasting and sufficient in themselves, without any other Priest besides Aaron and his successors, and without any connection to Christ’s Passion or any other redemption or forgiveness than what their Levitical duties provided. They did not know that these were all figures <note>symbolic previews</note> of Christ’s death, and were to be ended and fulfilled in the same. This point, if well understood and kept in mind, will clarify the entire controversy between Catholics and Protestants regarding the sacrifice of the Church <note>the Mass</note>. For, as the goal of the Apostle’s argument was to affirm the dignity, superiority, necessity, and eternal fruit and effect of Christ’s Passion, he did not need to discuss the other sacrifice at all, which is a sacrifice depending on his Passion. This was especially true when writing to the Hebrews, who needed to be instructed and reformed first regarding the sacrifice of the Cross before they could fruitfully hear anything about the other. However, in a hidden way and by the most evident logical consequence, the learned and faithful may easily perceive the foundation of the said Sacrifice of the Church (which is the Mass). Therefore, *St. Jerome says in letter 126 that all these praises of Melchizedek represent Christ, "whose effects are the sacraments of the Church."* <note>original Latin: "cuius profectus Ecclesiae sacramenta sunt."</note>

<margin>No lawful state of people exists without an external Priesthood.</margin>
12. *Changed.*] Note this passage well, and you shall perceive by it that every lawful form of law, state, or government of God’s people depends on a Priesthood; it rises, stands, falls, or changes along with the Priesthood. In the Law of Nature, the state of the people depended on one kind of Priesthood; in the Law of Moses, another; in the state of Christianity, another. Therefore, in the previous sentence, the Apostle said that the Jewish people or Commonwealth had their law under the Levitical Priesthood; and the Greek expresses the matter more properly: <margin>was established by law <note>original Greek: "nenomothe tēto"</note></margin> meaning they were *legitimated*—that is, made a lawful people or community under God—by the Priesthood. For there is no just or lawful Commonwealth in the world that is not made legal and God’s own property (and distinguished from unlawful Commonwealths that belong to false gods or to none at all) except by a Priesthood.

<margin>External Priesthood is necessary for the state of the New Testament.</margin>
From this, it is clear that the New Law, and all Christian people who follow it, is made lawful by the Priesthood of the New Testament. The Protestants are shamefully deceived, and they deceive others, by wanting Christian Commonwealths to lack an external Priesthood, or by claiming Christ’s death abolished it. For this is a logical proof: if Christ abolished the Priesthood, he abolished the New Law, which is the New Testament and the state of Grace that all Christian Commonwealths live under. Nor would it be true that the Priesthood was "changed" along with the Law if all external Priesthood ended with Christ’s death when the New Law began; for in that case, the Law would not depend on the Priesthood, but would endure after all Priesthood had ended—which is against St. Paul’s doctrine.

<margin>External sacrifice is also necessary for the same.</margin>
Furthermore, it is to be noted that this "legitimation," or the placing of communities under Law and Priesthood (of whatever order), happens in no other way than by joining them together in a single act of external sacrifice, which is the proper work of a Priesthood. For, just as no lawful state can exist without a priesthood, so no priesthood can exist without a sacrifice. And we always mean "Priesthood" and "Sacrifice" taken in their own proper, literal sense, as St. Paul uses them here. For the constitution, difference, alteration, or change of states and laws does not arise from any change of a spiritual or metaphorically understood Priesthood or sacrifice, but from these things in their literal sense, as is most plain.

->Lastly<-

It asserts that just as the Law of Moses required the Levitical priesthood, the Christian "New Law" requires a visible, external priesthood and sacrifice (the Mass) to remain valid.</summary>

<page-num>617</page-num>
<header>CHAPTER VII. TO THE HEBREWS.</header>

<margin>The transfer <note>The author uses "translation" in the sense of a formal transfer or change from one state to another.</note> of the old Priesthood and sacrifices must necessarily lead into the aforementioned Priesthood and sacrifice of the Church.</margin>
Lastly, it follows from this that although Christ truly sacrificed himself upon the Cross (acting there also as a Priest according to the order of Melchizedek) and there achieved the full redemption of the world, confirmed and perfected his compact and Testament, and established the law and priesthood of this his new and eternal state by his blood: yet that <note>the Crucifixion</note> cannot be the specific form of sacrifice into which the old Priesthood and sacrifices were transferred, upon which the Apostle bases the changing of the Law. For all of those <note>Old Testament rites</note> were figures of Christ’s death and effectively ended at his death, yet they were not altered into that specific kind of sacrifice which was to be made only once. That sacrifice was performed in such a way that Christian peoples and nations could not meet often to worship at it, nor have their law and Priests established within it. Nevertheless, for the honor, duty, remembrance, and representation of that event, not only we Christians, but also all faithful people among both Jews and Gentiles, have had their priesthood and sacrifices according to the difference of their states. These kinds of sacrifices were transferred from one into another: and so, without doubt, the Levitical Priesthood is properly turned into the Priesthood and sacrifice of the Church, according to Melchizedek’s rite and Christ’s institution in the forms of bread and wine. See the next note.

<margin>How Christ is a Priest forever.</margin>
<margin>Christ's eternal priesthood consists in the perpetual sacrifice of his body and blood in the Church.</margin>
17. *A Priest forever.*] Christ is not called a Priest forever only because his person is eternal, or because he sits at the right hand of God and perpetually prays or makes intercession for us, or because the effect of his death is everlasting. For all of this does not prove that, in a literal sense, his Priesthood is perpetual. Rather, according to the judgment of all the Church Fathers—based upon this deep and divine discourse of St. Paul, the very nature and definition of Priesthood, the excellent act and order of Melchizedek, and the state of the new law—he is a Priest forever according to Melchizedek's order specifically regarding the sacrifice of his holy body and blood. This was instituted at his last supper and is carried out by his commission, commandment, and perpetual cooperation with his Priests in the forms of bread and wine; for in these things alone did the high Priest Melchizedek sacrifice. Although St. Paul makes no explicit mention of this here because of the depth of the mystery and the lack of faith or the weakness of those to whom he wrote, it is evident in the judgment of all the learned Fathers (without exception) who ever wrote either upon this epistle, or upon the 14th chapter of Genesis, or Psalm 109, or who have treated the sacrifice of the altar, that the eternity and proper act of Christ’s Priesthood—and consequently the unchangeable nature of the new law—consists in the perpetual offering of Christ’s body and blood in the Church.

<margin>The Protestants' quibbling over small words against Melchizedek’s sacrifice and Priesthood is directly against the Apostle.</margin>
This fact is so well known to the adversaries of Christ’s Church and Priesthood, and so admitted, that they are forced to impudently quibble over certain Hebrew particles to claim that Melchizedek did not offer bread and wine. Indeed, when that tactic fails, they plainly deny him to have been a Priest at all—which is to directly contradict the Apostle and overthrow his entire argument. Thus, while these wicked men pretend to defend Christ’s singular Priesthood, they actually abolish, as much as they can, the whole order, office, and state of his eternal law and Priesthood.

<margin>page 126. * That is, from Adam to the end of the world, presented by sacrifice.</margin>
<margin>Christ's eternal Priesthood and sacrifice in the Church is proved from the writings of the Fathers.</margin>
Arnobius says, *By the mystery of bread and wine he was made a Priest forever.* And again, *The eternal memory, by which he gave the food of his body to those who fear him.* (On Psalm 109, 110). Lactantius says, *In the Church he must necessarily have his eternal Priesthood according to the order of Melchizedek.* (Book 14, Institutions). St. Jerome writing to Evagrius says, *Aaron’s Priesthood had an end, but Melchizedek’s—that is, Christ’s and the Church’s—is perpetual,* \* *both for the time past and to come.* St. Chrysostom therefore calls the Church's sacrifice an "indestructible victim" <note>original: *hostiam inconsumptibilem*</note>, a sacrifice that cannot be consumed. (Homily 17 on Hebrews 9). St. Cyprian calls it "a sacrifice which, if taken away, would leave no religion remaining" <note>original: *hostiam qua sublata, nulla esset futura religio*</note>. (On the Lord’s Supper, number 2). Eusebius Emissenus calls it "a perpetual offering and a redemption that flows forever" <note>original: *perpetuam oblationem & perpetuo currentem redemptionem*</note>. (Homily 5 on Easter). And our Savior expresses as much in the very institution of the Blessed Sacrament of his body and blood: especially when he calls the latter kind *the new Testament in his blood*, signifying that just as the old law was established in the blood of beasts, so the new (which is his eternal Testament) should be dedicated and perpetual in his own blood—not only as it was shed on the Cross, but as given in the Chalice. And therefore into this sacrifice of the altar (says St. Augustine, City of God book 17, chapter 20; St. Leo, sermon 8 on the Passion; and the rest) were the old sacrifices to be transferred. See St. Cyprian, letter 63 to Cecil, number 2; St. Ambrose, On the Sacraments, book 5, chapter 4; St. Augustine, On Psalm 33, sermon 2, and City of God book 17, chapter 17; St. Jerome, letter 17 chapter 2 and letter 126; Epiphanius, Heresy 55; Theodoret on Psalm 109; Damascene book 4, chapter 14.

Finally, if any of the Fathers, or all of the Fathers, had either wisdom, grace, or understanding of God’s word and mysteries, this is the truth. If nothing will satisfy our adversaries, may Christ Jesus confound them and defend his eternal Priesthood and the state of his new Testament established within it.

<header>THE EPISTLE OF SAINT PAUL CHAPTER 7.</header>

<margin>The old commandment and the new. Why Maundy Thursday is so called.</margin>
18. *Of the former commandment.* ] The whole law of Moses, containing all their old Priesthood, sacrifice, sacraments, and ceremonies, is called the *Old commandment*: and the New Testament, containing the sacrifice of Christ’s body and blood, and all the sacraments and graces given by the same, is named the *New mandate* <note>Latin: *mandatum*</note>: for which reason our forefathers called the Thursday in Holy Week *Maundy Thursday*, because on that day, the new law and Testament were dedicated in the *Chalice* <note>The cup used in the Eucharist</note> of his blood. The *old mandate*, law, Priesthood, and sacrifices—because they were insufficient and imperfect—were taken away, and this new sacrifice, after the order of Melchizedek, was given in their place.

<margin>The introduction of a new Priesthood.</margin>
19. *The introduction.* ] Always observe that the abolition of the old law is not a total removal of all Priesthood, but an introduction of a new one, containing the hope of eternal things, whereas the old had only temporal ones.

<margin>The eternity of the new Priesthood confirmed by the Father’s oath and Christ’s passion.</margin>
21. *With an oath.* ] This oath signifies the infallible and absolute promise of the eternity of the new Priesthood and the state of the Church. Christ—by his death and blood shed in the sacrifice of the Cross—confirmed it, sealed it, and made himself the surety and pledge of it. For although the **new** Testament was instituted, given, and dedicated at the Last Supper, its warrant, confirmation, and eternal operation were achieved upon the Cross, in the one offering <note>original: "oblation"</note> and one general and everlasting redemption made there.

<margin>By the comparison of many priests and one, it is not meant that there is only one Priest of the New Testament. Isaiah chapter 61. * Priests <note>Greek: *hiereis*</note> * Ministers <note>Greek: *leitourgoi*</note></margin>
23. *Being many.* ] The Protestants, not understanding this passage, foolishly imagine that the Apostle makes this difference between the old state and the new: that in the old, there were many Priests, but in the new, none at all except Christ. This is against the Prophet Isaiah, who specifically prophesied about the Priests of the New Testament (as Saint Jerome declares regarding the same passage) in these words, *You shall be called the Priests of God; it shall be said to you: the ministers of our God.* Furthermore, such an idea takes away all visible Priesthood, and consequently the lawful state that the Church and God’s people have on earth, along with all Sacraments and external worship.

<margin>The meaning is that the absolute sacrifice of eternal redemption could not be performed by those many Aaronical priests but by one only, Christ Jesus: who lives as a Priest forever, has no successor, and—as Chief Priest—works and concurs with all Priests in their priestly functions.</margin>
The Apostle then means, first, that the absolute sacrifice of completion, perfection, and universal redemption was only one, done once, and performed by only one Priest. Therefore, it could not be any of the sacrifices, or all the sacrifices of the Jewish law, or wrought by any or all of them, because they were a great number at once, succeeding one another, each of their offices and functions ending at their death. They could not work such an eternal redemption as was wrought by Christ alone upon the Cross. Secondly, Saint Paul implies thereby that Christ never loses the dignity or practice of his eternal Priesthood through death or otherwise; he never yields it up to anyone and never has successors after him who might enter into his position or right of Priesthood, as Aaron and all others had in the Levitical Priesthood. Instead, he himself works and concurs with his ministers—the Priests of the New Testament—in all their acts of Priesthood, including sacrifice, Sacrament, blessing, preaching, praying, and the like.

This, therefore, was the fault of the Hebrews: they did not acknowledge that their Levitical sacrifices and Priesthood were reformed and perfected by Christ’s sacrifice on the Cross. The Apostle argues only against them, and not against our Priests of the Holy Church or their number, who all confess that their Priesthood and all its exercises depend upon Christ’s only perpetual Priesthood.

27. *This did he once.* ] This is the special preeminence of Christ: he offers for other people’s sins only, having none of his own to offer for, as all other Priests of both the old and new law have. And this, again, is the special dignity of his own person, not shareable with any other of whatever order of Priesthood, that he by his death (which is the only offering declared by the Apostle to be unrepeatable in itself) paid the one full and sufficient ransom for the redemption of all sins.

# CHAPTER 8. TO THE HEBREWS.

<margin>1</margin> Now the main point <note>original: "summe"</note> of the things being said is this: We have such a high priest, who is seated on the right hand of the throne of majesty in the heavens,
<margin>2</margin> <margin>Christ, living and reigning in heaven, continues his priestly function still, and is the minister not of Moses’ holy places and tabernacle, but of his own body and blood, which are the true holy things and tabernacle, formed not by man, but by God’s own hand.</margin> a minister of the holy places <note>original: "Sancta"</note>, and of the true tabernacle, which our Lord pitched <note>meaning: set up or established</note> and not man.

<margin>4</margin> if then he were upon the earth, he would not even be a priest, since there were already those who offered gifts according to the Law,

As it was answered to Moses when he finished the tabernacle: *See* (said he) *that you make all things according to the pattern which was shown to you on the mount.*

<margin>8</margin> <margin>Jeremiah 31, 1.</margin> <margin>The promises and effects of the Law were temporary, but the promises and effects of Christ’s Sacraments in the Church are eternal.</margin> For finding fault with them, he says: *Behold the days shall come, says our Lord: and I will complete for the house of Israel, and for the house of Judah, a new Covenant:*
<margin>9</margin> *not according to the covenant which I made with their fathers on the day that I took their hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt: because they did not continue in my covenant: and I neglected them, says our Lord.*
<margin>10</margin> *For this is the covenant which I will grant to the house of Israel after those days, says our Lord: Putting my laws into their mind, and upon their heart will I write them: and I will be their God, and they shall be my people:*

### ANNOTATIONS
#### CHAPTER 8.

<margin>Theodore Beza’s annotations on the New Testament, Hebrews chapter 7, number 8.</margin> <margin>Christ’s priesthood and sacrifice are external, not spiritual only.</margin> 3. *Necessary that he also.* ] Even now being in heaven, because he is a Bishop and Priest, he must necessarily have something to offer, and a means by which to perform sacrifice. This is not in a spiritual sense only, for that could not make him a Priest of any specific order. And it is most false and wicked to hold with the Calvinists <note>Followers of John Calvin, a leader of the Protestant Reformation</note> that Melchizedek's priesthood was entirely spiritual. For then Christ's death was not a physical, external, visible, and truly named sacrifice; neither could Christ or Melchizedek be a Priest in any way other than how every faithful person is.

### THE EPISTLE OF ST. PAUL CHAPTER 8.

...a faithful man is: which to hold (as the Calvinists following their own doctrine must necessarily do) is directly against the Scriptures, and no less against Christ's one offering <note>original: "oblation"</note> of his body upon the Cross, than it is against the daily sacrifice of his body upon the altar. Therefore he has a certain sacrificial victim <note>original: "host"</note> in an external and proper manner, to make perpetual offering thereby in the Church: for he does not exercise a visible and external act of sacrificing in heaven.

<margin>How Christ’s body is made fit to be sacrificed and eaten perpetually.</margin>
4. **If upon the earth.**] It is by his death, and resurrection to life again, that his body has become apt and fit in such a divine way to be sacrificed perpetually. For if he had lived in a mortal way still, that method of mystical representation—breaking his body and separating the blood from it—could not have been appropriate. And so the Church and Christian people would have lacked a priesthood and sacrifice, and Christ himself would not have been a Priest of a peculiar order, but either must have offered the same things that Aaron’s Priests did, or else have been no Priest at all. For to have offered only spiritually, as all faithful men do, could not be enough for his vocation, and our redemption, and the state of the New Testament. How his flesh was made fit to be offered and eaten in the Blessed Sacrament by his death, see Hesychius <note>Hesychius of Jerusalem, a 5th-century theologian</note> book 1 on Leviticus, chapter 2.

<margin>Kingdom of heaven, and heavenly things, spoken of the Church.</margin>
5. **Heavenly things.**] As the Church or state of the New Testament is commonly called the **Kingdom of Heaven** <note>original: "Regnum cælorum"</note> and **of God** <note>original: "Dei"</note> in the Scriptures, so these heavenly things are likely understood by learned men to be the mysteries of the New Testament. And it seems that the pattern given to Moses to build his tabernacle by was the Church, rather than the heavens themselves: all of St. Paul’s discourse tending to show the difference between the New Testament and the Old, and not to make a comparison between the state of heaven and the Old Law. Though occasionally, because the condition of the New Testament more nearly resembles heaven than the Old state does, he sometimes may speak somewhat of that also.

<margin>Grace, the effect of the new Testament.</margin>
10. **Into their mind.**] This also and the rest following is fulfilled in the Church, and is the proper effect of the New Testament, which is the grace and spirit of love, grafted in the hearts of the faithful by the Holy Ghost, working in the Sacraments and sacrifice of the New Law to that effect.

<margin>The new Testament or covenant between God and man.</margin>
<margin>Luke 22.</margin>
10. **Their God.**] This mutual covenant made between God and the faithful is that which was dedicated and established, first in the chalice of his blood, called therefore **the New Testament in his blood:** and which was straight after ratified by the death of the testator upon the Cross.

<margin>Scriptures abused for fantastical inspirations.</margin>
<margin>Acts 2, 10, 14.</margin>
11. **Shall not teach.**] So it was in the primitive Church, especially among those who were the first founders of our new state in Christ. And that which was verified in the Apostles and other principal men, the Apostle speaks of generally as though it were so in everyone—just as St. Peter applies the like from Joel, and our Savior speaks so when he says that those who believe in him shall work miracles of various kinds. Christian men then must not abuse this place to claim new inspirations and such great knowledge that they need no Scriptures or teaching in this life, as some Heretics do: with much the same reason and appearance of Scripture as the Protestants have for refusing external sacrifice. And it is no less a "fantastical madness" to deny external sacrifice, sacraments, or priesthood, than it is to abolish teaching and preaching.

4 *A golden pot.*] The Protestants consider it superstitious to keep with honor and reverence the holy memories or monuments of God’s benefits and miracles, or the tokens of Christ’s Passion—such as his Cross, garments, or other things belonging to him or his Saints. They think it impossible that such things could last so long, yet they may see here the respectful and long-term preservation of Manna (which naturally rots very quickly), Aaron’s rod (which blossomed by a miracle), and the stone tables of the Covenant. See a notable passage in St. Cyril (Book 6, *Against Julian* <note>original Latin: "cont. Iulian"</note>), where he defends the keeping and honoring of the wood of the Cross on which Christ died against the blasphemies of Julian the Apostate. See also St. Paulinus (Epistle 11), and the reverence St. Jerome and the faithful of his time showed to the tombs of Christ and his Martyrs, and to their relics. *“We reverence and worship,”* he says, *“the tombs of Martyrs everywhere; we place the holy ashes to our eyes, and if we can, we touch them with our mouths. Do some then think that the monument where our Lord was buried should be neglected?”* But our Protestants do not understand this; they would rather...

<meta>This page continues the annotations and commentary on Chapter 9 of the Epistle to the Hebrews. ...rather follow Vigilantius <note>A 4th-century priest who opposed the veneration of relics and saints.</note>, Julian the Apostate <note>The Roman Emperor who famously renounced Christianity and attempted to revive paganism.</note>, and such masters, than the holy Doctors <note>The "Doctors of the Church" are influential ancient theologians recognized for their deep learning.</note> and the clear practice of the Church in all ages.

<margin>Images in Solomon's temple commanded by God.</margin>
### 5. *Cherubim.*] You see it is a foolish thing to conclude from the first or second commandment that there should be no sacred images in the Church. Even among those people who were most prone to idolatry and had limited understanding of spiritual things (such as Angels), and to whom the commandment was specifically given, the same God who forbade them from making carved idols also commanded these images of Angels to be made and placed in the most sovereign and holiest place of the entire Tabernacle and Temple. By this, it is plain that the images of Christ and his Blessed Mother and the Saints—who can be more truly portrayed than purely spiritual beings can—are not contrary to God's commandment, nor against his honor, nor repugnant to any other Scripture at all. Those Scriptures only condemn the idols or portraits of the Heathen made for the adoration of false gods.

<margin>Sacrifice was not taken away by the New Testament, but changed into something better.</margin>
### 10. *Until the time of correction.*] All those coarse and physical sacrifices, ceremonies, and observations were instituted to cleanse and purify the flesh from legal irregularities and impurities only. Because they did not reach the point of purging the souls and consciences of men, and were commanded not forever but until Christ's coming, they ceased then. In their place, better, more powerful, and more spiritual Sacraments were instituted. For we must not imagine that Christ took away the old system and put nothing in its place, or that he only changed the sacraments into other external sacraments without also transforming the sacrifices into something more excellent. For it is called <note>original: "tempus correctionis, non abolitionis sacrificij aut legis"</note> *the time of correction, not of abolishing sacrifice or law.* Nor do they have more reason to claim that Christ’s one offering upon the Cross took away all kinds of sacrifice than to say it took away all kinds of Sacraments. The time and state of the New Testament is not made lawless, without a host <note>meaning a sacrificial victim</note>, or without sacrifice; rather, it is the time of correction, or reformation and improving all the aforementioned things.

<margin>St. Augustine, *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 11.</margin>
<margin>The only sacrifice on the Cross is the redemption of the world, and there is only one Priest (Christ) who is its redeemer.</margin>
### 12. *Eternal redemption.*] No single sacrifice, nor all the sacrifices of the old law combined, could pay that one general price, ransom, and redemption of all mankind and all sins. This was achieved only by the highest Priest, Christ, and the one sacrifice of his blood offered once upon the Cross. This sacrifice of redemption cannot be performed often because Christ could die only once. However, the figures <note>symbolic previews</note> of that sacrifice in the law of nature and the law of Moses were truly called sacrifices. This is especially true of this high and marvelous commemoration of the same event in the Holy Sacrament of the Altar <note>The Mass</note>, according to the rite of the New Testament, which is most truly and uniquely a sacrifice (as St. Augustine calls it). But neither this kind, nor the others from the old law—being repeated often and performed by many priests (all of whom were and are sinners themselves)—could be the general redeeming and fulfilling sacrifice. Nor could any one of those priests, nor all of them together—whether from the Law of Nature, the order of Aaron, or the order of Melchizedek (except Christ alone)—be the general redeemers of the world.

<margin>The Apostle's argument is only against the error of the Jews regarding their sacrifices and priests; the Protestants are misapplying it against the sacrifice of the Mass and the priests of the New Testament.</margin>
And this is the Apostle's meaning in all this comparison and opposition of Christ's death to the old sacrifices, and of Christ to their priests. He does not mean that Christ's death or the sacrifice of the Cross should take away all sacrifices, or prove that those Aaronical offices <note>The duties of the priests descended from Aaron</note> were not true sacrifices, or those priests not truly priests. They were true priests and true sacrifices, though none of those sacrifices were the high, central, and general sacrifice of our price and redemption. None of them, or of those priests, could work anything for God's honor or the forgiveness of sins without looking toward this one sacrifice of Christ's death. The Jews falsely imagined otherwise, not referring their sacrifices to this general redemption and forgiveness by Christ, but thinking them to be absolute sacrifices in themselves. You may read that this was the error of the Hebrews in St. Augustine's <note>original: "li. 3. doct. Christ. c. 6."</note> *On Christian Doctrine, book 3, chapter 6.* This, we tell the Protestants, is the only purpose of the Apostle.

But they are so coarse, or ignorant of the Scriptures, and so maliciously set against the truth of God and the Church, that they perversely and foolishly turn the whole argument against the sacrifice of the Blessed Mass and the priests of the New Testament. They act as though we held that the sacrifice of the altar were the general redemption or the redeeming sacrifice itself, or that it had no relation to Christ's death, or that it were not the representation and most lively resemblance of the same, or were not instituted and performed to apply that other general benefit of Christ's one offering on the Cross to the specific use of those who participate. St. Paul, then, disputes only against the Jews and the false opinion they had of their priests and sacrifices, to which they attributed all forgiveness and redemption without regard for Christ's death.

### 15. *Of those prevarications.*] The Protestants unlearnedly imagine that because all sins are forgiven by the power of Christ's passion, there should be no other sacrifice after his death. However, they might as well say that there ought never to have been any sacrifice appointed by God, either in the Law of Nature or the Law of Moses. All their arguments made against the Sacrifice of the Church based on the Apostle's discourse prove just as well (or rather, only) that there were no sacrifices of Aaron’s order or Levitical law at all. For he disputes against the Jews' false opinion concerning them, and says not a word regarding the sacrifice of the Church, unto which...

# THE EPISTLE OF ST. PAUL CHAPTER IX.

In all this discourse he never opposes Christ’s sacrifice upon the Cross; all Christian men well know that the sacrificial victim <note>The original text uses "host," from the Latin *hostia*, meaning a sacrificial victim.</note> and offering <note>The original text uses "oblation."</note> of those two, though they differ in manner and external form, yet is in truth all one.

The Apostle then shows here plainly that all the sins that were ever remitted since the beginning of the world were not otherwise forgiven except by the force and in respect of Christ’s Passion. Yet it does not follow from that that the offerings of Abel, Abraham, Aaron, etc., were not sacrifices, as the Heretics' <note>The author uses "Heretics" to refer to the Protestant reformers who challenged Catholic doctrine on the Mass.</note> foolish deduction would have it. St. Paul does not oppose Christ’s Passion to them with the intent to prove them to have been no sacrifices, but to prove that they were not *absolute* sacrifices, nor the redeeming or consummating Sacrifice, which could not be many, nor performed by many Priests, but by one, and at one time, by a more excellent Priest than any of them, or any other mere mortal man.

<margin>Calvin’s argument against the sacrifice of the altar makes no less an argument against the sacrifices of the old Law.</margin>
And so that you may see the blasphemous pride and ignorance of Calvin, and in him, of all his fellows: read (as many as are permitted to read Heretical books) his commentary upon this place, and there you shall see him conclude from this that because Christ’s death had force from the beginning and was the remedy for all sins since the creation of the world, therefore there must be no more sacrifices but that one sacrifice of Christ’s death. Which must necessarily, by his deduction, hold true (as it indeed does) no less against the old sacrifices than the new sacrifice of the Church, and so take away all sacrifice, which is against the Apostle’s meaning and all religion.

<margin>The correspondence of words in dedicating both Testaments proves the real presence of blood in the Chalice.</margin>
20. **This is the blood.**] Christ’s death was necessary for the full confirmation, ratification, and accomplishment of the New Testament, though it was begun to be dedicated in the sacrifice of his last supper, being also within the scope of his Passion. This is evident by the words pronounced by Christ over the holy chalice, which are correspondent to the words that were spoken (as the Apostle here declares) in the first sacrifice of the dedication of the old law <note>Referencing Exodus 24:8.</note>, having also express mention of remission of sins thereby, as by the blood of the New Testament. By this it is plain that the Blessed Chalice of the altar has the very sacrificial blood in it that was shed upon the Cross, in and by which the New Testament (which is the law of spirit, grace, and remission) was dedicated and consists. And therefore it is also clear that many divine things, which to the Heretics or ignorant may seem to be spoken only of Christ’s sacrifice upon the Cross, are indeed verified and fulfilled also in the sacrifice of the altar. Regarding this, St. Paul, for the causes aforesaid, would not treat in plain terms. *See Hesychius <note>An 5th-century theologian and monk of Jerusalem.</note> book 1 on Leviticus, chapter 4, shortly after the beginning,* applying all these things to the offering of Christ also in the Sacrament.

<margin>In the old Testament were figures of the new: in the new, is a resemblance of the heavenly state.</margin>
23. **The exemplars.**] All the offices, places, vessels, and instruments of the old law were but figures and resemblances of the state and sacraments of the New Testament, which are here called celestials, because they are the living image of the heavenly state next ensuing. These are therefore specially dedicated and sanctified in Christ’s blood, sacrificed on the altar, and sprinkled upon the faithful, just as the old figures and people were cleansed by the blood of beasts. And therefore, by a transition usual in the holy Scriptures, the Apostle suddenly passes in the sentence immediately following and turns his talk to Christ’s entrance into heaven—the state of which is prefigured both by the Sacraments of the old law, and also more specially by those of the new.

<margin>Christ once offered in a bloody way, but unbloodily often, namely in the sacrifice of the altar.</margin>
25. **Offer himself often.**] As Christ never died but once, nor never shall die again, so in that violent, painful, and bloody way he can never be offered again, nor does he need to be so offered any more; having by that one action of sacrifice upon the Cross made the full ransom, redemption, and remedy for the sins of the whole world. Nevertheless, as Christ died and was offered in a certain sense in all the sacrifices of the Law and Nature since the beginning of the world (all of which were figures of this one offering upon the Cross), so is he much rather offered in the sacrifice of the altar of the New Testament, incomparably more nearly, divinely, and truly expressing his death, his body broken, and his blood shed, than did any figure of the old law or any other sacrifice that ever was. This is because it is indeed (though in a hidden, sacramental, mystical, and unbloody manner) the very self-same Blessed body and blood, the self-same victim <note>original: "host"</note>, offering, and sacrifice that was performed upon the Cross.

<margin>The sacrifice of the altar and that on the Cross are both one.</margin>
And this truth is most evident by the very form of words used by our Savior in the institution and consecration of the holy Sacrament, and by the profession of all the holy Doctors <note>Highly influential ancient theologians and saints.</note>. *Our sacrifice,* says St. Cyprian, *is correspondent to the Passion of Christ. And, The sacrifice that we offer is the Passion of Christ (Epistle 63, numbers 4 and 7).* St. Augustine in *On the Faith to Peter*, chapter 19: *In those fleshly sacrifices was the prefiguring of the flesh of Christ, which he was to offer for sins, and of the blood, which he was to shed. But in this Sacrifice is the commemoration of the flesh of Christ which he has now given, and of the blood which he has shed: in those he was foreshadowed as one to be killed; in this he is announced as having been killed <note>original: "in illis prænuntiabatur occidendus, in hoc annuntiatur occisus"</note>.* And St. Gregory Nazianzen says in his *Oration on his Sickness* that the Priest in this sacrifice *joins himself to the great Passions of Christ <note>original: "immiscet se magnis Christi Passionibus"</note>.* St. Ambrose in book 1 of *Duties*, chapter 48: *Christ is offered in an image as if receiving the passion <note>original: "Offertur Christus in imagine quasi recipiens passionem"</note>.* Alexander I <note>Early 2nd-century Pope.</note> in his *Epistle to all the Orthodox, number 4, volume 1 of the Councils: He whose body and blood are produced, his passion is also celebrated <note>original: "Cuius corpus & sanguis conficitur, passio etiam celebratur"</note>.* St. Gregory, *Homily 37 on the Gospels: So often as we offer the victim <note>original: "host"</note> of his Passion, so often we renew his Passion.* And, *He suffers for us again in mystery.* And Hesychius, book 2, chapter 8 on Leviticus, after the middle: *By the sacrifice of...*

# CHAPTER 10. TO THE HEBREWS.

<margin>Commentary on Hebrews 9.</margin>
through the only-begotten [Son], many things are given unto us: namely, the remission or pardoning of all mankind, and the singular introduction or bringing in of the mysteries of the New Testament.

<margin>The Church Fathers call it the unbloody sacrifice of the altar.</margin>
<margin>Calvin’s contempt for the Church Fathers.</margin>
And the said Fathers and others, because of the difference in the manner of Christ’s presence and offering <note>The original uses "oblation," a formal term for an offering to God.</note> in respect to that on the Cross, called this the unbloody sacrifice, as Calvin himself confesses. However, he answers them in the pride of a heretical spirit with these words: *I care nothing that the ancient writers speak thus* <note>original: "Nihil moror quod sic loquantur vetusti scriptores."</note>; that is, I do not care that the ancient writers speak so: calling the distinction between a bloody and unbloody sacrifice "scholastic and frivolous," and a *devilish device* <note>original: "diabolicum commentum"</note>. We have to deal with such ignorant and blasphemous men who think they understand the Scriptures better than all the Fathers.

## CHAPTER 10.

> Because in the yearly feast of Expiation <note>This refers to Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, the most solemn day of the Jewish year.</note> there was only a commemoration of sins, therefore in place of all those old sacrifices the Psalm tells us of the offering of Christ’s body. **10** Which he offered bloodily but once (while the Levitical Priests offer every day) because that one time was sufficient forever, **15** in that it purchased (as the prophet also witnesses) remission of sins. **19** After all this, he proceeds and exhorts them to perseverance, partly by the opening of Heaven by our High Priest, **26** and partly by the terror of damnation if they fall away again: **32** bidding them remember how much they had already suffered, and not to lose their reward.

<margin>Leviticus 16:14.</margin>
<image-desc>Woodcut ornamental initial 'F' with floral scrollwork and leaves.</image-desc>
**1** **F**OR the Law, having a "shadow of good things to come," and not the very image of the things: can never make those who approach it perfect by the same sacrifices <note>The original uses "hostes," from the Latin "hostia," meaning a sacrificial victim.</note> which they offer incessantly every year. **2** Otherwise, "they would have ceased to be offered," because the worshippers, once cleansed, would have no consciousness of sin any longer. **3** But in those sacrifices, a commemoration of sin is made every year. **4** For it is impossible that sins should be taken away by the blood of oxen and goats. <margin>Psalm 39:7.</margin> **5** Therefore, coming into the world, he says: > "Sacrifice and offering <note>original: "Host and oblation"</note> thou wouldst not: but a body thou hast prepared for me:" **6** "Burnt offerings <note>original: "Holocausts"</note> and <gloss>c</gloss> for sin did not please thee." **7** Then I said: "Behold, I come: in the scroll <note>original: "head"</note> of the book it is written of me: That I may do thy will, O God." <margin>c "For sin" is the proper name of a certain sacrifice called in Hebrew *chattat* <note>original: חטאת</note>: just as "Holocaust" is another kind. # ANNOTATIONS
## CHAPTER 10.

<margin>
The old sacrifices obscurely foreshadowed, but the sacrifice of the altar most plainly represents the sacrifice on the Cross.
</margin>

1. *A shadow.*] The sacrifices and ceremonies of the old law were so far from the truth of Christ’s Sacraments, and from giving spirit, grace, remission <note>Forgiveness or cancellation of the debt of sin.</note>, redemption, and justification—and therefore the entrance into heaven and celestial joys—that they were but mere shadows, imperfectly and obscurely representing the graces of the New Testament and of Christ’s death. Whereas all the holy Church’s rites and actions instituted by Christ in the priesthood of the new law contain and give grace, justification, and everlasting life to the faithful and worthy receivers. Therefore, they are not shades or dark resemblances of Christ’s passion (which is the fountain of all grace and mercy), but perfect images and most lively representations of the same, especially the sacrifice of the altar <note>The Mass or Eucharist.</note>. Because it is the same offering, the same host <note>From the Latin *hostia*, meaning a sacrificial victim.</note>, and offered by the same Priest, Jesus Christ (though through the ministry of man and in mystery), it is the most pure and near image, character, and correspondence to the sacrifice of Christ’s passion in substance, force, and effect that can be.

<margin>
The Jews' sacrifices were not absolute and independent, because they were often repeated.
</margin>

<margin>
The Apostle proves by the frequent repeating of the Jews' sacrifices, not that they were not sacrifices, but that they were not absolute and sufficient.
</margin>

2. *They should have ceased.*] If the hosts and offerings of the old law had been of themselves perfect for all effects of redemption and remission—as the Hebrews (against whom the Apostle disputes) believed—and had had no relation to Christ’s sacrifice on the Cross or any other absolute and universal offering or remedy for sin, but by their own efficacy could have generally purged and cleansed man of all sin and damnation, then they should never have needed to be so often repeated and reiterated. For if they were generally available for all (in their opinion) and particularly applied to the several infirmities of every offender, there would have been no sins left. But sins did remain—even those sins for which they had offered sacrifices before—notwithstanding their sacrifices were particularly applied to them. For, by offering yearly, they did not only offer sacrifices for newly committed crimes, but even for the old ones for which they had often sacrificed before. The sacrifices were records and attestations of their sins rather than a redemption or full remission, as Christ’s death is. Once Christ's death is applied to a person by Baptism, it wipes away all past sins, with God never remembering them any more. No sacrifice, sacrament, or ceremony is ever performed for those same sins again, though for new sins other remedies are daily required. Their sacrifices, then, could not of themselves remit sins, much less achieve general redemption without relation to Christ’s Passion. And so you see it is plain everywhere that the Apostle proves, by the frequent repetition of the Jewish sacrifices, not that they were no sacrifices at all, but that they were not of that absolute force or efficacy to achieve redemption or any remission without dependence on the one universal redemption by Christ. His whole purpose was to instill in them the necessity of Christ’s death and the offering of the New Testament. As for the Church’s holy sacrifice <note>The Catholic Mass.</note>, it is of an entirely different kind than those of the Jews. Therefore, he makes no opposition between it and Christ’s death or sacrifice on the Cross in all this Epistle; but rather, as a consequence of that one general offering, he always covertly implies it: as being, in a different manner, the very same host and offering that was done upon the Cross, and is continually performed by the same Priest.

4. *Impossible.*] The hosts and sacrifices of the old law, which the carnal Jews made...
