# THE EPISTLE OF ST. PAUL CHAPTER 10.

<margin>The old sacrifices did not take away sins, but were only signs of it.</margin>
...all those sacrifices, without relation to Christ’s death, were not only not perfect and absolutely sufficient in themselves, but they did not, nor could not, remit <note>Take away the guilt or punishment of sin.</note> any sins at all, being but only signs thereof, referring the offenders for actual remission to Christ’s Passion. For the blood of brute beasts could have no other effect, nor any other element or creature, before Christ’s death; the fruit whereof, before it was accomplished, could be no otherwise properly applied unto them, but by belief in him.

<margin>God refuses the Jews' sacrifices, but not all sacrifice.</margin>
**5. *Host and oblation.*]** <term>Host</term> <note>From the Latin *hostia*, referring to a sacrificial victim.</note> He means not that God would have no host nor sacrifice any more, as the Protestants falsely imagine: for that would be to take away not only the sacrifice of Christ’s body upon the altar, but the sacrifice of the same body upon the Cross also. Therefore the Prophet speaks only of the legal and carnal sacrifices of the Jews, signifying that they did never of themselves please God, but only in respect of Christ, by whose offering of his own body they should please.

<margin>That Christ should have a body was necessary for his Priesthood and sacrifice.</margin>
<margin>The body of Christ is the sacrifice of the altar.</margin>
**5. *But a body.*]** If Christ had not had a body, he could not have had any worthy matter—or any matter at all—to sacrifice in a visible manner, other than the offerings of the old law. Neither could he either have made the general redemption by his one offering upon the Cross, nor the daily sacrifice of the Church: for both of which, his body was fitted by divine wisdom. This is a high conclusion, not understood by Jews, Pagans, nor the heretics of our time: that Christ’s human nature was taken to make the Son of God (who in his divine nature could not be either Priest or host) fit to be the sacrifice and Priest of his father, in a more worthy sort than all the Priests or offerings of the old law. And that this body was given him, not only to be the sacrifice upon the Cross, but also upon the altar, St. Augustine affirms in these words: *The table which the Priest of the New Testament does exhibit is of his body and blood: for that is the sacrifice which succeeded all those sacrifices that were offered as a shadow of that to come.* <note>original Latin: *Liber 17 De Civitate Dei, caput 20* (Book 17 of The City of God, chapter 20)</note> For which also we acknowledge that voice of the same Mediator in the psalm, <margin>Psalm 39</margin> BUT A BODY YOU HAVE FITTED TO ME, because instead of all those sacrifices and offerings his body is offered, and is administered to the partakers or receivers. <note>original Latin: *Liber 4 de Trinitate, caput 14* (Book 4 on the Trinity, chapter 14)</note> And again: *Who is so just and holy a Priest as the only Son of God? What might so conveniently be offered for men, by men, as man's flesh? And what so fit for this immolation or offering as mortal flesh? What so clean for cleansing the vices of mortal men as the flesh born of the virgin’s womb? And what can be offered and received so gratefully as the flesh of our sacrifice, made the body of our Priest?*

<margin>The Jews' sacrifices are refused, not all sacrifice.</margin>
**8. *Neither did they please thee.*]** By his statement that the things offered in the Law did not please God, and likewise by saying the first is taken away so that the second may have its place, it is evident that all hosts and sacrifices are not taken away by Christ, as the heretics foolishly conceive: but rather that the old hosts of brute beasts are abolished to give place to that which is the proper host of the new law, that is, Christ’s own body.

<margin>We must often note that the Apostle's speech concerning many Priests and frequent sacrificing concerns only the Jews' Priests and sacrifices, not the Priests and sacrifice of the New Testament.</margin>
**11. *Often offering the same hosts.*]** Just as St. Paul is forced to frequently repeat that one principle of the efficacy and sufficiency of Christ’s death—because the Hebrews attributed too much to their legal sacrifices and did not refer them to Christ’s single offering—so we, through the intolerable ignorance and persistence of the heretics of this time (who abuse the words of the Apostle spoken in the proper defense and declaration of the value and efficacy of Christ’s Passion above the sacrifices of the Law), are forced to repeat often: that the Apostle’s reasons regarding many Priests and the frequent repetition of the self-same sacrifices concern the sacrifices of the Law only. To these, he opposes Christ’s sacrifice and Priesthood. He speaks no word of or against the Sacrifice of the New Testament, which is the sacrifice of Christ’s own Priesthood, Law, and institution—indeed, the same sacrifice performed daily in an unbloody manner that was once performed bloodily. It is made by the same Priest, Christ Jesus, though by his ministers' hands; and it is not many hosts, as those of the old law were, but the very same one in number, even Christ’s own body that was crucified. And so that you may see that this is the judgment of all antiquity, and their explanation of these and similar words of this Epistle—and that they, seeing the very same arguments that the Protestants now make such a fuss with among the simple and unlearned, yet well perceived that they were not at all against the daily offering or sacrifice of the altar, and therefore answered them 1200 years before the Protestants even existed—we will set down some of their words. Their authority and explanation of the Scriptures must prevail in all who have wisdom or the fear of God, above the false and vain interpretations of Calvin and his followers.

<margin>The Calvinists' arguments against Christ's body being often offered, and in many places, were answered by the Church Fathers long ago.</margin>
Thus, then, first says St. Ambrose: <margin>On chapter 10 of Hebrews</margin> *What then do we do? Do we not offer every day? We offer surely: but this sacrifice is a representation of that one: for we offer always the self-same, and not now one lamb, tomorrow another, but always the self-same thing: therefore it is one sacrifice. Otherwise, by this reason, because it is offered in many places, there should be many Christs. Not so; but it is one Christ in every place, here whole, and there whole, one body. But this which we do, is done for a commemoration of that which was done. For we offer not another sacrifice, as the high Priest of the old law, but always the self-same.* Primasius, St. Augustine’s scholar, also anticipates these Protestant objections thus: *What shall we say then? Do not our Priests daily offer...*

<summary>This page provides a Catholic defense of the Mass, arguing that Christ's "one sacrifice" does not exclude the "daily sacrifice" of the altar. It uses patristic sources like St. Augustine and St. Ambrose to clarify that the Eucharist is a commemoration and continuation of the same singular sacrifice on the Cross, unlike the repetitive animal sacrifices of the Old Covenant.</summary>

### CHAPTER 10 TO THE HEBREWS.

<margin>The general redemption upon the Cross is particularly applied in the sacrifice of the altar.</margin>
...offer sacrifice? They offer surely, because we sin daily and daily have need to be cleansed: and *because he cannot die, he has given us the Sacrament of his body and blood: so that as his Passion was the redemption and absolution of the world, so also this oblation <note>A formal offering or sacrifice.</note> may be redemption and cleansing to all that offer it in truth and verity.* So says this holy father <note>Referring to Primasius.</note>, to wit, that as the sacrifice of the Cross was a general redemption, so this of the altar is, to all that use it, a particular redemption or application of Christ’s redemption to them. In which sense also the Venerable Bede calls the holy Mass, *everlasting redemption of body and soul* <note>original Latin: "redemptionem corporis & animæ ſempiternam"</note>. (Book 4, chapter 22 of the *History of the English People*).

<margin>Primasius, in the place cited.</margin>
Again the same Primasius says: *the divinity of the Word of God which is everywhere makes it so that there are not many sacrifices, but one, although it be offered by many; and just as it is one body which he took from the Virgin’s womb, not many bodies, even so also there is one sacrifice, not diverse ones like those of the Jews were.*

<margin>* Homily 17 on the Epistle to the Hebrews.</margin>
* St. Chrysostom also, and after him Theophylact, and Oecumenius, and among the Latins, Haimo, Paschasius, Remigius, and others, object to themselves thus: *Do we not also offer every day? We offer surely, but this sacrifice is an exemplar <note>A pattern or representation.</note> of that one, for we offer always the self-same: and not now one lamb, and tomorrow another, but the self-same: therefore this is one sacrifice. Otherwise, because it is offered in many places, there would be many Christs. And a little after: Not another sacrifice, like the high priest of the Old Law, but the self-same we do always offer, rather working a remembrance or commemoration of the sacrifice.* See the Annotation on Luke 22:19 upon these words, *A commemoration.* Thus did all the ancient fathers, Greek and Latin, treat of these matters; and so they said Mass, and offered daily, and many of them composed such forms of celebrating the divine sacrifice as the Greeks and Latins use in their Liturgies and Masses. And yet they saw these places of the Apostle and made commentaries upon them, and understood them (I believe) as well as the Protestants.

<margin>Councils and fathers.</margin>
He that for his further confirmation or comfort wishes to see what the ancient Councils and Doctors believed, taught, and practiced in this thing, let him read the first holy Council of Nicaea (chapter 14 and at the end of the Council from the Greek); the Council of Ephesus (Anathema 11); the Council of Chalcedon (Act 3, page 112); the Council of Ancyra (chapters 1, 4, and 5); Neocaesarea (canon 13); Laodicea (canon 19); Carthage II (chapter 8); Carthage III (chapter 24); and Carthage IV (chapters 33 and 41). See also St. Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite.</note> (chapter 3, *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*); St. Andrew in the *History of the Passion*; St. Ignatius (*Epistle to the Smyrneans*); St. Martial (*Epistle to the people of Bordeaux*); St. Justin Martyr (*Dialogue with Trypho*); St. Irenaeus (Book 4, chapters 32 and 34); Tertullian (*On the Apparel of Women* and *On the Soldier's Crown*); Origen (*Homily 13 on Leviticus*); St. Cyprian (*Epistle to Caecilius*, number 2, and *On the Lord's Supper*, number 14); and Eusebius (*Demonstration of the Gospel*, Book 1, chapter 10), and the rest which we have cited by occasion before, and might cite but for tediousness: a truth most known and agreed upon in the Christian religion.

<margin>When the Apostle seems to say there is no oblation for sins committed after Baptism.</margin>
<margin>The willful remission by Baptism.</margin>
18. ** *Now there is not.*]** Christ’s death cannot be applied unto us in that full and ample sort as it is in Baptism, more than once. Christ appointed that large remission and application to be made but once in every man, as Christ died but once. For it is not meant that all sin shall cease after Christ’s sacrifice upon the Cross, nor that there should be no oblation for sins committed after Baptism, or that a man could not sin at all after Baptism, or that if he sinned afterward, he could have no remedy or remission by God’s ordinance in the Church—various falsehoods which sundry heretics gather from this and such like places. But only the Apostle tells the Hebrews, as he did before in chapter 6, and as he does immediately afterward, that if they fall now (whereunto they seemed very prone) back to their old law, and voluntarily after the knowledge and profession of Christian faith by Baptism, commit this sin of incredulity and apostasy, they can never have that abundant remission applied unto them by Baptism, which can never be ministered to them again. And that general full pardon he calls here *oblation*, and afterward in the 26th verse, *a victim for sin* <note>original Latin: "hostiam pro peccato"</note>.

<margin>The Calvinists' heresy against remission of sins.</margin>
<margin>All sins may be remitted by penance, but not so fully as by Baptism.</margin>
<margin>Perilous reading of the Scriptures.</margin>
<margin>2 Peter 3.</margin>
26. ** *If we sin willingly.*]** As the Calvinists abuse other like places against the holy sacrifice of the Mass, so they abuse this as the Novatians did before them, to prove that a heretic, an apostate, or anyone who willfully forsakes the truth, can never be forgiven. Which (as is before declared in the 6th chapter) is most wicked blasphemy. The meaning hereof is, as is said there, only to terrify the Hebrews: that falling from Christ they cannot so easily have the victim of Christ’s death applied unto them, because they cannot be baptized anymore, but must pass by sacramental penance, and satisfaction, and other hard remedies which Christ has prescribed after Baptism in the Church's discipline. Therefore St. Cyril says (Book 5 on John, chapter 17): *Penance is not excluded by these words of Paul, but the renewing by the washing of regeneration <note>Baptism.</note>.* He does not here take away the second or third remission of sins (for he is not such an enemy to our salvation), but he denies that the victim, which is Christ, is to be offered again upon the Cross. So says this holy Doctor. And by this place and the like you see how perilous a thing it is for heretics and ignorant persons to read the Scriptures, which by following their own fantasy they pervert to their damnation.

<margin>Contempt of Christ’s blood in the Sacrament.</margin>
<margin>Luke 22.</margin>
29. ** *The blood of the Testament.*]** Whosoever makes no more account of the blood of Christ’s sacrifice, either as shed upon the Cross, or as in the holy Chalice of the altar (for our Savior calls that also the blood of the New Testament), than he does of the blood of calves and goats, or of other common drinks, is worthy of death. And God will in the next life, if it be not punished here, revenge it with grievous punishment.

<margin>Penance.</margin> 31. *It is horrible.*] <note>Referring to Hebrews 10:31: "It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God."</note> Let all Christian people do satisfaction and penance for their sins in this life. For the judgments of God in the next life, carried out by God himself—of whatever sort they may be, whether temporal as in Purgatory, or eternal as in Hell—are exceedingly grievous.

<margin>Mercy to those imprisoned for religion.</margin> 34. *You had compassion.*] To be merciful to those afflicted for their religion, and to be partakers in their miseries, is a very meritorious work <note>A "meritorious work" in Catholic theology is an action performed through grace that is worthy of a reward from God.</note>, and gives great confidence before God on the day of repayment or reward for the same.

<margin>Loss of goods for religion.</margin> 34. *With joy.*] If all Christian men would consider this, they would not think it such a great matter to lose their land or goods in defense of the Catholic faith.

<margin>Faith is the comfort of the afflicted.</margin> 38. *Lives by faith.*] Faithful men afflicted in this life have their comfort in their assured faith and hope of Christ’s coming to deliver them once and for all from these miseries; and so by that faith and comfort they live, whereas otherwise this miserable life would be a death.

## CHAPTER 11.

->*He exhorts them by the definition of faith to stick close to God, though they do not yet see his reward; showing that all the Saints of former times did the same, being all constant in faith, though not one of them received the promise—that is, the inheritance in heaven—but they and we now, after the coming of Christ, receive it together.*<-

<margin>:: By this word "substance" is meant that faith is the ground of our hope.</margin>
<margin>proof <note>original Greek: "ἔλεγχος" (elenchos), meaning a conviction or evidence.</note></margin>

AND faith is the substance of things to be hoped for, the proof of things not appearing. † For by this, the men of old obtained a good testimony. 

<margin>Genesis 1:13</margin>

<margin>Genesis 4:4; Matthew 23:35.</margin>

-> A N N O T A T I O N S <-
-> CHAPTER 11. <-

<margin>Not only or a special faith.</margin>
1. *Faith is.*] By this description of faith, and by all the commendation thereof through the whole chapter, you may well perceive that the Apostle knew not the forged "special faith" of the Protestants, whereby every one of these new sect-masters and their followers believe their sins are forgiven <note>original: "remitted"</note>, and that they themselves shall be saved, though their sects be completely contrary to one another.

<margin>Faith is of things not seen: as in the Blessed Sacrament.</margin>
1. *Not appearing*] This is the praise of faith, says Saint Augustine, *if that which is believed, be not seen. For what great thing is it, if that be believed, which is seen?* <note>original Latin: "si id quod creditur, non videtur. Quid enim magnum est, si id creditur, quod videtur?"</note> according to that sentence of our Lord when he rebuked his disciple, saying: *Because you have seen me Thomas, you have believed: blessed are they that have not seen and have believed.* <note>original Latin: "Quia vidisti me Thoma, credidisti: beati qui non viderunt & crediderunt."</note> Augustine on the Gospel [of John], Tract 79. Which may be a rebuke also and a check to all those faithless speeches, "I would see him, taste him, touch him and feel his very flesh in the Sacrament <note>the Eucharist</note>, otherwise I will not believe."

<margin>Nothing profitable or meritorious without faith.</margin>
6. *He that comes.*] Faith is the foundation and ground of all other virtues and worship of God, without which no man can please God. Therefore if one be a Jew, a Heathen, or a heretic—that is to say, be without the Catholic faith—all his works shall profit him nothing toward salvation.

<meta>This page continues the annotations on Hebrews chapter 11, focusing on the defense of Catholic traditions such as the veneration of holy objects, the necessity of good works alongside faith, and the authority of the Vulgate and Septuagint translations against Protestant critiques.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<page-num>633</page-num>
<header>CHAPTER 11. TO THE HEBREWS.</header>

<margin>Genesis 47:31.</margin>
<margin>* Augustine, *The City of God*, Book 15, Chapter 14.</margin>
<margin><note>Hebrew: *matteh*, meaning staff, rod, or tribe.</note></margin>
<margin>The citations in the New Testament are not only according to the Hebrew, but also the Septuagint <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note></margin>
<margin>The Vulgate Latin translation.</margin>
<margin>* <note>Greek: *rhabdos*, meaning rod; *klinē*, meaning bed.</note></margin>
**21. Adored the top of his rod.]** The learned may see here that the Apostle does not tie himself to the Hebrew text in the passage from Genesis where this is cited, but follows the Septuagint, even though it differs from the Hebrew. The other Apostles, the Evangelists, and our Savior himself did the same. They were not overly concerned (as men are nowadays) with examining everything by the Hebrew alone, because writing and speaking by the Holy Spirit, they knew very well that this translation <note>the Septuagint</note> also reflects the sense of the Holy Spirit, and is as true and as directly intended as the other. Therefore, that translation always remained authentic in the Greek Church, despite its differences from the Hebrew. In the same way, we who are Catholics follow, along with all the Latin Fathers, the authentic Latin translation <note>the Vulgate</note>, even though it is not always in agreement with the Hebrew or Greek as they exist now. But Calvin is not only very insolent but very ignorant when he says that the Septuagint translators were deceived, and yet that the Apostle was content to follow them out of a lack of care. It is evident that since the Hebrew was then written without vowel points, the word <note>the Hebrew *m-t-h*</note> could be translated either way <note>as "staff" or "bed"</note> just as well as the other. They understood this so well (and therefore were not deceived) that within three lines, at the beginning of the next chapter, they translate the same word exactly as Calvin would have it in this place.

<margin>* Joshua 7:6.</margin>
<margin>* Oecumenius in his collection.</margin>
<margin>* 1 Kings 11, 12. <note>Cited as 3 Kings in the original Latin system.</note></margin>
<margin>Adoration of creatures, specifically of holy things.</margin>
<margin>Corrupt translation used against the doctrine of Dulia <note>The honor given to saints and holy objects, distinguished from *Latria*, which is worship given to God alone.</note>.</margin>
Again, observe in those words, *He adored the top of his rod*, that adoration (as the Scripture uses this word) may be given to creatures, or to God at and before a creature: such as at or before the Ark of the Testament in the old days, and now at or before the crucifix, relics, and images. As in Psalms 98 and 131: *Adore his footstool. Adore toward his holy mountain. We will adore toward the place where his feet stood:* or (which in the Hebrew phrase is all the same) *Adore his holy mountain. We will adore the place where his feet stood.* The Greek Fathers—such as St. John Damascene in Book 1 *On Images*, and Leontius whom he cites, and even St. Chrysostom—handle these passages, specifically this one by the Apostle which we now speak of. They interpret the Greek as our Latin does, and as we do: "He adored the rod" or "the top of his rod," meaning the scepter of Joseph, who was then Prince of Egypt. This fulfilled Joseph’s dreams which foretold this <note>Genesis 37</note>, and it also signified, by this prophetic act, the kingdom of Israel or of the ten tribes that was to come from Joseph through Ephraim his younger son under the first king, Jeroboam—so say the Greek Fathers. To this may be added that all of this was done as a type and figure of Christ’s scepter and kingdom, whom Jacob adored by and in His Cross, just as he did Joseph by or in his rod and scepter. Therefore the Apostle says he did it by faith, having respect toward things to come. By all this, it is evident that it is false what the Calvinists teach—that we may not adore an image, crucifix, or any visible creature—that is, that we may not adore God at or by such creatures, nor kneel before them. Therefore, their corrupt translation of this passage for that same purpose is intolerable, saying: *(LEANING) upon his staff he adored (GOD),* adding no fewer than two words that are not in the Greek. Even though that might be the sense of the passage, and St. Augustine explains it that way, they should not turn his commentary into the text of Holy Scripture, especially since he is the only one of all the ancient Fathers (as Beza admits) who explains it so.

<margin>James 2.</margin>
<margin>Book 4 of the *Stromata*, page 240.</margin>
<margin>Not by faith only.</margin>
**33. Wrought justice.]** Men are not made just by belief alone, as the Protestants affirm, but by working justice <note>meaning doing righteous deeds</note>. We may note that in all this long commendation of faith in the Fathers and holy persons, their good works are also specifically recounted: Rahab’s harboring the spies, Abraham’s offering his son (works which St. James also emphasizes), Noah’s making the ark <margin>Genesis 6</margin>, Abel’s offering which was better than Cain’s <margin>Genesis 4 &amp; Hebrews 11:4</margin>, and so forth. Therefore, St. Clement of Alexandria says that these persons were just by faith and obedience, by faith and hospitality, by faith and patience, by faith and humility.

<margin>No works of the Patriarchs or anyone else are profitable except by their faith in Christ. This is always the Apostle's meaning when commending faith.</margin>
The Apostle’s purpose is nothing else but to prove to the Hebrews (who highly valued their Patriarchs and ancestors and their famous acts) that all these glorious personages and their works were commendable and acceptable only through the faith they had in Christ. Without this faith, none of their lives or works would have profited them at all. The Gentiles do many noble acts (as Heretics may also do) which are of no value before God because they lack faith. This is the goal of St. Paul’s Epistle to the Romans and all other passages where he commends faith. He further proves, especially in this Epistle to the Hebrews, that all their sacrifices were nothing else but figures and testimonies of the Christian faith in Christ and his death. All this high resolution and conclusion against the Jews and Gentiles—that the Christian faith is the true faith and religion—is ignorantly and brutally abused by the Heretics of our time against Christian works, sacrifice, and Sacraments, which the Apostle actually meant to commend and establish by his high praise of faith in Christ.

<margin>The Patriarchs and other just people were not in heaven before Christ.</margin>
**40. Without us should not.]** The Fathers before Christ could not be "accomplished"—that is, not admitted to the heavenly joys, the vision, and the enjoyment of God—until the Apostles and others of the New Law were joined with them, and the way to everlasting glory was opened by our Lord’s death and Ascension. Neither they nor we shall be fully perfected in glory, in both body and soul, until the general resurrection. God’s providence is such that we should not be brought to completion without one another, as we are all of one faith and redeemed by one Lord, Christ.

# ANNOTATIONS
## CHAPTER 12.

<margin>Temporal punishment after the forgiveness of sins, either here or in purgatory.</margin>
6. *He scourges.*] By this we prove that God often punishes the sins even of his beloved children—though not with eternal damnation, yet with temporary discipline and correction. It shows that he does not always, along with the forgiveness of deadly sins and eternal punishment, exempt the offender who has been received back into his grace from all fatherly correction, either in this life or in the next. The heretics of this time have no reason or scripture in the world to deny this.

# ANNOTATIONS
## CHAPTER 13.

<margin>Hospitality.</margin>
<margin>Angels harboured.</margin>
2. *Hospitality.*] Hospitality—that is, receiving and sheltering poor pilgrims, persecuted, and desolate persons—is so acceptable to God and so honorable, that oftentimes it has been men's good fortune to harbor Angels instead of poor folk unawares. This must always be a great blessing to them and their families, as we see by **Abraham and Lot** (*Genesis 18 & 19*) (and the same also happened to St. Gregory, as **John the Deacon** writes, to whose ordinary table of poor men, not only Angels but Christ also came in a Pilgrim's garment. *In the Life, book 1, chapter 10, and book 2, chapters 22, 23.*). If we did not have the example and warrant for this in St. Paul’s words here, and many other express Scriptures of the Old Testament, these scornful **miscreants** <note>A term used here by the translators to refer to those who reject Catholic traditions.</note> of this time, who make so little account of both good works and such miraculous appearances of Christ and his Angels in holy men's homes, would make this also seem like a fable, as they do other similar things.

<margin>How marriage is honorable in all, if the Apostle did say so, as he does not.</margin>
<margin>One short place manifoldly corrupted by the Protestants.</margin>
<margin>1 Corinthians 7, verse 38.</margin>
4. *Marriage honorable.*] The Apostle (says a holy doctor) says: *Marriage is honorable in all, and the bed undefiled. And therefore the servants of God, in that they are not married, do not think the good of marriage to be a fault; but yet they do not doubt that perpetual <term>continency</term> <note>Voluntary self-restraint from marriage and sexual relations.</note> is better than good marriage, especially in this time when it is said of continency: He that can take it, let him take it.* <note>original Latin: "De fide ad Petrum c. 3. apud Augustinum in fine" (On Faith to Peter, chapter 3, found at the end of Augustine's works).</note> Note the doctrine of the fathers and of the Catholic Church concerning matrimony: that it is honorable, and so honorable that it is a **holy sacrament**, but yet inferior to virginity and perpetual continency. It is "honorable in all"—that is, all such as may lawfully marry and are lawfully married—not in brothers and sisters, nor in persons who have **vowed** the contrary, to whom the same Apostle says it is damnable (*1 Timothy 5, verse 11*). And this would be the meaning of this place, if it were to be read thus: *Marriage is honorable.*

But it is notorious to see how the Protestants in all their translations, to deceive the simple, falsify this sentence of the Apostle to make it serve for the marriage of **Votaries** <note>Those who have taken religious vows, such as monks or nuns.</note>. First, they use deceit by adding the verb "is" which is missing in the original, making it the indicative mood: *Marriage is honorable etc.*, as though the Apostle affirmed all marriage to be

<margin>They restrain the sense to their Heretical fancy.</margin>
honorable or lawful, where the verb to be supplied ought rather to be the Imperative mood, *Let marriage be honorable*, so that the speech may be an exhortation or commandment to those who are or will be married, to conduct themselves in that state in all fidelity, cleanliness, and conjugal continence one toward another: as when St. Peter also and this Apostle exhort married men to give honor to their wives as to the weaker vessels, and to <margin>1 Peter 3. 1 Thessalonians 4.</margin> possess their vessel in honor, not in the passions of ignominy and uncleanness: this is honorable or chaste marriage, to which he here exhorts. And that it is rather an exhortation than an affirmation is evident by the other parts and circumstances of this place both before and after: all of which are exhortations in their own translations: this only being in the middle, and as indifferent to be an exhortation as the rest (by their own confession) they restrain on purpose. Our text therefore and all Catholic translations leave the sentence <margin>* τιμιος ὁ γα-μος ἐν πᾶσι <note>original: "honorable marriage in all [things/men]"</note></margin> indifferent as it is in the Greek, and as true translators ought to do, not presuming to addict it to one side, lest they should restrain the sense of the Holy Ghost to their own particular fantasy.

<margin>* The English Bible 1577.</margin>
Again, * our new Translators corrupt the text in that they translate *in omnibus* as "among all men," <note>original: "in omnibus"</note> because they think it would sound better to the ignorant, suggesting that Priests, Religious, and all whosoever may marry: whereas they cannot tell either by the Greek or Latin whether *in omnibus* should be the masculine gender, rather than the neuter (as not only Erasmus, <margin>* Oecumenius in Collections.</margin> but * the Greek doctors also take it) to signify that marriage should be honorably kept between man and wife in all points and in all respects. See *St. Chrysostom* and *Theophylact on this place.* For there may be many filthy abuses in wedlock, which the Apostle warns them to take heed of, and to keep their marriage-bed undefiled. But the third corruption for <margin>* Beza in the Greek-Latin New Testament, year 1565.</margin> their purpose aforesaid, and most impudent, is * that some of the Calvinists translate *in omnibus* as "among whomsoever," with a marginal interpretation to signify all orders, conditions, states, and qualities of men. So boldly they take away all indifference of senses, and make God’s word to speak exactly what they themselves wish, as their heresy requires; in which kind they surpass all impudence and all heretics that ever were.

<margin>We must have regard to the faith and doctrine of the fathers.</margin>
7. *Remember your Prelates.*] We are here warned to have great regard in our life and belief for the holy fathers, Doctors, and glorious Bishops who have gone before us in God's Church, not doubting but they, being our lawful Pastors, held and taught the truth: of whom St. Augustine said, *That which they found in the Church, they held fast: that which they learned, they taught: that which they received of their fathers, the same they delivered to their children. Against Julian, book 2, chapter 10.* Which respect to our holy forefathers in faith is now, in this wicked contempt by the Heretics, so much the more to be maintained. See the said holy doctor's second book against Julian the Pelagian throughout, what great account he makes of them in the confutation of heresies, and how far he prefers them above the proud Sect-masters of that <margin>Memories and feasts of Saints</margin> time: as we must now do against our new doctors. This place also is rightly used to prove that the Church of God should keep the memories of Saints departed, by solemn holidays and other devout ways of honor.

<margin>Judaical abstinence from meats.</margin>
9. *Not with meats.*] He speaks not of Christian fasts, but of the legal difference of meats, which the Hebrews were still prone to; not considering that by Christ's faith they were made free from all such observations of the Law.

<margin>Material altars for the sacrifice of Christ's body.</margin>
10. *We have an altar.*] He reminds them by these words that in following their old Jewish rites so much, they deprived themselves of another manner and a more excellent sacrifice and meat: meaning, the holy altar and Christ's own blessed body offered and eaten there, of which those who continue in the figures of the old Law could not be partakers. *This altar (says Hesychius) is the altar of Christ's body, which the Jews, because of their incredulity, must not behold. Book 6, chapter 21 on Leviticus.* And the Greek word (as also the Hebrew <margin>θυσιαστήριον <note>original: thysiasterion</note> מזבח <note>original: mizbeach</note></margin> answering to it in the Old Testament) signifies properly an altar to sacrifice on, and not a metaphorical and spiritual altar. By this we prove against the Heretics that we have not a common table or profane communion board to eat mere bread upon, but a very altar in the proper sense, to sacrifice Christ’s body upon; and so it was called by the fathers in respect of the said body sacrificed. *Gregory Nazianzen in his oration on his sister Gorgonia; Chrysostom in "Demonstration that Christ is God"; Socrates, book 1, chapters 20 and 25; Augustine, letter 86; The City of God, book 8, chapter 27 and book 22, chapter 10; Confessions, book 9, chapters 11 and 13; Against Faustus the Manichaean, book 20, chapter 21; Theophylact on Matthew 23.* And when it is called a table, it is in respect of the heavenly food of Christ's body and blood received.

<margin>The Sacrifice of the altar is the principal host of praise and thanksgiving, therefore called, Eucharistia.</margin>
15. *The host of praise.*] Although it may signify spiritual sacrifices of praise and thanksgiving of whatever sort, it may specifically be thought to signify the great Sacrifice of the Blessed body and blood of Christ: not as on the Cross, which was done but once in a bloody manner, but as in the Church and New Testament, where it is daily done unbloodily, being the proper host of praise and thanksgiving, and therefore called the *Eucharist* <note>original: "Eucharistia," meaning thanksgiving.</note>, and being the fruit and effect of Christ's and his Priests' lips or words—that is, of consecration—because this sacrifice is made by the force of the holy words. And when we read in the psalms and other places of the Old Testament...

### CHAPTER XIII. TO THE HEBREWS.

Testament, of the sacrifice of praise, it may be thought to be a prophecy of the new Sacrifice, and not of every ordinary thanksgiving. And so the old fathers in the primitive Church, to hide the <term>mysteries<note>The 'mysteries' refers to the Sacraments, particularly the Eucharist, which early Christians often kept hidden from non-believers to prevent desecration.</note></term> from the unworthy or the heathen, often speak. <margin>St. Augustine</margin> *What is (says St. Augustine) a more holy sacrifice of praise, than that which consists in thanksgiving, all of which the faithful know in the sacrifice of the Church.* <note>original Latin: "Quid est... sanctius sacrificium laudis, nisi quod consistit in gratiarum actione, quod totum fideles norunt in sacrificio Ecclesiæ."</note> *Against the Adversaries of the Law and Prophets, Book 1, chapter 18. Again, chapter 20: The Church from the times of the Apostles by the most certain successions of Bishops, offers to God in the body of Christ the sacrifice of praise.* <note>original Latin: "Ecclesia ab apostolorum temporibus per certissimas successiones Episcoporum, offert Deo in corpore Christi sacrificium laudis."</note> And a little afterward, *Now Israel according to the spirit, that is, the Church, offers a singular sacrifice according to the spirit: from whose house he will not take calves nor goats, but will take the Sacrifice of praise, not according to the order of Aaron, but according to the order of <term>Melchizedek<note>Melchizedek was a priest-king in the Old Testament who offered bread and wine; Christians see him as a 'type' or foreshadowing of Christ and the Mass.</note></term>.* <note>original Latin: "Jam Israel secundum spiritum... offert singulare sacrificium secundum spiritum... non secundum ordinem Aaron, sed secundum ordinem Melchisedec."</note> See *Epistle 120, chapter 19 and Epistle 57, at the end of question 1.* Thus you see, when the holy fathers handle the Scriptures, they find the Mass and Sacrifice in many places, where the ignorant heretics or the simple might think they speak only of a common thanksgiving.

<margin>
The Protestants avoid the word merit.
<br/>
Good works are meritorious.
</margin>
16. *God is <term>promerited<note>A term derived from the Latin 'promeretur,' meaning to earn or deserve God's favor through actions.</note></term>.* ] This Latin word *promeretur* cannot be expressed effectively in any one English word. It signifies God's favor being procured by the aforesaid works of alms and charity, as by the deserts and merits of the doers. Which doctrine and word of "merits" the Adversaries <note>The 'Adversaries' refers to Protestant Reformers like Luther and Calvin.</note> like so poorly that they flee both here and elsewhere from the word, translating here as, *God is pleased*, rather than *God is promerited*, claiming this is closer to the Greek. Which indeed helps them no more than the Latin, which is agreeable to the most ancient copies, as we see by Primasius, St. Augustine's scholar. For if God be pleased with good works and shows favor for them, then they are meritorious, and then faith alone is not the cause of God's favor to men.

<margin>
The Apostle emphasizes obedience to the Priests and Bishops of God’s Church.
<br/>
No person is exempt from this obedience in matters of religion.
</margin>
17. *Obey your <term>Prelates<note>High-ranking clergy members, such as bishops, who hold authority over the spiritual life of the community.</note></term>.* ] There is nothing more emphasized in the holy Scriptures than the obedience of the laypeople to the Priests and Prelates of God's Church in matters of the soul, conscience, and religion. Whereof the Apostle gives this reason: because they have the charge of men's souls and must answer for them; which is an infinite preeminence and superiority joined with a heavy burden, and requires marvelous submission and obedience. There is no exception nor exemption for kings nor Princes, be they ever so great. If they have souls and are Christian men, they must be subject to some Bishop, Priest, or other Prelate. And whatsoever he be (though he were Emperor of all the world), if he takes it upon himself to prescribe and give laws of religion to the Bishops and Priests, whom he ought to obey and be subject to in religion, he shall be damned undoubtedly, unless he repents, because he acts against the express word of God and the law of nature. And by this you may see the difference between a heretical and disordered time and other Catholic Christian days. For heresy and similar damnable revolts from the Church of God are nothing more than a rebellion and disobedience to the Priests of God's Church, when men refuse to be under their discipline, to hear their doctrine and interpretation of Scriptures, or to obey their laws and counsels. This disobedience and rebellion against the Spiritual Governor, under the pretense of obedience to the Temporal Governor <note>Referring to the English Monarch's claim to be the Supreme Head of the Church.</note>, is the bane of our days, and especially of our Country, where these new Sects are specifically maintained by this false principle: That the Prince in matters of soul and religion may command the Prelate. This is directly and evidently against this Scripture and all others that command the sheep of Christ's fold to obey their spiritual Officers.

<meta>This page serves as the "Argument" or introduction to the Epistle of St. James. It continues the theological transition from the Epistle to the Hebrews, shifting from a focus on Christ's priesthood to the practical necessity of good works in the Christian life. The text specifically aims to counter the Reformation doctrine of "faith alone" by appealing to the authority of St. James and St. Augustine.</meta>

<image-desc>A decorative horizontal woodcut band featuring a repeating pattern of ornate scrolls and stylized floral motifs.</image-desc>

# THE ARGUMENT OF THE
# EPISTLE OF ST. JAMES.

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'T' within a decorative border, depicting a figure of a man (likely St. James) holding a staff, surrounded by foliate patterns.</image-desc>
THIS *Epistle (as with the others following) is directed specially, as* St. Augustine *says, against the error of* **faith alone**, *which some held at that time also, by misconstruing* St. Paul's *words. Yea, not only that, but many other errors (which then also were annexed unto it, as they are now) does this* Apostle *here touch expressly.*

*He says therefore, that not only faith, but also good works are necessary: that not only faith, but also good works do justify: that they are acts of Religion, or service and worship of* God: *that to keep all the commandments of* God, *and so to abstain from all mortal sin, is not impossible, but necessary: that* God *is not the author of sin, no, not so much as of temptation to sin: that we must stay ourselves from sinning, with fear of our death, of the Judgment, and of hell: and stir ourselves to doing of good, with the reward that we shall have for it in heaven. These points of the* Catholic *faith he commends earnestly unto us, inveighing vehemently against them that teach the contrary errors. However, he does at the same time admonish us not to neglect such people, but to seek their conversion, showing them how meritorious a thing that is. Thus then he exhorts generally to all good works, and dissuades from all sin; but yet also specifically to certain ones, and from certain ones: such as, from favoritism <note>original: "acception of persons," meaning showing partiality based on status.</note>, from detraction and rash judging, from <term>concupiscence<note>Strong worldly desire or lust.</note></term> and love of this world, and from swearing: and, toward prayer, alms, humility, confession, and penance: but most copiously toward patience in persecution.*

<margin>Which James wrote this epistle.</margin>
*Now, who this* James *was: It is not he whose feast the Church keeps on the 25th of* July, *who was* St. John’s *brother, and whose martyrdom we have in* Acts 12; *but he whom the Church worships on the first of* May, *who is called the* Brother of the Lord <note>original Latin: "Frater Domini." In Catholic tradition, this refers to a close relative or cousin, as James the Just.</note>, *and brother to* Jude, *and who was the first Bishop of* Jerusalem, *of whom we read in* Acts 15 & 21, *and also* Galatians 2; *of whose wonderful austerity and purity of life, the Ecclesiastical histories do report.* *Eusebius, Book 2, chapter 22. Jerome, in the Catalog.*

*Therefore, just as the old* High-priest *had power and charge over the* Jews, *not only in* Jerusalem *and* Judea, *but also dispersed in other countries (as we understand from* Acts 9, verses 1 & 2*), so* St. James *likewise, being Bishop of* Jerusalem, *and having care not only of those* Jews *with whom he was resident there in*
<margin>James 1.</margin>
*Judea, but of all the rest also, writes this Epistle, To the twelve tribes that are in dispersion; and in them, to all* Christians *universally dispersed through the world.*

## ANNOTATIONS
## CHAPTER 1.

<margin>What faith is required in prayer.</margin>
6. *Ask in faith, nothing doubting.*] The Protestants try to prove by this that no one ought to pray without an absolute assurance that they shall obtain what they ask. However, the Apostle means nothing else but that the person asking for lawful things must not mistrust God’s power and ability, nor be in despair of His mercy; rather, our only "doubt" should be regarding our own unworthiness or if we are asking improperly.

<margin>God is not the author of evil.</margin>
13. *Let no man say that he is tempted by God.*] We see by this that when the Scriptures (as in the Lord’s Prayer and other places) seem to say that God sometimes tempts us or leads us into <term>temptation|testing or trial</term>, they do not mean that God is in any way the author, cause, or mover of any person to sin. He does so only by permission, and because through His gracious power He does not always shield the offender from temptations. Therefore, the blasphemy of <term>Heretics|In this context, a polemical term for the Reformers like Calvin or Luther</term> who make God the author of sin is intolerable. <note>original Latin: "See S. August. ser. 9 de diuers. c. 9" — See St. Augustine, Sermon 9 *On Various Subjects*, chapter 9.</note>

<margin>Partial and willful translation.</margin>
<margin>*not tempted by / not a tempter of evils.* <note>original Greek: ἀπείραστος κακῶν (apeirastos kakōn)</note></margin>
13. *God is not a tempter of evils.*] The Protestants, as much as they can, try to diminish the force of the Apostle’s conclusion against those who attribute their evil temptations to God (for God does send other temptations to try men's patience and prove their faith). They translate the word <term>passively|receiving the action</term>, in the sense that God is "not tempted by" our evils. However, it is more consistent with the literal text and the surrounding context—and just as agreeable to the Greek—that it should be taken <term>actively|performing the action</term> as it is in the Latin: that God is "no tempter" to evil. For if it is taken passively, there is no logical connection to the Apostle's other words.

<margin><term>Concupiscence|Disordered desire</term> of itself is no sin.</margin>
15. *Concupiscence when it hath conceived.*] We see here that concupiscence (disordered desire) is not sin in and of itself, as Heretics falsely teach. It is only when we obey it or yield to it through the consent of the mind that sin is birthed and formed within us.

<margin>Not every sin is mortal.</margin>
15. *Sin consummate engenders death.*] Here we see that not all sin, nor all consent to desire, is <term>mortal|deadly or deserving of damnation</term>. It only becomes so when it is "consummate"—that is, when the consent of the human mind fully and perfectly yields to committing or liking the act or motion to which the desire incites us.

<margin>What the law of liberty is in the New Testament.</margin>
25. *The law of perfect liberty.*] The law of the Gospel and the grace of Christ is called the "law of liberty" because it replaces the yoke and burden of old physical ceremonies, and because Christ, by His blood of the New Testament, has delivered all who obey Him from the slavery of sin and the Devil. It does not mean, as the <term>Libertines|A radical group that claimed Christian freedom excused them from following any laws</term> and other Heretics of this time would have it, that in the New Testament every man may follow his own liking and conscience, choosing whether or not to be under the laws and obedience of Spiritual or Temporal Rulers.

<margin>Good works are a part of man's justice.</margin>
27. *Religion clean.*] True religion consists not only in talking about the Scriptures, or in "faith alone," or in Christ’s justice; it consists of purity of life and good works—especially acts of charity and mercy done through the grace of Christ. This is the Apostolic doctrine, and it is far from the "heretical vanity" of this current time.

This is shown by the example of Abraham in Romans 4: for Abraham was indeed justified by works also, 25 and likewise Rahab.*

-> A N N O T A T I O N S <-
-> C H A P T E R II. <-

<margin>
Scripture abused by the Anabaptists to make no distinction of persons.
What the Apostle means by "respect of persons."
</margin>
1. *In respect of persons.*] The Apostle does not mean—as the <term>Anabaptists|A radical Reformation group known for rejecting infant baptism and, in some cases, advocating for the total equality of all social classes</term> and other <term>seditious|rebellious or inciting trouble</term> persons sometimes gather from this—that there should be no difference in commonwealths or assemblies between the magistrate and the subject, the free man and the slave, the rich and the poor, or between one rank and another. For God, nature, and the needs of mankind have made such distinctions, and men are bound to observe them. But it is meant only, or especially, that in spiritual gifts and graces, in matters of faith, Sacraments, and salvation, and in the bestowing of spiritual functions and the care of souls, we must value a poor man or a slave no less than the rich man and the free, or than the Prince or the Gentleman. Because as Christ himself calls all, and endows all sorts with his graces, so in such things we must not be partial, but count all to be fellows, brothers, and members of one head. And therefore the Apostle says with a special clause, *That we should not hold or have the Christian faith with or in such differences or partialities.*

<margin>
How he who offends in one commandment is guilty of all.
</margin>
10. *Is made guilty of all.*] He does not mean that whoever is a thief is also a murderer, or that every murderer is also an adulterer; or that all sins are equal, according to the <term>Stoics|Ancient Greek philosophers who believed all moral failings were equally bad</term> and the heresy of <term>Jovinian|A 4th-century monk who argued that all sins were equal after baptism</term>. Much less does he mean that he shall suffer as great a damnation for breaking one commandment as if he had offended against every precept. But the sense is that it shall not help him toward salvation that he seems to have kept certain commandments and not broken all of them; seeing that any one <term>transgression|breaking</term> of the Law proves that he has not observed the whole, which he was bound to do as far as is required and possible for a man in this life. St. Augustine, disputing profoundly in his 29th Letter to St. Jerome regarding this passage of St. James, explains it thus: that he who offends in one, that is, against the general and great commandment of love or <term>charity|Christian love for God and neighbor</term> (because it is in a way everything, being the sum of all, the fullness of the law, and the perfection of the rest), breaks in a certain way and transgresses all, as no sin is committed that is not against either the love of God or of our neighbor.

<margin>
Works of mercy are exceedingly pleasing to God.
</margin>
13. *Judgment without mercy.*] Nothing gives more hope of mercy in the next life than the works of alms, charity, and mercy done to our neighbors in this life. Neither shall any be treated with extreme rigor in the next world except those who did not show mercy in this world. <note>original: "August. de pec. merit. li. 2 c. 3." — St. Augustine, *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, book 2, chapter 3.</note> This is true not only in respect of the judgment to everlasting damnation, but also of the <term>temporal|temporary</term> punishment in <term>Purgatory|A state of purification for souls before entering heaven</term>, as St. Augustine indicates, declaring that our <term>venial|lesser, pardonable</term> sins are washed away in this world with daily works of mercy, which otherwise would be punished in the next. <note>original: "See epist. 29 aforesaid in fine. and li. 21 de Ciu. Dei c. 27 in fine." — See Letter 29 mentioned before at the end, and book 21 of *The City of God*, chapter 27, at the end.</note>

<margin>
The proud and shameless behavior of the heretics against this Epistle, because it is clearly against "faith alone."
</margin>
14. *What shall it profit, if a man say he has faith?*] This whole passage of the Apostle is so clear against justification or salvation by "only faith"—a doctrine <term>damnably|in a way that leads to damnation</term> defended by the Protestants—and so evident for the necessity, merit, and cooperation of good works, that their first author <term>Luther|Martin Luther, the German reformer</term> and those who exactly follow him, boldly (after the manner of heretics) deny the book to be Canonical Scripture when they can find no excuse or false interpretation for the text. But <term>Calvin|John Calvin, the French reformer</term> and his companions, disagreeing with their masters, confess it to be Holy Scripture. However, their excuses and plain...

<meta>This page continues the polemical commentary on the Epistle of James, specifically addressing the Protestant doctrine of "faith alone" (sola fide) by contrasting it with the teachings of Church Fathers like St. Augustine and the internal consistency of the New Testament.</meta>

<page-num>646</page-num>
<header>THE EPISTLE CHAP. II.</header>

<term>foolish glosses|silly or superficial interpretations</term> as an answer for such plain passages, would be as impudent as the denial of the Epistle was in others—who would never have denied the book (thereby showing themselves to be Heretics) if they had thought those <term>vulgar|common or low-level</term> evasions that the <term>Zwinglians|Followers of Huldrych Zwingli</term> and <term>Calvinists|Followers of John Calvin</term> use (of which they were not ignorant) could have served their purpose. In both sorts of people, the Christian Reader may see that all the Heretics' vaunting of express Scriptures and the word of God is nothing more than a way to delude the world. Whereas, indeed, even when the Scriptures are ever so plain against them, they must either be <term>wrested|distorted or twisted</term> to sound as they say, or else they must be rejected as Scriptures altogether. And to see Luther, Calvin, Beza, and their fellows sit, as it were, in judgment of the Scriptures—to allow or disallow them at their pleasure—it is the most notorious example of heretical pride and misery that can be. See their prefaces and censures upon this Canonical Epistle, the <term>Apocalypse|The Book of Revelation</term>, the <term>Maccabees|Books of the Old Testament rejected by many Reformers</term>, and others.

<margin>Only faith, an old heresy.</margin>
<margin>St. James and the rest emphasize good works against the error of "only faith" falsely gathered from St. Paul's words.</margin>
21. *Abraham, was he not justified by works?*] It is much to be noted that St. Augustine, in his book <note>original: "de fide & operibus c. 14"</note> *On Faith and Works, chapter 14*, writes that the heresy of "only faith justifying" was an old heresy even in the Apostles' time. It was gathered by the false interpretation of some of St. Paul's profound disputations in the Epistle to the Romans, wherein he commended so highly the faith in Christ that they thought good works were not <term>available|effective or necessary</term>. He adds further that the other three Apostles—James, John, and Jude—purposely wrote so much about good works to correct the said error of "only faith," which had been gathered by the misconstruction of St. Paul's words. Indeed, when St. Peter <margin><note>original: "loco citato"</note> in the place cited.</margin> (*2 Peter 3*) warns the faithful that many things are hard in St. Paul's writings, which light and unlearned men mistake to their own <term>perdition|spiritual ruin</term>, the said St. Augustine affirms that he meant Paul's disputation concerning faith, which so many Heretics mistook as a reason to condemn good works. And in the preface of his commentary upon the 31st Psalm, he warns all men that this deduction based on St. Paul’s speech—*Abraham was justified by faith, therefore works are not necessary to salvation*—is the right way to the gulf of Hell and damnation.

<margin>St. Augustine's whole disputation on this point is very notable, and directly against "only faith."</margin>
And lastly (which is in itself very plain), so that we may see this Apostle purposely commended to us the necessity of good works and the <term>inanity|emptiness</term> and insufficiency of "only faith" to correct the error of such as misconstrued St. Paul's words, the said holy Doctor <note>St. Augustine</note> notes that James purposely took the very same example of Abraham, whom St. Paul said to be justified by faith <margin><note>original: "Li. 83 q. q. 76"</note> Book of 83 Different Questions, question 76.</margin>, and declares that he was justified by good works. He specifies the good work for which he was justified and blessed by God—namely, his obedience and the <term>immolation|offering as a sacrifice</term> of his only son. But regarding how St. Paul says that Abraham was justified by faith, see the Annotations upon that place (*Romans 4:1*).

<margin>Heresies against good works.</margin>
<margin>Works concur with faith as a cause of justification.</margin>
22. *Faith did work with.*] Some Heretics hold that good works are <term>pernicious|harmful or destructive</term> to salvation and justification. Others hold that, though they are not hurtful but required, yet they are not causes or workers of salvation (much less meritorious), but are merely effects and fruits issuing necessarily out of faith. Both of these fictions, falsehoods, and flights from the plain truth of God’s word are refuted by these words, when the Apostle says: *That faith worked together with good works*. He makes faith a <term>coadjutor|helper</term> or cooperator with works, and so both jointly concur as causes and workers of justification. Indeed, afterward he makes works the more principal cause when he resembles faith to the body and works to the spirit or life of man.

<margin>Works make us just indeed before God.</margin>
23. *The friend of God.*] By this also, another false and frivolous evasion of the Heretics is overtaken, when they feign that the Apostle here (when he says works justify) means that they show us to be just before men, but do not avail to our <term>justice|righteousness</term> before God. For the Apostle evidently declares that Abraham, by his works, was made or truly called the "friend of God," and therefore was not (as the Heretics say) approved as just before man only.

<margin>The Protestants say, "by faith only": St. James says the clean contrary, "Not by faith only."</margin>
<margin>See the annotations upon the Epistle to the Romans, chapter 2, verse 13.</margin>
24. *Not by faith only.*] This proposition or speech is directly opposite or contradictory to that which the Heretics hold. For the Apostle says, "Man is justified by good works, and not by faith only"; but the Heretics say, "Man is not justified by good works, but by faith only." Neither can they pretend that there is a similar contradiction or contrariety between St. James's speech and St. Paul's. For though St. Paul says man is justified by faith, he never says "by faith only," nor does he ever mean that faith which is alone, but always that faith which works through <margin>Galatians 5.</margin> charity, as he explains himself. Though concerning works also, there is a difference between the "first justification" (of which St. Paul specially speaks) and the "second justification" (of which St. James treats more specially). Of which thing enough has been said elsewhere.

<margin>The manifold meaning of certain fathers, when they say, "Only faith."</margin>
The <term>Fathers|Early Church theologians</term> indeed sometimes use this exclusive term, <note>original: "sola"</note> *only*, but in a far different sense than the Protestants do. For some of them thereby exclude only the works of Moses' Law (against the Jews). Some exclude the works of nature and moral virtues without the grace or knowledge of Christ (against the Gentiles). Some exclude the necessity of external good works where the parties lack time and means to do them (as in the case of the <term>penitent thief|The man crucified alongside Jesus</term>). Some exclude false opinions, sects, and religions contrary to the Catholic faith (against Heretics and <term>miscreants|unbelievers</term>). Some exclude reason, sense, and arguing in matters of faith and mystery (against those who will believe nothing but what they see or understand). Some exclude the

<meta>This page continues the Roman Catholic commentary on the Epistle of James, specifically focusing on the relationship between faith and works in the process of justification, while refuting the Protestant doctrine of "faith alone."</meta>

# CHAPTER II OF ST. JAMES

merit of works done in sin before the first <term>justification|the process by which a person is transitioned from a state of sin to a state of grace</term>: some, the arrogant Pharisaical vaunting of man's own proper works and justice, against such as do not refer their actions and good deeds to God's grace. To these purposes the holy <term>Doctors|theologians and teachers of the early Church</term> say sometimes, that only faith saves and serves: but never (as the Protestants would have it) to exclude from justification and salvation the cooperation of man's free will, the dispositions and preparations of our hearts by prayers, penance, and sacraments, the virtues of hope and charity, the purpose of well-working and of the observation of God's commandments: much less, the works and merits of the children of God, proceeding from grace and charity, after they are justified and are now in his favor: which are not only dispositions and preparations to justice, but the meritorious cause of greater justice, and of salvation.

<margin>St. Paul names faith, and St. James works, as causes of justification: but neither the one, faith only: nor the other, works only.</margin>
25. *Rahab*.] This Apostle alleges the good works of Rahab by which she was justified, and St. Paul (Hebrews 11) says she was justified by faith. Which are not contrary to one another, for both are true: that she was saved by faith, as one says; and that she was saved by her works, as the other says. But it would be untruly said that she was saved either by **only** faith, as the <term>Heretics|Protestant reformers</term> say; or by **only** good works, as no Catholic man ever said. But because some Jews and Gentile Philosophers did affirm—the Jews, that they should be saved by the works of Moses' law; the Gentiles, by their moral works—therefore St. Paul, in the letter to the Romans, disputed specially against both, proving that no works done without or before the faith of Christ can serve for justification or salvation.

<margin>Faith without works is a true faith, but not available; just as the body without the spirit is a true body, though it be dead.</margin>
26. *Faith without works is dead*.] St. James (as the Protestants <term>feign|falsely claim</term>) says that faith without good works is no faith, and that therefore it does not justify because it is no faith. For he says that it is dead without works, as the body is dead without the soul, and therefore being dead has no activity or efficacy to justify or save. But there is a great difference between saying that the body is dead, and saying that it is no body. Even so there is the same difference between saying that faith without works is dead, and saying that faith without works is no faith. And if a dead body is nonetheless a true body, then according to St. James's comparison here, a dead faith is nonetheless a true faith, but yet not <term>available|effective</term> for justification, because it is dead; that is, because it is only faith without good works.

<margin>What faith the Apostle speaks of: and that he knew no "special faith."</margin>
And therefore it is a great impudence in Heretics, and a <term>hard shift|desperate or clumsy argument</term>, to say that the faith which the Apostle disputes about all this while is no true or properly called faith at all. It is the same faith that St. Paul defined and commended in all the 11th chapter of Hebrews, and the same which is called the Catholic faith, and the same which, being formed and made alive by charity, justifies. Indeed, it is true that it is not that <term>special faith|the Protestant doctrine of personal assurance of salvation</term> which the Heretics feign alone justifies—namely, when a man does firmly believe as an article of his faith that he himself shall be saved. This "special faith" is not that of which the Apostle here speaks; for neither he, nor St. Paul, nor any other sacred writer in all the Holy Scriptures ever spoke or knew of any such forged faith.

<margin>Many masters are many proud Sect-masters.</margin>

# CHAPTER IV.

<margin>Man's working with God’s grace is no detraction from it.</margin>
8. *Purify your hearts.*] Man (we see here) makes himself clean and purges his own heart. This detracts nothing from the grace of God, which is the principal cause of the same. Yet Protestants think we detract from Christ’s Passion when we attribute such effects to our own works, or to other secondary helps and causes. <note>This reflects the Counter-Reformation debate over "Faith alone" versus the Catholic view of "Cooperative Grace," where human effort is seen as working alongside God's gift rather than replacing it.</note>

<margin>
The sins crying to heaven.
</margin>
4. *The hire.*] To withhold from the poor or laborer the hire or wages that is due or promised to him for his service or work done, is a great iniquity, and one of those five sins which in holy Writ be said to call for vengeance at God's hand, as we see here. They be called in the Catechism, *Sins crying to heaven*. The other four be, Murder, *Genesis* 18 v. 20. Usury, *Exodus* 22. v. 27. The sin against nature, *Genesis* 18. v. 20. The oppression and vexation of widows, pupils <note>orphans</note>, strangers, and such like. *Ibid. & Exodus* 3. v. 9.

<margin>
What oaths are lawful, what are not.
</margin>
12. *Swear not.*] He forbiddeth not all oaths, as the Anabaptists <note>A radical Reformation group that refused to take any oaths, even in court</note> falsely say. For in justice and judgment we may be by our lawful Magistrate put to swear, and may lawfully take an oath, as also for the advantaging of any necessary truth when time and place require. But the custom of swearing, and all vain, light, and unnecessary oaths in our daily speech do displease God highly, and are here forbidden by the Apostle, as also by our Savior. *Matthew* 5.

<margin>
Heretical translation against Priesthood.
</margin>
14. *Let him bring in the Priests.*] The Protestants for their special hatred of the holy order of Priesthood, as elsewhere often, so here they corrupt the text evidently, translating <term>Presbyteros</term> <note>original: "Presbyteros" — the Greek word for elders or priests</note> as "elders." As though the Apostle had meant men of age, and not such as were by holy office, Priests. St. Chrysostom who knew the sense and signification of the Greek word according to the Ecclesiastical use and the whole Church's judgment, better than any Protestant alive, taketh it plainly for <term>Sacerdotes</term> <note>original: "Sacerdotes" — Latin for sacrificial priests</note>, that is, Priests *in book 3 of "On the Priesthood," near the beginning*. And if they confess that it is a word of office with them also, though they call them Elders, and not Priests: then we demand whether the Apostle mean here men of that function which in their new Churches call Elders. If they say no, as they must needs (for Elders with them are not deputed specially to public praying or administration of the Sacraments, such as the Apostle here requireth to be sent for) then they must needs grant, that their Elders answer not to the function of those which in the new Testament are called <term>Presbyteri</term> in Greek and Latin, and therefore both their translation to be false and fraudulent, and also their naming of their new degrees or orders to be fond and incongruous.

They might do this with as much justification as calling those they have appointed in place of our Catholic Priests "Ministers." This word, being in its broad sense common to all who have to do with the celebration of divine things, was never designated by the use of either Scripture or the holy Church for that higher function of public administration of the Sacraments and Service, which is the Priesthood. Instead, it was designated for the order next below it, which is the Deaconship. Therefore, if anyone should be called "Ministers," their Deacons should properly be so named. And the Protestants have no more reason to keep the ancient Greek word "Deacon," assigned to that office by ancient usage, than to keep the word "Priest," which is no less specific to the status of those alone who minister the holy Sacraments and offer the Sacrifice of the Altar. But these fellows follow neither God's word nor Ecclesiastical usage, nor any reason, but mere fantasy, novelty, and hatred of God's Church. And how little they follow any good rule or reason in these things may appear by this: that here they avoid translating the word as "Priests," and yet in their own Communion book, in their order for visiting the sick, they commonly name the Minister "Priest."

<margin>The Sacrament of EXTREME UNCTION.</margin>
14. *Anointing with oil.*] Here is the Sacrament of <term>Extreme Unction</term> <note>The historical name for the Sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick, typically administered to those near death.</note> so plainly proclaimed—for it was instituted, like all other Sacraments of the New Testament, by our Savior Christ himself, and, as <term>Venerable Bede</term> <note>An 8th-century English monk and scholar.</note> and other ancient writers think, the anointing of the sick with oil in *Mark 6* pertains to it—that some Heretics, because of the evidence of this passage (as with the other passage regarding good works), deny the Epistle's authority entirely. Others (such as the Calvinists), through their confidence in clever excuses and interpretations, confess that St. James is the author, yet condemn the Church of God for using it and treating it as a Sacrament. But what dishonor to God is it (we ask them) that a Sacrament should be instituted using the material of oil, any more than in the element of water? Why may not grace and the forgiveness of sins be attached to the one as well as to the other, without taking away from God's glory?

<margin>The heretics' objections against the said Sacrament answered; and furthermore, it is proved to be a Sacrament.</margin>
But they say, "Sacraments endure forever in the Church, but this was only for a season in the Primitive Church." What Scripture tells them that this general and absolute instruction of the Apostle in this case should last only for a season? When was it taken away, abolished, or altered? They see that the Church of God has always used it based on this warrant from the Apostle, who knew Christ’s meaning and the institution of it better than these deceived men, who value their own foolish guesses and conjectures—grounded neither on Scripture, the context of the text, nor any one authentic author that ever wrote—more than the express word of God. It was (they say) a miraculous practice of healing the sick, lasting only during the Apostles' time and not long after. We ask them whether Christ appointed any certain physical object or external element for the Apostles to work miracles with generally. He himself used sometimes clay and spit, and sometimes he sent those who were diseased to wash themselves in waters; but we do not read that he appointed any of those or similar things as a general medicine or for miraculous healing only. For in the beginning, to better lead the people to faith and devotion, Christ willed that miracles be performed through various Sacraments as well. Even though those miraculous works have ceased, the Sacraments still remain until the end of the world.

Again we ask: have they ever read or heard that men were generally commanded to seek their health through miraculous means? Thirdly, did all Priests (or "Elders" as they call them) have the gift of miracles in the early Church? No, it cannot be; for though some had it, not all of those of whom the Apostle speaks had the gift indiscriminately. Conversely, many who were not Priests had the gift—both men and women—who yet could not be called upon as Priests were in this case. And though the Apostle and others could both cure men and bring them back to life, there was no such general command for sick or dead men as this: to call for the Apostles to heal or restore them to life again. Lastly, did any external element or miraculous practice, unless it were a Sacrament, have the promise of the forgiveness of all kinds of actual sins joined to it? Or could St. James institute such a ceremony himself that could save both body and soul by giving health to the one and grace and forgiveness to the other?

<margin>Forgiveness of sins attached to physical objects.</margin>
<margin>Holy water.</margin>
At other times these argumentative complainers rail against God’s Church for attaching only the forgiveness of <term>venial sins</term> <note>Sins considered less serious that do not entail a complete break with God's grace.</note> to the element of water made holy by the Priest’s blessing in the name of Christ and his word; and yet here they are forced to hold that St. James prescribed a miraculous oil or object which had much more power and efficacy. Such miscreants are brought into these difficult positions because they will not believe the express word of God as interpreted by the practice of God’s universal Church.

<margin>Holy oil blessed by the Bishop.</margin>
<margin>The people's devotion toward such hallowed objects.</margin>
*Venerable Bede in his commentary on Luke 9 says: "It is clear that this custom was delivered to the holy Church by the Apostles themselves: that the sick should be anointed with oil consecrated by the Bishop's blessing."* See also for this assertion and the use of this Sacrament: St. Innocent <note>original: "ep. 1 ad Decentium Eugubinum cap. 8" — Epistle 1 to Decentius of Gubbio, chapter 8.</note>, Volume 1 of the Councils; and Book 2 *On the Visitation of the Sick* <note>original: "de visitatione infirmorum"</note> in St. Augustine, chapter 4; the Second Council of Chalon, chapter 48; the Council of Worms, chapter 72; Volume 3 of the Councils, Aachen, chapter 8; the Council of Florence, and other later Councils; and St. Bernard in the *Life of Malachy* at the end. Because the faithful saw that this holy oil had such virtue in the early Church, many carried it home and used it for their illnesses—not using it in the Sacramental manner which the Apostle prescribes, as our opponents ignorantly object.

<summary>This page presents a Roman Catholic defense of the Sacrament of Extreme Unction (Anointing of the Sick), arguing that it is a permanent Sacrament instituted by Christ rather than a temporary miraculous gift. The author critiques Protestant translations of "Priest" as "Minister" and cites various Church Fathers and Councils to support the traditional practice.</summary>
