# CHAPTER V. OF ST. JAMES.
### Nnnn iij
<meta>catchword: CHAPTER</meta>

unto us: but as Christians now do (and then also did) concerning the water of Baptism, which they used to take home with them after it was hallowed <note>Blessed or made holy</note>, and to give it to their diseased to drink.

<margin>The sacramental words.</margin>
15. *The prayer of faith.*] He means the form of the Sacrament, that is, the words spoken at the same time when the party is anointed <note>original: "anoiled," an archaic term for ritual anointing with oil</note>, which no doubt are most ancient and Apostolic. Not that the word or prayer alone should have that great effect here mentioned, but joined with the aforementioned unction <note>The act of anointing with oil</note>, as is plain.

<margin>The three effects of this Sacrament.</margin>
15. *Shall save.*] The first effect of this Sacrament is to save the soul, by giving grace and comfort to withstand the terrors and temptations of the enemy <note>The Devil</note>, who goes about (especially in that extremity of death) to drive men to desperation or distress of mind and other damnable inconveniences. This effect is signified in the physical matter of this Sacrament specifically.

15. *Shall lift him up.*] When it shall be good for the salvation of the party, or agreeable to God’s honor, this Sacrament also restores a man to bodily health again, as experience often teaches us. Yet this is not done by way of a miracle, to make the party suddenly whole, but by God’s ordinary providence and use of second causes <note>Natural means or processes through which God works</note>, which otherwise would not have had that effect if not for the said Sacrament. This is the second effect.

<margin>
Is any sick? <note>original Greek: "ἀσθενεῖ τις" (astheneî tis)</note>
</margin>
<margin>Priests (and not Elders) are the ministers of this sacrament.</margin>
15. *They shall be remitted him.*] Whatever sins remain unremitted, they shall be remitted in this Sacrament and by its grace, if the persons receive it worthily. This is the third effect. St. Chrysostom says of this effect: *They (speaking of Priests) do not only remit sins in baptism, but afterward also, according to the saying of St. James, "If any be sick, let him bring in the Priests," etc.* <note>original Latin: "li. 3 de Sacerd. prope initiū" referring to Book 3 of "On the Priesthood," near the beginning</note>. Let the Protestants mark that he calls *Presbyteros* "Priests" <note>original Latin: "sacerdotes"</note>, and makes them the only ministers of this Sacrament, and not elders or other laymen. By all of which you see this Sacrament, above all others, is marvelously and plainly set forth by the Apostle. Only sick men and (as the Greek word implies) men who are very weak must receive it; only Priests must be the ministers of it; its matter is holy oil; its form is prayer, in the same manner as we see used now; and the effects are as stated before. Yet the enemy, through Heretics, would wholly abolish such a plain matter and profitable Sacrament.

<margin>On this passage. <note>original Latin: "In hunc locum"</note></margin>
<margin>Confession</margin>
16. *Confess therefore.*] It is not certain that he speaks here of sacramental Confession; yet the context of the text supports it, and it is very probable that he means it. Origen expounds it as such <note>original Latin: "ho. 2 in Leuit." referring to Homily 2 on Leviticus</note>, and the Venerable Bede writes thus: *In this sentence (he says) there must be this discretion: that we confess our daily and small sins to one another—to our equals—and believe we are saved by their daily prayer. But let us open the uncleanness of the greater leprosy <note>Significant or "mortal" sins</note> to the Priest according to the law; and at his pleasure, in whatever manner and for however long he shall command, let us be careful to be purified.* But the Protestants, fleeing from the very word "confession" out of spite for the Sacrament, translate it as: *Acknowledge your faults one to another.* They do not like to have Priests, praying over the sick, anointing them, forgiving them their sins, and confession all in one sentence.

<margin>Truths unwritten and known by tradition.</margin>
17. *He prayed.*] The Scriptures to which the Apostle alludes make no mention of Elijah’s <note>original: "Elias"</note> prayer; therefore, he knew of it by tradition or revelation. By this, we see that many unwritten things are of equal truth with those that are written.

<margin>Converting of souls</margin>
20. *Maketh to be converted.*] Here we see the great reward for those who seek to convert Heretics or other sinners from error and wickedness, and how necessary an office it is, especially for a Priest.

<margin>Our salvation attributed to men, without derogation to Christ.</margin>
20. *Shall save.*] We see that it does not detract from God to attribute our salvation to any man or Angel in heaven or earth, acting as the workers of salvation under God through their prayers, preaching, correction, counsel, or otherwise. Yet the Heretics are so foolish and critical in this regard that they cannot patiently hear that our Blessed Lady or others should be counted as means or workers of our salvation.

It emphasizes the roles of Priests, the efficacy of holy oil, and the importance of sacred tradition alongside Scripture.</summary>

# THE ARGUMENT OF BOTH
## THE EPISTLES OF ST. PETER, THE
### FIRST, AND THE SECOND.

<margin>chapter 10, verse 2.</margin>
Of St. Peter we read at length, both in the *Gospels* and in the *Acts of the Apostles*: namely, that Christ designated him and also made him his vicar <note>A representative or deputy; here, the earthly head of the Church</note>. For this reason, *St. Matthew*, in his list of the Apostles, calls him *Primus* <note>original: "Primus," meaning "The First"</note>, and all ancient tradition calls him *Princeps Apostolorum* <note>original: "Princeps Apostolorum," meaning "The Prince of the Apostles"</note>. We also read that he accordingly executed that office after Christ’s departure, establishing the Church first among the Jews in Jerusalem and in all that country and the surrounding coasts, just as Christ himself had previously preached to the Jews alone.

<margin>1 Peter 1.</margin>
But eventually preaching to the Gentiles <note>Non-Jewish people</note> as well, according to Christ’s commission (*Matthew 28:19*) and having now come to Rome—the capital city of the Gentiles—he wrote this Epistle from there to his Christian Jews. He cared for them in his absence no less than when he was present. He did not write to the Jews who were at home (likely because they had *St. James*, or his successor *St. Simon of Cleophas*, living with them), but * to those who were scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, and Bithynia.

<margin>* See the Annotation 1 Peter 5:13.</margin>
<margin>1 Peter 5.</margin>
And he indicates himself that he writes it from Rome, saying: *The Church that is in Babylon greets you.* By "Babylon," he means Rome, as all ancient writers interpret him. He does not call the Church of Rome "Babylon," but rather the pagan state of the Roman Empire. This empire, at that time and for 300 years afterward until the conversion of the Emperor *Constantine*, persecuted the chosen Church of Rome, so much so that the first thirty-three Bishops of Rome, up until *St. Sylvester*, were all martyrs.

<margin>2 Peter 3.</margin>
<margin>1 Peter 5.</margin>
<margin>* See the Annotation upon St. James epistle chapter 2, verse 21.</margin>
As for the subject he writes about, he indicates it himself in these words: 
> "Behold, this second Epistle I write to you, my dearest, in which (Epistles) I stir up your sincere mind by way of a reminder, so that you may be mindful of those words," etc. 
He says this regarding both letters together. And again, concerning the first letter for the same purpose, he says in another place: 
> "I have written briefly, beseeching and testifying that this is the true grace of God, in which you stand." 
For at that time, there were certain deceivers (as *St. Augustine* has also told us) who went about teaching "*Faith alone*," as if good works were neither necessary nor meritorious <note>Deserving of spiritual reward or favor in the eyes of God</note>. There were also great persecutions intended to terrify them into denying Christ and all of his religion. He therefore encourages them accordingly not to forsake the faith, neither due to persecution nor by deception. However, in the first letter, his encouragement is mainly against persecution; and in the second, it is mainly against deception. The first epistle is noted to be very similar to *St. Paul's* epistle to the Ephesians, even in its wording, and it is so filled with references to Scripture that it seems as if he speaks of nothing else.

The time when the first was written is uncertain; the second was written a little before his death, as is gathered from his words in that same letter (*Chapter 1, verse 14*).

-> C H A P T E R  II. <-

<margin>Spiritual hosts and Priests.</margin> 5. *Spiritual hosts <note>meaning sacrifices</note>.*] Here we see that as he speaks of spiritual hosts, which every Christian man offers, so he speaks not properly of priesthood when he makes all Priests, but of a spiritual priesthood. Which spiritual priesthood was also in all the Jews: but the priesthood (properly so called) was only in the sons of Aaron, and they offered the sacrifices (properly so called) which none besides might offer.

<margin>Obedience to temporal princes.</margin> 13. *Be subject.*] Not only our Master Christ, but the Apostles and all Christians were ever charged by such as thought to bring them into hatred with Princes, with disobedience to kings and temporal Magistrates; therefore both * St. Paul and this Apostle do specially warn the faithful, that <margin>Romans 13.</margin> they give no occasion by their ill demeanor to secular Princes, that the Heathen should count them disobedient or seditious workers against the States of the world.

<margin>God instituted the Spiritual government in more excellent manner than the temporal.</margin> 13. *To every human creature.*] So he calls the temporal Magistrate elected by the people, or holding their Sovereignty by birth and carnal propagation, ordained for the worldly wealth, peace, and prosperity of the subjects: to put a difference between that human Superiority and the spiritual Rulers and government, guiding and governing the people to a higher end, and instituted by God himself immediately. For Christ did expressly constitute the form of government used ever since in the Church. He made one the chief, placing Peter in the Supremacy: he called the Apostles <margin>Acts 1.<br/>Acts 20.</margin> and Disciples, giving them their several authorities. Afterward * God guided the lot for the choice of St. Matthias in Judas' place: and the Holy Ghost expressly and namely separated and chose Paul and Barnabas unto their Apostolical function: and generally the Apostle says of all spiritual Rulers, *The Holy Ghost has placed you to rule the Church of God.*

And although all power be of God, and kings rule by him, yet that is no otherwise, but by his ordinary concurrence, and providence, whereby he procures the earthly commodity <note>benefit</note> or wealth of men, by maintaining of due superiority and subjection one towards another, and by giving power to the people and Commonwealth to choose to themselves some kind or form of Regiment <note>system of government</note>, under which they be content to live for their preservation in peace and tranquility. But Spiritual superiority is far more excellent, as in more excellent sort depending, not of man’s ordinance, election, or (as this Apostle speaks) creation, but of the Holy Ghost, who is always resident in the Church (which is Christ’s body mystical, and therefore another manner of Com-<meta>monwealth</meta>

Lest therefore the people, being then in so precise a manner always warned of the excellence of their Spiritual governors <note>The clergy and Church hierarchy.</note> and of their obedience toward them, might neglect their duties to Temporal Magistrates—especially being infidels, and many times tyrants and persecutors of the faith, as Nero and others were then—therefore St. Peter here warns them to be subject, for their bodies and goods, and other temporal things, even to the worldly Princes, both infidels and Christians, whom he calls human creatures <note>This refers to the human origin of civil government institutions, distinguishing them from the divine origin of the Church.</note>.

<margin>Heretical translation. The King's excellence of power is in respect to the nobility and lay magistrates under him.</margin>
13. *To the king as excelling.*] Some simple heretics and others also who were not unlearned at the beginning, for lack of better scriptural evidence, would have proved by this that the king was head of the Church and above all Spiritual rulers. To make it sound better that way, they falsely translated it as, *To the king as to the chief head*, in the Bible of the year 1562 <note>This refers to the "Great Bible" or early Protestant translations that used language supporting Royal Supremacy.</note>. But it is evident that he calls the king the <term>precellent<gloss>surpassing others; preeminent</gloss></term> or more excellent, in respect to his Vicegerents <note>Deputies or representatives.</note> which he calls Dukes or Governors that are at his appointment; he does not mean "excelling" in respect to Popes, Bishops, or Priests in their rule over men's souls. Clergy could not be under such Kings or Emperors as the Apostle speaks of in that spiritual capacity, any more than the kings or Emperors of that time could be heads of the Church, being Heathen men and not even members of it, much less its chief members. See a notable passage in St. Ignatius's *Epistle to the Smyrnaeans* <note>original: "ep. ad Smyrnenses"</note>, where he exhorts them first to honor God, next the Bishop, and then the king.

<margin>Christian Princes have no more right to be supreme heads in spiritual causes than the Heathen.</margin>
This is an invincible demonstration that this text does not support any spiritual claim for earthly kings, because it gives no more to any Prince than what may and ought to be granted to a Heathen Magistrate. Neither is there anything in all the New Testament that proves the Prince to be the head or chief governor of the Church in spiritual or Ecclesiastical causes any more than it proves any heathen Emperor of Rome to have been so. For they were bound in temporal things to obey the heathen, being lawful kings; to be subject to them, even for conscience's sake; to keep their temporal laws; to pay them tribute; to pray for them; and to do all other natural duties. The scriptures bind us to do no more than this even for Christian kings.

<margin>Libertines.</margin>

<margin>Deadly sins of Princes or Superiors do not exempt the subjects from obedience, as Wycliffe held.</margin>
18. *But also the wayward.*] The <term>Wycliffites<gloss>Followers of John Wycliffe, who taught that authority is forfeited by those in a state of mortal sin.</gloss></term> and their followers in these days sometimes try to move the people to sedition by teaching that masters and magistrates lose their authority over their servants and subjects if they fall into deadly sin, and that the people in that case need not in conscience obey them. This is a pernicious and false doctrine, as is plain by this passage, where we are expressly commanded to obey even the ill-conditioned <note>Original: "vvaivvard," meaning perverse or difficult to please.</note>, provided they command nothing against God. ## ANNOTATIONS
### CHAP. III.

<margin>
18.
Christ in soul descended into hell, while his body lay in the grave.
</margin>
19. **To them that were in prison.]** St. Augustine, at the beginning of his 99th Epistle, confesses this passage is exceedingly hard to understand, and contains many difficulties which he could never explain to his own satisfaction. Yet to heretics, this and all other texts seem easy; they do not doubt that the meaning is whatever they themselves imagine, regardless of what other men think. St. Augustine finds himself sure of only this: that Christ’s descent into hell in soul after his death is plainly proved by this passage. He declares there that this is consistent with various other express
<margin>
Acts 2.
The Calvinists, by denying St. Augustine’s judgment, are (by St. Augustine’s judgment) infidels.
</margin>
words of Holy Writ, namely to this same Apostle’s sermon in *Acts 2.* And at length he concludes thus: "Therefore who but an infidel will deny that Christ was in hell?" <note>original: "Quis ergo nisi infidelis negauerit fuisse apud inferos Christum?"</note> You see then that Calvin and all his followers are infidels, for in place of this descent of Christ in soul after his death, they have invented another desperate kind of Christ being in "hell" while he was yet alive on the Cross. St. Athanasius also (in his epistle cited by St. Epiphanius in the beginning of *heresy 77*, and in his book *On the Incarnation of the Word* near the beginning), St. Cyril in *On the Right Faith to Theodosius*, Oecumenius, and various others upon this passage, prove Christ’s descending to hell. They likewise declare, based on the following words, that he preached to the spirits or souls of men detained in hell or in prison.

<margin>
Certain difficulties about which St. Augustine is uncertain.
</margin>
But whether this word "prison" or "hell" refers to the lower place of the damned, or to the *Limbo of the Fathers* <term>Limbo of the Fathers: traditionally called "Abraham’s bosom," the place where the righteous dead waited for Christ's redemption</term> called Abraham’s bosom, or some other place of temporal punishment; and to whom he preached there, and who were delivered by his preaching or presence there, and who those were called "unbelieving in the days of Noah"—all these things St. Augustine calls great depths, confessing himself unable to reach the full understanding of it. He only holds fast and assured to this article of our faith: that Christ delivered none assigned to damnation in the lowest hell, and yet he does not
<margin>
Purgatory.
</margin>
doubt that he released several out of places of pain there, which cannot be any place other than Purgatory. See the said Epistle, where he also suggests other expositions to explain the many difficulties of this hard text, which would be too long to rehearse here; our special purpose being only to briefly note the things that touch upon the controversies of this time.

<margin>
Who were the unbelieving persons of whom the Apostle speaks here.
</margin>
20. **Unbelieving sometime.]** Those who interpret the previous words as Christ’s descent to hell to deliver certain people detained there, explain this verse not as referring to those who died in their infidelity or without any faith in God (for such were not delivered), but either as referring to some who were once unbelieving and afterward repented before their death, or rather and especially to those who were otherwise faithful but did not trust Noah’s preaching by his work and word—that God would destroy the world by water. These people, being otherwise good men, were sorry for their error when the event occurred and died physically by the flood, but were in a state of salvation. Being punished for their fault in the next life, they were delivered by Christ’s descent there, and not they only, but all others in a similar condition. For the Apostle gives those of Noah's time only as an example.

<margin>
Noah’s Ark and the water, a figure of Christ’s Cross and Baptism.
</margin>
21. **Of the like form.]** The water bearing up the Ark from sinking, and the persons in it from drowning, was a figure of Baptism, which likewise saves the worthy receivers from everlasting perishing. "As Noah," says St. Augustine, "with his family, was delivered by the water and the wood, so the family of Christ is delivered by Baptism signed with Christ’s Passion on the Cross." <note>original: "Li. 12. Cont: Faustum c. 14."</note>
<margin>
ibid. v. 17.
Book 12, Against Faustus, ch. 14.
</margin>
Again he says, "that as the water saved none outside of the Ark, but was rather their destruction; so the Sacrament of Baptism received outside the Catholic Church at the hands of heretics or schismatics—though it be the same water and Sacrament that the Catholic Church has—yet profits no one to salvation, but rather works their perdition." This, however, is not meant for cases of extreme necessity, when a 
<margin>
Baptism received from heretics or schismatics; when it is damnable, and when it is not.
</margin>
person might die without the said Sacrament unless he took it from a heretic or schismatic. Neither is it meant for the case of infants, for whom the Sacrament is the cause of salvation; they are not at fault for receiving it at the hands of the unfaithful,
<margin>
Epistle 57.
</margin>
though their parents and friends who offer them to such people to be baptized are in no small fault. St. Jerome, writing to Pope Damasus of Rome, compares that See to the Ark, and those who communicate with it to those who were saved in the Ark; all other schismatics and heretics he compares to the rest who were drowned.

<margin>
The ceremonies of Baptism, namely "I renounce," etc.
</margin>
21. **The examination of a good conscience.]** The Apostle seems to allude here to the very form of Catholic Baptism, containing certain questions and solemn promises made regarding the articles of the Christian faith, a good life, and the renouncing of Satan and all his pomps and works. No doubt—regardless of what the Calvinists think of them—these are the very Apostolic ceremonies used in the administration of this Sacrament. See *St. Dionysius at the end of Ecclesiastical Hierarchy; St. Cyril, book 12 on John, ch. 64; St. Augustine, epistle 23; St. Basil, On the Holy Spirit, ch. 12 and 15; St. Ambrose, On those initiated into the mysteries, ch. 2, 3, and 4.*

## A N N O T A T I O N S
### CHAP. IV.

9. *Charity covereth.* <margin>Not only faith.</margin> <margin>Works of mercy.</margin> Faith alone cannot justify, seeing that charity also causes the remission of sins. And by saying "charity," he means love and charitable works toward our neighbors; the Scriptures especially attribute the power to extinguish sins to these works of mercy. See St. Augustine, <note>original: "c. 69 Enchiridij"</note> *Chapter 69 of the Enchiridion (The Manual)* and <note>original: "tract. 1. in ep. 1. Io. c. 2."</note> *Tractate 1 on the First Epistle of John, Chapter 2*, and the Venerable Bede’s commentary *upon this place.* In the same sense, the Holy Scriptures commonly recommend alms and deeds of mercy to us for the redemption of our sins. *Proverbs chapter 10; Ecclesiasticus 12 verse 2; Daniel chapter 4 verse 24.*

17. *That judgement begin.* <margin>The better men are most afflicted in this life.</margin> In this era of the New Testament, the faithful and all those who intend to live godly lives (especially the Clergy) must first and foremost be subject to God’s chastisement and temporal afflictions, which are here called "judgment." The Apostle records this for the comfort and encouragement of Catholic Christians, who were, at the time of this writing, being exceedingly persecuted by heathen princes and people.

18. *If the just.* <margin>The just man himself is hardly saved.</margin> <margin>Against the vain security of "faith alone."</margin> This does not mean that a person who dies in a state of justice and in the favor of God can afterward doubt their salvation or be rejected by God. Rather, it means that the just are subject to assaults, temptations, troubles, and the danger of falling away from God in this life. They also must often give a strict account and be temporally chastised in the next life <note>A reference to the doctrine of Purgatory</note>; thus, they cannot be saved without great watchfulness, fear, trembling, much labor, and discipline. This is quite contrary to the Protestant doctrine, which places no justice in anything but faith alone, denies that anyone is made truly just in deed and truth, and teaches men to be so certain of their salvation that even a person who has lived wickedly their whole life—if they only have "faith" at their death (meaning they steadfastly believe they are one of the elect)—shall be as certain of salvation immediately after death as the most virtuous person in the world.

---

# ANNOTATIONS
### CHAP. V.

<margin>The term "Senior" in the common Latin translation.</margin>
1. *Seniors [Elders].*] Although the Latin word *Senior* is not strictly reserved for holy orders in common speech—neither in Latin nor in our own language—it is plain that the Greek word *Presbyter*, which the Apostle uses here, is also here (as is common in other places of the New Testament) a word signifying an Ecclesiastical office, and not merely age. It is the same as saying Priest or Bishop. For the Apostle himself, being of that order, speaks (as is plain by his words) to such as had the charge of souls, saying, *Feed the flock of God which is among you.*

<meta>The catchword at the bottom of the page is "Because," indicating the start of the next section of annotations or text on the following page.</meta>

<summary>This page concludes the First Epistle of Peter, focusing on the duties of the clergy to lead by example rather than for profit, and urging the faithful to remain humble and vigilant against spiritual adversity. It identifies the "Babylon" church as a sister congregation, often interpreted as the early church in Rome.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the First Epistle of Peter, specifically focusing on the instructions to the elders (priests) in Chapter 5. It transitions from moral exhortations to a scholarly and polemical defense of the terms "Clergy" and "Priest," and argues for the historical presence of St. Peter in Rome.</meta>

<page-num>665</page-num>
<header>CHAPTER 5. OF ST. PETER.</header>

Because we follow the common Latin translation <note>The Vulgate</note>, we use the terms *Seniors* and *Senior*; otherwise, we could and should say according to the Greek, *The Priests therefore I beseech, myself a fellow-priest with them.* St. Jerome reads it this way <note>original Latin: "Presbyteros compresbyter"</note> and explains it in his 85th letter. Erasmus translates it this way, and even Beza <note>Theodore Beza, a major Protestant reformer</note> himself does so.

<margin>lording it over <note>original Greek: κατακυριεύοντες</note>. Matthew 20:25.</margin>
<margin>Not superiority but tyranny and lordliness is forbidden among the Clergy.</margin>
3. **Overruling.]** Neither superiority, preeminence, sovereignty, nor rule on one side—nor obedience, subjection, and inferiority on the other—are forbidden in the Clergy. Instead, tyranny, pride, and ambitious domination are forbidden, while humility, meekness, and moderation are commended in <term>Ecclesiastical|Related to the organized Christian Church and its hierarchy</term> officers. The Greek word here for "ruling" or "overruling" is the same one our Savior uses in the Gospel regarding the tyrannical rule of secular pagan <note>original: "Heathen"</note> princes, telling his Apostles that it shall not be so among them. Thus, the "prince of the Apostles" <note>St. Peter</note> teaches his brothers, the Church rulers.

<margin>Heretical translation.

The name of Clergy and Clerk.</margin>
3. **The Clergy.]** Some of the new English translations <note>referring to Protestant versions</note> translate this corruptly as *Parishes*; others as *heritages*. Both do so to avoid the most well-known, true, and common word in all Christian languages, namely, *Clergy*. This is a word that, by ancient usage and in agreement with the Holy Scriptures, is specifically designated for the <term>Spirituality|The body of individuals ordained for religious service; the clergy</term> or Clergy. Although in another more common sense it may apply to all of Christ’s chosen heritage—laypeople as well as Priests—the Protestants prefer that common meaning because they wish to eliminate any difference between the laity and the clergy. But the Holy Fathers thought very differently even from the beginning. Concerning this, see St. Cyprian’s letters 4, 5, 6, etc., and St. Jerome’s 2nd letter to Nepotianus, chapter 5, where he interprets this word. "Therefore," he says, "a <term>Clericus|A member of the clergy</term>—that is, a clergyman who serves the Church of Christ—should first interpret his own name. Once the meaning of the name is declared, let him strive to be what he is called. If *kleros* <note>original Greek: κλῆρος</note> in Greek is called *Sors* <note>original Latin: "lot" or "portion"</note> in Latin, then they are called Clergy <note>original Latin: Clerici</note> because they are of the lot of our Lord, or because our Lord himself is the lot or portion of clergymen, etc."

<margin>inheritance <note>original Greek: κληρονομία</note>.
lot <note>original Greek: κλῆρος</note>.
portion <note>original Greek: μερίς</note>.</margin>
This title was undoubtedly taken from the Holy Scriptures, specifically Numbers 18 and Deuteronomy 18, where God is called the inheritance, lot, and portion of the Priests and Levites. Even now, when men enter the Clergy, they say, *The Lord is the portion of my inheritance* <note>original Latin: "Dominus pars hæreditatis meæ"</note>. It comes especially from the New Testament (Acts 1:17, 25 and 8:21), where the "lot" or office of the Church ministry is called by this word *Clerus* <note>original Greek: κλῆρος</note>. Regarding the "Venerable Priests' crown" <note>the tonsure, or shaved crown of a priest's head</note>, see the reasons why this holy state, being separated by name from the Laity, also wears a round <note>original: "rōd"</note> crown on their head for distinction (Bede, *History of the English People*, Book 5, chapter 22).

<margin>The heavenly crown of Doctors and preachers.</margin>
4. **Crown of glory.]** Just as everlasting life shall be the reward of all the righteous, so the preachers and Pastors who do well shall receive that reward in a more excellent degree, expressed here by the words *Crown of glory*. This follows the saying of Daniel (chapter 12): *Those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, others to everlasting rebuke. But those who are learned shall shine as the brightness of the firmament, and those who instruct many in justice shall be like stars for all eternity.*

<margin>St. Peter writes from Babylon, that is, Rome.

Why Rome was called Babylon.</margin>
31. **That is in Babylon.]** The Protestants show themselves here (as in all places where any controversy exists, or that goes against them) to be most dishonest and biased handlers of God’s word. The ancient fathers—specifically St. Jerome in his *Catalog of Ecclesiastical Writers* under the entry for 'Mark'; Eusebius (Book 2, chapter 14 of his history); Oecumenius on this passage; and many more—agree that Rome is meant by the word "Babylon" here, just as it is in the 16th and 17th chapters of the <term>Apocalypse|The Book of Revelation</term>. They state plainly that St. Peter wrote this Epistle at Rome, which is called Babylon because of its resemblance to the great city of Babylon in <term>Chaldea|An ancient region in Mesopotamia</term> (where the Jews were captives). This resemblance lay in its magnificence, its status as a world power <note>original: "Monarchie"</note>, the gathering and confusion of all peoples and tongues, and because it was, before Christ and long after, the seat of all pagan <note>original: "Ethnike"</note> superstition and idolatry, and the slaughterhouse of the Apostles and other Christian men, where the pagan Emperors kept their chief residence. See St. Leo’s 1st Sermon on the Nativity of Peter and Paul.

<margin>The Protestants want Babylon to signify Rome in other places but not here.</margin>
This being most clear, and consistent with what follows regarding St. Mark (whom all church histories agree was Peter's student at Rome and that he wrote his Gospel there), our adversaries still deny he was ever there. They fear the logical conclusion of Peter’s or the Pope's <term>supremacy|The doctrine of the Pope's authority</term> at Rome, so they deny he was ever there, or that this letter was written there, or that "Babylon" here signifies Rome. Instead, they say Peter wrote this letter in Babylon in Chaldea, even though they have never read in the Scriptures or any other holy or secular history that this Apostle was ever in that town. See their shameless bias: here they say Babylon is *not* taken for Rome, because it would follow that Peter was at Rome. But in the Book of Revelation, where all evil is said of Babylon, they insist it signifies nothing but Rome—and the Roman Church specifically—not (as the Fathers interpret it) the temporary state of the pagan Empire there. Thus, they follow no rule but the advantage of their own <term>heresy|Beliefs contrary to established church doctrine</term>. See the annotations on the last chapter of Romans (verse 16) and on the 17th of the Apocalypse (verse 5).

<margin>The Protestants argue about the timing of Peter being at Rome.</margin>
And as for their arguing over the calculation of the time of his arrival there, the number of years he stayed, and the differences that seem to exist among Church writers regarding these dates, read Bishop <note>original: "B."</note> Fisher and others who substantially answer all such trivial objections <note>original: "cavils"</note>. If such argumentative reasoning were allowed, we could hardly believe any of the principal things recorded in Church histories or even in the Scriptures themselves. Concerning the time of...

<header>THE SECOND EPISTLE. CHAP. V.</header>

<margin>Many things most true (even in the Scriptures) are not agreed upon concerning the time.</margin>
Regarding Christ’s fleeing into Egypt, the coming of the Sages <note>The Magi or Three Wise Men</note> to adore him, and even the years of his age and the time of his death, all ancient writers do not agree. Concerning the day of his last supper and the institution of the holy Sacrament, there is also a diversity of opinions. Shall we therefore infer that he never died, and that the other things never were? Can the Heretics <note>The Protestant reformers, from the author's perspective</note> reconcile all the histories that seem to have contradictions even in holy Scripture? Can they tell us certainly when David first came to Saul, and the like? Do they doubt whether the world was ever created, because the count of the years is diverse? Do they not believe that Paradise ever was, because no man knows where it is? and such other like things, infinite to rehearse? Which, when they were done, were plain and known things in the world: and now for us to call them to an account, after so many years, ages, and worlds, is but sophistication and plain infidelity. And this sect of the Protestants, standing only upon detraction and negatives, and dealing with our religion even as Julian, Porphyry, and Lucian <note>Three famous ancient critics and "enemies" of early Christianity</note> did, it is an easy thing for them to bestow their time in picking of quarrels.

# ANNOTATIONS
## CHAP. I.

<margin>Good works must concur with God’s predestination for its effect.</margin>
<margin><note>original Greek: "διὰ τῶν καλῶν ἔργων" (dià tōn kalōn ergōn)</note> through good works</margin>
10. *By good works.*] Here we see that God’s eternal predestination and election consist with good works: indeed, that the certainty and effect thereof is procured by man’s free will and good works, and that our well-doing is a means for us to attain the effect of God’s predestination, which is life everlasting. Therefore, it is a desperate folly and a great sign of reprobate persons to say, "If I be predestined, do what I will, I shall be saved." Nay, the Apostle says, "If thou hope to be one of the predestined (for know it thou canst not), do well, that thou mayest be the more assured to attain to that which thou hopest for: or, make it sure by good works." The Protestants, in such cases, not much liking these words, *by good works*—though the Latin versions have it universally, and some Greek copies also, as Beza <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), a major Protestant theologian and successor to Calvin.</note> confesses—leave them out in their translations, by their usual policy.

<margin>The heretics (according to their custom) exclude this meaning altogether by their false translation.</margin>
<margin>Oecumenius on this place. <note>Oecumenius was a 10th-century Greek commentator; Gagnæus was a 16th-century French theologian.</note> Gagnæus.</margin>
15. *After my decease also.*] These words, though they may be easily altered by construction into various senses which are not untrue, yet the correspondence of the parts of the sentence going before and following gives most plainly this meaning: that, as during his life he would not omit to put them in memory of the things he taught them, so after his death (which he knew should be shortly) he would not fail to endeavor that they might be mindful of the same. This signifies that his care over them should not cease by death, and that by his intercession before God after his departure, he would do the same thing for them that he did before in his life by teaching and preaching. This is the sense that the *Greek Scholia* <note>Ancient marginal commentaries on the New Testament.</note> speak of, and this is most proper to the text, and consonant to the old usage of this Apostle and other Apostolic Saints and fathers of the primitive Church.

<margin>St. Peter’s Pastoral care and protection of the Church after his death.</margin>
<margin>Luke 22:32. John 21.</margin>
St. Clement <note>Regarded as the third successor to St. Peter as Pope.</note>, in his Epistle to St. James, our Lord’s brother, witnesses that St. Peter, encouraging him to take the charge of the Apostolic Roman See after his decease, promised that after his departure he would not cease to pray for him and his flock, thereby to ease him of his Pastoral burden. *Volume 1 of the Councils, Epistle 1 of St. Clement, in the beginning.* And St. Leo the Great, one of his successors in the said See, often attributes the good administration and government thereof to St. Peter’s prayers and assistance: namely in these goodly words from *Sermon 3 on the anniversary of his assumption to the Pontificate*: 
> We are much bound (says he) to give thanks to our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, who has given so great power to him whom he made the Prince of the whole Church: so that if in our time also anything be done well and be rightly ordered by us, it is to be imputed to his works and his government, to whom it was said, *And thou being converted, confirm thy brethren:* and to whom our Lord after his resurrection said thrice, *Feed my sheep.* Which now also, without doubt, the godly Pastor executes, confirming us with his exhortations, and not ceasing to pray for us, that we be overcome by no temptation, etc.

<margin>The Saints in heaven pray for the living.</margin>
Indeed, it was a common thing in the primitive Church among the ancient Christians, and always since among the faithful, to make a covenant in their lifetime that whichever of them went to heaven before the other, he should pray for his friend and fellow yet alive. See the Ecclesiastical history of the holy virgin and Martyr Potamiæna <note>An early Christian martyr of Alexandria (d. c. 205 AD).</note>, promising at the hour of her martyrdom that after her death she would procure mercy from God for Basilides, one of the soldiers that led her to execution, and so she did. *Eusebius, book 6, chapter 4.* Also St. Cyprian, *Epistle 57 at the end*: *Let us (says he) pray mutually one for another, and whichever of us two shall by God’s clemency be first called for, let his love continue, and his prayer not cease for his brethren and sisters in the world.* So said this holy Martyr at that time when Christians were so far from Calvinism (which abhors the prayers of Saints and praying to them) that, to be sure, they bargained beforehand to have the martyrs and other Saints pray for them. The same St. Cyprian also in his book *On the discipline and dress of virgins*, at the end, after a godly exhortation made to the holy Virgins or Nuns in his time, speaks thus to them:
> <note>original Latin: "Tantùm tunc mementote noſtri, cum incipiet in vobis virginitas honorari."</note> *Only then remember us, when your virginity shall begin to be honored.*
That is, after their departure.

<margin>Feasts of holy Virgins.</margin>
Wherein he insinuates the use of the Catholic Church in keeping the festival days and other duties toward the holy Virgins in heaven. St. Jerome <note>Hierom; a prominent Father of the Church known for translating the Vulgate Bible.</note> also in the same manner speaks to Heliodorus, saying that when he is once in heaven, then he will pray for him who exhorted and incited him to the blessed state of the Monastical life. *Epistle 1, chapter 2.*

<margin>Invocation of Saints.</margin>
And so does he speak to the virtuous matron Paula after her death, desiring her to pray for him in his old age, affirming that she shall the more easily obtain it, the nearer she is now joined to Christ in heaven. *In the Epitaph of Paula, at the end.* It would be too long to report how St. Augustine desires to be helped by St. Cyprian’s prayers (then and long before a Saint in heaven) toward the understanding of the truth concerning the peace and regiment of the Church. *Book 5, On Baptism against the Donatists, chapter 17.* And in another place the same holy Doctor alleges the said St. Cyprian saying that great numbers d —

### CHAPTER II. OF ST. PETER.

...members of our parents, brothers, children, friends, and others, await us with great concern and care for our salvation, being certain of their own. <note>St. Augustine, *On the Predestination of the Saints*, Book 1, Chapter 14.</note> St. Gregory Nazianzen, in his orations in praise of St. Cyprian at the end, and of St. Basil also at the end, declares how they pray for the people. He invokes these two saints there, as all the ancient fathers did—both saints in general and (as the occasion required) their specific patrons. Deipara," from the Greek *Theotokos*.</note> prayed to our Blessed Lady using the same terms of Advocate, Hope, and Reconciler that the faithful still use today, but which the Protestants cannot tolerate. <note>References: St. Basil's *Homily on the 40 Martyrs*; St. Athanasius's *Sermon on the Holy Mother of God*; St. Hilary on Psalm 124; St. Chrysostom's *Homily 66 to the people of Antioch*; and Theodoret's *On the Cure of Greek Affections*, Book 8.</note> Finally, all the church fathers are full of these things; they knew the meaning of Scripture and the intent of the Holy Spirit better than these new [Protestant] interpreters do.

<margin>Private and imaginative interpretations.</margin>
20. *Private.*] The Scriptures cannot be correctly explained by the private spirit or imagination of every common reader, but must be understood by the same Spirit through which they were written, which resides in the Church.

*Just as there were not only prophets but also false prophets in the Old Testament, so now there shall be masters of heresy, leading both themselves and their followers to damnation. 4 He proclaims their damnation using historical examples (while comforting virtuous Catholics and true believers with the example of Lot). # A N N O T A T I O N S
## C H A P. III.

<margin>The heretical proud spirit of private interpretation of Scriptures.</margin>
16. *Certain things hard.*] This is a plain text to convince the Protestants, who (as all heretics usually do and have done from the beginning) say the Scriptures are easy to understand, and therefore may be not only read safely, but also expounded boldly by all the people, as well unlearned as learned: and consequently every one by himself and his private spirit, without respect for the expositions of the learned fathers, or waiting for the judgment of the Church, its Pastors, and Prelates, may determine and make choice of such sense as he himself likes or thinks agreeable. For this is partly their saying, and partly the necessary consequence of their foolish opinion, which admits nothing but the bare Scriptures. And Luther said that the Scriptures were more plain than all the fathers' commentaries; and so all were to be superfluous but the Bible. <note>original: "Præfat. assert. art. damnat." — Preface to the Assertion of the Articles Condemned (referring to Martin Luther's response to the papal bull of 1520).</note>

<margin>The Scriptures are hard, namely S. Paul’s epistles, especially where he speaks of justification by faith.</margin>
Against all which devilish and seditious arrogance—tending to make the people esteem themselves learned or sufficient without their Pastors' and spiritual rulers' help to guide themselves in all matters of doctrine and doubts in religion—the holy Apostle here tells and forewarns the faithful that the Scriptures are full of difficulty, and especially Saint Paul’s epistles above all other parts of holy writ. He warns that ignorant men and unstable or fantastical fellows, tossed to and fro with every blast of doctrine and heresy, abuse, pervert, and misconstrue them to their own damnation. And Saint Augustine says <margin>* On Faith and Works, chapter 14.</margin> that the special difficulty in Saint Paul’s epistles, which ignorant and evil men so pervert and which Saint Peter means, is his difficult speech and high commendation of that faith which he says justifies. This the ignorant, even from the Apostles' time and much more now, have misconstrued and do so today, as though he had meant that faith alone without good works could justify or save a man. Against which wicked collection and abuse of Saint Paul’s words, the said father says all these Canonical or Catholic epistles were written.

<margin>The Protestants' idle distinction between difficulty in the Epistles and difficulty in the things.</margin>
But the Heretics here, to evade the matter and to creep out after their fashion, answer that Saint Peter does not say Saint Paul’s epistles are hard, but that many *things* in them are hard. This may be for Catholics an example of their sophistical evasions from the evidence of God’s word. As though it were not all one to say, "Such an author or writer is hard," and "There are many things in that writer hard to be understood." For, whether it be that the argument and matter are high and beyond common capacity—such as that of predestination, reprobation, the calling of the Gentiles, and justifying faith—or whether it be his manner of style and writing that is obscure; all prove that his epistles are hard, and other Scriptures also: because

# CHAP. III. OF S. PETER.

<margin>The Greek copies have both: some ἐν οἷς <note>original: "en hois"</note>, meaning "in which things"; some ἐν αἷς <note>original: "en hais"</note>, meaning "in which epistles."</margin>
S. Peter here affirmeth that by reason of the difficulties in them, whether in the style, or in the depth of the matter, the ignorant and unstable (such as Heretics be) do pervert his writings, as also other Scriptures, to their own damnation. Whereby it is plain that it is a very dangerous thing for such as be ignorant, or for wild-witted fellows, to read the Scriptures. For such conditioned men be they that become Heretics, and through ignorance, pride, and private fantasy, meeting with hard places of S. Paul's epistles or other Scriptures, breed Heresies.

<margin>Not only the matter, but the style of the Scriptures is hard.</margin>
<margin>
Ps. 118.
Act. 8.
Luc. 24. v. 45.
</margin>
And that not only the things treated of in the holy Scriptures, but also that the very manner of writing and enditing thereof, is high and hard, and purposely by God's providence appointed to be written in such sort, see S. Augustine in book 2 of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 6, and epistle 119. S. Ambrose, epistle 44 in the beginning. S. Jerome to Paulinus, epistle 103 chapters 5, 6, 7; who also (in epistle 65, chapter 1) saith, that in his old age when he should rather have taught than be taught, he went as far as Alexandria, only to hear Didymus <note>Didymus the Blind (c. 313–398), a famous theologian and head of the Catechetical School of Alexandria</note>, and to have his help for the understanding of the Scriptures, and confesseth with great thanks to the said Didymus, that he learned of him that which before he knew not. David saith, *Give me understanding, and I will search thy law* <note>Psalm 118:34 in the Vulgate numbering; Psalm 119:34 in modern Bibles</note>. The Eunuch in the Acts said, *How can I understand without an interpreter?* [Acts 8:31]. The Apostles, till Christ opened their sense to understand the scriptures, could not understand them [Luke 24:45]. The holy Doctors <note>Doctor: a title for an eminent saint whose writings have significantly advantaged the Church</note> by continual study, watching, fasting, and praying, had much ado to understand them: that great clerk <note>clerk: a scholar or man of letters</note> S. Augustine confessing in the aforesaid epistle 119, chapter 21, that there were many more things that he understood not, than that he understood. The Heretics say the fathers did commonly err. And how could such great wise learned men be deceived in reading and expounding the Scriptures, if they were not hard? and if they were hard to them, how are they easy to these new masters the Heretics? finally, why do they write so many new glosses <note>gloss: a brief explanatory note or interpretation</note>, scholies <note>scholies: grammatical or logic-based commentaries</note>, commentaries, as a cart cannot carry? Why do Luther, Zwingli, Calvin, and their Companions agree no better upon the interpretation of the Scriptures, if they be not hard? whereat stumbled all the old heretics and the new—Arius, Macedonius, Vigilantius, Nestorius, Eutyches, Berengarius, Wycliffe, Protestants, Puritans, Anabaptists, and the rest—but at the hardness of the Scriptures? They be hard then to understand, and Heretics pervert them to their own damnation.

## THE ARGUMENT OF SAINT JOHN’S THREE EPISTLES.

<margin>Pope Hyginus, Epistle 1, Volume 1 of the Councils. Augustine, Book 2 of *Questions on the Gospels*, Question 39.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative initial letter 'O' containing a portrait of an elderly bearded man, presumably Saint John, holding a book.</image-desc> Concerning Saint John, much was said in the "Argument" <note>An "Argument" in this context is a formal introduction or summary of a book's themes and purpose.</note> preceding his Gospel. Now here follow his three Epistles: one addressed to all Catholics (though some ancient writers call it <note>original: "Ad Parthos"</note> *To the Parthians*); the other two being very short, addressed to a certain Lady and to one Gaius. The purpose of them all is to bear witness to the certainty of the Catholic faith and to exhort them to continue steadfast in it. He also encourages them to love the Catholic Church and, in doing so, to neither become heretics nor schismatics <note>Schismatics are those who create a division or "schism" within the Church, even if they hold the same basic beliefs.</note>. Rather, they are to avoid all such people as the forerunners of Antichrist. He reminds them that Catholics have no need to attend the schools of such teachers, for they have at home, within the Catholic Church, the doctrine of the Holy Ghost himself, who was given to the Church visibly in the beginning to lead her into all truth and to remain with her forever. Therefore he says:

<margin>1 John 2:24.</margin>
> That which you have heard from the beginning, let it abide in you. 

Likewise a little after, in verse 27 and Epistle 2, verse 6: *This is the commandment: that as you have heard from the beginning, you walk in the same, because many seducers are gone out into the world* (and verses 8 and 9).

<margin>Augustine, *On Faith and Works*, chapter 14.</margin>
And he does not only speak thus in general terms, but also specifically identifies the points which the heretics of that time were calling into question. Some errors concerned Christ himself: for they denied that Jesus is Christ, that he is the true Son of God, or that he is incarnate <note>Incarnate: God taking on human flesh.</note> (1 John 2:22 and 2 John 7). It was against such people that he wrote his Gospel as well, as he indicates there (John 20:31). Other points concern our justification, arguing against the idea of "faith alone" and in favor of good works, as Saint Augustine also noted in the words cited previously. Upon this point he says: *If we say we have society with God, and walk in darkness, we lie* (1 John 1). Again:
<margin>1 John 2 and 5.</margin>
*He that says he knows God, and keeps not his commandments, is a liar.* Again: *This is the charity of God, that we keep his commandments, and his commandments are not heavy.* Finally: *Children, let no man seduce you; he that does justice is just, even as he is just* (1 John 3:7–9, likewise 2:29). Indeed, throughout all three Epistles, he emphasizes the importance of performing good works and keeping the commandments against the heresy of "faith only" <note>The author is likely contrasting the Catholic position with the Protestant doctrine of "Sola Fide" (faith alone) prevalent during the time this commentary was written.</note>.

# ANNOTATIONS
## CHAPTER I.

<margin>No salvation but in the Society of the Church.</margin> 3. *You may have society.*] Saint John shows clearly that whoever desires to be a partakers with God must first be united to the Church’s society. They must learn that faith and receive those Sacraments which the Disciples received from the Truth itself <note>referring to Jesus Christ</note>, who lived among them in the flesh. This is what <term>Venerable Bede</term> <note>An 8th-century English monk and influential theologian</note> says regarding this passage. By this, we see there is no society with God in sects or <term>schisms</term> <note>Formal divisions or splits within the Christian Church</note>, nor anywhere else but in the unity, fellowship, and communion of that Church which can prove its descent from the Apostles.

<margin>Many means and instruments for the forgiveness of sin, but all through the power and merit of Christ's blood applied through them.</margin> 7. *The blood of Jesus.*] Whether sins are forgiven <note>original: "remitted"</note> by prayers, by fasting, by alms, by faith, by charity, by sacrifice, by Sacraments, and by the Priests—as the holy Scriptures clearly attribute forgiveness to each of these—none of these forgive in any other way than by the power, merit, and virtue of Christ's blood. These are simply the appointed means and instruments through which Christ intends his holy blood to work effectively in us. Whoever despises these means deprives himself of the benefit <note>original: "commoditie"</note> of Christ's own blood and continues still in sin and uncleanness, no matter how much he boasts of Christ's death. The <term>Protestants</term> <note>Followers of the 16th-century Reformation who challenged these Catholic views on the necessity of secondary means for grace</note> should take careful note of this and stop deceiving their poor, misled followers by claiming that Catholics take away from Christ's blood or seek forgiveness elsewhere. In reality, Catholics humbly use the means appointed by Christ to apply the benefit of his holy blood to themselves.

<margin>All forgiveness of sins is through the Passion of Christ, though also through secondary means.</margin> 7. *From all sin.*] From original and actual sin, from <term>venial</term> and <term>mortal</term> sin, *from the guilt and the punishment* <note>original Latin: "a culpa & pœna"</note> due for the same. Bede says that Christ's <term>Passion</term> <note>The suffering and death of Jesus</note> does not only forgive in Baptism the sins committed before, but also all others done afterward through human frailty—provided that we use the necessary means Christ has appointed for their forgiveness, some of which he lists. See Bede on this passage, as well as Saint Augustine in *volume 9* <note>original Latin: "to. 9."</note> and Saint Jerome in *Against the Pelagians, book 2, chapter 3* <note>original Latin: "di. 2 con. Pelag. c. 3."</note>.

<margin>Some sins are venial. A person may be truly righteous despite venial sins.</margin> 8. *That we have no sin.*] We gather from these words and the previous ones that there are two types of sins: one is mortal, which excludes us from light and the society of God; the other is venial, which is found even in those who walk in the light and remain in the society of God. We also note against the <term>Pelagians</term> <note>A group who believed humans could achieve perfection without divine grace</note> that we are truly called the sons of God and are indeed righteous, even though we are not without all sins. Every one of us, the righteous as well as the unrighteous, is taught and required to confess our offenses and ask for pardon daily from God through this petition of the <term>Pater noster</term> <note>The "Our Father" or Lord's Prayer</note>: *Forgive us our debts*. Therefore, Saint Augustine, in his book *On Nature and Grace, chapter 36* <note>original Latin: "li. de natura & grat. c. 36."</note>, lists all the holy Patriarchs, Prophets, and renowned righteous persons as having been sinners, even while they were in a state of grace and righteousness. He always excepts our <term>Blessed Lady</term> <note>The Virgin Mary</note>, *concerning whom, for the honor of our Lord, I wish to have no question at all when we are discussing sins* <note>original Latin: "de qua propter honorem Domini, nullam prorsus, cùm de peccatis agitur, habere volo quæstionem"</note>. And when Pelagius asked what sins Abel and such righteous men committed, Saint Augustine answered <note>original: "e. 38."</note> that they might have laughed too much at times, or desired something a bit too intemperately, or picked fruit too greedily, or eaten a bit more than was easily digested, or had their attention wander during prayer, and similar things. <margin>Examples of venial sins.</margin> This is the general sense of Augustine's words. By this, we may learn which are venial sins—those that can exist alongside true righteousness and <note>original: "de dono perseuerat. c. 20."</note> cannot always be avoided even by holy people in this life. In the book *On Faith to Peter, chapter 41* <note>original: "de fide ad Petrum c. 41."</note>, children who have been newly baptized and do not yet have the use of reason to sin either mortally or venially are excepted from this common rule of sinners.

-> C H A P T E R II. <-

1. *That you sin not.*] Saint John (says the Venerable Bede <note>An influential 8th-century English monk and historian.</note> upon this place) is not contrary to himself, in that he seeks here to make them without sin, whom he said in the last chapter could not be without all sins. But in the former place he warned us only of our frailty, that we should not <term>arrogate</term> <note>To claim or take for oneself without justification.</note> to ourselves perfect innocence: here he provokes us to watchfulness and diligence in resisting and avoiding sins, especially the greater, which by God's grace may more easily be repelled.

<margin>How Christ is our only Advocate.</margin>
1. *An advocate.*] The calling and office of an Advocate is in many things proper to Christ, and in every condition more singularly and excellently agreeing to him than to any Angel, Saint, or creature living. Though these also be rightly and truly so called, and that not only without any <term>derogation</term> <note>A lessening or taking away of someone's authority or honor.</note>, but much to the honor of Christ's advocacy. To

The annotations argue that while Christ is the primary Advocate, human righteousness is achieved through good works fueled by grace, rather than faith alone.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the First Epistle of John, Chapter 2, specifically expanding on verse 1 and transitioning into verses 2 through 19. It addresses the theological roles of Christ as the primary advocate and the Saints as secondary intercessors, while defining the nature of "antichrists" and heresy.</meta>

# CHAPTER II. OF ST. JOHN.

To him solely and only it belongs to obtain mercy for us before God's face, by the general ransom, price, and payment of his blood for our delivery, as is said in the following sentence: *And he is the propitiation <note>Atonement or the act of regaining God's favor.</note> for our sins, and not for ours only, but for the whole world's.* In this way he is our only advocate, because he is our only redeemer; and therefore he alone immediately, by and through himself, and without the aid or assistance of any other—man or Angel—in his own name, right, and merits, confidently deals with our causes before God our judge, and so procures our pardon, which is the highest degree of advocacy that can be.

<margin>How Angels, Saints, and living men are our advocates.</margin>
All this notwithstanding, yet the Angels, and Saints, and our fellow Christians alive, may and do pray for us; and because they deal with God by intercession to obtain mercy for us, they may justly be called our advocates. They are not advocates in the same way Christ is—who demands all things immediately by his own merits—but as secondary intercessors, who never ask nor obtain anything for us, but *through Christ our Lord* <note>original Latin: "per Christum Dominum nostrum"</note>, by and through Christ our common Lord, Advocate, and Redeemer of mankind. And behold how St. Augustine (in his *first treatise on the Epistle of John, upon these very words*) anticipated the heretics' objections. *But someone will say, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Sed dicit aliquis &c."</note> *But someone will say, "Do not the Saints then pray for us? Do not Bishops then or Prelates and Pastors pray for the people?" Yes, says he: Mark the Scriptures, and you shall find that the Apostles prayed for the people, and again desired the people to pray for them; and so the head prays for all, and the members one for another.* And likewise (lest the heretics should <margin>Saints in heaven pray for us.</margin> say there is a difference between the living and the dead in this case), the same holy father writes this at the end of his commentary on the 85th Psalm: *Our Lord Jesus Christ does yet make intercession for us; all the Martyrs that be with him pray for us: neither will their intercession cease, until we cease our groanings.*

<margin>Irenaeus, book 3, chapter 33 & book 5 after the middle. Eusebius. St. Jerome on Matthew chapter 18.</margin>
<margin>The Blessed Virgin is our advocate.</margin>
In this sense, therefore, whosoever prays for us, whether alive or dead, is our advocate, just as St. Augustine (in his *59th letter to Paulinus, near the middle* <note>original Latin: "circa med."</note>) calls Bishops the "people's advocates" when they give them their benediction or blessing. So does the holy Church call our Blessed Lady our advocate, using the very words of St. Irenaeus, so that you may see such speech is no new invention of later ages, but is Apostolic. *The obedient Virgin MARY* (he says) *is made the advocate of the disobedient virgin Eve.* And to clearly confound the Protestants—in that they think or pretend that the advocacy or patronage of Saints would be injurious to Christ—remember that our Savior acknowledges <margin>Angels are our protectors.</margin> Angels to be assigned for the protection (which is nothing else but advocacy) of infants before the face of God; besides the plain examples in the Old Testament (*Genesis 48:16; Tobit 5:27 and 12:12; Daniel 10*). And this is not only held by the Catholic Church, but even the English Protestants themselves in their service book <note>The Book of Common Prayer.</note> and in the Prayer for Michaelmas Day <note>A feast day honoring the Archangel Michael.</note>, profess and pray for the same protection or advocacy of Angels, defending this against their younger brethren, the Puritans.

<margin>The Catholic Church is the only true Church.</margin>
2. *For the whole world's.*] St. Augustine gathers from this, against the Donatists <note>A schismatic sect that claimed the true Church existed only in their own group in North Africa.</note> and all other heretics who would drive the Church into corners or specific countries, that from the universality of all Nations (for which it was named "Catholic" by the Apostles), the true religion, the Church, and consequently the effect of Christ's propitiation, death, and advocacy, pertain not to one age, nation, or people, but to the whole world. (St. Augustine on this place, *Volume 9, Treatise 1 on the Epistle of John*).

<margin>Not only faith</margin>
4. *He that saith he knoweth.*] To "know" God here signifies (as it often does in the Scriptures) to love him; that is, as in the last chapter, to be in fellowship with him and to have familiar and experimental knowledge of his graces. If any boast that they know God in this way, yet do not keep his commandments, they are liars—such as all Calvinists and Lutherans who profess themselves to be in the favor of God by "faith alone," while affirming that they neither keep, nor possibly can keep, his commandments.

<margin>All heretics are antichrists, the forerunners of the great Antichrist.</margin>
18. *Many antichrists.*] The holy Apostle St. John (says St. Cyprian) did not make a distinction between one heresy or schism and another, nor did he mean any specific group that separated themselves, but generally called all without exception "antichrists" who were adversaries to the Church or had gone out from it. And a little after: *It is evident that all are here called antichrists who have severed themselves from the charity and unity of the Catholic Church.* So he writes in *Letter 76, number 1, to Magnus*. By this we may learn that all heretics, or rather arch-heretics, are properly the precursors of that one and special Antichrist who is to come at the last end of the world, and who is called here immediately before *the Antichrist* <note>original Greek: "ὁ ἀντίχριστος"</note>, that peculiar and singular Antichrist.

<margin>The mark of all heretics is their going out of the Catholic society.</margin>
19. *They went out from us.*] This is an evident note and mark by which to convict all heretics and false teachers: namely, that having once been part of the common Catholic Christian fellowship, they forsook it and went out from it. Simon Magus, Nicolas the Deacon, Hymenaeus, Alexander, Philetus, Arius, Macedonius, Pelagius, Nestorius, Eutyches, Luther, Calvin, and the like, were once of the common society of all of us who are Christian Catholics; they went out from us, whom they saw living in unity of faith and religion together, and made for themselves new assemblies <note>original: "conventicles," meaning unauthorized religious meetings.</note>. Therefore they were (as the Apostle here shows) antichrists. And we, and all who abide in the ancient fellowship of Christian religion—who did not go out of their fellowship (in which we never were) nor out of any other society of known Christians—cannot be schismatics or heretics, but must necessarily be true Christian Catholic men. Let our adversaries tell us, out of what Church...

It also defines heretics as "antichrists" characterized by their departure from the original, universal Catholic fellowship.</summary>

# THE FIRST EPISTLE, CHAPTER III.

<vocab>Heretics, Catholics, unity, charity, sons of God, iniquity, justice</vocab>

<margin>Catholics cannot be proven to have left the Church.</margin>
...Church we ever departed, when, and where, and under what persons it was that we revolted, just as we can tell them the year, the places, and the ringleaders of their own revolt.

<margin>How heretics are part of the Church before they fall away.</margin>
19. **_They were not of us._**] He does not mean that heretics were not, or could not be, in or part of the Church before they left or fell into their heresy or schism <note>A formal split or division within a religious body.</note>. Rather, he means partly that many of those who later fall away—even though they were previously with the rest and shared in all the Sacraments with their fellows—were actually of wicked life and conscience while they were inside. Being more like "ill humors" or "superfluous waste" rather than true and living parts of the body, they can be said, in a way, not to have belonged to the body at all. St. Augustine explains these words this way in his commentary on this passage, *Tractate 3*. But elsewhere, in a more fitting way, he suggests the Apostle means that those who will not stay in the Church but finally forsake it are not "of" or "in" the Church in the foreknowledge <note>original: "prescience"</note> of God. In respect to the small benefit they will gain from their temporary stay there, they are not of the Church, even though according to their current state they are truly members. <note>original Latin: "Li. de corrept. & gr. c. 9 & de dono perseuer. c. 8" (Book on Correction and Grace, ch. 9 and On the Gift of Perseverance, ch. 8)</note>

<margin>Constant Catholics are made known through heresies.</margin>
19. **_That they may be manifest_**] God allows heresy to exist so that those who are permanent, constant, and chosen members and children of the Catholic Church—who were previously known only to God—may now also be made manifest to the world. They are shown by their constant remaining in the CHURCH, even when the wind and blast of every heresy or temptation drives out those who are light and unstable.

<margin>Every good Catholic is sufficiently taught by the Church for salvation.</margin>
20. **_Know all things._**] Those who stay in the unity of Christ’s Church have the *unction* <note>Anointing; the spiritual influence or grace of the Holy Spirit.</note>, that is, the Holy Spirit, who teaches all truth. This does not mean that every individual member possesses all knowledge personally, but that everyone who belongs to that happy society—to which Christ promised and gave the Holy Spirit—shares in the gifts and graces of others through the same holy Spirit for their salvation. Nor does anyone need to seek truth from heretics or others who have left, when truth is within themselves, and only within themselves, in God’s Church. <note>original Latin: "If thou loue vnitie (saith S. Augustine) for thee also hath he, vvhosoeuer hath any thing in it. take avvay enuie, it is thine vvhich I haue, it is mine vvhich thou hast. &c. Tract. 32 in Euang. Ioan." (If you love unity, then whatever anyone else has in it, he has for you as well. Remove envy: what I have is yours, and what you have is mine.)</note>

### ANNOTATIONS
### CHAPTER III.

<margin>Inclination to sin remaining after Baptism is not sin without consent.</margin>
4. **Sin is iniquity** ] Iniquity is not used here to mean general "wickedness," as it is commonly used in English or Latin. This is clear from the original Greek word *anomia* <note>original: 'ανομια</note>, which simply signifies a swerving or declining from the straight line of the law of God or nature. The Apostle means that every sin is a deviation from the rule of the law; however, it does not mean that every such deviation is properly a "sin." The Heretics <note>The author is referring to Protestant reformers.</note> wrongly use this to argue that <term>concupiscence<gloss>The natural inclination toward worldly desires or sin that remains even after religious conversion.</gloss></term> remaining after Baptism is a true sin, even if we never give our consent to it. Although in chapter 5, verse 17, the Apostle says every "iniquity" is a sin, he uses a different Greek word there, *adikia* <note>original: 'αδικια</note>, which refers to a person’s actual and willful transgression, which must indeed be a sin. See St. Augustine, *Against Julian*, book 5, chapter 3; and St. Ambrose, *On the Defense of David*, chapter 13.

<margin>Heretical interpretation of the Scriptures.</margin>
<margin>No one in a state of grace commits mortal sin.</margin>
6. **Does not sin.** ] Jovinian and Pelagius <note>Early Christian figures whose views on sin and perfection were declared heretical by the Church.</note> falsely argued from these words and those in verse 9 that either a baptized person could never sin again, or that a righteous man could not sin. However, among the many good interpretations of this passage, the most agreeable is this: the Apostle is saying that <term>mortal sin<gloss>A grave sin that destroys the relationship with God's grace.</gloss></term> cannot exist alongside the grace of God. Therefore, it cannot be committed by a man as long as he remains a child of God. See St. Jerome, *Against Jovinian*, book 2, chapter 1.

<margin>True righteousness.</margin>
7. **He who does justice.** ] He emphasizes this often: that a person's true righteousness <note>original: "iustice"</note> consists in doing or working righteous deeds. This is how one becomes "just." He warns them not to be deceived by heretics on this point.

<margin>How the Devil sinned from the beginning.</margin>
8. **Sins from the beginning.** ] The Devil was created holy and in a state of grace, not in sin; he fell by his own free will from God. Therefore, these words, "from the beginning," can be interpreted as the "beginning of sin"—meaning the Devil committed the first sin. St. Augustine explains it this way in *The City of God*, book 11, chapter 15. The simplest meaning seems to be that he has sinned since the beginning of the world, following his fall shortly after creation.

<margin>Not by faith alone.</margin>
22. **We shall receive, because.** ] Let the Protestants be ashamed to say that we obtain everything from God by faith alone, as the Apostle here attributes it to the "keeping of God's commandments." Note also that God's commandments are not impossible to keep; they were observed then, and are observed now, by godly people.
