<header>THE FIRST EPISTLE CHAPTER 4.</header>

## ANNOTATIONS
### CHAPTER 4.

<margin>Heretical boasting of the spirit.</margin>
1. **Believe not every spirit.]** That is, do not receive every doctrine from those who boast that they possess the spirit. For there are many false prophets—which is to say, heretics—who will leave the Church and claim to have the spirit, boasting of God’s word, Scripture, and the Gospel, when in deed they are seducers.

<margin>Only the Church, not every private man, has the authority to prove and discern spirits. 1 Corinthians 12:10; 14:26.</margin>
1. **Prove the spirits.]** This passage does not mean, as the Protestants would have it, that every individual person should examine, try, or judge for themselves who is a true or false teacher, or what is true or false doctrine. Rather, the Apostle here wants everyone to discern these different spirits by looking to those to whom God has given the gift of "discerning spirits" and doctrines (which Saint Paul expressly says is given only to some, and not to everyone, in 1 Corinthians 12) and by obeying the Church of God, to whom Christ has given the Spirit of truth. This is the only sure way to test the spirits and doctrines of these days. All those who would lead us away from our Pastors and the Church's judgment to our own private trial seek nothing else but to drive us into <margin>Calvin.</margin> miserable uncertainty in all our beliefs—as Calvin does, who says regarding this passage that private men may examine the doctrines of general Councils.

<margin>To confess or deny any article which the Catholic Church teaches is at all times a certain mark of a Catholic or a heretic.</margin>
2. **Every spirit that confesses.]** The Apostle is speaking according to that time, and regarding that specific part of Christian doctrine which then had to be especially confessed, taught, and maintained against certain wicked heretics like Cerinthus, Ebion, and their followers, who taught wickedly against the person and both natures of Christ Jesus. The Apostle therefore gives the faithful this sign to distinguish the true teachers of those days from the false. This mark was not intended to serve for all times or for all other false doctrines, but it was a necessary note then. It is as if a good Catholic writer, Pastor, or parent today were to warn their followers to listen only to those teachers who acknowledge Christ our Savior to be really present and sacrificed in the Blessed Mass, and that all such are true preachers from God, and the rest are of the Devil, or possess the spirit of Antichrist. This spirit of Antichrist (he says) had already arrived then, and is undoubtedly much more present now in all heretics, who are all precursors to that great Antichrist who shall come toward the very end.

<margin>Many ancient heresies that "dissolved" Christ.</margin>
3. **That dissolves.]** To "dissolve," loose, or separate Jesus apart was characteristic of all those old heretics who taught against either his Divinity, his Humanity, or the Unity of his person (him being of two natures), such as Cerinthus, Ebion, Nestorius, Eutyches, Manes (or Manichaeus), Cerdon, Apelles, Apollinaris, and the like. This is one place where we can see that the common Greek copies are not always authentic <note>The author argues that the Latin version used by the Church is more reliable than the Greek manuscripts available to Protestants in the 16th century.</note>, and that our old, <margin>The Greek text corrupted by old heretics.</margin> approved translation should not always be judged by the Greek as it exists now (which the Protestants follow exclusively). Instead, it should be assumed that when our old Latin text differs plainly from the Greek, in ancient times either all or the most approved Greek readings were different, and that the current Greek was often corrupted then or since by heretics or other means. Among the Greeks, Saint Irenaeus (Book 3, Chapter 18), and among the Latin fathers, Saint Augustine (Tract 6 at the end), Saint Leo (Epistle 10, Chapter 5), and Venerable Bede all read the text as we do. This reading is more effective against the mentioned heretics than the version in the common Greek today, which says: *Every spirit that confesses not Christ to have come in flesh, is not of God.* This was already effectively said in verse 2. To see how it was corrupted and altered by heretics, look at the words of Socrates (a Greek writer) <margin>Book 7, Chapter 32.</margin> which are very relevant. *Nestorius* (he says), *being naturally eloquent (a trait often found in heretics), considered himself learned and disdained studying the ancient interpreters, thinking himself better than them all; he was ignorant that in Saint John's Catholic epistle the old Greek copies had:* EVERY ONE THAT DISSOLVES JESUS, IS NOT OF GOD. *So he says, adding moreover that those who wished to separate the divinity from the humanity of Christ's nature took this sense out of the old copies. For this reason, the old commentators noted that those who would "loose" Jesus had corrupted this Epistle.* See also the Tripartite History, Book 12, Chapter 4.

<margin>A sure mark of true or false teachers.</margin>
6. **In this we know.]** This is the most certain and general sign to distinguish true spirits and prophets from the false: those who are of God will hear and obey their Apostles and the lawful pastors succeeding the Apostles, and submit themselves to the Church of God. The others, who are not of God, will not listen to Apostle, pastor, or Church, but insist on being their own judges.

<margin>Against the Protestant concept of "special faith" and [assurance].</margin>
17. **That we may have confidence.]** Confidence, called in Latin *Fiducia* <note>original: "Fiducia"</note>, is not the same thing as faith. Nor is it an infallible persuasion that makes a man just as secure and certain of his salvation as he is of the things we are bound to believe, as the Protestants falsely teach.

<meta>The text cuts off here with the catchword "teach," indicating the argument about Protestant theology and the nature of "certainty of salvation" continues on the next page.</meta>

<summary>This page provides Catholic commentary on 1 John 4, arguing that the true "test of spirits" is obedience to the Church hierarchy rather than private interpretation. It notably defends the Latin Vulgate's reading of verse 3 ("Every spirit that dissolves Jesus") as the original version, claiming heretics corrupted the Greek manuscripts to support their views.</summary>

The words both following and preceding this also clearly prove, contrary to the Protestants, that our confidence and hope on the Day of Judgment does not rely solely on our grasping Christ's merits through faith, or on His grace and mercy. <margin>The fear of God in righteous men is compatible with charity.</margin>
18. **Fear is not in charity.]** The heretics <note>referring to Protestant reformers</note> very falsely interpret this passage to mean that godly Christian men ought to have no doubt, mistrust, or fear of hell and damnation. This is most evidently against the Scriptures, which everywhere commend to us the awe and fear of God and His judgments. *Fear him* (says our Savior in Matthew 10) *who can cast both body and soul into hell.* And *Psalm 118: Pierce my flesh with your fear.* This fear of God’s judgments caused Saint Paul and all good men to discipline their bodies, lest they should be rejected and damned. For this cause, the wise man affirms that the person who is always fearful is happy. Holy Job says, *I feared all my works.* And the Apostle says, *With fear and trembling work out your salvation.* This kind of fear exists even in the most righteous men who are most full of charity; it fits well with that virtue and is called *Filial fear* <note>original: "Filialis timor"</note>, because it is the kind of fear a good child should have toward their father.

Proverbs 28.

Philippians 2.

<margin>What kind of fear does not agree with charity.</margin>
But there is a kind of fear which is incompatible with charity and is also entirely against hope—the kind that brings such distress and anxiety of conscience that it leads a person to mistrust or despair of God's mercies. There is also *servile fear* <term>servile fear: fear motivated by punishment rather than love</term>, which often makes a person stop sinning and perform the eternal works of justice, not out of any love or delight in God or His laws, but only for fear of damnation. Although this is not evil in itself—and is actually very useful as it helps lead one toward the love of God—it still does not coexist with charity. Instead, it is daily diminished and eventually driven out by charity. It is of these kinds of fear that the Apostle speaks, and (as some explain) also the fear of men, of which our Savior said, *Do not fear those who kill the body.*

Servile fear is not evil.
Matthew 10.

### ANNOTATIONS
### CHAPTER V.

<margin>The commandments are possible to be kept.</margin>
v 3. *His commandments are not heavy.*] How can the Protestants say that God’s commandments cannot possibly be fulfilled or kept in this life, seeing the Apostle says, *they be not heavy:* and Christ says, *his yoke is sweet, and his burden light?* <note>original: Matthew 11:30</note> See for the full understanding of this place, *Matthew 11, Saint Augustine, verse 30.* <note>The author argues against the Reformers' view that human nature is so fallen that it is impossible to perfectly obey God's law; the Catholic view presented here is that with God's grace, obedience is achievable.</note>

<summary>This page concludes the First Epistle of John, emphasizing the witness of the Trinity and the effectiveness of prayer. It includes a theological defense of the possibility of keeping God's commandments against Protestant interpretations.</summary>

--- Page 719 ---
<meta>This page continues the commentary on 1 John Chapter 5, specifically focusing on the Catholic interpretation of verses regarding the Trinity, the nature of sin, and the legitimacy of praying for the deceased. It directly follows the discussion of verse 16 regarding "sin unto death."</meta>

<page-num>687</page-num>
<header>CHAPTER V OF SAINT JOHN.</header>

<margin>Heretical translation.</margin>
<margin>* [This refers to a specific Greek or Latin textual variant cited by the author]</margin>
3. <insert>*</insert> <gloss>Saint Augustine, *On the Perfection of Justice*, chapter 10.</gloss> The Heretics <note>In this context, "Heretics" refers to Protestant reformers, likely Calvinists or Lutherans.</note>, in favor of their aforementioned error, prefer to translate: *His commandments are not grievous*, rather than: *are not heavy.* <note>The author argues that "grievous" implies the commandments are impossible to keep, whereas "heavy" suggests they are a manageable burden with God's grace.</note>

<margin>Three persons and one substance in the Blessed Trinity.</margin>
<margin>The Arians corrupt the text of Scripture.</margin>
7. **Three which give testimony.**] An express passage for the distinction of three persons, and the unity of nature and essence in the Blessed Trinity: against the Arians <note>Arians: A group in the early Church who believed Jesus Christ was not co-eternal or co-equal with God the Father.</note> and other similar Heretics, who have in various ages found themselves so pressed by these plain Scriptures, that they have (as it is thought) altered and corrupted the text in both Greek and Latin in many ways; just as the Protestants handle those texts that go against them. But because we are not now troubled with Arianism as much as with Calvinism, we need not dwell on the variety of readings or interpretations of this passage. See Saint Jerome in his epistle placed before the seven Canonical or Catholic Epistles.

<margin>What is a sin unto death.</margin>
16. **A sin unto death.**] A sin unto death is something different than a mortal sin. For it is that mortal sin only which a man never repents of before his death, or in which he continues until death, and dies in it. I affirm (says Saint Augustine, *On Rebuke and Grace*, chapter 12) *that a sin unto death is to leave faith working through charity even until death.* <note>original: "hoc est enim peccatum ad mortem, fidem quae per dilectionem operatur deserere usque ad mortem"</note> Similarly, in the words before, *a sin not unto death* is not what we call a venial sin, but any sin that a man commits but does not continue in until death.

<margin>Prayer for the dead.</margin>
<margin>Some of the dead may not be prayed for.</margin>
16. **For that I say not.**] If the "sin unto death" he speaks of is the sin in which a man dies without repentance, according to Saint Augustine’s words previously quoted: then the prayer which he speaks of must necessarily be prayer for the dead. This is because he speaks of praying, or not praying, for those who died in deadly sin, exhorting us to pray and encouraging us to do it with confidence of being heard if we pray for those who departed this life not in deadly sin; and conversely, in a way, dissuading and discouraging us from praying for those who continued in wickedness even until their life's end. And Saint Augustine sets down the Church's practice as agreeable to the Apostle's meaning in Book 21, Chapter 24 of *The City of God*. *If there be any (he says) that persist until death in impenitence of heart, does the Church now pray for them—that is, for the souls of those who have so departed?* <note>original: "Si qui autem usque ad mortem in impoenitentia cordis perseverant, numquid nam pro eis jam Ecclesia, id est, pro animabus eorum qui ita defuncti sunt, orat?"</note> So he says. And this is the cause that the first *Council of Braga* <note>original: "Concilium Bracharense"</note>, chapter 34, forbids praying for those who die in desperation, or kill themselves; and the reason why the Church refrains from praying for Heretics who die in their heresy, or maintain heresy until death and by their death.

<margin>It is proved that the Apostle speaks of praying for the dead.</margin>
<margin>The Calvinists' blasphemy, to avoid this sense of the Apostle.</margin>
And that this passage is most properly or only meant as praying for the departed is proven by this: neither the Church nor any man is discouraged here from praying for any sinner still living, nor for the forgiveness of any sin in this life. All sins (of whatever sort) are pardonable as long as the person who committed them is in a state to repent, as they are as long as they are in this world. And we see that the Church prays, and is often heard, for Heretics, Jews, Turks, Apostates, and whatever other infidels or evil men exist during their lives. And it is great blasphemy that the Calvinists utter regarding this passage: namely, that Apostasy and certain other sins of the reprobate <note>Reprobate: In Calvinist theology, those predestined to damnation.</note> cannot be forgiven at all in this life. They hold this only to avoid the logical conclusion of praying for the dead based on these words of Saint John. Additionally, they must presumptuously take it upon themselves to know and discern God’s secrets—who is reprobate and who is not—and according to that, pray for some and not for others, all of which is most wicked and absurd presumption.

As for their allegation that Saint Jeremy <note>Jeremiah</note> the Prophet was forbidden to pray for the Jews and warned that he should not be heard (Chapter 7, 11, 14), there is a great difference. First, he had a revelation by the words of God that they would continue in their wickedness, which we do not have regarding any specific person of whom Saint John speaks here. Secondly, Jeremiah was not forbidden to pray for the forgiveness of their sins, nor was he denied being heard in any man's particular case (which the Apostle speaks of here); rather, he was told that they should not escape the temporal punishment and affliction which God had designed for them, and that He would not hear him in that regard.

<margin>Heretical translation against sacred images.</margin>
<margin>The 2nd Council of Nicaea pronounces anathema against the Calvinists.</margin>

21. **From idols.**] It is such a well-known treachery of Heretics to translate *idola* as "images" (as seen here and in many places, especially in the English Bible printed in the year 1562) that we need not dwell on it. It is also visible to all the world that they do this on purpose to seduce poor, ignorant people, and to make them think that whatever is spoken in the Scriptures against the idols of the Gentiles (which the Prophet calls *Likenesses of the Gentiles* <note>original: "Simulachra Gentium"</note>) is meant for pictures, sacred images, and holy memorials of Christ and His Saints. Against such deceivers, the second sacred Council of Nicaea, called the Seventh Synod, decrees thus in Act 4, page 122: *Anathema to all those who bring the sentences of Holy Scripture regarding idols against venerable images. Anathema to those who call venerable images "idols." Anathema to those who say that Christians adore images as gods.* <note>original: "Quicunque sententias sacrae scripturae de Idolis, contra venerandas imagines adducunt, anathema. Qui venerandas imagines idola appellant, anathema. Qui dicunt quod Christiani adorant imagines ut Deos, anathema." Anathema is a formal curse and excommunication.</note>

But concerning this matter, it is most evident that neither is every idol an image, nor every image an idol: and that, however the origin or etymology of the word *idol* may be taken in the Greek, yet both the words and the things are in truth and by the use of all tongues very different. The great dragon that the Babylonians adored (<term>Daniel 14</term> <note>This refers to the story of Bel and the Dragon, found in the deuterocanonical portions of Daniel.</note>) was an idol, but not an image; the Cherubim in Solomon’s temple were images, but not idols; and the face of the Queen on her coin or elsewhere—just as Caesar’s face upon the coin convinces us—proves that the Heretics <note>The term "Heretics" here refers to the Protestant Reformers who opposed the use of religious statues and paintings.</note> are false and corrupt translators in this place and other similar ones, confounding these two words as if they were all one.

### ANNOTATIONS

<margin>To hold fast to the old received faith.</margin>
4. *From the beginning.*] This is the rule for a Christian Catholic: to walk in that faith and worship of God which he has received from the beginning. This is what we now call, according to the Scriptures, *the tradition of the Apostles*: that which has come to us from man to man, from Bishop to Bishop, and so from the Apostles. In this way, a faithful person shall avoid seducers who rise up in every age teaching new doctrine.

<margin>To willfully bring another doctrine than what the Catholic Church sets down is always a mark of seducers and Heretics.</margin>
10. *This doctrine.*] The Apostles, and true Pastors (their lawful successors), and the Church of God in holy Council, are accustomed to set down the true doctrine in those points which Heretics call into controversy. Once this is done and declared to the faithful, they need no other mark or description to know a Heretic or false teacher by, other than that he comes with a different doctrine than the one set down for them. Neither can the Heretics shift themselves—as they try to do nowadays—by saying, "O, let us first be proved Heretics by the Scriptures, let them define what a Heretic is." No, this is not the Apostle’s rule. Many a good, honest shepherd knows a wolf even if he cannot provide a formal definition for one. But the Apostle says: "If he does not bring this set doctrine, he is a seducer." So the holy Church says now: "Christ is really in the Blessed Sacrament under the forms of bread and wine, etc." If, therefore, someone does not bring this doctrine, he is a seducer and a Heretic; and we must avoid him, whether he considers himself a Heretic in his own definitions and judgments or not.

<margin>When and in what circumstances it is tolerable to converse with heretics; when it is not.</margin>
10. *Receive him not.*] Although in such times and places where the community or the majority are infected, necessity often forces the faithful to converse with such people in worldly affairs—to salute them, to eat and speak with them—the Church (by decree of Council, for the peace of fearful consciences) provides that they do not incur excommunication or other censures for communicating in worldly affairs with anyone of this kind, unless they be by name excommuni-

<margin>When and in what ways it is damnable.</margin>
...communicated or declared to be heretics: yet even in worldly conversation and secular acts of our life, we must avoid them as much as we may, because their familiarity is in many ways contagious and harmful to good men, namely to the simple: but in matters of religion—in praying, reading their books, hearing their sermons, presence at their service, partaking of their Sacraments, and all other communicating with them in spiritual things—it is a great and damnable sin to deal with them.

<margin>St. John would not be in the same bath with Cerinthus the heretic.</margin>
10. *Nor say, God save you.*] St. Irenaeus <note>A prominent early Christian theologian and bishop of Lyon (c. 130–202 AD).</note> (Book 3, Chapter 3) reports a notable story of this holy Apostle touching this point, from the account of St. Polycarp, which is this: *“There are some,”* says he, *“that have heard Polycarp say, that when John the disciple of our Lord was going to Ephesus, into a bath to wash himself, and saw Cerinthus the heretic <note>Cerinthus was an early Gnostic teacher who denied that God created the physical world and challenged the orthodox view of Jesus's divinity.</note> within the same, he suddenly skipped out, saying that he feared lest the bath should fall, because Cerinthus the enemy of truth was within.”* So he says of St. John, and adds also a similarly worthy example of St. Polycarp himself: who on one occasion meeting Marcion the heretic <note>Marcion of Sinope was a famous 2nd-century heretic who rejected the Old Testament and the God of the Jews.</note>, and the said Marcion calling out to him, asking him whether he knew him or not: *“Yes,”* said Polycarp, *“I know you for Satan’s son and heir.”* So great a fear (says St. Irenaeus) had the Apostles and their disciples to communicate in word only with such as were adulterers or corrupters of the truth. 
<margin>Titus 3.</margin>
As St. Paul also warned, when he said, *A man that is a heretic, after the first and second admonition, avoid.* So far says Irenaeus. If then, to speak with them or salute them is so earnestly to be avoided according to this Apostle’s example and doctrine: what a sin is it to flatter them, to serve them, to marry with them, and so forth?
<margin>The similar zeal of St. Polycarp, and other Apostolic men in not communicating with heretics.</margin>

<header>OF ST. JUDE.</header>

### ANNOTATIONS

<margin>Truths unwritten, and known by tradition.</margin>
**9. For the body of Moses.]** When, why, or how this dispute or combat took place between St. Michael and the Devil regarding Moses’s body, no one can fully explain. Only this we see: that many truths and stories were kept in the mouths and hearts of the faithful that were not written in the canonical Scriptures, just as this one was among the Jews. <note>The author is arguing that "Tradition"—religious knowledge passed down orally—is a legitimate source of truth alongside the Bible.</note>

<margin>Ignorance makes Heretics blaspheme.</margin>
**10. They blaspheme.]** He speaks of Heretics who, being ignorant of God's mysteries and the divine doctrine of his Church, when they cannot disprove the teachings, resort to curses, mockery, and blasphemies against the Priests, the Church, the Sacraments, and whatever is holy.

<margin>Heretics compared to Cain, Balaam, and Korah.</margin>
**11. Cain, Balaam, Korah <note>original: "Core"</note>.]** The Apostle would have Heretics specifically identified by the resemblance they have to three figures: first to Cain, who—out of envy that his brother's service and sacrifice were accepted while his own were rejected—slew his brother and became a fugitive from the face and city of God, which is the Church. Secondly, by their resemblance to Balaam, who was induced to curse God’s people for money; greed is commonly the cause that first creates Heretics and false Prophets. Upon this, St. Augustine says, "He is a Heretic who, for the sake of worldly advantages, either invents or follows new opinions." <note>original: *S. August. li. de Vtil. cred. cap. 1.* (St. Augustine, *On the Utility of Believing*, chapter 1)</note> And lastly, by the resemblance they have with the ancient and notorious schismatic Korah <note>original: "Core"</note> and his companions, who abandoned the ordinary Priesthood appointed by God and insisted on performing sacrifices themselves without a lawful calling.

Such indeed are all Heretics, and such are all their sacraments, services, and offices in their church, just as Korah’s were in his schismatic tabernacles. And as pride was the cause of his rebelling against the obedience of Moses and Aaron, his Priests and true Governors, so is intolerable pride the cause of all Heretics abandoning their lawful Pastors and Rulers—namely, abandoning Christ's own Vicar on earth, our true Aaron, as St. Bernard calls him. <note>original: *De confid. li. 2. cap. 8.* (St. Bernard, *On Consideration*, book 2, chapter 8)</note> To all such deserters, the Apostle here gives the curse and the "Woe" <note>original: *Væ*</note> due to those three—Cain, Balaam, and Korah—and tells them that the storm of darkness and eternal damnation is prepared for them. He gives a most vivid description of all Heretics (as we unfortunately have experience with through their behaviors in our own days) throughout this entire passage even to the end of the epistle.

<margin>All Heretics separate themselves.</margin>
**19. These are they which separate <note>original: "segregate"</note> themselves.]** The characteristics of Heretics in the latter days—that is, ever since Christ's time, not just those of our own age. For there were many who abandoned God's Church and separated themselves from the fellowship of the faithful even in the early Church. We should therefore marvel less at these men separating themselves and leaving the rest to go into various sects, which St. Augustine therefore calls "Separations" <note>original: *Segregations*</note>.

# THE ARGUMENT OF THE
## REVELATION <note>original: "APOCALYPSE"</note> OF ST. JOHN.

*That which the Old Testament predicted about Christ himself, the Apostles were able to report as a historical fulfillment in the New Testament, from his Conception to his Glorification. But of his Church, they could not do the same: because in their time it was only beginning. It was to continue long after them, even to the end of the world, and then at length to be glorified, just as Christ her Spouse already is. Because of this, God willed for St. Luke to report in the Acts of the Apostles the story of the Church's beginning; and for the rest of its history until the end (so that we might receive this benefit also by the Apostles' hands), he willed St. John to tell us about it in this book by way of a prophecy.*

<margin>Jerome to Paulinus <note>original: "Hier. ad Paulin." This refers to St. Jerome’s Letter 53, a famous introduction to the study of the Bible.</note></margin>
*Of which book St. Jerome says: The <term>Revelation<gloss>original: "Apocalypse"</gloss></term> of St. John has as many <term>sacraments<gloss>In this context, "sacraments" refers to sacred mysteries or hidden meanings rather than the seven ritual sacraments.</gloss></term> or mysteries as it has words. Yea, more than that: in every word there are hidden manifold and various senses. Therefore, very little can be noted here in comparison to the whole. Yet to give the good Catholic (whose comfort is found here) some little help, the book may be divided into five parts.*

<margin>Chapters 1, 2, 3.</margin>
<margin>Part 1.</margin>
*The first part (after the <term>Proem<gloss>An introductory preface.</gloss></term>) contains seven Epistles from Christ, now in glory, to seven Churches of Asia, or (for he makes these all one) to the seven Bishops of those Churches. This means not only to those specific men, but to all his Churches and Bishops throughout the world; saying therefore in every one of them to all in general:*

> *He that has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the Churches.*

*As also in every one he exhorts us to fight manfully (in this spiritual warfare of ours against sin) for the victory, and in every one accordingly promises us a reward in heaven. But before this, in the beginning of every one, he partly commends, partly reprehends, and exhorts to <term>penance<gloss>Repentance and acts of contrition.</gloss></term>. It is much to be noted and feared that among so many, he reproves something in all except only two, which are the second and the sixth. In the beginning also of every one, he takes some piece out of the vision going before, to frame his style according to the matter of each Epistle.*

<margin>Chapters 4 to 8.</margin>
<margin>Part 2.</margin>
*After this admonition to Pastors and their flocks, the second part follows, wherein the Church and its whole course from the beginning to the end is expressed in the opening of a book in God's hand, and the seven seals thereof, by Christ. For this, John sees praise sung now in heaven and earth, not only to the Godhead, as before, but also (in a new manner) to Christ according to his Manhood. And here, when he has come to the opening of the last seal, signifying <term>Doomsday<gloss>The Day of Judgment.</gloss></term>, he leaves 그 matter alone for a while; and to speak more fully yet of the said course of the Church, he brings in another <term>pageant<gloss>original: "pagent" - a dramatic sequence or display.</gloss></term> as it were, of seven Angels with seven Trumpets. The effect of both the Seals and Trumpets is this: That as the Church begins and proceeds, there should be raised against it cruel persecutions and pestilent heresies; and at length, after all heresies, a certain most blasphemous Apostasy, being the next preparation to the*

<margin>Chapters 8 to 12.</margin>

comming <note>This "catchword" at the bottom of the page indicates the first word of the next page is "comming" (coming).</note>

It outlines the first two of five parts of the book: the letters to the seven churches and the opening of the seven seals.</summary>

coming of Antichrist: After all which, Antichrist himself in person shall appear in the time of the sixth seal and sixth trumpet, persecuting and seducing (for the short time of his reign) more than all those before him. <margin>Chapters 12, 13, 14</margin>
3. Of which judgment, deferring for a while to speak at length, he first in the third part treats more fully of the Devil’s working through Antichrist and his company against the Church, so that the justice of Christ afterward in judging may be more manifest.

<margin>Chapters 15 to 21</margin>
4. At length, therefore, in the fourth part he comes to the seven last plagues, the seventh of them containing the final damnation of the whole multitude, society, or body of the wicked, from the beginning of the world to the end. <margin>1 John 2; Revelation 17</margin> Which multitude, in the Gospel and first Epistle of this same St. John (as also in the other Scriptures commonly) is often called the <term>World<gloss>original Latin: "Mundus"</gloss></term>; and here he calls it partly a <term>Whore or Harlot<gloss>original Latin: "Meretricem"</gloss></term>, because with her lustful desires <note>original: "concupiscence"</note> she entices carnal and earthly men away from God; and partly the <term>City of Babylon<gloss>original Latin: "Ciuitatem Babylon"</gloss></term>, because it makes war against Jerusalem <note>original: "Hierusalem"</note>, the City of God, and labors to hold God’s people captive in sin—as was foreshadowed in Nebuchadnezzar <note>original: "Nabuchodonosor"</note> and his Babylonians, who led and held the Jews with their Jerusalem in captivity until Cyrus (acting as a figure of Christ) delivered them. 

But whether all these seven plagues should be understood (like the seventh) as referring to <term>Judgment Day<gloss>original: "Domesday"</gloss></term> itself, it is hard to define. It is more likely that the first six are to go before Judgment Day; but whether physically and literally (in the way Moses plagued Egypt) or rather spiritually, it is more difficult to determine. Yet it seems easier to understand them physically, as also the plagues with which Elijah <note>original: "Elias"</note> and his companion <note>A reference to the "Two Witnesses" of Revelation 11, traditionally identified by many commentators as Elijah and Enoch.</note> shall in the time of Antichrist plague the wicked (which perhaps shall be the same last plagues) of which we read in this book, chapter 11, verse 6. But not content to have described thus the damnation of the whole adulterous and bloody society, he also expressly reports the damnation of their three grand Captains, which are these: Antichrist, his False Prophet, and the Devil himself, the author of all this mischief.

<margin>Chapters 21, 22</margin>
5. Finally, on the other side, in the fifth part he reports the unspeakable and everlasting glory that the Church, after all this suffering, shall be taken up <note>original: "assumpted"</note> into by Christ her glorious Spouse. And so he concludes the book.

**1. APOCALYPSE.**] Of the Apocalypse thus writes the ancient father Dionysius, Bishop of Corinth, as Eusebius alleges him in Book 7, chapter 20 of the *Ecclesiastical History*. <note>original: "hist. Eccl."</note> *Of this book (he says) this is my opinion: to the reader, the matter thereof is far more profound than my wit can reach unto, and I doubt not but almost in every sentence of it, there lies hidden a certain sense exceeding mystical and marvelous. Which though I understand not, yet I conceive that under the words there is a deep meaning, and I measure not the matter by my own reason, but attribute all to faith, taking it to be more high and divine than I can by thought comprise: not reproving that which I understand not, but therefore I admire with reverence, because my wit cannot attain to it.* Again St. Augustine says, that in the *Apocalypse many things are obscurely spoken, to exercise the mind of the reader: and yet some few things left evident, that through them a man may with labor search out the rest. Especially because the author so repeats the same things in various ways, that while seeming to speak of different matters, he is indeed found to utter the same things in diverse manners. --- Page 732 ---
<meta>This page continues the commentary on the first chapter of the Apocalypse (Revelation), focusing on the mystical significance of the number seven, the role of angels, the nature of the Christian priesthood, and the transition of the Sabbath to Sunday.</meta>

<page-num>700</page-num>
<header>THE APOCALYPSE. CHAPTER 1.</header>

Which we see set down here in the beginning, to warn the good Christian reader to be humble and wise in reading both all other holy Scriptures, and specifically this divine and profound prophecy. We further give the reader to understand that we will, in our annotations—following our previous method and purpose—chiefly note for the studious those places that may be used by Catholics, or abused by <term>Heretics<note>In this context, the authors are referring to Protestant reformers who challenged Catholic interpretations.</note></term>, in the controversies of this time. We will also note other passages that offer special matter for <term>edification<note>Spiritual improvement or moral guidance.</note></term>, doing so as briefly as possible, as the volume is growing quite large.

<margin>Mystical numbers.</margin>
4. *To the 7 Churches.*] That certain numbers may be observed as significant and mystical is plain from many places in holy Scripture, and from the ancient Doctors' special noting of the same for many purposes. Hereby we see the rashness of our adversaries in generally condemning all religious respect for certain numbers in our prayers, fasts, or actions. Specifically, the number *Seven* is mystical, prophetic, and perfect; as Saint Augustine says, the Church knows through the Scriptures that it is specially dedicated to the Holy Spirit and pertains to spiritual <term>mundation<note>Cleansing or purification.</note></term>. Examples include the Prophet appointing Naaman to wash seven times in the Jordan, and the sprinkling of blood seven times against the tabernacle. <note>original: "li. 4 quaest. in numer. q. 33. See li. 5. c. 5 de Gen. ad lit. & li. 5 quaest. in Deuter. q. 42" — These refer to St. Augustine’s "Questions on Numbers" (Book 4, Q. 33), "On the Literal Meaning of Genesis" (Book 5, Ch. 5), and "Questions on Deuteronomy" (Book 5, Q. 42).</note>

<margin>The number Seven is mystical: especially in this book.</margin>
All these visions are built upon Sevens: seven Churches, seven Angels, seven stars, seven spirits, seven candlesticks, seven lamps, seven trumpets, seven vials, seven horns of the Lamb, seven hills, seven thunders, seven heads of the Dragon (signifying the Devil), seven of the beast that is Antichrist, and seven of the beast that the harlot rode upon. Finally, the number of the visions themselves is specifically marked to be seven in this book. Every time this number is used in this prophecy, it holds a mystery and a larger meaning than the nature of that number is precisely and commonly understood to be. For instance, when he writes to seven Churches, it is to be understood as all the Churches in the world; just as the seven Angels represent all the Angels or governors of the whole Catholic Church. This applies to the rest as well, because the number *Seven* contains the perfection of universality, as Saint Augustine says. <note>See Augustine, "Questions on Deuteronomy," Book 5, Question 42.</note>

<margin>Grace and peace from God and the holy Angels.</margin>
<margin>God and our Lady save us, and the like.</margin>
4. *From the 7 spirits.*] The Holy Spirit may be meant here, so called for his sevenfold gifts and graces, as some commentators think. However, it seems more probable that he speaks of the holy Angels, by comparing this to a similar passage in Chapter 5 following. There, he seems to call these the seven spirits sent into all the world, just as Saint Paul speaks of Angels in the letter to the Hebrews (*Chapter 1, verse 14*). Even the Protestants accept this in their commentaries. We note this because they must therefore confess that the Apostle here gives or wishes grace and peace, not from God alone, but also from his Angels. Although that blessing comes one way from God, and another way from his Angels or Saints (who are but his creatures), they may learn that the faithful often join them in one speech: *God and our Lady, our Lord and any of his Saints, help us or bless us*. This is not superstitious, but an Apostolical way of speaking. As the Patriarch said (*Genesis 48, verse 16*): *The Angel that delivers me from all evils, bless these children.* <note>See the Annotation for Acts 15:28.</note>

<margin>How all Christians are both kings and Priests.</margin>
6. *A kingdom and Priests.*] Just as all who truly fear God and have dominion over their <term>concupiscences<note>Strong worldly desires or lusts that lead to sin.</note></term> and whatever would induce them to sin are "kings," so too are all who employ their works and themselves to serve God—offering all their actions as an acceptable sacrifice to him—"priests." Nevertheless, if any man were to argue from this that there ought to be no other earthly powers or kings to govern worldly affairs over Christians, he would be a seditious heretic. In the same way, those who use this or similar places (where all Christians are called priests in a spiritual sense) to infer that everyone is a Priest in the proper sense, or that all are Priests alike, or that there should be no priests except these spiritual ones, are also in error. For this is the seditious voice of <term>Korah<note>A biblical figure who led a rebellion against Moses and Aaron, questioning their unique authority.</note></term>, saying to Moses and Aaron: *Let it suffice you, that all the multitude consists of holy ones, and the Lord is in them. Why are you exalted over the people of the Lord?* (Numbers 16).

<margin>Difference between holy days and workdays.</margin>
10. *On the Dominical day.*] Many notable points may be marked here. First, that even in the time of the Apostles there were days designated for the service of God, thus made holy and different—though not by nature, but by use and blessing—from other profane or (as we call them) workdays.

<margin>Sunday made a holiday by the Apostles and the Church's authority.</margin>
<margin>Other feasts ordained by the Church.</margin>
<margin>Just as Saturday was in memory of creation, so Sunday is of Christ's resurrection.</margin>
Secondly, the Apostles and the faithful abolished the Sabbath, which was the seventh day, and established a holy day in its place: the next day following, being the eighth day in the count from creation. This was done without any Scripture or commandment from Christ that we read of. In fact, it was done not only differently than what was observed by the Law, but plainly otherwise than what was prescribed by God himself in the second commandment—even otherwise than he ordained at the first creation when he precisely sanctified the Sabbath day and not the day following. Such great power did Christ leave to his Church, and for such causes did he give the Holy Spirit to reside in it: to guide it into all truths, even those not expressed in the Scriptures. And if the Church had the authority and inspiration from God to make Sunday (which was a workday before) an everlasting holy day, and to make Saturday (which was a holy day before) a common workday, why may the same Church not prescribe and appoint the other holy feasts of Easter, Whitsuntide, Christmas, and the rest? For she has the same warrant for the one as she has for the other.

Thirdly, it should be noted that the cause of this change was because we Christians now value our redemption more than our first creation. Therefore, we have the holy day which was previously for...

It focuses on the transition from the Jewish Sabbath to the Christian Sunday, the role of Bishops as "Angels" of the Church, and the specific priestly vestments of Christ as seen in John’s vision. This text reflects a Counter-Reformation perspective, emphasizing the authority of the Catholic Church and its traditional terminology over "heathenish" or Protestant alternatives.</meta>

<header>CHAPTER II. THE APOCALYPSE. 701</header>

...the remembrance of God’s accomplishment of the creation of things, *now* for the memory of the accomplishment of our redemption. Which therefore is kept upon that day on which our Lord rose from death to life, which was the day after the Sabbath, being called by the Jews, *the first of the Sabbath* <note>original Latin: "una or prima Sabbathi"</note>. *Matthew 28, Acts 20, 1 Corinthians 16.* Fourthly, it is to be marked, that this holy day by the Apostles’ tradition also, was named *the Lord’s day* <note>original Latin: "Dominicus dies"</note>, or, the <term>Dominike<note>From the Latin 'Dominicus,' meaning 'belonging to the Lord.' This was a traditional term for Sunday in the early Church.</note></term>, which is also an old ecclesiastical word in our language; for the name "Sunday" is a heathenish calling, as all other names of the week days are in our language: some imposed after the names of planets, as in the Romans’ time; some by the name of certain idols that the Saxons did worship, and to which they dedicated their days before they were Christians. Which names the Church uses not, but has appointed to call the first day, the *Dominike*, after the Apostle here: the others by the name of <term>Feries<note>From 'feria,' a Latin ecclesiastical term for weekdays. For example, Monday is 'Feria Secunda' (the second fair/day).</note></term>, until the last of the week, which she calls by the old name, *Sabbath*, because that was of God, and not by imposition of the heathen. See the marginal Annotation *Luke 24:1.*

<margin>The Church does not use the heathenish names of days: but the Lord’s Day, weekday, and Sabbath.</margin>

<margin>God gives greater grace at holy times of prayer and fasting.</margin>
Lastly observe, that God reveals such great things to Prophets rather upon holy days, and in times of contemplation, sacrifice, and prayer, than on other profane days; and therefore as Saint Peter (*Acts 10*) had a revelation at the sixth hour of prayer, and Zachary (*Luke 1*) at the hour of incense, and Cornelius (*Acts 10*) when he was at his prayers the ninth hour, so here Saint John notes that he had these marvelous visions upon a Sunday.

<margin>Priestly garments.</margin>
13. *Vested in a Priestly garment.*] He appeared in a long garment or vestment proper unto Priests (for so the word, <term>poderes<note>A Greek term for a robe reaching to the feet, used in the Septuagint for the High Priest's garment.</note></term>, does signify, as *Wisdom 18:24*) and that was most agreeable for him that represented the person of Christ the high Priest, and appeared to John being a most holy Priest, and who is specially noted in ecclesiastical history for his Priestly garment called a <term>pétalon<note>A Greek word meaning 'leaf' or 'thin plate,' referring to the golden plate on the High Priest's miter.</note></term> or <term>lamina<note>Latin for a thin plate or blade.</note></term>. *Eusebius, Book 3 of Ecclesiastical History, chapter 25, & Book 5, chapter 23.*

<margin>Matthew 5:15</margin>
<margin>The true religion is manifest as the light on a candlestick.</margin>
20. *The seven stars.*] The Bishops are the stars of the Church, as the Churches themselves are the golden candlesticks of the world: no doubt to signify, that Christ preserves the truth only in and by the lawful Bishops and Catholic Church, and that Christ’s truth is not to be sought for in corners or <term>conventicles<note>Secret or illegal religious meetings, here referring to Protestant gatherings.</note></term> of Heretics, but at the Bishops’ hands, and upon the candlestick which shines to all in the house.

<margin>Malachi 2:7.</margin>
<margin>Angels as Protectors. Bishops and Priests are called Angels.</margin>
20. *The Angels of the Churches.*] The whole Church of Christ has Saint Michael for her keeper and Protector, and therefore keeps his holy day only by name, among all Angels. And as earthly kingdoms have their special Angel Protectors, as we see in the 10th Chapter of Daniel: so much more the particular Churches of Christendom. See Saint Jerome on chapter 34 of *Ezekiel.* But of those Angels it is not here meant, as is manifest. And therefore "Angels" here must needs signify the Priests or Bishops specially of the Churches here, and in them, all the governors of the whole and of every particular Church of Christendom. They are called Angels, for that they are God’s messengers to us, interpreters of his will, our keepers and directors in religion, our intercessors, the carriers and offerers of our prayers to him, and mediators unto him under Christ; and for these causes and for their great dignity they are here and in other places of Scripture called Angels.

### A N N O T A T I O N S
### C H A P T E R  II.

<margin>Christ’s care of his Church.</margin>
1. *Holdeth the seven.*] It is much to be observed that Christ has such care over the Church and the Bishops thereof, that he is said here to bear them up in his right hand, and to walk in the midst of them: no doubt to uphold and preserve them and to guide them in all truth.

<margin>Special virtues required in a Bishop.</margin>
2. *Thy works, labour, patience &c.*] Things required in a Bishop. First, good works, and great patience in tribulation. Next, zeal and sharp discipline toward offenders is here commended in them. Thirdly, wisdom and diligence in trial of false Apostles and preachers coming in sheepskins: where is signified the watchful providence that ought to be in them, so that Heretics enter not into their flocks.

<margin>Sin is the cause that God takes the Catholic faith from countries.</margin>
5. *Will move.*] Note that the cause why God takes the truth from certain countries, and removes their Bishops or Churches into captivity or desolation, is the sin of the <term>Prelates</term> <note>High-ranking clergy, such as bishops.</note> and people. And that is the cause (no doubt) that Christ has taken away our golden candlestick, that is, our Church in England. God grant us to remember our fall, to do penance and the former works of charity which our first Bishops and Church were notable and renowned for.

<margin>Zeal against Heretics.</margin>
6. *Because thou hatest.*] We see here that of all things, Christian people (especially Bishops) should have great zeal against Heretics and hate them—that is, their wicked doctrine and conditions—even as God hates them. For which zeal alone, our Lord says here that he bears with some Churches and Prelates, and saves them from perishing.

<meta>This page continues the annotations and text of the Apocalypse (the Book of Revelation), specifically concluding the commentary on Chapter 2 and beginning the text and summary for Chapter 3. It maintains the polemical tone of the Counter-Reformation, comparing early biblical heretics to contemporary Protestant figures like Luther and Zwingli.</meta>

# THE APOCALYPSE. CHAPTER III.

<margin>The Nicolaites were the first heretics, named after their leader, serving as a pattern for Arians, Lutherans, and other such specific names.</margin>
6. **Of the Nicolaites.**] Heretics take their names from certain persons, as is noted at length in *Acts 11:26*. These had their name from Nicolas, one of the seven first Deacons who were chosen in *Acts 6*. He is thought to have taught the "community of women" (sharing wives) and that it was lawful to eat of <term>meats offered to idols</term> <note>original Greek: "Idolothyta"</note>. This latter point is the same as if someone today held it lawful to receive the bread or wine of the new Protestant Communion, which is a kind of idolatrous meat. For though such creatures are good by creation, they are made execrable by the profane blessings of heretics or idolaters. Concerning the name "Nicolaites" given here by our Lord himself to those heretics, it is a clear pattern and mark for the faithful forever to identify what kind of men they are who are called by similar names, such as Arians, Macedonians, Nestorians, Lutherans, Zuinglians, and so on. See *St. Jerome, Against the Luciferians, at the end.* <note>original Latin: "S. Hierom cont. Lucifer. in fine"</note>

<margin>Balaam, who overcame God's people by persuading them toward lechery and gluttony, was a type of heretic.</margin>
<margin>*Josephus, Antiquities, Book 4, Chapter 6.*</margin>
<margin>*2 Peter 2:15; Jude v. 11.*</margin>
14. **To cast a scandal.**] Josephus writes that when Balaam could not curse God's people nor otherwise harm them, he taught Balac a way to overthrow them: namely, by presenting to them their beautiful heathen women and delicate dishes of meat offered to the idol <term>Bel-phegor</term> <note>The Moabite god Baal-Peor.</note>. He did this so that, being tempted, they might fall into heathen customs and displease God. The Apostle compares the fraud of heretics to this crafty counsel of Balaam; they cause many more to fall through their preaching of "liberty" regarding food, women, Church goods, the breaking of religious vows, and other such licentious allurements than they do by their actual sermons.

<margin>Zeal against heretics.</margin>
<margin>Ahab and Jezebel.</margin>
<margin>*3 Kings 18.* <note>Modern 1 Kings 18.</note></margin>
20. **The woman Jezebel.**] He warns Bishops to be zealous and stout against false prophets and heretics of every sort. He does this by alluding covertly to the example of holy Elijah, who in his zeal killed 450 false prophets of Jezebel and spared neither Ahab nor Jezebel themselves, but told them to their faces that they troubled Israel—that is, the faithful people of God. Whether there was actually a specific powerful woman at that time who promoted the Nicolaites, whom the Prophet means here, is difficult to say.

<margin>Free will. God is not the author of evil.</margin>
21. **She will not repent.**] Observe free will here most plainly. God is not the proper cause of a hardened heart or impenitence, but man himself alone. Our Lord gives sinners a long life specifically so they may seek amendment; but Jezebel (to whom the Apostle here alludes) would never repent.

<margin>Those who communicate with heretics shall be damned with them.</margin>
<margin>*3 Kings 19:18; Romans 11.* <note>Modern 1 Kings 19.</note></margin>
22. **They that commit adultery with her.**] Those who <term>communicate</term> <note>Meaning to participate in religious services or fellowship.</note> with heretics shall, alas, be damned with them. For it was not only those who were in their hearts of Jezebel's religion, or who inwardly believed in Baal, but also those who externally worshipped him (which the Scriptures call "bowing their knees to Baal") who are guilty. Just so, many today bow their knees to the [Protestant] Communion who do not bow their hearts.

<margin>Saints are also Patrons, not only Angels.</margin>
26. **I will give him power.**] Observe that not only do Angels have power and rule over countries under God, but now—for the honor of Christ’s human nature and for his ministry in the world—the deceased Saints in heaven also have government over men and provinces, and therefore they are involved in our affairs in the world. This is against the heretics of these days who, in order to take away our prayers to Saints, would strip them of the sovereign dignities that the Scriptures show are equal to those of Angels.

### CHAPTER III.

*He is commanded to write to the Churches of Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea: recalling those who err to penance through threats, but praising the rest and promising a reward to those who overcome. He detests the "cold," indifferent Christian. He says that God knocks at the door of men's hearts by offering his grace, intending to enter into whoever will open to him by the consent of their free will.*

# ANNOTATIONS
## CHAPTER III.

<margin>Doing well in respect of reward.</margin>
5. *He that shall overcome.*] In all these speeches to various Bishops and their Churches, he continually encourages them to constancy in faith and a good life, by setting before their eyes the reward of the next life. And yet the <term>Calvinists</term> <note>Followers of John Calvin. The commentators are criticizing the Protestant view that performing good works for the sake of a heavenly reward is self-serving or improper.</note> would have no man do good in respect of such reward.

<margin>Adoration of creatures, called Dulia.</margin>
9. *Adore before thy feet.*] You see this word of adoration is in the Scriptures used for the worship of creatures also, and that to fall before the feet of holy men or Angels for duty and reverence is not idolatry, unless the proper honor due to God alone is given to them. See the Annotations upon the 19th and 22nd Chapters concerning the Apostle's prostration before the Angel. And the adversaries' evasion—saying that the adoration was of God only, and that "before the feet of the party" signifies nothing else but "in his presence"—is false and against the phrase of the Scriptures. For example, 4 Kings 4 <note>original: "4 Reg. 4" — modern 2 Kings 4.</note>, where the <term>Shunammite</term> <note>original: "Sunamite"</note> adored <term>Elisha</term> <note>original: "Elisæus"</note>, falling down before his feet; and 4 Kings 2 <note>original: "4 Reg. 2" — modern 2 Kings 2.</note>, the sons of the Prophets adored him in the same sort. And here, this adoration cannot be meant for anyone but the Bishop or Angel of Philadelphia, because he promises this honor as a reward, and as an effect of his love toward him, saying, *And they shall know that I have loved thee.* And that which he says in the 22nd Chapter, *I fell down to adore before the feet of the Angel:* the very same he expresses thus in the 19th Chapter, *I fell before his feet to adore him:* making it all one to "adore before his feet" and to "adore him."

<margin>Perseverance in good and continuing to the end.</margin>
11. *That no man take thy crown.*] That is, his crown of everlasting life and glory, if he does not persevere to the end in faith and good works; otherwise another shall enter into his place, just as <term>Matthias</term> did—taking both the dignity of the Apostleship and the heavenly crown due for the well-using and executing of that same function—which Judas might and should have had, if he had persevered to the end. And just as the Gentiles came into the grace and place of the Jews. Other difficulties concerning this kind of speech are resolved by the <term>Schoolmen</term> <note>Academic theologians of the Middle Ages, such as Thomas Aquinas.</note> and are not to be dwelt upon here.

<margin>Neuters or indifferents in religion.</margin>
16. *Lukewarm.*] Zeal and fervor are commendable, especially in God’s cause; and the <term>Neuters</term> <note>A term used here for those who remain indifferent or uncommitted in the religious conflicts between Catholicism and Protestantism.</note> that be neither hot nor cold are burdensome and loathsome to Christ and his Church, just as lukewarm water is to a man’s stomach, provoking him to vomit; and therefore he threatens to cast such Neuters out of his mouth.

->A N N O T A T I O N S<-
->C H A P T E R V.<-

<margin>The Saints in heaven offer our prayers to God.</margin>
8. *The prayers of Saints.*] From this it is clear that the Saints in heaven offer up the prayers of faithful and holy persons on earth (called here "saints," as they often are in Scripture) unto Christ. Among so many divine and unsearchable mysteries set down without explanation, it pleased God that the Apostle himself should clarify this one point: that these fragrances are the praises and prayers of the faithful, ascending and offered up to God as incense by the Saints in heaven. This is so that the Protestants may have no excuse for their error in claiming that the Saints have no knowledge of our affairs or desires.

<margin>Spiritual kings and Priests.</margin>
10. *A kingdom and priests.*] To serve God and subdue vices and sins is to reign or to be a king spiritually. Likewise, to offer to him the sacrifices of good works is to be a priest in a certain sense, though neither are meant in the literal sense of the words. See the Annotation before Chapter 1, verse 6.

<margin>Limbo of the Fathers and Purgatory.</margin>
13. *Every creature.*] He means the creatures in heaven, such as Angels and Saints; the holy persons on earth; and those who were in <term>Limbo of the Fathers <gloss>A place of rest for the souls of the righteous who died before Christ's resurrection.</gloss></term> or are in <term>Purgatory <gloss>A state of purification for souls before entering heaven.</gloss></term> (for he cannot be speaking of the damned in hell in this context). Lastly, he refers to the people in the islands (here called "the sea"), which the Prophets often name separately when they foretell the spreading of Christ’s glory through the world, as in Isaiah chapter 49: *Listen, you islands, and pay attention, you people from far away.* <note>original Latin: "Audite insulae et attendite populi de longe."</note>

->ANNOTATIONS<-
->CHAPTER VI.<-

<margin>
Consecration of altars with Saints' relics.
</margin>
9. **Under the altar.]** Christ as man (no doubt) is this altar, under which the souls of all Martyrs live in heaven, awaiting their bodies, just as Christ their head already has his body there. And for correspondence to their place or state in heaven, the Church commonly lays their bodies also, or relics, near or under the altars where our Savior’s body is offered in the holy Mass. The Church has a special rule <note>A "proviso" or ecclesiastical requirement.</note> that no altars be erected or consecrated without some part of a Saint’s body or relics. <note>original: "Conc. African. can. 50. Carthag. 5. can. 14."</note> Council of Africa, canon 50; Council of Carthage 5, canon 14. See Saint Jerome *Against Vigilantius*, chapter 3. Saint Augustine, *The City of God*, book 8, chapter 27. Saint Gregory, book 5, letter 50; book 1, letter 52; book 2, letter 58. To which the Prophet seems here to allude, describing their souls as having their being in heaven, as it were, under the altar. But for this purpose, note well the words of Saint Augustine (or whatever other ancient writer was the author of it) in *Sermon 11 on the Saints*: *Under the altar of God (he says) I saw the souls of the slain. What is more reverent or honorable than to rest under that altar on which sacrifice is done to God, and in which our Lord is the Priest: as it is written, Thou art a Priest according to the order of Melchizedek? Rightly do the souls of the just rest under the altar, because upon the altar our Lord’s body is offered. Neither without cause do the just there call for revenge of their blood, where also the blood of Christ is shed for sinners.* and many other excellent words to that purpose.

<margin>
Saints are present at their tombs and relics.
The Calvinist heresy concerning the Saints refuted by Saint Jerome long ago.
</margin>
This passage was also abused by the wicked heretic Vigilantius (as Saint Jerome witnesses in writing against him, chapter 2) to prove that the souls of Martyrs and other Saints were confined to a certain place, and that they could not be present at their bodies and monuments (where Christian people used to pray to them in the primitive Church, as Catholics still do), nor be wherever they wish, or where men pray to them. To which the holy doctor answers at length: that they are wherever Christ is according to his humanity, for they are under that altar. Part of his words are these, so that you may see how this blessed father refuted the Calvinists in that Heretic so long before they were born: *Do you (he says) prescribe laws to God? Do you fetter the Apostles, so that they must be kept in prison until the day of judgment, and be kept from their Lord, of whom it is written: They follow the Lamb wherever he goes? If the Lamb is in every place, then they who are with the Lamb must be everywhere. And if the devil and wicked spirits, wandering abroad in the world with passing speed, are present everywhere: shall holy Martyrs, after the shedding of their blood, be kept closed under an altar, unable to stir out from there?* So answers this learned doctor.
<margin>Apocalypse 14.</margin>

<margin>
They ignorantly accuse Saint Jerome as an Ubiquitist.
How Saint Jerome says Christ and his Saints are everywhere.
</margin>
This displeases our Calvinists so much that they charge him with a great error for saying that Christ, according to his humanity, is everywhere—as though he were an <term>Ubiquitarian Protestant</term> <note>A term referring to the "Ubiquity" doctrine, which suggested Christ's physical body could be everywhere at once; the author argues Jerome meant spiritual speed and power, not physical presence.</note>. In this, if they had any judgment, they might perceive that he does not mean that Christ or his Saints should be personally present at once in every place alike, as God is: but that their motion, speed, and agility to be where they wish is incomparable, and that their power and operation are according. You may learn this to be the holy doctor's meaning by the words that follow concerning the Devil and his ministers: whom he affirms to be everywhere in no other way but by their exceeding speed of being and working mischief now in one place, now in another, and that in a moment. For though they are spirits, yet they are not everywhere at once according to their essence. And for our new theologians, it would be a hard thing to determine how long Satan (who told our Lord he had circled the earth) was on his journey, and in the particular consideration and temptation of Job: and how many men he assaulted in that one circuit of his. No, no. Such curious companions know nothing, nor believe nothing, but what they see with their physical eyes, and teach nothing but the way to unbelief.
<margin>Job 1.</margin>

<margin>
Saint Jerome proves against the Heretic Vigilantius.
</margin>
10. **And they cried.]** Saint Jerome also, against the said Vigilantius, reports that he used an argument against the prayers of Saints from this passage: because these Martyrs cried for revenge and could not obtain it. But we will report his words, so that you may see how like one heretic is to another—those of our days to those of old. *You say in your book (says Saint Jerome, chapter 3) that while we are alive, one of us may pray for another: but after we are dead, no man's prayer shall be heard for another: especially seeing the Martyrs, asking revenge for their blood, could not obtain it.* So said the Heretic. Against which the holy Doctor makes a long refutation, proving that they pray much more after they are in heaven than they did here on earth:

earth: and that they shall be much sooner heard by God than when they were in the world.
   But as for the Heretics' <note>In this 16th-century Catholic commentary, "Heretics" refers to the Protestant Reformers.</note> argument framed out of these words of the Revelation thus: *These Martyrs did not obtain their request, therefore <note>original: "ergo"</note> Saints do not pray for us:* it was so frivolous, and the premise so manifestly false, that he <note>Likely referring to a specific commentator like St. Jerome or a contemporary Catholic apologist.</note> did not think it worth his time to address it. For it is plain that the Martyrs here were heard, and that their petition should be fulfilled in the time appointed by God (to which they did and do always conform themselves): for it was said to them, *That they should rest yet a little time, until &c.* And that Martyrs' prayers are heard in this case, our Savior testifies in *Luke 18* saying, *And will not God avenge <note>original: "reuenge"</note> his elect that cry to him day and night? I say to you, he will quickly avenge them.* And if God does not hear the Saints sometimes or grant their requests, is it therefore a consequence that they do not or may not pray? If so, Christ himself should not have prayed to his father to remove the bitter cup of death from him, because that petition was not granted.
<margin>How Martyrs cry for vengeance.</margin>
   10. *Do you not avenge?*] They do not desire vengeance upon their enemies out of hatred, but out of charity and zeal for God's honor, praying that his enemies, and the persecutors of his Church and Saints who will not repent, may be confounded; and that our Lord would hasten <note>original: "accelerate"</note> his general judgment, so that they might attain the perfect crown of glory promised to them, in both body and soul. This is to desire the resurrection of their bodies, which shall then triumph perfectly and fully over the persecutors who so cruelly handled the bodies of the elect, which shall then appear glorious to the confusion of their enemies.
   11. *Until their fellow servants be complete.*] There is a certain number that God has ordained to die for the testimony of truth and the Catholic faith, for the conformity of the members to the head, CHRIST our chief Martyr; and until that number is accomplished, the general condemnation of the wicked persecutors shall not come, nor the general reward of the elect.

### ANNOTATIONS
#### CHAP. IX.

<margin>
Who are seduced by Heretics.
</margin>
**4. *Nor any green thing.*]** The Heretics never hurt or seduce the green tree, that is, such as have a living faith working by charity. But commonly they corrupt him in faith who should otherwise have perished for an ill life, and him that is reprobate, that hath neither the sign of the Cross (which is God's mark) in the forehead of his body, nor the note of election in his soul.

<margin>
The manifold hypocrisy of Heretics.
</margin>
**7. *Prepared into battle.*]** Heretics being ever ready to contend, do pretend victory, and counterfeit gold: in shape as men, as smooth and delicate as women, their tongues and pens full of gall and venom: their hearts obdurate: full of noise and shuffling: their doctrine as pestiferous and full of poison, as the tail and sting of a scorpion. But they endure for a little season.

<margin>
Heretical translation.
</margin>
**21. *Idols of gold.*]** Here again the new Translators <note>A reference to Protestant translators of the era, whom the author accuses of bias.</note> abuse the people, for *idols* saying *images*: the place being plainly against the portraits of the Heathen Gods, which are here and in the Psalm 95 called, *demons* <note>original: "dæmonia," meaning devils or evil spirits.</note>, Devils.

### ANNOTATIONS
->CHAPTER XII.<-

<margin>
The Church shall flee as to a desert in Antichrist's time, but not decay or be unknown, no, not even for a very short time.
</margin>
*6. The woman fled.]* This great persecution that the Church shall flee from is in the time of Antichrist, and shall endure but three years and a half, as is noted in the margin of verse 14. In which time, despite everything, she shall not lack our Lord's protection, nor true Pastors, nor be so secret but all faithful men shall know and follow her. Much less shall she decay, err in faith, or degenerate and follow Antichrist, as Heretics wickedly imagine. Just as the Catholic Church now in England is in this time of persecution—because it has no public state of government nor open free exercise of holy functions—it may be said to be fled into the desert; yet it is neither unknown to the faithful who follow it, nor to the enemies that persecute it. This is unlike the "hidden company" that the Protestants talk about, which they claim existed for some centuries together, yet was known to neither their friends nor foes because, in truth, no such company existed for many ages. And this is true if we take this "flight" as a physical retreat into the wilderness. However, it may be, and is by most explained, to be a spiritual flight: forsaking the joys and comforts of the world and giving herself to contemplation and penance during the time of persecution under Antichrist. By enlarging the sense, it may also well signify the desolation and affliction that the Church suffers and has suffered from time to time in this wilderness of the world by all the forerunners and ministers of Antichrist, including Tyrants and Heretics.

<margin>
Saint Michael, protector of the Church.
</margin>
*7. A great battle.]* In the Church there is a perpetual combat between Saint Michael (protector of the <term>Church militant</term> <note>The "Church militant" refers to the Christian community on earth, currently engaged in spiritual warfare against sin and evil.</note> as he was formerly of the Jews' Synagogue, Daniel 10:21) and his Angels, fighting against the Devil and his ministers. The perfect victory over them shall be at the judgment. Note here also the reason why Saint Michael is commonly painted fighting with a dragon.

<margin>
Antichrist's attempts to draw people from the true faith.
</margin>
*15. To be carried away.]* By great persecution he would draw her—that is, her children—from the true faith; but every one of the faithful elect, gladly bearing their part of it, overcome his temptations. Because he is even more offended by their constancy, he works malicious attempts in assaulting the frailer sort, who are here signified by the "rest of her seed" that keep the commandments but are not as perfect as the former.

->ANNOTATIONS<-
->CHAPTER XIII.<-

<margin>Many mysteries expounded.</margin>
1. *A beast coming up.*] This beast is the universal company of the wicked, whose head is Antichrist: & the same is called (Apocalypse 17) the whore of Babylon. The 7 heads are expounded (Apocalypse 17) as seven kings: five before Christ, one present, and one to come. The 10 horns are also there expounded to be 10 kings that shall reign a short while after Antichrist. This dragon is the Devil, by whose power the whore or beast or Antichrist works. For in the words following (verses 3 & 4) Antichrist is called the beast, to whom the dragon, that is, the Devil gives that power of feigned miracles. and as we adore God for giving power to Christ and his followers, so they shall adore the Devil for assisting Antichrist and giving him power.

<margin>Great persecution by Antichrist and his ministers.</margin>
<margin>Their blessedness that continue constant.</margin>
7. *To make battle with the saints.*] He shall kill the saints then living, Elias and Enoch <note>The prophets Elijah and Enoch were traditionally believed to return to Earth to oppose the Antichrist before the Second Coming</note>, and infinitely more that profess Christ. whereby we must learn, not to marvel when we see the wicked persecute and prevail against the just, in this life. Then shall his great persecution and cruelty try the saints' patience, as his wonderful means to seduce shall try the steadfastness of their faith, which is signified by these words following, *Here is the patience and the faith of saints.* And when it is said, *They adored the beast, whose names are not written in the book of life of the Lamb*, it gives great solace and hope to all them that shall not yield to such persecutions, that they are of God's elect, and their names written in the book of life.

<margin>The honor of Christ's image is for the honor of Christ.</margin>
14. *The image of the beast.*] They that now refuse to worship Christ's image <note>A reference to Protestant iconoclasm, or the removal of statues and crucifixes from churches</note>, would then worship Antichrist's. And we may note here, that as the making or honoring of this image was not against the honor of Antichrist, but wholly for it, as also the image erected of Nebuchadnezzar <note>original: "Nabuchodonosor"</note>, and the worship thereof, was altogether for the honor of him, so is the worship of Christ's image, the honor of Christ himself, and not against him, as Protestants madly imagine.

<margin>Antichrist's triple honor against the honor of Christ.</margin>
17. *The character or the name.*] As likely for the perverse imitation of Christ, whose image (especially as on the Rood <note>A large crucifix, typically positioned above the entrance to the chancel of a medieval church</note> or crucifix) he sees honored and exalted in every Church, he will have his image adored (for that is Antichrist, in emulation of like honor, adversary to Christ) so for that he sees all true Christian men to bear the badge of his Cross in their foreheads, he likewise will force all his to have another mark, to abolish the sign of Christ. By the like emulation also and wicked opposition he will have his name and the letters thereof to be sacred, and to be worn in men's caps, or written in solemn places, and to be worshipped, as the name of JESUS is, and ought to be among Christian men. And as the ineffable name of God was among <margin>Yahweh <note>original: "יהוה" (the Tetragrammaton)</note></margin> the Jews expressed by a certain number of 4 characters (therefore called <term>Tetragrammaton: the four-letter Hebrew name of God, Y-H-W-H</term>) so it seems the Apostle alludes here to the number of Antichrist's name.

<margin>The Protestants by abolishing of Christ's image, & cross and irreverence to the name JESUS, make a ready way to the honor of Antichrist.</margin>
And here it is much to be noted, that the Protestants plucking down the image of Christ out of all Churches, & his sign of the cross from men's foreheads, and taking away the honor and reverence of the name JESUS, do make room for Antichrist's image, & mark, and name. And when Christ's images and ensigns or arms shall be abolished, and the Idol of Antichrist set up in stead thereof, as it is already begun: then is the abomination of desolation which was foretold by Daniel and our Savior.
