# THE APOCALYPSE. CHA. XIIII. 724

...here signifying, that it is a point of high understanding, illuminated extraordinarily by God’s spirit, to reckon correctly and decipher truly beforehand, Antichrist’s name and person.

18. *It is the number of a man.*] A man he must be, and not a Devil or spirit, as it is clear here, and by St. Paul in *2 Thessalonians 2*, where he is called *the man of sin.* Again, he must be one particular person, and not a number, a succession, or a whole order of any degree of men: because his proper name, man, and of a peculiar name, <note>The author argues that Antichrist must be a single individual, rather than a line of rulers like the Papacy.</note> reproves the wicked vanity of Heretics <note>Referring to Protestant reformers of the era.</note> who would have Christ’s own Vicars, the successors of his chief Apostle, even the whole order of them for many ages together, to be this Antichrist. Who, by the description here and in the said Epistle to the Thessalonians, must be one special man, and of a particular proper name, as our Lord JESUS is. And whoever he may be, these Protestants undoubtedly are his precursors; for as they prepare his way by getting rid of Christ’s images, the cross, and his name, so they exceedingly promote the matter by removing Christ’s chief minister <note>The Pope</note>, so that all may be clear for Antichrist.

<margin>The Pope cannot be Antichrist.</margin>
If the Pope had been Antichrist, and had been revealed now a good many years since, as these fellows say he is to them, then the number of this name would agree with him. If the prophecy were now fulfilled, it would evidently appear that he bore the name and number noted here. For (no doubt) when he comes, this count of the letters or number of his name, which before is so hard to know, will be easy. For he will set up his name in every place, even as we faithful men do now advance the name of JESUS. And what name, proper or common, of all or any of the Popes do they find to agree with this number? This is despite their boast that they have found the whole order, and every one of them for these thousand years, to be Antichrist—and the rest before them, even from St. Peter, to be forerunners toward his kingdom.

<margin>All framing of letters to express Antichrist's name is uncertain.</margin>
18. *The number 666.*] Because the ancient expositors and others think (for no mortal man can have certain knowledge of this without an express revelation) that his name consists of so many and such letters in Greek, as—according to their manner of numbering by the alphabet—make 666. And because the letters making that number may be found in various names, both proper and common: (as St. Irenaeus finds them in *Latinos* <note>original: "Latinos"; written in Greek as Lateinos, this was a common early interpretation referring to the Roman/Latin empire</note> and *Teitan* <note>Titan</note>; Hippolytus in "I deny" <note>original: "ἀρνoῦμαι" (arnoumai)</note>; *Irenaeus book 5 at the end*; Aretas in *Lampetis*; and some of this age in *Ludérus*, which was Luther’s name in the German tongue); in the end, we see there can be no certainty, and everyone frames and applies the letters to his own purpose. It is the most absurd folly of the Heretics to apply the word *Latinos* to the Pope; neither the whole order in common, nor any particular Pope was ever so called. St. Irenaeus, the first who observed it in that word, applied it to the Empire and state of the Roman Emperor, which was then Heathen, and not to the Pope of his days or after him. Yet he preferred the word *Teitan* as more agreeable, with this admonition: that it is a very perilous and presumptuous thing to define any certainty beforehand regarding that number and name. And truly, whatever the Protestants presume here concerning the Pope, we may boldly discharge Luther of that dignity. He is undoubtedly one of Antichrist’s precursors, but not Antichrist himself.

## ANNOTATIONS
### CHAPTER 14.

<margin>Praying for the dead, and unto Saints, at the altar.</margin>
13. *From henceforth now.*] This being specially spoken of Martyrs (as not only Saint Augustine seems to take it, but the Calvinists themselves, translating "in the Lord" as "for our Lord's cause") <note>original Latin: "in domino"</note> the <margin>*Beza.*</margin> Protestants have no reason to use this passage against <term>Purgatory</term> <note>A place or state of suffering inhabited by the souls of sinners who are expiating their sins before going to heaven.</note> for the departed. For the Catholic Church and all her children confess that all Martyrs are, immediately after their death, in bliss and need no prayers. Regarding this, there is Saint Augustine's well-known sentence: *He does injury to the Martyr, who prays for the Martyr.* <note>original: "He doeth iniurie to the Martyr, that praieth for the Martyr. Ser. 17 de verb. Apoſt. c. 1." (Sermon 17 on the words of the Apostle, chapter 1)</note> and again to this purpose he writes most excellently: *We do not keep a memory of Martyrs at our Lord’s table, as we do of others who rest in peace (that is, for the intent to pray for them), but rather so that they may pray for us, etc.* <note>original: "tract. 84 in Ioan." (Tractate 84 on the Gospel of John)</note>

<margin>The passage abused against Purgatory, answered.</margin>
But if we take the words generally for all who deceased in a state of grace, as it may also be, then we say that even such people—though they be in Purgatory and under God’s chastisement in the next life and need our prayers—yet (according to the aforesaid words of Saint Augustine) do "rest in peace." They are discharged from the labors, afflictions, and persecutions of this world, and (what is more) possess unspeakable comfort of conscience. Such people are indeed more happy and blessed than any living person, who are nonetheless usually called "blessed" in the Scriptures even in the midst of the tribulations of this life. Whereby we see that these words, *from henceforth they shall rest from their labors*, may truly apply to those also who are in Purgatory; and so, there is nothing proved here against Purgatory. Lastly, this adverb, *from now on* in Latin, as in the Greek *aparti*, does not properly signify "from <margin>*from now on [ἀπάρτι] Photius in his Lexicon.*</margin> <note>original: "á modo ἀπάρτι"</note> this present time forward," as though the Apostle had said that they are happy only after their death and so forward. Rather, it notes and joins the time past together with the time present, in this sense: that such as have died since Christ’s Ascension—when he first entering into heaven opened it for others—go not to the *Limbo of the Fathers*, as they were accustomed to do before Christ’s time, but are in a position to go straight to bliss, unless the impediment be in themselves. <note>The "Limbo of the Fathers" (Limbus Patrum) was believed to be the place where righteous souls waited before Christ opened the gates of Heaven.</note> Therefore they are here called blessed, who die now in this state of grace and of the New Testament, in comparison to the old faithful and good persons.

# ANNOTATIONS
### CHAPTER XVII.

<margin>The Protestants here insist that Babylon must be Rome, but they refuse this interpretation for Saint Peter's epistle.</margin>
*5. Babylon.]* In the end of Saint Peter’s first Epistle, where the Apostle dates it at Babylon, which the ancient writers (as we noted there) affirm to be meant of Rome: the Protestants will not by any means have it so, because they would not be driven to confess that Peter was ever at Rome. But here, because they think it supports their opinion that the Pope is Antichrist, and Rome the seat and city of Antichrist, they insist that Rome is this Babylon, this great whore, and this purple harlot. For such fellows, in the exposition of holy Scripture, are led only by their prejudiced opinions and heresies, to which they distort all things without any fairness or sincerity.

<margin>By Babylon (according to all the Church fathers), is signified partly the whole society of the wicked, and partly the city of Rome, but only in respect to its earthly and worldly nature.</margin>
But Saint Augustine, Aretas, and other writers, most commonly interpret it neither as Babylon itself (a city of Chaldea or Egypt), nor of Rome, nor any one specific city which may be so called spiritually (as Jerusalem in Chapter 11 is named spiritual Sodom and Egypt); but of the general society of the impious, and of those who prefer the earthly <note term="terrene">From the Latin *terrenus*, meaning worldly, earthly, or secular as opposed to heavenly.</note> kingdom and convenience of the world before God and eternal happiness. The author of the Commentaries upon the Apocalypse, published under Saint Ambrose's name, writes thus: *This great whore sometimes signifies Rome, especially which at that time when the Apostle wrote this, did persecute the Church of God. But otherwise it signifies the whole city of the Devil, that is, the universal body of the reprobate.* Tertullian also takes it for Rome in his book *Against the Jews* <note>original: "li. aduers. Iudæos."</note> thus: *Babylon (he says) in Saint John is a figure of the city of Rome, being so great, so proud of its Empire, and the destroyer of the saints.* This is plainly spoken of that city when it was heathen—the head of the earthly dominion of the world, the persecutor of the Apostles and their successors, the seat of Nero, Domitian, and the like, Christ's special enemies, the sink of idolatry, sin, and false worship.

<summary>This page concludes the description of the seven-headed beast and the ten kings, followed by a theological commentary arguing that "Babylon" refers to the wicked world or ancient pagan Rome, rather than the contemporary Papacy as claimed by Reformers.</summary>
<keywords>Seven heads, ten kings, Lamb of God, Babylon, Rome, Antichrist, Protestants, Saint Augustine, Tertullian, Counter-Reformation, Papacy, paganism</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the 16th-century Catholic commentary on Revelation 17. Following the previous page’s description of the "Whore of Babylon," the author here argues against Protestant interpretations, asserting that "Babylon" refers to the pagan Roman Empire of the past or a future persecuting state, rather than the Catholic Church or the Papacy.</meta>

<page-num>731</page-num>
<header>CHAPTER XVII. THE APOCALYPSE.</header>
<sig>Zzzz ij</sig>
<meta>catchword: called</meta>

<margin>the heathen state of those who persecuted the Church</margin>
false worship of the Pagan gods. Then was it Babylon, when Saint John wrote this, and then was Nero <note>Nero (37–68 AD) was the first Roman emperor to systematically persecute Christians.</note> and the rest figures of Antichrist, and that city the resemblance of the principal place (wherever it may be) that Antichrist shall reign in, toward the later end of the world.

Now to apply that to the Roman Church and Apostolic See, either now or then, which was spoken only of the earthly <note term="terrene">From the Latin 'terrenus,' meaning worldly or of the earth, as opposed to the spiritual realm.</note> state of that city—as it was the seat of the Emperor, and not of Peter—when it did slay above thirty Popes, Christ’s Vicars, one after another, and endeavored to destroy the whole Church: that is most blasphemous and foolish.

<margin>The Church of Rome is never called Babylon.</margin>
The Church in Rome was one thing, and Babylon in Rome another thing. Peter sat in Rome, and Nero sat in Rome. But Peter sat as in the Church of Rome; Nero sat as in the Babylon of Rome. Which distinction the Heretics <note>In this context, "Heretics" refers to the Protestant Reformers who claimed the Pope was the Antichrist.</note> might have learned by Saint Peter himself in his *first epistle, chapter 5*, writing thus: *The Church greets you, which is in Babylon, co-elect.* <note>original Latin: "Ecclesia quae est in Babylone coëlecta." Peter used "Babylon" as a code for pagan Rome.</note> So that the Church, and the very chosen Church, was in Rome when Rome was Babylon. Whereby it is plain that, whether Babylon or the Great Whore signify Rome here or not, yet it cannot signify the Church of Rome: which is now, and ever was, differing from the earthly Empire of the same. And if, as in the beginning of the Church, Nero and the rest of the persecuting Emperors (who were figures of Antichrist) did principally sit in Rome, so also the great Antichrist shall have his seat there, as it may well be (though others think that Jerusalem rather shall be his principal city). Yet even then shall neither the Church of Rome, nor the Pope of Rome, be Antichrist, but shall be persecuted by Antichrist, and driven out of Rome, if it be possible. For, toward Christ’s Vicar and the Roman Church, he will bear as much goodwill as the Protestants now do, and he shall have more power to persecute him and the Church than they have.

Saint Jerome, in his *17th Letter, chapter 7*, writing to Marcella to draw her out of the city of Rome to the Holy Land, warning her of the manifold allurements to sin and evil life that are in so great and populous a city, alludes at length to these words of the Apocalypse, and makes it to be Babylon and the purple whore. But straight away, lest some wicked person might think he meant that of the Church of Rome, which he spoke of the society of the wicked only, he adds: *There is there indeed the holy Church, there are the triumphant monuments of the Apostles and Martyrs, there is the true confession of Christ, there is the faith praised* <margin>Romans 1.</margin> *by the Apostle, and Gentility trodden under foot, the name of Christian daily advancing itself on high.* <note>Jerome argues that while the city's secular vices resemble Babylon, the presence of the Church makes it holy.</note> Whereby you see that whatever may be spoken or interpreted of Rome out of this word Babylon, it is not meant of the Church of Rome, but of the earthly state; so much so that the said holy Doctor, in his *second book Against Jovinian, chapter 19*, signifies that the holiness of the Church there has wiped away the blasphemy written in the forehead of her former iniquity. But regarding the difference between the old state and dominion of the Heathen there (for which it is compared to Antichrist) and the Priestly state which it now has, read a notable passage in Saint Leo’s *first sermon on the feast of Peter and Paul*.

<margin>Mystery.</margin>
5. ***Mystery.***] Saint Paul calls this secret and close working of abomination the "mystery of iniquity" in *2 Thessalonians 2*. And it is called a little after in this chapter, in *verse 7*, the *Sacrament* (or mystery) of the woman, and it is also the mark of reprobation and damnation.

<margin>This woman signifies all persecutors of saints.</margin>
<margin>Putting heretics to death is not the shedding of the blood of saints.</margin>
6. ***Drunken with the blood.***] It is plain that this woman signifies the whole body of all the persecutors who have and shall shed so much blood of the just: of the Prophets, Apostles, and other Martyrs from the beginning of the world to the end. The Protestants foolishly interpret it of Rome because there they put Heretics to death, and allow their punishment in other countries; but their blood is not called the blood of saints, no more than the blood of thieves, man-killers, and other evildoers, for the shedding of which by order of justice no Commonwealth shall answer.

<margin>The Protestants' madness in interpreting the seven hills as Rome: the Angel himself interpreting it otherwise.</margin>
9. ***Seven hills.***] The Angel himself here interprets these seven hills to be all one with the seven heads and the seven kings; and yet the Heretics, blinded exceedingly with malice against the Church of Rome, are so mad as to take them for the seven hills literally upon which in old time Rome stood, so that they might make the unlearned believe that Rome is the seat of Antichrist. But if they had any consideration, they might mark that the Prophet’s visions here are most of them by Sevens, whether he talks of heads, horns, candlesticks, Churches, kings, hills, or other things; and that he alluded not to the hills because they were exactly seven, but that Seven is a mystical number, as sometimes Ten is, signifying universally all of that sort of which he speaks. As in, the seven heads, hills, or kingdoms (which are here all one) should be all the kingdoms of the world that persecute the Christians, being "heads" and "mountains" for their height in dignity above others. And some take it that there were seven special Empires, kingdoms, or States that were or shall be the greatest persecutors of God's people: such as Egypt, Canaan, Babylon, the Persians, and Greeks, which make five. Sixthly, the Roman Empire, which once persecuted most of all others, and which (as the Apostle here says) *now is*, or stands. But the seventh, then when Saint John wrote this, was not come, nor is it yet come in our days: which is Antichrist's state, which shall not come so long as the Empire of Rome stands, as Saint Paul did prophesy in *2 Thessalonians 2*.

<margin>What is the eighth beast.</margin>
11. ***The same is the eighth.***] The beast itself, being the congregation of all these wicked persecutors, though it consists of the aforesaid seven, yet because the malice of all is complete in it, it may be called the eighth.

<margin>The double interpretation of Babylon.</margin>
18. *The great city.*] If it be meant of any one city, and not of the universal society of the rejected <note>original: "reprobate" — those traditionally understood as being outside the state of grace or predestined to damnation.</note> (which is the city of the Devil, just as the Church and the universal fellowship of the faithful is called the city of God) it is most likely to be old Rome, as some of the Greeks explain it, from the time of the first Emperors until Constantine's <note>Constantine the Great (r. 306–337 AD) was the first Roman Emperor to convert to Christianity and stop the state persecution of the Church.</note> days, who made an end of the persecution. All which Antichristian persecutions ceased when Constantine reigned and yielded up the city to the Pope, who holds not the kingdom or Empire over the world as the Heathen did, but the fatherhood and spiritual rule of the Church. However, the more probable sense is the other: that of the city of the Devil, as the author of the homilies upon the Apocalypse in Saint Augustine declares.

## C H A P T E R XIX.

<margin>4. Amen, Alleluia.]</margin> <margin><note>original Hebrew: אמן הללויה; "Amen, Hallelujah"</note> Amen, Alleluia, not translated.</margin> These two Hebrew words (as others elsewhere) are religiously kept in both the Greek and Latin text and are not translated, unless it be once or twice in the Psalms. Indeed, even the Protestants themselves keep them in the text of their English Testaments in many places. It is a wonder why they do not use them in all places, but sometimes change *Amen* into *verily* (concerning which, see the Annotation for **John 8:34**) and in their Service book <note>Referring to the Anglican Book of Common Prayer</note> they translate *Alleluia* into,

# THE APOCALYPSE. CHAPTER XIX.

into, *Praise ye the Lord*. as though *Alleluia* had not as good a grace in the act of serving God, (where it is indeed properly used) as it hath in the text of the Scripture.

<margin>Alleluia is often used in the Church, especially in Easter time.</margin>
The Catholic Church does often and especially use this sacred word, to join with the Church triumphant <note>The "Church Triumphant" refers to the saints and angels already in heaven, as opposed to the "Church Militant" on earth.</note>, consisting of Angels and Saints, who here are said to laud and praise God with great rejoicing, by this word *Alleluia*, and by often repetition thereof: as the Catholic Church also uses, namely in Easter time even until Whitsuntide <note>Whitsuntide is the week following Pentecost.</note>, for the joy of Christ’s resurrection, which (as Saint Augustine declares in his *Letter to Januarius*, chapters 17 and 15 <note>original: "Epist. ad Ian. c. 17. & 15."</note>) was the general use of the Primitive Church, making a greater mystery and matter of it, than our Protestants now do. At other times of the year also he says it was sung in some Churches, but not in all, and Saint Jerome numbers it among the heresies of Vigilantius <note>Vigilantius was a 4th-century priest who opposed the veneration of relics and certain liturgical practices.</note>, That *Alleluia* could not be sung but at Easter. (See *Against Vigilantius, chapter 1* <note>original: "Aduers. Vigilant. c. 1."</note>).

<margin>It signifies more than (as the Protestants translate it) "praise ye the Lord."</margin>
The truth is, by the use of the Scriptures it has more in it than, *Praise ye the Lord*, signifying with laud, glorifying, and praising of God, a great rejoicing withal, mirth, and exultation of heart in the singers thereof, and that is the cause why the holy Church says, *Praise be to thee, O Lord* <note>original: "Laus tibi Domine"</note>, in Lent and times of penance and mourning, but not *Alleluia*. which (as Saint Augustine also declares) is a term of significance and mystery, joined with that time, and then used specially in the Church of God, when she represents to us in her Service, the joys and beatitude of the next life: which is done specially at Easter, by the joyful celebrating of Christ's glorious Resurrection and Ascension, after the penal time of Lent which represents the misery of this life. See Saint Augustine's *Sermons 1 and 5, chapter 9; and 6, chapter 9 on Various Subjects, volume 10* <note>original: "Ser. 1. & 5. c. 9. & 6. c. 9 de Diuersis to. 10."</note> and his commentary upon the 148th Psalm. for in the titles and ends of diverse holy Psalms this *Alleluia* is full of mystery and sacred significance. <margin>False translation.</margin> Where we must ask the Protestants, why they have left it out altogether, being in the Hebrew, saying neither *Alleluia*, nor, *Praise ye the Lord*, in the Bible of 1577: and that nine times in the six last Psalms.

<margin>Amen and Alleluia should not be translated into vulgar tongues.</margin>
Moreover the said holy Doctor (in book 2 of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 11 <note>original: "li. 2 de doct. Christ. c. 11"</note>) affirms that *Amen* and *Alleluia* should not be translated into any other language, *because of its more sacred authority* <note>original: "propter sanctiorem authoritatem"</note>, for the more sacred authority of the words so remaining, and in *letter 178* <note>original: "ep. 178."</note> he says that it is not lawful to translate them. *For it must be known, etc. for it is to be known (says he) that all nations do sing Amen and Alleluia in the Hebrew words, which neither the Latin speaker nor the foreigner <note>original: "Barbarous"</note> may translate into his own language.* See Saint Jerome also in *letter 137* <note>original: "epist. 137."</note>. And namely for our Nation, Saint Gregory will bear us witness that <margin>All nations in the Primitive Church sang Amen and Alleluia.</margin> our country received the word *Alleluia* with their Christianity, saying thus in book 27 of his *Morals*, chapter 6 <note>original: "li. 27 Moral. c. 6."</note>: *The British tongue, which knew nothing else but to mutter barbarously, has for a long time now begun to sound the Hebrew Alleluia in Divine praises.* <note>original: "Lingua Britannia quæ nihil aliud nouerat quàm barbarum frendere, iamdudum in Diuinis laudibus Hebræum cœpit resonare Alleluia."</note> And for Judea, Saint Jerome in *letter 17, chapter 7* <note>original: "ep. 17. c. 7"</note> writes, that the husbandmen at the plough sang *Alleluia*, which was not then their common speech. Yes, he says that in Monasteries the singing of *Alleluia* was instead of a bell to call them together *to the Gathering* <note>original: "ad Collectam" – referring to the assembly for prayer</note>. (See *In the Epitaph of Paula, chapter 10* <note>original: "in Epitaph. Paulæ c. 10."</note>).

<margin>The Protestants profane this word by translating it, and diminish the significance thereof.</margin>
This word is a sacred, Christian, mystical, and Angelical song, and yet in the new service book <note>The author is likely referring to the Anglican Book of Common Prayer.</note> it is turned into, *Praise ye the Lord*, and *Alleluia* is quite gone, because they care neither to agree with the Church of God, nor with the use of holy Scriptures, no, nor with their own translations. But it is no marvel that they cannot sing the song of our Lord and of Angels in a strange country, <margin>Psalm 136.</margin> that is, out of the Catholic Church, in the captivity of schism and heresy. Lastly, we might ask them whether it be all one to say in Matthew 21 *Hosanna*, and *Save us we beseech thee*? whereas *Hosanna* is withal a word of exceeding congratulation and joy which they expressed toward our Savior. Even so *Alleluia* has another manner of power <note>original: "offense" – used here in the sense of 'effect' or 'striking power'</note> and significance in it, than can be expressed by, *Praise ye the Lord.*

<margin>Justifications are good works, not as the effects of faith justifying, but because themselves also with faith justify a man.</margin>
8. *Justifications of Saints.* <note>This refers to Revelation 19:8, describing the fine linen of the bride.</note> Here the Heretics <note>The Catholic author uses "Heretics" to refer to Protestant reformers.</note> in their translations could not alter the word *justifications* into *ordinances*, or *constitutions*, as they did falsely in the first chapter of Saint Luke (whereof see the Annotation there, verse 6). But they are forced to say in Latin, *justificationes*, as Beza <note>Theodore Beza was a major Protestant reformer and scholar.</note> does: and in English, *righteousness*, (for *justifications* they will not say in any case for fear of inconvenience.) Yes, and they cannot deny but these justifications be the good works of saints. But where <margin>Beza.</margin> they make this explanation <note>original: "gloss"</note>, that they be so called because they are the fruits or effect of faith and of the justice which we have by faith alone, it is most evidently false, and against the very text, and nature of the word. For there is no cause why anything should be called a man's justification, except that it makes him just. So that, *justifications*, be the virtues of faith, hope, charity, and good deeds, justifying or making a man just, and not merely effects of justification. Neither faith alone, but they all together be the very ornaments and inward garments, beauty, and justice of the soul, as here it is evident.

<margin>Saint John’s adoring of the Angel, explained against the Protestants abusing the same.</margin>
10. *And I fell.*] The Protestants abuse this place, and the example of the Angel forbidding John to adore him because he was but his fellow servant, and appointing him to adore God, against all honor, reverence, and adoration of Angels, Saints, or other sanctified creatures, teaching that no religious worship ought to be done unto them. But in truth it makes for no such purpose, but only warns us that Divine honor and the adoration due to God alone <note>The Church distinguishes between 'latria' (worship for God) and 'dulia' (honor for saints).</note>, may not be given to any Angel or other creature. (Saint Augustine, *On True Religion, last chapter*). And when the Adversaries reply that so great an Apostle as John was could not be ignorant of that point, nor would have given divine honor unto an Angel (for so he would have been an Idolater) and therefore that he was not

# CHAPTER XIX. THE APOCALYPSE.

<margin>The Protestants are refuted by their own reasoning.</margin>
He was not rebuked for that, but for offering any religious reverence or other honor whatsoever to his fellow-servant. We answer that by the same reasoning, Saint John being so great an Apostle, if this later kind of reverence had been unlawful and deserving of rebuke—as the Protestants hold it is no less than the other—he could not have been ignorant of that fact, nor would he have done it.

<margin>Revelation 1.</margin>
<margin>Saint John erred only regarding the person, taking the Angel to be Christ himself, and so adoring him as God.</margin>
<margin>Isaiah 9 in the Greek <note>original: "Esa. 9 in Græco"</note>. Malachi 3.</margin>
Therefore, they might much better have learned from Saint Augustine (*Question 61 on Genesis*), how this act of Saint John was corrected by the Angel, and where the error lay. In effect, it is this: That the Angel, being so glorious and full of majesty, representing Christ’s person and using various words in his name that are proper to God—such as, *I am the first and the last, and alive and was dead*, and such like—might well be mistaken by Saint John, through an error of identity, for Christ himself. The Apostle, assuming him to indeed be Christ, adored him with Divine honor. The Angel, correcting this, told him he was not God, but one of his fellow-servants, and therefore that he should not adore him in that way, but adore God. Thus we see that John was neither so ignorant as to think that any undue honor might be given to any creature, nor so evil as to commit idolatry by performing improper worship to any Angel in heaven. Therefore, he was not at all blameworthy in his action, but only erred "materially" (as the Scholastic theologians <note>The "Scholemen" or Scholastics were medieval scholars who used logic to explain Christian doctrine.</note> call it); that is, by mistaking one for another, thinking that he who was an Angel was actually our Lord. This was because he knew that our Lord himself is also called an "Angel" <note>In some Old Testament passages, the "Angel of the Lord" is interpreted by theologians as a pre-incarnate appearance of Christ.</note> and has often appeared in the visions of the faithful.

<margin>Saint John did not sin in this adoration.</margin>
<margin>Another explanation of this passage.</margin>
And the same is to be thought of the Angel appearing in the 22nd chapter of the Apocalypse, whether it was the same one or another. For that one also appeared in such a way that John could not tell whether it was Christ himself or not, until the Angel told him. This much is certain: John did not "formally" (as they say) commit idolatry, nor did he sin at all in this, as he knew all the duties of a Christian man as well as an Angel of heaven, being also in as great honor with God—and even more so than many Angels. This perhaps may be the cause (and consequently another explanation of this passage) why the Angel, knowing John's great graces and merits before God, would not accept any worship or submission from his hands, though John again did it out of similar humility, as also happens immediately afterward in chapter 22. Likely John would not have done this if he had been strictly warned by the Angel only a moment before of an error or lack of duty in the act. However that may be, it is evident that this refusal of adoration by the Angel does not take away the due reverence and respect we ought to have for Angels or other sanctified persons and creatures. Thus these words, *See thou do it not*, signify an earnest refusal rather than an indication of a crime being committed.

<margin>Augustine, *On True Religion*, chapter 55 <note>original: "Aug. de vera relig. c. 55."</note>.</margin>
<margin>The Protestants, by comparing Scriptures, might find religious adoration of creatures.</margin>
<margin>Three points herein examined and proved by Scriptures.</margin>
<margin>Hebrew: *Hishtachavah* (השתחוה); Greek: *Proskynein* (προσκυνεῖν) <note>Both terms refer to the act of bowing down or prostrating oneself in respect or worship.</note>.</margin>
And it is a marvel that the Protestants—who make themselves so sure of the true sense of every doubtful passage by the "conference" (comparison) of other Scriptures—do not follow here the comparison of Scriptures that they themselves so strongly require. We will give them an occasion and a method to do so, as follows. He who doubts this passage finds three things in question which must be tested by other Scriptures. The first is whether there ought to be, or may be, any religious reverence or honor done to any creatures—taking the word "religion" or "religious worship" not for that special honor which is properly and only due to God (as Saint Augustine sometimes uses the term), but for reverence due to anything that is holy by sanctification or application to the service of God. The second thing is whether, by the usage of Scripture, that honor is called "adoration" in Latin, or by an equivalent word in other languages: Hebrew, Greek, or English. Lastly, whether we may, according to the Scriptures, fall down prostrate before the things, or at the feet of the persons, that we so adore. As for the civil duty shown to our superiors by tipping one's cap, kneeling, or other courtesy, I think the Protestants will not disagree with us—though indeed, their arguments work as much against the one as the other.

<margin>Psalms 5, 137. Daniel 6. 3 Kings 8 <note>In modern Bibles, this is 1 Kings 8.</note>. Joshua 7. Psalms 98, 131.</margin>
<margin>1. Religious worship of creatures.</margin>
<margin>2. The name is called adoration.</margin>
<margin>3. Falling prostrate before the persons or things adored.</margin>
<margin>Genesis 18. Exodus 3. Joshua 5.</margin>
<margin>Adoring before Angels.</margin>
But regarding the religious worship of creatures (of which we speak), let them look in the Scriptures, both Old and New. First, see whether the Temple, the Tabernacle, the Ark, the mercy seat, the Cherubim, the altar, the showbread, the Sabbath, and all their holy things were not reverenced by all signs of devotion and religion. See whether the Sacraments of Christ, the Priests of our Lord, the Prophets of God, the Gospel, the Scriptures, the name of JESUS, and such things (which are made holy by use, significance, or sanctification) are not now to be reverenced. They shall find all these things to have been reverenced by all the faithful, without any dishonor to God, and much to his honor. Secondly, that this reverence is named "adoration" in the Scriptures is proved by these phrases: Psalm 98, *Adore ye his footstool, because it is holy* <note>In many modern versions, this is translated as "worship at his footstool."</note>; and Hebrews 11, *He adored the top of his rod*. Thirdly, the Scriptures also warrant us (as the nature of the word "adoration" implies in all three languages) to bow down our bodies, to fall flat on the ground in the presence of such things and at the feet of holy persons, especially Angels, as John does here. These examples prove it: Abraham adored the Angels that appeared to him; Moses also adored the Angel that showed himself out of the bush—who were creatures, though they represented God’s person, just as this Angel here did who spoke to Saint John. Balaam adored the Angel that stood before him with a drawn sword (Numbers 22). Joshua adored, falling flat down...

<summary>This page defends the Catholic practice of venerating angels and holy objects, arguing that Saint John's attempt to adore the angel was a mistake of identity rather than a sin of idolatry. It uses scriptural precedents like Abraham and Moses to show that "religious reverence" (as distinct from divine worship) is a biblical practice.</summary>

<margin>Adoring of Prophets and holy persons.</margin>
Yea, not only to Angels, but even to great Prophets this devotion was done, as to Daniel by Nebuchadnezzar, who fell flat upon his face before him, and did other great offices of religion, which the Prophet refused not, because they were done to God rather than to him, as Saint Jerome defendeth the same against Porphyry <note>Porphyry was a 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively against Christianity.</note>, who charged Daniel with intolerable pride therein; and the said holy doctor alleges the fact of Alexander the Great, who did the like to \* Jehoiada the high priest of the Jews. Howsoever <margin>Daniel 2.</margin> <margin>\* or, Jaddus. <note>Historical accounts of Alexander the Great often refer to the High Priest as Jaddua.</note></margin> that be (for of the sacrifice there mentioned there may be some doubt, which the Church does always immediately to God, and to no creature) the fact of the prophets (4 Kings 2) <note>original: "4 Reg 2"; in modern Bibles, this is 2 Kings 2.</note> to Elisha, is plain: where they, perceiving that the double grace and spirit of Elijah was given to him, fell flat down at his feet and adored. So did \* the Shunammite. To omit that <margin>4 Kings 4. Judith 13.</margin> Achior adored Judith, falling at her feet, as a woman blessed of God, and infinite other places.

All which things, by comparing the Scriptures, our Adversaries <note>A common term in this period for Protestant reformers.</note> should have found to be lawfully done to men, and Angels, and sovereign holy creatures. Whereby they might convince themselves, and perceive that the thing could not be forbidden Saint John to do to the Angel, which they pretend; though the Angel for certain causes might refuse even that which Saint John did lawfully unto him, as Saint Peter did refuse the honor given him by Cornelius, according to Saint Chrysostom’s opinion (*Homily 23 on Acts 10*). Yea, even in the third chapter of this book (if our Adversaries would look no further) they might see where this Angel prophesieth and promiseth that the Jews should fall down before the feet of the Angel of Philadelphia and adore. See the Annotations there.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Chapter 20 of the Apocalypse (the Book of Revelation), focusing on the theological interpretation of the "thousand years," the nature of the first resurrection, the priesthood of the faithful, and the eventual release of Satan. It specifically engages with the interpretations of Saint Augustine to refute both ancient heresies and contemporary Protestant views.</meta>

### THE APOCALYPSE. CHAPTER 20.

<margin>(Within this militant Church) the saints reign with Christ in soul only. <note>The "militant Church" refers to the Christian community currently living on earth, struggling against sin and temptation.</note></margin>
*They are not separated from the Church, which is even now the kingdom of Christ. For otherwise, no memory of them would be kept at the altar of God during the communication of the body of Christ <note>A reference to the Eucharist or Holy Communion.</note>; nor would it be useful to hasten to Baptism in the perils of death for fear of ending our life without it; nor to hasten to be reconciled <note>Meaning the Sacrament of Penance or Confession.</note> if we happen to be separated from that same body by penance or an uneasy conscience. And why are all these things done, except because the faithful departed are also members of the Church? And though the Martyrs are the only ones named here as an example, it is intended to include others also who die in the state of grace.*

<margin>The rest are dead and damned in soul during the same time.</margin>
5. *The rest lived not.*] The rest, who are not part of the happy number mentioned before but lived and died in sin, do not reign with Christ in their souls during this time of the New Testament. Instead, they are dead spiritually in soul and naturally in body until the day of judgment. <note>original: "S. August. ibidem." Saint Augustine, in the same place (The City of God, Book 20).</note>

<margin>The first resurrection is of the soul only.</margin>
3. *This is the first resurrection.*] Just as there are two regenerations—one by faith, which happens now in Baptism, and another according to the flesh, when at the last day the body shall be made immortal and incorruptible—so there are two resurrections. One happens now, for souls to achieve salvation when they die in grace (which is called the first), and the other is for the bodies at the last day. <note>original: "S. August. li. 20 de Ciuit. c. 6." Saint Augustine, *The City of God*, Book 20, Chapter 6.</note>

<margin>Priests: some properly so called, some improperly.</margin>
<margin>1 Peter 2</margin>
6. *They shall be Priests.*] This is not spoken (says Saint Augustine <note>original: "li. 20 de Ciuit. c. 10." *The City of God*, Book 20, Chapter 10.</note>) only of Bishops and Priests, who are properly called Priests in the Church now. Rather, just as we call everyone "Christians" because of the mystical chrism <note>The "chrism" is the holy oil used in anointing.</note> or ointment, so we call all "Priests" because they are members of the one Priest, of whom the Apostle Peter says: *A holy people, a kingly Priesthood.* These words are significant for the education of those who think there are no men properly called "Priests" in the New Testament—thinking they are no different than any other Christian men and women. This is a rebuke to those who have, for that reason, changed the name "Priests" into "Ministers."

<margin>The binding and loosening of Satan, explained by S. Augustine.</margin>
7. *Satan shall be loosed.*] In the entire eighth chapter of the aforementioned 20th book of *The City of God* by Saint Augustine, there is a notable commentary on these words. There, he first declares that neither this binding nor loosening of Satan refers to whether he can seduce the Church of God; he proves that whether he is bound or loose, he can never seduce the Church. The state of the Church at the time when the Devil is to be loosed, he says, *will be the same as it was since it was instituted, and as it shall be in her children who succeed each other by birth and death.* And a little later: *I thought this should be mentioned so that no one would think that during the short time when the Devil is loosed, the Church will not exist on the earth—either because he does not find it here when let loose, or because he consumes it when he persecutes it by all means.* Secondly, he declares that the Devil being "bound" simply means he is not permitted by God to use all his force or fraud in temptations. To be "loosed" means to be allowed by God for a short time—that is, for three and a half years—to practice and test all his power and arts of temptation against the Church and her children, and yet still not prevail against them. Thirdly, this Doctor of the Church shows by what great mercy our Lord has tied Satan and shortened his power during the entire "millenary" or thousand years (which is the entire time of the New Testament until then). He also shows with what wisdom God permits him to break loose for that little time of three years and six months toward the final day, which shall be the reign of Antichrist. Lastly, he shows what kind of men will be most subject to the Devil’s seduction (even those who now, by the temptation of Heretics, leave the Church) and who will avoid it.
<margin>The short reign of Antichrist.</margin>

<margin>Millenary or Chiliasts. <note>"Chiliasts" (from the Greek word for "thousand") is another name for Millenarians, who believe in a literal 1,000-year earthly kingdom.</note></margin>
By all this, we may refute various false explanations by old and recent Heretics. First, the ancient sect of the Millenarians, who based their heresy on these thousand years named by the Prophet. They claimed there would be a thousand years after the resurrection of our bodies in which we would reign with Christ in this world, in our bodies, enjoying all bodily delights and pleasures of food, drink, and the like. They called this the "first resurrection." The author of this heresy was Cerinthus. <note>original: "Epiph. har. 77 in fine. Hiero. Comment. in c. 19 Mat. August. har. 8 ad Quodvult Deum." References to Epiphanius (*Against Heresies*), Jerome (*Commentary on Matthew*), and Augustine (*To Quodvultdeus on Heresies*).</note> Eusebius also <note>original: "li. 3 historie c. 33." *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 3, Chapter 33.</note> shows that some prominent men held this opinion in part (though in a more honorable way regarding those bodily delicacies) by misinterpreting these words of Saint John. From this we learn, and all the world may see, that the holy Scriptures are difficult when even such great scholars erred; there is no security except in the sense which the Church approves.
<margin>The Scriptures are difficult.</margin>

<margin>By Saint Augustine’s previous explanation, it is clearly shown against the Protestants that the Church cannot err, and that the Pope cannot possibly be Antichrist.</margin>
Modern Heretics <note>In this context, "Heretics" refers to the Protestant reformers.</note> are also fully refuted by Saint Augustine’s words. They claim not only that the Church may be seduced during the great persecution of the Devil’s loosening, but that it has been seduced for a large portion of this time while the Devil is bound. They hold that the true Church may err or fall from truth into error and idolatry—and even more blasphemously, that the chief governor of the Church is Antichrist himself, and the Church under him is the "whore of Babylon." They claim that this Antichrist (who the Scriptures in many places, and here clearly by Saint Augustine’s explanation, testify will reign only a short time toward the last judgment) was revealed long ago to be the Pope himself, Christ’s own Vicar, and that he has persecuted the "Saints" of their sect for at least a thousand years. This is nothing more than claiming the Devil has been loose and Antichrist has reigned for the entire thousand years, or most of it—which is the majority of the Church's existence in the New Testament. This evidently contradicts this and other Scriptures that appoint this as the time of the Devil’s binding. Indeed, it would make Antichrist and the Devil weaker toward the day of judgment than [they were before...]

<summary>This page provides a Roman Catholic commentary on Revelation 20, using Saint Augustine to argue that the 'thousand years' represents the entire age of the Church, not a literal future kingdom. It refutes the 'Millenarian' heresy of earthly pleasures and the Protestant claim that the Pope is the Antichrist, asserting the Church's inability to be fully seduced by Satan.</summary>

### CHAPTER 20. THE APOCALYPSE.

<margin>Matthew 24. Luke 18:8.</margin>
<margin>An invincible demonstration.</margin>
...before, and the truth better to be known, and the faith more common, the nearer we come to the same judgment: which is expressly against the Gospel and this prophecy of Saint John. We see that the sects of Luther, Calvin, and others, are more spread through the world than they were ever before, and consequently the Pope and his religion lessened, and his power of punishing (or, as they call it) persecuting the said Sectaries <note>The term "Sectaries" was used by the author to refer to followers of the Protestant Reformation, such as Lutherans and Calvinists.</note>, through the multitude of his adversaries, diminished. How then is the Pope Antichrist, whose force shall be greater at the later end of the world, than before? Or how can it be otherwise, but these Sect-Masters should be Antichrist’s near precursors, who make Christ’s chief Ministers and the Church’s chief governors—who have been for these thousand years and more—to be Antichrists? And they make themselves and their sects to be true, even though they come so near the time of the Devil’s loosening and seduction, and of the personal reign of Antichrist?

<margin>The camp of Saints is the Catholic Church throughout the world.</margin>
<margin>As now Heretics in particular countries, so Antichrist shall persecute the Churches of all nations.</margin>
8. *The camp of the Saints.*] Saint Augustine, in the said 20th book of *The City of God* <note>original: "de Civitate Dei"</note>, chapter 11: *It is not,* says he, *to be taken that the persecutors shall gather to any one place, as though the camp of the saints or the beloved city should be in only one place, which in deed are no other thing but the Church of Christ spread through the whole world. And therefore wherever the Church shall then be (which shall be in all Nations even then, for so much is suggested by this "breadth of the earth" specified here) there shall the tents of saints be, and the beloved city of God, and there shall she be besieged by all her enemies, who shall be in every country where she is, in the most cruel and forceful way.* So writes this profound holy Doctor. Whereby we see, that just as now the particular Churches of England, Scotland, Flanders, and such like, are persecuted by their enemies in those countries, so in the time of Antichrist, the Churches of all Nations—such as Italy, Spain, France, and all others which now are quiet—shall be assaulted just as the aforementioned are now, and much more so; for the general persecution of the whole Church shall be greater than the particular persecution of any individual Churches in the world.

<margin>What is meant by fire from heaven.</margin>
9. *There came down a fire.*] It is not meant to be the fire of Hell (says Saint Augustine in the same book, chapter 12 <note>original: "ib. c. 12"</note>) into which the wicked shall be cast after the resurrection of their bodies, but of an extraordinary help that God will send from heaven to give rescue to the Saints of the Church who shall then fight against the wicked; or, it refers to the very fervent and burning zeal of religion and God’s honor, which God will kindle in the hearts of the faithful to remain constant against the forces of that great persecution.

<margin>The book of every man’s works, opened in the day of judgment.</margin>
12. *Another book.*] This is the book of God’s knowledge or predestination, wherein that which was previously hidden from the world shall be opened, and wherein the true record of every man’s works shall be contained; and they receive their judgment differently according to their works, and not according to faith only, or lack of faith only. For all infidels (such as Turks <note>In this historical context, "Turks" was a common term for Muslims.</note>, obstinate Jews, and Heretics) shall never come to that examination, being otherwise already condemned.

### A N N O T A T I O N S
### CHAPTER 22.

11. *He that hurts.*] This is not an encouragement [to do evil], but a <term>commination</term> <note>original: "commination"; a formal threat of divine punishment or vengeance.</note> or warning, that however far the wicked increase in their wickedness, God has provided a matching punishment for them.

<margin>The curse against commentators who add or subtract from the text is aimed at heretics.</margin>
18. *If any man shall add.*] The author of the commentaries on this book, bearing the name of St. Ambrose, says this regarding this point: <note>The text refers to "Pseudo-Ambrose," an ancient commentary once thought to be by St. Ambrose of Milan, but now attributed to other early medieval authors.</note> *He does not make this protest against those who explain the prophecy by adding or taking away [words], but against heretics. For the commentator adds or takes away nothing, but instead opens up the obscurity of the narrative, or shows its moral or spiritual meaning. He therefore curses heretics, who used to add something of their own that was false, and take away other things that were contrary to their heresies.* So says this ancient writer. And this was the characteristic of them in all ages, and so it is with our opponents now, as we have noted throughout the whole Bible, and as we have in various places shown to the sight of all <term>indifferent</term> <note>In this context, "indifferent" means "impartial" or "unbiased" readers.</note> readers in the New Testament; so that all the world may see that the Apostle's curse has fallen upon them, and may beware of them.

<margin>A brief prayer to JESUS Christ, to come as St. John speaks here, and to judge the cause of Catholics and Protestants.</margin>
20. *Come Lord Jesus.*] And now, O Lord Christ, most just and merciful, we your poor creatures who are so afflicted for the confession and defense of the holy, Catholic, and Apostolic truth—contained in this your sacred book and in the infallible doctrine of your dear spouse, our mother the Church—we also cry unto your Majesty with unspeakable tenderness of heart: COME, LORD JESUS, QUICKLY, and judge between us and our adversaries. In the meantime, give patience, comfort, and constancy to all who suffer for your name and trust in you. O Lord God, our only helper and protector, do not delay long. AMEN.

# HARD WORDS EXPLAINED.

### E

*Evacuated* from Christ, that is, made void and having no part with him. page 508.
The scandal of the cross *evacuated*, that is, made void, entirely taken away. ibid. <note>The translators often used "evacuated" to mean "rendered powerless" or "emptied of effect."</note>
*Evangelize*, signifies such preaching of good tidings as concerns the Gospel. *See the preface.*
*Eunuchs*, castrated men.
*Euro-aquilo*, A north-east wind. page 368. <note>A specific Mediterranean wind mentioned in the account of Saint Paul's shipwreck.</note>
*Exinanited*, abased or humbled exceedingly. page 528. <note>From the Latin 'exinanivit,' referring to Christ "emptying" himself of his glory.</note>

### G

*Gratis*, a common word to signify "for nothing," freely, as a matter of grace, without merit.

### H

*Holocaust*, a kind of sacrifice where everything was burnt in honor of God. page 625.
*Hosts*, sacrifices. page 445. <note>From the Latin 'hostia,' meaning a sacrificial victim.</note>

### I

*Invocated*, called upon, prayed to. page 316. From this we say, "Invocation of Saints," and "to invocate."
*Issue*, a good outcome or event. page 445.
*Justice*, used in the New Testament not as it refers to legal fairness or injury, but for that quality by which a man is just and justified. page 391. <note>The translators use 'justice' where modern bibles often use 'righteousness.'</note>

### N

*Neophyte*, explained on page 569. <note>A new convert or "newly planted" believer.</note>

### P

*Paraclete*, <note>OCR reads "Paradele," but refers to the Holy Spirit as the Comforter.</note> explained on page 260.
*Parasceve*, the Jews' Sabbath-eve, Good Friday. page 130, verse 43. *See the Preface.*

<column-break/>

*Pasch*, Easter, and the Paschal lamb. page 201.
*Pentecost*, Whitsuntide, etc., the space of fifty days.
*Predefinition*, A determination made beforehand. page 517.
*Prepuce*, explained on page 387. <note>The state of being uncircumcised.</note>
*Prescience*, foreknowledge. page 294.
*Prevaricator*, transgressor; and *prevarication*, transgression. page 386, 387.
*Loaves of Proposition*, so called because they were proposed <note>Meaning "set forth" or "displayed."</note> and set upon the table in the Temple, before God. page 31.

### R

*Repropitiate* the sins, page 605, that is, make a reconciliation for them.
*Resolution*, the separation of the body and the soul, the departing out of this life. page 592.
*Resuscitate* the grace, that is, raise, quicken, renew and revive the grace which otherwise languishes and decays. page 586.

### S

*Sabbatism*, A time of resting and ceasing from labors. page 607.
*Sacrament*, used for "mystery." page 513.
*Sancta Sanctorum*, The Holy of Holies, that is, the inmost and holiest place of the Jews' Temple, similar to the Sanctuary or Chancel. page 621.
*Superedified*, Built upon Christ, the principal stone. page 657.

### T

*Tetrarch*, Governor or Prince of the fourth part of a country. page 38.
*Thrones*, a higher order of Angels. page 537.

### V

*Victims*, Sacrifices. page 308.

# HARD WORDS EXPLAINED.

*Dominical day*, Sunday. <note>original: "Dies Dominica." Literally, the "Lord’s Day."</note> See Annotations pages 701, 702.
*Donaries*, gifts offered to God for his Temple, etc. page 199. <note>From the Latin "donarium," referring to a votive offering or a place where such gifts are kept.</note>

### E

*Evacuated* from Christ, that is, made void and having no part with him. page 508.
The scandal of the cross *evacuated*, that is, made void, entirely taken away. ibid. <note>original: "evacuatum." The translators used "evacuated" to mean "made of no effect" or "emptied of power."</note>
*Evangelize*, signifies such preaching of good tidings as concerns the Gospel. *See the preface.* <note>From the Greek "evangelion," meaning "good news."</note>
*Eunuchs*, castrated men.
*Euro-aquilo*, A north-east wind. page 368. <note>original: "Euro-aquilo." A specific Mediterranean wind mentioned in the account of Saint Paul's shipwreck in the Book of Acts.</note>
*Exinanited*, abased or humbled exceedingly. page 528. <note>original: "exinanivit." Used in Philippians 2:7 to describe how Christ "emptied" himself of his divine glory to become human.</note>

### G

*Gratis*, a common word to signify "for nothing," freely, as a matter of grace, without merit.

### H

*Holocaust*, a kind of sacrifice where everything was burnt in honor of God. page 625. <note>From the Greek "holokaustos," meaning "completely burnt."</note>
*Hosts*, sacrifices. page 445. <note>original: "hostia." In this context, it refers to a sacrificial victim, from which the Catholic "Host" in the Eucharist derives its name.</note>

### I

*Invocated*, called upon, prayed to. page 316. From this we say, "Invocation of Saints," and "to invocate."
*Issue*, a good outcome or event. page 445.
*Justice*, used in the New Testament not as it refers to legal fairness or injury, but for that quality by which a man is just and justified. page 391. <note>The Rheims translators preferred "justice" where modern Bibles usually use the word "righteousness," reflecting the Latin "iustitia."</note>

### N

*Neophyte*, explained ... <note>original: "neophytus." Literally "newly planted," referring to a person recently converted to the faith.</note>

These definitions were provided to help English readers understand the formal theological vocabulary the translators chose over more common Germanic words.</summary>
